(Surat al-A'raf)
Makkiyya (Meccan), except for the verses from 163 to 170, which are Madaniyya (Medinan).

Its verses number 206. It was revealed after Surat Sad.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book has been sent down to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast about it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder to the believers.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad. A Book has been sent down to you, so let there be no constriction in your breast about it, that you may warn by it, and as a reminder to the believers.﴾

Concerning the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ means "I am God, the Clarifier (Afsil)." He also said: "I am God, the All-Knowing, and the Clarifier." Al-Wahidi said: On this interpretation, these letters occupy the position of sentences. Sentences that consist only of a subject (mubtada') and a predicate (khabar) have no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). So his saying "I am God, the All-Knowing" has no place in i'rab: "I" (ana) is the subject, and its predicate is "God," and "the All-Knowing" is a second predicate following the first. When the meaning of ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ is "I am God, the All-Knowing," its i'rab is like the i'rab of the thing that explains it.

Al-Suddi said: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ is spelled like our saying of God's names: "He is the Fashioner (al-Musawwir)." 

Al-Qadi said: This wording is no more appropriate for our reading "I am God, the Clarifier" than for "I am God, the Reformer," or "I am God, the Tester," or "I am God, the King." For if the criterion is the letter Sad, it is present in "I am God, the Reformer" (Muslih). And if the criterion is the letter Mim, then just as it is present in "the All-Knowing," it is also present in "the King" and "the Tester." So to interpret ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ as that particular meaning is pure arbitrariness. Moreover, if the interpretation of words is based on the letters they contain, without the word being laid down in the language for that meaning, the way is opened for the Batiniyya (the esoteric sect) to interpret all the words of the Qur'an in a manner resembling this method.

As for the saying of some that it is one of God's names, it is more remote, because making it a name for God is no more appropriate than making it a name for some of His messengers from among the angels or prophets. For a name becomes a name for the named only through imposition and convention, and that is absent here. Rather, the truth is that ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ is a title (laqab) for this surah, and names given as titles do not convey meaning regarding the things named; they stand in place of pointing gestures. God may name this surah with the words ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾, just as when one of us has a child, he names him Muhammad.

[p. 14]

Having understood this, we say: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿A Book﴾ is its predicate (khabar), and ﴿sent down to you﴾ is a qualifier of that predicate. That is: the surah named by our saying ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ is ﴿a Book sent down to you﴾.

If it is said: The proof that establishes the validity of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) is that God singled him out by sending down this Qur'an to him. So if we do not know this meaning, we cannot know his prophethood, and if we do not know his prophethood, we cannot argue from this statement. Thus if we establish that this surah was sent down to him from God by this very statement, it entails circular reasoning.

We say: By pure reason alone we know that this surah is a Book sent down to him from God. The evidence for this is that he (peace be upon him) did not become a student of any teacher, did not learn from any instructor, did not study any book, and did not associate with scholars, poets, or people of narratives. Forty years of his life passed without any of these circumstances occurring for him. Then after the forty years, this glorious Book was revealed to him, comprising the knowledge of the earlier and later generations. Sound reason testifies that this could only happen through revelation from God Most High.

Thus it has been established by this rational proof that ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ is a Book sent down upon Muhammad (ﷺ) from his Lord and his God.

The second issue: Those who hold that the Qur'an is created argued from His saying ﴿a Book sent down to you﴾. They said: God described it as sent down, and sending down entails moving from one state to another, which is not befitting to the Eternal (qadim). This shows that it is originated (muhdath).

The answer to this: What is described as sent down and revealed, in a figurative sense, is these letters, and there is no dispute that they are originated and created. And God knows best.

If it is said: Suppose that what is meant is the letters. Still, letters are accidents (a'rad) that do not endure, as evidenced by the fact that they follow one another in succession, and their succession indicates that they do not persist. If that is so, how can it be conceived to describe as "sent down" an accident that does not persist for two moments?

The answer: God brought these inscriptions and engravings into being on the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). Then the angel gazes at those engravings, descends from heaven to earth, and teaches Muhammad those letters and words. So the meaning of those letters being sent down is that their bearer descended from heaven to earth with them.

The third issue: Those who affirmed that God has a place held on to this verse and said: The word "min" (from) denotes the starting point of a limit, and the word "ila" (to) denotes the endpoint of a limit. So His saying ﴿sent down to you﴾ requires the existence of a distance whose starting point is God Most High and whose endpoint is Muhammad. This indicates that God is specifically located in the direction of above, because descent is movement from above to below.

The answer to this: Since it has been established by compelling proofs that place and direction are impossible for God Most High, it is necessary to interpret it according to the interpretation we have mentioned, namely that the angel moved with it from the height to below.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿so let there be no constriction in your breast about it.﴾ Regarding the explanation of "constriction" (haraj), there are two views:

The first: Haraj means narrowness. The meaning is: let your breast not be constricted because they deny you in conveying the message.

The second: ﴿so let there be no constriction in your breast about it﴾ means doubt about it, [p. 15] as in His saying: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [Yunus: 94]. Doubt is called haraj because the doubter is narrow of breast and constricted in chest, just as the one who is certain is open of breast and expansive of heart.

* * *

Then God Most High said: ﴿that you may warn by it.﴾ To what does this "li" (the lam of purpose) relate?

On this there are several opinions:

The first: Al-Farra' said: It relates to His saying ﴿sent down to you﴾, by way of anteposition and postposition (taqdim wa ta'khir). The implied meaning is: A Book sent down to you that you may warn by it, so let there be no constriction in your breast about it.

If it is asked: What is the benefit of this anteposition and postposition?

We say: Because proceeding to warn and convey the message is not completed and perfected except when constriction is removed from the breast. For this reason God Most High commanded him to remove constriction from the breast, and then after that commanded him to warn and convey.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: The lam here has the meaning of "kay" (in order that). The implied meaning is: let there be no doubt in your breast, so that you may warn others.

The third: The author of al-Nazm (Sahib al-Nazm) said: The lam here has the meaning of "an" (that). The implied meaning is: let your breast not be narrowed, nor your resolve weakened, from warning by it. The Arabs place this lam in the position of "an," as God says: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of God with their mouths﴾ [al-Tawba: 32], and in another place: ﴿They wish to extinguish﴾ [al-Saff: 8], and both have one meaning.

The fourth: The implied meaning of the speech is: This Book, God has sent it down upon you. When you know that it is the revelation of God Most High, know that God's care is with you. When you know this, let there be no constriction in your breast, for whoever has God as his guardian and helper does not fear anyone. When fear and narrowness are removed from the heart, one proceeds to warn, convey, and remind like brave men, and pays no heed to any of the people of deviation, error, and falsehood.

Then He said: ﴿And a reminder for the believers﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means admonitions for those who affirm the truth. Al-Zajjaj said: It is a noun in the place of the verbal noun (maṣdar). Al-Layth said: (al-dhikrā) is a noun for reminder (tadhkira), and regarding its grammatical position (iʿrāb) there are several possibilities.

Al-Farraʾ said: It may be in the accusative position, meaning: "so that you may warn by it and remind." It may also be in the nominative position, as a coordination with His saying (kitāb), and the sense is: "a Book that is true, and a reminder." It may also be that the implied sense is "and it is a reminder." It may also be in the genitive position, because the meaning of "so that you may warn by it" is "for warning and reminding," so it is in the genitive position, since the meaning is for warning and reminder.

If it is asked: Why did He restrict this reminder to the believers?

We say: This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾. The rational investigation regarding this is that human souls are of two kinds: dull, ignorant souls, far from the world of the unseen, drowned in the pursuit of bodily pleasures and corporeal desires; and noble souls, illuminated by divine lights, prepared for spiritual events. The sending of prophets and messengers, with regard to the first kind, is a warning and a frightening, for they have drowned in the sleep of heedlessness and the slumber of ignorance, so they need one who awakens them and one who alerts them. As for the second kind, it is a reminder and an alert. This is because these souls, by the requirement of their original essences, are prepared to be drawn toward the world of holiness and to be joined with the Eternal Presence; yet at times veils from the world of body cover them, so a kind of stupor and heedlessness befalls them. When they hear the call of the prophets and the lights of the spirits of God's messengers join with them, they remember their origin, perceive their source, and long for what is there of spirit, rest, and fragrance. Thus it is established that He, Exalted is He, sent down this Book upon His Messenger so that it would be a warning for one group and a reminder for another group. And God knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow, apart from Him, any protectors. Little do you remember.﴾

Know that the matter of prophethood is completed only by the sender, who is Allah, glorified and exalted is He; the one sent, who is the Messenger; and the one to whom he is sent, who is the community (ummah). So when He commanded the Messenger in the first verse to convey and warn with a strong heart and a sound resolve, He commanded the one to whom he is sent, namely the community, to follow the Messenger, saying: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾. There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: al-Hasan said: O son of Adam, you have been commanded to follow the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger.

Know that His saying: ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ encompasses the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

If it is said: Why did He say ﴿sent down to you﴾ when it was sent down to the Messenger?

We say: It is sent down to all in the sense that it is an address to all.

Having understood this, we say: this verse indicates that restricting the general (ʿumum) wording of the Qur'an by analogy (qiyas) is not permissible, because the general wording of the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, exalted is He. Allah has made following it obligatory, so acting upon the general wording of the Qur'an is obligatory; and since acting upon it is obligatory, acting upon analogy is prohibited, otherwise contradiction would follow.

If they say: When the command to use analogy came in the Qur'an, namely His saying: ﴿So take warning﴾ [al-Hashr: 2], acting upon analogy was acting upon what Allah has sent down.

We say: Grant that this is so; yet we say that the verse indicating the obligation to act upon analogy only indicates the ruling established by analogy, not directly but through that analogy. As for the general wording of the Qur'an, it indicates the establishment of that ruling directly, not through an intermediary. And when a conflict occurred, what was indicated directly by what Allah sent down was more deserving of regard than the ruling indicated by what Allah sent down through something else. So the preference lies on our side. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not follow, apart from Him, any protectors﴾. They said: its meaning is, do not take as allies, apart from Him, protectors from among the devils of the jinn and of mankind, who would lead you to worship idols, desires and innovations.

One may say: the verse indicates that what is followed is either that which Allah has sent down, or something else. As for the first, it is what Allah commanded to be followed. As for the second, it is what Allah forbade to be followed. So the meaning is that whatever contradicts the ruling which Allah has sent down, it is not permissible to follow it.

Having established this, we say: those who deny analogy have relied on it in negating analogy. They said: the verse indicates that it is not permissible to follow other than what Allah has sent down, and acting upon analogy is following other than what Allah has sent down, so it must be impermissible.

If they say: since His saying "so take warning" indicates the acting upon analogy, acting upon analogy is acting upon what Allah has sent down.

صفحة ١٧
It is answered: if acting upon analogy were acting upon what Allah has sent down, then whoever abandons acting upon the requirement of analogy would be an unbeliever, according to His saying: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. Since the community has agreed on not declaring such a person an unbeliever, we know that acting upon the ruling of analogy is not acting upon what Allah has sent down, and then the argument is complete.

Those who affirm analogy answered this: the fact that analogy is a proof was established by the consensus of the Companions, and consensus is a definitive proof, whereas what you have mentioned is reliance on the apparent generality of a text, which is a speculative proof, and the definitive is preferable to the speculative.

The first group answered: you have established that consensus is a proof by the generality of His saying: ﴿And follows a path other than the path of the believers﴾ [al-Nisa': 115], and the generality of His saying: ﴿Thus We have made you a middle nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], and the generality of His saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 110], and by the generality of his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: "My community will not agree upon error." Accordingly, establishing that consensus is a proof is a branch of relying on the general texts, and a branch cannot be stronger than its root.

Those who affirm analogy replied: since the verses, the hadiths and the consensus converged in establishing analogy, its strength was multiplied and preference was achieved. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: the Hashwiyya, who deny rational reflection and rational proofs, relied on this verse, and that is far-fetched, because knowledge that the Qur'an is a proof depends on the soundness of relying on rational proofs. So if we made the Qur'an cast doubt on the soundness of rational proofs, contradiction would follow, and that is invalid.

The fourth issue: Ibn ʿAmir read (qalīlan mā yatadhakkarūn) with the yaʾ at one time and the tāʾ at another. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ḥafs from ʿAsim read with the tāʾ and with the dhal lightened; the rest read with the tāʾ and with the dhal doubled. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: its original form is tatadhakkarūn, so the tāʾ of tafaʿʿala was assimilated into the dhal, because the tāʾ is voiceless (mahmusah) and the dhal is voiced (majhurah), and the voiced is louder in sound than the voiceless, so it was good to assimilate the weaker into the stronger. The mā is a relative pronoun joined to the verb, and it together with it has the status of a verbal noun (maṣdar). So the meaning is: little is your remembering. As for the reading of Ibn ʿAmir (yatadhakkarūn) with a yaʾ and a tāʾ, its explanation is that this is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, meaning: little do those who were admonished with this address remember. As for the reading of Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ḥafs, with the dhal light and the kaf doubled, they omitted the tāʾ which the first readers assimilated, and that is good because of the coming together of three closely related letters. And Allah knows best.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: Malik ibn Dinar read (wa lā tabtaghū), from al-ibtighā' in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 85].

[Page 18]

Know that when God, exalted is He, commanded the Messenger, upon him be peace, to warn and to convey the message, and commanded the people to accept and follow it, He mentioned in this verse the threat that comes with abandoning that following and turning away from it. The verse raises several issues:

**First issue:** Al-Zajjaj said: The position of *kam* (how many) is nominative, as the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is *ahlaknaha* (We destroyed it). He said: This is better than its being in the accusative position, because your saying "Zayd, I struck him" (*Zaydun darabtuhu*) is more eloquent than your saying "Zayda, I struck him" (*Zaydan darabtuhu*). The accusative is also good Arabic, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49].

**Second issue:** It has been said that there is an omission in the verse, and the intended meaning is: "And how many of the people of a town," and there are several indications of this:

First: His saying, ﴿then Our punishment came upon it﴾, since punishment (*ba's*) befits only people.

Second: His saying, ﴿or they were resting at midday﴾, where the pronoun refers back to the people of the town.

Third: Warning and admonition reach the responsible persons only through their destruction.

Fourth: The meaning of *bayat* (night raid) and *qa'ilah* (midday rest) is valid only with respect to people.

If it is asked: Why did He say "We destroyed it"? They answered: God, exalted is He, returned the speech to the wording rather than to the meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town that defied the command of its Lord﴾ [al-Talaq: 8], where He returned to the wording. Then He said: ﴿God has prepared for them﴾, where He returned to the meaning rather than the wording. For this reason, al-Zajjaj said: "If he had said, 'then Our punishment came upon them,' it would have been correct." Others said: There is no omission in the verse, and what is meant is the destruction of the town itself, because destroying it by demolition, by sinking into the earth, or by other means is the destruction of those in it. Moreover, on this interpretation, His saying ﴿then Our punishment came upon it﴾ is taken in its apparent sense, and there is no need for interpretation.

**Third issue:** Someone may say: His saying ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, then Our punishment came upon it﴾ implies that the destruction preceded the coming of the punishment, but the matter is not so, since the coming of the punishment precedes the destruction. The scholars answered this objection in several ways:

The first: What is meant by His saying "We destroyed it" is: We decreed its destruction, and then Our punishment came upon it.

The second: "How many a town did We intend to destroy, then Our punishment came upon it," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

The third: If He had said, "And how many a town We destroyed, then Our destruction came upon them," the objection would not arise. Likewise here, since He expressed that destruction by the word "punishment" (*ba's*). If they say: The objection remains, because the *fa'* in His saying ﴿then Our punishment came upon it﴾ is the *fa'* of sequence, which requires difference. We reply: The *fa'* may come with the meaning of explanation, as in the saying of the Prophet, upon him be peace: "God does not accept the prayer of any one of you until he places the purification in its proper places, then washes his face and his hands." Here the *fa'* in "then washes" is explanatory, because washing the face and hands is like an explanation of placing the purification in its proper places. Similarly here, "punishment" serves as an explanation of that destruction, since destruction may occur through ordinary death, and it may occur through the imposition of punishment and affliction upon them. So the mention of "punishment" is an explanation of that destruction.

The fourth: Al-Farra' said: It is not far-fetched to say that punishment and destruction occur together, just as one says, "You gave me and you did well (*fa-ahsanta*)," and the doing well did not come after the giving nor before it, but they occurred together. So likewise here. As for His saying "bayatan" (by night), al-Farra' said: One says, "The man spent the night (*bata*) spending the night (*bayta*)," and they sometimes say "bayatan." They said: The house (*bayt*) was so named because one spends the night in it. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: His saying "bayatan" is a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), in the sense of "spending the night." As for His saying ﴿or they were resting at midday﴾, there are two points of discussion:

**First point:** It is a circumstantial clause conjoined to "bayatan," as if it were said: "Then Our punishment came upon them spending the night or resting at midday."

Al-Farra' said: There is a hidden *wa* (and) in it, and the meaning is: "We destroyed it, and then Our punishment came upon it spending the night, or they were resting at midday." However, they found the joining of two conjunctive particles burdensome. Had it been said, it would have been correct. Al-Zajjaj said: It is not correct, because the *wa* of circumstance is close to the *wa* of conjunction, so combining them requires combining two like things, which is not permitted. If you say, "Zayd came to me on foot (*rajilan*) while he was a horseman (*wa huwa faris*)," you do not need the *wa* of conjunction there.

**Second point:** The particle *aw* (or) enters here with the meaning that the punishment came upon them once by night and once by day. As for *qa'ilah* (midday rest), there are two views. Al-Layth said: *Qa'ilah* is the sleep at midday. Al-Azhari said: *Qa'ilah*, in the usage of the Arabs, is the rest at midday when the heat is intense, even if there is no sleep with it. The evidence for this is that there is no sleep in Paradise, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their abode and finer in their resting place (*maqil*)﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. The meaning of the verse is that Our punishment came upon them while they did not expect it, either by night while they were asleep, or by day while they were resting at midday. The purpose is that the punishment came upon them in a moment of heedlessness, without any prior sign indicating its descent. It is as if it were said to the disbelievers: Do not be deceived by the causes of security, comfort, and leisure, for when the punishment of God comes, it comes suddenly and without any preceding sign. So do not be deceived by your circumstances.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So their claim (*da'wa*) was not⦅...⦆﴾. The people of language said: *Da'wa* is a noun standing in the place of *idda'a'* (claiming) and in the place of *du'a'* (supplication). Sibawayh related: "O God, include us among the good supplications (*du'a'*) of the Muslims and their claims (*da'wa*)."

Ibn Abbas said: Their supplication (*tadarru'*) was not, when Our punishment came upon them, except that they said, "We were indeed wrongdoers," so they confessed against themselves to polytheism.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Their saying, when Our punishment came upon them, was nothing but the acknowledgment of wrongdoing and the confession of evil. As for His saying, ﴿except that they said﴾, the preferred view among the grammarians is that the position of *an* (that) is nominative as the subject of *kana* (was), and His saying *da'wahum* (their claim) is accusative as the predicate, as in His saying: ﴿So their answer was not except that they said﴾ [al-Naml: 56], and His saying: ﴿So the end of both of them was that they were in the Fire﴾ [al-Hashr: 17], and His saying: ﴿Their argument was not except that﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 25]. He said: It is also permissible to do the opposite, by making *da'wa* nominative and the other accusative, as in God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], according to the reading of one who made *al-birr* (righteousness) nominative. The basic rule in this matter is that when two definites come after the verb *kana*, you have the choice to make either of them nominative and the other accusative. For example, you say, "Zayd was your brother," and if you wish, "Zayda was your brother," with the other reversed.

Al-Zajjaj said: However, the preferred form, if we take His saying *da'wahum* to be nominative, is to say, "*fa-ma kanat da'wahum*" (their claim was not). When He said *kana* (masculine), this shows that *da'wa* is in the accusative position. It may be answered that it is permissible to make *da'wa* masculine even if it is nominative, so one says *kana da'wahu batilan* and *batilatan* (his claim was false). And God knows best.

We reply: The *fa'* may come with the meaning of explanation, as in the saying of the Prophet, upon him be peace: "God does not accept the prayer of any one of you until he places the purification in its proper places, then washes his face and his hands." Here the *fa'* in "then washes" is explanatory, because washing the face and hands is like an explanation of placing the purification in its proper places. Similarly here, "punishment" serves as an explanation of that destruction, since destruction may occur through ordinary death, and it may occur through the imposition of punishment and affliction upon them. So the mention of "punishment" is an explanation of that destruction.

The fourth: Al-Farra' said: It is not far-fetched to say that punishment and destruction occur together, just as one says, "You gave me and you did well (*fa-ahsanta*)," and the doing well did not come after the giving nor before it, but they occurred together. So likewise here. As for His saying "bayatan" (by night), al-Farra' said: One says, "The man spent the night (*bata*) spending the night (*bayta*)," and they sometimes say "bayatan." They said: The house (*bayt*) was so named because one spends the night in it. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: His saying "bayatan" is a verbal noun standing in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), in the sense of "spending the night." As for His saying ﴿or they were resting at midday﴾, there are two points of discussion:

**First point:** It is a circumstantial clause conjoined to "bayatan," as if it were said: "Then Our punishment came upon them spending the night or resting at midday."

Al-Farra' said: There is a hidden *wa* (and) in it, and the meaning is: "We destroyed it, and then Our punishment came upon it spending the night, or they were resting at midday." However, they found the joining of two conjunctive particles burdensome. Had it been said, it would have been correct. Al-Zajjaj said: It is not correct, because the *wa* of circumstance is close to the *wa* of conjunction, so combining them requires combining two like things, which is not permitted. If you say, "Zayd came to me on foot (*rajilan*) while he was a horseman (*wa huwa faris*)," you do not need the *wa* of conjunction there.

**Second point:** The particle *aw* (or) enters here with the meaning that the punishment came upon them once by night and once by day. As for *qa'ilah* (midday rest), there are two views. Al-Layth said: *Qa'ilah* is the sleep at midday. Al-Azhari said: *Qa'ilah*, in the usage of the Arabs, is the rest at midday when the heat is intense, even if there is no sleep with it. The evidence for this is that there is no sleep in Paradise, and God, exalted is He, says: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their abode and finer in their resting place (*maqil*)﴾ [al-Furqan: 24]. The meaning of the verse is that Our punishment came upon them while they did not expect it, either by night while they were asleep, or by day while they were resting at midday. The purpose is that the punishment came upon them in a moment of heedlessness, without any prior sign indicating its descent. It is as if it were said to the disbelievers: Do not be deceived by the causes of security, comfort, and leisure, for when the punishment of God comes, it comes suddenly and without any preceding sign. So do not be deceived by your circumstances.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So their claim (*da'wa*) was not⦅...⦆﴾. The people of language said: *Da'wa* is a noun standing in the place of *idda'a'* (claiming) and in the place of *du'a'* (supplication). Sibawayh related: "O God, include us among the good supplications (*du'a'*) of the Muslims and their claims (*da'wa*)."

Ibn Abbas said: Their supplication (*tadarru'*) was not, when Our punishment came upon them, except that they said, "We were indeed wrongdoers," so they confessed against themselves to polytheism.

Ibn al-Anbari said: Their saying, when Our punishment came upon them, was nothing but the acknowledgment of wrongdoing and the confession of evil. As for His saying, ﴿except that they said﴾, the preferred view among the grammarians is that the position of *an* (that) is nominative as the subject of *kana* (was), and His saying *da'wahum* (their claim) is accusative as the predicate, as in His saying: ﴿So their answer was not except that they said﴾ [al-Naml: 56], and His saying: ﴿So the end of both of them was that they were in the Fire﴾ [al-Hashr: 17], and His saying: ﴿Their argument was not except that﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 25]. He said: It is also permissible to do the opposite, by making *da'wa* nominative and the other accusative, as in God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], according to the reading of one who made *al-birr* (righteousness) nominative. The basic rule in this matter is that when two definites come after the verb *kana*, you have the choice to make either of them nominative and the other accusative. For example, you say, "Zayd was your brother," and if you wish, "Zayda was your brother," with the other reversed.

Al-Zajjaj said: However, the preferred form, if we take His saying *da'wahum* to be nominative, is to say, "*fa-ma kanat da'wahum*" (their claim was not). When He said *kana* (masculine), this shows that *da'wa* is in the accusative position. It may be answered that it is permissible to make *da'wa* masculine even if it is nominative, so one says *kana da'wahu batilan* and *batilatan* (his claim was false). And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 6–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ ﴿And We will surely relate to them with knowledge, for We were not absent﴾.

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: In establishing the connection of the composition (wajh al-nazm) there are two aspects.

The first aspect: When Exalted is He commanded the messengers in the preceding verse to convey the message, and commanded the community to accept and follow it, and mentioned the threat against those who abandon acceptance and following by mentioning the descent of punishment in this world, He followed it with another kind of threat, namely that Exalted is He
صفحة ٢٠
will question everyone about how they conducted their deeds on the Day of Resurrection.

The second aspect: When Exalted is He said: ﴿So their claim when Our punishment came to them was only that they said, "Indeed, we were wrongdoers"﴾, He followed it by stating that on the Day of Resurrection, what occurs is not limited to their confession. Rather, there is added to it that Exalted is He questions everyone about how they conducted their deeds, and He made clear that this questioning is not specific to the people of punishment. Rather, it is general to the people of punishment and the people of reward.

The second issue: Those to whom messengers were sent are the community (ummah), and the messengers are the messengers. Thus He made clear that He will question these two groups. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all, about what they used to do﴾ (al-Hijr: 92).

One may say: The purpose of questioning is that the one questioned informs about how he conducted his deeds. So since God informed in the preceding verse that they acknowledge that they were wrongdoers, what is the benefit of mentioning this questioning after it?

Also, Exalted is He said after this verse: ﴿And We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾. If He relates to them with knowledge, what is the meaning of this questioning?

The answer: When they acknowledged that they were wrongdoers and negligent, they were then asked about the cause of that wrongdoing and negligence, and the purpose of it is reproach and rebuke.

If it is said: What is the benefit of questioning the messengers, given the knowledge that no negligence at all proceeded from them?

We say: Because when they affirm that no negligence at all proceeded from them, the negligence is entirely attributed to the community, so God's honour toward the messengers is multiplied, due to the manifestation of their innocence from all causes of negligence, and the causes of disgrace and humiliation toward the disbelievers are multiplied, because it is established that all the negligence came from them.

* * *

Then Exalted is He said: ﴿And We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾. The meaning is that Exalted is He repeats and makes clear to the people what they made public and what they concealed of their deeds, and relates the reasons which led them to undertake those deeds. Then Exalted is He made clear that it is only proper for Him to relate those states to them because He was not absent from their conditions, but was knowing of them, and nothing of them went outside His knowledge. This indicates that divinity is not perfected except when He knows all particulars, so that He can distinguish the obedient from the disobedient, and the good-doer from the evil-doer. Thus it becomes clear that whoever denies that He, Exalted is He, knows the particulars, is thereby prevented from acknowledging that He is commanding, forbidding, rewarding and punishing. For this reason, wherever Exalted is He mentions the states of resurrection and the Last Day, He makes clear that He knows all that is known.

The third issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely relate to them with knowledge﴾ indicates that Exalted is He is knowing with knowledge (ʿilm), and that the saying of whoever says that God has no knowledge is a false saying.

If it is said: How is one to reconcile His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾ with His saying: ﴿So on that Day, no one will be questioned about his sin, neither man nor jinn﴾ (al-Rahman: 39) and His saying: ﴿And the criminals will not be questioned about their sins﴾ (al-Qasas: 78)?

We say: There are aspects to this:

One of them: The people are not questioned about the deeds, because the books contain them, but they are questioned about the motives which prompted them to the deeds, and about the deterrents which turned them away from them.

The second: Questioning may be for the sake of seeking guidance and benefit, and may be for the sake of reproach and humiliation, like the saying of one who says: "Did I not give you?" and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam﴾ (Ya-Sin: 60). The poet said:

صفحة ٢١

Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts?

Knowing this, we say: Exalted is He does not question anyone for the sake of benefit and guidance, and He questions them for the sake of reproaching and humiliating the disbelievers. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And some of them turn to others, questioning one another﴾ (al-Saffat: 27), then He said: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they question one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101). The first verse indicates that the questioning occurring between them was in the manner of some blaming others, and the evidence for this is His saying: ﴿So some of them turn to others, blaming one another﴾ (al-Qalam: 30). And His saying: ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they question one another﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 101) means that some of them will not ask others in the manner of compassion and gentleness, because kinship necessitates inclination, mercy and honour.

The third aspect in the answer: The Day of Resurrection is a long day with many standing-places, so He informed about some times that questioning occurs, and about others that there is no questioning.

The fourth issue: The verse indicates that Exalted is He calls all His servants to account, because they do not go outside being either messengers or those to whom messengers were sent, and it refutes the saying of whoever claims that there is no reckoning for the prophets and the disbelievers.

The fifth issue: The verse indicates that Exalted is He is transcendent above place and direction, because He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿and We were not absent﴾, and if He were upon the Throne, He would be absent from us.

If they say: We interpret it to mean that He was not absent from them in knowledge and encompassing.

We say: This is an interpretation, and the basic principle in speech is to take it in its literal sense.

If they say: Since you say that He, Exalted is He, is not particular to any of the spaces or directions, you have also said that He is absent.

We say: This is false, because the absent is the one who is conceivable to be present after an absence, and that is conditioned on his being particular to a place and direction. As for the one who is not particular to a place and direction, and for whom that is impossible, it is impossible to describe Him with absence and presence. Thus the difference becomes clear, and God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 8:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the weighing on that Day is the truth. So whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful.﴾ ﴿And whoever's scales are light, those are the ones who have lost themselves, for they used to wrong Our signs.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained in the first verse that among the events of the Resurrection are the questioning and the reckoning, He explained in this verse that among the events of the Resurrection is also the weighing of deeds. There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: *al-Waznu* (the weighing) is the subject (*mubtada'*, the topic of the sentence), *yawma'idhin* (on that Day) is an adverbial phrase (*zarf*) modifying it, and *al-haqqu* (the truth) is the predicate (*khabar*, the comment of the sentence). It is also permissible that *yawma'idhin* be the predicate and *al-haqqu* be an attribute of *al-wazn*, meaning: "and the weighing is the truth," i.e., the justice, on the Day when Allah questions the nations and the messengers.

The second issue: concerning the interpretation of the weighing of deeds there are two views.

The first: according to the report, He, exalted is He, sets up on the Day of Resurrection a scale that has a tongue and two pans, by which the deeds of the servants, good and bad, are weighed. Then Ibn 'Abbas said: As for the believer, his deed comes to him in the most beautiful form, and it is placed in a pan of the scale, and his good deeds outweigh his bad deeds. This is His saying: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy, those are the successful﴾, meaning the saved. He said: This is as He said in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be wronged in the least﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47). As for the manner of weighing deeds according to this view, there are several possibilities:

One of them: the deeds of the believer take the form of a good image, and the deeds of the disbeliever take the form of an ugly image, and that image is weighed, as Ibn 'Abbas mentioned.

The second: the weighing refers to the pages on which the deeds of the servants are written. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about what is weighed on the Day of Resurrection, and he said: "The pages." This view is the position of the majority of the exegetes regarding this verse. It is reported from 'Abdullah ibn Salam that the scale of the Lord of the worlds will be set up between the jinn and mankind, and it will be faced toward the Throne. One of the two pans of the scale is over Paradise, and the other is over Hell. If the heavens and the earth were placed in one of them, it would contain them. Jibril will be holding its pillar and looking at its tongue.

It is also reported from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection to the scale, and there will be brought to him ninety-nine registers, each register as far as the eye can see, containing his sins and his offenses, and they will be placed in one pan of the scale. Then there will be brought out for him a small scroll like a fingertip, in which is the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His servant and messenger, and it will be placed in the other pan, and it will outweigh them."

And it is reported from al-Hasan: "One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was resting his head in the lap of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, and he had fallen asleep, when tears flowed from her eyes. He said: 'What has befallen you that makes you weep?' She said: 'I remembered the gathering of the people, and whether anyone will remember anyone.' He said to her: 'They will be gathered barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised. Each person among them on that Day will have a concern that occupies him. No one will remember anyone at the pages, and at the weighing of the good and bad deeds.'"

And it is reported from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr: "A man, large, a great eater and a great drinker, will be brought, and he will not have the weight of a gnat."

The second view, which is the view of Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and al-A'mash, is that what is meant by the scale is justice and judgment. Many of the later scholars adopted this view and said: Interpreting the word "weighing" in this sense is valid in the language, and the evidence for it is [what follows]. The proof that interpreting the word "weighing" in this sense is permissible in the language is that justice in giving and taking appears in the world only through measuring and weighing, so it is not far-fetched to make the weighing a metaphor for justice. What strengthens this is that when a man has no power or standing with others, it is said: "So-and-so does not give so-and-so any weight." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So We will not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (al-Kahf: 105). It is also said: "So-and-so belittled so-and-so," and it is said: "This statement is the weight of this one and its equal," meaning it counterbalances and equals it, even though there is no literal weight. The poet said:

*Before meeting you, I was indeed strong;*
*With me, for every opponent, there is his scale.*

He meant: With me, for every opponent, there is a statement that counterbalances his statement. So he made "the scale" a figure for justice.

When this is established, we say: It is necessary that the meaning of this verse be this meaning alone. The evidence for this is that the scale is only intended so that the magnitude of a thing may be known through it, and the magnitudes of reward and punishment cannot be displayed by a scale, because the deeds of the servants are accidents (*a'rad*), and they have passed away and ceased to exist, and weighing what does not exist is impossible. Moreover, even if they were to persist, their weighing would be impossible. As for their saying: "What is weighed is the pages of the deeds, or created forms according to the measures of the deeds," we say: The responsible person on the Day of Resurrection either acknowledges that He is just and wise, or does not acknowledge that. If he acknowledges that, then the judgment of Allah, exalted is He, concerning the measures of reward and punishment suffices him, in his knowledge that it is just and correct. If he does not acknowledge that, then the preponderance of the pan of good deeds over the pan of bad deeds, or the reverse, does not reveal the preponderance, because it is possible that He displayed that preponderance not by way of justice and equity. Thus it is established that this weighing has no benefit whatsoever.

The earlier scholars answered and said: All the responsible persons will know on the Day of Resurrection that He is free from injustice and oppression, and the benefit in setting up that scale is that the preponderance may become manifest to the people of the Resurrection. If the preponderance appears on the side of good deeds, his joy and happiness increase because of the manifestation of his virtue and the perfection of his rank before the people of the Resurrection. If it is the opposite, his grief, sorrow, and fear increase, and his disgrace in the place of the Resurrection [increases].

Then they differed about the manner of that preponderance. Some said: a light will appear in the preponderance of good deeds, and a darkness in the preponderance of bad deeds. Others said: rather, by the appearance of a preponderance in the pan.

The third issue: the more apparent view is the affirmation of multiple scales on the Day of Resurrection, not one single scale. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ (al-Anbiya': 47), and He said in this verse: ﴿So whoever's scales are heavy﴾. Based on this, it is not far-fetched that there be a scale for the actions of the hearts, a scale for the actions of the limbs, and another scale for what relates to speech.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah gathered "the scales" here, saying ﴿whoever's scales are heavy﴾ and not "whoever's scale," for two reasons:

The first: the Arabs sometimes apply the plural form to the singular. They say: "So-and-so went out to Mecca on mules."

The second: what is meant by "the scales" here is the plural of "the weighed things" (*mawzun*), not the plural of "scale" (*mizan*), and by "the scales" He meant the deeds that are weighed.

Someone may say: These two aspects necessitate deviating from the apparent meaning of the expression, and that is resorted to only when it is impossible to take the speech in its apparent sense, and there is no impediment here to that. Therefore it is necessary to apply the wording to its literal meaning. Just as there is no impossibility in affirming a scale that has a tongue and two pans, so there is no impossibility in affirming multiple scales with this attribute. So what compels abandoning the apparent meaning and turning to interpretation?

[Page 24]

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those whose scales are light, those are the ones who have lost their souls because they wronged Our signs﴾.

Know that this verse contains several issues.

The first issue: it indicates that the people of the Resurrection are of two groups. Among them are those whose good deeds outweigh their evil deeds, and among them are those whose evil deeds outweigh their good deeds. As for a third category, in which their good and evil deeds are equal and balanced, it does not exist.

The second issue: Most of the commentators (mufassirun) said: What is meant by ﴿And those whose scales are light﴾ is the disbeliever. The evidence for this is the Qur'an, the report (khabar) and the transmitted statement (athar). As for the Qur'an, it is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿those are the ones who have lost their souls because they wronged Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 9]. Being a wrongdoer toward the signs of God has no meaning except being an unbeliever in them and denying them. This shows that what is meant by this verse is the people of disbelief. As for the report, it is what is narrated: "When the good deeds of a believer are light, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) brings out from his chamber a small slip like a finger joint, and places it in the right pan of the scale, where his good deeds are, and the good deeds then outweigh. That believing servant says to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'May my father and mother be your ransom, how beautiful is your face and how beautiful is your character! Who are you?' He says: 'I am your Prophet Muhammad, and this is your prayer which you used to send upon me; I have fulfilled it for you at the time you most need it.'" This report was related by al-Wahidi in al-Basit. As for the majority of scholars, they related here the report we mentioned, that God, may He be exalted, places in the pan of good deeds the written record that includes the testimony that there is no god but God and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God.

Al-Qadi said: This must be understood to mean that he came with the two testimonies with their due rights from the acts of worship, because if that were not taken into account, then whoever came with the two testimonies would know that sins do not harm him, and that would be an incitement to disobedience of God, may He be exalted.

Someone may say: Reason indicates the soundness of what this report indicates, because whatever act is more noble and higher in rank must be greater in reward. It is known that knowing God, may He be exalted, and loving Him are higher in status and greater in rank than all other acts, so it must be that they are fuller in reward and higher in rank than all other acts. As for the athar, it is because Ibn 'Abbas and most of the commentators understood this verse to refer to the people of disbelief.

Since this principle is established, we say: The Murji'ah (a sect who say that sin does not harm along with faith) who say "sin does not harm alongside faith" held fast to this verse and said: He, may He be exalted, limited the people of the station of the Resurrection to two groups:

One of them: those whose good deeds' pan outweighed, and who were judged to be among the successful.

The second: those whose evil deeds' pan outweighed, and who were judged to be people of disbelief who used to wrong the signs of God. This indicates that the believer is not punished at all.

We say in reply: At most, the matter is that He, may He be exalted, did not mention this third category in this verse, but He mentioned it in other verses, saying: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. The explicit statement (mantuq) takes precedence over the implied meaning (mafhum), so it is necessary to turn to affirming it. Furthermore, He, may He be exalted, said regarding this category: ﴿those are the ones who have lost their souls﴾, and we concede that this is only fitting for the disbeliever. As for the sinful believer, he is punished for days, then he is pardoned and attains the mercy of God, may He be exalted. So in reality he has not lost his soul; rather he has triumphed with the mercy of God forever, without cessation or end. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood; little are you grateful.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when Exalted God commanded creation to follow the prophets, peace be upon them, and to accept their call, then warned them of the punishment of this world, which is His saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾, then He warned them of the punishment of the Hereafter in two respects:

The first of them: the questioning, which is His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾.

The second: the weighing of deeds, which is His saying: ﴿And the weighing that Day is the truth﴾. He encouraged them to accept the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, in this verse by another way, namely that God's blessings upon them were abundant, and abundance of blessings necessitates obedience. So He said: ﴿And We have certainly established you on the earth and made for you therein means of livelihood﴾. His saying: ﴿established you on the earth﴾ means: We made for you therein a place and a settled abode, and We established you therein, and We empowered you to dispose of it. And "made for you therein means of livelihood" — the meaning of "means of livelihood" is the aspects of benefit, and these are of two kinds: some of them are obtained by God's creation directly, such as the creation of fruits and other things, and some are obtained by acquisition. Both, in reality, have come about only through God's bounty, His empowering and His establishing. Therefore the whole of it is a favour from God, Exalted, and abundance of favour undoubtedly necessitates obedience and submission. Then God, Exalted, explained that, despite this bounty and favour, He knows that they do not perform His thanks as they should, so He said: ﴿little are you grateful﴾. This indicates that they do sometimes give thanks, and the matter is so, because the acknowledgment of the existence of the Creator is like a necessary matter inherent in the natural disposition of every rational mind, and God's blessings upon man are numerous, so there is no human being who does not thank God at some times for His blessings; the difference is only that some of them are often very thankful, and some are seldom thankful.

The second issue: Narrated Kharijah, from Nafi', that he hamzated (maʿāʾish). Al-Zajjaj said: All the Basran grammarians maintain that hamzating maʿāʾish is an error, and they mentioned that changing the yāʾ into a hamzah is permissible only when the yāʾ is augmentative, as in ṣaḥīfah and ṣaḥāʾif. As for maʿāyish, it is from al-ʿaysh (livelihood), and the yāʾ is original (radical). I do not know a valid basis for Nafi's reading, except that the yāʾ of this word, which is from the root of the word itself, is made quiescent in maʿīshah, so this word came to resemble our saying ṣaḥīfah, and so maʿāʾish was made similar to our saying ṣaḥāʾif; just as they inserted a hamzah in our saying ṣaḥāʾif, so too in our saying maʿāʾish, by way of analogy. The only difference is what we have mentioned: that the yāʾ in maʿīshah is original, while in ṣaḥīfah it is augmentative.

The Most High says: ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you, then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," and they prostrated, except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated.﴾

In this verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that the Most High encouraged the nations to accept the call of the prophets, peace be upon them, first through warning and then through encouragement, as we have explained. The encouragement was intended to draw attention to the abundance of God's blessings upon creation. So He began explaining those blessings with His words: ﴿And We have established you upon the earth and provided for you therein means of livelihood﴾. Then He followed this with mention that He created our father Adam and made him one to whom the angels prostrate. A favour bestowed upon a father is treated like a favour bestowed upon his son. This is the manner of arrangement (wajh al-nazm) in these verses. A parallel to this is His saying at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life?﴾ (al-Baqarah: 28). Here He forbade disobedience with His words, ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾, and justified that prohibition by the abundance of His blessings upon creation: that they were dead and He gave them life, then He created for them everything on the earth of benefit, and then He followed that benefit by making Adam a khalifah (vicegerent) on the earth, one to whom the angels prostrate. The purpose of all of this is to establish that, given these great blessings, rebellion and denial are not fitting for them. Likewise, in this surah the Most High mentioned the very same meaning in a different order. This is the explanation of the manner of arrangement in the best way.

The second issue: Know that the Most High mentioned the story of Adam, peace be upon him, together with the story of Iblis in the Qur'an in seven places:

The first is in Surah al-Baqarah. The second is in this surah. The third is in Surah al-Hijr. The fourth is in Surah Bani Isra'il. The fifth is in Surah al-Kahf. The sixth is in Surah Ta-Ha. The seventh is in Surah Sad.

[Page 26 continues]

Having understood this, we say: In this verse there is a difficulty. The words of the Most High, ﴿And We created you, then We fashioned you﴾, indicate that the one addressed by this address is us. Then He said after it, ﴿then We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾, and the word "then" (thumma) indicates delay. The apparent meaning of the verse therefore requires that the command to the angels to prostrate to Adam occurred after Our creating and fashioning of you. It is known that this is not the case. For this reason, people differed in interpreting this verse, giving four opinions:

The first: The words, ﴿And We created you﴾, mean: We created your father Adam, and ﴿We fashioned you﴾ means: We fashioned Adam. Then ﴿We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. This is the view of al-Hasan and Yusuf al-Nahwi (the grammarian), and it is the preferred view. This is because the command to the angels to prostrate to Adam came after the creation and fashioning of Adam, and it did not come after Our creating and fashioning of you.

At most, one might ask: How is it appropriate to make Our creating and fashioning of you a metonym for the creation and fashioning of Adam?

We answer: Adam, peace be upon him, is the origin of mankind, so this metonymy is appropriate. A parallel to this is the words of the Most High: ﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you﴾ (al-Baqarah: 63), meaning the covenant of your forefathers from the Children of Israel at the time of Musa, peace be upon him. It is also said: "The Banu Asad killed so-and-so," when in fact only one of them killed him. He, peace be upon him, said: "Then you, O Khuza'ah, have killed this victim, when in fact only one of them killed him." And the Most High, addressing the Jews at the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), said: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾ (al-A'raf: 141) and ﴿And when you killed a soul﴾ (al-Baqarah: 72). What is meant by all these addresses is their forefathers. So likewise here.

The second: The meaning of His words, ﴿We created you﴾, is Adam, and ﴿then We fashioned you﴾ means: We fashioned the offspring of Adam, peace be upon him, in his loins. Then after that We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam." This is the view of Mujahid. It states that the Most High first created Adam, then brought forth his offspring from his loins in the form of dhurr (tiny particles), and after that commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam.

The third aspect: "We created you, then We fashioned you, then We inform you that We said to the angels, 'Prostrate to Adam.'" This conjunction indicates the sequence of one report after another report, and does not indicate the sequence of the reported event after another reported event.

The fourth aspect: In the linguistic usage, "creation" (khalq) is an expression for "decree" (taqdir), as we have established in this book. The decree of God is an expression for His knowledge of things and His will to assign each thing its specific measure. So His words, "We created you," point to God's ruling and decree for the bringing into being of mankind in this world. And His words, "We fashioned you," point to the fact that He, the Most High, recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) the form of everything that will exist and be created until the Hour, according to what came in the report that He, the Most High, said: "Write what will be until the Day of Resurrection." So the creation of God is an expression for His ruling and His will, and the fashioning is an expression for recording the forms of things in the Preserved Tablet. Then after these two matters, God, the Most High, brought Adam into being and commanded the angels to prostrate to him. This interpretation is, in my view, closer to the truth than all the other aspects.

The third issue: We mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah that concerning this prostration there are three opinions:

One of them: What is meant by it is merely honouring, not the actual prostration.

The second: What is meant is the actual prostration, but the one to whom it was directed is God, the Most High; Adam was like the qiblah (direction of prayer).

The third: The one to whom prostration was directed is Adam. We also mentioned that people differed as to whether the angels whom God, the Most High, commanded to prostrate to Adam are the angels of the heavens and the Throne, or whether what is meant is the angels of the earth. There is disagreement on this, and these discussions were already mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah.

[Page 27]

The fourth issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that the Most High made an exception of Iblis from the angels, and therefore he must be one of them. We have also thoroughly examined this issue in Surah al-Baqarah. Al-Hasan used to say: Iblis was not one of the angels, because he was created from fire, and the angels from light. The angels do not act arrogantly against worshipping Him, nor do they weary of it, nor do they disobey, whereas Iblis is not like that: he disobeyed and acted arrogantly. The angels are not of the jinn, whereas Iblis is of the jinn. The angels are messengers of God, whereas Iblis is not like that. Iblis is the first creation of the jinn and their father, just as Adam, peace be upon him, is the first creation of mankind and their father.

Al-Hasan said: Since Iblis was commanded together with the angels, God, the Most High, made an exception of him, and the name "Iblis" was something else. When he disobeyed God, the Most High, he was named by it. He had been a believer and a worshipper in the heaven until he disobeyed his Lord, and so he was sent down to the earth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "What prevented you from not prostrating when I commanded you?" He said, "I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay."﴾ ﴿He said, "Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein. So get out, for you are among the debased."﴾

There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: This verse indicates that when God commanded the angels to prostrate, that command included Iblis. The apparent meaning is that Iblis was among the angels. However, the proofs we have mentioned indicate that this is not the case. As for the exception (istithna'), we have answered it in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of the verse requires that God asked Iblis what prevented him from abandoning prostration, but that is not the case. The intended meaning is to ask what prevented him from prostrating. Because of this difficulty, two views have arisen concerning the verse.

The first view, which is the well-known one, is that the word (la, "not") is a superfluous particle (silah za'idah), and the meaning is: "What prevented you from prostrating?" It has parallels in the Qur'an, such as His saying: ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 1), meaning "I swear." And His saying: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they should not return﴾ (Al-Anbiya': 95), meaning "that they should return." And His saying: ﴿So that the People of the Scripture would not know﴾, meaning "so that the People of the Scripture would know." This is the view of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', al-Zajjaj, and most scholars.

The second view is that the word (la) here is meaningful and is not redundant (laghw). This is the correct view, because ruling that a word in the Book of God is redundant, with no benefit in it, is a serious problem. According to this view, there are two interpretations of the verse:

The first: The meaning is, "What was it that prevented you from abandoning prostration?" This question is in the form of a denunciation, and its meaning is: "Nothing prevented you from abandoning prostration." It is like the saying of a person to one who struck him unjustly: "What prevented you from striking me? Is it your religion, or your intellect, or your modesty?" The meaning is that none of these matters existed, and you did not refrain from striking me.

The second: Al-Qadi said: God mentioned the prevention but intended the motive, as if He said: "What motivated you to not prostrate?" This is because disobeying God's command is a grave state at which one marvels and asks about the motive for it.

(Page 28)

The third issue: Scholars have used this verse as evidence that the form of a command (sighat al-amr) indicates obligation (wujub). They said: God censured Iblis in this verse for abandoning what he was commanded to do, and if the command did not indicate obligation, then merely abandoning the commanded act would not warrant censure.

If it is said: "Grant that this verse indicates that that command was indicative of obligation; perhaps that particular form of command indicated obligation. Why do you claim that all forms of command must be like that?"

We reply: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ indicates that the censure is grounded merely in abandoning the command, because His saying ﴿when I commanded you﴾ is mentioned in the context of giving a reason. What is mentioned in His saying ﴿when I commanded you﴾ is the command insofar as it is a command, not its being a specific command in a specific form. Since that is so, abandoning a command insofar as it is a command must warrant censure, and that indicates that every command requires obligation, which is what was to be proved.

The fourth issue: Whoever holds that a command indicates immediacy (al-fawr) has used this verse as evidence. He said: God censured Iblis for not prostrating at once, and if the command did not indicate immediacy, he would not have deserved this censure for not prostrating at once.

The fifth issue: Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ seeks the motive that led him to abandon prostration. God related from Iblis the mention of that motive, which is that he said: ﴿I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay.﴾ The meaning is that Iblis said: "I did not prostrate to Adam only because I am better than him, and whoever is better than another, it is not permissible to command that more perfect one to prostrate to the less worthy one." Then he explained the first premise, which is his saying ﴿I am better than him﴾, by saying ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾. Fire is superior to clay, and what is created from the superior is superior. Therefore it follows that Iblis is better than Adam.

As for showing that fire is superior to clay: fire is luminous, elevated, subtle, light, hot and dry, adjacent to and touching the substances of the heavens. Clay is dark, low, dense, heavy, cold and dry, far from the proximity of the heavens. Furthermore, fire has a strong effect and action, whereas earth has only receptivity and being affected, and action is nobler than being affected. Also, fire is suited to innate heat, which is the substance of life, while earthiness, cold and dryness are suited to death, and life is nobler than death. Also, the ripening of fruits depends on heat. Also, the time of growth in plants, when heat is at its peak, is the time when the perfection of animal life is attained in these two periods, whereas the time of old age is the time of suitable cold and dryness. Undoubtedly, this period is the worst of the stages of human life.

As for showing that what is created from the superior is superior, this is obvious, because the nobility of origins necessitates the nobility of branches.

As for showing that the more noble may not be commanded to serve the less noble, this is because it is established in intellects that whoever commands Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and the other great jurists to serve a jurist of low rank would be acting in a way that intellects find repugnant. This is the formulation of Iblis's argument.

We say: this argument is composed of three premises.

The first: that fire is superior to dust. We have discussed this in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for the second premise, namely that whoever has a superior material has a superior form, this is the point of dispute and investigation, because since excellence is a gift from God granted from the outset, excellence of material does not necessitate excellence of form. Do you not see that a disbeliever emerges from a believer, and a believer from a disbeliever, and light from darkness and darkness from light? This shows that excellence is attained only by the grace of God, not because of the excellence of the origin or the substance.

Also, obligation (taklif) applies to a living being only after it reaches the limit of the perfection of intellect, so what counts is what it attains, not what it was created from. Also, excellence comes only through deeds and what is connected to them, not through the material. Do you not see that a believing Abyssinian is preferred over an unbelieving Qurashi?

The sixth issue: Whoever said that it is not permissible to specify the general meaning of a text by analogy (qiyas, analogical reasoning) argued: If specifying the general meaning of a text by analogy were permissible, Iblis would not have deserved this severe censure and great rebuke. Since this censure did occur, it shows that specifying the general meaning of a text by analogy is not permissible. The implication is as follows: God's saying to the angels, ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, is a general address that includes all the angels. Then Iblis removed himself from this generality by analogy. He reasoned that he was created from fire, fire is nobler than clay, and whoever has a nobler origin is nobler, so Iblis must be nobler than Adam, peace be upon him. Whoever is nobler than another may not be commanded to serve the lower and less worthy. The evidence for this is that this ruling holds in all comparable cases, and analogy means nothing other than this. Thus it is established that Iblis did nothing in this event except specify the generality of God's saying to the angels, ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, by this analogy. Therefore, if specifying a text by analogy were permissible, Iblis should not have deserved censure for this act. Since he deserved severe censure for it, we know that specifying a text by analogy is not permissible.

Also, the verse provides evidence for the soundness of this issue from another angle. When Iblis mentioned this analogy, God said: ﴿Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein.﴾ He described Iblis as arrogant after relating to us that analogy, which necessitates specifying the text. This implies that whoever attempts to specify the general meaning of a text by analogy is arrogant toward God. Since this verse shows that specifying the general meaning of a text by analogy is arrogance toward God, and this verse shows that arrogance toward God necessitates severe punishment, expulsion from the ranks of the friends of God, and inclusion among the accursed, it is established that specifying a text by analogy is not permissible. This is what is meant by what al-Wahidi transmitted in al-Basit from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Obedience was more fitting for Iblis than analogy, so he disobeyed his Lord and analogized. Iblis was the first to analogize, and he disbelieved by his analogy. Whoever measures the religion by some of his own opinion, God will join him with Iblis." This is the whole of the wording that al-Wahidi transmitted in al-Basit from Ibn 'Abbas.

If it is said: "Analogy that nullifies the text entirely is invalid. As for analogy that specifies the text in some instances, why do you claim it is invalid?"

Its formulation is: if it were repugnant for one created from fire to prostrate to one created from earth, then it would be even more repugnant, and more fitting, for one created from pure light to prostrate to one created from earth, because light is nobler than fire. This analogy requires that the command of any of the angels to prostrate to Adam be repugnant, so this analogy requires lifting the meaning of the text entirely, and it is invalid.

As for the analogy that requires specifying the meaning of the general text, why do you claim it is invalid? This is a good question that I have raised regarding this method, and I have not seen anyone raise this question who could be answered. It may be answered as follows: that he is nobler than others necessitates the repugnance of commanding one who would not accept to resort to serving the lower and less worthy. But if that noble one accepts that service, it is not repugnant, because there is no objection to his waiving his own right. As for the angels, they accepted that, so there is no harm in it. As for Iblis, he did not accept waiving this right, so his being commanded to prostrate was repugnant. This is an appropriate analogy, and it requires specifying the text, not lifting it entirely or nullifying it. If specifying a text by analogy were permissible, he would not have deserved great censure. Since he deserved this great censure on his part, we know that this was only because specifying a text by analogy is not permissible. And God knows best.
