We reply: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ indicates that the censure is grounded merely in abandoning the command, because His saying ﴿when I commanded you﴾ is mentioned in the context of giving a reason. What is mentioned in His saying ﴿when I commanded you﴾ is the command insofar as it is a command, not its being a specific command in a specific form. Since that is so, abandoning a command insofar as it is a command must warrant censure, and that indicates that every command requires obligation, which is what was to be proved.

The fourth issue: Whoever holds that a command indicates immediacy (al-fawr) has used this verse as evidence. He said: God censured Iblis for not prostrating at once, and if the command did not indicate immediacy, he would not have deserved this censure for not prostrating at once.

The fifth issue: Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ seeks the motive that led him to abandon prostration. God related from Iblis the mention of that motive, which is that he said: ﴿I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay.﴾ The meaning is that Iblis said: "I did not prostrate to Adam only because I am better than him, and whoever is better than another, it is not permissible to command that more perfect one to prostrate to the less worthy one." Then he explained the first premise, which is his saying ﴿I am better than him﴾, by saying ﴿You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾. Fire is superior to clay, and what is created from the superior is superior. Therefore it follows that Iblis is better than Adam.

As for showing that fire is superior to clay: fire is luminous, elevated, subtle, light, hot and dry, adjacent to and touching the substances of the heavens. Clay is dark, low, dense, heavy, cold and dry, far from the proximity of the heavens. Furthermore, fire has a strong effect and action, whereas earth has only receptivity and being affected, and action is nobler than being affected. Also, fire is suited to innate heat, which is the substance of life, while earthiness, cold and dryness are suited to death, and life is nobler than death. Also, the ripening of fruits depends on heat. Also, the time of growth in plants, when heat is at its peak, is the time when the perfection of animal life is attained in these two periods, whereas the time of old age is the time of suitable cold and dryness. Undoubtedly, this period is the worst of the stages of human life.

As for showing that what is created from the superior is superior, this is obvious, because the nobility of origins necessitates the nobility of branches.

As for showing that the more noble may not be commanded to serve the less noble, this is because it is established in intellects that whoever commands Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i and the other great jurists to serve a jurist of low rank would be acting in a way that intellects find repugnant. This is the formulation of Iblis's argument.

We say: this argument is composed of three premises.

The first: that fire is superior to dust. We have discussed this in Surat al-Baqarah.

As for the second premise, namely that whoever has a superior material has a superior form, this is the point of dispute and investigation, because since excellence is a gift from God granted from the outset, excellence of material does not necessitate excellence of form. Do you not see that a disbeliever emerges from a believer, and a believer from a disbeliever, and light from darkness and darkness from light? This shows that excellence is attained only by the grace of God, not because of the excellence of the origin or the substance.

Also, obligation (taklif) applies to a living being only after it reaches the limit of the perfection of intellect, so what counts is what it attains, not what it was created from. Also, excellence comes only through deeds and what is connected to them, not through the material. Do you not see that a believing Abyssinian is preferred over an unbelieving Qurashi?

The sixth issue: Whoever said that it is not permissible to specify the general meaning of a text by analogy (qiyas, analogical reasoning) argued: If specifying the general meaning of a text by analogy were permissible, Iblis would not have deserved this severe censure and great rebuke. Since this censure did occur, it shows that specifying the general meaning of a text by analogy is not permissible. The implication is as follows: God's saying to the angels, ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, is a general address that includes all the angels. Then Iblis removed himself from this generality by analogy. He reasoned that he was created from fire, fire is nobler than clay, and whoever has a nobler origin is nobler, so Iblis must be nobler than Adam, peace be upon him. Whoever is nobler than another may not be commanded to serve the lower and less worthy. The evidence for this is that this ruling holds in all comparable cases, and analogy means nothing other than this. Thus it is established that Iblis did nothing in this event except specify the generality of God's saying to the angels, ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, by this analogy. Therefore, if specifying a text by analogy were permissible, Iblis should not have deserved censure for this act. Since he deserved severe censure for it, we know that specifying a text by analogy is not permissible.

Also, the verse provides evidence for the soundness of this issue from another angle. When Iblis mentioned this analogy, God said: ﴿Then descend from it, for it is not for you to be arrogant therein.﴾ He described Iblis as arrogant after relating to us that analogy, which necessitates specifying the text. This implies that whoever attempts to specify the general meaning of a text by analogy is arrogant toward God. Since this verse shows that specifying the general meaning of a text by analogy is arrogance toward God, and this verse shows that arrogance toward God necessitates severe punishment, expulsion from the ranks of the friends of God, and inclusion among the accursed, it is established that specifying a text by analogy is not permissible. This is what is meant by what al-Wahidi transmitted in al-Basit from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "Obedience was more fitting for Iblis than analogy, so he disobeyed his Lord and analogized. Iblis was the first to analogize, and he disbelieved by his analogy. Whoever measures the religion by some of his own opinion, God will join him with Iblis." This is the whole of the wording that al-Wahidi transmitted in al-Basit from Ibn 'Abbas.

If it is said: "Analogy that nullifies the text entirely is invalid. As for analogy that specifies the text in some instances, why do you claim it is invalid?"

Its formulation is: if it were repugnant for one created from fire to prostrate to one created from earth, then it would be even more repugnant, and more fitting, for one created from pure light to prostrate to one created from earth, because light is nobler than fire. This analogy requires that the command of any of the angels to prostrate to Adam be repugnant, so this analogy requires lifting the meaning of the text entirely, and it is invalid.

As for the analogy that requires specifying the meaning of the general text, why do you claim it is invalid? This is a good question that I have raised regarding this method, and I have not seen anyone raise this question who could be answered. It may be answered as follows: that he is nobler than others necessitates the repugnance of commanding one who would not accept to resort to serving the lower and less worthy. But if that noble one accepts that service, it is not repugnant, because there is no objection to his waiving his own right. As for the angels, they accepted that, so there is no harm in it. As for Iblis, he did not accept waiving this right, so his being commanded to prostrate was repugnant. This is an appropriate analogy, and it requires specifying the text, not lifting it entirely or nullifying it. If specifying a text by analogy were permissible, he would not have deserved great censure. Since he deserved this great censure on his part, we know that this was only because specifying a text by analogy is not permissible. And God knows best.

The seventh issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ There is no doubt that the speaker of this statement is God, because His saying ﴿when I commanded you﴾ is fitting only for God, glorified is He.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿You created me from fire﴾, there is no doubt that the speaker of this statement is Iblis.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿He said, "Then descend from it"﴾, there is no doubt that the speaker of this statement is God, exalted is He. A dialogue like this one between God, glorified is He, and Iblis is mentioned in Surah Sad in detail.

Having established this, we say: No one among the great prophets, peace be upon them, has been granted a conversation with God like the one granted to Iblis. God magnified the honor of Moses by speaking to him, when He said: ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him﴾ (Al-A'raf: 143), and He said: ﴿And God spoke to Moses with speech﴾ (An-Nisa': 164). If this conversation indicates great honor, how did Iblis obtain it in the highest form? And if it does not confer great honor, how did God mention it in the context of complete honor for Moses, peace be upon him?

The answer: some scholars said that God said to Iblis, through the words of whichever angel conveyed it to him: "What prevented you from prostrating?" It is not conceded that God spoke with Iblis directly, without an intermediary. They said: "This is because it is established that God does not address anyone other than the prophets except through an intermediary." Others said that God did speak with Iblis directly, but in a manner of humiliation, as evidenced by His saying to him: ﴿So get out, for you are among the debased﴾. He spoke with Musa and with all the other prophets, peace be upon them, in a manner of honour. Do you not see that He said to Musa: ﴿And I have chosen you﴾ (Ta-Ha: 13), and said to him: ﴿And I have made you for Myself﴾ (Ta-Ha: 41)? This is the utmost honour.

The eighth issue: God's saying: ﴿Then descend from it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means from the Garden. They were in the Garden of ʿAdn (Eden), and Adam was created in it. Some of the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasised divine justice and human free will) said: He was only commanded to descend from the heaven. We have thoroughly discussed this issue in the commentary on Surat al-Baqarah. ﴿It is not for you to be arrogant therein﴾, meaning in the heaven. Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means that the people of the heavens are angels who are humble and submissive. ﴿So get out, for you are among the debased﴾. The debasement (ṣaghār) is abasement. Al-Zajjaj said: Iblis sought arrogance, so God tested him with abasement and humiliation, as an indication of the truth of what the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever humbles himself for God, God will raise him, and whoever is arrogant, God will lower him." Some of them said: When he displayed arrogance, he was clothed in debasement. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 7, verses 14–15:**

*Allah the Exalted said:* ﴿He said, "Give me respite until the day they are raised."﴾ ﴿He said, "You are among those given respite."﴾ ﴿He said, "Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path.﴾ ﴿Then I will come at them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful."﴾

Concerning the verse, there are several issues.

[p. 31]

**First issue:** His saying, ﴿He said, "Give me respite until the day they are raised"﴾, indicates that he asked Allah the Exalted for respite until the time of resurrection, which is the time of the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thāniyah), when people stand before the Lord of the worlds.

His aim was that he would not taste death, and Allah the Exalted did not grant him that.

Rather, He said, ﴿"You are among those given respite"﴾. Here there are two opinions:

The first: Allah the Exalted granted him respite until the first blast, because He said in another verse, ﴿"So you are among those given respite, until the day of the appointed time"﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:37–38]. What is meant by it is the day on which all living things die. Others said: Allah did not specify a fixed term for him, but rather said, ﴿"You are among those given respite"﴾, and His saying in the other verse, ﴿"until the day of the appointed time"﴾ [al-Ḥijr 15:38], means the time that is known in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted.

They said: The evidence for the soundness of this opinion is that Iblis was a responsible being (mukallaf), and a responsible being cannot be allowed to know that Allah the Exalted has postponed his term to a specific time. This is because such a responsible being would know that whenever he repents, his repentance is accepted. So if he knew that the time of his death was a specific time, he would proceed to disobedience with an empty heart, and when the time of his death drew near he would repent of those sins. Thus it is established that defining the exact time of death amounts to encouraging (ighrā') the commission of evil, and that is impermissible for Allah the Exalted.

The first group replied: Allah's informing him that he is among those given respite until the Day of Resurrection does not entail encouraging him to do evil, because Allah the Exalted knew that he would die upon the most evil kinds of disbelief and wickedness, whether or not He informed him of the time of his death. So that information did not necessitate encouraging him to evil. An example of this is that Allah the Exalted informed His prophets that they would die in purity and infallibility, and that did not necessitate encouraging them to evil, because Allah knew about them, whether or not He made them aware of this state, that they would die in purity and infallibility.

Since their state does not change because of this information, that information was not, for that reason, an encouragement to evil. The same applies here. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**Second issue:** Iblis's saying, ﴿"Because You have led me astray"﴾, indicates that he attributed his misguidance to Allah the Exalted. His saying in another verse, ﴿"By Your might, I will surely mislead them all"﴾ [Ṣād 38:82], indicates that he attributed the misguiding of the servants to himself.

The first points to his being on the doctrine of determinism (jabr), and the second points to his being on the doctrine of free will (qadar).

This indicates that he was confused on this question. Or it may be said that he believed misguidance could only occur through one who misguides, so he made himself a misguider of others from among the misguided, and then claimed that the one who misguided him was Allah the Exalted, in order to avoid an infinite regress (tasalsul).

People have differed in interpreting this word. As for our companions (ashābunā, the Ash'arī theologians), they said: *al-ighwā'* is the placing of error (ghayy) in the heart, and *ghayy* is false belief. This indicates that he believed truth and falsehood only occur in the heart from Allah the Exalted.

As for the Mu'tazilah (a theological school that emphasized human free will and divine justice), they have two positions here:

One: to interpret *ghayy* in the way we have mentioned.

Two: to mention another meaning in its interpretation.

As for the first meaning, they have several excuses:

The first: They say, "This is the saying of Iblis. Grant that Iblis believed that the creator of error, ignorance and disbelief is Allah the Exalted, yet his saying is not evidence."

The second: They said, "When Allah the Exalted commanded the prostration to Adam, his error and disbelief became manifest at that point. So it is permissible to attribute that error to Allah the Exalted in this sense, just as a speaker may say, 'Do not make me hit you,' meaning: do not do what makes me hit you."

The third: ﴿"He said, 'Because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them'"﴾, meaning: "Since You cursed me because of Adam, for the sake of this enmity I cast whisperings into their hearts."

The fourth: ﴿"My Lord, because You have led me astray"﴾, meaning: "You cast me out of Your Garden as a punishment for my deed, so I will sit in ambush for them."

[p. 32]

The second meaning: In interpreting *ighwā'* (misleading), it means destruction. From this is His saying, ﴿"They will meet with ghayy"﴾ [Maryam 19:59], meaning destruction and perdition. From this also is the saying of the Arabs: *ghawā al-faṣīl yaghwī ghawan*, when a young camel drinks too much milk until its insides are spoiled and it approaches destruction and ruin. They also interpreted His saying, ﴿"If Allah wills to mislead you"﴾ [Hūd 11:34], as: "If Allah wills to destroy you because of your obstinacy."

This is the whole body of the stated interpretations.

Know that we do not insist that what is meant by *ighwā'* in this verse is leading astray, because its outcome returns to the saying of Iblis, and that is not evidence. However, we establish the certain proof that the one who misled Iblis is Allah the Exalted. This is because the one who is in error must have a misleader, just as the moving thing must have a mover, the still thing must have a stiller, and the one who is guided must have a guide. Since Iblis is in error, he must have a misleader. The misleader is either himself, or another created being, or Allah the Exalted. The first is false, because a rational being does not choose error while knowing it is error. The second is false, for otherwise either an infinite regress (tasalsul) or circularity (dawr) would follow. The third is the intended conclusion. And Allah knows best.

Third issue: The preposition in His words ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾ (fa-bima aghwaytani) has several possible readings.

The first: it is the particle of oath (bā' al-qasam). The meaning is: "By Your misguiding me, I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path," that is: "By Your power over me and the effectiveness of Your authority over me, I will surely sit in wait for them on the straight path which they travel to Paradise, by making falsehood appealing to them and by what earns them sins." Since the bā' is the bā' of oath, the lam is the answer of the oath, and mā is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), with ﴿aghwaytani﴾ as its relative clause.

The second: that His words ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾ mean "because of Your leading me astray I will surely sit in wait for them." The intended meaning is that since You led me astray, I too strive to lead them astray.

The third: some have said that mā in His words ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾ is interrogative, as if it were said: "By what did You lead me astray?" and then he began and said: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them﴾. There is a difficulty in this: the retention of the alif when the preposition enters on the interrogative "mā" is rare.

Fourth issue: In His words ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ there is no disagreement among the grammarians that "ʿalā" (on) is elided, and the implied phrase is: "I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path."

Al-Zajjaj said: its example is your saying: "Zayd struck the back and the belly," meaning "on the back and the belly." Omitting the word ʿalā is permissible, because the path (ṣirāṭ) is a place-adverb in meaning, so it admits what the day and the night admit, in your saying: "I will come to you tomorrow" and "on tomorrow."

Having understood this, we say: His words ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ contain several investigations:

The first investigation: what is meant is that he persists in corruption with a persistence from which he never slackens. For this reason he mentioned sitting (qu'ud), because whoever wishes to be thorough in completing a matter sits down until he becomes free of mind, so that he can accomplish the aim. His persistence in corruption is his persistence in whispering, so that he never slackens from it.

The second investigation: this verse indicates that he was knowledgeable about the true religion and the correct method, because he said: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾, and the straight path of God is His true religion.

The third investigation: the verse indicates that Iblis knew that the doctrine and belief he held was pure error and misguidance, because if he had not been like that, he would not have said: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾. Also, he knew the true religion, and had he not known it, he would not have said: ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾.

If this is established, how can it be possible for Iblis to be content with that doctrine while knowing that it is error and misguidance, and that it opposes the true religion and contradicts the straight path? For a person only holds a corrupt belief when it has become dominant in his estimation that it is true; but with knowledge that it is falsehood, error and misguidance, it is impossible that he would choose it, be pleased with it, and believe in it.

Know that some people have said: Iblis's disbelief was disbelief of obstinacy (kufr ʿinād), not disbelief of ignorance (kufr jahl), because whenever he knew that his doctrine was error and misguidance, he knew that its opposite was the truth, so his denial was a denial merely by the tongue, and that was disbelief of obstinacy. Others said: No, rather his disbelief is disbelief of ignorance, and his words ﴿Because You have led me astray﴾ and his words ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ are meant according to the opponent's assumption and his own belief. And God knows best.

* * *

Fifth issue: Our companions (the Ashʿarites) have argued from this verse that it is not obligatory upon God to safeguard the interests of the servant in his religion or in his worldly life. The argument is that Iblis requested a long period of respite, and God granted him respite. Then He made clear that he requested it only in order to mislead creatures, to lead them astray and to cast whisperings into their hearts. God, exalted, knew that most creatures would obey him and accept his whispering, as He said: ﴿And Iblis did indeed verify his assumption about them, so they followed him, except a party of the believers﴾ (Saba': 20). Thus it is established that granting Iblis respite and allowing him this long period entails the occurrence of great corruptions and great disbelief. Had God been caring for the interests of His servants, He would have refrained from granting him respite and from enabling him to do these corruptions. Since He granted him respite and reprieve, we know that nothing at all of safeguarding interests is obligatory upon Him. What strengthens this is that God sent the prophets as callers to the creatures, and He knew from Iblis's condition that he calls only to disbelief and error. Then God caused the prophets, who are the callers of creatures, to die, and left alive Iblis and the rest of the devils, who call creatures to disbelief and falsehood. Whoever wished the interests of the servants would have refrained from doing that.

The Muʿtazilites said: Our shaykhs have differed on this question. Al-Jubbaʾi said: The state does not differ by reason of his existence or non-existence, and no one is led astray by his speech except one who, were we to assume Iblis's non-existence, would also go astray. The evidence for this is God's words: ﴿You cannot lead astray [anyone] except one who is destined for the Blazing Fire﴾ (al-Saffat: 162–163). Also, if anyone were led astray by him, his remaining would be a corruption.

Abu Hashim said: It is possible that a people are led astray by him, and his creation is like the creation of an increase in desire. This increase in desire does not necessitate committing an ugly act, but refraining from it becomes harder, and because of that increase in hardship, an increase in reward is obtained. Likewise here, through Iblis's continuance, refraining from ugly acts becomes stronger and harder, but it does not reach the point of compulsion and coercion.

The reply: As for the statement of Abu ʿAli, it is weak, because the devil must adorn ugly deeds in the heart of the disbeliever and make them appealing to him, and remind him of the kinds of pleasures and good things in those ugly deeds. It is well known that a person's state, when this reminding and adorning occurs, is not equal to his state when this reminding and adorning is absent. The evidence for this is custom: when a person has companions who encourage him toward a matter, make it appealing in his eyes, facilitate the way to reach it, and persistently call him to it, his disposition to undertake that act is not like his disposition when this reminding, beautifying and adorning does not exist. Knowledge of this is necessary. As for the statement of Abu Hashim, it is also weak, because when this reminding and adorning becomes present for a person to undertake that ugly act, that is striving to throw him into corruption. And what he mentioned about the creation of an increase in desire is another proof for us that God, exalted, does not safeguard the interest. How can he use it as an argument? What best establishes it is that because of that increase in desire, a person falls into disbelief and the punishment of eternity; and if he refrains from that desire, the most that happens is that his reward from God increases because of the increase in that hardship. The occurrence of this increase in reward is something not needed at all, whereas averting eternal punishment is among the greatest of needs. Had the God of the worlds been caring for the interests of the servants, it would be impossible for Him to neglect the most important, most perfect and greatest matter in order to seek an increase that is neither needed nor necessary. Thus the corruption of these doctrines is established, and it is established that nothing at all is obligatory upon God, exalted. And God knows best what is correct.

Regarding His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them, and from their right and from their left; and You will not find most of them grateful.﴾ On this there are several issues.

**The first issue:** Concerning the mention of these four directions there are two views.

**The first view:** Each of them is specific to a particular kind of harm to the religion. Those who hold this view have given several explanations.

One of them: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾ means that I will make them doubt the soundness of the resurrection and the Last Day, ﴿and from behind them﴾ means that I will suggest to them that the world is eternal and without beginning.

The second: ﴿Then I will surely come to them from before them﴾ means that I will make them lax in desiring the felicities of the Hereafter, ﴿and from behind them﴾ means that I will strengthen their desire for the pleasures of this world and its good things, and make them appear attractive in their eyes. On these two explanations, what is meant by ﴿before them﴾ is the Hereafter, because they are heading towards it and will reach it, so it is before them; and when the Hereafter is before them, the world is behind them, because they leave it behind.

The third, which is the view of al-Hakim and al-Suddi: ﴿from before them﴾ means the world, and ﴿from behind them﴾ means the Hereafter. We have explained ﴿before them﴾ as the world because it is before a person, who strives in it and sees it, whereas the Hereafter comes after that.

The fourth: ﴿from before them﴾ refers to denying the prophets and messengers who are present, and ﴿from behind them﴾ refers to denying those prophets and messengers who came before.

* * *

As for His words, ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾, there are several explanations:

One: ﴿and from their right﴾ refers to disbelief and innovation (bid'ah), and ﴿and from their left﴾ refers to various kinds of sins.

The second: ﴿and from their right﴾ refers to turning them away from the truth, and ﴿and from their left﴾ refers to encouraging them towards falsehood.

The third: ﴿and from their right﴾ means that I will make them lax regarding good deeds, and ﴿and from their left﴾ means that I will strengthen their motives towards evil deeds. Ibn al-Anbari said: the statement of those who say that "the right" is a metaphor for good deeds and "the left" a metaphor for evil deeds is a good statement, because the Arabs say: "Place me on your right and do not place me on your left," meaning: "Place me among those who are brought forward in your sight and do not place me among those who are put back." Abu 'Ubayd narrated from al-Asma'i that it is said: "He is with us on the right," i.e., in a good position; and when his position is bad, one says: "You are with me on the left." This is a summary of what the exegetes have mentioned in explaining these four directions.

As for the wise men of Islam (hukama' al-Islam, i.e., the philosophers), they have mentioned other explanations regarding them:

The first, which is the strongest and most noble, is that in the body there are four powers, which are the cause of the strengths of spiritual felicities:

The first of them is the imaginative faculty (al-quwwah al-khayaliyyah), in which the likenesses of sensible things and their images are gathered. It is located in the front chamber of the brain, and images of sensible things reach it from its front; and to this refers His words: ﴿from before them﴾.

The second power is the estimative faculty (al-quwwah al-wahmiyyah), which judges, regarding non-sensible things, by judgments appropriate to sensible things. It is located in the rear chamber of the brain, and to it refers His words: ﴿and from behind them﴾.

The third power is appetite (al-shahwah), which is located in the liver, and the liver is on the right side of the body.

The fourth power is anger (al-ghadab), which is located in the left chamber of the heart. These four powers are the ones from which states arise that cause the loss of spiritual felicities. As long as the external devils do not seek help from any of these four powers, they cannot cast whisperings; this is the reason for specifying these four directions, and it is a true and noble explanation.

The second: His words ﴿I will surely come to them from before them﴾ mean doubts based on anthropomorphism (tashbih), either regarding the essence and attributes, like the doubts of the mujassimah (those who literally corporealise God), or regarding the actions, like the doubts of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) concerning God's justice, promise and threat, and the beautifying and the ugliness of acts. ﴿And from behind them﴾ means doubts arising from negation (ta'til, i.e., denying God's attributes). We have made His words ﴿from before them﴾ refer to the doubts of anthropomorphism because a person observes these corporeal things and their states, so they are present before him, and he believes that the unseen must be like this seen thing. We have made His words ﴿from behind them﴾ a metaphor for negation (ta'til), because anthropomorphism is the very same as negation; and since we made ﴿from before them﴾ a metaphor for anthropomorphism, we must make ﴿from behind them﴾ a metaphor for negation. As for His words ﴿and from their right﴾, they mean encouraging them to abandon the commands, and ﴿and from their left﴾ means encouraging them to commit the prohibited acts.

The third: It is reported from Shaqiq, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "Not a morning passes but that Satan comes to me from the four directions: from before me and behind me, and from my right and from my left. As for from before me, he says: 'Do not fear, for Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.' So I recite: ﴿And indeed, I am Forgiving to whoever repents and believes and does righteousness﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:82). As for from behind me, he frightens me that my children will fall into poverty, so I recite: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that upon Allah is its provision﴾ (Hud 11:6). As for from my right, he comes to me from the direction of praise, so I recite: ﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous﴾ (al-A'raf 7:128). As for from my left, he comes to me from the direction of desires, so I recite: ﴿And a barrier will be placed between them and what they desire﴾ (Saba' 34:54)."

**The second view:** In this verse, He, exalted, relates the statement of Satan mentioning these four directions, and the purpose of it is that he exaggerates in casting whisperings and does not fall short in any of the possible directions at all. The sense of the verse is: "Then I will surely come to them from all possible directions, by all possible considerations."

It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Satan sat in wait for the son of Adam on the path of Islam, and said to him: 'Will you abandon the religion of your fathers?' He disobeyed him and embraced Islam. Then he sat in wait for him on the path of emigration (hijrah), and said to him: 'Will you abandon your homeland and become a stranger?' He disobeyed him and emigrated. Then he sat in wait for him on the path of jihad, and said to him: 'Will you fight and be killed, and your property be divided, and your wife be married off?' He disobeyed him and fought." This report indicates that Satan does not leave any direction of whispering without casting it into the heart.

If it is said: why did He not mention "from above them and from beneath them" along with the four directions?

We say: As for the reality, we have mentioned that the powers from which arise what causes the loss of spiritual felicities are located in these four sides of the body. As for the outward sense: it is narrated that when Satan said these words, the hearts of the angels were moved with compassion for the human beings. They said: "O our God, how can a human being be saved from Satan, given that he dominates him from these four directions?" So Allah, exalted, revealed to them that two directions remain for the human being: above and below. When he raises his hands upward in supplication in humility, or places his forehead upon the earth in submission, I shall forgive him the sin of seventy years. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The second issue:** He said ﴿from before them and from behind them﴾, mentioning these two directions with the word (min, "from"). Then He said ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾, mentioning these two directions with the word (ʿan, "from/away from"). There must be a benefit in this distinction. We say: when someone says "he sat on his right" (jalasa ʿan yamīnih), it means that he sat apart from the companion on the right, not adjoining him. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿on the right and on the left, a companion sits﴾ (Qaf 50:17), so He clarified that two angels are present on these two sides, while no two angels are present in front or behind. Satan keeps away from the angel. For this reason He specified the right and the left with the word (ʿan), because it indicates distance and separation. Also, we have mentioned that what is meant by ﴿from before them and from behind them﴾ is imagination and estimation, and the harm arising from them is the acquisition of false beliefs, which is disbelief. What is meant by ﴿and from their right and from their left﴾ is appetite and anger, and the harm arising from them is the performance of appetitive and angry acts, which is disobedience. There is no doubt that the harm resulting from disbelief is permanent, because its punishment is everlasting. As for the harm resulting from disobedience, it is lighter, because its punishment is finite. For this reason He specified these two categories with the word (ʿan), as an indication that these two categories are more connected and continuous than the first category. And Allah knows best His intention.

**The third issue:** The judge (al-Qadi) said: this statement from Iblis is like evidence against what is said, that he enters the body of the son of Adam and mixes with it, because if that were possible, he would have been more entitled to mention it in the context of exaggeration.

Then He, exalted, said, relating from Iblis, that he said: ﴿and You will not find most of them grateful.﴾ There is a question here: this is a matter of the unseen, so how did Iblis know it? For this reason the scholars differed about it. Some said: he had seen it in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), so he said it with certainty and conviction. Others said: he said it on the basis of conjecture, because he was determined to exaggerate in adorning desires and beautifying good things, and he knew that these are things people are inclined towards; so it became his conjecture that they would accept his words about them in most cases and generally. This view is confirmed by His statement: ﴿And Iblis had already confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a group of believers﴾ (Saba' 34:20). It is strange that Iblis said to the Truth, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿and You will not find most of them grateful﴾, and the Truth replied with what corresponds to it: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾ (Saba' 34:13).

There is another explanation. It is that the soul has nineteen powers, all of which call the soul to corporeal pleasures and appetitive good things. Five of them are the outward senses, five others are the inward senses, two are appetite and anger, and seven are the hidden faculties, namely: the attractive (jadhibah), the retentive (masikah), the digestive (hadimah), the expulsive (dafi'ah), the nutritive (ghadhiyah), the growth-promoting (namiyah), and the generative (muwallidah). Their total is nineteen, and all of them call the soul to the world of the body and encourage it to seek bodily pleasures. As for the intellect, it is a single power, and it is the one that calls the soul to worship Allah, exalted, and to seek spiritual felicities. There is no doubt that the domination of nineteen powers is more complete than the domination of a single power. Especially since those nineteen powers are strong from the beginning of creation, while the intellect is very weak; and after their strength, it is difficult to make them weak and subordinate. Since this is so, it is necessary to conclude that most creatures will be seeking these bodily pleasures and turning away from knowing the Truth and loving it. For this reason He said: ﴿and You will not find most of them grateful.﴾ And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 18:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Go forth from it, reproached and expelled. Whoever of them follows you – I will surely fill Hell with you all.﴾

Page 37
Know that when Iblis promised to cause the corruption he had mentioned, Allah, Exalted is He, addressed him with words indicating rebuke and humiliation, and said: (Go forth from it) from the Garden, or from the heavens, (mad'uman) reproached. Al-Layth said: "I reproached the man, so he is mad'um, meaning despised; al-dhamm (reproach) is contempt." Al-Farra' said: "I reproached him when I found fault with him; they say in the proverb, 'The beautiful woman never lacks reproach.'" Ibn al-Anbari said: al-mad'um is al-madhum (the blamed). Ibn Qutaybah said: mad'uman: blamed with the most eloquent blame. Umayya said:

And the Lord of the servants said to Iblis: "Go forth, banished, cursed, reproached."

His saying: (madhuran) (expelled). Al-dahr in the language means expulsion and distancing. It is said: "He dahara him, dahran and duhuran," when he expelled him and distanced him. From this is His saying: ﴿And they are pelted from every side﴾ ﴿with expulsion (duhuran)﴾. Umayya said:

And by His permission they all prostrated to Adam, except a cursed, sinful, expelled one.

His saying: ﴿Whoever of them follows you﴾: the lam in it is the lam of oath, and its answer is His saying: (I will surely fill). The author of al-Kashshaf said: Isma transmitted from Asim: (li-man tabi'aka) with a kasra on the lam, meaning "for whoever of them follows you, this threat is for them," and it is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell with you all﴾. It was also said that (la-amla'anna) is in the position of the subject, and (wa-li-man tabi'aka) is its predicate. Abu Bakr ibn al-Anbari said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿whoever of them follows you﴾ refers to the children of Adam, because when He said ﴿And We certainly created you﴾, He was addressing the children of Adam, so the pronoun returned to them.

The judge (al-Qadi) said: This verse indicates that the follower and the one followed are both meant in that Hell is filled with them. Then, since the disbeliever follows him, the sinner likewise follows him, so it is necessary to affirm with certainty that the sinner enters the Fire. Its answer: what is mentioned in the verse is that He, Exalted is He, fills Hell with those who follow Him, and the verse does not say that everyone who follows him enters Hell, so this argument falls. We say: this verse indicates that all the people of innovations and misguidances enter Hell, because all of them are followers of Iblis. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 19:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers.﴾

Know that this verse comprises several issues:

The first: His saying "dwell" (uskun) is either a command of worship (amr ta'abbud) or a command of permission and release (amr ibahah wa-itlaq), since there is no hardship in it. Therefore, obligation (taklif) is not attached to it.

The second: the wife of Adam is Hawwa' (Eve), and we must mention how God created Hawwa'.

The third: that Garden was either the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld), or a garden of the gardens of heaven, or a garden of the gardens of the earth.

The fourth: His saying ﴿eat﴾ is a command of permission, not a command of obligation.

The fifth: His saying ﴿do not approach﴾ is either a prohibition of disapproval (nahy tanzih) or a prohibition of forbiddance (nahy tahrim).

The sixth: His saying ﴿this tree﴾ means one tree, either by individual or by kind.

The seventh: that tree, whichever tree it was.

The eighth: whether that sin was minor or major.

The ninth: what is meant by His saying ﴿or you will be among the wrongdoers﴾, and whether being a wrongdoer by this approach necessarily entails falling under His saying: ﴿Surely the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers﴾ (Hud: 18).

The tenth: whether this event occurred before the prophethood of Adam, peace be upon him, or after it. These ten issues have already been explained and established in Surat al-Baqarah, so we will not repeat them. What remains for us from this verse is one point,

page 38
namely that He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And eat from it freely﴾ (al-Baqarah: 35) with the particle wa (and), while here He said: (fa-kula) with the particle fa (so). What is the reason for this?

Its answer is in two respects:

The first: the particle wa indicates absolute joining (al-jam' al-mutlaq), while the particle fa indicates joining in the manner of sequence (al-ta'qib). So what is understood from fa is a kind that falls under what is understood from wa, and there is no contradiction between a species and a genus. Thus, in Surat al-Baqarah He mentioned the genus, and in Surat al-A'raf He mentioned the species.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 20:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them to reveal to them that which was concealed from them of their private parts, and he said, "Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels or become of the eternal."﴾ ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you a sincere advisor."﴾ ﴿So he made them fall through deception. And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to fasten over themselves from the leaves of Paradise. And their Lord called to them, "Did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that indeed Satan is to you a clear enemy?"﴾

It is said: waswasa (وسوس) means that he spoke a hidden speech which he repeated. From this, the sound of ornaments is called waswas. It is an intransitive verb, like our saying walwalat al-mar'a (the woman ululated) and wa'wa'a al-dhi'b (the wolf howled). A man is musawwis with a kasra on the waw, and one does not say musawwas with a fatha; rather, one says musawwas lahu and musawwas ilayhi. The one to whom the whisper is cast is the musawwas ilayhi. The meaning of waswasa lahu is that he performed the whispering for his sake, and waswasa ilayhi is that he cast it to him. Here there are questions:

The first question: How did he whisper to him when Adam was in the Garden and Iblis had been expelled from it?

The answer: al-Hasan said: he used to whisper from the earth to the sky and to the Garden by the upward power which Allah the Exalted had given him. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: rather, Adam and Iblis were both in the Garden, because this Garden was one of the gardens of the earth. As for what some people say, that Iblis entered into the belly of the serpent and the serpent entered the Garden, that story is weak and well known. Others said: Adam and Hawwa' may have approached the gate of the Garden, while Iblis was standing outside the Garden at its gate, so one of them would approach the other and the whispering would take place there.

The second question: Adam, peace be upon him, knew the enmity between himself and Iblis, so how did he accept his words?

The answer: It is not far-fetched to say that Iblis met Adam many times and encouraged him to eat from the tree by many means. Because of the persistence and continuity of this deception, his speech affected Adam, peace be upon him.

Page 39
The third question: Why did he say: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them﴾?
The answer: The meaning of waswasa lahu is that he performed the whispering for his sake, and Allah knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿to reveal to them﴾, there are two opinions regarding this lam:

One of them: it is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas: 8). This is because Satan did not intend by the whispering the exposure of their private parts, and he did not know that if they ate from the tree their private parts would become apparent; rather, his purpose was only to bring them to disobedience.

The second: It is also not far-fetched to say that it is the lam of purpose (lam al-gharad). Then there are two aspects to it:

One of them: that the exposure of the private part be taken as a metaphor for the loss of dignity and the cessation of honor. The meaning is that his aim in casting that whisper to Adam was the removal of his dignity and the loss of his rank.

The second: Perhaps he saw in the Preserved Tablet, or heard from some of the angels, that if he ate from the tree his private part would be exposed, and that indicates the utmost harm and the loss of dignity, so he whispered to him in order to achieve this aim.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾, there are discussions concerning it:

The first discussion: má wūriya (what was concealed) is derived from al-muwara (concealment). It is said: wāraytuhu, meaning I covered him. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿He conceals the private part of his brother﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Ali when he informed him of his father's death: "Go and bury him."

The second discussion: al-sawà'a is the private part of the man and the woman, because its exposure distresses (yasu'u) a person. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: It was as if they had been clothed with a garment that covered their private parts, and when they disobeyed, that garment was removed from them. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾.

The third discussion: This verse indicates that uncovering the private part is among the reprehensible things, and that it has never ceased to be abhorrent in natures and repugnant to intellects. His saying: ﴿Your Lord has only forbidden you this tree, lest you become angels or become of the eternal﴾ (al-A'raf: 20) may be a statement which Iblis mentioned in a way that addressed Adam and Hawwa', and it may also be a whisper which he cast into their hearts. Both possibilities are transmitted, but the more prevalent view is that it was by way of direct address, as is evident from His saying: ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you a sincere advisor."﴾ The meaning of the speech is that Iblis said to them in the whispering: "Unless you become two angels," intending: that you become in the rank of the angels if you eat from it, or that you become of the eternal if you eat. He encouraged them by making them imagine that whoever eats from it becomes like that, and that Allah only forbade them from it so that they would not become like the angels nor live forever. Here there are questions:

The first question: How did Iblis make Adam hope to become an angel by eating from the tree, when he had witnessed the angels humbly prostrating to him, acknowledging his excellence? The answer has several aspects:

The first: This meaning is one of the things which indicates that the angels who prostrated to Adam were the angels of the earth. As for the angels of the heavens, the dwellers of the Throne and the Footstool, and the near angels, they did not prostrate to Adam at all; had they prostrated to him, this enticement would have been corrupt and defective.

Second: al-Wahidi transmitted from some people that he said: Adam knew that the angels do not die until the Day of Resurrection, but he did not know this for himself, so Iblis presented to him that he would become like an angel in endurance. I say: this answer is weak, because on this assumption the thing sought from the angels is immortality, and then there would be no difference between His saying: ﴿unless you become two angels﴾ and His saying: ﴿or become of the eternal﴾.

Page 40
The second aspect: al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas used to read (malikayn, with a kasra on the lam, meaning "two kings") and would say: they did not hope to become two angels, but they aspired to become two kings, and the accursed one came to them from the direction of kingship. This is supported by His saying: ﴿Shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?﴾ (Ta-Ha: 120). I say: this answer is also weak, and its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: Suppose the answer is obtained by this reading: does Ibn 'Abbas then say that the well-known reading is false, or does he not say that? The first is invalid, because that reading is a mutawatir reading, so how could it be challenged?

As for the second: on this assumption the difficulty remains, because on that reading the enticement would have been that by means of that eating they would become among the angels, and then the question returns.

The second aspect: He, exalted is He, made the prostration of the angels and of creation to him a result of his dwelling in the Garden, and of his eating from it freely as he wished and willed; and there is no greater increase in dominion beyond this rank.

The second question: Does this verse indicate that the rank of the angels is more complete and more excellent than the rank of prophethood?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: If we say that this event occurred before prophethood, it does not indicate that, and because when Adam sought to reach the rank of the angels, he was not among the prophets; on this assumption the argument falls away.

The second: If we take the "an" (that) to mean that this event occurred during the time of prophethood, then perhaps Adam, peace be upon him, desired to become one of the angels in power, strength and might, or in the nature of his essence by becoming a luminous substance, and in becoming one of the dwellers of the Throne and the Footstool; on this assumption the argument falls away.

The third question: It is reported that 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd said to al-Hasan concerning His saying: ﴿unless you become two angels or become of the eternal﴾ and concerning His saying: "and he swore to them." 'Amr said: I said to al-Hasan: Then did they believe him in that? Al-Hasan said: Allah forbid! If they had believed him, they would have been among the disbelievers. The point of the question is: how does this declaration of disbelief follow, on the assumption that they believed Iblis in that statement?

The answer: They mentioned in establishing that declaration of disbelief that if he had believed Iblis regarding eternity, that would necessitate denying the resurrection and the Last Day, and that is disbelief. One may say: We do not grant that it follows from that belief that disbelief results? Its explanation is from two aspects:

The first: The word "khulud" is to be understood as long remaining, not as perpetuity, and on this aspect what they mentioned is refuted.

The second aspect: Suppose "khulud" is explained as perpetuity; still, we do not grant that believing in perpetuity necessitates disbelief. Its explanation is that the knowledge of whether Allah causes this accountable being to die or does not cause him to die is a knowledge which can only be obtained through the evidence of revelation. Perhaps Allah, the Exalted, had not made clear at the time of Adam, peace be upon him, that He causes creation to die; and since that revelatory evidence did not yet exist, Adam, peace be upon him, considered the continuation of endurance possible, and for this reason he desired it. On this assumption, the declaration of disbelief does not follow.

The fourth question: It has been established from what preceded that if Adam and Hawwa' had believed Iblis in what he said, their declaration of disbelief would not follow. Do they then say that they believed him in it with certainty? And if certainty was not achieved, do they say that they supposed the matter was as he said? Or do they deny this supposition as well?

Page 41
The answer: The verifying scholars denied that this belief occurred, either with certainty or with supposition. Rather, the correct view is that they only proceeded to eat due to the dominance of desire, not that they believed him, either by knowledge or by supposition, just as we find ourselves, when desire is present, proceeding to an act when another has made attractive to us what we desire, even though we do not believe that the matter is as he said.

The fifth question: His saying: ﴿unless you become two angels or become of the eternal﴾ — did this encouragement and enticement occur in both matters together, or in one of them?

The answer: Some said: the encouragement was in both matters together, because it was introduced as encouragement. It was also said: rather, it is on its apparent sense, by way of alternatives (al-takhyir).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 21–22:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And he swore to them both, "Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisors."﴾ That is, he swore to them both, "Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisors."

If it is asked: al-Muqasamah (mutual swearing) means that you swear to your companion and he swears to you. One says: qasamtu fulanan, meaning ḥālaftuhu (I swore an oath to him), and taqasama means taḥālafa (they swore oaths to one another). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Swear to one another by Allah, "We will surely attack him and his family by night."﴾ (al-Naml: 49).

We say: In this there are several interpretations.

The first: the meaning is that he said, "I swear to you both that I am to you both among the sincere advisors," and they said to him, "Do you swear by Allah that you are among the sincere advisors?" So he made that a mutual swearing between them.

The second: he swore to them both by the sincere advice, and they both swore to him by accepting it.

The third: he gave the oath of Iblis the form of the mufā'alah (the reciprocal verbal pattern), because he exerted himself in it as one who swears in return.

Having understood this, we say: Qatadah said: "He swore to them both by Allah until he deceived them, and a believer in Allah may be deceived." His saying ﴿Indeed, I am to you both among the sincere advisors﴾ means that Iblis said: "I was created before you both, and I know many matters of benefit and harm that you do not know, so obey my word and I will guide you."

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he brought them down by deception.﴾ Abu Mansur al-Azhari mentioned two roots for this word:

One of them: its origin is a thirsty man who lowers his legs into a well to take water, but finds no water in it. So the word tadliyah (lowering) was used for hoping for something that has no benefit. It is said: dallāhu, when he made him hope (for something).

The second: ﴿fa-dallāhumā bi-ghurūr﴾ means that Iblis emboldened them to eat from the tree through deception. The root of it is dallalahumā, from al-dall (coquetry), and al-dāllah, which is boldness.

Having understood this, we say: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ means he deceived them with the oath, and Adam thought that no one swears by Allah falsely. It is also reported from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that whenever he saw in his slave obedience and good prayer, he would free him, so his slaves would do that seeking manumission. It was said to him, "They are deceiving you," and he said, "Whoever deceives us by Allah, we are deceived by him."

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they tasted the tree﴾ and this indicates that they took a small amount intending to know its taste. Had He not mentioned in another verse that they both ate from it, what is in this verse would not indicate eating, because one who tastes may be a taster without eating.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿Their private parts became apparent to them﴾ meaning their nakedness became visible, and the light departed from them. ﴿And they began to join over themselves⟩ (yakhṣifān). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ṭafiqa is "began to do the act"; (yakhṣifān) means they place one leaf upon another leaf. From this it is said of the one who mends a sandal: khaṣṣāf. In this there is evidence that exposing the nakedness is ugly from the time of Adam. Do you not see that they hastened to cover themselves because the ugliness of exposing the nakedness was established in their intellects? ﴿And their Lord called out to them﴾. 'Ata' said: "It reached me that Allah called out to them, 'Did you flee from Me, O Adam?' He said, 'Rather, out of shame before You, O Lord. I did not think that anyone would swear by Your name falsely.' Then his Lord called to him, 'Did I not create you with My own hands? Did I not breathe into you of My spirit? Did I not command My angels to prostrate to you? Did I not settle you in My Garden, in My neighborhood?'"

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And did I not forbid you from that tree and tell you that Satan is to you both a manifest enemy?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: he made the enmity clear when he refused to prostrate, and said: ﴿I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ (al-A'raf: 16).

Know that this verse is explained in Surat al-Baqarah. There we mentioned that this verse indicates that a great sin proceeded from Adam (عليه السلام). However, we say: this sin proceeded from him before prophethood (النُّبُوَّة, nubuwwah). On this assumption, the question is removed.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قالَ اهْبِطُوا بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ ولَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ ومَتاعٌ إلى حِينٍ﴾ ﴿قالَ فِيها تَحْيَوْنَ وفِيها تَمُوتُونَ ومِنها تُخْرَجُونَ﴾

Know that what has been mentioned above refers to Adam, Hawwa' (Eve), and Iblis. Given this, His saying "Go down" (اهْبِطُوا) must include these three. ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ means: enmity is established between the jinn and the humans and never ceases at all. As for His saying "in it you will live" (فِيها تَحْيَوْنَ), the pronoun refers to the earth in His saying ﴿and for you on the earth﴾. The meaning is: you will live on the earth, in it you will die, and from it you will be brought out to the resurrection (البَعْث) and the Day of Resurrection (القِيامَة).

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read (تَخْرُجُونَ) with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the rā', and likewise in al-Rūm, al-Zukhruf and al-Jāthiyah. Ibn 'Āmir read it here and in al-Zukhruf with a fatḥah on the tā', and in al-Rūm and al-Jāthiyah with a ḍammah on the tā'. All the others read it with a ḍammah on the tā' in all of these places.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿يابَنِي آدَمَ قَدْ أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْكم لِباسًا يُوارِي سَوْآتِكم ورِيشًا ولِباسُ التَّقْوى ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ ذَلِكَ مِن آياتِ اللَّهِ لَعَلَّهم يَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾

There are two aspects to the arrangement (نَظْم, naẓm) of this verse:

The first aspect: When He explained that He commanded Adam and Hawwa' to descend to the earth, and made the earth a settlement for them, He then explained that He sent down everything they need in religion and in worldly life, and among it is the clothing that is needed in both religion and worldly life.

[Page 43]

The second aspect: When He mentioned the incident of Adam, in which the private parts were exposed and he began covering them with leaves, He followed it by explaining that He created clothing for creation so that they might cover their private parts with it. Through this He drew attention to the great favour upon creation, because He made them able to conceal themselves.

If it is asked: What is the meaning of sending down clothing?

We say: He sent down rain, and through rain the things from which clothing is obtained come into being. So it is as if He had sent down the clothing itself. The clarification of the matter is that the things that come into being on the earth, since they are dependent upon the matters that descend from the sky, it is as if He had sent them down from the sky. From this is His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ (al-Zumar: 6), and His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which there is great might﴾ (al-Ḥadīd: 25).

As for His saying ﴿and plumage (ریشا)﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Rīsh (الرِّيش) is clothing of adornment. It is borrowed from the plumage of birds, because it is their clothing and their adornment. That is, He sent down to you two garments: a garment that covers your private parts, and a garment that adorns you. This is because adornment is a legitimate purpose, as He said: ﴿that you may ride them and as adornment﴾ (al-Naḥl: 8), and He said: ﴿and in them there is beauty for you﴾ (al-Naḥl: 6).

The second discussion: A non-widely-known transmission from 'Āṣim reads (ورِياشًا, wa-riyāshan), and this is also transmitted from 'Uthmān (may Allah be pleased with him). The others read (ورِيشًا, wa-rīshan). Scholars differed over the distinction between al-rīsh and al-riyāsh. It was said: riyāsh is the plural of rīsh, like dhiyāb and dhayb, qidāḥ and qidḥ, shi'āb and shi'b. It was also said: they are one and the same, like libās and libs, and jilāl and jill. Tha'lab reported from Ibn al-A'rābī who said: everything by which a person lives, whether goods, wealth or food, is rīsh and riyāsh. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: riyāsh is specific to clothing and household goods, while rīsh may be applied to all kinds of wealth.

His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ has two discussions:

The first discussion: Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir and al-Kisā'ī read (ولِباسَ, wa-libāsa) in the accusative, coordinated with His saying (لِباسًا, libāsan), and the governing element for it is (أنْزَلْنا, anzalnā). On this reading, His saying (ذَلِكَ, dhālika) is the subject (مُبْتَدَأ, mubtada'), and His saying (خَيْرٌ, khayrun) is its predicate (خَبَر, khabar). The others read it in the nominative. On this reading, His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ is the subject, and His saying (ذَلِكَ) is an adjective (صِفَة, ṣifah), or an apposition (بَدَل, badal), or an explicative apposition (عَطْف بَيان, 'aṭf bayān), and His saying (خَيْرٌ) is the predicate of ﴿the clothing of righteousness﴾. The meaning of our saying "adjective" is that (ذَلِكَ) points to the clothing, as if it were said: "and the clothing of righteousness, that being referred to, is best."

The second discussion: They differed over the interpretation of His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾. The governing principle here is that some took it to refer to the garment itself, and others took it to refer to something other than that.

As for the first view, there are several opinions:

One: The meaning is that the clothing which Allah sent down to cover your private parts is the clothing of righteousness. On this assumption, the clothing of righteousness is the first clothing, and Allah only repeated it in order to inform about it that it is best, because a group of the people of ignorance (الجاهِلِيَّة) used to worship by going naked and removing their clothes while circumambulating the House. So this in the repetition goes in the manner of someone saying: "I have made you know truthfulness in the chapters of righteousness, and truthfulness is better for you than other than it." So he repeats the mention of truthfulness in order to inform about it in this sense.

Two: The meaning of the clothing of righteousness is the armour that is worn, such as coats of mail, tunics and helmets, and other things by which one guards oneself in wars.

Three: The meaning of the clothing of righteousness is the garments prepared for the purpose of performing the prayers.

The second view: That His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ should be taken as figurative (مَجاز, majāz). Then they differed. Qatādah, al-Suddī and Ibn Juraij said: the clothing of righteousness is faith (الإيمان). Ibn 'Abbās said: the clothing of righteousness is righteous deeds. It was said: it is a good bearing (السَّمْت الحَسَن). It was said: it is chastity (العَفاف) and monotheism (التَّوْحِيد), because the believer's private parts are not exposed even if he is naked of clothes, whereas the sinner's private parts are always exposed even if he is clothed. Ma'bad said: it is modesty (الحَياء). It was said: it is what appears on a person of tranquillity, humility and righteous deeds. We have taken the word "clothing" in these figurative senses only because the clothing that brings about righteousness is nothing but these things.

As for His saying ﴿that is best﴾, Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī said: the meaning of the verse is that the clothing of righteousness is better for its wearer if he adopts it, and closer to him to Allah the Exalted than the clothing and finery that He created, by which one adorns oneself. He said: the clothing is attributed to righteousness just as it is attributed to hunger in His saying: ﴿so Allah made them taste the clothing of hunger and fear﴾ (al-Naḥl: 112). And His saying ﴿that is among the signs of Allah﴾ means: among the signs of Allah that point to His grace and mercy upon His servants, namely the sending down of clothing upon them, ﴿that they may be reminded﴾, so that they recognise the great blessing in it.

And His saying ﴿that is among the signs of Allah﴾ means: among the signs of Allah that point to His grace and mercy upon His servants, namely the sending down of clothing upon them, ﴿that they may be reminded﴾, so that they recognise the great blessing in it.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قالا رَبَّنا ظَلَمْنا أنْفُسَنا وإنْ لَمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنا وتَرْحَمْنا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ الخاسِرِينَ﴾

Know that this verse is explained in Surat al-Baqarah. There we mentioned that this verse indicates that a great sin proceeded from Adam (عليه السلام). However, we say: this sin proceeded from him before prophethood (النُّبُوَّة, nubuwwah). On this assumption, the question is removed.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قالَ اهْبِطُوا بَعْضُكم لِبَعْضٍ عَدُوٌّ ولَكم في الأرْضِ مُسْتَقَرٌّ ومَتاعٌ إلى حِينٍ﴾ ﴿قالَ فِيها تَحْيَوْنَ وفِيها تَمُوتُونَ ومِنها تُخْرَجُونَ﴾

Know that what has been mentioned above refers to Adam, Hawwa' (Eve), and Iblis. Given this, His saying "Go down" (اهْبِطُوا) must include these three. ﴿Some of you are enemies to others﴾ means: enmity is established between the jinn and the humans and never ceases at all. As for His saying "in it you will live" (فِيها تَحْيَوْنَ), the pronoun refers to the earth in His saying ﴿and for you on the earth﴾. The meaning is: you will live on the earth, in it you will die, and from it you will be brought out to the resurrection (البَعْث) and the Day of Resurrection (القِيامَة).

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read (تَخْرُجُونَ) with a fatḥah on the tā' and a ḍammah on the rā', and likewise in al-Rūm, al-Zukhruf and al-Jāthiyah. Ibn 'Āmir read it here and in al-Zukhruf with a fatḥah on the tā', and in al-Rūm and al-Jāthiyah with a ḍammah on the tā'. All the others read it with a ḍammah on the tā' in all of these places.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿يابَنِي آدَمَ قَدْ أنْزَلْنا عَلَيْكم لِباسًا يُوارِي سَوْآتِكم ورِيشًا ولِباسُ التَّقْوى ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ ذَلِكَ مِن آياتِ اللَّهِ لَعَلَّهم يَذَّكَّرُونَ﴾

There are two aspects to the arrangement (نَظْم, naẓm) of this verse:

The first aspect: When He explained that He commanded Adam and Hawwa' to descend to the earth, and made the earth a settlement for them, He then explained that He sent down everything they need in religion and in worldly life, and among it is the clothing that is needed in both religion and worldly life.

[Page 43]

The second aspect: When He mentioned the incident of Adam, in which the private parts were exposed and he began covering them with leaves, He followed it by explaining that He created clothing for creation so that they might cover their private parts with it. Through this He drew attention to the great favour upon creation, because He made them able to conceal themselves.

If it is asked: What is the meaning of sending down clothing?

We say: He sent down rain, and through rain the things from which clothing is obtained come into being. So it is as if He had sent down the clothing itself. The clarification of the matter is that the things that come into being on the earth, since they are dependent upon the matters that descend from the sky, it is as if He had sent them down from the sky. From this is His saying: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ (al-Zumar: 6), and His saying: ﴿And We sent down iron, in which there is great might﴾ (al-Ḥadīd: 25).

As for His saying ﴿and plumage (ریشا)﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: al-Rīsh (الرِّيش) is clothing of adornment. It is borrowed from the plumage of birds, because it is their clothing and their adornment. That is, He sent down to you two garments: a garment that covers your private parts, and a garment that adorns you. This is because adornment is a legitimate purpose, as He said: ﴿that you may ride them and as adornment﴾ (al-Naḥl: 8), and He said: ﴿and in them there is beauty for you﴾ (al-Naḥl: 6).

The second discussion: A non-widely-known transmission from 'Āṣim reads (ورِياشًا, wa-riyāshan), and this is also transmitted from 'Uthmān (may Allah be pleased with him). The others read (ورِيشًا, wa-rīshan). Scholars differed over the distinction between al-rīsh and al-riyāsh. It was said: riyāsh is the plural of rīsh, like dhiyāb and dhayb, qidāḥ and qidḥ, shi'āb and shi'b. It was also said: they are one and the same, like libās and libs, and jilāl and jill. Tha'lab reported from Ibn al-A'rābī who said: everything by which a person lives, whether goods, wealth or food, is rīsh and riyāsh. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: riyāsh is specific to clothing and household goods, while rīsh may be applied to all kinds of wealth.

His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ has two discussions:

The first discussion: Nāfi', Ibn 'Āmir and al-Kisā'ī read (ولِباسَ, wa-libāsa) in the accusative, coordinated with His saying (لِباسًا, libāsan), and the governing element for it is (أنْزَلْنا, anzalnā). On this reading, His saying (ذَلِكَ, dhālika) is the subject (مُبْتَدَأ, mubtada'), and His saying (خَيْرٌ, khayrun) is its predicate (خَبَر, khabar). The others read it in the nominative. On this reading, His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ is the subject, and His saying (ذَلِكَ) is an adjective (صِفَة, ṣifah), or an apposition (بَدَل, badal), or an explicative apposition (عَطْف بَيان, 'aṭf bayān), and His saying (خَيْرٌ) is the predicate of ﴿the clothing of righteousness﴾. The meaning of our saying "adjective" is that (ذَلِكَ) points to the clothing, as if it were said: "and the clothing of righteousness, that being referred to, is best."

The second discussion: They differed over the interpretation of His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾. The governing principle here is that some took it to refer to the garment itself, and others took it to refer to something other than that.

As for the first view, there are several opinions:

One: The meaning is that the clothing which Allah sent down to cover your private parts is the clothing of righteousness. On this assumption, the clothing of righteousness is the first clothing, and Allah only repeated it in order to inform about it that it is best, because a group of the people of ignorance (الجاهِلِيَّة) used to worship by going naked and removing their clothes while circumambulating the House. So this in the repetition goes in the manner of someone saying: "I have made you know truthfulness in the chapters of righteousness, and truthfulness is better for you than other than it." So he repeats the mention of truthfulness in order to inform about it in this sense.

Two: The meaning of the clothing of righteousness is the armour that is worn, such as coats of mail, tunics and helmets, and other things by which one guards oneself in wars.

Three: The meaning of the clothing of righteousness is the garments prepared for the purpose of performing the prayers.

The second view: That His saying ﴿and the clothing of righteousness﴾ should be taken as figurative (مَجاز, majāz). Then they differed. Qatādah, al-Suddī and Ibn Juraij said: the clothing of righteousness is faith (الإيمان). Ibn 'Abbās said: the clothing of righteousness is righteous deeds. It was said: it is a good bearing (السَّمْت الحَسَن). It was said: it is chastity (العَفاف) and monotheism (التَّوْحِيد), because the believer's private parts are not exposed even if he is naked of clothes, whereas the sinner's private parts are always exposed even if he is clothed. Ma'bad said: it is modesty (الحَياء). It was said: it is what appears on a person of tranquillity, humility and righteous deeds. We have taken the word "clothing" in these figurative senses only because the clothing that brings about righteousness is nothing but these things.
