**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 7, verse 27**

﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise, stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts. Indeed, he sees you, he and his soldiers, from where you do not see them. Indeed, We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe.﴾

Know that the purpose of mentioning the stories of the prophets (peace be upon them) is that a lesson may be drawn by whoever hears them. So when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the story of Adam and showed in it the severity of Satan's enmity toward Adam and his descendants, He followed it by warning the children of Adam against accepting Satan's whispering, saying: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from Paradise﴾. This is because when the effect of Satan's scheming, the subtlety of his whispering, and the intensity of his determination reached the point that he was able to cast Adam into the sin that caused his removal from Paradise, then his being able to bring about similar harms against the children of Adam is more likely. By this method, Allah, exalted is He, warned the children of Adam to guard against Satan's whispering, saying: ﴿let not Satan tempt you﴾. The consequence of this is that you would not enter Paradise as he tempted your parents, and the consequence of that was their departure from it. The original meaning of *fitnah* (temptation, trial) is placing gold in fire to separate it from impurities. Then in the Qur'an it is used in the sense of a trial (*mihnah*). Here there are two discussions.

**The first discussion:** Al-Ka'bi said: This verse is a proof against those who attribute the departure of Adam and Eve, and all forms of disobedience, to Satan, and this indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is free of them. It is said to him: Why do you say that the attribution of this act to Satan prevents its attribution to Allah, exalted is He? And why is it not permissible to say that, since He, exalted is He, created the power and the motive that necessitate that act, it is attributed to Allah, exalted is He? And since He has established His custom that He creates that motive after Satan adorns those acts and makes them appear good to that disbeliever, it is attributed to Satan.

**The second discussion:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that Allah, exalted is He, removed Adam and Eve from Paradise only as a punishment for them for that lapse. The apparent meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:30) indicates that He, exalted is He, created them for the succession (*khilafah*) on earth and sent them down from Paradise to earth for this purpose. So how can the two be reconciled?

[p. 45]

Its answer: It may be said that it was for the combination of both matters, and Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿He strips them of their clothing to show them their private parts﴾, and concerning this there are discussions.

**The first discussion:** ﴿He strips them of their clothing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject). That is, he brought them out while stripping off their clothing. The stripping of the clothing is attributed to Satan even though he did not personally carry it out, because it occurred through a cause from him. So it is ascribed to him, just as you say to someone who did that action through a cause, "Did you do this?", even if he did not directly perform it. Likewise, since the stripping of their clothing came about through Satan's whispering and deception, it was ascribed to him.

**The second discussion:** The *lam* in His saying ﴿to show them﴾ (*li-yurayahuma*) is the *lam* of consequence (*lam al-'aqibah*), as we mentioned in His saying ﴿to reveal to them﴾ (*li-yubdiya lahuma*). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Adam would not see Eve's private part, and Eve would not see Adam's private part.

**The third discussion:** They differed concerning the clothing that was stripped from them. Some said it was light, some said it was piety, and some said it was the clothing that is the garments of Paradise. This last view is closest to the truth, because the unqualified use of the word "clothing" requires it. The purpose of this statement is to emphasize the warning to the children of Adam, because when the effect of Satan's whispering upon Adam, despite his lofty rank, reached this extent, how then would the condition of ordinary creatures be? Then Allah, exalted is He, emphasized this warning by His saying: ﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his soldiers, from where you do not see them﴾. And concerning this there are discussions:

**The first discussion:** ﴿Indeed, he sees you﴾ means Iblis (Satan). ﴿He and his soldiers﴾: the pronoun was repeated so that the conjunction would be good, like His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:35).

**The second discussion:** Abu 'Ubaydah said, on the authority of Abu Zayd: *al-qabil* is a group of three or more from different peoples, and its plural is *qubul*. And *al-qabilah* is the sons of one father. Ibn Qutaybah said: *qabiluhu* means his companions and his army. Al-Layth said: ﴿he and his soldiers﴾ means he and whoever is of his offspring.

**The third discussion:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: They see humans because Allah, exalted is He, created perception in their eyes, while humans do not see them because Allah, exalted is He, did not create this perception in human eyes. The Mu'tazilah said: The reason humans do not see the jinn is the fineness and subtlety of the jinn's bodies. The reason the jinn see humans is the density of human bodies. As for some jinn seeing others, it is because Allah, exalted is He, strengthens and increases the ray of the jinn's sight. If Allah increased the strength of our sight, we would see them just as some of us see others. And if He made their bodies dense while our sight remained in this state, we would see them. According to this, humans' ability to see the jinn is, for the Mu'tazilah, contingent either upon increasing the density of the jinn's bodies or upon increasing the strength of human sight.

**The fourth discussion:** His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from where you do not see them﴾ indicates that humans do not see the jinn, because His saying ﴿from where you do not see them﴾ covers future times without specification. Some scholars said: If the jinn were able to change the forms of their selves into any form they wished and intended, then the trust in people's recognition would be lost. Perhaps this one I see, whom I judge to be my son or my wife, is a jinni who has made himself into the likeness of my son or my wife. According to this assumption, confidence in recognizing persons is eliminated. Also, if they were able to confuse people and remove their minds, while Allah has explained the severe enmity between them and humans, why do they not do that to most of mankind, and to the scholars, the virtuous, and the ascetics? For this enmity between them and the scholars and ascetics is greater and stronger. Since nothing of that has been found, it is established that they have no power over humans in any way whatsoever. This is confirmed by His saying: ﴿I had over you no authority except that I invited you and you responded to me﴾ (Ibrahim 14:22). Mujahid said: Iblis said: "We have been given four attributes: we see and are not seen, we emerge from beneath the earth, and our old man becomes a youth."

* * *

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾. Our companions have used this text as evidence that it is Allah, exalted is He, who empowered the accursed Satan over them until he misguided and led them astray. Al-Zajjaj said: This text is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have We not sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ (Maryam 19:83). The Qadi said: The meaning of His saying ﴿We have made the devils allies of those who do not believe﴾ is that We have judged that Satan is an ally of whoever does not believe. He said: The meaning of His saying ﴿We sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ (Maryam 19:83) is that We left between them and between the devils [no barrier], just as it is said of one who ties his dog at his house and does not prevent it from pouncing on the one who enters: "He sent his dog upon him."

The answer: When a speaker says, "So-and-so made this garment white or black," it is not understood from him that he judged it so; rather it is understood that the blackness or whiteness came to be in it. Likewise here, the word *ja'l* (making) must be interpreted as causing and effecting, not as mere judgment. Also, suppose He, exalted is He, did judge it so; still, opposing the judgment of Allah, exalted is He, would make Him a liar, and that is impossible. Whatever leads to an impossibility is itself impossible. So the servant's being able to act contrary to that must be impossible.

As for his statement that His saying ﴿We sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ means that We left between them and the disbelievers, it is also weak. Do you not see that the people of the marketplace harm one another and insult one another? Then if Zayd and 'Amr do not prevent one another [from harming each other], it is not said that he sent some of them upon others. Rather, the term "sending" is only truly applied when the empowering of some over others comes about through a cause from Him. So it is likewise here. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they commit an immorality, they say, "We found our fathers doing it, and Allah has commanded us to it." Say, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality. Do you say about Allah that which you do not know?"﴾

Know that among the people there are those who take fahisha (immorality) to refer to what they used to forbid of the bahira (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was released), the sa'iba (a camel set free for the gods), and other things. Among them are those who take it to mean that they used to circumambulate the House naked, men and women alike. The better view is to apply the general sense, and fahisha is an expression for every major sin, so that all the major sins fall within it.

Know also that the intended meaning is not that the people acknowledged these acts to be immoral and then claimed that Allah had commanded them. That is not something any sensible person would say. Rather, the intended meaning is that these things were in themselves immoral, while the people believed them to be acts of obedience and believed that Allah had commanded them. Then, exalted is He, He relates of them that they argued for their persistence in those immoralities with two things:

One of them: "We found our fathers upon it."

The second: "Allah has commanded us to it."

Page 47
As for the first argument: Allah mentions no answer to it, because it is a mere pointing to blind imitation (taqlid). It is firmly established in the intellect of everyone that this is a corrupt method, since taqlid occurs in mutually contradictory religions. If taqlid were a true path, it would necessitate judging that each of two contradictories is true, and it is known that this is false. Since the corruption of this path was manifest and clear to everyone, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention an answer to it.

As for the second argument, their saying: "Allah has commanded us to it," Allah has answered it with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not command immorality.﴾ The meaning is that it has been established through the tongues of the prophets and messengers that these acts are reprehensible and ugly, so how is it possible to say that Allah, exalted is He, has commanded us to them? I say: The Mu'tazila may use this verse to argue that a thing is ugly only for a reason that returns to it, and that God, exalted is He, forbade it because it includes that reason. For His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed, Allah does not command immorality," is an indication that, since that thing is described in itself as being of the immorality, it is impossible for Allah to command it. This requires that its being in itself an immorality be distinct from the connection of command and prohibition to it, and that yields the desired conclusion.

Its answer: It is possible that, since it has been established by induction that He, exalted is He, commands only what is beneficial to the servants and forbids only what is harmful to them, this rationale for this meaning is valid. And Allah knows best.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do you say about Allah that which you do not know?﴾ In this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The intended meaning is that it may be said: You say that Allah commanded you these particular acts, so your knowledge that Allah commanded you them has been attained, either because you heard the speech of Allah, exalted is He, directly without an intermediary, or because you came to know that through the way of revelation to the prophets.

As for the first, its falsity is known necessarily.

As for the second, it is false according to your view, because you deny the prophethood of the prophets absolutely. This debate occurred with the disbelievers of Quraysh, and they denied the very principle of prophethood. If that is the case, they have no path to attaining knowledge of the rulings of Allah, exalted is He. So their saying, "Allah has commanded us to it," was a saying about Allah, exalted is He, of something that is not known. And that is false.

The second discussion: Those who deny qiyas (analogical reasoning) say: A ruling established by qiyas is conjectural (mazhnun) and not known, and what is not known is not permissible to assert. This is because of His saying, exalted is He, in a context of reproach and derision: ﴿Do you say about Allah that which you do not know?﴾ The answer of those who affirm qiyas to such proofs has been mentioned by us many times. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 29–30:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice. And set your faces (in worship) at every place of prayer, and call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him. Just as He originated you, you will return.﴾ ﴿A group He has guided, and a group has deserved misguidance. Indeed, they have taken the devils as allies instead of Allah, and they think that they are guided.﴾

Page 48

Know that when He, the Exalted, explained the command to indecency, He explained that He commands justice and equity. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿My Lord has commanded justice﴾, indicates that a thing is in itself just, for reasons that return to it in its essence, and then He, the Exalted, commands it because it is so in itself. This also indicates that goodness is good only for reasons that return to it. Its answer has already been mentioned.

The second issue: ʿAṭāʾ and al-Suddī said: ﴿justice﴾ means equity, and what is apparent to reason as being good and correct. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is the statement "There is no god but Allah." The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but Him, and the angels and those of knowledge, standing in justice﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 18). And that justice is nothing but the testimony that there is no god but Allah. Thus it is established that justice is nothing but the statement "There is no god but Allah."

Having understood this, we say: In this verse He, the Exalted, commanded three things:

The first of them: He commanded justice, which is the statement "There is no god but Allah." It includes knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, in His essence, His acts and His rulings, and then knowledge that He is One with no partner.

The second of them: He commanded prayer, which is His saying: ﴿and set your faces at every place of prayer﴾. And in this there are discussions:

The first discussion: One may say: ﴿My Lord has commanded justice﴾ is a report, and ﴿and set your faces﴾ is a command, and coordinating a command with a report is not permissible. Its answer: the implied meaning is: "Say: My Lord has commanded justice," and "Say: set your faces at every place of prayer, and call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him."

The second discussion: In the verse there are two opinions:

One of them: what is meant by His saying "set (your faces)" is facing the qibla.

The second: what is meant is sincerity (ikhlāṣ). The reason for mentioning these two opinions is that setting the face in worship may be by facing the qibla, and it may be by sincerity in that worship. The closer is the first, because sincerity is mentioned afterward; and if we took it to mean sincerity, it would be as if He had said: "Be sincere at every place of prayer and call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him," and that is not sound.

If it is said: that is sound if you attach sincerity to calling alone.

We say: since it is possible for it to refer to both together, it is not permissible to restrict it to one of them, especially with His saying ﴿sincere in devotion to Him﴾, for it encompasses everything that is called religion.

Having established this, we say: concerning His saying ﴿at every place of prayer﴾, they differed as to whether what is meant is the time of prayer or its place. The closer is the first, because it is the place where it is possible to set the face toward the qibla. So it is as if He, the Exalted, has shown us that we should not regard places, but should regard the qibla; the meaning is: turn your faces wherever you are in prayer toward the Kaʿba. Ibn ʿAbbās said: what is meant is that when prayer comes due and you are at a mosque, pray in it, and let none of you say, "I will not pray except in the mosque of my people."

One may say: taking the wording of the verse this way is remote, because the wording of the verse indicates the obligation of setting the face in every mosque, and does not indicate that it is not permissible for him to move from one mosque to another.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and call upon Him, sincere in devotion to Him﴾, know that when He, the Exalted, commanded in the first verse turning toward the qibla, He commanded after it calling upon Him. My clear view is that what is meant by it is the acts of prayer, and He called them "calling" because prayer in its basic linguistic sense is an expression for supplication, and because the most noble parts of prayer are supplication and remembrance. He explained that this supplication must be made with sincerity. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And they were commanded only to worship Allah, sincere in devotion to Him﴾ (al-Bayyina: 5). Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Just as He originated you, you will return.﴾ On this there are two opinions:

The first opinion: Ibn ʿAbbās said: ﴿Just as He originated you﴾ means He created you believer or disbeliever; ﴿you will return﴾ means He resurrects the believer as a believer and the disbeliever as a disbeliever. For whoever Allah created at the beginning for wretchedness, He makes him act by the deeds of the people of wretchedness, and his end is wretchedness; and whoever He created for happiness, He makes him act by the deeds of the people of happiness, and his end is happiness.

The second opinion: al-Ḥasan and Mujāhid said: ﴿Just as He originated you﴾ means He created you in this world when you were nothing; likewise you will return living. Those who hold the first opinion argued for its soundness by the fact that He mentioned after it His saying: ﴿A group He has guided, and a group has deserved misguidance﴾, and this goes in the manner of an explanation of His saying ﴿Just as He originated you, you will return﴾, and that necessitates what we have said. The judge (al-Qāḍī) said: this opinion is false, because no one says that He originated us as believers or disbelievers, since in belief and disbelief there must be something that arises. This objection is weak, because its answer is to say: just as He originated you with belief, disbelief, happiness and wretchedness, so the state will be upon it on the Day of Resurrection.

Know that He, the Exalted, commanded in the verse first with the word "justice," which is the word "There is no god but Allah," then He commanded prayer second, then He explained that the benefit of performing these acts only appears in the Hereafter. Its parallel is His saying, the Exalted, to Mūsā, peace be upon him, in Ṭā-Hā: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾ (Ṭā-Hā: 14–15).

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿A group He has guided, and a group has deserved misguidance﴾. On this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: Our companions (the Ashʿarites) used this verse to argue that guidance and misguidance are from Allah, the Exalted. The Muʿtazilites said: what is meant is that He guided a group to Paradise and reward, and a group has deserved misguidance, i.e., punishment and being turned away from the path of reward. The judge said: because this is what is due to them and not to others, since the servant does not deserve to be led astray from the religion; for if he deserved that, it would be permissible for Him to command His prophets to mislead them from the religion, just as He commanded them to establish the due prescribed punishments, and in that is the loss of trust in prophethood.

Know that this answer is weak in two respects:

The first: His saying ﴿A group He has guided﴾ refers to the past, and on the interpretation they mention the meaning becomes that He will guide them in the future. If what is meant were that He, in the past, decreed that He would guide them to Paradise, this would be a departure from the apparent meaning without need, because we have shown by decisive rational proofs that guidance and misguidance are only from Allah, the Exalted.

The second: We say, suppose that what is meant by guidance and misguidance is Allah's judgment concerning that; nevertheless, once this judgment has taken place, it is impossible for the servant to produce anything other than it, otherwise that judgment would turn into a lie, and lying about Allah is impossible, and what leads to the impossible is impossible. So it was impossible for the servant to produce any act other than that, and this necessitates the invalidity of the Muʿtazilite doctrine in this respect. And Allah knows best.

The second discussion: The accusative of His saying ﴿and a group has deserved misguidance﴾ is governed by a verb that its following clause explains, as if it were said: "and He abandoned a group that has deserved misguidance." Then Allah, the Exalted, explained that the reason for which misguidance was decreed upon this group is that they took the devils as allies instead of Allah, so they accepted what they called them to, and did not reflect in distinguishing truth from falsehood.

Page 50

If it is said: how does this explanation accord with your statement that guidance and misguidance arise only through Allah's creation at the outset? We say: in our view, the totality of capacity together with the motive necessitates the act, and the motive that prompted them to that act is: that they took the devils as allies instead of Allah.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and they think that they are guided﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: He means what ʿAmr ibn Luḥayy showed them. This is remote; rather it is to be taken in its general sense: whoever embarks upon falsehood deserves blame and punishment, whether he supposes it to be true or does not suppose so. This verse indicates that mere supposition and assumption are not sufficient for the soundness of religion; rather it requires certainty, conviction and firm knowledge, because He, the Exalted, faulted the disbelievers for supposing that they were guided; and if this supposition were not blameworthy, He would not have blamed them for it. And Allah knows best.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Indeed, He does not love the excessive.﴾ ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?" Say, "They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely [for them] on the Day of Resurrection. Thus do We detail the verses for a people who know."﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded justice (qist) in the first verse, and clothing and food and drink are among the components of justice, He therefore followed it with mention of these two. Also, when He commanded the establishment of prayer in His statement, ﴿And set your faces upright at every place of prayer﴾, and covering the awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered) is a condition for the validity of prayer, He therefore followed it with mention of clothing. There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: Ibn Abbas said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) among the Arab tribes used to circumambulate the House naked: the men by day and the women by night. When they reached the mosque of Mina, they would take off their clothes and come to the mosque naked. They said, 'We will not circumambulate in garments in which we have committed sins.' Some of them said, 'We do this as an omen, so that we may be stripped of sins just as we have stripped off clothes.' Women among them would make a veil and tie it around their hips to conceal themselves from the Hums, who were the Quraysh, for they did not do this. They prayed in their clothes, and did not eat food except a little sustenance, and did not eat fat. The Muslims said, 'O Messenger of Allah, we have more right to do this.' So Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse, meaning: 'Wear your clothes, and eat meat and fat, and drink, but do not be excessive.'"

The second issue: The intended meaning of adornment (zina) is wearing clothes, and the evidence for this is His statement, ﴿and not reveal their adornment﴾ (Al-Nur: 31), meaning clothing. Also, adornment is not attained except through complete concealment of the awrah, and for this reason adorning oneself with the finest clothes on congregational occasions and on festivals became a sunnah (recommended practice). Also, He, exalted is He, said in the preceding verse: ﴿We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts, and as plumage﴾ (Al-A'raf: 26). So He made clear that the clothing which covers the private parts is among the category of finery and adornment. Then He commanded the taking of adornment in this verse. Therefore it is necessary that the intended meaning of this adornment is what was mentioned in that verse, and so this adornment must be understood as covering the awrah. Also, the exegetes have agreed (ajma'a) that the intended meaning of adornment here is wearing a garment that covers the awrah. Also, His statement, ﴿Take your adornment﴾, is a command, and a command implies obligation (lil-wujub). Thus it is established that taking adornment is obligatory, and everything other than clothing is not obligatory. Therefore it is necessary to interpret adornment as clothing, acting upon the text to the extent possible.

Having understood this, we say: His statement, ﴿Take your adornment﴾, is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. This indicates the obligation of covering the awrah at the establishment of every prayer. Here there are two questions.

The first question: He, exalted is He, joined to it His statement, ﴿and eat and drink﴾, and there is no doubt that this is a command of permissibility (amr ibahah). So it is necessary that His statement, ﴿Take your adornment﴾, is also a command of permissibility.

Its answer: It does not follow that abandoning the apparent meaning in the conjoined element entails abandoning it in the element to which it is conjoined. Also, eating and drinking may themselves be obligatory in ruling.

The second question: This verse was revealed concerning the prohibition of circumambulating while naked.

The answer: We have explained in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that what matters is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation (sabab).

Having understood this, we say: His statement, ﴿Take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾, requires the obligation of wearing complete clothing at every prayer, because complete clothing is adornment. The application of this is set aside regarding the portion of the body whose covering is not obligatory, by consensus (ijma'), and what remains falls under the wording. And if it is established that covering the awrah is obligatory in prayer, then prayer must be invalidated upon its omission, because omitting it entails omitting what is commanded, and omitting what is commanded is disobedience, and disobedience entails punishment, as we have explained this method in usul.

The third issue: The followers of Abu Hanifa used this verse in the question of removing impurity (najasah) with rose water. They said: He commanded us to pray in His statement, ﴿Establish prayer﴾ (Al-An'am: 72), and prayer is an expression of supplication (du'a'), and he has performed it, and performing what is commanded results in discharging the obligation. So the implication of this evidence is that the validity of prayer should not depend on covering the awrah. However, we have made this meaning obligatory in acting upon His statement, ﴿Take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾. Wearing a garment washed with rose water, in the utmost degree of cleanliness, is taking adornment, so it must be sufficient for the validity of prayer.

Our answer: The definite article in His statement, ﴿Establish the prayer﴾, refers to a previously known referent (al-ma'hud al-sabiq), and that is the practice of the Messenger ﷺ. So why do you say that the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace, prayed in a garment washed with rose water? And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His statement, ﴿and eat and drink﴾: know that we have mentioned that the people of the Jahiliyyah used to eat only a little food during the days of their pilgrimage, and did not eat fat, glorifying their pilgrimage by this. So Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse to explain the corruption of that practice.

The second opinion: They used to say that Allah, exalted is He, had forbidden them some of what is in the bellies of cattle, so He forbade them the baḥīrah and the sā'ibah. So Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse as an explanation of the corruption of their statement in this matter.

Know that His statement, ﴿and eat and drink﴾, is unrestricted, encompassing times and circumstances, and encompassing all foods and drinks. Therefore the original ruling concerning them must be permissibility at all times and for all foods and drinks, except what is excluded by a separate textual proof (dalil munfasil). Also, they forbade for themselves during the time of pilgrimage things that Allah, exalted is He, had made lawful for them, and that is excess.

Know that interpreting the word "excess" as excessive consumption is no less appropriate than interpreting it as prohibiting what is not permissible and what is proper.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the excessive﴾. This is the utmost of warning, because whatever Allah, exalted is He, does not love remains deprived of reward, since the meaning of Allah's love for a servant is that He bestows reward upon him. Thus the absence of this love is an expression of the absence of attaining reward, and whenever reward is not attained, punishment has been attained, because there is consensus that there is no accountable being in existence who is neither rewarded nor punished.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?"﴾ And in this there are issues:

The first issue: The apparent form of this verse is interrogative, but its intended meaning is the affirmation of denial and the emphasis of that denial. There are two opinions regarding the verse:

The first opinion: the intended meaning of adornment in this verse is the clothing with which the awrah is covered. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and of many exegetes.

The second opinion: it encompasses all kinds of adornment. Thus all forms of beautification fall under adornment, and cleansing the body in all its aspects falls under it, and mounts fall under it, and types of jewelry fall under it, because all of that is adornment. Were it not for the explicit text prohibiting gold, silver and silk for men, this would have been included in this generality. The good things of provision encompass everything that is pleasant and desired among types of food and drink, and they also encompass enjoying women and perfume. It is narrated from Uthman ibn Maz'un that he came to the Messenger ﷺ and said: "My inner self has overwhelmed me; I resolved to castrate myself." He said: "Gently, O Uthman, the castration of my community is fasting." He said: "My inner self tells me to adopt monasticism." He said: "The monasticism of my community is sitting in the mosques awaiting prayer." He said: "My inner self tells me to travel." He said: "The travel of my community is jihad, Hajj and 'Umrah." He said: "My inner self tells me to give away what I possess." He said: "It is better that you suffice yourself and your dependents, and that you show mercy to the orphan and the needy, giving them something better than that." He said: "My inner self tells me to divorce Khawlah." He said: "The emigration (hijrah) of my community is emigrating from what Allah has forbidden." He said: "My inner self tells me not to approach her." He said: "When a Muslim approaches his wife or what his right hand possesses, if he does not produce a child from that intercourse, it will be for him a servant in Paradise. And if he has a child who dies before him or after him, it will be for him a delight of the eye, and he will rejoice on the Day of Resurrection. And if he dies before reaching puberty, it will be for him an intercessor and a mercy on the Day of Resurrection." He said: "My inner self tells me not to eat meat." He said: "Gently. I eat meat when I find it, and if I asked Allah to feed me it every day, He would do so." He said: "My inner self tells me not to touch perfume." He said: "Gently, for Jibril commanded me to use perfume at intervals, and said: 'Do not abandon it on Friday.'" Then he said: "O Uthman, do not turn away from my sunnah, for whoever turns away from my sunnah and dies before repenting, the angels will turn his face away from my Basin."

Know that this hadith indicates that this complete Shari'ah indicates that all kinds of adornment are permissible and authorized, except what is excluded by a textual proof. For this reason we included all of them under His statement, ﴿Say, "Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah?"﴾.

The second issue: the implication of this verse is that whatever a person adorns himself with must be permissible, and likewise whatever is found good (yustaṭāb) must be permissible. Thus this verse entails the permissibility of all benefits. This is a principle upheld throughout the whole Shari'ah, because every event that occurs either has benefit that is pure or predominant, or harm that is pure or predominant, or harm and benefit are equal, or neither exists. As for the last two divisions, namely that harm and benefit are equal, or that neither has ever existed, then in these two cases it must be ruled that what was is left as it was. If the benefit is pure, then permissibility is required by the implication of this verse. If the benefit is predominant and the harm is subordinate, then like is set against like, and the excess remains as pure benefit, so it joins the division in which benefit is pure. If the harm is pure, then abandoning it is pure benefit, so it joins the earlier division. If the harm is predominant, then the excess remains as pure harm, so abandoning it is pure benefit. By this route this verse becomes indicative of rulings without limit concerning permissibility and prohibition. Then, if we find an explicit text concerning the event, we decide permissibility where there is pure benefit and prohibition where there is pure harm. By this route all rulings without limit come within the scope of the text.

The deniers of analogy (nufāt al-qiyās) then said: If God the Exalted had obligated us to act by analogy (qiyās), the ruling of that analogy would either agree with the ruling of this general text, in which case it would be idle, since this text is independently sufficient for it; or it would contradict it, in which case that analogy would be specifying the generality of this text, and it would be rejected, because acting upon the text is preferable to acting upon analogy.

They said: By this route the Qur'an alone is sufficient to explain all the rulings of the Shari'ah, and there is no need with it for any other method. This is the articulation of the view of one who says: the Qur'an suffices to explain all events. And God knows best.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but do not be excessive. Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded justice (qist) in the first verse, and clothing and food and drink are among the components of justice, He therefore followed it with mention of these two. Also, when He commanded the establishment of prayer in His statement, ﴿And set your faces upright at every place of prayer﴾, and covering the awrah (the parts of the body that must be covered) is a condition for the validity of prayer, He therefore followed it with mention of clothing. There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: Ibn Abbas said: "The people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance) among the Arab tribes used to circumambulate the House naked: the men by day and the women by night. When they reached the mosque of Mina, they would take off their clothes and come to the mosque naked. They said, 'We will not circumambulate in garments in which we have committed sins.' Some of them said, 'We do this as an omen, so that we may be stripped of sins just as we have stripped off clothes.' Women among them would make a veil and tie it around their hips to conceal themselves from the Hums, who were the Quraysh, for they did not do this. They prayed in their clothes, and did not eat food except a little sustenance, and did not eat fat. The Muslims said, 'O Messenger of Allah, we have more right to do this.' So Allah, exalted is He, sent down this verse, meaning: 'Wear your clothes, and eat meat and fat, and drink, but do not be excessive.'"

The second issue: The intended meaning of adornment (zina) is wearing clothes, and the evidence for this is His statement, ﴿and not reveal their adornment﴾ (Al-Nur: 31), meaning clothing. Also, adornment is not attained except through complete concealment of the awrah, and for this reason adorning oneself with the finest clothes on congregational occasions and on festivals became a sunnah (recommended practice). Also, He, exalted is He, said in the preceding verse: ﴿We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts, and as plumage﴾ (Al-A'raf: 26). So He made clear that the clothing which covers the private parts is among the category of finery and adornment. Then He commanded the taking of adornment in this verse. Therefore it is necessary that the intended meaning of this adornment is what was mentioned in that verse, and so this adornment must be understood as covering the awrah. Also, the exegetes have agreed (ajma'a) that the intended meaning of adornment here is wearing a garment that covers the awrah. Also, His statement, ﴿Take your adornment﴾, is a command, and a command implies obligation (lil-wujub). Thus it is established that taking adornment is obligatory, and everything other than clothing is not obligatory. Therefore it is necessary to interpret adornment as clothing, acting upon the text to the extent possible.

Having understood this, we say: His statement, ﴿Take your adornment﴾, is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. This indicates the obligation of covering the awrah at the establishment of every prayer. Here there are two questions.

The first question: He, exalted is He, joined to it His statement, ﴿and eat and drink﴾, and there is no doubt that this is a command of permissibility (amr ibahah). So it is necessary that His statement, ﴿Take your adornment﴾, is also a command of permissibility.

Its answer: It does not follow that abandoning the apparent meaning in the conjoined element entails abandoning it in the element to which it is conjoined. Also, eating and drinking may themselves be obligatory in ruling.

The second question: This verse was revealed concerning the prohibition of circumambulating while naked.

The answer: We have explained in usul al-fiqh (the principles of jurisprudence) that what matters is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion of revelation (sabab).

Having understood this, we say: His statement, ﴿Take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾, requires the obligation of wearing complete clothing at every prayer, because complete clothing is adornment. The application of this is set aside regarding the portion of the body whose covering is not obligatory, by consensus (ijma'), and what remains falls under the wording. And if it is established that covering the awrah is obligatory in prayer, then prayer must be invalidated upon its omission, because omitting it entails omitting what is commanded, and omitting what is commanded is disobedience, and disobedience entails punishment, as we have explained this method in usul.

The third issue: The followers of Abu Hanifa used this verse in the question of removing impurity (najasah) with rose water. They said: He commanded us to pray in His statement, ﴿Establish prayer﴾ (Al-An'am: 72), and prayer is an expression of supplication (du'a'), and he has performed it, and performing what is commanded results in discharging the obligation. So the implication of this evidence is that the validity of prayer should not depend on covering the awrah. However, we have made this meaning obligatory in acting upon His statement, ﴿Take your adornment at every place of prayer﴾. Wearing a garment washed with rose water, in the utmost degree of cleanliness, is taking adornment, so it must be sufficient for the validity of prayer.

So why do you say that the Messenger, upon whom be prayers and peace, prayed in a garment washed with rose water? And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know.﴾

In the verse there are two issues:

The first issue: Hamzah (the reciter) pronounced the yā' in (rabbiya) with sukūn (silent), while the rest read it with a fatḥah (vowel).

The second issue: Know that when, in the previous verse, He, exalted is He, clarified that what they had made forbidden is not forbidden, He clarified in this verse the categories of forbidden things. He first forbade the fawāḥish (indecencies), and second, the ithm (sin). The scholars differed about the distinction between the two in several respects:

The first: The fawāḥish are a term for the major sins, because its ugliness has become excessive (tafāḥasha) meaning it has increased, and the ithm is a term for the minor sins. So the meaning of the verse becomes: He has forbidden both the major and the minor sins. Al-Qadi criticised this, saying: This requires that one say that fornication, theft, and disbelief are not ithm. And this is far-fetched.

The second view: The fāḥishah is a name for what does not entail a ḥadd (prescribed punishment), while ithm is a name for what entails a ḥadd. Although this differs from the first, it is close to it, and the objection to it is what preceded.

The third view: The fāḥishah is a name for the major sin, and the ithm is a name for sin in general, whether major or minor. Its benefit is that, when He forbade the major sin, He followed it with the prohibition of sin in general, lest it be supposed that the prohibition is aimed only at the major sin. This is the view chosen by al-Qadi.

The fourth view: Although fāḥishah, according to the linguistic origin, is a name for everything that has become excessive and increased in any matter, in custom it is specific to the increase (in what is evil). The evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, said about fornication: ﴿Indeed it was an indecency﴾ (al-Nisa larger: 22), and because the word fāḥishah, when used without qualification, is not understood from it except that; and when it is said: "So-and-so is faḥḥāsh," it is understood that he insults people with obscene words. Therefore the word fāḥishah must be restricted to fornication alone.

Having established this, we say: In His saying: ﴿what is apparent of them and what is concealed﴾, according to this explanation, there are two possibilities:

The first: It means the secret of fornication, which occurs by way of passion and love, and what is apparent of it is that it occurs openly.

The second: What is apparent of fornication may mean the touching and embracing, and (what is concealed) the penetration. As for ithm, it must be specified as wine, because He, exalted is He, said in describing wine: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ (al-Baqarah: 219). With this interpretation the distinction between the two terms becomes clear.

The third category of forbidden things: His saying: ﴿and oppression without right﴾. We say: As for those who said that fawāḥish means all major sins and ithm means all sins, they said: Oppression and shirk must necessarily be included under the fawāḥish and under the ithm, but Allah, exalted is He, singled them out for mention to alert that they are the worst kinds of sins, as in His saying: ﴿and His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ (al-Baqarah: 98), and in His saying: ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you and from Nuh﴾ (al-Ahzab: 7). As for those who said that fāḥishah is specific to fornication and ithm to wine, they said: On this reading, oppression and shirk are not included under the fawāḥish or the ithm. We say: Oppression is not used except for aggression against another's self, property, or honour; and also oppression may mean rebellion against the authority of the time.

If it is said: Oppression is only ever without right, so what is the benefit of mentioning this condition?

We say: It is like His saying: ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right﴾ (al-An'am: 151). The meaning is: Do not undertake to harm people by killing and coercion, except where you have a right in it; then in that case it ceases to be oppression.

The fourth category of forbidden things: His saying: ﴿and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority﴾. There is an objection: this gives the impression that there is some shirk with Allah for which He has sent down an authority. Its answer: What is meant is that affirming a thing for which there is no proof of its establishment, nor any authority, is impossible. Since the existence of proof and indication of the soundness of the claim of shirk is impossible, it must be that the claim of it is false absolutely. This verse is among the strongest proofs that the claim based on mere imitation (taqlid) is false.

The fifth category of forbidden things mentioned in this verse: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾. The explanation of this verse has already passed in this surah at His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah does not command indecency. Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ Two questions remain concerning the verse:

The first question: The word ﴿innama﴾ ("only") indicates restriction (ḥaṣr). So His saying: ﴿My Lord has only forbidden﴾ such-and-such indicates restriction, yet the forbidden things are not confined to these matters.

The answer: If we say that fāḥishah is applied to all major sins, and ithm to all sin, then every sin is included in it. And if we take fāḥishah to mean fornication, and ithm to mean wine, then we say: The crimes are confined to five kinds:

One: crimes against lineage, which occur only through fornication, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿My Lord has only forbidden the fawāḥish﴾.

Two: crimes against the intellect, which is the drinking of wine, and to it refers His saying: (and sin).

Three: crimes against honour.

Four: crimes against lives and against property, and to these two refers His saying: ﴿and oppression without right﴾.

Five: crimes against religion, and these are of two aspects:

One: impugning the Oneness of Allah, exalted is He, to which refers His saying: (and that)

Two: speaking about the religion of Allah without knowledge, to which refers His saying: ﴿and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾. Since the roots of crimes are these things, and the rest are like branches and followers, He, exalted is He, therefore made the mention of these operate as the mention of the whole, and included in it the word ﴿innama﴾ which indicates restriction.

The second question: The fawāḥish and the ithm are what Allah has forbidden, so the sense of the verse becomes: "My Lord has only forbidden the forbidden things," which is a statement devoid of benefit.

The answer: That an act is a fāḥishah is an expression for its containing, in its very nature, matters on account of which its prohibition is required. On this reading the question falls away. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And for every nation there is a term. When their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: When He, exalted is He, had explained the lawful and the unlawful and the states of obligation (taklif), He explained that for every person there is a specified term that cannot be advanced or delayed, and when that term comes, the person dies without doubt. The purpose of this is to instill fear, so that a person may be earnest in fulfilling the obligations as they should be.

The second issue: Know that the ajal (term) is the appointed time set for the expiry of a respite. In this verse there are two views:

The first view: This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and Muqatil: the meaning is that God, exalted is He, gave respite to every nation that denied its messenger until a specified time. He does not punish them until they reach that time, at which point they become deserving of the punishment of annihilation (isti'sal). When that time comes, that punishment descends without doubt.

The second view: The intended meaning of this term is the lifespan. When that term ends and is complete, advancing or delaying it is impossible. The first view is preferable, because He said: ﴿And for every nation﴾ and did not say: "And for every person there is a term." On the second view, He said: ﴿for every nation﴾ and did not say "for every person," because the nation is the community in every age, and it is known of its condition that its terms are close to one another, since mention of the nation in what runs in the manner of a warning is more forceful. Also, the first view requires that every nation among the nations has a specified time for the descent of the punishment of annihilation upon them, and the matter is not so, because our nation is not like that.

The third issue: If we take the verse according to the second view, it follows that every person has a term in which advancing or delaying does not occur, so that the one who is killed dies at his term. It does not mean that He, exalted is He, is unable to keep him alive longer or shorter than that, nor that He is unable to cause him to die at that time, because this would require that He, exalted is He, leave being capable and choosing, and become like something that necessitates its own essence, and that is impossible with regard to God, exalted is He. Rather, the meaning is that He, exalted is He, informed that the matter occurs in this manner.

The fourth issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They cannot delay it by an hour, nor can they advance it.﴾ The meaning is that they do not come late from that specified term, not by an hour nor by anything less than an hour, except that He, exalted is He, mentioned the hour because this word is the least of the names of times.

If it is said: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿nor can they advance it﴾? For when the term arrives, it is rationally impossible for that term to occur at a time before it?

We say: His saying ﴿When their term comes﴾ is taken to mean the approach of the arrival of the term. The Arabs say: "The winter has come" when its time has drawn near, and with the nearness of the term, advancing upon it at times and delaying from it at other times is valid.

O Children of Adam, if messengers from among you come to you, relating to you My verses, then whoever fears God and makes amends, there shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve. And those who deny Our verses and turn arrogantly away from them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.

Know that when God, exalted is He, explained the conditions of moral obligation (al-taklif) and explained that for every person there is a determined term (ajal) that neither advances nor delays, He then explained that after death, those who were obedient will have no fear and no grief, whereas if they were rebellious, they will fall into the severest punishment.

His saying: ﴿إمّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ﴾ ("in-ma ya'tiyannakum", "if ever there come to you"): "in" is the conditional particle, to which "ma" has been joined as an emphasizer of the meaning of the condition; for this reason the heavy nun (al-nun al-thaqila) is attached to its verb. The response (jaza') of this condition is the "fa" and what follows it of condition and response, which is His saying: ﴿فَمَنِ اتَّقى وأصْلَحَ﴾ ("fa-man ittaqa wa-aslah", "then whoever fears God and makes amends"). He said "messengers" (rusul), although the address is to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, who is the Seal of the Prophets, upon him and upon them be peace, because He, exalted is He, framed the speech according to what His practice requires regarding the nations. He said "from among you" (minkum) because the messenger being from among them is more decisive for their excuse and clearer for the proof against them, in several respects:

First: their knowledge of his circumstances and his purity is prior.

Second: their knowledge of what befits his capacity is prior, so there is no doubt or suspicion whatsoever concerning the miracles that appear through him, that they came about by the power of God, exalted is He, and not by his own power. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿ولَوْ جَعَلْناهُ مَلَكًا لَجَعَلْناهُ رَجُلًا﴾ ("Had We made him an angel, We would have made him a man") [al-An'am: 9].

Third: the familiarity and tranquillity of the heart that arises toward those of one's own kind, unlike one who is not of the same kind, with whom familiarity does not arise.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿يَقُصُّونَ عَلَيْكم آياتِي﴾ ("relating to you My verses"), it has been said: those verses are the Qur'an. It has been said: they are the proofs. It has been said: they are the rulings and the laws. The preferable view is that all of these are included, because all of these things are verses of God, exalted is He, since when messengers come they must mention all these categories.

Then God, exalted is He, divided the state of the community, saying: ﴿فَمَنِ اتَّقى وأصْلَحَ﴾. The combination of these two states is among what necessitates reward, because the one who fears God is the one who guards against everything God, exalted is He, has forbidden, and His saying "and makes amends" includes that he has done everything he was commanded.

Then God, exalted is He, said concerning their description: ﴿فَلا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ i.e., because of future circumstances, ﴿ولا هم يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ i.e., because of past circumstances; for when a person considers that harm may reach him in the future, he fears, and when he reflects and knows that some of what is not fitting has reached him in the past, grief arises in his heart for this reason. The preferable interpretation of the negation of grief is that what is meant is that they do not grieve over what they missed in this world, because their grief over the punishment of the Hereafter must be removed by what they have gained of the cessation of fear, so it becomes like a return (to the start); and reading it as an additional benefit is preferable. Thus God, exalted is He, made clear that their state in the Hereafter differs from their state in this world, for in the Hereafter no fear or grief whatsoever arises in their hearts.

The scholars differed as to whether believers among the people of obedience will experience fear and grief at the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. Some held that they will not experience that, and the proof for this is this verse; and also His saying: ﴿لا يَحْزُنُهُمُ الفَزَعُ الأكْبَرُ﴾ ("The greatest terror will not grieve them") [al-Anbiya': 103]. Others held that they will experience that terror, based on His saying: ﴿يَوْمَ تَرَوْنَها تَذْهَلُ كُلُّ مُرْضِعَةٍ عَمّا أرْضَعَتْ وتَضَعُ كُلُّ ذاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَها وتَرى النّاسَ سُكارى وما هم بِسُكارى﴾ ("On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed, and every pregnant woman will drop her burden, and you will see people drunk though they are not drunk") [al-Hajj: 2], i.e., from the intensity of fear.

Those who held this view answered regarding this verse: its meaning is that their affair will end in safety and joy, like the physician's saying to the patient: "There is no harm upon you," i.e., your affair will end in health and well-being, even if at the present time he is in distress from his illness.

Then God, exalted is He, made clear that those who denied these verses which the messengers bring, ﴿واسْتَكْبَرُوا﴾ i.e., they disdained accepting them and rebelled against committing to them, ﴿أُولَئِكَ أصْحابُ النّارِ هم فِيها خالِدُونَ﴾ ("those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever"). Our companions (the Ash'arites) have relied on this verse to show that the sinful person among the people of prayer does not remain eternally in the Fire, because He, exalted is He, made clear that those who deny the signs of God and are arrogant toward accepting them are the ones who remain eternally in the Fire, and the word "hum" (they) denotes restriction; this implies that whoever is not described by that denial and arrogance does not remain eternally in the Fire. And God knows best.

[Page 59]

God Most High says: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, or denies His signs? Those will receive their portion of the Book, until when Our messengers come to them to take them in death, they say: "Where is that which you used to call upon besides God?" They say: "They have strayed from us," and they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers.﴾

Know that God Most High's words ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against God, or denies His signs﴾ refer back to His words ﴿And those who denied Our signs and were arrogant towards them﴾. His words "Who is more unjust" mean: who is greater in wrongdoing than one who says about God what He has not said, or denies what He has said. The first is the judgment that something exists which does not exist, and the second is the judgment that denies what exists.

The first category includes the statement of one who ascribes partners to God, whether that partner is an idol, a star, or the doctrine of those who speak of Yazdan and Ahriman. It also includes the statement of one who attributes daughters and sons to God Most High, and includes the statement of one who attributes false rulings to God Most High.

The second category includes the statement of one who denies that the Qur'an is a Book sent down from God Most High, and the statement of one who denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ).

[Page 60]

Then God Most High said: ﴿Those will receive their portion of the Book﴾. The scholars differed over what is meant by that portion, giving two views:

The first: that what is meant by it is punishment, and the meaning is that this specific punishment, which He made their portion in the Book, will befall them. Then they differed over that specific punishment. Some of them said: it is the blackening of the face and the blueness of the eye. The evidence for this is God Most High's words: (﴿And on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied against God, their faces blackened﴾ [al-Zumar: 60]). Al-Zajjaj said: it is what is mentioned in God Most High's words: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾ [al-Layl: 14], and in His words: ﴿He will make him enter a severe punishment﴾ [al-Jinn: 17], and in His words: ﴿When the shackles are around their necks and the chains﴾ [Ghafir: 71]. These things are their portion of the Book in proportion to their sins in their disbelief.

The second view: that what is meant by this portion is something other than punishment. They differed over it. It was said: they are the Jews and Christians, for whom it is obligatory upon us, when they are under our protection (dhimma), that we not transgress against them, that we deal justly with them, and that we defend them. That is the meaning of the portion from the Book.

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: ﴿Those will receive their portion of the Book﴾ means: what has preceded for them in God's judgment and His will of wretchedness and happiness. If God decrees for them that they be sealed in wretchedness, He leaves them in their disbelief; and if He decrees for them that they be sealed in happiness, He transfers them to faith and monotheism.

Al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd said: it means what He has written for them of provisions, deeds and lifespans. When these are exhausted and come to an end, and they finish with them, ﴿Our messengers come to them to take them﴾.

Know that this disagreement arose only because He, Most High, said: ﴿Those will receive their portion of the Book﴾, and the word "portion" (nasib) is general, admitting of all the aspects mentioned.

Some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqin) said: understanding it as lifespan and provision is more preferable, because God Most High clarified that even if they reach that great extent in disbelief, this does not prevent what has been written for them of provision and lifespan from reaching them, as a bounty from God Most High, so that they might reform and repent. Also, His words ﴿until when Our messengers come to them to take them﴾ indicate that the coming of the messengers for taking (the souls) is like the endpoint for the attainment of that portion. It is therefore necessary that the attainment of that portion precede the occurrence of death, and what precedes the occurrence of death is nothing but lifespan and provision.

As for His words ﴿until when Our messengers come to them to take them, they say: Where is that which you used to call upon﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Al-Khalil and Sibawayh said: the imala (vocalic inclination of the alif toward the i-sound) of "hatta" (until), "alla" (unless) and "amma" (as for) is not permitted. These are alifs that are obligatorily pronounced with fath (the a-vowel), because they are final letters of particles that carry meanings, and they are separated from the final letters of nouns that contain an alif, such as hublā and hudan. However, "hatta" was written with a yā' because it has four letters, so it resembled "sakrā". Some grammarians said: the imala of "hatta" is not permitted, because it is a particle that does not inflect, and imala is a type of inflection.

The second issue: His words ﴿until when Our messengers come to them to take them﴾ have two views:

The first view: what is meant is the seizing of souls, because the word "wafat" (taking in death) conveys this meaning. Ibn 'Abbas said: death is the resurrection of the disbeliever, so the angels demand these things from them at death by way of rebuke, reproach and threat. These messengers are the Angel of Death and his assistants.

The second view, which is the view of al-Hasan and one of the two views of al-Zajjaj, is that this does not occur in the Hereafter. The meaning of His words ﴿until when Our messengers come to them﴾ is: the angels of punishment, ﴿to take them﴾ means: they complete their term when they are gathered to the Fire, in the sense that they complete their count, so that not one of them escapes.

[Page 60]

The third issue: His words ﴿Where is that which you used to call upon﴾ mean: where are the partners whom you used to call upon and worship besides God. The word "ma" was written joined to "ayna" in the script of the Mushaf. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it should have been separated, because it is joined in meaning: where are the gods whom you used to call upon.

Then He, Most High, related of them that they said: ﴿They have strayed from us﴾, meaning they vanished, departed and were gone, and ﴿they will bear witness against themselves that they were disbelievers﴾ at the moment of witnessing death.

Know that in all these aspects, the purpose of the verse is to deter the disbelievers from disbelief, because the awe-inspiring mention of these states moves the intelligent person to exert the utmost effort in reflection and reasoning, and to be vigilant in guarding against blind imitation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 38–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will say, "Enter into nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and humankind, into the Fire." Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them, "Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say, "For each there is double, but you do not know."﴾ ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them, "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾

Know that this verse is part of the continuing description of the condition of the disbelievers, namely that He, exalted is He, causes them to enter the Fire.

As for His saying, exalted is He, (He will say, "Enter"), there are two views:

The first: that Allah, exalted is He, says this.

The second: Muqatil said it is from the speech of the keeper of the Fire.

This disagreement is based on whether He, exalted is He, speaks with the disbelievers or not. We have already discussed this question at length.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Enter into nations﴾, there are two views:

The first view: the sense is, "Enter into the Fire along with nations." On this view, there is an ellipsis (iḍmār, a implied element not stated) and a figurative usage (majāz, non-literal use of a word). The ellipsis is because we have implied in it the phrase "into the Fire." The figurative usage is because we have taken the word "fī" (in) to mean "maʿa" (with), since we say the meaning of His saying "in nations" is "with nations."

The second view: one does not posit an ellipsis or a figurative usage. The sense is, "Enter into nations in the Fire." The meaning of entering into nations is entering among them. His saying, ﴿that have passed away before you, of jinn and humankind﴾, means that their time has gone before your time. This indicates that He, exalted is He, does not cast all the disbelievers into the Fire at once, but one group after another, so that among them there is one who precedes and one who follows, in order for this statement to be true, and so that the one entering from the nation sees in the Fire those who went before it.

His saying, ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾: the intended meaning is that the people of the Fire curse one another, so some of them disown others, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

By His saying, "its sister," is meant sister in religion. The meaning is that polytheists curse polytheists, and likewise Jews curse Jews, Christians curse Christians, and the same applies to Magians, Sabians, and the rest of the religions of misguidance.

His saying, ﴿until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾: that is, they caught up with one another (tadārakū), in the sense of following one another closely and gathering together in the Fire, and some of them overtook others and settled together with them. ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them﴾. There are two issues here.

First issue: regarding the explanation of "the first" and "the last," there are two views:

The first: Muqatil said: "the last of them" means the last to enter the Fire, and "the first of them" means the first to enter it.

The second: "the last of them" in rank, who are the followers and the lowly, and "the first of them" in rank, who are the leaders and chiefs.

Second issue: the "lām" in His saying, "to the last of them," is the lām of purpose (lām al-ajal), and the meaning is: for their sake and for their misleading of them, they said, ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us﴾. It is not meant that they spoke this statement to the first of them, because they did not address the first of them; rather they addressed Allah, exalted is He, with this speech.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us﴾, the meaning is that the followers say: the earlier ones misled us. Know that this misleading occurs from the earlier ones to the later ones in two ways:

One of them: by calling to falsehood and adorning it in their eyes, and striving to conceal the proofs that refute those falsehoods.

The second way: that the later ones venerate those earlier ones, so they imitate them in those falsehoods and fabrications which they devised, and take them as examples, so that this becomes a resemblance to the earlier ones' undertaking of misleading.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related about these later ones that they call down for the earlier ones an increase in punishment, which is His saying: ﴿So give them a double punishment of the Fire.﴾ Regarding the "double" (ḍiʿf), there are two views:

The first view: Abu ʿUbayda said: "ḍiʿf" is the equivalent of a thing once. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said something close to this, when he said about a man who made a bequest, "Give so-and-so double the share of my son." He said: he is given an equal amount twice.

The second view: al-Azhari said: "ḍiʿf" in the speech of the Arabs means an equal amount and whatever exceeds it, and it is not restricted to two equal amounts. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to say, "This is its double," meaning two equal amounts or three equal amounts. This is because ḍiʿf in origin is an unlimited increase. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿As for those, they will have the recompense of the double for what they did﴾ [Saba: 37], and He did not intend by it one equal amount nor two, but the most appropriate thing for it is that it be made ten times, based on His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-Anʿam: 160]. So it is established that the least of the ḍiʿf is bounded, which is the equal amount, while its greater part is unbounded, extending to no end.

As for the question of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him: know that the estate is tied to the rights of the heirs. However, for the sake of the bequest we have directed a portion of it to the beneficiary, and the certain amount in the bequest is the equal amount, while the rest is doubtful. So we took the certain and set aside the doubtful. For this reason, in that case we took ḍiʿf to mean two equal amounts.

[p. 62]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 38–40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He will say, "Enter into nations that have passed away before you, of jinn and humankind, into the Fire." Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister, until, when they have all overtaken one another therein, the last of them will say of the first of them, "Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire." He will say, "For each there is double, but you do not know."﴾ ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them, "You had no superiority over us, so taste the punishment for what you used to earn."﴾

Know that this verse is part of the continuing description of the condition of the disbelievers, namely that He, exalted is He, causes them to enter the Fire.

As for His saying, exalted is He, (He will say, "Enter"), there are two views:

The first: that Allah, exalted is He, says this.

The second: Muqatil said it is from the speech of the keeper of the Fire.

This disagreement is based on whether He, exalted is He, speaks with the disbelievers or not. We have already discussed this question at length.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Enter into nations﴾, there are two views:

The first view: the sense is, "Enter into the Fire along with nations." On this view, there is an ellipsis (iḍmār, a implied element not stated) and a figurative usage (majāz, non-literal use of a word). The ellipsis is because we have implied in it the phrase "into the Fire." The figurative usage is because we have taken the word "fī" (in) to mean "maʿa" (with), since we say the meaning of His saying "in nations" is "with nations."

The second view: one does not posit an ellipsis or a figurative usage. The sense is, "Enter into nations in the Fire." The meaning of entering into nations is entering among them. His saying, ﴿that have passed away before you, of jinn and humankind﴾, means that their time has gone before your time. This indicates that He, exalted is He, does not cast all the disbelievers into the Fire at once, but one group after another, so that among them there is one who precedes and one who follows, in order for this statement to be true, and so that the one entering from the nation sees in the Fire those who went before it.

His saying, ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾: the intended meaning is that the people of the Fire curse one another, so some of them disown others, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the righteous﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 67].

By His saying, "its sister," is meant sister in religion. The meaning is that polytheists curse polytheists, and likewise Jews curse Jews, Christians curse Christians, and the same applies to Magians, Sabians, and the rest of the religions of misguidance.

His saying, ﴿until, when they have all overtaken one another therein﴾: that is, they caught up with one another (tadārakū), in the sense of following one another closely and gathering together in the Fire, and some of them overtook others and settled together with them. ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them﴾. There are two issues here.

First issue: regarding the explanation of "the first" and "the last," there are two views:

The first: Muqatil said: "the last of them" means the last to enter the Fire, and "the first of them" means the first to enter it.

The second: "the last of them" in rank, who are the followers and the lowly, and "the first of them" in rank, who are the leaders and chiefs.

Second issue: the "lām" in His saying, "to the last of them," is the lām of purpose (lām al-ajal), and the meaning is: for their sake and for their misleading of them, they said, ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us﴾. It is not meant that they spoke this statement to the first of them, because they did not address the first of them; rather they addressed Allah, exalted is He, with this speech.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us﴾, the meaning is that the followers say: the earlier ones misled us. Know that this misleading occurs from the earlier ones to the later ones in two ways:

One of them: by calling to falsehood and adorning it in their eyes, and striving to conceal the proofs that refute those falsehoods.

The second way: that the later ones venerate those earlier ones, so they imitate them in those falsehoods and fabrications which they devised, and take them as examples, so that this becomes a resemblance to the earlier ones' undertaking of misleading.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related about these later ones that they call down for the earlier ones an increase in punishment, which is His saying: ﴿So give them a double punishment of the Fire.﴾ Regarding the "double" (ḍiʿf), there are two views:

The first view: Abu ʿUbayda said: "ḍiʿf" is the equivalent of a thing once. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him, said something close to this, when he said about a man who made a bequest, "Give so-and-so double the share of my son." He said: he is given an equal amount twice.

The second view: al-Azhari said: "ḍiʿf" in the speech of the Arabs means an equal amount and whatever exceeds it, and it is not restricted to two equal amounts. It is permissible in the speech of the Arabs to say, "This is its double," meaning two equal amounts or three equal amounts. This is because ḍiʿf in origin is an unlimited increase. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿As for those, they will have the recompense of the double for what they did﴾ [Saba: 37], and He did not intend by it one equal amount nor two, but the most appropriate thing for it is that it be made ten times, based on His saying: ﴿Whoever brings a good deed will have ten times its like﴾ [al-Anʿam: 160]. So it is established that the least of the ḍiʿf is bounded, which is the equal amount, while its greater part is unbounded, extending to no end.

As for the question of al-Shafiʿi, may Allah have mercy on him: know that the estate is tied to the rights of the heirs. However, for the sake of the bequest we have directed a portion of it to the beneficiary, and the certain amount in the bequest is the equal amount, while the rest is doubtful. So we took the certain and set aside the doubtful. For this reason, in that case we took ḍiʿf to mean two equal amounts.
