[Page 63]

The purpose of this verse is to complete the discussion of the threat against the disbelievers. In the preceding verse He said: ﴿And those who denied Our signs and were arrogant towards them, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾. Then, in this verse, God explains the manner of that eternal abiding for those deniers who were arrogant, through His saying: ﴿who denied Our signs﴾, meaning the proofs that point to the matters that are the foundations of religion. The Dahriyya (materialists who deny a Creator) deny the proofs for the affirmation of the Essence and the Attributes; the polytheists deny the proofs of Divine Oneness (tawhid); those who deny prophethood deny the proofs that indicate the validity of prophethood; those who deny the prophethood of Muhammad deny the proofs that indicate the validity of his prophethood; and those who deny the Return (ma'ad) deny the proofs that indicate the validity of the Return. So His saying ﴿denied Our signs﴾ encompasses all of these. The meaning of istikbar (arrogance) is seeking to elevate oneself through falsehood, and this word, when applied to human beings, indicates blame. God said concerning Pharaoh: ﴿And he and his hosts were arrogant in the land without right﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: Abu 'Amr read (lā tuftaḥu) with a ta' and without emphasis (tashdid), Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a ya' and without emphasis, and the rest read it with a ta' and with emphasis. As for the reading with emphasis, its basis is God's saying: ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ [al-An'am: 44], and ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven﴾ [al-Qamar: 11]. As for the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, its basis is that the verb is preceded (by its subject in the feminine, so the verb is marked as masculine).

The second issue: concerning His saying: ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ there are several views. Ibn 'Abbas said: it means they will not be opened for their deeds, nor for their supplications, nor for anything they intend by it the obedience of God. This interpretation is derived from God's saying: ﴿To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it﴾ [Fatir: 10], and from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in 'Illiyyin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 18]. Al-Suddi and others said: the gates of heaven will not be opened for their souls, while they are opened for the souls of the believers.

This interpretation is supported by what is narrated in a long hadith: "Indeed the soul of the believer is raised up to heaven, and it is asked to be admitted, and it is said: 'Welcome to the good soul that was in the good body,' and this is said to it until it reaches the seventh heaven. And for the soul of the disbeliever it is asked to be admitted, and it is said to it: 'Return, reproached, for indeed the gates of heaven will not be opened for you.'"

The third view: Paradise is in heaven, so the meaning is that they are not permitted to ascend to heaven, and there is no path for them to it, so that they might enter Paradise.

The fourth view: blessing and good will not descend upon them. This is derived from His saying: ﴿So We opened the gates of heaven with water pouring forth﴾ [al-Qamar: 11]. I say: this verse indicates that souls are only happy either because goods of every kind descend upon them from heaven, or because the deeds of those souls ascend to the heavens. This indicates that the heavens are the place of the joy of souls and the places of their happiness, from them descend the goods and blessings, and to them ascend the souls when they attain the perfection of happiness. Since the matter is so, His saying ﴿the gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾ is among the greatest kinds of warning and threat.

As for His saying: ﴿and they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾, there are several issues concerning it.

The first issue: al-Wulūj means entering. The camel is well known. Al-summ, with a fatha or a damma on the sin, is the eye of the needle. Ibn Sirin read (summ) with a damma. The author of al-Kashshaf said: it is narrated with all three vowel forms (summ, samm, simm). Every small opening in the body is a summ, and its plural is sumum; from this comes the saying "al-summ" (poison), because it penetrates by its subtlety into the pores of the body until it reaches the heart. And al-khiyat is that with which one sews. Al-Farra' said: it is also said khiyat and mikhyat, just as one says izar and mi'zar, lihaf and milhaf, qina' and miqna'. The camel was singled out from among all animals because it is the largest animal in body according to the Arabs. The poet said:

The bodies of camels and the dreams of sparrows.

So the body of the camel is the largest of bodies, and the eye of the needle is the narrowest of openings, so the camel passing through that narrow opening is impossible. When God made their entry into Paradise conditional upon the fulfilment of this condition, and this condition is impossible, and it is established in the intellects that what is conditional upon the impossible is impossible, it is necessary that their entry into Paradise be definitively despaired of.

The second issue: the author of al-Kashshaf said: Ibn 'Abbas read (al-jummal) on the pattern of al-qummal, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr read (al-jumal) on the pattern of al-nughar. It was also read (al-jumul) on the pattern of al-qufl, (al-jumul) on the pattern of al-nusub, and (al-jaml) on the pattern of al-habl. Its meaning is a thick rope (qalas), because it is strands of rope gathered together and made into a single bundle. And it is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that God is too exalted to be compared to a camel, meaning that a rope is suitable for the thread that passes through the eye of the needle, while a camel is not suitable for it. However, we have mentioned the benefit in it.

The third issue: those who believe in metempsychosis (tanasukh, the transmigration of souls) argued with this verse, saying: the souls that were in human bodies, when they disobeyed and sinned, after the death of the bodies they are returned from one body to another, and they continue to remain in punishment until they transfer from the body of a camel to the body of a worm that penetrates the eye of the needle. Then they become purified from those sins and disobediences, and then they enter Paradise and reach happiness. Know that the doctrine of metempsychosis is false, and this argument is weak. And God knows best.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And thus We recompense the criminals﴾, meaning: and like what We have described, We recompense the criminals. The criminals here, God knows best, are the disbelievers, because the characteristics of them that were previously mentioned are denial of God's signs and arrogance towards them.

Know that when God explained their condition, that they will not enter Paradise at all, He also explained that they will enter the Fire, so He said: ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hellfire and above them coverings﴾. And in this there are two issues.

The first issue: al-mihad is the plural of mahd, which is a bed. Al-Azhari said: the root of mahd in the language is spreading out, and a bed is called mihad because it is spread out. The plural of ghawashi is the plural of ghashiya, which is everything that covers you, meaning that envelops you. Jahannam is not declined because of the combination of feminine gender and definiteness in it. It was also said its derivation is from al-jahmah, which is harshness, as one says: a man with a harsh (jahm) face, meaning coarse of face, and it was named this because of the severity of its punishment. The exegetes said: the intent of this verse is to report that the Fire encompasses them from every side, so for them there is a covering and a spread, a bed and a blanket.

The second issue: one may say: ghawashi, on the pattern of fawa'il, would then be undeclinable, so how did tanwin (nunation) enter it? Its answer, according to the school of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is that this is a plural, and the plural is heavier than the singular, and it is also the greatest plural to which pluralities culminate, so that added to its heaviness, then the ya' fell at its end, and it is heavy, so when these things were combined in it they lightened it by deleting its ya'. When the ya' was deleted it fell short of the pattern fawa'il and became ghawashin on the pattern of janah, so tanwin entered it because it had fallen short of that pattern.

As for His saying: ﴿And thus We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: it means those who associated partners with God and took besides Him a god. According to this determination, the wrongdoers here are the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 42–43 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believed and did righteous deeds — We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity. Those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts; rivers will flow beneath them. And they will say, "Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this. And we would never have been guided if Allah had not guided us. The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth." And they will be called, "This is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had completed the discussion of the threat (wa'id), He followed it with the promise (wa'd) in this verse. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that most of the scholars of meanings (ashab al-ma'ani) hold that His saying, ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) that occurred between the subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence) and the predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence). The construction would be: "Those who believed and did righteous deeds — those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein eternally." It is good for this statement to occur between the subject and predicate because it is of the same kind as this statement: when He mentioned their righteous deeds, He mentioned that those deeds lie within their capacity and do not exceed their power. It also serves as an admonition to the disbelievers that Paradise, despite its great station, is reached by easy action without enduring hardship. Others said: its place is a predicate of that subject, and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted; as if it were said: "We do not burden any soul of them except according to its capacity." The returning pronoun was omitted because it is known.

The second issue: The meaning of wus' (capacity) is what a person can do in a state of ease and facility, not in a state of constriction and hardship. The evidence for this is that Mu'adh ibn Jabal said regarding this verse: "Except its ease, not its hardship." As for the utmost effort, it is called juhd (exertion), not wus'. Whoever thinks that wus' means expending the utmost effort has erred.

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i said: This indicates the invalidity of the doctrine of the Mujbira (determinists) that Allah, exalted is He, imposes on the servant what he is not able to do, because Allah, exalted is He, has denied this about them. When this principle is established, their view on the creation of actions is also invalidated. For if the creator of the actions of the servants were Allah, exalted is He, that would be imposing what cannot be borne. For if He imposes that act upon him at the time He creates it in him, then this is imposing what cannot be borne, since it is a command to achieve what is already achieved, which is not within one's power. And if He imposes it upon him at a time when He has not created that act in him, that too would be imposing what cannot be borne, because on this assumption the servant has no power to bring about and effect that act. They said: Furthermore, when this principle is established, it becomes evident that the capability (istita'ah) is prior to the act. For if it were present together with the act, then the disbeliever would have no power to believe while being commanded to do so, and this would be imposing what cannot be borne. Since this verse indicates the negation of imposing what cannot be borne, the invalidity of these two principles is established.

For He imposes on the servant the bringing about of the act in a state where the motives toward the act and its abandonment are equal, or in a state where one of the two motives outweighs the other. The first is false, because bringing about (ijad) is preponderance (tarjih) for the side of the act, and the occurrence of preponderance in a state of equality is impossible. The second is also false, because in the state of preponderance the occurrence is necessary. If the command is directed at the preponderant side, it is a command to achieve what is already achieved. If it is directed at the outweighed side, it is a command to achieve the outweighed while it is outweighed, which is a command to combine two contradictories, and that is impossible. Therefore, whatever you propose as an answer to this question is our answer to your statement. And Allah knows best.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾, know that naz' (removal) of a thing is uprooting it from its place, and ghill is hatred (hiqd). The lexicographers said: It is that which penetrates with its subtlety to the core of the heart; that is, it enters. From it comes ghulul (embezzlement), which is reaching minor sins by stratagem. It is said: ingharra fi al-shay' and taghalghala fihi when he enters it subtly, like love that penetrates to the core of the heart.

Having known this, we say: This verse has two interpretations.

The first interpretation: The meaning is that We removed the grudges that some of them had against others in the worldly life. The meaning of removing resentment is the purification of natures, the elimination of whisperings, and the prevention of their reaching the hearts, for since Satan is in punishment, he is not free to cast whisperings into the hearts. To this meaning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) alluded when he said: "I hope that I, 'Uthman, Talha, and al-Zubayr are among those of whom Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts﴾."

The second interpretation: The meaning is that the ranks of the people of Paradise vary according to their perfection and deficiency, and Allah, exalted is He, removed envy from their hearts, so that the one of lower rank does not envy the one of higher rank.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: This interpretation is preferable to the first, so that it may stand in contrast to what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned about some of the people of the Fire disowning others and cursing one another, so that it may be known that the state of the people of Paradise in this respect too is different from the state of the people of the Fire.

If they say: How is it conceivable that a person sees great blessings and lofty ranks, and sees himself deprived of them and unable to attain them, yet his nature does not incline toward them and he does not grieve because of being deprived of them? If that is conceivable, why is it not also conceivable that Allah, exalted is He, would restore them and not create in them the desire for eating, drinking, and sexual intercourse, and render them independent of these?

We say: All of this is possible, and Allah, exalted is He, is capable of it. However, He, exalted is He, promised to remove rancor and envy from the hearts, and He did not promise to remove the desire for eating and drinking from the souls. Thus the difference between the two categories becomes evident.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rivers will flow beneath them﴾. The meaning is that just as He freed them from the bond of rancor, envy, and greed for seeking more, He bestowed upon them great pleasures. His saying ﴿rivers will flow beneath them﴾ is part of Allah's mercy, His favor, His kindness, and kinds of unveilings (mukashafat) and spiritual felicities.

[66]

Then He, exalted is He, related about the people of Paradise that they said: ﴿Praise be to Allah, who guided us to this.﴾ Our companions said: The meaning of "Allah guided us" is that He gave capability and added to it the decisive motive, and He made the combination of capability and that motive a cause for the occurrence of that virtue. For if He gave capability but did not create that motive, the effect would not occur; and if Allah created a counter-motive opposing the other diverting motives, the act would also not occur. But when He created capability and created the decisive motive, and the combination of capability with the specific motive became a cause for the act, guidance was in reality accomplished by the decree of Allah, exalted is He, and His creation and bringing into being.

The Mu'tazila said: The praise came only because He, exalted is He, gave reason, set up the proofs, and removed the obstacles; at this point the matter returns to the discussions of compulsion and destiny in their full detail.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And we would never have been guided if Allah had not guided us.﴾ Regarding this there are issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Amir recited "wa-ma kunna" without the waw (conjunction), and it is so in the codices of the people of Syria; the rest recited it with the waw. The reason for Ibn 'Amir's reading is that His saying ﴿And we would never have been guided if Allah had not guided us﴾ functions as an explanation (tafsir) of His saying ﴿He guided us to this﴾. Since one of them is the very same as the other, it is necessary to omit the conjunctive particle.

The second issue: His saying ﴿And we would never have been guided if Allah had not guided us﴾ is evidence that the one who is guided is the one whom Allah guides, and if Allah does not guide him, he is not guided. Indeed, we say: The doctrine of the Mu'tazila is that everything Allah, exalted is He, did regarding the prophets, peace be upon them, and the friends of Allah of kinds of guidance and direction, He has also done for all the disbelievers and wrongdoers; the distinction between the believer and the disbeliever, and between the rightly guided and the falsifier, came about only through his own striving and his own choice. Therefore it would be obligatory upon him to praise himself, because it was he who obtained faith for himself, he who brought himself to the ranks of the Gardens, and he who delivered himself from the levels of the Fire. But since he did not praise himself at all, and praised only Allah, we know that the Guide is none other than Allah, glorified is He.

Then He, exalted is He, related about them that they said: ﴿The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth.﴾ This is from the speech of the people of Paradise when they saw directly what the messengers had promised them, and they said: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth."

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they will be called, "This is Paradise."﴾ Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: That calling is either from Allah, exalted is He, or from the angels, and the more appropriate view is that the caller is Allah, glorified is He.

The second issue: Al-Zajjaj mentioned two possibilities regarding the particle "an" here:

The first: It is a lightened form of the heavy (an) (anna), and the implied pronoun is for the matter (ash-shan), and the meaning is: "They were called, that it is this Paradise," i.e., they were called with this statement.

The second: He said: The better view in my opinion is that "an" is in the sense of explaining the calling, and the meaning is: "And they were called, i.e., this is Paradise." The meaning: It was said to them: "This is Paradise," like His saying: ﴿And the chiefs among them set off, saying, "Walk on and be steadfast."﴾ [Sad: 6], meaning: "walk on." He said: He said "this" (tilkum) because they had been promised it in the world; as if it were said to them: "This is that which you were promised." As for His saying "you have been made to inherit it" (uwritum-uha), there are two views:

The first view, which is the view of the scholars of meanings, is that its meaning is: it has come to you as inheritance comes to its heirs. Inheritance may be used in the language without meaning the removal of ownership from the dead to the living, as one says: "This deed will bequeath you honor" (yuwrithuka al-sharaf), i.e., will bring you to it, and "will bequeath you shame." Some say: They were given those dwellings without toil at that moment, so it became like inheritance.

The second view: The people of Paradise inherit the dwellings of the people of the Fire. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is not a disbeliever or a believer but that he has a dwelling in Paradise and in the Fire. When the people of Paradise enter Paradise and the people of the Fire enter the Fire, Paradise is raised up for the people of the Fire, and they look at their dwellings therein. It is said to them: 'These would have been your dwellings had you obeyed Allah.' Then it is said: 'O people of Paradise, inherit them for what you used to do,' and the dwellings of the people of the Fire are divided among the people of Paradise."

* * *

As for His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾, there are issues:

The first issue: The one who says that "the deed necessitates this reward" holds on to this verse, for the particle "bi" (for/because of) in His saying ﴿for what you used to do﴾ indicates causation (al-'illiyyah), and this indicates that the deed necessitates this reward. Our answer: It is a cause of the reward, but because the Law made it a cause for it, not because it is in itself necessitating that reward. The evidence for this is that the blessings of Allah upon the servant have no end, so when the servant performs some acts of obedience, these acts fall in exchange for those past blessings, and it is impossible for them to become a cause necessitating a reward that comes later.

The second issue: Some objected and said: This verse indicates that the servant enters Paradise only by his deeds, while His statement, upon him be peace: "None will enter Paradise by his deeds, but he enters it by the mercy of Allah, exalted is He," contradicts it. Our answer to what we have mentioned is: Deeds do not necessitate entry into Paradise in themselves; rather, they necessitate it because Allah, exalted is He, by His grace made them a sign of it and a means of knowing it. Furthermore, since the one who fulfills the righteous deed is Allah, exalted is He, entry into Paradise in reality is nothing but by the grace of Allah, exalted is He.

Question three: The judge (al-Qadi) said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿And they will be called out: "This is the Garden; you have been made its inheritors for what you used to do."﴾ are a general address concerning all the believers. This indicates that everyone who enters the Garden enters it by his deeds. Given this, the view of those who say that the sinners (al-fussaq) enter the Garden by the grace (tafaddul) of God, exalted is He, is untenable.

Having established this, we say: it is necessary that the sinner not leave the Fire. For if he were to leave it, he would either enter the Garden or not enter it. The second is invalid by consensus (ijma'). As for the first, it must be either that he enters the Garden by way of grace or by way of entitlement (istihqaq). The first is invalid, because we have shown that this verse indicates that no one enters the Garden by grace.

The second is also invalid, because once he has entered the Fire, it must be said that he was deserving of punishment. So if he were admitted to the Garden by way of entitlement, it would follow that he deserves reward. In that case, it would follow that the combination of deserving reward and deserving punishment occurs, and this is impossible, because reward is a lasting benefit free of any admixture of harm, while punishment is a lasting harm free of any admixture of benefit. The combination of the two is impossible. Since this is so, the combination of the occurrence of the entitlement to both is impossible.

The answer: this is based on the premise that the entitlement to reward and to punishment cannot coincide. We have gone to great lengths in refuting this argument in the chapter of al-Baqarah. And God knows best.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 44–45:

﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire, "We have found true what our Lord promised us. Have you found true what your Lord promised you?" They will say, "Yes." Then a caller will proclaim between them, "The curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers, who avert [people] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked, and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter."﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the threat against the disbelievers and the reward of the people of faith and righteous deeds, He followed it with mention of the debates that take place between the two groups. These are the circumstances mentioned in this verse.

Know also that when He mentioned in the preceding verse His saying, ﴿And they will be called out to: "That is the Garden which you have been made to inherit"﴾, this indicates that they had settled in the Garden at the time of this calling. When He then said, ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾, this indicates that this calling took place after they had settled. Ibn 'Abbas said: "We have found true what our Lord promised us in the world of reward, so have you found true what your Lord promised you of punishment?" The purpose of this question is to show that they have reached complete happiness, and to cause grief to the heart of the enemy.

Here there are some questions:

**The first question:** If the Garden is in the highest heavens and the Fire is in the lowest depths of the earth, how can this calling be valid despite such great distance?

The answer: This is valid according to our view, because for us great distance and great nearness are not barriers to perception. Al-Qadi accepted this and said: Among the scholars there are those who say that sound has a special property, that distance alone does not prevent it from being heard.

**The second question:** Does this calling take place from all the people of the Garden to all the people of the Fire, or from some of them to some of them?

The answer: His saying, ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾, conveys generality. When a plural is set against a plural, each individual is distributed against each individual. Each group of the people of the Garden calls out to whoever among the disbelievers they knew in the world.

**The third question:** What is the meaning of (an) in His saying, ﴿an qad wajadna﴾ ("that we have found")?

The answer: It may be the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah) form, and it may be the explanatory (mufassirah) form, like the one that preceded in His saying, ﴿an tilkumu al-jannah﴾ ("that this is the Garden"), and likewise in His saying, ﴿an la'natu Allahi 'ala al-zalimin﴾ ("that the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers").

**The fourth question:** Why was it not said, "What your Lord promised you as true," just as it was said, ﴿ma wa'adana rabbuna﴾ ("what our Lord promised us")?

The answer: His saying, ﴿ma wa'adana rabbuna haqqan﴾ indicates that He, exalted is He, addressed them with this promise. Being addressed by Allah, exalted is He, with this promise necessitates additional honour, and additional honour is fitting for the state of the believers. As for the disbeliever, he is not worthy that Allah, exalted is He, should address him. For this reason, Allah, exalted is He, did not mention that He addressed them with this address, but rather mentioned that He explained this ruling.

[Page 70]

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿Qalu na'am﴾ ("They will say, 'Yes'"), there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The verse indicates that the disbelievers, on the Day of Resurrection, will acknowledge that the promise and threat of Allah are true and truthful, and this is not possible unless they, on the Day of Resurrection, know the Essence of Allah and His attributes.

If it is said: Since they know His Essence and attributes, and it is established that among His attributes is that He accepts repentance from His servants, and they know by necessity that upon the acceptance of repentance they will be freed from punishment, then why do they not repent so as to free themselves from punishment?

It is not open to anyone to say that He accepts repentance only in this world, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants and pardons evil deeds﴾ [al-Shura: 25] is general across all circumstances. Furthermore, repentance is an acknowledgment of sin and an affirmation of humiliation and wretchedness, and what befits the Merciful, the Wise, is to overlook this condition, whether in this world or in the Hereafter.

The theologians (al-mutakallimun) answered: The intensity of their preoccupation with those severe pains prevents them from undertaking repentance. One might say: If those pains do not prevent them from these debates, how can they prevent them from repentance, through which they would be freed from those severe pains?

Know that the Mu'tazilah, who say that it is obligatory upon Allah to accept repentance, have no escape from this question. As for our companions (the Ash'arites), since they say that this is not obligatory by reason, they say: It is for Allah, exalted is He, to accept repentance in this world, and not to accept it in the Hereafter, so the question is resolved. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** Sibawayh said: (na'am) is a affirmation of a promise and an affirmation of truth. Those who explained his words said: Its meaning is that it is used sometimes to affirm a promise and sometimes to affirm truth, not that it is both at once. Do you not see that if one says, "Will you give me?" and the other says, "Na'am," it is a promise with no affirmation of truth in it? And if one says, "Such and such has happened," and you say, "Na'am," you have spoken the truth with no promise in it. Also, if you ask about an affirmative matter, as one says, "Will Zayd stand?" and you say, "Na'am." Had the affirmation been a negation, you would say, "Bala," and not "Na'am." So the word na'am is specific to answering an affirmative, and the word bala is specific to negation, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Bala"﴾ [al-A'raf: 172].

**The third issue:** al-Kisa'i (in his reading) read (na'im) with a kasra on the 'ayn in the whole Qur'an. Abu al-Hasan said: They are two dialects. Abu Hatim said: The kasra is not well known. Al-Kisa'i argued that it was narrated from 'Umar that he asked some people about something, and they said, "Na'am." 'Umar said: "As for al-na'am, it is camels." Abu 'Ubayda said: This narration from 'Umar is not well known.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Fa-adhdhana mu'adhdhinun baynahum﴾ ("Then a caller proclaimed among them"), there are two issues:

**The first issue:** The meaning of ta'dhin in the language is calling out and making a sound to inform. The adhan for prayer is an informing of it and of its time. They said regarding ﴿adhdhana mu'adhdhin﴾: a caller called out and made both parties hear. Ibn 'Abbas said: That caller is one of the angels, and he is the one who holds the trumpet (sur).

**The second issue:** His saying (baynahum) ("among them") may be an adverbial complement (zarf) of (adhdhana) ("proclaimed"), the meaning being: the caller made that proclamation among them, in their midst; and it may be an attribute of (mu'adhdhin) ("caller"), the meaning being: a caller from among them proclaimed with that proclamation. The first is preferable. And Allah knows best.

**The third attribute:** His saying: ﴿wa-yabghunaha 'iwajan﴾ ("and seek to make it crooked"). What is meant by it is casting doubts and misgivings upon the proofs of the true religion.

Know that when He, exalted is He, made clear that this caller pronounced that curse upon the wrongdoers described with these three attributes, this was an explicit statement that this curse fell only upon the disbelievers. This indicates the corruption of what al-Qadi stated, that the curse encompasses both the sinner and the disbeliever. And Allah knows best.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights (al-A'raf) are men who recognize each by their marks. They call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," though they have not entered it, yet they aspire to it.﴾ ﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And between them is a barrier﴾ means between Paradise and the Fire, or between the two groups. This barrier is the well-known one mentioned in His saying: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them, having a gate﴾ [al-Hadid: 13].

If it is asked: what need is there for this wall to be erected between Paradise and the Fire, since it is established that Paradise is above the heavens and that Hell is in the lowest of the lowest?

We say: the distance of one from the other does not prevent a wall and a barrier from being between them. As for al-A'raf, it is the plural of 'urf, which is every high, elevated place. From it come the mane of the horse ('urf al-faras) and the crest of the rooster ('urf al-dik), and every elevated thing on the earth is an 'urf, because by its elevation it becomes more distinct (a'raf) than what is lower than it.

Having understood this, we say: regarding the interpretation of the word al-A'raf there are two opinions.

The first opinion, which most scholars hold, is that al-A'raf means the upper parts of that wall struck between Paradise and the Fire. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. It is also related from him that he said: "al-A'raf is the high ground of the bridge (al-Sirat)."

The second opinion is that of al-Hasan and of al-Zajjaj, in one of his two views: that His saying ﴿and upon the heights﴾ means "and upon the knowledge (ma'rifah) of the people of Paradise and Hell are men who recognize every one of the people of Paradise and Hell by their marks." It was said to al-Hasan: "Are they a people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal?" He struck his thigh and then said: "They are a people whom Allah the Exalted has placed in recognizing the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, distinguishing some from others. By Allah, I do not know, perhaps some of them are with us now."

As for those who hold the first opinion, they differ regarding who the people upon the A'raf are. Opinions on this are numerous, but they are restricted to two:

One: it is said that they are the nobles among the people of obedience and the people of reward.

The second: it is said that they are groups who occupy the lower rank among the people of reward.

As for the first assumption, there are several views:

One of them: Abu Mijlaz said: "They are angels who recognize the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire." It was said to him: "Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And upon the heights are men﴾, and you claim they are angels?" He said: "The angels are males, not females."

One may say: the description by manhood is only appropriate in a place where a female is in opposition to a man, and since it is impossible for an angel to be female, it is impossible to describe them as men.

The second view: they say they are the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah the Exalted seated them upon the high points of that wall, to distinguish them from the rest of the people of the Resurrection and to show their nobility and the loftiness of their rank. He seated them in that high place so that they would be overlooking the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, observing their conditions and the measures of their reward and punishment.

The third view: they say they are the martyrs, because He the Exalted described the companions of al-A'raf as recognizing every one of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire.

Then some people said: they recognize the people of Paradise by their faces being bright and joyful, and the people of the Fire by the blackness of their faces and the blueness of their eyes. But this view is invalid, because He the Exalted specified the people of al-A'raf as recognizing every one of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire by their marks. If what they mentioned were intended, the people of al-A'raf would have no distinction in this recognition, because every one of the people of Paradise and of the Fire recognizes these conditions of the people of Paradise and of the Fire. Since this view is invalid, it is established that what is meant by His saying ﴿they recognize each by their marks﴾ is that they used to recognize, in the world, the people of goodness, faith and righteousness, and the people of evil, disbelief and corruption. They were, in the world, witnesses of Allah over the people of faith and obedience and over the people of disbelief and disobedience. So He the Exalted seats them upon al-A'raf, which are the lofty and elevated places, so that they may be overseeing all,
[Page 73]
bearing witness over each one concerning what befits him, and knowing that the people of reward have reached the ranks, and the people of punishment have reached the depths.

If it is said: these three views are invalid, because He the Exalted said regarding the companions of al-A'raf that they ﴿have not entered it, though they aspire to it﴾, meaning they have not entered Paradise while they aspire to enter it, and this description is not fitting for prophets, angels, or martyrs.

Those who hold this view answered by saying: it is not far-fetched to say that He the Exalted has made clear among the attributes of the companions of al-A'raf that their entry into Paradise is delayed. The reason for this is that He the Exalted distinguished them from the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire and seated them upon those lofty battlements and elevated places, so that they may witness the conditions of the people of Paradise and the conditions of the people of the Fire, and great joy will reach them by witnessing those conditions. Then, when the people of Paradise settle in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, Allah the Exalted will then move them to their lofty places in Paradise. Thus it is established that their not yet having entered Paradise does not prevent the perfection of their nobility or the loftiness of their rank. As for His saying ﴿while they aspire﴾, the aspiration here means certainty. Do you not see that He the Exalted said, relating about Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my error on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]; and that hope was a hope of certainty, so it is likewise here. This is the explanation of the view of those who say that the companions of al-A'raf are the nobles of the people of Paradise.

The second opinion is that of those who say: the companions of al-A'raf are groups who occupy the lower rank among the people of reward. Those who hold this opinion mentioned several views:

One of them: they are a people whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal, so they were neither of the people of Paradise nor of the people of the Fire. Allah the Exalted stopped them upon these A'raf, because it is an intermediate rank between Paradise and the Fire. Then Allah the Exalted will admit them into Paradise by His bounty and mercy, and they will be the last people to enter Paradise. This is the view of Hudhayfah and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the preference of al-Farra'.

Al-Juba'i and the Qadi criticized this view and argued against its invalidity with two arguments:

The first: they said that His saying the Exalted: ﴿And they will be called: "This is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."﴾ indicates that everyone who enters Paradise must necessarily be deserving of entering it, and this prevents the claim that there exist people who deserve neither Paradise nor the Fire, and then they enter Paradise by sheer grace, not by way of deserving.

The second: that their being of the companions of al-A'raf indicates that He the Exalted distinguished them from all the people of the Resurrection by seating them upon lofty places overlooking the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, and this is a great honor, and such honor is fitting only for the nobles. Without doubt, those whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal have a deficient rank, so such honor is not fitting for them.

The answer to the first: it is possible that His saying ﴿This is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit﴾ is addressed to specific people, so it does not necessarily follow that this applies to all the people of Paradise.

The answer to the second: we do not accept that He the Exalted seated them upon those places in the manner of specifically honoring them with additional honor and esteem. Rather, He seated them there because it is like an intermediate rank between Paradise and the Fire. And is the dispute about anything other than this? Thus it is established that the argument on which they relied to refute this view is weak.

* * *

The second of the views mentioned in the interpretation of the companions of al-A'raf: they said the meaning of the companions of al-A'raf is groups who went out to the raid without the permission of their parents, were martyred, and were detained between Paradise and the Fire.

[Page 74]

Know that this view falls under the first opinion, because these people became companions of al-A'raf only because their disobedience equaled their obedience through jihad. This is one of the matters included under the first view. And even granting that this view is correct, there is no sense in restricting this case and confining the wording of the verse to it.

The third view: Abdullah ibn al-Harith said: "They are the poor among the people of Paradise."

The fourth view: some said: "They are the sinful among the people of prayer, whom Allah pardons and settles in al-A'raf." All of this is the explanation of the view of those who say that al-A'raf refers to the lofty places upon the wall struck between Paradise and the Fire.

As for those who say that al-A'raf refers to the men who recognize the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, this view is also not far-fetched, except that these people must have an elevated place from which they overlook the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire. In that case, this view returns to the first view. These are the details of people's opinions on this subject. And Allah knows best.

Then He the Exalted informed that the companions of al-A'raf recognize each of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire by their marks (simah). They differed regarding the meaning of His saying "bi-simahum" (by their marks) into several views:

The first view, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas: the mark (sima) of the righteous man among the people of Paradise is the whiteness of his face, as He the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]; and their faces being radiant, smiling and joyful; and each of them being bright-marked (aghharr muhajjal) from the traces of ablution; and the sign of the disbelievers is the blackness of their faces, and their faces having dust upon them, covered with gloom; and their eyes being blue.

One may say: when they have witnessed the people of Paradise in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, what need is there to infer that they are of the people of Paradise through these signs? For this would be like inferring what is already known through the senses, and that is invalid.

Furthermore, this verse indicates that the companions of al-A'raf are specifically characterized by this recognition, and if we interpret it according to this view, this specificity would not remain, because these conditions are perceptible matters, and so no one person is specifically distinguished in recognizing them over another.

The second view concerning the interpretation of this verse is that the companions of al-A'raf used to recognize the believers in the world through the manifest signs of faith and acts of obedience upon them, and they also used to recognize the disbelievers in the world through the manifest signs of disbelief and wickedness upon them. So when they witness those people in the assembly of the Resurrection, they distinguish some from others by those signs which they witnessed upon them in the world. This view is the one preferred.

As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And they call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you"﴾, the meaning is that when they look at the people of Paradise, they greet the people of Paradise, and at this point the speech of the companions of al-A'raf is complete.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿They have not entered it, though they aspire to it﴾. The meaning is that He the Exalted informed that the companions of al-A'raf have not entered Paradise, and yet they aspire to enter it. Then, if we say that the companions of al-A'raf are the nobles of the people of Paradise, we have already mentioned that He the Exalted seated them upon al-A'raf and delayed their entry into Paradise so that they may witness the conditions of the people of Paradise and the Fire. Then He the Exalted moves them to the lofty ranks in Paradise, as it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The people of the highest ranks will be seen by those beneath them as you see the bright star on the horizon of the sky, and Abu Bakr and 'Umar are among them."

The essence of the matter is that the companions of al-A'raf are the noblest of the people of the Resurrection. So when the people of the Resurrection stand at the station of standing, Allah seats the people of al-A'raf upon the A'raf,
[Page 75]
which are the lofty and noble places. Then when He admits the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of the Fire into the Fire, He moves them to the lofty ranks in Paradise, so they will always sit only in the lofty ranks.

Now, if we interpret the people of the A'raf as those who occupy the lower rank among the people of salvation, we say: God makes them sit on the A'raf while they hope, through His grace and kindness, that He will move them from those positions to Paradise.

* * *

As for God's words, ﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire﴾, al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: *al-tilqa'* (تِلْقاءُ) means the direction of meeting, that is, the direction of facing one another. For this reason it is used as a spatial adverb, as one says: "So-and-so is *tilqa'uka*" (in front of you), just as one says: "He is *hidha'uka*" (opposite you). Originally it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adverb. Then al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, related with his chain of transmission from Tha'lab, from the Kufans, and from al-Mubarrad, from the Basrans, that both said: Among the verbal nouns of the pattern *tif'āl* (تِفْعالٌ), only two words have come: *tibyān* (تِبْيانٌ, "explanation") and *tilqā'* (تِلْقاءٌ, "encounter/front"). If these two are set aside, the rule is regular: one says *tif'āl* with a fatḥah on the *tā'* (تَفْعالٌ) for every verbal noun, such as *tasyār* (تَسْيارٌ) and *tarsāl* (تَرْسالٌ). And one says *tif'āl* with a kasrah on the *tā'* (تِفْعالٌ) for every noun (ism), such as *timthāl* (تِمْثالٌ, "statue") and *tiqsār* (تِقْصارٌ). The meaning of the verse is: whenever the eyes of the people of the A'raf fall upon the people of the Fire, they humbly beseech God, Exalted, not to place them among their company. The purpose of all these verses is to instill fear, so that a person will proceed to reflection and inquiry (*nazar* and *istidlāl*), and will not be content with *taqlīd* (blind imitation of tradition without examination), in order to attain the true religion. Thereby he will reach the reward mentioned in these verses and be delivered from the punishment mentioned in them.

[Page 72]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And between them is a barrier, and upon the heights (al-A'raf) are men who recognize each by their marks. They call out to the companions of Paradise, "Peace be upon you," though they have not entered it, yet they aspire to it.﴾ ﴿And when their eyes are turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord, do not place us with the wrongdoing people."﴾

Know that His saying ﴿And between them is a barrier﴾ means between Paradise and the Fire, or between the two groups. This barrier is the well-known one mentioned in His saying: ﴿So a wall will be struck between them, having a gate﴾ [al-Hadid: 13].

If it is asked: what need is there for this wall to be erected between Paradise and the Fire, since it is established that Paradise is above the heavens and that Hell is in the lowest of the lowest?

We say: the distance of one from the other does not prevent a wall and a barrier from being between them. As for al-A'raf, it is the plural of 'urf, which is every high, elevated place. From it come the mane of the horse ('urf al-faras) and the crest of the rooster ('urf al-dik), and every elevated thing on the earth is an 'urf, because by its elevation it becomes more distinct (a'raf) than what is lower than it.

Having understood this, we say: regarding the interpretation of the word al-A'raf there are two opinions.

The first opinion, which most scholars hold, is that al-A'raf means the upper parts of that wall struck between Paradise and the Fire. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. It is also related from him that he said: "al-A'raf is the high ground of the bridge (al-Sirat)."

The second opinion is that of al-Hasan and of al-Zajjaj, in one of his two views: that His saying ﴿and upon the heights﴾ means "and upon the knowledge (ma'rifah) of the people of Paradise and Hell are men who recognize every one of the people of Paradise and Hell by their marks." It was said to al-Hasan: "Are they a people whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal?" He struck his thigh and then said: "They are a people whom Allah the Exalted has placed in recognizing the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, distinguishing some from others. By Allah, I do not know, perhaps some of them are with us now."

As for those who hold the first opinion, they differ regarding who the people upon the A'raf are. Opinions on this are numerous, but they are restricted to two:

One: it is said that they are the nobles among the people of obedience and the people of reward.

The second: it is said that they are groups who occupy the lower rank among the people of reward.

As for the first assumption, there are several views:

One of them: Abu Mijlaz said: "They are angels who recognize the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire." It was said to him: "Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And upon the heights are men﴾, and you claim they are angels?" He said: "The angels are males, not females."

One may say: the description by manhood is only appropriate in a place where a female is in opposition to a man, and since it is impossible for an angel to be female, it is impossible to describe them as men.

The second view: they say they are the prophets, peace be upon them. Allah the Exalted seated them upon the high points of that wall, to distinguish them from the rest of the people of the Resurrection and to show their nobility and the loftiness of their rank. He seated them in that high place so that they would be overlooking the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, observing their conditions and the measures of their reward and punishment.

The third view: they say they are the martyrs, because He the Exalted described the companions of al-A'raf as recognizing every one of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire.

Then some people said: they recognize the people of Paradise by their faces being bright and joyful, and the people of the Fire by the blackness of their faces and the blueness of their eyes. But this view is invalid, because He the Exalted specified the people of al-A'raf as recognizing every one of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire by their marks. If what they mentioned were intended, the people of al-A'raf would have no distinction in this recognition, because every one of the people of Paradise and of the Fire recognizes these conditions of the people of Paradise and of the Fire. Since this view is invalid, it is established that what is meant by His saying ﴿they recognize each by their marks﴾ is that they used to recognize, in the world, the people of goodness, faith and righteousness, and the people of evil, disbelief and corruption. They were, in the world, witnesses of Allah over the people of faith and obedience and over the people of disbelief and disobedience. So He the Exalted seats them upon al-A'raf, which are the lofty and elevated places, so that they may be overseeing all,
[Page 73]
bearing witness over each one concerning what befits him, and knowing that the people of reward have reached the ranks, and the people of punishment have reached the depths.

If it is said: these three views are invalid, because He the Exalted said regarding the companions of al-A'raf that they ﴿have not entered it, though they aspire to it﴾, meaning they have not entered Paradise while they aspire to enter it, and this description is not fitting for prophets, angels, or martyrs.

Then, when the people of Paradise settle in Paradise and the people of the Fire in the Fire, Allah the Exalted will then move them to their lofty places in Paradise. Thus it is established that their not yet having entered Paradise does not prevent the perfection of their nobility or the loftiness of their rank. As for His saying ﴿while they aspire﴾, the aspiration here means certainty. Do you not see that He the Exalted said, relating about Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿And the one from whom I hope that He will forgive my error on the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 82]; and that hope was a hope of certainty, so it is likewise here. This is the explanation of the view of those who say that the companions of al-A'raf are the nobles of the people of Paradise.

The second opinion is that of those who say: the companions of al-A'raf are groups who occupy the lower rank among the people of reward. Those who hold this opinion mentioned several views:

One of them: they are a people whose good deeds and bad deeds were equal, so they were neither of the people of Paradise nor of the people of the Fire. Allah the Exalted stopped them upon these A'raf, because it is an intermediate rank between Paradise and the Fire. Then Allah the Exalted will admit them into Paradise by His bounty and mercy, and they will be the last people to enter Paradise. This is the view of Hudhayfah and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, and the preference of al-Farra'.

Al-Juba'i and the Qadi criticized this view and argued against its invalidity with two arguments:

The first: they said that His saying the Exalted: ﴿And they will be called: "This is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do."﴾ indicates that everyone who enters Paradise must necessarily be deserving of entering it, and this prevents the claim that there exist people who deserve neither Paradise nor the Fire, and then they enter Paradise by sheer grace, not by way of deserving.

The second: that their being of the companions of al-A'raf indicates that He the Exalted distinguished them from all the people of the Resurrection by seating them upon lofty places overlooking the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, and this is a great honor, and such honor is fitting only for the nobles. Without doubt, those whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal have a deficient rank, so such honor is not fitting for them.

The answer to the first: it is possible that His saying ﴿This is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit﴾ is addressed to specific people, so it does not necessarily follow that this applies to all the people of Paradise.

The answer to the second: we do not accept that He the Exalted seated them upon those places in the manner of specifically honoring them with additional honor and esteem. Rather, He seated them there because it is like an intermediate rank between Paradise and the Fire. And is the dispute about anything other than this? Thus it is established that the argument on which they relied to refute this view is weak.

* * *

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 7, verses 48–50:**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the companions of the Heights will call out to men whom they recognize by their marks, saying, "Neither your gathering nor your arrogance availed you."﴾ ﴿"Are these the ones you swore that Allah would not reach with mercy?" "Enter Paradise; no fear will be upon you, nor will you grieve."﴾

Know that when the Exalted, by His saying ﴿And when their sight is turned toward the companions of the Fire, they say, "Our Lord..."﴾, had explained the situation, He followed it by stating that the companions of the Heights call out to men from among the people of the Fire. He omitted mention of the people of the Fire because the speech being quoted befits only them, namely their saying ﴿"Neither your gathering nor your arrogance availed you."﴾ That speech befits only one who rebukes and reproaches, and it also befits only their leaders. By "gathering" is meant either the gathering of wealth or the assembly and multitude. ﴿"Nor your arrogance"﴾ means their arrogance in refusing the truth and their arrogance toward the people who held to the truth. It is recited as (تَسْتَكْثِرُونَ), from "abundance," and this is like an indication of the gloating of the companions of the Heights over the punishment befalling those addressed, and of a great rebuke that those addressed suffer because of this speech. Then they increased this rebuke with their saying ﴿"Are these the ones you swore that Allah would not reach with mercy?"﴾ They pointed to a group of the people of Paradise whom the addressees used to belittle, deeming their conditions insignificant, and perhaps mocking them, and scorning to share their religion with them. So when one who used to claim precedence sees those he had regarded as weak attain a lofty station, he becomes distressed, and his anguish and regret over what he had done within himself become great.

* * *

As for the saying of the Exalted ﴿"Enter Paradise"﴾, scholars have differed concerning it. It was said that those who speak are the companions of the Heights, and Allah the Exalted says this to them, or it is some of the angels whom Allah the Exalted commands to say this. It was also said that rather some of them say it to others. The meaning is that the Exalted urges the companions of the Heights to enter Paradise and join the station that Allah the Exalted has prepared for them. On this reading, the saying ﴿"Are these the ones you swore that Allah would not reach with mercy?"﴾ is from the speech of the companions of the Heights, and the saying ﴿"Enter Paradise"﴾ is from the speech of Allah the Exalted. Here there must be an implied element (idmar), and the sense is: "Allah said this to them," as in His saying ﴿"He wants to drive you out of your land"﴾ [al-A'raf: 110]. The speech of the council (al-mala') ends here. Then Pharaoh said ﴿"What do you advise?"﴾, and his speech is joined to theirs without any clear separation, so likewise here.

The commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 51–52:

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of the Garden: "Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided for you." They will say: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers, those who took their religion as amusement and play, and whom the worldly life deceived." So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their Day, and as they used to deny Our signs.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained what the companions of the Heights (Ashab al-A'raf, the people standing on the elevated barrier between Paradise and Hell) say to the people of the Fire, He followed it with mention of what the people of the Fire say to the people of the Garden. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: When the companions of the Heights reached the Garden, the people of the Fire, having despaired, began to hope for relief. They said: "O Lord, we have relatives among the people of the Garden, so permit us to see them and speak with them." Allah then commanded the Garden and it drew back. The people of Hell looked at their relatives in the Garden and at the bliss they were in, and they recognised them. The people of the Garden looked at their relatives among the people of Hell and did not recognise them, for their faces had blackened and they had become a different creation. So the companions of the Fire called out to the companions of the Garden by their names, saying: ﴿Pour upon us some water.﴾ They asked specifically for water only because of the intensity of the burning and blazing within their insides caused by the severe heat of Hell. His saying ﴿Pour﴾ indicates that the people of the Garden are higher in place than the people of the Fire.

If it is asked: did they ask with hope and expectation, or with despair?

We say: what we have related from Ibn 'Abbas indicates that they asked for water while the granting of it was still considered possible. But al-Qadi (the judge, i.e. al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) said: rather, they asked in despair, because they knew the perpetuity of their punishment and that it would never be lifted from them. Yet one who despairs of something may still seek it, as the proverb says: "The drowning man clutches at the foam, even though he knows it will not save him."

As for His saying ﴿or some of what Allah has provided﴾, it was said that this refers to fruits, and it was said that it refers to food. This statement indicates that they suffered from intense thirst and intense hunger. It is related from Abu al-Darda' that Allah, exalted is He, sends hunger upon the people of the Fire so that their punishment increases. They then cry out for help and are given relief with ad-Dari' (a thorny plant) which neither nourishes nor relieves hunger. Then they cry out again and are given food that chokes in the throat. Then they mention drink, cry out for help, and are given boiling water and pus, dragged to them with iron hooks, which cuts up what is in their bellies. They then cry out to the people of the Garden, as in this verse, and the people of the Garden say: "Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers." They also say to Malik (the keeper of Hell): ﴿Let your Lord put an end to us﴾ (Az-Zukhruf 43:77), and he answers them after a thousand years, as it was said. And they say: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:107), and He answers them: ﴿Be driven away into it, and do not speak to Me﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:108). At that, they despair of every good, and they begin to groan and wail.

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that in describing the people of the Garden he mentioned that they see Allah, Mighty and Majestic, every Friday, and that each of them has a dwelling with a thousand doors. When they see Allah, Exalted, an angel enters through every door bearing noble gifts and says: "The palm trees of the Garden have wood of emerald and soil of red gold, their fronds are garments and clothing for the people of the Garden, and their fruit is like pitchers or buckets, whiter than silver, softer than butter, and sweeter than honey, with no stone in it."

This is the description of the people of the Garden and the description of the people of the Fire. I have also seen in some books that a reciter recited His saying, related as the words of the disbelievers: ﴿Pour upon us some water, or some of what Allah has provided﴾, in the Tadhkira of the Ustadh (teacher) Abu 'Ali al-Daqqaq. The Ustadh said: "Their desire and craving in the world were for drinking and eating, and in the Hereafter they remain in this same state. This indicates that a man dies upon what he lived upon, and is resurrected upon what he died upon."

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that when these disbelievers asked the people of the Garden for water and food, the people of the Garden said: ﴿Allah has forbidden both to the disbelievers.﴾ Without doubt this conveys complete disappointment. Then He, exalted is He, described these disbelievers as those who took their religion as amusement and play. In this there are two interpretations:

The first interpretation: that which they believed to be their religion, they treated with levity, and they were not earnest in it.

The second interpretation: they took amusement and play as a religion for themselves. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: this refers to the mockers, the ones who divided (the Qur'an).

Then He said: ﴿and the worldly life deceived them﴾. This is a metaphor, because the worldly life does not in reality deceive; rather, what is meant is that deception occurred in the presence of this worldly life, since a person hopes for long life, a good living, abundant wealth and strength of status. Because of his intense desire for these things, he becomes veiled from seeking religion and immersed in pursuing the world.

Then, after Allah, exalted is He, described those disbelievers with these attributes, He said: ﴿So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their Day.﴾ Regarding the meaning of this forgetting there are two opinions:

The first opinion: forgetting means abandoning. The meaning is: We leave them in their punishment as they abandoned work for the meeting of this their Day. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, al-Suddi and most scholars.

The second opinion: the meaning of ﴿We will forget them as they forgot﴾ is that We treat them as one who has forgotten is treated, leaving them in the Fire as they themselves turned away from Our signs. In sum, Allah called the recompense for their forgetting "forgetting," as in His saying: ﴿and the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ (Ash-Shura 42:40). What is meant by this forgetting is that He will not answer their supplication and will not show them mercy.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that all these severities were only because they used to deny Our signs. There is a subtle and wondrous point in this verse, namely that He described them as disbelievers, then explained their condition: first they took their religion as amusement, then as play, then the worldly life deceived them, and finally the outcome of these states and stages was that they denied the signs of Allah. This indicates that love of the world is the source of every calamity, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The love of this world is the root of every sin," and the love of this world may lead to disbelief and misguidance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 53:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We had detailed with knowledge, as guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the states of the people of Paradise, the people of Hell, and the people of the A'raf, and then explained the words circulating among these three groups in a manner whereby hearing those debates would move the responsible person to caution and avoidance, and would call him to reflection and reasoning, He explained the nobility of this noble Book and the ultimate benefit of it, saying: ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book﴾, which is the Qur'an. (﴿We had detailed﴾) meaning We distinguished some of it from others, with a distinction that guides to right direction and protects from error and confusion.

As for His saying: ﴿with knowledge﴾, the meaning is that this detailing and distinguishing occurred with complete knowledge of what is in each of those sections of manifold benefits and increasing advantages. And His saying: ﴿as guidance and mercy﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "(guidance)" is in the accusative position, meaning We detailed it as guiding and as possessing mercy. His saying: ﴿for a people who believe﴾ indicates that the Qur'an was made guidance for specific people, and the meaning is that they are the ones who were guided by it and not others. It is like His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2]. Our companions (the Ash'aris) argued with His saying: ﴿detailed with knowledge﴾ that He, exalted is He, is knowing with knowledge, contrary to what the Mu'tazilah say, that God has no knowledge. And God knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they await anything but its final outcome? The day its final outcome comes, those who had forgotten it before will say: "The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth. So are there any intercessors for us who would intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?" They have certainly lost themselves, and what they used to fabricate has departed from them﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had explained the removal of the excuse by means of the sending down of this detailed Book which necessitates guidance and mercy, He then explained the state of those who denied, saying: ﴿Do they await anything but its final outcome?﴾ Here "await" (al-nazar) has the meaning of waiting and expecting.

If it is said: How can they expect and await while denying it and rejecting it?

We say: Perhaps among them are groups who doubted and hesitated, and for this reason they awaited it. Also, though they are deniers, they are in the position of those who await, inasmuch as those conditions will certainly come upon them. As for His saying: (﴿anything but its final outcome﴾), al-Farra' said: The pronoun in His saying "its" refers to the Book, meaning the outcome of what they were promised through the tongues of the messengers of reward and punishment. And ta'wil (final outcome) is the return and destination of a thing, from their saying: "the thing returned" (ala al-shay'u ya'ulu).

Those who held that His saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7] means that none knows the outcome of the matter in it except God have argued with this verse. And His saying: ﴿The day its final outcome comes﴾ means the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Zajjaj said: His saying "the day" is in the accusative governed by "says". As for His saying: ﴿those who had forgotten it before will say﴾, its meaning is that they became, in their turning away from it, like one who has forgotten it. It is also possible that the meaning of "forgotten it" is that they abandoned acting upon it and believing in it, and this is as we mentioned in His saying: ﴿as they forgot the meeting of this day of theirs﴾. Then He, exalted is He, explained that those who forgot, on the Day of Resurrection, will say: ﴿The messengers of our Lord had certainly come with the truth﴾.

Page 79
The meaning is that they acknowledged that what the messengers brought regarding the reality of the gathering, the resurrection, the raising, the Day of Resurrection, reward and punishment, all of that was true, and they acknowledged the reality of these things only because they witnessed and beheld them. God, exalted is He, explained that when they saw themselves in punishment they said: ﴿So are there any intercessors for us who would intercede for us, or could we be sent back so that we might do other than what we used to do?﴾ The meaning is that there is no way for us to escape what we are in of severe punishment except one of these two matters: that an intercessor intercede for us, and by that intercession this punishment would cease; or that God, exalted is He, return us to the world so that we might do other than what we used to do, meaning that we would affirm the oneness of God instead of disbelief, and obey Him instead of disobedience.

If it is said: Did they say this statement with hope or with despair? Our answer to it is similar to what we mentioned regarding His saying: ﴿Pour upon us some of the water﴾. Then, by His saying: ﴿They have certainly lost themselves﴾, God, exalted is He, indicated that what they requested will not happen, because if that sought-after thing had occurred, God would not have judged against them that they had lost themselves.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿and what they used to fabricate has departed from them﴾. He means that they did not benefit from the idols they worshipped in the world, nor did they benefit from the support of the false religions for which they strove greatly. Al-Jubba'i said: This verse indicates two rulings.

The first ruling:

He said: The verse indicates that they, during the time of responsibility, were able to believe and repent, which is why they asked to be returned so that they might believe and repent. Had they been unable in the world, as the Jabriyyah (determinists) say, there would be no benefit in returning them and it would not have been permissible for them to ask that.

The second ruling:

The verse indicates the invalidity of the view of the Jabriyyah and of those who claim that the people of the Hereafter are still under obligation, because if that were so they would not have asked to be returned to a state while they are in the same state at present; rather they would have repented and believed in the moment. Thus what is related from al-Najjar and his circle is invalidated, that obligation remains upon the people of the Hereafter.

[p. 80]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself upon the Throne. He covers the night with the day, which pursues it swiftly, and [He created] the sun, the moon, and the stars, subjected by His command. Unquestionably, creation and command belong to Him. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of the worlds.﴾

Know that we have explained that the core of the Qur'an's message rests on establishing these four matters: divine unity (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwah), the Return (ma'ad), and divine decree and destiny (qada' and qadar). Undoubtedly, the proof of the Return rests on the proof of divine unity, power, and knowledge. When Allah the Exalted had fully established the matter of the Return, He returned to mentioning the proofs that indicate divine unity and the perfection of His power and knowledge, so that these proofs would both confirm the foundations of divine unity and also confirm the proof of the Return. There are several issues concerning this verse:

**The first issue:** Al-Wahidi related from al-Layth that he said: "The original form of *sitt* and *sittah* (six) is *sidsun* and *sidsah*. The sin was replaced with a taa'. Since the articulation points of the dal and the taa' are close, one of them was assimilated into the other, and the taa' was retained. For this reason, the diminutive of *sittah* is *sudaysah*, and similarly *asdas* and all its derivations indicate this." And Allah knows best.

**The second issue:** *Al-khalq* (creation) means determination (taqdir), according to what we have established. Thus, the creation of the heavens and the earth refers to the determination of a state of their conditions, and this determination admits of many aspects:

The first: The determination of their essences with a specific measure, although reason judges that a greater or lesser measure is also possible. Therefore, the specification of each of them with its particular measure must be due to a specifier, and this indicates that the creation of the heavens and the earth requires a free-choosing agent.

The second: That these bodies being in motion from eternity is impossible, because motion is a transition from one state to another. Motion必 must be preceded by another state, and eternity precludes being preceded. Thus, combining motion with eternity is impossible.

Having established this, we say: These spheres and stars either had their essences non-existent in eternity and then came into existence, or they were existent but were stationary and at rest in eternity, and then began to move. In either case, those motions began to come into being at a specific time, although it was possible for them to occur before or after that time. Since this is so, the specification of the beginning of those motions at those specific times, by way of determination and creation, can only occur through the specification of a capable and free-choosing specifier.

The third: The bodies of the spheres, stars, and elements are composed of small parts, and it must be said that some of those parts are located inside those bodies while others are located on their surfaces. Therefore, the specification of each of those parts in its particular place and particular position must be due to the specification of a capable, free-choosing specifier.

The fourth: Some spheres are higher than others, and some stars are located in the zodiac belt while others are located at the poles. Therefore, the specification of each of them in its particular place must be due to the specification of a capable, free-choosing specifier.

The fifth: Each of the spheres moves toward a specific direction, with a motion specific to a particular measure of slowness or speed. This too is creation and determination, and it indicates the existence of a capable specifier.

The sixth: Each of the stars is distinguished by a particular color, such as the dullness of Saturn, the brightness of Jupiter, the redness of Mars, the light of the sun, the radiance of Venus, the yellowness of Mercury, and the whiteness of the moon. Bodies are identical in their complete quiddity. Thus, the specification of each of them with its particular color is creation, determination, and evidence of their need for a free-choosing agent.

The seventh: The spheres and elements are composed of small parts, and the Necessary Existent cannot be more than one. Therefore, these are possible in their essences. Whatever is possible in its essence is in need of an effector. The need for an effector does not exist in the state of permanence, for otherwise it would entail the existent coming into being [while already existing]. Thus, that need only occurs at the time of origination or at the time of non-existence. In either case, it follows that these parts are originated, and whenever they are originated, their origination is specified to a particular time. That is creation and determination, and it indicates the need for a capable, free-choosing Creator.

The eighth: These bodies are never free of motion and rest, and both are originated. Whatever is never free of the originated is itself originated.
