Therefore, these bodies are originated, and every originated thing has its origination occur at a specific time. That is creation and determination, and it necessarily requires a capable, free-choosing Creator.

The ninth: Bodies are identical. Thus, the specification of some of them with the attributes by which they became heavens and stars, and the other [bodies] with the attributes by which they became earth, water, air, or fire, must be something permissible. This only occurs through the determination of a determiner and the specification of a specifier, and that is what was sought.

The tenth: Just as the aforementioned distinction occurred between the spheres and the elements, a similar distinction has also occurred between the stars, between the spheres, and between the elements. Indeed, a similar distinction has occurred between each one of the stars themselves. This indicates the need for a capable, free-choosing agent.

Know that *al-khalq* is an expression for determination. When we have demonstrated that bodies are identical, it becomes necessary to affirm with certainty that every attribute that comes to be in a particular body is possible for all other bodies. When this is the case, the specification of that particular body with that particular attribute is creation and determination. Thus it falls under His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth.﴾ And Allah knows best.

\* \* \*

**The third issue:** A questioner may ask: "Can the fact that these things were created in six days not be used as a proof for establishing the Creator?" Its explanation is through several aspects:

First: The way in which these originated things indicate the existence of the Creator is their origination, or their possibility, or both together. As for whether that origination occurred over six days or in one day, this has no effect on that whatsoever.

Second: Reason indicates that origination is permissible at all times. Given this, it is not possible to be certain that this origination occurred over six days except through the report of a truthful informant. That in turn depends on knowing the existence of God, the Free-Choosing Agent. Therefore, if we made this premise a premise in establishing the Creator, it would entail circular reasoning (dawr).

Third: The origination of the heavens and the earth all at once is a greater indication of the perfection of power and knowledge than their origination over six days.

Having established the three aspects we have mentioned, we now ask: What is the benefit of mentioning that He created them over six days, in establishing what indicates the existence of the Creator?

Fourth: What is the reason that He limited Himself here to mentioning the heavens and the earth, and did not mention the creation of all other things?

**The fifth question:** The day is distinguished from the night only through the rising and setting of the sun. So before the creation of the sun and the moon, how is it conceivable that days existed?

**The sixth question:** He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 54:50], and this seems contradictory to His saying: ﴿created the heavens and the earth in six days.﴾

**The seventh question:** He, the Exalted, created the heavens and the earth over a stretched-out period. So what is the wisdom in restricting and fixing it to six days?

We say: As for our school of thought, the matter in all of these is easy and clear, because He does what He wills and decides what He desires. No one can object to Him regarding any matter, and everything is His creation, with no cause for His action. Then we say:

As for the first question, its answer is that He, glorified is He, mentioned at the beginning of the Torah that He created the heavens and the earth in six days, and the Arabs used to mix with the Jews, and it is apparent that they heard this from them. So it is as if He, glorified is He, were saying: Do not occupy yourselves with worshipping idols and images, for your Lord is the One whom you have heard from the wise among people to be the One who created the heavens and the earth, in their utmost greatness and final majesty, in six days.

As for the third question, its answer is that the intended meaning is that He, glorified and exalted is He, although He is capable of bringing all things into existence at once, has nevertheless set for each thing a defined limit and an appointed time, so He does not bring it into existence except in that manner. Thus, although He is capable of delivering reward to the obedient immediately, and punishment to the wrongdoers immediately, He delays both until a known, appointed term.

This delay is not because He has neglected His servants. Rather, it is for the reason we mentioned: He has specified each thing with an appointed time through His preceding will, and so He does not falter in it. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, in Surat Qaf: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, and no fatigue touched Us﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Qaf 50:38-39], after He had said before this: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed before them, who were stronger than them in might, so they roamed through the lands—was there any escape?﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart or gives ear while he is present﴾ [Qaf 50:36-37]. He informed them that He had destroyed, from among the polytheists who associated partners with Him and the deniers of His prophets, those who were stronger in might than the polytheists of the Arabs. Yet He granted respite to these for what contains of benefit, just as He created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six consecutive days, not because of any fatigue that befell Him in granting respite. When He clarified by this method that He, exalted is He, created the world not all at once but gradually, He said after it: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Qaf 50:39], regarding their polytheism and denial, and do not seek to hasten punishment for them. Rather, rely upon Allah, the Exalted, and entrust the matter to Him. This is the meaning of what the exegetes say: that He, exalted is He, created the world in six days in order to teach His servants gentleness in affairs and patience in them, and so that the responsible person would not take the delay of reward and punishment as neglect or abandonment.

Some scholars mentioned two other aspects regarding this:

The first aspect: When a thing is originated all at once and then the path of origination is cut off, it may occur to some that this happened by way of mere coincidence. But if things come into being in succession and continuity, while also being consistent with benefit and wisdom, this is stronger in indicating that they occurred by the origination of an eternal Originator who is Wise, Capable, Knowing, and Merciful.

The second aspect: It has been established by proof that He, exalted is He, creates the rational being first and then creates the heavens and the earth after him. Then, when that rational being witnesses, at every hour and moment, the origination of another thing in succession and continuity, this increases his knowledge and insight, because the manifestation of this proof repeatedly appears to his intellect moment after moment. This is therefore stronger in conveying certainty.

As for the fourth question, its answer is that the mention of the heavens and the earth in this verse also includes what is between them. The evidence for this is that He, exalted is He, mentioned the rest of the created things in other verses, saying: ﴿Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne; you have no protector or intercessor besides Him﴾ and He said: ﴿And rely upon the Ever-Living who does not die, and glorify Him with His praise, and He is sufficient as Knower of the sins of His servants﴾ ﴿Who created the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ [al-Furqan 25:58-59], and He said: ﴿And We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days﴾ [Qaf 50:38].

[Page 83]

As for the fifth objection, its answer is that the meaning is that God created the heavens and the earth within the span of six days, and this is like His saying: ﴿And they will have their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam 19:62]. The meaning is according to the measure of morning and evening in this world, because there is no night or day there.

[Page 83, continued]

As for the sixth objection, its answer is that His saying: ﴿And Our command is but one, like a glance of the eye﴾ [al-Qamar 54:50] is to be understood as referring to the bringing into existence of each individual being and the annihilation of each individual being. This is because bringing a single being into existence, and annihilating a single existent, does not admit of gradation, so it cannot be achieved except in a single instant. As for respite and duration, these only occur over a period of time.

As for the seventh objection, namely the specification of this period as six days, it is not a valid objection. This is because if He had originated it over a different span of time, the same objection would recur. Also, some have said: the number seven has great honour, and this is mentioned in the argument that the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr) is the night of the twenty-seventh. Once this is established, they say: the six days are for the creation of the world, and the seventh day is for the attainment of the full dominion and sovereignty (malakut). By this route, perfection was achieved in the seven days. End of quotation.

The fourth issue: in this verse there is a great glad tidings for the intelligent, because He said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. The meaning is that the One who nurtures you, sets right your affairs, brings good things to you, and repels harmful things from you, is the One who has reached such perfection of power, knowledge, wisdom and mercy that He created these great things and placed within them kinds of benefits and varieties of goods. And whoever has a Lord described with this wisdom, power and mercy, how is it fitting that he should turn to another in seeking good things, or rely upon another for attaining felicities?

Then there is another subtle point in the verse: He did not say "you are His servants," but rather said "He is your Lord." And another subtle point: when He attributed Himself to us, He named Himself in this situation as "the Lord (al-Rabb)," which indicates nurturing and abundance of grace and kindness. It is as if He is saying: whoever has a Lord with such abundant mercy and grace, how is it fitting for him to busy himself with worshipping another?

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾, know that it is impossible for its meaning to be that He is settled upon the Throne. Several rational arguments and several transmitted arguments prove its invalidity.

As for the rational arguments, they are several matters.

The first: if He were settled upon the Throne, then on the side that faces the Throne He would have to be bounded (mutanahiyan), otherwise it would follow that the Throne is inside His essence, which is impossible. Whatever is bounded, reason decides that it is not impossible for it to become larger than it or smaller than it by a particle; and knowledge of this possibility is necessary. So if the Creator, the Exalted, were bounded from some sides, His essence would be receptive to increase and decrease. And whatever is such, its being specified with that determinate magnitude requires a specifier (mukhassis) and a determiner (muqaddir). And whatever is such is originated (muhdath). It is therefore established that if He were upon the Throne, then from the side facing the Throne He would be bounded; and if He were such, He would be originated; and this is impossible. So His being upon the Throne must be impossible.

The second: if He were in a place and a direction (jihah), He would either be unbounded from all directions, or bounded in all directions, or bounded from some directions and not others. All of these are false, so the claim that He is in place and in space (ḥayyiz) is false with certainty.

The demonstration of the invalidity of the first division: it would follow that His essence mixes with all the lower and upper bodies, and that it mixes with filth and impurities, and God is exalted above that. Also, on this assumption the heavens would be indwelling in His essence, and the earth too would be indwelling in His essence.

Once this is established, we say: the thing that is the locus of the heavens is either the very thing that is the locus of the earths, or something other than it. If the first, it follows that the heavens and the earths are two indwelling things in one locus, without any distinction between their two loci at all; and every two indwelling things that inhere in one locus are not distinct from one another. So it must be said: the heavens are not distinguished from the earths in essence, and this is false. If the second, it follows that the essence of God, the Exalted, is composed of parts and components, and this is impossible.

The third: if the essence of God, the Exalted, is present in all spaces and directions, then either it is said: the thing that is above is the very thing that is below. In that case the one essence would be present all at once in many spaces. And if this is conceivable, why would it not also be conceivable for one body to be present in many spaces all at once? And that is impossible by the immediate judgment of reason.

But if it is said: the thing that is above is other than the thing that is below, then composition and partition would necessarily occur in the essence of God, the Exalted, and this is impossible.

As for the second division, namely that He is bounded from all directions: we say that whatever is such is, by immediate reason, receptive to increase and decrease. And whatever is such, its being specified with a determinate measure is for the sake of a specifier's specification. And whatever is such is originated. Moreover, if it were possible for a thing bounded from all sides to be eternal, without beginning, and the agent of the world, then why could it not be said that the creator of the world is the sun, or the moon, or another star? And that is false by consensus.

As for the third division, namely that He is bounded from some sides and unbounded from the remaining sides, this too is false, in several respects:

One: the side that is truly described as bounded is other than the side that is truly described as unbounded; otherwise the two contradictories would both be true together, and that is impossible. And when there is difference, it follows that He, the Exalted, is composed of parts and components.

Two: the side on which reason's judgment applies that it is bounded is either equal to the side on which reason's judgment applies that it is unbounded, or it is not so. The first is false, because things equal in their complete quiddity (māhiyyah): whatever holds of one of them holds of the rest. And given this, the side that is unbounded could become bounded, and the side that is bounded could become unbounded.

And when this is the case, growth, withering, increase, decrease, dispersal and disintegration become possible upon His essence. And whatever is such is originated; and that is impossible for the eternal God. Thus it is established that if He, the Exalted, were located in space and direction, then He would either be unbounded from all directions, or bounded from all directions, or bounded from some directions and unbounded from the rest. It has been established that the three divisions are false. Therefore it is necessary to say that the claim that He, the Exalted, is located in space and direction is impossible.

The third demonstration: if the Creator, the Exalted, were located in place and direction, then the thing called "direction" would either be an existent pointed to, or not so. Both alternatives are false, so the claim that He, the Exalted, is located in space and direction is false.

As for the demonstration of the invalidity of the first alternative: if what is called "space and direction" were an existent pointed to, then what is called "space and direction" would be an extension and a dimension. And what is located in it must also have in itself a dimension and extension; otherwise its being located in it would be impossible. And then it would follow that the two dimensions interpenetrate, and that is impossible, by the many well-known proofs in this domain. Moreover, it would follow from the Creator, the Exalted, being eternal and without beginning that space and direction are eternal too. Then it would follow that there existed in eternity a self-subsisting existent other than God, the Exalted; and that is false by the consensus of the majority of intellects.

As for the demonstration of the invalidity of the second alternative, it is from two aspects:

One of them: that non-existence is pure negation and absolute nothingness, and whatever is such cannot be a container for another, nor a direction for another.

The second of them: that whatever is located in a direction, its direction is distinguished perceptibly from the direction of others. So if that direction were pure non-existence, it would follow that pure non-existence is pointed to by the senses; and that is false. Thus it is established that if He, the Exalted, were located in a space and direction, it would lead to one of these two false divisions, so it must be that the claim of His being so is false.

If it is said: this objection applies to you too, in your saying that body is located in space and direction.

We say: on this approach we do not affirm for the body any space or direction at all, in the sense that the essence of the body is penetrating in it and pervading it. Rather, "place" (makān) is an expression for the inner surface of the containing body which is in contact with the outer surface of the contained body. And this meaning is impossible, by consensus, with respect to God, the Exalted. So this objection falls away.

The fourth demonstration: if the existence of the Creator, the Exalted, were impossible except in a way that He is specified by space and direction, then the essence of the Creator would be dependent for its realization and existence on another. And whatever is such is possibly existent in its essence. The conclusion is that if the existence of the Creator were impossible except in direction and space, it would follow that He is possibly existent in His essence. And since this is impossible, the claim that it is necessary for Him to be located in space is impossible.

Explanation of the first stage: it is that, since the realization of the essence of God, the Exalted, is impossible except if He is specified by space and direction. We say: there is no doubt that space and direction is something other than the essence of God, the Exalted. Then the essence of God, the Exalted, would be dependent in its realization on a thing other than it. And whatever's realization depends on something other than it, is possibly existent in its essence.

The proof of this is that the necessary-in-essence (wājib al-wujūd li-dhātihi) is that whose non-existence does not entail the non-existence of another; and the dependent on another is that whose non-existence entails the non-existence of another. So if the necessary-in-essence were dependent on another, it would follow that both contradictories are true of it; and that is impossible. It is thus established that if He, the Exalted, were necessarily located in space, He would be possibly existent in His essence, not necessary in His essence; and that is impossible.

The second way of formulating this argument: the possible existent needs space and direction. As for those who affirm the void (khalā'), there is no doubt that space and direction are established even without occupation. But as for those who deny the void, it is not so; for although he believes that there must be an occupant that is located in the direction, he does not say that there must be a determinate occupant for that direction; rather, whatever thing it may be, it suffices to make it occupy that space. When this is established: if the essence of God, the Exalted, were specified with a direction and space, then His essence would be dependent on that space, and that space would be independent in its realization of the essence of God, the Exalted. And then it would follow that one must say: space is necessary in its essence and independent of another; and one must say: the essence of God, the Exalted, is dependent in its essence and necessary through another. And this undermines our saying: God the Exalted is necessary of existence in His essence.

If it is said: space and direction is not an existent thing, such that it could be said the essence of God, the Exalted, is dependent on it and in need of it.

We say: this is false with certainty. For on the assumption that the essence of God, the Exalted, is specified with the direction of "above," we distinguish perceptibly between that direction and the rest of the directions. And how can it be conceived that what is perceptibly distinguished is a pure non-existence and absolute negation? And if that were permissible, the same would be permissible for all perceptible things, and that would entail doubt about the existence of every perceptible thing; and no rational person says that.

[Page 86]

The fifth proof, establishing that He, may He be exalted, cannot be specifically confined to a space (ḥayyiz) and direction (jihah):

We say: space and direction have no meaning except pure emptiness and sheer void, and sound reason witnesses that this concept is one single concept with absolutely no difference in it. If this is the case, then all spaces are equal in their entire quiddity.

Having established this, we say: If God, exalted is He, were specifically confined to a space, He would be originated (ḥādith), and this is impossible; therefore that is impossible.

The proof of the implication: since it has been established that all spaces are equal, if the essence of God, exalted is He, were specifically confined to a particular space, its being confined to that space would be because some specifier had specified it to that space. Everything that is the act of a choosing agent is originated. Therefore it is necessary that the specification of God's essence to a particular space is originated. Since His essence cannot be free of being in a space, and it has been established that being in a space is originated, and the immediate judgment of reason testifies that what cannot be free of the originated is itself originated, it follows that we must be certain that if He were present in a space, He would be originated. Since this is impossible, that also is impossible.

If they say: the spaces differ according to the fact that some are high and some are low, so why not say that God's essence is specifically confined to the direction of height? We say: this is false, because some of those directions being high and others low are conditions that arise only in relation to the existence of this world. Since this world is originated, before its origination there was no high, no low, no right, and no left, but only pure void. If that is so, then the aforementioned implication returns in full.

Also: if it were permissible to say that God's essence is confined by necessity to some of the spaces, why could it not also be conceived that some bodies are confined by necessity to some of the spaces? In that case, that thing would be something not capable of motion and rest, so the proof of the origination of bodies would not apply to it. The one who holds this view cannot establish the proof of the origination of all bodies by way of motion and rest. The Karramiyya (a sect) agreed with us that permitting this view entails disbelief. And God knows best.

The sixth proof: If the Creator, exalted, were present in a space and direction, He would be indicated by sensory perception (ḥiss). Whatever is so indicated either does not accept division in any way, or accepts division.

If we say that He can be indicated by sensory perception while not accepting quantitative division at all, then that would be a point that cannot be divided, an indivisible single atom (jawhar fard), and it would be at the utmost smallness and insignificance. This is false by the consensus of all rational people. That is because those who deny His being in a direction deny that He is like this, and those who affirm His being in a direction deny that He is in smallness and insignificance like the indivisible part. Thus it is established that this is false by the consensus of rational people.

Also: if that were permissible, why could it not be conceived to say that the God of the world is a part of one thousandth of the head of a needle, or an atom attached to the tail of a louse or an ant? It is known that every doctrine that leads to such things, sound reason requires that God be exalted above them.

As for the second division, that He accepts division: we say that whatever is so has a composite essence, every composite is possible in its essence, and every possible in its essence is in need of the one who brings it into being and the one who effects it. That is impossible for the Necessary Existent in His essence.

The seventh proof: We say: every self-subsisting essence that is indicated by sensory perception is divisible, and every divisible is possible. Therefore every self-subsisting essence indicated by sensory perception is possible. Whatever is not possible in its essence but necessary in its essence, it is impossible for it to be indicated by sensory perception.

As for the first premise: because every self-subsisting essence indicated by sensory perception must have its right side different from its left side, and whatever is so is divisible.

As for the second premise, that every divisible is possible: it needs each one of its parts, and each one of its parts is other than it. Everything divisible is in need of something other than itself, and everything in need of something other than itself is possible in its essence.

Know that the first premise of this proof is complete only with the negation of the indivisible atom.

[p. 87]

The eighth proof: If His being in a space were established, He would either be greater than the Throne, or equal to it, or smaller than it. If the first, He would be divisible, because the portion that equals the Throne would be different from the portion that exceeds the Throne. If the second, He would be divisible, because the Throne is divisible, and what equals the divisible is divisible. If the third, then it would follow that the Throne is greater than Him, and this is false by the consensus of the community. As for us, it is clear; as for our opponents, they deny that anything other than God, exalted, is greater than God, exalted. Thus this doctrine is established as false.

The ninth proof: If God, exalted, were present in a space and direction, He would either be finite from all directions, or not. Both are false.

That He cannot be finite from all directions: on this assumption, there would be empty spaces above Him, and He, exalted, is able to create a body in that empty space. On this assumption, if He created another world there, He would be located beneath that world, which, according to the opponent, is impossible. Also, He could create other bodies on the six sides of that essence, and on this assumption His essence would be located in the middle of those bodies, confined within them, and between Him and the bodies there would be union at times and separation at others. All of this is impossible for God, exalted.

As for the second division, that He is infinite in some directions: this too is impossible, because it has been established by proof that an infinite dimension cannot exist. Also, on this assumption, it is not possible to establish a proof that the world is finite, because every proof offered for the finitude of dimensions is refuted by God's essence, since on the opponent's doctrine it is an infinite dimension. Although he would not accept this wording, he agrees with the meaning, and rational discussions are built upon meanings, not upon disputing over words.

The tenth proof: If God, exalted, were present in a space and direction, then His being there would either prevent another body from being there, or it would not. Both are false, so the doctrine of His being in a space is false.

As for the falsity of the first: since His being there would prevent another body from being there, He would be equal to all bodies in being a volume, extended, occupying space and direction, and preventing others from being in the space where He is. Once equality in this concept between Him and all bodies is established, then either a difference arises between Him and them in all other respects, or it does not. The first is false for two reasons:

[p. 88]

The first: if the commonality between God's essence and the essences of bodies is in some respects and difference is in all others, then what makes them common is other than what makes them differ, and thus God's essence would be composed of these two aspects. We have demonstrated that every composite is possible, so the Necessary Existent in His essence would be possible in His essence. This is a contradiction.

The second: what makes them common, namely the nature of extension and dimension, either is a substrate for what makes them differ, or inheres in it, or it is said that it has no substrate and does not inhere in anything.

As for the first: that it is a substrate for what makes them differ. Then the nature of extension and dimension is the self-subsisting substance, and the things by which difference occurs are accidents and attributes. Since the essences are equal in their entire quiddity, whatever is valid of some of them must be valid of the rest. So whatever is valid of all bodies must be valid of the Creator, and vice versa. This would entail that separation, dispersal, growth, decay, putrefaction and corruption are valid of God's essence, and all of this is impossible.

As for the second division, that what makes them differ is a substrate and an essence, while what makes them common is an inhering attribute: this is impossible, because on this assumption the nature of extension and dimension would be an attribute subsisting in a substrate. If that substrate also has specification to a space and direction, it would require another substrate, ad infinitum. If it does not, then it would be a pure existent with no connection at all to space, direction, or sensory indication. The nature of extension and dimension necessarily requires specification to space, direction, and sensory indication, and the inherence of something with this characteristic in that substrate entails the combination of contradictories, which is impossible.

As for the third division, that neither inheres in the other nor is a substrate for it: we say that on this assumption each of the two is separate from the other. And on this assumption God's essence would be equal to the other corporeal essences in its entire quiddity, because what makes God's essence differ from the other essences is neither inhering in these essences nor being a substrate for them, but matters external to them. So God's essence would be equal to the essences of bodies in its entire quiddity, and then the aforementioned implication returns. Thus it is established that the saying that God's essence is specifically confined to a space and direction in such a way that it prevents another body from being in that space leads to these three false divisions, so it must be false.

As for the second division: that it is said that God's essence, although specifically confined to a space and direction, does not prevent another body from being in that same space and direction. This too is impossible, because it entails that His essence would be mixing with and pervading the essence of that body which comes to be on that side and in that space, and this is impossible by consensus. Moreover, if that were conceivable, why could it not be conceived that many bodies exist in one space?

Thus it is established that if He, exalted, were present in a space, then either He would prevent another body from being in that space or He would not. The falsity of both divisions has been established, so the saying that He is present in a space and direction is impossible and false.

The eleventh proof, showing that the presence of God's essence in a space and direction is impossible: we say that if He were specifically confined to a space and direction, then either He would be in a state in which He could move from that direction, or He would not be able to do so. Both divisions are false, so the doctrine of His being present in a space is false.

As for the first division, that He is able to move: we say that this essence is not free of motion and rest, and both

[Page 90 begins below]

...muhdath (originated), because on this assumption stillness is possible for Him and motion is possible for Him. And when this is the case, the agent of that motion and that stillness is not His essence itself. Otherwise, the arrival of its opposite would be impossible. The assumption is that He is able to move and able to be still. When this is so, the agent that brings about that motion and that stillness is the free-choosing agent (al-fa'il al-mukhtar). Every act of a free-choosing agent is muhdath. Therefore motion and stillness are muhdath, and whatever is not free from the muhdath is itself muhdath. So it follows that His essence, exalted is He, would be muhdath, and this is impossible.

As for the second case, namely that He is particularized to a location and a direction (hayyiz wa jiha) while being unable to move from it, this too is impossible, for two reasons.

The first: on this assumption He would be like a paralyzed, helpless invalid, and that is a deficiency, and deficiency is impossible for God.

The second: if it is not impossible to suppose an existent that is present in a specific location, such that its presence there is necessarily fixed and its removal impossible, then it is also not far-fetched to suppose other bodies particularized to specific locations, such that their leaving those locations is impossible. On this assumption, the origination of these bodies cannot be proven by the argument from motion and stillness. The Karramiyya (a sect) agree that this is unbelief (kufr).

The third: since He, exalted is He, is present in a location and a direction, He would be equal to bodies in being a spatially occupying entity that fills locations. Then we establish the aforementioned argument that, since spatially occupying entities are equal in the attribute of spatial occupation, they must be equal in their entire quiddity (tamam al-mahiyya). For if some of them differed from others, the thing by which they differ would either be inherent in the spatially occupying entity or be its substrate, or neither inherent nor a substrate. The three divisions are invalid, as has been shown. And when they are equal in their entire quiddity, just as motion is valid for these bodies, so it must be affirmed that motion is valid for the essence of God, exalted is He. Then the argument is complete.

The twelfth argument: If God, exalted is He, were particularized to a specific location, then, if we suppose a person reaching the edge of that thing and attempting to enter it, either it is possible for him to penetrate and enter it, or it is not possible. If the first, then it would be like subtle air or subtle water, and then it would be susceptible to separation and tearing apart. If the second, then it would be solid like hard stone, which he cannot penetrate. Thus it is established that if He were particularized to a place, a spatial location, and a direction, He would either be fine and easily separated and torn like water and air, or solid and hard like hard stone. The Muslims have unanimously agreed that affirming either of these two attributes for the God, exalted is He, is unbelief and deviation in His attributes.

Also, on the assumption that He is particularized to a place and direction, He would either be luminous or dark. Most of the Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists) believe that He is pure light, because they believe that light is noble and darkness base. However, general induction shows that luminous things are subtle and do not prevent a penetrating thing from penetrating them and entering between their parts. On this assumption, that which penetrates into it would become mixed with it, its parts would be separated, and that thing would be like air, which at times connects and at times separates, at times gathers and at times disperses. This is not fitting for a Muslim to attribute to the Lord of the worlds. And if this were permissible, why would it not be permissible to say that the Creator of the world is one of these winds that blow, or that He is one of these lights and radiances that shine upon the walls?

As for those who say that He does not accept separation or tearing and that what penetrates cannot penetrate Him, the essential result of their statement is that a solid, hard mountain has come to exist above the world, and the God of this world is that solid mountain standing in the higher location. Also, if He has an edge, a boundary, and an end, does that thing have depth and thickness, or not?

If the first, then its outer surface would be other than its inner and its inner other than its outer, so it would be composed and compounded of outer and inner, while its inner is other than its outer and its outer other than its inner. If the second, then His essence would be a thin surface of extreme thinness, like the skin of garlic, rather, a million million times thinner than that, and a sane person would not accept making such a thing the God of the world. Thus it is established that His being in a location and direction leads to opening the door to these false and corrupt divisions.

The thirteenth argument: The world is a sphere, and if this is the case, it is impossible for the God of the world to be present in the direction "above."

As for the first point: it is explained at length in the science of astronomy (ilm al-hay'a), but we say: if we consider a lunar eclipse that occurred at the beginning of the night in the western lands, the very same eclipse is present in the eastern lands at the beginning of the day. Thus we know that the beginning of the night in the western lands is precisely the beginning of the day in the eastern lands. That is not possible unless the earth is spherical from east to west. Also, if we head toward the northern side, the further we proceed, the higher the North Pole rises, and in proportion to the rise of the North Pole, the South Pole descends. This indicates that the earth is spherical from north to south. The combination of these two considerations shows that the earth is a sphere.

Having established this, we say: if we suppose two people, one standing at the point of the east and the other at the point of the west, the soles of their feet become opposite. What is "above" in relation to one of them is "below" in relation to the other. So if we suppose that the God of the world is present in the location that is above in relation to one of them, that very location is below in relation to the other, and vice versa. Thus it is established that if He were present in a specific location, that location would be below in relation to specific peoples. But His being below the people of this world is impossible by consensus. Therefore He must not be present in a specific location.

Also, on this assumption, whatever is above in relation to some peoples is below in relation to other peoples, to the right in relation to a third, to the left in relation to a fourth, in front of the face in relation to a fifth, and behind the head in relation to a sixth. The earth's being a sphere necessitates this. But the occurrence of these states, by the unanimous agreement of rational people, is impossible regarding the God of the world, unless it is said that He encompasses the earth from all sides, and then this would be a sphere (falak) encompassing the earth. Its ultimate result returns to saying that the God of the world is one of the spheres encircling this world, and no Muslim says that. And God knows best.

The fourteenth argument: If the God of the world were above the Throne ('arsh), then He would either be touching the Throne, or separate from it by a finite distance, or by an infinite distance. All three divisions are invalid, so the claim that He is above the Throne is invalid.

As for the explanation of the corruption of the first division: on the assumption that He becomes touching the Throne, then His lowest part would be touching the Throne. Is there anything of Him above that part which is not touching the Throne, or is there not? If the first, then the part of Him that has become touching the edge of the Throne is other than the part of Him that is not touching the edge of the Throne. It follows that the essence of God, exalted is He, would be composed of parts and portions, and His essence would in reality be composed of contiguous surfaces placed one above another. This is the claim that He is a body composed of parts and portions, and that is impossible. If the second, then the essence of God, exalted is He, would be a thin surface with no thickness at all. Then the division recurs: if it has extension to the right, left, front, and back, it is composed of parts and portions; and if it has no extension and no movement through locations according to the six directions, it would be one of the atoms, an indivisible part mixed with the vapors, and no sane person says that.

* * *

[Page 91 begins below]

As for the second division: that it is said that between Him and the world there is a finite distance. This too is impossible, for on this assumption there is nothing preventing the world from rising from its location toward the direction in which the essence of God, exalted is He, is situated, until the world becomes touching Him, and then the impossibility mentioned in the first division recurs.

As for the third division: that it is said that He, exalted is He, is separate from the world by an infinite separation. This is more evidently corrupt than all the divisions, for since He, exalted is He, is separate from the world, the separation between Him and other than Him is bounded by two extremities, namely the essence of God, exalted is He, and the essence of the world, and is confined between these two confining limits. And a distance confined between two confining limits and bounded between two limits and extremities cannot be an infinite distance.

If it is said: Is He not preceding the world from eternity (al-azal) to eternity (al-abad), so that His precedence over the world is confined between two confining limits and bounded between two limits and extremities: one of them is eternity (al-azal) and the second is the first existence of the world? And it does not follow from this precedence being confined between two confining limits that this precedence has a first and a beginning. So too here? This is what Muhammad ibn al-Haytham relied upon to dispel this difficulty regarding this division.

The answer: This is pure sophistry. For eternity (al-azal) is not an expression for a specific time and a specific period, such that it could be said that He precedes the world from that time to the time that is the beginning of the world. Rather, every specific time supposed from that time to the other time is bounded between two limits and confined between two confining limits, and that cannot be conceived as infinite. Rather, eternity (al-azal) is an expression for the negation of priority (al-awwaliyya) without indicating by it any specific time whatsoever.

Having known this, we say: either we say that He is particularized to a specific direction and present in a specific location, or we do not say that. If we affirm the first, then the distance existing between those two extremities is bounded between those two limits, and the distance confined between the two confining limits cannot be conceived as infinite, because being infinite means the absence of limit, termination, and extremity, while being confined between confining limits means the affirmation of limit, termination, and extremity. Combining them entails combining two contradictories, which is impossible. A parallel to what we have mentioned: whenever we specify a specific time before the world, the distance between it and the time in which the beginning of the world occurred is necessarily a finite distance. As for if we affirm the second division, namely that He is not particularized to a specific location and not present in a specific direction, then this is an expression for the negation of His being in a direction, because the specific essence being present without a specific direction in itself is an impossible statement. A parallel to this is the statement of one who says: eternity (al-azal) is not an expression for a specific time, but an indication of the negation of priority and origination. Thus it becomes clear that what Ibn al-Haytham said is an imagining devoid of substance.

The fifteenth argument: It has been established in the rational sciences that place (al-makan) is either the inner surface of the containing body, or pure extension and expanded space, and there is no third thing conceivable regarding place.

[p. 92]

Having understood this, we say: if place is the first meaning, then we say that it has been established that the bodies of the world are finite. Beyond the physical world there is no void, no plenum, no place, and no direction. Therefore it is impossible for God to be located in a place outside the world.

If place is the second meaning, then we say: the nature of extension is one nature, identical in its whole quiddity. So if God were located in a *hayyiz* (a bounded space), He would be capable of being located in all other spaces. In that case, motion and rest would be applicable to Him. Whatever is like this is originated (*muhdath*) by the well-known proofs mentioned in the science of *uṣūl* (the foundational principles of theology, *ʿilm al-uṣūl*), and these proofs are accepted by the majority of the *mutakallimun* (scholars of kalam). It would then follow that God is originated, and this is impossible. Thus it is established that the claim that He, exalted is He, is present in a *hayyiz* and a direction is false under every consideration.

The sixteenth argument: this is an inductive, considerative argument, very subtle. It is that we have observed that whenever the attribute of corporeality (*jismiyya*) is stronger and more firmly established in a thing, its active power is weaker and more deficient. And whenever the attribute of corporeality in a thing is less and weaker, its active power is stronger and more perfect. Its elaboration is that we say: we find the earth to be the densest of bodies and the most solid in volume, so it has only the property of receiving effects, and nothing more. As for the pure earth having any effect on other things, it is very little. As for water, it is less dense and less solid in volume than the earth, so it has acquired an effective power. Flowing water, by its nature, when mixed with earth, affects it with various kinds of effects. As for air, it is less in volume and density than water, so it is stronger in effecting than water. For this reason some said that life is not complete except by breath, and they claimed that the spirit (*rūḥ*) means nothing but the inhaled air. As for fire, it is less dense than air, so it is the strongest of the elemental bodies in effecting. By the strength of heat, cooking and ripening occur, and the three generated kingdoms come into being, namely minerals, plants, and animals. As for the celestial spheres (*aflāk*), they are finer than the elemental bodies, so they are the ones that dominate the mixing of the elemental bodies with one another and the generation of the various kinds and species from those combinations.

This consistent induction indicates that whenever a thing is greater in volume, mass and corporeality, it is less in power and effect, and whenever it is stronger in power and effect, it is less in volume, mass and corporeality. Since the matter is so, this induction gives a strong conjecture that wherever perfect power and capacity for origination and innovation are found, there is absolutely no meaning of volume, mass, or specification by a *hayyiz* or a direction. This, although it is an inductive inquiry, is, upon thorough reflection, very closely related to the certainty that He, exalted is He, is far above corporeality, locality and *hayyiz*. And success is from God. This is the total of the rational aspects in explaining that He, exalted is He, is far above being specified by a *hayyiz* and a direction.

* * *

As for the transmitted proofs (*al-dalāʾil al-samʿiyya*), they are numerous.

The first of them: the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Say: He is God, the One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. He described Him as *aḥad* (the One), and *aḥad* is an intensive form of being one. What fills the Throne and overflows beyond the Throne would be composed of a very great number of parts, far exceeding the parts of the Throne, and that contradicts His being *aḥad*. Many of the Karramiyya (followers of Ibn Karram), when confronted with this objection, say: He, exalted is He, is a single essence, and while He is one, He is present in all these spaces at once. They said: because He is present in all the spaces at a single instant, the Throne is filled by Him. I say: the substance of this speech returns to the claim that it is permissible for an essence that occupies space and direction to be present in many spaces at a single instant. The rational people agree that knowledge of the falsity of this is among the most sublime necessary sciences. Moreover, if you permit that, why do you not permit saying that the entire world, from the Throne to what lies beneath the earth, is one substance and one existent, except that this indivisible part is present in all of these spaces, so that it is supposed that they are many things? It is known that whoever permits this has committed himself to a very great abomination of speech.

If they say: we know here that there is a difference between these essences because some of them perish while the others remain, and that requires difference. Also, we see some of them moving and some at rest, and the moving is not the resting, so difference must be affirmed. These meanings do not apply to God's essence, so the difference is evident. We say: as for your claim that we witness that this part remains while that other part perishes, which requires difference: we do not grant that any of the parts perished. Rather, we say: why is it not permissible to say that all the parts of the world are only one part? Then it is present here and there, and also it is present described as black and white and all colours and tastes. What perishes is only its presence there. As for saying that it perished in itself, that is not granted.

As for your statement: we see some bodies moving and some at rest, and that requires difference, because motion and rest do not coexist: we say, when we judge that motion and rest do not coexist, this is because we believe that one body cannot be present at one instant in two spaces. When we see that the resting thing remains here and the moving thing is not here, we decide that the moving thing is not the resting thing. But on the assumption that it is permissible for one essence to be present in two spaces at a single instant, it is not impossible that one essence be moving and resting together. For the most that can be said is that because of the rest it remained here, and because of the motion it came to be in the other space. But since we have permitted that one essence be present in two spaces at once, it is not far-fetched that the resting essence be the very same as the moving essence. Thus it is established that if it is permissible to say that He, exalted is He, is one in His essence, not admitting division, and yet the Throne is filled by Him, then it is also not far-fetched to say that the Throne in itself is a single substance and an indivisible part, and yet it is present in all those spaces, and the whole Throne is produced by Him. It is known that permitting this leads to opening the door of ignorance.

The second: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And there shall bear the Throne of your Lord above them that Day eight [angels]﴾ [al-Haqqa: 17]. If the God of the world were in the Throne, then the bearer of the Throne would be bearing God. It would follow that God is carried and bearing, and guarded and guarding. No intelligent person says that.

The third: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And God is the Rich (al-Ghaniyy)﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. He judged Him to be rich absolutely, and this requires that He, exalted is He, be free of need of place and direction.

The fourth: when Pharaoh sought the reality of God, exalted is He, from Moses, peace be upon him, Moses did not go beyond mentioning the attribute of creating (*khallāqiyya*) three times. When [Pharaoh] said: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 23], Moses said the first time: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you are certain﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 24]. The second time he said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 26]. The third time he said: ﴿The Lord of the East and the West and what is between them, if you use reason﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 28]. All of that is an indication of the attribute of creating. As for Pharaoh, may God curse him, he said: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses﴾ [Ghafir: 36-37]. So he sought God in the sky. Thus we know that describing God as Creator, and not describing Him with place and direction, is the religion of Moses and all the prophets, while describing God as being in the sky is the religion of Pharaoh and his brethren among the disbelievers.

The fifth: God, exalted is He, said in this verse: ﴿Indeed your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then He established Himself above the Throne﴾. The word *thumma* ("then") indicates sequence in time, and this shows that He, exalted is He, established Himself above the Throne only after the creation of the heavens and the earth. If the meaning of *istiwāʾ* (establishment) is settling, then it must be said that He was not settled on the Throne but was inclined and agitated, and then He settled upon it after that. This would require describing Him with the attributes of all bodies, of agitation and motion at one time and rest at another. No intelligent person says that.

The sixth: God, exalted is He, related of Abraham, peace be upon him, that he only criticized the divinity of the star, the moon and the sun on the grounds that they set and disappear. So if the God of the world were a body, He would always be setting and disappearing, and moving from agitation and inclination to establishment, rest and settlement. Therefore, whatever Abraham, peace be upon him, made a criticism of the divinity of the sun, star and moon would be present in the God of the world. How then is it possible to acknowledge His divinity?

The seventh: God, exalted is He, mentioned before His words ﴿then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ something, and after it something else. What He mentioned before this word is His words: ﴿Indeed your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾,

[p. 93]

and we have already explained that the creation of the heavens and the earth indicates the existence of the Creator, His power and His wisdom in many respects. As for what He mentioned after this word, there are several things:

The first: His words ﴿He covers the night over the day, which pursues it rapidly﴾. This is one of the proofs that indicate the existence of God, and of His power and wisdom.

The second: His words ﴿And the sun and the moon and the stars are subjected by His command﴾. This is also among the proofs indicating existence, power and knowledge.

The third: His words ﴿Unquestionably, His is the creation and the command﴾. This is also an indication of the perfection of His power and wisdom.

Having established this, we say: the beginning of the verse is an indication of mentioning what indicates existence, power and knowledge, and its end also indicates this same aim. Since the matter is so, His words ﴿then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ must also be a proof of perfect power and knowledge. For if it did not indicate that, but rather the intended meaning were His being settled upon the Throne, that would be a statement unrelated to what comes before it and what comes after it. For God's being settled upon the Throne cannot be made a proof of His perfection in power and wisdom, nor is it among the attributes of praise and commendation. For He is capable of seating all the countless numbers of gnats and mosquitoes upon the Throne and upon what is above the Throne. Thus it is established that His sitting upon the Throne is neither among the proofs establishing the attributes and essence, nor among the attributes of praise and commendation. So if the intended meaning of His words ﴿then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ were His sitting upon the Throne, that would be a statement unrelated to what precedes it and what follows it, and this would entail the utmost incoherence. Therefore it is established that this is not the intended meaning. Rather, the intended meaning is the perfection of His power in the governance of the dominion and the kingdom (*malakūt*), so that this word becomes relevant to what precedes it and what follows it, and that is the aim.

Eighthly: The heaven (samā') is a term for everything that is raised up, elevated and high. The evidence for this is that God, exalted is He, called the clouds "heaven" when He said: ﴿And He sends down upon you water from the heaven, to purify you thereby﴾ [al-Anfal: 11]. If this is the case, then everything that has height, loftiness and elevation is a heaven. So if the God of the worlds were existing above the Throne, then the very essence of God, exalted is He, would be a heaven for the dwellers of the Throne. Thus it is established that if He, exalted is He, were above the Throne, He would be a heaven. Yet God has ruled that He is the Creator of all the heavens in many verses, among them this verse, which is His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. So if He were above the Throne as a heaven for the inhabitants of the Throne, He would be the creator of Himself, and that is impossible.

When this is established, we say: His saying ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾ is a clear (muḥkam) verse indicating that His saying ﴿then He istawā upon the Throne﴾ is among the ambiguous (mutashābih) verses which must be interpreted (ta'wīl). This is a subtle point. A parallel to this is that God said at the beginning of Surat al-An'am: ﴿And He is God in the heavens﴾ [al-An'am: 3], then said shortly after: ﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth? Say: To God﴾ [al-An'am: 12]. This later verse indicates that everything in the heavens belongs to God; so if God were in the heavens it would follow that He belongs to Himself, and that is impossible. The same applies here.

Thus it is established, by the totality of these rational and transmitted proofs, that His saying ﴿then He istawā upon the Throne﴾ cannot be taken to mean sitting, settling, occupying a place and a space. At this point the learned scholars (al-'ulamā' al-rāsikhūn) have two positions:

The first: that we affirm with certainty that He, exalted is He, is transcendent above place and direction, and we do not delve into the detailed interpretation of the verse, but commit its knowledge to God. This is what we have established in our commentary on His saying: ﴿And none knows its interpretation except God. And those firm in knowledge say: We believe in it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 7]. This is the position we choose, adopt and rely upon.

The second position: that we delve into its interpretation in detail, and on this there are two summarized views:

The first is what al-Qaffal (may God have mercy on him) mentioned. He said: "The Throne ('arsh), in their speech, is the couch upon which kings sit. Then the Throne became a metonymy for the king himself; it is said: 'His throne collapsed,' meaning his rule was shaken and corrupted. And when his rule is firm and his command and judgment prevail, they say: 'He istawā upon his throne,' and 'he settled upon the couch of his kingdom.'" This is what al-Qaffal said. I say: what he said is true, right and correct. A parallel to it is their saying of a tall man: "So-and-so has long cords (ṭawīl al-nijād)," and of a man who entertains much: "much ash (kathīr al-ramād)," and of an old man: "So-and-so's head has blazed with white hair." None of these expressions intends its literal meaning; rather they intend to make the meaning known by way of metonymy. Likewise here, He mentions istiwā' upon the Throne, and what is meant is the penetration of power and the flow of will.

Then al-Qaffal, may God have mercy on him, said: When God, exalted is He, indicated His essence, His attributes and the manner of His governance of the world in the way they were accustomed to with their kings and chiefs, the greatness of God and the perfection of His majesty settled in their hearts. Yet all of this is conditional upon the negation of likeness (tashbīh). So when He says that He is Knowing, they understand from it that nothing is hidden from Him, exalted is He; then they know by their intellects that this knowledge was not acquired through thought, reflection, or use of a sense. When He says that He is Capable, they understand from it that He is able to bring the beings into existence and form the possibilities; then they know by their intellects that He is independent, in that act of bringing into being and forming, of instruments and tools, and that He precedes matter, duration, thought and deliberation. The same holds for all His attributes. When He informs that He has a House which His servants must pilgrimage to, they understand from it that He has set up for them a place they intend for asking their Lord and seeking their needs, just as they intend the houses of kings and chiefs for this purpose; then they know by their intellects the negation of likeness, and that He did not make that House a dwelling for Himself, nor benefit from it in warding off heat and cold in its very self. When He commands them to praise and glorify Him, they understand from it that He commanded them to the utmost of exalting Him; then they know by their intellects that He is not delighted by that praise and exaltation, nor grieved by its neglect and their turning away from it.

Having understood this introduction, we say: He, exalted is He, informed that He created the heavens and the earth as He willed and wished, without any contender or opponent. Then He informed after that that He istawā upon the Throne, that is, the governance of creation came to Him as He willed and wished. So His saying ﴿then He istawā upon the Throne﴾ means: after He created them, He istawā upon the Throne of dominion and majesty. Then al-Qaffal said: The evidence that this is what is meant is His saying in Surat Yunus: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then istawā upon the Throne, governing the affair﴾ [Yunus: 3]. So His saying ﴿governing the affair﴾ serves as an explanation of His saying ﴿istawā upon the Throne﴾. And in this verse we are explaining, He said: ﴿then istawā upon the Throne, He covers the night over the day, pursuing it swiftly, and the sun and the moon and the stars, subjected by His command. Surely to Him belong creation and command﴾. This indicates that His saying ﴿then He istawā upon the Throne﴾ refers to what we have mentioned.

If it is said: If you interpret His saying ﴿then He istawā upon the Throne﴾ to mean "He istawā over dominion," it must follow that God was not istawā before the creation of the heavens and the earth.

We reply: Before the creation of the worlds, He, exalted is He, was only capable of creating and forming them, and was not actually their creator or originator in their very existence; for the giving of life to Zayd, the causing of death to 'Amr, feeding this one and quenching that one, occur only under these conditions. So when we interpret the Throne as dominion, and dominion as these conditions, it is correct to say that He, exalted is He, istawā over His dominion only after the creation of the heavens and the earth, meaning that His disposal of these things and His governance of them became manifest only after the creation of the heavens and the earth. This is a true and correct answer in this context.

The second answer: it may be said that istawā here means istawlā (to take dominion/prevail). We have already lengthened the explanation of this aspect in the commentary on Surat Ta-Ha, so we will not repeat it here.

The third answer: we interpret the Throne as dominion, and interpret istawā as "to rise and to prevail over the dominion," so the meaning is that He, exalted is He, prevailed over the dominion, in the sense that His power penetrated the arrangement of the kingdom and the malakūt. Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned His saying ﴿istawā upon the Throne﴾ in seven surahs: first here; second in Yunus; third in al-Ra'd; fourth in Ta-Ha; fifth in al-Furqan; sixth in al-Sajdah; seventh in al-Hadid. In each place we have mentioned many benefits, and whoever gathers these benefits together, some with others, they become abundant and reach a considerable degree, sufficient to remove the doubts of likeness from the heart and the mind.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿He covers the night over the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾, there are several issues:

Issue one: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim in the transmission of Hafs read "yughshī" with a light ghayn, and so in al-Ra'd. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr read it with doubling (tashdīd), and so in al-Ra'd. Al-Wahidi (may God have mercy on him) said: al-ighshā' and al-taghshiyah mean covering one thing with another, and revelation has come with both doubled and light forms. From the doubled form is His saying: ﴿So there covered them that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 54], and from the second form His saying: ﴿And We covered them, so they do not see﴾ [Ya-Sin: 9], where the second object is omitted, meaning: We covered them with blindness and the loss of sight.

Issue two: His saying ﴿He covers the night over the day, pursuing it swiftly﴾ may mean that He brings the night upon the day, and it may mean that He brings the day upon the night; the wording admits both together without any alteration. The evidence for the second is the reading of Humayd ibn Qays, "yaghshā al-layla al-nahāru" with a fatha on the yā', the night accusative and the day nominative, meaning: the day overtakes the night and pursues it. Al-Qaffal (may God have mercy on him) said: When He, glorified is He, informed His servants of His istiwā' upon the Throne, He, as it were, showed them by sight, in what they witness of the most difficult of creatures, its continuance according to His will, so that sight would join report and doubts would vanish from every direction. So He said: ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, because God, exalted is He, informed in this Noble Book of the great benefits in the alternation of night and day and the sublime advantages in it; for by their alternation the affair of life is completed and benefit and welfare are perfected.

Issue three: His saying ﴿pursuing it swiftly﴾. Al-Layth said: al-hathth means haste; it is said: "I urged so-and-so and he hastened (iḥtatha)," so he is ḥathīth and maḥthūth, meaning diligent and swift.

Know that He, glorified is He, described this motion with swiftness and intensity, and that is the truth; for the alternation of night and day occurs only through the motion of the greatest sphere, and that motion is the most swift of motions and the most perfect in intensity. So much so that researchers into the states of existing things have said: if a human is running at the utmost intense speed, then in the time it takes to raise his foot and set it down, the greatest sphere moves three thousand miles. Since the matter is so, that motion is at the utmost of intensity and speed. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿pursuing it swiftly﴾. A parallel to this verse is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; and each is floating in an orbit﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]. He likened that course and that motion to swimming in water, and the purpose is to draw attention to its speed, its ease, and the perfection of its progress.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿and the sun and the moon and the stars, subjected by His command﴾. On this there are issues:

Issue one: Ibn 'Amir read "wa-al-shamsu wa-al-qamaru wa-al-nujūmu musakhkharātun" in the nominative, on the sense of a new beginning (ibtidā'). The rest read it in the accusative, on the sense of "and He made the sun and the moon." Al-Wahidi said: The accusative is the preferred reading, because of His saying: ﴿and prostrate to God who created them﴾ [Fussilat: 37]. Just as He stated in that verse that He subjected the sun and the moon, so it must be understood here that He created them in His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ and ﴿the sun and the moon and the stars﴾. This accusative is a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause, meaning: He created these things in a state in which they are described by these attributes, effects and actions. The argument of Ibn 'Amir is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He subjected to you what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾; and among what is in the heaven are the sun and the moon. So when He informed that He subjected them, it is fitting to report of them that they are subjected, just as when you say "I struck Zayd," it is correct to say "Zayd is struck."

Issue two: In this verse there are subtleties.

The first: the sun has two kinds of motion. One of the two: its motion by its own nature, which is completed in a full year, and by this motion the year is produced. The second: its motion by means of the motion of the greatest sphere, and this motion is completed in a day and night.

Knowing this, we say: night and day do not occur through the motion of the sun; they occur through the motion of the outermost heaven which is called the Throne. For this reason, when He mentioned the Throne in His saying ﴿then He istawā upon the Throne﴾, He linked to it His saying ﴿He covers the night over the day﴾, as an indication that the cause of the occurrence of night and day is the motion of the outermost sphere, not the motion of the sun and the moon. This is a subtle and wondrous point.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 7, verse 54 (part 7 of 7):**

The second point: When He, exalted is He, explained how the heavens were created, He said: ﴿Then He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command﴾ [Fussilat: 12]. That verse indicates that He, glory be to Him, specified all of that with a subtle, luminous, lordly essence from the realm of command (ʿālam al-amr).

Then, after it, He said: ﴿Surely, to Him belong the creation and the command﴾. This is an indication that everything other than God, exalted is He, is either from the realm of creation (ʿālam al-khalq) or from the realm of command. As for what belongs to the realm of creation, "creation" means measurement (taqdir). Everything that is a body or corporeal is specified by a determined quantity, so it belongs to the realm of creation. Everything that is free of corporeality and quantity belongs to the realm of spirits and to the realm of command. This shows that He, glory be to Him, assigned to each of the bodies of the spheres and stars, which belong to the realm of creation, an angel from among the angels, who belong to the realm of command. The sound hadiths agree with this, such as what is reported in the traditions that God has angels who move the sun and the moon at their rising and at their setting, and likewise for the rest of the stars. Also, His statement, glory be to Him: ﴿And eight will bear the throne of your Lord above them that Day﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17] is an indication that the angels who sustain the Throne are eight. Then, if you examine closely, you will know that the realm of creation is under God's subjection (taskhir), the realm of command is under God's governance (tadbir), and the dominance of spiritual beings over corporeal beings is by God's decree. For this meaning He said: ﴿Surely, to Him belong the creation and the command﴾.
