**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 55–56 (part 1 of 3):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation, and call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the proofs that indicate the perfection of power, wisdom and mercy, and at this point the obligation directed toward acquiring the knowledge of the soul and the true sciences was complete, He followed it by mentioning the actions that are fitting for those cognitions, which is occupying oneself with supplication (du'a') and humble entreaty (tadarru'), for supplication is the marrow of worship (mukh al-'ibadah). So He said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly.﴾ There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, concerning which there are two opinions. Some said: it means "worship" (u'budu). Others said: it means supplication (al-du'a').

Whoever holds the first view understands from supplication that it is seeking good from Allah, exalted is He, and this is the characteristic of worship, because it is done seeking nearness and seeking reward. Also, Allah, exalted is He, coupled with it His saying: ﴿and call upon Him in fear and hope﴾, and the coupled element ought to be different from the element it is coupled with. The second view is the more apparent, because supplication differs from worship in meaning.

Having understood this, we say: people have differed concerning supplication. Some of them denied it, and they argued for the soundness of their position with several things.

The first: If the thing sought by supplication is known to occur, it is necessarily going to occur, since change in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, and what is necessarily going to occur has no benefit in seeking it. And if it is known not to occur, it is impossible to occur, so there is also no benefit in seeking it.

The second: If Allah, exalted is He, had willed in eternity to bring about that sought thing, it will be realized whether or not this supplication occurs. And if He had willed in eternity not to give it, it is impossible to occur, so there is no benefit in seeking it. And if we say that He did not will in eternity to bring that thing into being, neither its existence nor its non-existence, and then at the time of that supplication He became willing to it, this would entail change occurring in the essence of Allah and in His attributes, and that is impossible. For on this assumption, the servant's undertaking of supplication would become a cause for the occurrence of an attribute in the essence of Allah, exalted is He, so the servant would be disposing of the attribute of Allah through alteration and change, and that is impossible.

The third: If the thing sought by supplication is what wisdom and benefit require to be given, then He, exalted is He, gives it without this supplication, because He is exalted above being miserly. And if wisdom requires withholding it, then He does not give it, whether or not the servant undertakes supplication.

The fourth: Supplication is other than command, and there is no difference between the two categories except that the one who supplicates is of lower rank and the one who commands is of higher rank. And for the servant to undertake to command Allah is bad manners, and it is not permissible.

The fifth: Supplication resembles the case where the servant undertakes to guide his Lord and his Deity to the doing of what is better and more correct, and that is bad manners; or it means he alerts the Deity to something He was not aware of, and that is disbelief; or it means that He fell short in beneficence and bounty, and so by this you are bringing Him to undertake beneficence and bounty, and that is ignorance.

The sixth: Undertaking supplication indicates that the one who does so is not content with the decree, for if he were content with what Allah has decreed for him, he would have abandoned the disposing of his own self and would not have asked Allah for anything specific. And abandoning contentment with the decree is among the reprehensible matters.

The seventh: Often the servant thinks that something is beneficial and good, but then, when it comes into existence, it becomes a cause of many afflictions and great corruptions. Since this is so, seeking a specific thing from Allah is impermissible; rather, it is better to seek what is the benefit and good, and that is granted by Allah, exalted is He, whether or not the servant seeks it by supplication. So nothing of benefit remains in supplication.

The eighth: Supplication is an expression of the heart's turning toward seeking something from Allah, exalted is He. And the heart's turning toward seeking that specific thing prevents the heart from being absorbed in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, in His love, and in servanthood to Him. These are lofty and noble stations, and whatever prevents the attainment of lofty and noble stations is blameworthy.

The ninth: It is narrated that he, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said, relating from Allah, glorified is He: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give those who ask." And this indicates that the better course is to abandon supplication.

The tenth: The knowledge of the Truth encompasses the servant's need, and when the servant knows that his Master is aware of his need, and he remains silent and does not mention that need, this is more conducive to good manners and to the magnification of the Master than if he were to begin explaining the state of that need and asking for what would remove it. And if the matter is this way among the witnessed (human relations), it is necessary to consider the like of it regarding the right of Allah, glorified is He. That is why it is said that when the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, was placed in the catapult to be thrown into the fire, Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, said: "Call upon your Lord!" And the Friend, peace be upon him, said: "My knowledge of my state is sufficient for me in place of asking Him."

These are the aspects mentioned in this chapter. Know that supplication is a kind of worship, and the questions mentioned apply to all kinds of acts of worship: it is said that if this person is happy in the knowledge of Allah, there is no need for acts of obedience and worship, and if he is wretched in His knowledge, there is no benefit in those acts of worship. Also it is said that a person should not eat bread or drink water, for if this person is sated in the knowledge of Allah, there is no need to eat bread, and if he is hungry, there is no benefit in eating bread. And just as this argument is false here, so too is what they have mentioned. Rather, we say: supplication conveys knowledge of the humility of servanthood and conveys knowledge of the might of Lordship, and this is the noblest and highest purpose of all acts of worship. Its explanation is that the one who supplicates does not undertake supplication except when he recognizes in himself that he is in need of that sought thing and that he is incapable of attaining it, and recognizes of his Lord and his Deity that He hears his supplication, knows his need, is able to remove that need, and is merciful, such that His mercy requires the removal of that need. And when this is the case, he does not undertake supplication except when he recognizes that he is characterized by need and by incapacity, and recognizes that the Deity, glorified is He, is characterized by perfect knowledge, power and mercy. So there is no purpose in all the obligations except knowledge of the humility of servanthood and the might of Lordship. When supplication combines these two stations, it is inevitably the greatest of the kinds of worship.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ is an indication of the meaning we have mentioned, because humble entreaty (tadarru') arises only from the deficient in the presence of the perfect. So unless the servant believes in the deficiency of his own self and the perfection of his Master in knowledge, power and mercy, he will not undertake humble entreaty. Thus it is established that the purpose of supplication is what we have mentioned, and so it is established that the wording of the Qur'an is evidence for it. What strengthens what we have mentioned is what is narrated, that he, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said: "Nothing is more honoured by Allah than supplication," and "supplication is worship." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated.﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. The full discussion of the realities of supplication is mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: concerning the establishment of the conditions of supplication.

Know that the purpose of supplication is that the servant becomes a witness to the need of his own self and to the incapacity of his own self, and a witness to the fact that his Master is characterized by perfect knowledge, power and mercy. All these meanings are included in His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly﴾. Then, when these states are attained in sincerity, it is necessary to safeguard them from ostentation (riya'), which nullifies the reality of sincerity, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and secretly﴾. The purpose of mentioning humble entreaty is to establish the original state required of supplication, and the purpose of mentioning concealment is to protect that sincerity from the admixtures of ostentation. When you understand this meaning, it becomes clear to you that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿humbly and secretly﴾ comprises everything that is intended to be realized and attained among the conditions of supplication, and that it does not exceed it at all in any respect. As for the detailed discussion of those conditions, Shaykh Sulayman al-Halimi, may Allah have mercy on him, elaborated on their explanation in the book al-Minhaj, so it is to be sought there.

The third issue: "al-tadarru'" means humbling oneself and showing submission, and it is the displaying of the self's humiliation, from the expression: "Fulan was submissive (ḍari'a) to Fulan," and "tadarra'a lahu" when he displayed humility toward him in the context of asking. "Al-khufyah" is the opposite of openness (al-'alaniyyah); it is said: "akhfaytu al-shay'" when I concealed the thing. It is also said "khifyah" with a kasra. ʿāṣim alone, in the narration of Abu Bakr from him, recited "khifyah" with a kasra on the kh here and in al-An'am, and the rest recited it with a damma, and both are dialects.

Know that concealment is required in supplication, and this is indicated by several aspects.

The first: this verse, for it indicates that He, exalted is He, commanded supplication coupled with concealment, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. If obligation is not established, then it is at least recommended.

* * *

Then, after this, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾. The more apparent meaning is that He does not love those who transgress in abandoning these two matters that were mentioned, namely humble entreaty and concealment. For Allah does not love such a person, and the love of Allah, exalted is He, is an expression for reward. So the meaning is that whoever abandons humble entreaty and concealment in supplication, Allah will by no means reward him or show beneficence to him. And whoever is like this is inevitably among the people of punishment. Thus it becomes clear that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ is like a severe warning against abandoning humble entreaty and concealment in supplication.

The second argument: He, exalted is He, praised Zakariyya, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3], that is, he concealed it from the servants, made it sincere for Allah, and devoted himself to Him through it.

The third argument: what Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated: that they were on a campaign, and they came upon a valley and began to exclaim "Allahu Akbar" and "La ilaha illa Allah" with raised voices. Then he, peace be upon him, said: "Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, Near, and He is with you."

The fourth argument: his saying, peace be upon him: "A supplication in secret equals seventy supplications in public." And from him, peace be upon him: "The best remembrance is the hidden one, and the best provision is that which suffices." And it is related from al-Hasan that he used to say: "A man would gather the Qur'an and his neighbour would not perceive it; he would comprehend much and people would not perceive it; he would pray a long prayer at night while his visitors were present and they would not perceive it. We have known peoples who used to go to great lengths in concealing their deeds. The Muslims used to strive in supplication while their voices were not heard except as whispers, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, and Allah mentioned His servant Zakariyya, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]."

The fifth argument: the rational one, which is that the soul has a strong inclination and a great desire for ostentation and reputation. So when a person raises his voice in supplication, ostentation mingles with that supplication, and then no benefit remains in it at all. Therefore it is better to conceal supplication so that it remains protected from ostentation.

Here are some key points to note about the Mu'tazila's position on Hadith, and the dispute over whether the first or second version of the rule holds.

Part 2 of the commentary is a long passage. What you have sent is the text of part 2 itself, which I was asked to translate. I should be direct about what I produced: the previous reply did not translate the passage. It offered an unrelated summary of Mu'tazili views on hadith, which was not what the passage says, and I should not have presented it as a rendering.

Here is the translation of the passage you sent:

Here there are issues over which the scholars of the path (arbab al-tariqa) have differed greatly. They are: Is it better to conceal acts of worship or to make them public? Some said: concealing them is better, to protect them from riya' (showing off). Others said: making them public is better, so that others may be eager to follow him in performing those acts of worship. Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi took a middle position and said: if one fears for oneself from riya', concealment is better, to protect one's deed from being invalidated; but if one has reached such purity and strength of certainty that one is safe from any trace of riya', then making it public is better for him, so that the benefit of being followed is achieved.

The fourth issue: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: concealing the "ta'min" (saying "amin" aloud or silently in prayer) is better. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: announcing it is better. Abu Hanifa argued for the soundness of his view, saying: regarding the word "amin" there are two aspects:
First, that it is a supplication.
Second, that it is one of the names of Allah.
If it is a supplication, then concealing it is obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. If it is one of the names of Allah, then concealing it is obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear﴾ [al-A'raf: 205]. If obligation is not established, then it is at least recommended. And we say according to this view.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: The Muslims have agreed that love is an attribute of Allah, Exalted, because the Qur'an speaks of it in many verses. They agreed that its meaning is not the desire of the soul, the inclination of nature, or the seeking of pleasure in something, because all of that is impossible for Allah, Exalted, by consensus. They differed in interpreting love with respect to Allah, Exalted, in three views:
The first view: it is an expression for Allah's bestowing reward, goodness, and mercy upon the servant.
The second view: it is an expression for His being willing to bestow reward and goodness upon the servant. This difference is based on another issue: whether He, Exalted, is described with the attribute of will or not. Al-Ka'bi and Abu al-Husayn said: He, Exalted, is not described with will at all. So His being willing for His own acts means that He brings them into existence and is their agent, and His being willing for the acts of others means that He commands them. It is not permissible for Him to be described with the attribute of will. As for our companions (the Ash'aris) and the Mu'tazila of Basra, they affirmed that He is described with the attribute of willing.
Given this, whoever denies will with respect to Allah interprets Allah's love as merely the bestowing of reward on the servant, and whoever affirms will for Allah interprets His love as His willing to bestow reward upon him.
Page 108
The third view: it is not far-fetched that Allah's love for the servant is an attribute beyond His being willing to bestow reward upon him. This is because we observe in the visible world that a father loves his son, and from that love follows the will to bestow good upon that son. So this will is an effect of that love, a fruit of its fruits, and a benefit of its benefits.
At most, it may be said: in the visible world this love is an expression for desire, inclination of nature, and eagerness of the soul, and that is impossible for Allah, Exalted. But we say: why is it not permissible to say that Allah's love is another attribute, other than desire and inclination of nature, from which follows the will to bestow goodness and reward upon the servant? At most, we do not know what that love is or how it is. But the lack of knowledge of a thing does not necessitate knowledge of its non-existence. Do you not see that the People of the Sunna affirm that He is seen, and then say that this seeing differs from the seeing of bodies and colors, rather it is seeing without modality (bila kayf)? So why do they not say here as well: Allah's love for the servant is a love exalted above the inclination of nature and the desire of the soul, rather it is love without modality? Thus it is established that the certainty of the theologians that there is no meaning to Allah's love except the will to bestow reward has no conclusive proof on this restriction. At most, it may be said that there is no proof for affirming another attribute besides will, so it must be negated. But we have shown in the book Nihayat al-'Uqul that this method is weak and invalid.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ means: those who exceed what they were commanded. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Jurayj said: among transgression is raising the voice in supplication.

The third issue: Know that everyone who opposes the command and prohibition of Allah, Exalted, has transgressed and exceeded, so he falls under His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾. We have shown that whoever Allah does not love, He punishes. So the apparent meaning of this verse requires that everyone who opposes Allah's command and prohibition will be punished. The Mu'tazila relied on this verse to assert with certainty the threat of punishment for grave sinners, and they said: it is not permissible to say that what is meant is transgression in raising the voice in supplication. Its explanation is in two ways:
First: the word "al-mu'tadin" is a general term with the definite article, so it conveys comprehensiveness. Its being revealed in this particular case does not restrict it, because it is established that what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.
Second: raising the voice in supplication is not one of the forbidden acts; at most it may be said that the better course is to avoid it. And if it is not forbidden, it does not fall under this threat.
The thorough answer is what we mentioned in Surat al-Baqara: relying on these general expressions does not establish certainty regarding the threat.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾, and there are two issues here:

The first issue: His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ means: do not cause corruption in anything on the earth. It includes the prohibition of corrupting souls by killing and by cutting off limbs; corrupting property by usurpation, theft, and ways of trickery; corrupting religions by disbelief and innovation; corrupting lineages by committing adultery, sodomy, and by slander; and corrupting minds by drinking intoxicants. This is because the interests considered in this world are these five: souls, property, lineages, religions, and minds. So His saying: ﴿do not cause corruption﴾ is a prohibition against bringing the reality of corruption into existence, and prohibiting the bringing of a reality into existence requires prohibiting all its kinds and types, so it includes the prohibition of corruption in these five categories. As for His saying: ﴿after its reformation﴾, it may mean: after He had reformed its creation in the manner that fits the benefits of creatures and suits the interests of those under obligation; and it may mean: after the reformation of the earth through the sending of prophets and the revelation of books, as if He, Exalted, said: since I have reformed the interests of the earth through sending prophets, revealing books, and detailing the laws, then submit to them, and do not proceed to deny the messengers, reject the books, or rebel against accepting the laws, for that would bring about chaos and disorder on the earth, so corruption would occur after reformation, and that is abhorrent to sound reason.

The second issue: This verse indicates that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition, absolutely.

Having established this, we say: if we find a specific text indicating permissibility of engaging in some harms, we judge accordingly, giving priority to the specific over the general; otherwise it remains under the prohibition indicated by this text.

Know that we mentioned in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-A'raf: 32] that this verse indicates that the basic principle regarding benefits and pleasures is permissibility and lawfulness. Then we showed that since the matter is so, all the rulings of Allah, Exalted, fall under that verse. Likewise in this verse, it indicates that the basic principle regarding harms and pains is prohibition.

Once this is established, all the rulings of Allah, Exalted, are included under the generality of this verse, and everything we have discussed of investigations and subtleties in that verse is present in this verse. So that verse indicates that the basic principle regarding benefits is lawfulness, and this verse indicates that the basic principle regarding all harms is prohibition. Each of these two verses corresponds to the other, reinforces its meaning, and establishes its sense, and they indicate that the rulings of all events fall under these generalities. Also, this verse indicates that every contract to which both parties have consented is concluded, valid, and established, because annulling it after it has been established would be corruption after reformation, and the text indicates that this is not permitted.

Once this is established, we say: the indication of this verse in this respect is reinforced by the generality of His saying: ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1], and by the generality of His saying, Exalted: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2-3], and under His saying: ﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant, observers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 8], and under all the general texts concerning the obligation of fulfilling covenants and contracts.

Once this is established, we say: if we find a text indicating that some contract to which both sides consented is not valid, we judge it void, giving priority to the specific over the general; otherwise we judge it valid, observing the indication of these generalities. By this clear and evident method it is established that the Qur'an is sufficient to explain all the rulings of the Shari'a from beginning to end.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾, and there are questions regarding it:

The first question: In the beginning of the verse He said: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, then He said: ﴿and do not cause corruption﴾, then He said: ﴿and call upon Him﴾. This requires attributing a thing to itself, which is invalid.

The answer: Those who said, in explaining His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly﴾, that it means "worship Him," only said that out of concern for this difficulty. If we adopt this explanation, the question is resolved. If we say that what is meant by His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly﴾ is supplication, the answer is that His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ indicates that supplication must be accompanied by humility and concealment. Then He explained in His saying: ﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾ that the benefit of supplication is one of these two matters. So the first verse explains a condition for the validity of supplication, and the second verse explains the benefit and advantage of supplication.

The second question: The theologians agreed that whoever worships and supplicates for the sake of fear of punishment and hope for reward, his worship is not valid. This is because the theologians are of two groups: some said that the obligations were revealed according to the requirement of divinity and servitude, so that His being our God and our being His servants requires that it be proper for Him to command His servants as He wills, and thus what is considered is not that it is in itself good and beneficial. This is the view of the People of the Sunna. Others said: the obligations were revealed because they are in themselves interests; this is the view of the Mu'tazila.

Once you know this, we say: As for the first view, the basis for the obligation of some acts and the prohibition of others is simply God's command to what He made obligatory and His prohibition of what He forbade. So whoever performs these acts of worship has them valid. But whoever performs them out of fear of punishment or hope for reward must be deemed invalid, because he did not perform them for the sake of the reason they are obligatory. As for the second view, the basis for their obligation is that they are in themselves interests, so whoever performs them out of fear of punishment or hope for reward has not performed them for the reason of their obligation, and so they must be deemed invalid. Thus it is established that according to both schools, whoever performs supplication and the rest of the acts of worship out of fear of punishment or hope for reward, they must be deemed invalid.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 55–56 (part 3 of 3):

Having established this, we say: the apparent meaning of His words, ﴿Call upon Him in fear and hope﴾, implies that God commanded the responsible person to make supplication for this purpose. The invalidity of this has been established by proof. So how can the apparent meaning of this verse be reconciled with what we have mentioned from the rational arguments?

The answer: The verse does not mean what you suppose. Rather, it means: call upon Him with fear of falling short in some of the conditions required for the acceptance of that supplication, and with hope that all of those conditions will be fulfilled. On this reading, the question falls away.

Third question: Does this verse indicate that the one who supplicates must necessarily have this fear and hope in his heart?

The answer: The servant cannot be certain that he has fulfilled all the conditions required for the acceptance of supplication, and for this reason fear arises. Likewise, he cannot be certain that those conditions are absent, so he must be hopeful of their being accepted. Therefore, we say: the one who supplicates is not a supplicant unless he is in this state. So His words, ﴿fear and hope﴾, mean that you should be combining in your souls fear and hope in all your deeds, and not be certain that, even if you strive, you have fulfilled the right of your Lord. This is reinforced by His words: ﴿They give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:60).

* * *

Then God said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾. On this there are several issues:

First issue: They differ on whether mercy (rahmah) is the bestowal of good and blessing, or the will to bestow good and blessing. On the first view, mercy is among the attributes of acts; on the second, it is among the attributes of essence. We have thoroughly examined this issue in our commentary on "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

[p. 111]

Second issue: Some of our companions said: For the disbeliever, God has neither mercy nor blessing. They argued from this verse, and its explanation is as follows: this verse indicates that whatever is mercy is near to the doers of good. It follows that whatever is not near to the doers of good is not mercy. What has come to the disbeliever is not near to the doers of good, so it must be that it is not mercy from God, nor a blessing from Him.

Third issue: The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that the mercy of God is near to the doers of good. Since the whole of this reality belongs to the doers of good, it is necessary that no portion of it be given to non-doers of good. Therefore, no part of God's mercy should reach the disbelievers. Yet pardon from punishment is mercy, and deliverance from the Fire after entering it is mercy. So it is necessary that this not be granted to one who is not among the doers of good. The disobedient and the people of major sins are not doers of good, so it is necessary that pardon from punishment not be granted to them, and that deliverance from the Fire not be granted to them.

The answer: Whoever believes in God and affirms the oneness of God and prophethood has done good. The proof is that if a child reaches maturity at the time of mid-morning, believes in God, His Messenger and the Last Day, and dies before midday, the community (ummah) has agreed that he is included in His words: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward)﴾ (Yunus 10:26). It is known that this person did not perform any act of obedience except knowledge and affirmation, because when he reached maturity after the dawn, the dawn prayer was not obligatory upon him, and when he died before noon, the noon prayer was not obligatory upon him. The apparent meaning is that the rest of the acts of worship were not obligatory upon him. Thus it is established that he is a doer of good, and it is established that nothing proceeded from him except knowledge and affirmation. Therefore, this amount must count as good, and its doer is a doer of good.

Having established this, we say: Everyone who has attained affirmation and knowledge is among the doers of good. This verse indicates that the mercy of God is near to the doers of good. Therefore, by the ruling of this verse, the mercy of God must reach the person who has committed a major sin among the people of prayer, and then this verse turns into proof against them.

If they say: "The doers of good are those who have brought all the aspects of goodness," we say: This is false, because the doer of good is one from whom the name of goodness proceeds, and it is not a condition of being a doer of good that one bring all aspects of goodness, just as the knowing person is one who has knowledge, and it is not a condition of him that he attain all kinds of knowledge. Thus it is established by this that the objection they raised falls away, and that the truth is what we have upheld.

Fourth issue: One may say: The grammatical rule would require that it be said, "Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near (qarib) to the doers of good." So what is the reason for the omission of the feminine marker (ta' al-ta'nith)? They gave several answers to this:

The first: The feminine form of "mercy" is not real (haqiqi), and whatever is like this may be treated as either masculine or feminine according to the people of the language.

The second: Al-Zajjaj said: He said "qarib" because mercy, forgiveness, pardon and bounty have one meaning. So His words, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾, mean: the bounty of Allah is near, and the reward of Allah is near. Thus the ruling of one of the two terms was applied to the other.

The third: Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "Mercy" is a verbal noun (masdar), and verbal nouns by right are masculine, as in His words: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:275). This goes back to al-Zajjaj's view, because "admonition" is intended to mean "exhortation," and therefore it was mentioned in that form. The poet said:

Indeed, generosity and manliness have been joined
in a tomb in Marw, on the clear road.

It was said: By "generosity" he meant bounty, and by "manliness" he meant nobility.

The fourth: The interpretation may be that the mercy of Allah is something with a near place, close to the doers of good, as they say: "hā'iḍ" (a woman in menses), "laban" (milk-bearing) and "tamr" (dates-bearing), meaning: possessing menstruation, milk and dates. Al-Wahidi said: al-Arudi told me, from al-Azhari, from al-Mundhiri, from al-Harrani, from Ibn al-Sikkit, who said: The Arabs say: "He is near to me" (huwa qarib minni), "they two are near to me" (huma qarib minni), "they are near to me" (hum qarib minni), and "she is near to me" (hiya qarib minni), because it is in the sense of "he is in a place near to me." It is also permissible to say "qarib" (feminine) and "ba'idah" (feminine) to point to the meaning that they (the things) have come near or gone far by themselves.

Fifth issue: The explanation of this nearness is that a person grows nearer to the Hereafter and further from this world every moment, for the world is like the past and the Hereafter is like the future. A person, at every hour, moment and glance, grows further from the past and nearer to the future. For this reason the poet said:

May what you love never cease to be nearer than tomorrow,
and may what you fear never cease to be further than yesterday.

Since it is established that the world grows further away every hour, and the Hereafter grows nearer every hour, and since it is established that the mercy of God is only attained after death, it follows that God, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾, on the basis of this interpretation.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 55–56 (part 1 of 3):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly. Indeed, He does not love the transgressors.﴾ ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation, and call upon Him in fear and hope. Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the proofs that indicate the perfection of power, wisdom and mercy, and at this point the obligation directed toward acquiring the knowledge of the soul and the true sciences was complete, He followed it by mentioning the actions that are fitting for those cognitions, which is occupying oneself with supplication (du'a') and humble entreaty (tadarru'), for supplication is the marrow of worship (mukh al-'ibadah). So He said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly.﴾ There are several issues in the verse.

The first issue: His saying, ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, concerning which there are two opinions. Some said: it means "worship" (u'budu). Others said: it means supplication (al-du'a').

Whoever holds the first view understands from supplication that it is seeking good from Allah, exalted is He, and this is the characteristic of worship, because it is done seeking nearness and seeking reward. Also, Allah, exalted is He, coupled with it His saying: ﴿and call upon Him in fear and hope﴾, and the coupled element ought to be different from the element it is coupled with. The second view is the more apparent, because supplication differs from worship in meaning.

Having understood this, we say: people have differed concerning supplication. Some of them denied it, and they argued for the soundness of their position with several things.

The first: If the thing sought by supplication is known to occur, it is necessarily going to occur, since change in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, and what is necessarily going to occur has no benefit in seeking it. And if it is known not to occur, it is impossible to occur, so there is also no benefit in seeking it.

The second: If Allah, exalted is He, had willed in eternity to bring about that sought thing, it will be realized whether or not this supplication occurs. And if He had willed in eternity not to give it, it is impossible to occur, so there is no benefit in seeking it. And if we say that He did not will in eternity to bring that thing into being, neither its existence nor its non-existence, and then at the time of that supplication He became willing to it, this would entail change occurring in the essence of Allah and in His attributes, and that is impossible. For on this assumption, the servant's undertaking of supplication would become a cause for the occurrence of an attribute in the essence of Allah, exalted is He, so the servant would be disposing of the attribute of Allah through alteration and change, and that is impossible.

The third: If the thing sought by supplication is what wisdom and benefit require to be given, then He, exalted is He, gives it without this supplication, because He is exalted above being miserly. And if wisdom requires withholding it, then He does not give it, whether or not the servant undertakes supplication.

The fourth: Supplication is other than command, and there is no difference between the two categories except that the one who supplicates is of lower rank and the one who commands is of higher rank. And for the servant to undertake to command Allah is bad manners, and it is not permissible.

The fifth: Supplication resembles the case where the servant undertakes to guide his Lord and his Deity to the doing of what is better and more correct, and that is bad manners; or it means he alerts the Deity to something He was not aware of, and that is disbelief; or it means that He fell short in beneficence and bounty, and so by this you are bringing Him to undertake beneficence and bounty, and that is ignorance.

The sixth: Undertaking supplication indicates that the one who does so is not content with the decree, for if he were content with what Allah has decreed for him, he would have abandoned the disposing of his own self and would not have asked Allah for anything specific. And abandoning contentment with the decree is among the reprehensible matters.

The seventh: Often the servant thinks that something is beneficial and good, but then, when it comes into existence, it becomes a cause of many afflictions and great corruptions. Since this is so, seeking a specific thing from Allah is impermissible; rather, it is better to seek what is the benefit and good, and that is granted by Allah, exalted is He, whether or not the servant seeks it by supplication. So nothing of benefit remains in supplication.

The eighth: Supplication is an expression of the heart's turning toward seeking something from Allah, exalted is He. And the heart's turning toward seeking that specific thing prevents the heart from being absorbed in the knowledge of Allah, exalted is He, in His love, and in servanthood to Him. These are lofty and noble stations, and whatever prevents the attainment of lofty and noble stations is blameworthy.

The ninth: It is narrated that he, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said, relating from Allah, glorified is He: "Whoever is preoccupied with My remembrance from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give those who ask." And this indicates that the better course is to abandon supplication.

The tenth: The knowledge of the Truth encompasses the servant's need, and when the servant knows that his Master is aware of his need, and he remains silent and does not mention that need, this is more conducive to good manners and to the magnification of the Master than if he were to begin explaining the state of that need and asking for what would remove it. And if the matter is this way among the witnessed (human relations), it is necessary to consider the like of it regarding the right of Allah, glorified is He. That is why it is said that when the Friend (Khalil, Abraham), peace be upon him, was placed in the catapult to be thrown into the fire, Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him, said: "Call upon your Lord!" And the Friend, peace be upon him, said: "My knowledge of my state is sufficient for me in place of asking Him."

These are the aspects mentioned in this chapter. Know that supplication is a kind of worship, and the questions mentioned apply to all kinds of acts of worship: it is said that if this person is happy in the knowledge of Allah, there is no need for acts of obedience and worship, and if he is wretched in His knowledge, there is no benefit in those acts of worship. Also it is said that a person should not eat bread or drink water, for if this person is sated in the knowledge of Allah, there is no need to eat bread, and if he is hungry, there is no benefit in eating bread. And just as this argument is false here, so too is what they have mentioned. Rather, we say: supplication conveys knowledge of the humility of servanthood and conveys knowledge of the might of Lordship, and this is the noblest and highest purpose of all acts of worship. Its explanation is that the one who supplicates does not undertake supplication except when he recognizes in himself that he is in need of that sought thing and that he is incapable of attaining it, and recognizes of his Lord and his Deity that He hears his supplication, knows his need, is able to remove that need, and is merciful, such that His mercy requires the removal of that need. And when this is the case, he does not undertake supplication except when he recognizes that he is characterized by need and by incapacity, and recognizes that the Deity, glorified is He, is characterized by perfect knowledge, power and mercy. So there is no purpose in all the obligations except knowledge of the humility of servanthood and the might of Lordship. When supplication combines these two stations, it is inevitably the greatest of the kinds of worship.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ is an indication of the meaning we have mentioned, because humble entreaty (tadarru') arises only from the deficient in the presence of the perfect. So unless the servant believes in the deficiency of his own self and the perfection of his Master in knowledge, power and mercy, he will not undertake humble entreaty. Thus it is established that the purpose of supplication is what we have mentioned, and so it is established that the wording of the Qur'an is evidence for it. What strengthens what we have mentioned is what is narrated, that he, peace be upon him (ﷺ), said: "Nothing is more honoured by Allah than supplication," and "supplication is worship." Then he recited: ﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated.﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. The full discussion of the realities of supplication is mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah: 186]. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: concerning the establishment of the conditions of supplication.

Know that the purpose of supplication is that the servant becomes a witness to the need of his own self and to the incapacity of his own self, and a witness to the fact that his Master is characterized by perfect knowledge, power and mercy. All these meanings are included in His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly﴾. Then, when these states are attained in sincerity, it is necessary to safeguard them from ostentation (riya'), which nullifies the reality of sincerity, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and secretly﴾. The purpose of mentioning humble entreaty is to establish the original state required of supplication, and the purpose of mentioning concealment is to protect that sincerity from the admixtures of ostentation. When you understand this meaning, it becomes clear to you that His saying, glorified is He: ﴿humbly and secretly﴾ comprises everything that is intended to be realized and attained among the conditions of supplication, and that it does not exceed it at all in any respect. As for the detailed discussion of those conditions, Shaykh Sulayman al-Halimi, may Allah have mercy on him, elaborated on their explanation in the book al-Minhaj, so it is to be sought there.

The third issue: "al-tadarru'" means humbling oneself and showing submission, and it is the displaying of the self's humiliation, from the expression: "Fulan was submissive (ḍari'a) to Fulan," and "tadarra'a lahu" when he displayed humility toward him in the context of asking. "Al-khufyah" is the opposite of openness (al-'alaniyyah); it is said: "akhfaytu al-shay'" when I concealed the thing. It is also said "khifyah" with a kasra. ʿāṣim alone, in the narration of Abu Bakr from him, recited "khifyah" with a kasra on the kh here and in al-An'am, and the rest recited it with a damma, and both are dialects.

Know that concealment is required in supplication, and this is indicated by several aspects.

The first: this verse, for it indicates that He, exalted is He, commanded supplication coupled with concealment, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. If obligation is not established, then it is at least recommended.

* * *

Then, after this, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾. The more apparent meaning is that He does not love those who transgress in abandoning these two matters that were mentioned, namely humble entreaty and concealment. For Allah does not love such a person, and the love of Allah, exalted is He, is an expression for reward. So the meaning is that whoever abandons humble entreaty and concealment in supplication, Allah will by no means reward him or show beneficence to him. And whoever is like this is inevitably among the people of punishment. Thus it becomes clear that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ is like a severe warning against abandoning humble entreaty and concealment in supplication.

The second argument: He, exalted is He, praised Zakariyya, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3], that is, he concealed it from the servants, made it sincere for Allah, and devoted himself to Him through it.

The third argument: what Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated: that they were on a campaign, and they came upon a valley and began to exclaim "Allahu Akbar" and "La ilaha illa Allah" with raised voices. Then he, peace be upon him, said: "Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, Near, and He is with you."

The fourth argument: his saying, peace be upon him: "A supplication in secret equals seventy supplications in public." And from him, peace be upon him: "The best remembrance is the hidden one, and the best provision is that which suffices." And it is related from al-Hasan that he used to say: "A man would gather the Qur'an and his neighbour would not perceive it; he would comprehend much and people would not perceive it; he would pray a long prayer at night while his visitors were present and they would not perceive it. We have known peoples who used to go to great lengths in concealing their deeds. The Muslims used to strive in supplication while their voices were not heard except as whispers, because Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾, and Allah mentioned His servant Zakariyya, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]."

The fifth argument: the rational one, which is that the soul has a strong inclination and a great desire for ostentation and reputation. So when a person raises his voice in supplication, ostentation mingles with that supplication, and then no benefit remains in it at all. Therefore it is better to conceal supplication so that it remains protected from ostentation.

Here are some key points to note about the Mu'tazila's position on Hadith, and the dispute over whether the first or second version of the rule holds.

Part 2 of the commentary is a long passage. What you have sent is the text of part 2 itself, which I was asked to translate. I should be direct about what I produced: the previous reply did not translate the passage. It offered an unrelated summary of Mu'tazili views on hadith, which was not what the passage says, and I should not have presented it as a rendering.

Here is the translation of the passage you sent:

Here there are issues over which the scholars of the path (arbab al-tariqa) have differed greatly. They are: Is it better to conceal acts of worship or to make them public? Some said: concealing them is better, to protect them from riya' (showing off). Others said: making them public is better, so that others may be eager to follow him in performing those acts of worship. Shaykh Muhammad ibn 'Isa al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi took a middle position and said: if one fears for oneself from riya', concealment is better, to protect one's deed from being invalidated; but if one has reached such purity and strength of certainty that one is safe from any trace of riya', then making it public is better for him, so that the benefit of being followed is achieved.

The fourth issue: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, said: concealing the "ta'min" (saying "amin" aloud or silently in prayer) is better. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: announcing it is better. Abu Hanifa argued for the soundness of his view, saying: regarding the word "amin" there are two aspects:
First, that it is a supplication.
Second, that it is one of the names of Allah.
If it is a supplication, then concealing it is obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. If it is one of the names of Allah, then concealing it is obligatory, based on His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear﴾ [al-A'raf: 205]. If obligation is not established, then it is at least recommended. And we say according to this view.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: The Muslims have agreed that love is an attribute of Allah, Exalted, because the Qur'an speaks of it in many verses. They agreed that its meaning is not the desire of the soul, the inclination of nature, or the seeking of pleasure in something, because all of that is impossible for Allah, Exalted, by consensus. They differed in interpreting love with respect to Allah, Exalted, in three views:
The first view: it is an expression for Allah's bestowing reward, goodness, and mercy upon the servant.
The second view: it is an expression for His being willing to bestow reward and goodness upon the servant. This difference is based on another issue: whether He, Exalted, is described with the attribute of will or not. Al-Ka'bi and Abu al-Husayn said: He, Exalted, is not described with will at all. So His being willing for His own acts means that He brings them into existence and is their agent, and His being willing for the acts of others means that He commands them. It is not permissible for Him to be described with the attribute of will. As for our companions (the Ash'aris) and the Mu'tazila of Basra, they affirmed that He is described with the attribute of willing.
Given this, whoever denies will with respect to Allah interprets Allah's love as merely the bestowing of reward on the servant, and whoever affirms will for Allah interprets His love as His willing to bestow reward upon him.
Page 108
The third view: it is not far-fetched that Allah's love for the servant is an attribute beyond His being willing to bestow reward upon him. This is because we observe in the visible world that a father loves his son, and from that love follows the will to bestow good upon that son. So this will is an effect of that love, a fruit of its fruits, and a benefit of its benefits.
At most, it may be said: in the visible world this love is an expression for desire, inclination of nature, and eagerness of the soul, and that is impossible for Allah, Exalted. But we say: why is it not permissible to say that Allah's love is another attribute, other than desire and inclination of nature, from which follows the will to bestow goodness and reward upon the servant? At most, we do not know what that love is or how it is. But the lack of knowledge of a thing does not necessitate knowledge of its non-existence. Do you not see that the People of the Sunna affirm that He is seen, and then say that this seeing differs from the seeing of bodies and colors, rather it is seeing without modality (bila kayf)? So why do they not say here as well: Allah's love for the servant is a love exalted above the inclination of nature and the desire of the soul, rather it is love without modality? Thus it is established that the certainty of the theologians that there is no meaning to Allah's love except the will to bestow reward has no conclusive proof on this restriction. At most, it may be said that there is no proof for affirming another attribute besides will, so it must be negated. But we have shown in the book Nihayat al-'Uqul that this method is weak and invalid.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ means: those who exceed what they were commanded. Al-Kalbi and Ibn Jurayj said: among transgression is raising the voice in supplication.

The third issue: Know that everyone who opposes the command and prohibition of Allah, Exalted, has transgressed and exceeded, so he falls under His saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾. We have shown that whoever Allah does not love, He punishes. So the apparent meaning of this verse requires that everyone who opposes Allah's command and prohibition will be punished. The Mu'tazila relied on this verse to assert with certainty the threat of punishment for grave sinners, and they said: it is not permissible to say that what is meant is transgression in raising the voice in supplication. Its explanation is in two ways:
First: the word "al-mu'tadin" is a general term with the definite article, so it conveys comprehensiveness. Its being revealed in this particular case does not restrict it, because it is established that what counts is the generality of the wording, not the specific cause.
Second: raising the voice in supplication is not one of the forbidden acts; at most it may be said that the better course is to avoid it. And if it is not forbidden, it does not fall under this threat.
The thorough answer is what we mentioned in Surat al-Baqara: relying on these general expressions does not establish certainty regarding the threat.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾, and there are two issues here:

The first issue: His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption on the earth after its reformation﴾ means: do not cause corruption in anything on the earth. It includes the prohibition of corrupting souls by killing and by cutting off limbs; corrupting property by usurpation, theft, and ways of trickery; corrupting religions by disbelief and innovation; corrupting lineages by committing adultery, sodomy, and by slander; and corrupting minds by drinking intoxicants. This is because the interests considered in this world are these five: souls, property, lineages, religions, and minds. So His saying: ﴿do not cause corruption﴾ is a prohibition against bringing the reality of corruption into existence, and prohibiting the bringing of a reality into existence requires prohibiting all its kinds and types, so it includes the prohibition of corruption in these five categories. As for His saying: ﴿after its reformation﴾, it may mean: after He had reformed its creation in the manner that fits the benefits of creatures and suits the interests of those under obligation; and it may mean: after the reformation of the earth through the sending of prophets and the revelation of books, as if He, Exalted, said: since I have reformed the interests of the earth through sending prophets, revealing books, and detailing the laws, then submit to them, and do not proceed to deny the messengers, reject the books, or rebel against accepting the laws, for that would bring about chaos and disorder on the earth, so corruption would occur after reformation, and that is abhorrent to sound reason.

The second issue: This verse indicates that the basic principle regarding harms is prohibition, absolutely.

Having established this, we say: if we find a specific text indicating permissibility of engaging in some harms, we judge accordingly, giving priority to the specific over the general; otherwise it remains under the prohibition indicated by this text.

Know that we mentioned in the explanation of His saying: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision?﴾ [al-A'raf: 32] that this verse indicates that the basic principle regarding benefits and pleasures is permissibility and lawfulness. Then we showed that since the matter is so, all the rulings of Allah, Exalted, fall under that verse. Likewise in this verse, it indicates that the basic principle regarding harms and pains is prohibition.

Once this is established, all the rulings of Allah, Exalted, are included under the generality of this verse, and everything we have discussed of investigations and subtleties in that verse is present in this verse. So that verse indicates that the basic principle regarding benefits is lawfulness, and this verse indicates that the basic principle regarding all harms is prohibition. Each of these two verses corresponds to the other, reinforces its meaning, and establishes its sense, and they indicate that the rulings of all events fall under these generalities. Also, this verse indicates that every contract to which both parties have consented is concluded, valid, and established, because annulling it after it has been established would be corruption after reformation, and the text indicates that this is not permitted.

Once this is established, we say: the indication of this verse in this respect is reinforced by the generality of His saying: ﴿Fulfill the contracts﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 1], and by the generality of His saying, Exalted: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do? Greatly hateful is it in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 2-3], and under His saying: ﴿And those who are, for their trusts and their covenant, observers﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 8], and under all the general texts concerning the obligation of fulfilling covenants and contracts.

Once this is established, we say: if we find a text indicating that some contract to which both sides consented is not valid, we judge it void, giving priority to the specific over the general; otherwise we judge it valid, observing the indication of these generalities. By this clear and evident method it is established that the Qur'an is sufficient to explain all the rulings of the Shari'a from beginning to end.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾, and there are questions regarding it:

The first question: In the beginning of the verse He said: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, then He said: ﴿and do not cause corruption﴾, then He said: ﴿and call upon Him﴾. This requires attributing a thing to itself, which is invalid.

The answer: Those who said, in explaining His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly﴾, that it means "worship Him," only said that out of concern for this difficulty. If we adopt this explanation, the question is resolved. If we say that what is meant by His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly﴾ is supplication, the answer is that His saying: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ indicates that supplication must be accompanied by humility and concealment. Then He explained in His saying: ﴿And call upon Him in fear and in hope﴾ that the benefit of supplication is one of these two matters. So the first verse explains a condition for the validity of supplication, and the second verse explains the benefit and advantage of supplication.

The second question: The theologians agreed that whoever worships and supplicates for the sake of fear of punishment and hope for reward, his worship is not valid. This is because the theologians are of two groups: some said that the obligations were revealed according to the requirement of divinity and servitude, so that His being our God and our being His servants requires that it be proper for Him to command His servants as He wills, and thus what is considered is not that it is in itself good and beneficial. This is the view of the People of the Sunna. Others said: the obligations were revealed because they are in themselves interests; this is the view of the Mu'tazila.

Once you know this, we say: As for the first view, the basis for the obligation of some acts and the prohibition of others is simply God's command to what He made obligatory and His prohibition of what He forbade. So whoever performs these acts of worship has them valid. But whoever performs them out of fear of punishment or hope for reward must be deemed invalid, because he did not perform them for the sake of the reason they are obligatory. As for the second view, the basis for their obligation is that they are in themselves interests, so whoever performs them out of fear of punishment or hope for reward has not performed them for the reason of their obligation, and so they must be deemed invalid. Thus it is established that according to both schools, whoever performs supplication and the rest of the acts of worship out of fear of punishment or hope for reward, they must be deemed invalid.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 55–56 (part 3 of 3):

Having established this, we say: the apparent meaning of His words, ﴿Call upon Him in fear and hope﴾, implies that God commanded the responsible person to make supplication for this purpose. The invalidity of this has been established by proof. So how can the apparent meaning of this verse be reconciled with what we have mentioned from the rational arguments?

The answer: The verse does not mean what you suppose. Rather, it means: call upon Him with fear of falling short in some of the conditions required for the acceptance of that supplication, and with hope that all of those conditions will be fulfilled. On this reading, the question falls away.

Third question: Does this verse indicate that the one who supplicates must necessarily have this fear and hope in his heart?

The answer: The servant cannot be certain that he has fulfilled all the conditions required for the acceptance of supplication, and for this reason fear arises. Likewise, he cannot be certain that those conditions are absent, so he must be hopeful of their being accepted. Therefore, we say: the one who supplicates is not a supplicant unless he is in this state. So His words, ﴿fear and hope﴾, mean that you should be combining in your souls fear and hope in all your deeds, and not be certain that, even if you strive, you have fulfilled the right of your Lord. This is reinforced by His words: ﴿They give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:60).

* * *

Then God said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾. On this there are several issues:

First issue: They differ on whether mercy (rahmah) is the bestowal of good and blessing, or the will to bestow good and blessing. On the first view, mercy is among the attributes of acts; on the second, it is among the attributes of essence. We have thoroughly examined this issue in our commentary on "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful."

[p. 111]

Second issue: Some of our companions said: For the disbeliever, God has neither mercy nor blessing. They argued from this verse, and its explanation is as follows: this verse indicates that whatever is mercy is near to the doers of good. It follows that whatever is not near to the doers of good is not mercy. What has come to the disbeliever is not near to the doers of good, so it must be that it is not mercy from God, nor a blessing from Him.

Third issue: The Mu'tazilah said: The verse indicates that the mercy of God is near to the doers of good. Since the whole of this reality belongs to the doers of good, it is necessary that no portion of it be given to non-doers of good. Therefore, no part of God's mercy should reach the disbelievers. Yet pardon from punishment is mercy, and deliverance from the Fire after entering it is mercy. So it is necessary that this not be granted to one who is not among the doers of good. The disobedient and the people of major sins are not doers of good, so it is necessary that pardon from punishment not be granted to them, and that deliverance from the Fire not be granted to them.

The answer: Whoever believes in God and affirms the oneness of God and prophethood has done good. The proof is that if a child reaches maturity at the time of mid-morning, believes in God, His Messenger and the Last Day, and dies before midday, the community (ummah) has agreed that he is included in His words: ﴿For those who did good is the best (reward)﴾ (Yunus 10:26). It is known that this person did not perform any act of obedience except knowledge and affirmation, because when he reached maturity after the dawn, the dawn prayer was not obligatory upon him, and when he died before noon, the noon prayer was not obligatory upon him. The apparent meaning is that the rest of the acts of worship were not obligatory upon him. Thus it is established that he is a doer of good, and it is established that nothing proceeded from him except knowledge and affirmation. Therefore, this amount must count as good, and its doer is a doer of good.

Having established this, we say: Everyone who has attained affirmation and knowledge is among the doers of good. This verse indicates that the mercy of God is near to the doers of good. Therefore, by the ruling of this verse, the mercy of God must reach the person who has committed a major sin among the people of prayer, and then this verse turns into proof against them.

If they say: "The doers of good are those who have brought all the aspects of goodness," we say: This is false, because the doer of good is one from whom the name of goodness proceeds, and it is not a condition of being a doer of good that one bring all aspects of goodness, just as the knowing person is one who has knowledge, and it is not a condition of him that he attain all kinds of knowledge. Thus it is established by this that the objection they raised falls away, and that the truth is what we have upheld.

Fourth issue: One may say: The grammatical rule would require that it be said, "Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near (qarib) to the doers of good." So what is the reason for the omission of the feminine marker (ta' al-ta'nith)? They gave several answers to this:

The first: The feminine form of "mercy" is not real (haqiqi), and whatever is like this may be treated as either masculine or feminine according to the people of the language.

The second: Al-Zajjaj said: He said "qarib" because mercy, forgiveness, pardon and bounty have one meaning. So His words, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾, mean: the bounty of Allah is near, and the reward of Allah is near. Thus the ruling of one of the two terms was applied to the other.

The third: Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "Mercy" is a verbal noun (masdar), and verbal nouns by right are masculine, as in His words: ﴿Whoever receives an admonition﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:275). This goes back to al-Zajjaj's view, because "admonition" is intended to mean "exhortation," and therefore it was mentioned in that form. The poet said:

Indeed, generosity and manliness have been joined
in a tomb in Marw, on the clear road.

It was said: By "generosity" he meant bounty, and by "manliness" he meant nobility.

The fourth: The interpretation may be that the mercy of Allah is something with a near place, close to the doers of good, as they say: "hā'iḍ" (a woman in menses), "laban" (milk-bearing) and "tamr" (dates-bearing), meaning: possessing menstruation, milk and dates. Al-Wahidi said: al-Arudi told me, from al-Azhari, from al-Mundhiri, from al-Harrani, from Ibn al-Sikkit, who said: The Arabs say: "He is near to me" (huwa qarib minni), "they two are near to me" (huma qarib minni), "they are near to me" (hum qarib minni), and "she is near to me" (hiya qarib minni), because it is in the sense of "he is in a place near to me." It is also permissible to say "qarib" (feminine) and "ba'idah" (feminine) to point to the meaning that they (the things) have come near or gone far by themselves.

Fifth issue: The explanation of this nearness is that a person grows nearer to the Hereafter and further from this world every moment, for the world is like the past and the Hereafter is like the future. A person, at every hour, moment and glance, grows further from the past and nearer to the future. For this reason the poet said:

May what you love never cease to be nearer than tomorrow,
and may what you fear never cease to be further than yesterday.

Since it is established that the world grows further away every hour, and the Hereafter grows nearer every hour, and since it is established that the mercy of God is only attained after death, it follows that God, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the doers of good﴾, on the basis of this interpretation.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 57–58 (part 1 of 3)**

God's words: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy, until when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water from it, and bring forth from it all kinds of fruits. Thus shall We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember.﴾ ﴿As for the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, but that which is bad yields only meagrely. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾

Know that there are two aspects regarding the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses:

The first: When God mentioned the proofs of divinity and the perfection of knowledge and power in the upper world, namely the heavens, the sun, the moon and the stars, He followed it with mention of proofs from some of the conditions of the lower world. Know that the conditions of this world are confined to four matters: the upper phenomena (al-ātharāt al-ʿulwiyya), minerals, plants, and animals. Among the upper phenomena are the winds, the clouds and the rains. The conditions of plants are consequent upon the descent of rain, and that is what is mentioned in this verse.

The second aspect of explaining the arrangement: When God established the proof in the first verse for the existence of the God who is capable, knowing, wise and merciful, He established in this verse the proof for the validity of the doctrine of the gathering (al-ḥashr), the scattering (al-nashr), the resurrection (al-baʿth) and the Last Day, so that through knowledge of these two verses one obtains all that is needed for knowing the Origin (al-mabda') and the Return (al-maʿād).

[Page 113]

There are issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *al-rīḥ* (الرِّيحَ, the singular), while the rest read *al-riyāḥ* (الرِّياحَ, the plural). Whoever reads *al-riyāḥ* in the plural finds its description with *bushran* appropriate, since it is the plural described with the plural. Whoever reads *al-rīḥ* in the singular reads *bushuran* (بُشُرًا) in the plural, because by *al-rīḥ* he means multiplicity, like their saying: "a lot of dirhams," "dinars," "sheep," and "camels," and like His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 2], then He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 3]. Since the intended meaning of *al-rīḥ* is the plural, He described it with the plural. As for His saying *bushran*, there are readings for it:

The first: The reading of the majority is *nushuran* (نُشُرًا), with a ḍamma on the nūn and the shīn, which is the plural of *nashūr*, like *rusul* for *rasūl*. *Nashūr* carries the meaning of *munsharā* (scattered), like *rakūb* in the sense of *marākūb* (ridden). The meaning is winds that are spread out (munashsharah), i.e., dispersed from every direction. *Al-nashr* is dispersal, and from it come *nashr al-thawb* (shaking out a garment) and *nashr al-khashaba* (sawing wood with a saw). Al-Farrā' said: *al-nashr* among the winds is the gentle, pleasant wind that spreads the clouds; its singular is *nushūr*, and its origin is from *al-nashr*, which is a pleasant fragrance. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "and the spreading of perfume" (*wa-nashr al-ʿiṭr*).

The second reading: Ibn ʿĀmir read *nushran* (نُشْرًا) with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn, lightening the ʿayn, as one says *kutb* and *rusl*.

The third reading: Hamza read *nashran* (نَشْرًا) with a fatḥa on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn. *Al-nashr* is the verbal noun of *nashartu al-thawb*, the opposite of *ṭawaytuhu* (I folded it), and the verbal noun here is used in the sense of the passive participle. It is as if the winds were folded, then God sent them spread out after their folding. So His saying *nashran* is a verbal noun functioning as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from *al-riyāḥ*; the implied meaning is: He sends the winds spreading out. It is also permissible that *al-nashr* here carries the meaning of life, from their saying: "God revived (*anshara*) the dead, so he was revived (*nushira*)." Al-Aʿshā said:

"O wonder at the dead who is revived!"

If you interpret it this way, which is the preferred view, then the verbal noun is intended in the sense of the active participle, as you say: "He came to me running" (*rakḍan*), meaning "running." It is also permissible to say that *arsala* and *nashara* are close in meaning, so it is as if it were said: "And He is the one who spreads the winds with spreading."

The fourth reading: The author of al-Kashshaf reported from Masruq the reading *nashran* in the sense of *manshūrāt* (spread things), a form *faʿl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*, like *naqḍ* and *ḥasb*. From it comes their saying: "He gathered its spread-out things" (*ḍamma nashrahu*).

The fifth reading: The reading of ʿĀṣim is *bushran* (بُشْرًا) with a single dot below the bā', the plural of *bashīr* as *bushr*, from His saying: ﴿He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾ [al-Rūm: 46], meaning they bring good news of rain and mercy. The author of al-Kashshaf also related *bushuran* with a ḍamma on the shīn and its lightening, and *bashran* with a fatḥa on the bā' and a sukūn on the shīn, a verbal noun from *bashsharahu* in the sense of *bashsharahu* (he gave him good news), meaning *bāshirāt* and *busrā*.

[Page 114]

**The second issue:** Know that His saying ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ is conjoined (ma'ṭūf) to His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. Then we say: the definition of wind is that it is moving air. We say: this air's being in motion is not due to its essence nor to the necessary attributes of its essence, for otherwise the motion would persist as long as its essence persists. Therefore it must be due to the moving of a choosing agent, who is God, majestic is His majesty. The philosophers said: here there is another cause, namely that earthly particles, which are fine, rise from the earth and heat it with a strong, intense heat; because of that intense heat it rises and ascends. When it reaches near the celestial sphere, the air adhering to the concave surface of the sphere is moving in the circular motion of the sphere, by the circular motion that has come about for that layer of air. So it prevents these vapours from ascending; rather it turns them back from the direction of their motion. Then those vapours return and disperse in every direction, and by that dispersal the winds arise. Then, the more those vapours are, and the stronger their ascent, the stronger their return will be in motion, so the winds become stronger and more intense. This is the summary of what they have mentioned, and it is false. Several points demonstrate its falsehood:

The first: The ascent of the earthly particles occurs only because of the intensity of their heating. There is no doubt that this heating is an accident, because the earth is by nature cold and dry. When those earthly particles ascend greatly, they become quickly affected. When they rise and reach the cold layer of air, it becomes impossible for the heat to persist in them; rather they become very cold. And when they become cold, it becomes impossible for them to reach, in their ascent, the air layer moving with the motion of the sphere. So what they claimed is refuted.

The second point: Suppose those smoky particles did ascend to the air layer moving with the motion of the sphere. Nevertheless, when they return, they must descend in a straight line, because the earth is a heavy body, and a heavy body moves only in a straight line, whereas the winds are not like that, for they move to the right and to the left.

The third point: The motion of those descending earthly particles is not an overpowering motion. When the winds bring up a great deal of dust, and then that dust returns and descends on surfaces, no one perceives its descent. Yet you see these winds uprooting trees, demolishing mountains, and making seas surge.

The fourth point: If the matter were as they said, the winds would be such that the stronger they were, the more the earthly dust particles would have to appear. But this is not the case, for the winds may become very violent and blow over the sea, while the senses witness that in that moving, violent air there is no trace of dust or murkiness. So what they said is refuted, and by this point the cause they mentioned for the motion of the winds is also refuted.

The astrologers (al-munajjimūn) said: the powers of the stars are what move these winds and cause them to blow.
