That too is far-fetched, because if the cause of the blowing of the winds is the nature of the stars, the winds must persist as long as that nature persists. And if the cause is the nature of the star on condition of its being in a specific sign of the zodiac and a specific degree, then the air of the whole world must move, and it does not. Furthermore, we have already shown that bodies are alike, and that the specialisation of a particular star and a particular sign (for a particular effect) must be by the choice of a choosing agent. The nature which, for its sake, produced that particular effect must necessarily be through the specification of a choosing agent. Thus it is established by this demonstration we have mentioned that the mover of the winds is God, glorified and exalted is He. And by rational proof the validity of His saying is established: ﴿who sends the winds﴾.

[Page 115]

**The third issue:** His saying: "*nashran bayna yadayy raḥmatihi*" (نَشْرًا بَيْنَ يَدَيْ رَحْمَتِهِ, spreading before His mercy) contains two benefits:

The first: His saying *nashran* means "spread out and dispersed." So one part of the wind's parts goes to the right, another goes to the left, and likewise for the rest of the parts, for each one goes in a different direction. We say: there is no doubt that the nature of air is one nature, and the relation of the spheres, the stars and the natures to each of the indivisible parts of that wind is one and the same relation. So the specification of some parts of the wind to go right and another part to go left must be due only to the specification of a choosing agent.

The second benefit in the verse: His saying ﴿before His mercy﴾ means before the rain, which is His mercy. The reason for the beauty of this metaphor is that the Arabs use "the two hands" (*al-yadān*) in the sense of precedence, by way of metaphor. They say: "Trials will occur before the Hour" (*bayna yadayi al-sāʿa*), meaning just before it. The reason for the beauty of this metaphor is that a person's hands are his forerunners (mutaqaddimāt), so whatever precedes something is called by the term "two hands" by way of metaphor because of this resemblance. Since the winds precede the rain, he therefore expressed it with this term.

If it is objected: we indeed find rain without winds preceding it. We reply: the verse does not say that this precedence occurs in all circumstances, so the objection does not arise. Also, it is possible that these winds precede it even though we do not perceive them.

God, the Exalted, then said: ﴿until, when they carry heavy clouds﴾. It is said: "*aqalla* so-and-so the thing" when he carried it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the derivation of *iqlāl* (carrying) is from *qilla* (fewness), because whoever lifts something sees what he lifts as light. His saying ﴿heavy clouds﴾ means heavy with water; *saḥāban* is the plural of *saḥāba*. The meaning is: until these winds carry heavy clouds laden with the water within them. The meaning is that the dense clouds that spread great waters remain suspended in the air only because God, in His wisdom, ordained that He move the winds with intense motion. Because of the intense movements in those winds, several benefits arise:

The first: The parts of the cloud join one another, pile up, and the dense rain-bearing cloud is formed.

The second: Because of those intense movements in those winds, going right and left, it becomes impossible for those watery particles to descend, so necessarily they remain suspended in the air.

The third: Because of the movements of those winds, the cloud is driven from one place to another, the place where God, the Exalted, knows their need for the descent of rain and their benefit from it.

The fourth: The movements of the winds are sometimes gathering the parts of the cloud, causing some of them to join others until the thick cloud is formed, and sometimes they scatter the parts of the cloud, nullifying it.

The fifth: These winds are sometimes strengthening for the crops and trees, completing what is in them of growth and increase; these are the fertilising winds (*al-riyāḥ al-lawāqiḥ*). And sometimes they nullify them, as happens in autumn.

The sixth: These winds are sometimes pleasant and delightful, agreeable to bodies, and sometimes destructive, either because of the intense heat within them, as in the simoom (*al-sumūm*), or because of the intense cold within them, as in the very destructive cold winds.

The seventh: These winds are sometimes from the east, and sometimes from the west, north and south. This classification was mentioned by some people; otherwise, the winds blow from every direction of the world, and there is no fixed pattern for them, nor is any direction of the world specific to them.

Eighth: these winds sometimes rise from the depths of the earth. Whoever rides the sea observes that the sea undergoes a violent churning because of the generation of winds in its depths, which rise to above the surface of the sea. At that point, the blowing of the winds over the surface of the sea becomes intense. At other times He sends down the wind from above. Thus the variation of the winds on account of these meanings is also wondrous.

It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The winds are eight: four of them are a punishment, namely the qasif (the crushing wind), the ʿasif (the storming wind), the sarsar (the freezing wind), and the ʿaqim (the barren wind); and four of them are mercy: the nashirat (the spreading winds), the mubashshirat (the bearers of glad tidings), the mursalat (the sent winds), and the dhariyat (the scattering winds)." And from the Prophet ﷺ: "I have been aided by the eastern wind (al-Saba), and ʿAd were destroyed by the western wind (al-Dabur)." The south wind (al-Janub) is from the wind of Paradise. And from Kaʿb: "If Allah were to withhold the wind from His servants for three days, most of the earth would stink." And from al-Suddi: that He, exalted is He, sends the winds, and they bring the clouds; then He, exalted is He, spreads them in the sky however He wills, then He opens the gates of the sky and the water flows upon the clouds, then He causes the clouds to rain after that. And His mercy is the rain.

Having understood this, we say: the variation of the winds in the aforementioned attributes, although the nature of the air is one and the influences of the natural elements, the stars and the spheres are one, indicates that these conditions came about only through the management of the Choosing Agent, glorified and exalted is He.

* * *
Page 116

Then the Exalted said: ﴿We drive it to a dead land﴾. The meaning is that We drive that cloud to a dead land on which no rain has fallen and in which no greenery has grown.

If it is said: if "cloud" (sahab) is masculine, it should be said "until when they carry a heavy cloud (saḥāban thaqīlan)," and if it is feminine, it should be said "suqnāhu"; so how is the reconciliation?

The answer: the word "sahab" is grammatically masculine, being the plural of sahaba. Therefore, referring back to it with masculine pronouns is permissible, looking to the word's form, and with feminine pronouns is also permissible, looking to its being a plural. As for the lām in His saying ﴿to a dead land﴾ (li-baladin), there are two views. Some said: this lām has the meaning of ilā ("to"), as one says: "I guided him to the religion" (lil-dīn) and "to the religion" (ilā al-dīn). Others said: this lām has the meaning of min ajl ("for the sake of"), and the sense is: We drive it for the sake of a dead land, having no living thing to water it. As for the baladh (land), every place on the earth, whether inhabited or uninhabited, empty or populated, is a balad; a portion of it is a baldah, and the whole is bilad; and wasteland is also called baldah. Al-Aʿsha said:

And a baldah like the back of a shield, desolate, where at night the jinn's chanting resounds at its edges.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So We send down water by it﴾. They differed as to what the pronoun in His saying "by it" (bihi) refers back to. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: it is permissible that it means "So We send down water upon the land," and it is permissible that it means "So We send down water by means of the cloud," since the cloud is the instrument for sending down water.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then We bring forth by it of all kinds of fruits﴾. The pronoun refers to the water, since the bringing forth of fruits was by water. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible that the sense is: "So We bring forth by the land of all kinds of fruits," since the land here is not specific to one land rather than another. On the first view, Allah, exalted is He, creates the fruits only through the intermediary of water. Most of the theologians said: fruits are not generated from water; rather Allah, exalted is He, established His custom of creating vegetation directly after water mixes with earth. The majority of the philosophers said: it is not impossible to say that He, exalted is He, deposited in water a natural power, and that this natural power necessitates the occurrence of specific conditions when water mixes with earth and specific natures come into being. The theologians argued against the soundness of this view: the nature of water and earth is one, yet we see that in a single plant there arise differing conditions, such as the grape, whose skin is cold and dry, whose flesh and juice are hot and moist, and whose seed is cold and dry. Thus the generation of bodies described by differing attributes from water and earth indicates that they came into being through the origination of the Choosing Agent, not by nature and inherent property.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Thus shall We bring forth the dead﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: the meaning is that just as He, exalted is He, creates plants through the sending down of rains, so too He brings the dead to life through a rain which He sends down upon those decayed bodies. It is related that He, exalted is He, will send down upon the bodies of the dead, between the two blasts, a rain like semen for forty days, and that they will then sprout and become living. Mujahid said: when Allah wishes to resurrect them, He will send rain upon them until the earth splits open over them, as trees split open to release blossoms and fruit; then He will send the spirits, and each spirit will return to its body.

The second view: the comparison is made only with the basic fact of bringing to life after having been dead. The meaning is: just as He, exalted is He, revived this land after its ruin, causing trees to grow in it and placing fruit in it, so He will bring the dead to life after they were dead; for whoever is able to create a body, and to put moisture and taste into it, is also able to put life into the body of the dead. The purpose of this is to establish proof that resurrection and the Last Day are true.

صفحة ١١٧

Know that those who adhere to the first view, if they believe that the bodies cannot be resurrected except by raining upon those decayed bodies a rain of the description of semen, then they have gone too far. Moreover, the One who is able to bring about in rainwater the attributes by which semen became semen initially, why would He not be able to create life and a body initially? Furthermore, suppose that this rain falls; yet the parts of the dead are not mixed together: some of them are in the East and some in the West, so how does the sending down of that rain benefit in generating those bodies?

If they say: He, by His power and wisdom, brings out those scattered parts, then why do they not say that by His power and wisdom He creates life in those parts initially, without the intermediary of that rain? And if they believe that He, exalted is He, is able to revive the dead initially, but that He revives them in this manner only because He has established His custom of not creating them except from two parents—just as He is able to create persons in this world initially, yet He has established His custom of not creating them except from the two parents—then this is permissible.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So that you may remember﴾. The meaning is: when you witnessed that this earth was adorned in spring and summer with flowers and fruits, then in winter it became dead and bare of that adornment, and then He, exalted is He, revived it once more, then the One who is able to revive it after its death must also be able to revive bodies after their death. So His saying "so that you may remember" means remembering that since this meaning was not impossible in one of the two instances, it must not be impossible in the other.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, while that which is bad comes forth only scantily﴾.

Concerning this there are issues:

First issue: concerning this verse there are two views:

The first view, and it is the well-known one: this is a parable which Allah, exalted is He, struck for the believer and the disbeliever, using the fertile land and the salty land, and He likened the descent of the Qur'an to the descent of rain. He likened the believer to the fertile land upon which rain falls, so that all kinds of flowers and fruits come forth in it. As for the salty land, although rain falls upon it, there comes forth from it only a meager amount of vegetation. Likewise, the pure, clean soul free from the impurities of ignorance and blameworthy character, when the light of the Qur'an reaches it, there appear in it various kinds of acts of obedience, knowledge, and praiseworthy character; while the foul, turbid soul, even when the light of the Qur'an reaches it, there appears in it only a little of knowledge and praiseworthy character.

The second view: the verse does not intend the comparison of the believer and the disbeliever; rather, the intended meaning is that the salty land yields little benefit and fruit, yet its owner does not neglect it but exhausts himself in its improvement, hoping to obtain what is fitting for it of benefit. Whoever seeks this small benefit with great hardship, it is then all the more fitting that he seek the great benefit promised in the Hereafter through the hardship that must necessarily be borne in performing acts of obedience.

Second issue: this verse indicates that the happy person is not turned into a wretch, nor the reverse. This is because it indicates that souls are of two kinds: some are, in the essence of their substance, pure and clean, disposed to know the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it; and some are, in the essence of their substance, coarse and turbid, slow to accept true knowledge and virtuous character, just as among lands some are salty and corrupt. And just as it is impossible for those flowers and fruits that grow in fertile land to arise in salty land, so too it is impossible for certainty-based knowledge and virtuous character to appear in a dull and turbid, coarse soul in the same way as they appear in a pure and clear soul.

صفحة ١١٨

And what strengthens this discourse is that we see souls differing in these qualities: some are disposed by nature to love the world of purity and divine matters, turning away from bodily pleasures, as the Exalted said: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83]. And among them are souls extremely hard and very averse to accepting these meanings, as He said: ﴿Then they are like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. And among them are souls intensely inclined to satisfying desire and distant from states of anger; and among them are souls intensely inclined to executing anger and distant from the acts of desire. Indeed, we say: among souls are some with a great desire for wealth but not for status, and among people some are the reverse; and among those who seek wealth are some with a great desire for real estate, whose desire for it exceeds their desire for cash, and among them are those whose desire for acquiring cash is great and who have no desire for estates and lands. When you reflect upon this kind of consideration, you will be certain that the conditions of souls differ in these matters with an essential, inherent difference that cannot be removed or changed. And if this is so, it is impossible that a coarse, ignorant soul inclined by nature to acts of wickedness should become a soul radiant with divine knowledge and virtuous character. Since this is established, imposing upon this soul those certainty-based knowledge and virtuous character is akin to imposing what cannot be borne.

Thus it is established by this explanation that the happy person is one who is made happy in his mother's womb, and the wretched one is one who is made wretched in his mother's womb; that the pure soul brings forth its vegetation of certainty-based knowledge and virtuous character by the permission of its Lord, while the foul soul brings forth its vegetation only scantily, little in benefit and good, abundant in excess and evil.

The second aspect of the inference from this verse on this question is His saying ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, which indicates that everything good and obedient that the believer does occurs only by Allah's grace (tawfiq), exalted is He.

Third issue: it has been read as "yukhriju nabatahu" (its vegetation comes forth), meaning the land brings it forth and causes it to grow.

As for His saying ﴿and that which is bad﴾, al-Farra' said: one says "khabutha al-shay'" (the thing became bad), "yakhbuthu khubthan wa khabatha" (it becomes bad in quality). As for His saying ﴿only scantily﴾, al-nakid is that which is difficult and withholds good out of stinginess. Al-Layth said: al-nakid is ill omen, meanness, and scarcity of giving; and a man is "ankad" and "nakid." He said:

And give what you have given, graciously; there is no good in the one who is stingy and the one who is miserly.

Once you understand this, we say: His saying, ﴿And the land that is bad﴾ is an attributive (adjective) describing "the land," and its meaning is: a bad land does not bring forth its vegetation except with difficulty. So the modifier that is "the vegetation" (nabat) was omitted, and the modified term that is the pronoun referring back to that land was placed in its position. However, it had been in the genitive and explicit, so it changed into a nominative concealed pronoun because it occupies the position of the subject (fa'il). Or it may be estimated as: "and the vegetation of that which is bad." It was also read as "nakadan" with a fatha on the kaf, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: possessing difficulty.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks﴾. It was read as "yusarrifu," meaning Allah varies them. He concluded this verse with His saying ﴿for a people who give thanks﴾ because what was mentioned earlier is that He, the Exalted, stirs the gentle, beneficial winds and makes them a cause for the descent of rain, which is mercy, and makes those winds and rains a cause for the emergence of kinds of beneficial, gentle, and delicious vegetation. This, from one of the two aspects, is a mention of the evidence indicating the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power, and His wisdom; and from the second aspect it is an alert to the delivery of this great blessing to the servants. Therefore, insofar as they are proofs of the existence of the Creator and His attributes, they are signs (ayat), and insofar as they are blessings whose thanks is obligatory, He said: ﴿We vary the signs for a people who give thanks﴾. He specified their being signs for the thankful people only because they are the ones who benefit from them, and this is like His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 57–58 (part 1 of 3)**

God's words: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as heralds of good news before His mercy, until when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land, and We send down water from it, and bring forth from it all kinds of fruits. Thus shall We bring forth the dead; perhaps you will remember.﴾ ﴿As for the good land, its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, but that which is bad yields only meagrely. Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks.﴾

Know that there are two aspects regarding the arrangement (naẓm) of the verses:

The first: When God mentioned the proofs of divinity and the perfection of knowledge and power in the upper world, namely the heavens, the sun, the moon and the stars, He followed it with mention of proofs from some of the conditions of the lower world. Know that the conditions of this world are confined to four matters: the upper phenomena (al-ātharāt al-ʿulwiyya), minerals, plants, and animals. Among the upper phenomena are the winds, the clouds and the rains. The conditions of plants are consequent upon the descent of rain, and that is what is mentioned in this verse.

The second aspect of explaining the arrangement: When God established the proof in the first verse for the existence of the God who is capable, knowing, wise and merciful, He established in this verse the proof for the validity of the doctrine of the gathering (al-ḥashr), the scattering (al-nashr), the resurrection (al-baʿth) and the Last Day, so that through knowledge of these two verses one obtains all that is needed for knowing the Origin (al-mabda') and the Return (al-maʿād).

[Page 113]

There are issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read *al-rīḥ* (الرِّيحَ, the singular), while the rest read *al-riyāḥ* (الرِّياحَ, the plural). Whoever reads *al-riyāḥ* in the plural finds its description with *bushran* appropriate, since it is the plural described with the plural. Whoever reads *al-rīḥ* in the singular reads *bushuran* (بُشُرًا) in the plural, because by *al-rīḥ* he means multiplicity, like their saying: "a lot of dirhams," "dinars," "sheep," and "camels," and like His saying: ﴿Indeed, mankind is in loss﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 2], then He said: ﴿except those who believe﴾ [al-ʿAṣr: 3]. Since the intended meaning of *al-rīḥ* is the plural, He described it with the plural. As for His saying *bushran*, there are readings for it:

The first: The reading of the majority is *nushuran* (نُشُرًا), with a ḍamma on the nūn and the shīn, which is the plural of *nashūr*, like *rusul* for *rasūl*. *Nashūr* carries the meaning of *munsharā* (scattered), like *rakūb* in the sense of *marākūb* (ridden). The meaning is winds that are spread out (munashsharah), i.e., dispersed from every direction. *Al-nashr* is dispersal, and from it come *nashr al-thawb* (shaking out a garment) and *nashr al-khashaba* (sawing wood with a saw). Al-Farrā' said: *al-nashr* among the winds is the gentle, pleasant wind that spreads the clouds; its singular is *nushūr*, and its origin is from *al-nashr*, which is a pleasant fragrance. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays: "and the spreading of perfume" (*wa-nashr al-ʿiṭr*).

The second reading: Ibn ʿĀmir read *nushran* (نُشْرًا) with a ḍamma on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn, lightening the ʿayn, as one says *kutb* and *rusl*.

The third reading: Hamza read *nashran* (نَشْرًا) with a fatḥa on the nūn and a sukūn on the shīn. *Al-nashr* is the verbal noun of *nashartu al-thawb*, the opposite of *ṭawaytuhu* (I folded it), and the verbal noun here is used in the sense of the passive participle. It is as if the winds were folded, then God sent them spread out after their folding. So His saying *nashran* is a verbal noun functioning as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from *al-riyāḥ*; the implied meaning is: He sends the winds spreading out. It is also permissible that *al-nashr* here carries the meaning of life, from their saying: "God revived (*anshara*) the dead, so he was revived (*nushira*)." Al-Aʿshā said:

"O wonder at the dead who is revived!"

If you interpret it this way, which is the preferred view, then the verbal noun is intended in the sense of the active participle, as you say: "He came to me running" (*rakḍan*), meaning "running." It is also permissible to say that *arsala* and *nashara* are close in meaning, so it is as if it were said: "And He is the one who spreads the winds with spreading."

The fourth reading: The author of al-Kashshaf reported from Masruq the reading *nashran* in the sense of *manshūrāt* (spread things), a form *faʿl* in the sense of *maf'ūl*, like *naqḍ* and *ḥasb*. From it comes their saying: "He gathered its spread-out things" (*ḍamma nashrahu*).

The fifth reading: The reading of ʿĀṣim is *bushran* (بُشْرًا) with a single dot below the bā', the plural of *bashīr* as *bushr*, from His saying: ﴿He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾ [al-Rūm: 46], meaning they bring good news of rain and mercy. The author of al-Kashshaf also related *bushuran* with a ḍamma on the shīn and its lightening, and *bashran* with a fatḥa on the bā' and a sukūn on the shīn, a verbal noun from *bashsharahu* in the sense of *bashsharahu* (he gave him good news), meaning *bāshirāt* and *busrā*.

[Page 114]

**The second issue:** Know that His saying ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ is conjoined (ma'ṭūf) to His saying ﴿Indeed your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. Then we say: the definition of wind is that it is moving air. We say: this air's being in motion is not due to its essence nor to the necessary attributes of its essence, for otherwise the motion would persist as long as its essence persists. Therefore it must be due to the moving of a choosing agent, who is God, majestic is His majesty. The philosophers said: here there is another cause, namely that earthly particles, which are fine, rise from the earth and heat it with a strong, intense heat; because of that intense heat it rises and ascends. When it reaches near the celestial sphere, the air adhering to the concave surface of the sphere is moving in the circular motion of the sphere, by the circular motion that has come about for that layer of air. So it prevents these vapours from ascending; rather it turns them back from the direction of their motion. Then those vapours return and disperse in every direction, and by that dispersal the winds arise. Then, the more those vapours are, and the stronger their ascent, the stronger their return will be in motion, so the winds become stronger and more intense. This is the summary of what they have mentioned, and it is false. Several points demonstrate its falsehood:

The first: The ascent of the earthly particles occurs only because of the intensity of their heating. There is no doubt that this heating is an accident, because the earth is by nature cold and dry. When those earthly particles ascend greatly, they become quickly affected. When they rise and reach the cold layer of air, it becomes impossible for the heat to persist in them; rather they become very cold. And when they become cold, it becomes impossible for them to reach, in their ascent, the air layer moving with the motion of the sphere. So what they claimed is refuted.

The second point: Suppose those smoky particles did ascend to the air layer moving with the motion of the sphere. Nevertheless, when they return, they must descend in a straight line, because the earth is a heavy body, and a heavy body moves only in a straight line, whereas the winds are not like that, for they move to the right and to the left.

The third point: The motion of those descending earthly particles is not an overpowering motion. When the winds bring up a great deal of dust, and then that dust returns and descends on surfaces, no one perceives its descent. Yet you see these winds uprooting trees, demolishing mountains, and making seas surge.

The fourth point: If the matter were as they said, the winds would be such that the stronger they were, the more the earthly dust particles would have to appear. But this is not the case, for the winds may become very violent and blow over the sea, while the senses witness that in that moving, violent air there is no trace of dust or murkiness. So what they said is refuted, and by this point the cause they mentioned for the motion of the winds is also refuted.

The astrologers (al-munajjimūn) said: the powers of the stars are what move these winds and cause them to blow. That too is far-fetched, because if the cause of the blowing of the winds is the nature of the stars, the winds must persist as long as that nature persists. And if the cause is the nature of the star on condition of its being in a specific sign of the zodiac and a specific degree, then the air of the whole world must move, and it does not. Furthermore, we have already shown that bodies are alike, and that the specialisation of a particular star and a particular sign (for a particular effect) must be by the choice of a choosing agent. The nature which, for its sake, produced that particular effect must necessarily be through the specification of a choosing agent. Thus it is established by this demonstration we have mentioned that the mover of the winds is God, glorified and exalted is He. And by rational proof the validity of His saying is established: ﴿who sends the winds﴾.

[Page 115]

**The third issue:** His saying: "*nashran bayna yadayy raḥmatihi*" (نَشْرًا بَيْنَ يَدَيْ رَحْمَتِهِ, spreading before His mercy) contains two benefits:

The first: His saying *nashran* means "spread out and dispersed." So one part of the wind's parts goes to the right, another goes to the left, and likewise for the rest of the parts, for each one goes in a different direction. We say: there is no doubt that the nature of air is one nature, and the relation of the spheres, the stars and the natures to each of the indivisible parts of that wind is one and the same relation. So the specification of some parts of the wind to go right and another part to go left must be due only to the specification of a choosing agent.

The second benefit in the verse: His saying ﴿before His mercy﴾ means before the rain, which is His mercy. The reason for the beauty of this metaphor is that the Arabs use "the two hands" (*al-yadān*) in the sense of precedence, by way of metaphor. They say: "Trials will occur before the Hour" (*bayna yadayi al-sāʿa*), meaning just before it. The reason for the beauty of this metaphor is that a person's hands are his forerunners (mutaqaddimāt), so whatever precedes something is called by the term "two hands" by way of metaphor because of this resemblance. Since the winds precede the rain, he therefore expressed it with this term.

If it is objected: we indeed find rain without winds preceding it. We reply: the verse does not say that this precedence occurs in all circumstances, so the objection does not arise. Also, it is possible that these winds precede it even though we do not perceive them.

God, the Exalted, then said: ﴿until, when they carry heavy clouds﴾. It is said: "*aqalla* so-and-so the thing" when he carried it. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the derivation of *iqlāl* (carrying) is from *qilla* (fewness), because whoever lifts something sees what he lifts as light. His saying ﴿heavy clouds﴾ means heavy with water; *saḥāban* is the plural of *saḥāba*. The meaning is: until these winds carry heavy clouds laden with the water within them. The meaning is that the dense clouds that spread great waters remain suspended in the air only because God, in His wisdom, ordained that He move the winds with intense motion. Because of the intense movements in those winds, several benefits arise:

The first: The parts of the cloud join one another, pile up, and the dense rain-bearing cloud is formed.

The second: Because of those intense movements in those winds, going right and left, it becomes impossible for those watery particles to descend, so necessarily they remain suspended in the air.

The third: Because of the movements of those winds, the cloud is driven from one place to another, the place where God, the Exalted, knows their need for the descent of rain and their benefit from it.

The fourth: The movements of the winds are sometimes gathering the parts of the cloud, causing some of them to join others until the thick cloud is formed, and sometimes they scatter the parts of the cloud, nullifying it.

The fifth: These winds are sometimes strengthening for the crops and trees, completing what is in them of growth and increase; these are the fertilising winds (*al-riyāḥ al-lawāqiḥ*). And sometimes they nullify them, as happens in autumn.

The sixth: These winds are sometimes pleasant and delightful, agreeable to bodies, and sometimes destructive, either because of the intense heat within them, as in the simoom (*al-sumūm*), or because of the intense cold within them, as in the very destructive cold winds.

The seventh: These winds are sometimes from the east, and sometimes from the west, north and south. This classification was mentioned by some people; otherwise, the winds blow from every direction of the world, and there is no fixed pattern for them, nor is any direction of the world specific to them.

Eighth: these winds sometimes rise from the depths of the earth. Whoever rides the sea observes that the sea undergoes a violent churning because of the generation of winds in its depths, which rise to above the surface of the sea. At that point, the blowing of the winds over the surface of the sea becomes intense. At other times He sends down the wind from above. Thus the variation of the winds on account of these meanings is also wondrous.

It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The winds are eight: four of them are a punishment, namely the qasif (the crushing wind), the ʿasif (the storming wind), the sarsar (the freezing wind), and the ʿaqim (the barren wind); and four of them are mercy: the nashirat (the spreading winds), the mubashshirat (the bearers of glad tidings), the mursalat (the sent winds), and the dhariyat (the scattering winds)." And from the Prophet ﷺ: "I have been aided by the eastern wind (al-Saba), and ʿAd were destroyed by the western wind (al-Dabur)." The south wind (al-Janub) is from the wind of Paradise. And from Kaʿb: "If Allah were to withhold the wind from His servants for three days, most of the earth would stink." And from al-Suddi: that He, exalted is He, sends the winds, and they bring the clouds; then He, exalted is He, spreads them in the sky however He wills, then He opens the gates of the sky and the water flows upon the clouds, then He causes the clouds to rain after that. And His mercy is the rain.

Having understood this, we say: the variation of the winds in the aforementioned attributes, although the nature of the air is one and the influences of the natural elements, the stars and the spheres are one, indicates that these conditions came about only through the management of the Choosing Agent, glorified and exalted is He.

* * *
Page 116

Then the Exalted said: ﴿We drive it to a dead land﴾. The meaning is that We drive that cloud to a dead land on which no rain has fallen and in which no greenery has grown.

If it is said: if "cloud" (sahab) is masculine, it should be said "until when they carry a heavy cloud (saḥāban thaqīlan)," and if it is feminine, it should be said "suqnāhu"; so how is the reconciliation?

The answer: the word "sahab" is grammatically masculine, being the plural of sahaba. Therefore, referring back to it with masculine pronouns is permissible, looking to the word's form, and with feminine pronouns is also permissible, looking to its being a plural. As for the lām in His saying ﴿to a dead land﴾ (li-baladin), there are two views. Some said: this lām has the meaning of ilā ("to"), as one says: "I guided him to the religion" (lil-dīn) and "to the religion" (ilā al-dīn). Others said: this lām has the meaning of min ajl ("for the sake of"), and the sense is: We drive it for the sake of a dead land, having no living thing to water it. As for the baladh (land), every place on the earth, whether inhabited or uninhabited, empty or populated, is a balad; a portion of it is a baldah, and the whole is bilad; and wasteland is also called baldah. Al-Aʿsha said:

And a baldah like the back of a shield, desolate, where at night the jinn's chanting resounds at its edges.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So We send down water by it﴾. They differed as to what the pronoun in His saying "by it" (bihi) refers back to. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari said: it is permissible that it means "So We send down water upon the land," and it is permissible that it means "So We send down water by means of the cloud," since the cloud is the instrument for sending down water.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Then We bring forth by it of all kinds of fruits﴾. The pronoun refers to the water, since the bringing forth of fruits was by water. Al-Zajjaj said: it is also permissible that the sense is: "So We bring forth by the land of all kinds of fruits," since the land here is not specific to one land rather than another. On the first view, Allah, exalted is He, creates the fruits only through the intermediary of water. Most of the theologians said: fruits are not generated from water; rather Allah, exalted is He, established His custom of creating vegetation directly after water mixes with earth. The majority of the philosophers said: it is not impossible to say that He, exalted is He, deposited in water a natural power, and that this natural power necessitates the occurrence of specific conditions when water mixes with earth and specific natures come into being. The theologians argued against the soundness of this view: the nature of water and earth is one, yet we see that in a single plant there arise differing conditions, such as the grape, whose skin is cold and dry, whose flesh and juice are hot and moist, and whose seed is cold and dry. Thus the generation of bodies described by differing attributes from water and earth indicates that they came into being through the origination of the Choosing Agent, not by nature and inherent property.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Thus shall We bring forth the dead﴾. Concerning this there are two views:

The first: the meaning is that just as He, exalted is He, creates plants through the sending down of rains, so too He brings the dead to life through a rain which He sends down upon those decayed bodies. It is related that He, exalted is He, will send down upon the bodies of the dead, between the two blasts, a rain like semen for forty days, and that they will then sprout and become living. Mujahid said: when Allah wishes to resurrect them, He will send rain upon them until the earth splits open over them, as trees split open to release blossoms and fruit; then He will send the spirits, and each spirit will return to its body.

The second view: the comparison is made only with the basic fact of bringing to life after having been dead. The meaning is: just as He, exalted is He, revived this land after its ruin, causing trees to grow in it and placing fruit in it, so He will bring the dead to life after they were dead; for whoever is able to create a body, and to put moisture and taste into it, is also able to put life into the body of the dead. The purpose of this is to establish proof that resurrection and the Last Day are true.

صفحة ١١٧

Know that those who adhere to the first view, if they believe that the bodies cannot be resurrected except by raining upon those decayed bodies a rain of the description of semen, then they have gone too far. Moreover, the One who is able to bring about in rainwater the attributes by which semen became semen initially, why would He not be able to create life and a body initially? Furthermore, suppose that this rain falls; yet the parts of the dead are not mixed together: some of them are in the East and some in the West, so how does the sending down of that rain benefit in generating those bodies?

If they say: He, by His power and wisdom, brings out those scattered parts, then why do they not say that by His power and wisdom He creates life in those parts initially, without the intermediary of that rain? And if they believe that He, exalted is He, is able to revive the dead initially, but that He revives them in this manner only because He has established His custom of not creating them except from two parents—just as He is able to create persons in this world initially, yet He has established His custom of not creating them except from the two parents—then this is permissible.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So that you may remember﴾. The meaning is: when you witnessed that this earth was adorned in spring and summer with flowers and fruits, then in winter it became dead and bare of that adornment, and then He, exalted is He, revived it once more, then the One who is able to revive it after its death must also be able to revive bodies after their death. So His saying "so that you may remember" means remembering that since this meaning was not impossible in one of the two instances, it must not be impossible in the other.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And the good land—its vegetation comes forth by the permission of its Lord, while that which is bad comes forth only scantily﴾.

Concerning this there are issues:

First issue: concerning this verse there are two views:

The first view, and it is the well-known one: this is a parable which Allah, exalted is He, struck for the believer and the disbeliever, using the fertile land and the salty land, and He likened the descent of the Qur'an to the descent of rain. He likened the believer to the fertile land upon which rain falls, so that all kinds of flowers and fruits come forth in it. As for the salty land, although rain falls upon it, there comes forth from it only a meager amount of vegetation. Likewise, the pure, clean soul free from the impurities of ignorance and blameworthy character, when the light of the Qur'an reaches it, there appear in it various kinds of acts of obedience, knowledge, and praiseworthy character; while the foul, turbid soul, even when the light of the Qur'an reaches it, there appears in it only a little of knowledge and praiseworthy character.

The second view: the verse does not intend the comparison of the believer and the disbeliever; rather, the intended meaning is that the salty land yields little benefit and fruit, yet its owner does not neglect it but exhausts himself in its improvement, hoping to obtain what is fitting for it of benefit. Whoever seeks this small benefit with great hardship, it is then all the more fitting that he seek the great benefit promised in the Hereafter through the hardship that must necessarily be borne in performing acts of obedience.

Second issue: this verse indicates that the happy person is not turned into a wretch, nor the reverse. This is because it indicates that souls are of two kinds: some are, in the essence of their substance, pure and clean, disposed to know the truth for its own sake and the good for the sake of acting upon it; and some are, in the essence of their substance, coarse and turbid, slow to accept true knowledge and virtuous character, just as among lands some are salty and corrupt. And just as it is impossible for those flowers and fruits that grow in fertile land to arise in salty land, so too it is impossible for certainty-based knowledge and virtuous character to appear in a dull and turbid, coarse soul in the same way as they appear in a pure and clear soul.

صفحة ١١٨

And what strengthens this discourse is that we see souls differing in these qualities: some are disposed by nature to love the world of purity and divine matters, turning away from bodily pleasures, as the Exalted said: ﴿And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83]. And among them are souls extremely hard and very averse to accepting these meanings, as He said: ﴿Then they are like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 74]. And among them are souls intensely inclined to satisfying desire and distant from states of anger; and among them are souls intensely inclined to executing anger and distant from the acts of desire. Indeed, we say: among souls are some with a great desire for wealth but not for status, and among people some are the reverse; and among those who seek wealth are some with a great desire for real estate, whose desire for it exceeds their desire for cash, and among them are those whose desire for acquiring cash is great and who have no desire for estates and lands. When you reflect upon this kind of consideration, you will be certain that the conditions of souls differ in these matters with an essential, inherent difference that cannot be removed or changed. And if this is so, it is impossible that a coarse, ignorant soul inclined by nature to acts of wickedness should become a soul radiant with divine knowledge and virtuous character. Since this is established, imposing upon this soul those certainty-based knowledge and virtuous character is akin to imposing what cannot be borne.

Thus it is established by this explanation that the happy person is one who is made happy in his mother's womb, and the wretched one is one who is made wretched in his mother's womb; that the pure soul brings forth its vegetation of certainty-based knowledge and virtuous character by the permission of its Lord, while the foul soul brings forth its vegetation only scantily, little in benefit and good, abundant in excess and evil.

The second aspect of the inference from this verse on this question is His saying ﴿by the permission of its Lord﴾, which indicates that everything good and obedient that the believer does occurs only by Allah's grace (tawfiq), exalted is He.

Third issue: it has been read as "yukhriju nabatahu" (its vegetation comes forth), meaning the land brings it forth and causes it to grow.

As for His saying ﴿and that which is bad﴾, al-Farra' said: one says "khabutha al-shay'" (the thing became bad), "yakhbuthu khubthan wa khabatha" (it becomes bad in quality). As for His saying ﴿only scantily﴾, al-nakid is that which is difficult and withholds good out of stinginess. Al-Layth said: al-nakid is ill omen, meanness, and scarcity of giving; and a man is "ankad" and "nakid." He said:

And give what you have given, graciously; there is no good in the one who is stingy and the one who is miserly.

Once you understand this, we say: His saying, ﴿And the land that is bad﴾ is an attributive (adjective) describing "the land," and its meaning is: a bad land does not bring forth its vegetation except with difficulty. So the modifier that is "the vegetation" (nabat) was omitted, and the modified term that is the pronoun referring back to that land was placed in its position. However, it had been in the genitive and explicit, so it changed into a nominative concealed pronoun because it occupies the position of the subject (fa'il). Or it may be estimated as: "and the vegetation of that which is bad." It was also read as "nakadan" with a fatha on the kaf, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: possessing difficulty.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus do We vary the signs for a people who give thanks﴾. It was read as "yusarrifu," meaning Allah varies them. He concluded this verse with His saying ﴿for a people who give thanks﴾ because what was mentioned earlier is that He, the Exalted, stirs the gentle, beneficial winds and makes them a cause for the descent of rain, which is mercy, and makes those winds and rains a cause for the emergence of kinds of beneficial, gentle, and delicious vegetation. This, from one of the two aspects, is a mention of the evidence indicating the existence of the Creator, His knowledge, His power, and His wisdom; and from the second aspect it is an alert to the delivery of this great blessing to the servants. Therefore, insofar as they are proofs of the existence of the Creator and His attributes, they are signs (ayat), and insofar as they are blessings whose thanks is obligatory, He said: ﴿We vary the signs for a people who give thanks﴾. He specified their being signs for the thankful people only because they are the ones who benefit from them, and this is like His saying: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing﴾.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 59–62 (part 1 of 2)**

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah to his people, and he said, "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day."﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of his people said, "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾ ﴿He said, "O my people, there is no error in me, but I am a Messenger from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and advise you, and I know from Allah that which you do not know."﴾

Know that when the Exalted, in establishing the principles of the origin and the return, mentioned clear proofs, compelling evidences and dazzling demonstrations, He followed them with the narration of the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them. In this there are several benefits:

The first: an alert that people's turning away from accepting these proofs and evidences is not peculiar to the people of Muhammad (ﷺ). Rather, this blameworthy habit was present among all the earlier nations. A calamity, when it becomes general, lightens. Thus, mentioning their stories and recounting their persistence in ignorance and obstinacy serves to console the Messenger (ﷺ) and lighten that burden on his heart.

The second: the Exalted, in these stories, relates that the outcome of those deniers was disbelief and curse in this world and loss in the Hereafter, while the outcome of the truthful was dominance in this world and happiness in the Hereafter. This strengthens the hearts of the truthful and breaks the hearts of the falsifiers.

The third: an alert that although the Exalted gives respite to these falsifiers, He does not neglect them, but takes vengeance upon them in the most perfect manner.

The fourth: a demonstration that these stories indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because he (ﷺ) was unlettered, had not read a book, and had not studied under a teacher. So when he narrates these stories in their proper form, without distortion or error, this shows that he knew them only through revelation from Allah, and this indicates the validity of his prophethood.

It may be said: reporting about past unseen matters does not indicate a miracle, since it is possible to claim that Iblis witnessed these events and conveyed them to him. But reporting about future unseen matters is a miracle, because knowledge of the unseen belongs only to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Know that the Exalted mentioned in this surah the story of Adam, peace be upon him, and its mention has already preceded.

[p. 120]

The second story: the story of Noah, peace be upon him, which is mentioned in this verse. He is Noah the son of Lamech the son of Methuselah the son of Enoch, and Enoch is the name of the Prophet Idris, peace be upon him. In this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the words ﴿Indeed, We sent﴾ are the answer to an omitted oath.

If it is asked: what is the reason that they hardly ever utter this *lam* (of emphasis) except with *qad*, and the use of this *lam* without *qad* is rare, as in his saying:

*"I swore to her by Allah an oath of a sinner: they surely slept."*

This is only so because the oath clause is not brought except as an emphasis for the sentence sworn about, which is its answer. Thus it was apt to prevent the expectation which is the meaning of *qad* when the addressee hears the word of oath.

**The second issue:** Al-Kisa'i read *ghayrihi* with a *kasra* on the *ra'* (*ghayrihi*), considering it an adjective of *ilah* according to its wording (lafz). The rest read it with a *damma* (*ghayruhu*), considering it an adjective of *ilah* according to its position (mawdi'), because the sense of the sentence is: "you have no god other than Him." Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: the basis for the one who reads it with *raf'* is His saying: ﴿There is no god except Allah﴾ [Al Imran: 62]. Just as His saying *"illa Allah"* is a substitute for *"ma min ilah,"* so His saying ﴿other than Him﴾ is a substitute for ﴿from god﴾; thus *ghayr* is in the nominative by way of exception. The author of al-Kashshaf said: *ghayr* has been read with the three vowels. He mentioned the basis for the nominative and genitive as already stated. He said: as for the accusative, it is by way of exception, in the sense of "you have no god except Him," like your saying: "there is no one in the house except Zayd and other than Zayd."

**The third issue:** Al-Wahidi said: there is an omission in the speech, namely the predicate of *ma* (the negative particle), because if you make *ghayruhu* an adjective of *ilah*, there remains no predicate for this negated term, and speech does not complete with an adjective and its noun alone, since if you say "Zayd the intelligent" and stop, it conveys nothing until you mention its predicate. The meaning would be: "you have no god other than Him in existence." I say: the grammarians agreed that our saying *la ilaha illa Allah* necessarily requires an implied element. The estimate is: "there is no god in existence," or "there is no god for us except Allah." They did not mention any proof for this speech. We say: why is it not permissible to say that the negative particle has entered upon this reality and this quiddity, so the meaning is that there is no realization of the reality of divinity except in the right of Allah? When we take the speech in this meaning, we dispense with the implied element they mentioned.

If it is said: directing negation to the quiddity is not possible, because realities cannot be negated. Thus one cannot say "no blackness" in the sense of the removal of this quiddity; rather what is possible is to say that those realities are not existent nor attained, and then the predicate must be implied.

We say: this speech is based on the premise that quiddity cannot be negated or removed, and that is certainly false. For if the matter were so, it would necessarily follow that the removal of existence is impossible, since existence too is a reality and a quiddity. So why would the removal of all other quiddities be impossible?

If it is said: when we say "there is no man," and we mean by it the negation of his being existent, this negation has not been directed to the quiddity of existence, but to the quiddity of the man being described by existence.

We say: that descriptiveness is impossible to be something additional to the quiddity and to existence, for if the descriptiveness were one quiddity, and existence another quiddity, then that quiddity would also be described by existence, and the discussion of it would be as the discussion of what preceded it, so there would be an infinite regress (*tasalsul*), and it would follow that the one existent is not one existent, but infinitely many existents, and this is impossible. Then we say: the descriptiveness of the quiddity by existence is either something distinct from the quiddity and existence, or it is not so. If it is not distinct from them, then that distinct thing has a quiddity and an existence, and its quiddity does not accept removal, and then the question mentioned returns. Thus it has been established by what we have mentioned that the quiddity does not accept negation and removal, so it is impossible to direct the negative particle to any of the concepts. But if the quiddity is capable of negation and removal, then it is possible to direct the word *la* in our saying "there is no god but Allah" to this reality, and then there is no need to accept the omission and the implied element that the grammarians mention. This is pure rational speech that occurred in this discussion mentioned by the grammarians.

**The fourth issue:** The Exalted's words ﴿Indeed, We sent﴾ have two views:

Ibn Abbas said: *ba'athna* (We raised up/dispatched).

Others said: the meaning of sending is that He entrusted him with a message to deliver. The message, according to this estimate, includes the sending, so the sending is subordinate, not the principal matter. This discussion is based on a legal-theoretical (*usuli*) question: is it a condition of sending a Messenger to a people that he informs them through his tongue of rulings that they have no way to know by their intellects, or is that not a condition, rather the purpose of sending the messengers is merely to confirm what is in the intellects? This disagreement is appropriate only to the branches of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and not appropriate to the branches of our school and principles.

**The fifth issue:** In the verse there are several benefits.

**The first benefit:** The Exalted related from Noah in this verse three things:

One: that he, peace be upon him, commanded them to worship Allah, the Exalted.

Two: that he judged that there is no god other than Allah. The purpose of the first statement is to establish the obligation (*taklif*), and the purpose of the second statement is the affirmation of monotheism.

* * *

Then he said after it: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ There is no doubt that what is meant by it is either the punishment of the Day of Resurrection—and on this assumption, he has warned them about the Day of Resurrection, and this is the third claim—or the punishment of the Day of the Flood. On this assumption, he has claimed revelation and prophethood from Allah. The summary is that the Exalted related from him that he mentioned these three claims, and he mentioned no proof or argument for the validity of any one of them. If he commanded them to be warned by them by way of *taqlid* (blind imitation), this is false, because the claim of *taqlid* is false. Moreover, Allah has filled the Qur'an with the censure of *taqlid*, so how is it becoming for the infallible Messenger to call to *taqlid*? And if he commanded them to affirm them along with mentioning the proof, then this proof is not mentioned.

Know that the Exalted mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah the proofs of monotheism, prophethood, and the validity of the return, and that is an alert from Him, the Exalted, that none of the prophets calls anyone to these foundations except with mention of argument and proof. The most that can be said is that the Exalted did not relate those proofs from Noah in this context; but since those proofs were known, there was no need to mention them in this context, so Allah, the Exalted, left out the mention of the proofs for this reason.

**The second benefit:** He, peace be upon him, first said: ﴿worship Allah﴾, and second said: ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾. The second is like the cause for the first, because if they have no god other than Him, then everything that reaches them of the forms of benefit, kindness, goodness and gentleness is from Allah, and the utmost of blessing necessitates the utmost of veneration. Thus the worship of Allah became obligatory only because of knowing that there is no god but Allah.

From this discussion arises an issue: before knowing whether there is one god or more than one god, we do not know who is the one who bestows upon us the forms of blessing that we have; is it this one or that one? And if we are ignorant of that, then we are ignorant of who is the bestower of blessing in our regard, and in that case his worship is not fitting. So according to this view, knowledge of monotheism is a condition for knowledge of the fittingness of worship.

**The third benefit** in this verse: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the god is the one who deserves worship, because His saying ﴿worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ is an affirmation and a negation, so both must converge upon one concept for the speech to be sound. The meaning is: "worship Allah; you have no worshipped one other than Him," so that the negation and affirmation correspond. Then it was established by proof that the god is not the worshipped one itself, otherwise idols would necessarily be gods, and the god would not be a god in eternity because in eternity he was not worshipped. Thus it is necessary to interpret the word *ilah* as meaning the one deserving worship.

Know that they differed about the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾: is it certainty, or is "fear" in the sense of supposition and doubt? A group said: what is meant is certainty and conviction, because he was certain that the punishment would descend upon them, either in this world or in the Hereafter, if they did not accept that religion. Others said: rather what is meant is doubt, and its explanation is in several ways:

The first: he only said ﴿I fear for you﴾ because he allowed that they might believe just as he allowed that they might persist in their disbelief, and with this allowance he would not be certain of the descent of the punishment, so it was necessary for him to express it with the word of fear.

The second: the occurrence of punishment for disbelief and disobedience is a matter known only by revelation, and perhaps Allah had not clarified to him the manner of this question, so he necessarily remained in suspense, allowing that the Exalted might punish them for that disbelief or not.

The third: it is possible that the meaning of fear is caution, as He said about the angels: ﴿they fear their Lord﴾ [An-Nahl: 50], that is, they guard against sins out of fear of punishment.

The fourth possibility is that he was certain that the punishment itself would descend, but did not know its magnitude, whether it would be very great or moderate. In that case, the doubt concerned a quality of the punishment, namely whether it would be great or not, and not its occurrence in principle.

Then God, exalted is He, related what he said to his people, so He said: ﴿The chiefs of his people said, "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) said: "al-Mala'" (the chiefs, the notables) are the great and the lords who made themselves the opponents of the prophets. The evidence for this is that His saying ﴿of his people﴾ implies that those chiefs were a part of his people, and that part must be characterized by a quality because of which they deserved this description. That is, they were the ones who filled the front of the assemblies, whose awe filled hearts, whose presence filled eyes, and toward whom gazes turned in gatherings. These qualities arise only in leaders, and this indicates that what is meant by al-Mala' is the leaders and the eminent.

His saying ﴿we see you﴾: this seeing must necessarily mean belief and assumption, not direct observation and sight.

His saying ﴿in manifest error﴾ means in clear mistake and evident misguidance. Their intention must necessarily be to attribute to Nuh misguidance in the four matters which we have explained Nuh, peace be upon him, mentioned: obligation (al-taklif), monotheism (al-tawhid), prophethood (al-nubuwwah), and the return (al-ma'ad). When they spoke this speech, Nuh, peace be upon him, answered with his saying: ﴿O my people, there is no misguidance in me.﴾

If it is said: the people said, "Indeed, we see you in manifest error." Then the answer is: "There is no misguidance in me" — why did he abandon this phrasing and say "there is no misguidance (dalalah) in me"?

I say: because his saying ﴿there is no misguidance in me﴾ means that there is not in me any kind of misguidance whatsoever, so this is more emphatic in the generality of negation. Then, when he, peace be upon him, negated from himself the defect they had attributed to him, and described himself with the most noble and exalted qualities, which is that he is a messenger to creation from the Lord of the worlds, he mentioned what is the purpose of the messengership, which is two matters:

The first: conveying the message.

The second: affirming counsel. So He said: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and I advise you﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr read "ublighukum" (ﺃُﺑْﻠِﻐُﻜُﻢ) with the light form (from abla'a), and the rest read it with the intensive form (from ballagha). al-Wahidi said: both forms have come in the revelation. The light form is His saying ﴿And if they turn away, then I have conveyed to you﴾ [Hud: 57], and the intensive form is ﴿So you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67].

The second issue: the difference between conveying the message and counsel is that conveying the message means that he informs them of the kinds of God's obligations and the categories of His commands and prohibitions. As for counsel, it means that he encourages them to obedience, warns them against disobedience, and strives to establish that encouragement and warning by the most eloquent means. His saying ﴿the messages of my Lord﴾ indicates that God entrusted him with many kinds of messages, which are the categories of obligations of commands and prohibitions, and explanation of the measures of reward and punishment in the Hereafter, and the measures of the prescribed punishments and deterrents in this world. As for His saying ﴿and I advise you﴾, al-Farra' said: the Arabs hardly say "nasahtuka" (I advised you); they say "nasahtu laka" (I advised for you), though "nasahtuka" is also permissible. al-Nabighah said:

"I advised the Banu 'Awf, but they did not accept my messenger, and my messages did not succeed among them."

The reality of counsel is sending toward what is beneficial together with sincerity of intention free from impurities of harm. The meaning is: I convey to you God's obligations, then I guide you to what is most correct and most beneficial, and I call you to what I was called to, and I make beloved to you what I love for myself.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And I know from God what you do not know﴾, and in it are aspects:

The first: "I know that if you disobey His command, He will punish you with the flood."

The second: "I know that He will punish you in the Hereafter with a severe punishment beyond what your minds can imagine."

The third: It is possible that what is meant is: "And I know, from the oneness of God and the attributes of His majesty, what you do not know." The purpose of mentioning this statement would be to move the people to return to him in seeking those sciences.

Know that when the Exalted, in establishing the principles of the origin and the return, mentioned clear proofs, compelling evidences and dazzling demonstrations, He followed them with the narration of the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them. In this there are several benefits:

The first: an alert that people's turning away from accepting these proofs and evidences is not peculiar to the people of Muhammad (ﷺ). Rather, this blameworthy habit was present among all the earlier nations. A calamity, when it becomes general, lightens. Thus, mentioning their stories and recounting their persistence in ignorance and obstinacy serves to console the Messenger (ﷺ) and lighten that burden on his heart.

The second: the Exalted, in these stories, relates that the outcome of those deniers was disbelief and curse in this world and loss in the Hereafter, while the outcome of the truthful was dominance in this world and happiness in the Hereafter. This strengthens the hearts of the truthful and breaks the hearts of the falsifiers.

The third: an alert that although the Exalted gives respite to these falsifiers, He does not neglect them, but takes vengeance upon them in the most perfect manner.

The fourth: a demonstration that these stories indicate the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), because he (ﷺ) was unlettered, had not read a book, and had not studied under a teacher. So when he narrates these stories in their proper form, without distortion or error, this shows that he knew them only through revelation from Allah, and this indicates the validity of his prophethood.

It may be said: reporting about past unseen matters does not indicate a miracle, since it is possible to claim that Iblis witnessed these events and conveyed them to him. But reporting about future unseen matters is a miracle, because knowledge of the unseen belongs only to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Know that the Exalted mentioned in this surah the story of Adam, peace be upon him, and its mention has already preceded.

This discussion is based on a legal-theoretical (*usuli*) question: is it a condition of sending a Messenger to a people that he informs them through his tongue of rulings that they have no way to know by their intellects, or is that not a condition, rather the purpose of sending the messengers is merely to confirm what is in the intellects? This disagreement is appropriate only to the branches of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), and not appropriate to the branches of our school and principles.

**The fifth issue:** In the verse there are several benefits.

**The first benefit:** The Exalted related from Noah in this verse three things:

One: that he, peace be upon him, commanded them to worship Allah, the Exalted.

Two: that he judged that there is no god other than Allah. The purpose of the first statement is to establish the obligation (*taklif*), and the purpose of the second statement is the affirmation of monotheism.

* * *

Then he said after it: ﴿Indeed, I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ There is no doubt that what is meant by it is either the punishment of the Day of Resurrection—and on this assumption, he has warned them about the Day of Resurrection, and this is the third claim—or the punishment of the Day of the Flood. On this assumption, he has claimed revelation and prophethood from Allah. The summary is that the Exalted related from him that he mentioned these three claims, and he mentioned no proof or argument for the validity of any one of them. If he commanded them to be warned by them by way of *taqlid* (blind imitation), this is false, because the claim of *taqlid* is false. Moreover, Allah has filled the Qur'an with the censure of *taqlid*, so how is it becoming for the infallible Messenger to call to *taqlid*? And if he commanded them to affirm them along with mentioning the proof, then this proof is not mentioned.

Know that the Exalted mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah the proofs of monotheism, prophethood, and the validity of the return, and that is an alert from Him, the Exalted, that none of the prophets calls anyone to these foundations except with mention of argument and proof. The most that can be said is that the Exalted did not relate those proofs from Noah in this context; but since those proofs were known, there was no need to mention them in this context, so Allah, the Exalted, left out the mention of the proofs for this reason.

**The second benefit:** He, peace be upon him, first said: ﴿worship Allah﴾, and second said: ﴿you have no god other than Him﴾. The second is like the cause for the first, because if they have no god other than Him, then everything that reaches them of the forms of benefit, kindness, goodness and gentleness is from Allah, and the utmost of blessing necessitates the utmost of veneration. Thus the worship of Allah became obligatory only because of knowing that there is no god but Allah.

From this discussion arises an issue: before knowing whether there is one god or more than one god, we do not know who is the one who bestows upon us the forms of blessing that we have; is it this one or that one? And if we are ignorant of that, then we are ignorant of who is the bestower of blessing in our regard, and in that case his worship is not fitting. So according to this view, knowledge of monotheism is a condition for knowledge of the fittingness of worship.

**The third benefit** in this verse: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the god is the one who deserves worship, because His saying ﴿worship Allah; you have no god other than Him﴾ is an affirmation and a negation, so both must converge upon one concept for the speech to be sound. The meaning is: "worship Allah; you have no worshipped one other than Him," so that the negation and affirmation correspond. Then it was established by proof that the god is not the worshipped one itself, otherwise idols would necessarily be gods, and the god would not be a god in eternity because in eternity he was not worshipped. Thus it is necessary to interpret the word *ilah* as meaning the one deserving worship.

Know that they differed about the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, I fear for you﴾: is it certainty, or is "fear" in the sense of supposition and doubt? A group said: what is meant is certainty and conviction, because he was certain that the punishment would descend upon them, either in this world or in the Hereafter, if they did not accept that religion. Others said: rather what is meant is doubt, and its explanation is in several ways:

The first: he only said ﴿I fear for you﴾ because he allowed that they might believe just as he allowed that they might persist in their disbelief, and with this allowance he would not be certain of the descent of the punishment, so it was necessary for him to express it with the word of fear.

The second: the occurrence of punishment for disbelief and disobedience is a matter known only by revelation, and perhaps Allah had not clarified to him the manner of this question, so he necessarily remained in suspense, allowing that the Exalted might punish them for that disbelief or not.

The third: it is possible that the meaning of fear is caution, as He said about the angels: ﴿they fear their Lord﴾ [An-Nahl: 50], that is, they guard against sins out of fear of punishment.

The fourth possibility is that he was certain that the punishment itself would descend, but did not know its magnitude, whether it would be very great or moderate. In that case, the doubt concerned a quality of the punishment, namely whether it would be great or not, and not its occurrence in principle.

Then God, exalted is He, related what he said to his people, so He said: ﴿The chiefs of his people said, "Indeed, we see you in manifest error."﴾ The exegetes (mufassirun) said: "al-Mala'" (the chiefs, the notables) are the great and the lords who made themselves the opponents of the prophets. The evidence for this is that His saying ﴿of his people﴾ implies that those chiefs were a part of his people, and that part must be characterized by a quality because of which they deserved this description. That is, they were the ones who filled the front of the assemblies, whose awe filled hearts, whose presence filled eyes, and toward whom gazes turned in gatherings. These qualities arise only in leaders, and this indicates that what is meant by al-Mala' is the leaders and the eminent.

His saying ﴿we see you﴾: this seeing must necessarily mean belief and assumption, not direct observation and sight.

His saying ﴿in manifest error﴾ means in clear mistake and evident misguidance. Their intention must necessarily be to attribute to Nuh misguidance in the four matters which we have explained Nuh, peace be upon him, mentioned: obligation (al-taklif), monotheism (al-tawhid), prophethood (al-nubuwwah), and the return (al-ma'ad). When they spoke this speech, Nuh, peace be upon him, answered with his saying: ﴿O my people, there is no misguidance in me.﴾

If it is said: the people said, "Indeed, we see you in manifest error." Then the answer is: "There is no misguidance in me" — why did he abandon this phrasing and say "there is no misguidance (dalalah) in me"?

I say: because his saying ﴿there is no misguidance in me﴾ means that there is not in me any kind of misguidance whatsoever, so this is more emphatic in the generality of negation. Then, when he, peace be upon him, negated from himself the defect they had attributed to him, and described himself with the most noble and exalted qualities, which is that he is a messenger to creation from the Lord of the worlds, he mentioned what is the purpose of the messengership, which is two matters:

The first: conveying the message.

The second: affirming counsel. So He said: ﴿I convey to you the messages of my Lord and I advise you﴾, and in it are issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr read "ublighukum" (ﺃُﺑْﻠِﻐُﻜُﻢ) with the light form (from abla'a), and the rest read it with the intensive form (from ballagha). al-Wahidi said: both forms have come in the revelation. The light form is His saying ﴿And if they turn away, then I have conveyed to you﴾ [Hud: 57], and the intensive form is ﴿So you have not conveyed His message﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67].

The second issue: the difference between conveying the message and counsel is that conveying the message means that he informs them of the kinds of God's obligations and the categories of His commands and prohibitions. As for counsel, it means that he encourages them to obedience, warns them against disobedience, and strives to establish that encouragement and warning by the most eloquent means. His saying ﴿the messages of my Lord﴾ indicates that God entrusted him with many kinds of messages, which are the categories of obligations of commands and prohibitions, and explanation of the measures of reward and punishment in the Hereafter, and the measures of the prescribed punishments and deterrents in this world. As for His saying ﴿and I advise you﴾, al-Farra' said: the Arabs hardly say "nasahtuka" (I advised you); they say "nasahtu laka" (I advised for you), though "nasahtuka" is also permissible. al-Nabighah said:

"I advised the Banu 'Awf, but they did not accept my messenger, and my messages did not succeed among them."

The reality of counsel is sending toward what is beneficial together with sincerity of intention free from impurities of harm. The meaning is: I convey to you God's obligations, then I guide you to what is most correct and most beneficial, and I call you to what I was called to, and I make beloved to you what I love for myself.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And I know from God what you do not know﴾, and in it are aspects:

The first: "I know that if you disobey His command, He will punish you with the flood."

The second: "I know that He will punish you in the Hereafter with a severe punishment beyond what your minds can imagine."

The third: It is possible that what is meant is: "And I know, from the oneness of God and the attributes of His majesty, what you do not know." The purpose of mentioning this statement would be to move the people to return to him in seeking those sciences.
