Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 88–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said: "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion." He said: "Even though we are unwilling?"﴾ ﴿We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it. It is not for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In Allah we have put our trust. Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of deciders.﴾

Know that when Shu'ayb had established those words, those who were arrogant and disdained to believe him and accept his speech said: there must be one of two matters:
Either we expel you and your followers from this town,
or you return to our religion.

The difficulty here is that it may be said: their saying, "or you will surely return to our religion," indicates that he (peace be upon him) was upon their religion, which is disbelief, and this requires that he was a disbeliever before that, and that is utterly corrupt. Also, their saying, "We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion," indicates this same meaning.

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the followers of Shu'ayb were disbelievers before entering his religion, so they addressed Shu'ayb with the address of his followers and applied to him their rulings.

The second: their leaders said that in a manner of deception toward the common people, making them imagine that he had been one of them, and Shu'ayb mentioned his answer in accordance with that imagination.

The third: that Shu'ayb, at the beginning of his affair, was concealing his religion and creed, so they imagined that he was upon the religion of his people.

The fourth: it is not far-fetched to say that Shu'ayb was upon their law, then Allah, exalted is He, abrogated that law by the revelation He sent to him.

The fifth: what is meant by His saying, "or you will surely return to our religion," is: "you will come to our religion," so the return is used in the sense of beginning. The Arabs say: "a disliked thing has returned to me from so-and-so," meaning a disliked thing has come to me from him at the start. The poet said:

If the days were the best of periods toward me, then sins have returned to them (i.e., have become theirs).

He meant: sins have become theirs, and he did not mean that sins were theirs before the good.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that when the people said that, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) answered their words in two ways:

The first: His saying, "Even though we are unwilling?" The hamza is for interrogation, and the waw is the waw of circumstance; its implied sense is: "Will you return us to your religion while we are in a state of hatred and being unwilling?"

The second: His saying, "We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it." The first answer works as an allusion to the fact that he would not return to their religion, while this second answer is an explicit statement that he will not do that; he said: if we did that, we would have invented a lie against Allah. The basis of the matter concerning prophethood and messengership is truthfulness of speech and freedom from lying, so returning to your religion would nullify prophethood and remove messengership.

As for His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it," there are several aspects:

The first: the meaning of "after Allah has saved us from it" is that He taught us its ugliness and corruption, and established the proofs that it is false.

The second: that what is meant is that Allah saved His people from that religion, but he placed himself among them in the sum, though he was innocent of it, applying the speech according to the rule of predominance (taghlib).

The third: that the people were made to imagine that he had been upon their religion, or they believed that he had been so; so His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it," means according to your belief and your assumption.

* * *

As for His saying, "It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills."

Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) hold fast to this verse to show that Allah, exalted is He, may will disbelief, while the Mu'tazilites hold fast to it to show that Allah, exalted is He, wills only good and righteousness. As for the manner in which our companions argue from it, it is from two aspects:

The first: His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it," indicates that the one who saves from disbelief is Allah, exalted is He. If faith came about by the creation of the servant, then salvation from disbelief would occur for a person from himself, not from Allah, exalted is He, and that is contrary to the implication of His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it."

The second: the meaning of the verse is that it is not for us to return to your religion unless Allah wills that He return us to that religion. Since that religion was disbelief, this was a permission from Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) that they be returned to disbelief, and this nearly amounts to an explicit statement from Shu'ayb that Allah, exalted is He, has willed the return of a Muslim to disbelief, and that is not our doctrine. Al-Wahidi said: The prophets and the great ones have always feared the outcome and the reversal of affairs. Do you not see the saying of the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], and Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) often used to say: "O Turner of hearts and sights, make our hearts firm upon Your religion and Your obedience." And Yusuf said: ﴿Take my soul as a Muslim﴾ [Yusuf: 101].

The Mu'tazilites answered this from several aspects:

The first: that His saying, "It is not for us to return to that religion unless Allah wills that He return us to it," is a conditional proposition, and there is no statement in it that He, exalted is He, willed that or did not will it.

The second: that this is mentioned by way of remoteness, as one says: "I will not do that unless the crow turns white and the raven grows gray." Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) made his return to their religion conditional upon His will. It is known that this is not a negation of that at all; it is by way of remoteness, not by way of condition.

The third: that His saying, "unless Allah wills," contains no statement of what Allah willed, so we take it to mean: unless our Lord wills by making us show this disbelief from ourselves when you compel us to it by killing; for at the compulsion to show disbelief by killing, it is permissible to show it, and what is permissible is willed by Allah, exalted is He. The fact that concealment (of faith) is better than outward display does not remove that display from being willed by Allah, exalted is He, just as wiping over the leather socks is willed by Allah, exalted is He, even though washing the feet is better.

The fourth: that His saying, "O Shu'ayb, we will surely expel you," means expulsion from the town, so His saying, "It is not for us to return to it," is understood as referring to the town; for He, exalted is He, had forbidden him, if they expelled him from the town, to return to it except by Allah's permission and will.

The fifth: we say that the will here must be understood as command; for His saying, "It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills," means: if He wills, it is for us to return to it, and His saying, "It is for us to return to it," means that return is permissible. According to the people of the Sunnah, will does not necessitate the permissibility of the act, for He, exalted is He, wills the disbelief of the disbeliever in their view, yet it is not permissible for him to do it. What necessitates permissibility is only command. Thus it is established that the meaning of will here is command, so the sense is: unless Allah commands our return to your religion, then we return to it. A law that has become abrogated is not far-fetched to be commanded again by Allah, and on this interpretation your argument falls away.

The sixth answer of the opponents: what al-Jubba'i mentioned. He said: what is meant by "religion" is the law in which the worship may differ according to times, such as prayer, fasting, and others. Shu'ayb said: ﴿It is not for us to return to it﴾, and since all that they were upon entered into that, and it was possible that some of those rulings and laws remained unabrogated, he therefore said: ﴿unless Allah wills﴾. The meaning: unless Allah wills the preservation of some of them, so He guides us to it, and then we return to them. This exception refers to the rulings in which abrogation and change may enter, and does not refer to what does not accept change at all. These are the objections of the opponents by this method, and they are good. There are many verses indicating the soundness of our doctrine, and the weakness of our companions' argument from this verse does not entail weakness entering the doctrine.

As for the Mu'tazilites, they held fast to this verse for the soundness of their view from two aspects:

The first aspect: when they said: the apparent sense of His saying, "It is not for us to return to it unless Allah our Lord wills," requires that if Allah willed our return to it, it would be for us to return to it; and that requires that whatever Allah wills to exist, its doing is permissible and authorized, and not forbidden. They said: and this is precisely our doctrine, that whatever Allah wills to occur is good and authorized, and whatever is forbidden is prohibited and not willed by Allah, exalted is He.

The second aspect for them: they said that His saying, "We will surely expel you," and "or you will surely return to our religion," there is no basis for distinguishing these two divisions according to the opponent's view; for in their view, their expulsion from the town is by the creation of Allah and their return to that religion is also by the creation of Allah, and if both divisions occur by Allah's creation, there remains no benefit in distinguishing between the two divisions.

Know that when the two sides' arguments from this verse conflicted, it became necessary to return to the other verses on this subject.

* * *

As for His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," there are several issues:

Issue one: regarding the connection of this statement with the earlier statement, there are several views. Al-Qadi said: we have transmitted from Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i that Shu'ayb's saying, "unless our Lord wills," means: unless He creates the benefit in those acts of worship, and then He obligates us with them; and the one who knows the benefits is none other than the one whose knowledge encompasses all things; therefore He followed it with this statement. Our companions said: the connection of this statement with what precedes it is that when the people said to Shu'ayb: either you leave our town or you return to our religion, Shu'ayb said: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, for perhaps in His knowledge there is a third division, namely that we remain in this town without returning to your religion, but He makes you subdued under our command, humbled and submissive under our rule. This view is better than what al-Qadi said, because His saying, "In Allah we have put our trust," fits this view and not what al-Qadi said.

Issue two: His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," indicates that He, exalted is He, was knowing in eternity of all things, because His saying "encompassed" is a past-tense verb, and so it encompasses every past. And when it is established that He was knowing in eternity of all knowables, and it is established that change in Allah's knowables is impossible, it follows that the rulings have been established, the pens have dried, and whoever is happy is happy in Allah's knowledge, and whoever is wretched is wretched in Allah's knowledge.

Issue three: His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," indicates that He knows the past, the present, and the future, and He knows the non-existent, how it would be were it to exist. These are four divisions. Then each of these four divisions occurs in four aspects. As for the past: He knows that, being past, how it was; He knows that, had it not been past but present, how it would be; He knows how it would be if it were future; and He knows how it would be if it were pure non-existence. These are four divisions according to the past. He considers these four divisions according to the present, according to the future, and according to pure non-existence, so the total becomes sixteen. Then He considers these sixteen divisions according to each of the essences, colors, tastes, and scents, and likewise the case for the remaining particulars of the kinds and genera of accidents. Thus there appears to your intellect, from His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," a sea whose extent the combined intellects of intelligent people do not reach to the first step of its shore.

**Fourth issue:** Al-Wahidi said: The phrase ﴿Our Lord has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ is in the accusative as a *tamyiz* (specification of the noun).

Know that he (peace be upon him) concluded his speech with two matters:

The first was reliance upon Allah. He said: ﴿In Allah we have put our trust﴾. This indicates restriction (*hasr*), meaning: upon Him alone we have relied, not upon anyone else. It seems that at this station he set aside the means and rose above them to the Causer of causes.

The second was supplication. He said: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: *"Judge and decide."* Al-Farra' said: "The people of ʿAmman call the judge *al-Fatih* and *al-Fattah*, because he opens up the places of truth." It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "I did not understand His words ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth﴾ until I heard the daughter of Dhi Yazan say to her husband: 'Come, let me *fatihk*,' meaning, 'let me bring you to judgment.'" Al-Zajjaj said: It is also possible that His words ﴿decide between us and our people in truth﴾ mean: "Make our matter manifest, until it becomes open between us and our people and is revealed." What is meant by this is that He should send down upon them a punishment that shows that they are falsifiers and that Shuʿayb and his people are truthful. On this interpretation, the meaning is disclosure and clarification.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And You are the best of those who decide﴾. What is intended by this is the praise of Allah. Our companions (the Ashʿariyyah) used this expression as evidence that it is He who creates faith in the servant. This is because faith is the most noble of created things. If we interpret *fath* as disclosure and clarification, there is no doubt that faith is likewise.

Having established this, we say: If the one who brings faith into existence were the servant, then the best of those who decide would be the servant, and that would negate His being the best of those who decide.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 88–89 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The chiefs of his people who were arrogant said: "We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, and those who believed with you, from our town, or you will return to our religion." He said: "Even though we are unwilling?"﴾ ﴿We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it. It is not for us to return to it unless Allah, our Lord, wills. Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge. In Allah we have put our trust. Our Lord, decide between us and our people in truth, for You are the best of deciders.﴾

Know that when Shu'ayb had established those words, those who were arrogant and disdained to believe him and accept his speech said: there must be one of two matters:
Either we expel you and your followers from this town,
or you return to our religion.

The difficulty here is that it may be said: their saying, "or you will surely return to our religion," indicates that he (peace be upon him) was upon their religion, which is disbelief, and this requires that he was a disbeliever before that, and that is utterly corrupt. Also, their saying, "We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion," indicates this same meaning.

The answer has several aspects:

The first: the followers of Shu'ayb were disbelievers before entering his religion, so they addressed Shu'ayb with the address of his followers and applied to him their rulings.

The second: their leaders said that in a manner of deception toward the common people, making them imagine that he had been one of them, and Shu'ayb mentioned his answer in accordance with that imagination.

The third: that Shu'ayb, at the beginning of his affair, was concealing his religion and creed, so they imagined that he was upon the religion of his people.

The fourth: it is not far-fetched to say that Shu'ayb was upon their law, then Allah, exalted is He, abrogated that law by the revelation He sent to him.

The fifth: what is meant by His saying, "or you will surely return to our religion," is: "you will come to our religion," so the return is used in the sense of beginning. The Arabs say: "a disliked thing has returned to me from so-and-so," meaning a disliked thing has come to me from him at the start. The poet said:

If the days were the best of periods toward me, then sins have returned to them (i.e., have become theirs).

He meant: sins have become theirs, and he did not mean that sins were theirs before the good.

Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that when the people said that, Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) answered their words in two ways:

The first: His saying, "Even though we are unwilling?" The hamza is for interrogation, and the waw is the waw of circumstance; its implied sense is: "Will you return us to your religion while we are in a state of hatred and being unwilling?"

The second: His saying, "We would have invented a lie against Allah if we returned to your religion after Allah has saved us from it." The first answer works as an allusion to the fact that he would not return to their religion, while this second answer is an explicit statement that he will not do that; he said: if we did that, we would have invented a lie against Allah. The basis of the matter concerning prophethood and messengership is truthfulness of speech and freedom from lying, so returning to your religion would nullify prophethood and remove messengership.

As for His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it," there are several aspects:

The first: the meaning of "after Allah has saved us from it" is that He taught us its ugliness and corruption, and established the proofs that it is false.

The second: that what is meant is that Allah saved His people from that religion, but he placed himself among them in the sum, though he was innocent of it, applying the speech according to the rule of predominance (taghlib).

The third: that the people were made to imagine that he had been upon their religion, or they believed that he had been so; so His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it," means according to your belief and your assumption.

* * *

As for His saying, "It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills."

Know that our companions (the Ash'arites) hold fast to this verse to show that Allah, exalted is He, may will disbelief, while the Mu'tazilites hold fast to it to show that Allah, exalted is He, wills only good and righteousness. As for the manner in which our companions argue from it, it is from two aspects:

The first: His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it," indicates that the one who saves from disbelief is Allah, exalted is He. If faith came about by the creation of the servant, then salvation from disbelief would occur for a person from himself, not from Allah, exalted is He, and that is contrary to the implication of His saying, "after Allah has saved us from it."

The second: the meaning of the verse is that it is not for us to return to your religion unless Allah wills that He return us to that religion. Since that religion was disbelief, this was a permission from Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) that they be returned to disbelief, and this nearly amounts to an explicit statement from Shu'ayb that Allah, exalted is He, has willed the return of a Muslim to disbelief, and that is not our doctrine. Al-Wahidi said: The prophets and the great ones have always feared the outcome and the reversal of affairs. Do you not see the saying of the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him: ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾ [Ibrahim: 35], and Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) often used to say: "O Turner of hearts and sights, make our hearts firm upon Your religion and Your obedience." And Yusuf said: ﴿Take my soul as a Muslim﴾ [Yusuf: 101].

The Mu'tazilites answered this from several aspects:

The first: that His saying, "It is not for us to return to that religion unless Allah wills that He return us to it," is a conditional proposition, and there is no statement in it that He, exalted is He, willed that or did not will it.

The second: that this is mentioned by way of remoteness, as one says: "I will not do that unless the crow turns white and the raven grows gray." Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) made his return to their religion conditional upon His will. It is known that this is not a negation of that at all; it is by way of remoteness, not by way of condition.

The third: that His saying, "unless Allah wills," contains no statement of what Allah willed, so we take it to mean: unless our Lord wills by making us show this disbelief from ourselves when you compel us to it by killing; for at the compulsion to show disbelief by killing, it is permissible to show it, and what is permissible is willed by Allah, exalted is He. The fact that concealment (of faith) is better than outward display does not remove that display from being willed by Allah, exalted is He, just as wiping over the leather socks is willed by Allah, exalted is He, even though washing the feet is better.

The fourth: that His saying, "O Shu'ayb, we will surely expel you," means expulsion from the town, so His saying, "It is not for us to return to it," is understood as referring to the town; for He, exalted is He, had forbidden him, if they expelled him from the town, to return to it except by Allah's permission and will.

The fifth: we say that the will here must be understood as command; for His saying, "It is not for us to return to it unless Allah wills," means: if He wills, it is for us to return to it, and His saying, "It is for us to return to it," means that return is permissible. According to the people of the Sunnah, will does not necessitate the permissibility of the act, for He, exalted is He, wills the disbelief of the disbeliever in their view, yet it is not permissible for him to do it. What necessitates permissibility is only command. Thus it is established that the meaning of will here is command, so the sense is: unless Allah commands our return to your religion, then we return to it. A law that has become abrogated is not far-fetched to be commanded again by Allah, and on this interpretation your argument falls away.

The sixth answer of the opponents: what al-Jubba'i mentioned. He said: what is meant by "religion" is the law in which the worship may differ according to times, such as prayer, fasting, and others. Shu'ayb said: ﴿It is not for us to return to it﴾, and since all that they were upon entered into that, and it was possible that some of those rulings and laws remained unabrogated, he therefore said: ﴿unless Allah wills﴾. The meaning: unless Allah wills the preservation of some of them, so He guides us to it, and then we return to them. This exception refers to the rulings in which abrogation and change may enter, and does not refer to what does not accept change at all. These are the objections of the opponents by this method, and they are good. There are many verses indicating the soundness of our doctrine, and the weakness of our companions' argument from this verse does not entail weakness entering the doctrine.

As for the Mu'tazilites, they held fast to this verse for the soundness of their view from two aspects:

The first aspect: when they said: the apparent sense of His saying, "It is not for us to return to it unless Allah our Lord wills," requires that if Allah willed our return to it, it would be for us to return to it; and that requires that whatever Allah wills to exist, its doing is permissible and authorized, and not forbidden. They said: and this is precisely our doctrine, that whatever Allah wills to occur is good and authorized, and whatever is forbidden is prohibited and not willed by Allah, exalted is He.

The second aspect for them: they said that His saying, "We will surely expel you," and "or you will surely return to our religion," there is no basis for distinguishing these two divisions according to the opponent's view; for in their view, their expulsion from the town is by the creation of Allah and their return to that religion is also by the creation of Allah, and if both divisions occur by Allah's creation, there remains no benefit in distinguishing between the two divisions.

Know that when the two sides' arguments from this verse conflicted, it became necessary to return to the other verses on this subject.

As for His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," there are several issues:

Issue one: regarding the connection of this statement with the earlier statement, there are several views. Al-Qadi said: we have transmitted from Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i that Shu'ayb's saying, "unless our Lord wills," means: unless He creates the benefit in those acts of worship, and then He obligates us with them; and the one who knows the benefits is none other than the one whose knowledge encompasses all things; therefore He followed it with this statement. Our companions said: the connection of this statement with what precedes it is that when the people said to Shu'ayb: either you leave our town or you return to our religion, Shu'ayb said: ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾, for perhaps in His knowledge there is a third division, namely that we remain in this town without returning to your religion, but He makes you subdued under our command, humbled and submissive under our rule. This view is better than what al-Qadi said, because His saying, "In Allah we have put our trust," fits this view and not what al-Qadi said.

Issue two: His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," indicates that He, exalted is He, was knowing in eternity of all things, because His saying "encompassed" is a past-tense verb, and so it encompasses every past. And when it is established that He was knowing in eternity of all knowables, and it is established that change in Allah's knowables is impossible, it follows that the rulings have been established, the pens have dried, and whoever is happy is happy in Allah's knowledge, and whoever is wretched is wretched in Allah's knowledge.

Issue three: His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," indicates that He knows the past, the present, and the future, and He knows the non-existent, how it would be were it to exist. These are four divisions. Then each of these four divisions occurs in four aspects. As for the past: He knows that, being past, how it was; He knows that, had it not been past but present, how it would be; He knows how it would be if it were future; and He knows how it would be if it were pure non-existence. These are four divisions according to the past. He considers these four divisions according to the present, according to the future, and according to pure non-existence, so the total becomes sixteen. Then He considers these sixteen divisions according to each of the essences, colors, tastes, and scents, and likewise the case for the remaining particulars of the kinds and genera of accidents. Thus there appears to your intellect, from His saying, "Our Lord encompasses all things in knowledge," a sea whose extent the combined intellects of intelligent people do not reach to the first step of its shore.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 90–93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the chiefs of those who disbelieved among his people said: "If you follow Shu'ayb, you will surely be losers."﴾ ﴿So the earthquake seized them, and they became prostrate in their homes by morning.﴾ ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb — it was as if they had never lived in them. Those who denied Shu'ayb — it was they who were the losers.﴾ ﴿So he turned away from them and said: "O my people, I had certainly conveyed to you the messages of my Lord and advised you sincerely, so how should I grieve over a disbelieving people?"﴾

Page 148

Know that He, exalted is He, showed the magnitude of their misguidance by their denial of Shu'ayb. Then He showed that they did not confine themselves to that, but went so far as to misguide others, and they blamed them for following him, so they said: ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb, you will surely be losers.﴾ They differed: some said, "losers in religion," and others said, "losers in worldly life, because he forbids you from taking excess from people's wealth." At this statement their condition was complete, first in misguidance and then in misguiding others, so they deserved destruction. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾, which is the intense, destroying quaking. When there is added to it the severe, frightening punishment mentioned by God, exalted is He, in the story of the wrongdoers, the destruction becomes greater, because the punishment encompassed them from above them and from beneath their feet. ﴿And they became in their homes﴾, that is, in their dwellings, ﴿prostrate﴾, that is, lifeless, still and motionless without life. The full explanation of these words has already passed.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb — it was as if they had never lived﴾, and in this there are two discussions:

The first discussion: concerning His saying ﴿as if they had never lived (lam yaghnaw)﴾ there are two views:

One: it is said, "the people lived (ghaniya) in their homes," when their stay in them was long.

The second: the dwellings in which their inhabitants dwelt, its singular being maghan. The poet said:

"Indeed they dwelt (ghanaw) in them in the finest of living, in the shade of a kingdom whose tent-pegs are firm."

He meant they remained in them. On this reading, His saying ﴿as if they had never lived (lam yaghnaw)﴾ means as if they had never dwelt or settled in them.
The second view: al-Zajjaj said: ﴿as if they had never lived (yaghnaw)﴾ means as if they had never lived in them in affluence. It is said, "the man became rich (ghaniya yaghna)" when he became wealthy, and this is from richness (ghina), which is the opposite of poverty.

Having known this, we say on both interpretations: God likened the condition of these deniers to the condition of one who had never been in those abodes at all. The poet said:

"As if there had never been between al-Hajun and al-Safa / any companion, and no one had conversed in Mecca at night.
Indeed, we were its people, but the vicissitudes of the nights and the fated misfortunes destroyed us."

The second discussion: His saying ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb — it was as if they had never lived﴾. ﴿Those who﴾ indicates that this punishment was specific to those deniers, and that indicates several things:

First: that this punishment occurred by the creation of a free-choosing agent, and that it was not the effect of the stars and nature; otherwise it would have befallen the followers of Shu'ayb just as it befell the disbelievers.

Second: it indicates that this free-choosing agent knows all particulars, so that He is able to distinguish between the obedient and the disobedient.

Third: it indicates a great miracle on behalf of Shu'ayb, because when the punishment descending from heaven fell upon one people and not another, although they were gathered in one town, that was among the greatest of miracles.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb — it was they who were the losers﴾. He repeated His saying ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾ to magnify their humiliation and to express the horror of the punishment they deserve for their ignorance. The Arabs repeat such a phrase for emphasis and magnification, as a man says to another: "your brother who wronged us, your brother who took our wealth, your brother who violated our honor." Also, when the people said ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb, you will surely be losers﴾, God, exalted is He, showed that those who did not follow him and opposed him were the losers.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So he turned away from them﴾. They differed as to whether he turned away after the punishment descended upon them or before that, and this question has already been mentioned. Al-Kalbi said: he went out from among them, and no prophet's people were punished until he had been taken out from among them.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿So how should I grieve over a disbelieving people?﴾ Al-asa (grief) is intense sorrow. Al-Ajjaj said:

"And his two eyes flowed from excess of grief."

Having known this, we say: there are two views concerning the verse:

The first view: his sorrow over his people was intense, because they were numerous, and he had been expecting from them a response to faith. When that great destruction befell them, there arose in his heart grief because of kinship, blood-relation and neighbourhood, and long familiarity. Then he consoled himself, saying: ﴿So how should I grieve over a disbelieving people?﴾, because it was they who destroyed themselves through their persistence in disbelief.

The second view: the meaning is, "I had certainly discharged my duty to you in conveying, advising and warning you of what has befallen you, but you did not hear my word and did not accept my counsel, so how should I grieve over you?" That is, they were not deserving that a person should grieve over them. The author of al-Kashshaf said: Yahya ibn Wathhab read "fa-kayfa iyas" with a kasra on the hamza.

One: it is said, "the people lived (ghaniya) in their homes," when their stay in them was long.

"And his two eyes flowed from excess of grief."

Having known this, we say: there are two views concerning the verse:

The first view: his sorrow over his people was intense, because they were numerous, and he had been expecting from them a response to faith. When that great destruction befell them, there arose in his heart grief because of kinship, blood-relation and neighbourhood, and long familiarity. Then he consoled himself, saying: ﴿So how should I grieve over a disbelieving people?﴾, because it was they who destroyed themselves through their persistence in disbelief.

The second view: the meaning is, "I had certainly discharged my duty to you in conveying, advising and warning you of what has befallen you, but you did not hear my word and did not accept my counsel, so how should I grieve over you?" That is, they were not deserving that a person should grieve over them. The author of al-Kashshaf said: Yahya ibn Wathhab read "fa-kayfa iyas" with a kasra on the hamza.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 94–95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send to any town a prophet except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship, that they might humble themselves﴾ ﴿Then We substituted good in place of evil until they multiplied and said, "Indeed, hardship and ease touched our fathers," so We seized them suddenly while they were unaware﴾.

Know that when Exalted God informed us of the circumstances of these prophets and of what befell their nations, it was possible to suppose that He sent the punishment of total destruction (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣāl) only in the time of these prophets alone. So in this verse He made clear that this kind of destruction He has inflicted upon others as well, and He explained the reason for which He does so. He said, exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send to any town a prophet except that We seized its people with adversity and hardship﴾. He mentioned "town" because it is the gathering place of the people to whom the messengers are sent, and the word includes the city, since it is the gathering place of peoples. His saying "a prophet" (min nabiyyin) contains an ellipsis and an implied element; the sense is: "a prophet was sent, and he was rejected, or his people rejected him, and We seized its people with adversity and hardship." Al-Zajjaj said: al-baʾsāʾ (adversity) is everything of hardship that befell them in their circumstances, and al-ḍarrāʾ (hardship) is what befell them of illnesses. It was also said the reverse.

Then Exalted God explained that He does this so that they would humble themselves (yaḍarraʿūn); its meaning is "that they would supplicate" (yatadarraʿūn). Tadarruʿ is submission and yielding to God, exalted is He. Since you know that His saying "perhaps" (laʿallahum) cannot be taken to mean doubt with respect to God, exalted is He, it is necessary to take it to mean that God, exalted is He, did this act so that they would humble themselves. The Muʿtazilah said: this indicates that God, exalted is He, willed from all accountable persons faith and obedience. Our companions (the Ashʿarites) said: since it has been established by proof that ascribing causes (taʿlīl) to God's acts and rulings is impossible, it is necessary to interpret the verse as meaning that God, exalted is He, did an act which, if another had done it, would have been similar to a cause and a purpose.

Then Exalted God explained that His management of the people of the towns does not proceed in one fixed pattern, but He manages them in whatever brings them closer to faith. So He said: ﴿Then We substituted good in place of evil﴾, because the arrival of blessing in body and wealth after adversity and hardship calls to submission and occupation with gratitude. The meaning of "good" (ḥasanah) and "evil" (sayyiʾah) here is hardship and ease. The people of lexicography said: "sayyiʾah" is everything that displeases its possessor, and "ḥasanah" is what the nature and intellect find pleasing. The meaning is that Exalted God informed us that He seizes the people of sin with hardship at one time and with ease at another.

His saying ﴿until they multiplied (ʿafaw)﴾: al-Kisa'i said: it is said "al-shaʿr wa ghayruhu ʿafa" when it increases, it "yaʿfū," so it is "ʿāfin." From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until they multiplied﴾, meaning they increased. From this is what has come in the hadith that he, peace be upon him, "commanded that the moustaches be trimmed and the beards be left (tuʿfā)," meaning they should grow and become abundant.

His saying ﴿and they said, "Indeed, hardship and ease touched our fathers"﴾: the meaning is that whenever hardship reached them, they said: "This is not because of the religion and deeds we follow; this is the custom of the age." What touched us of adversity and hardship was not a punishment from God. This narration indicates that they did not benefit from what God arranged for them of ease after hardship and security after fear, but rather they turned to the view that this is the custom of time toward its people: at times hardship and distress occur among them, and at times ease and comfort occur for them. So Exalted God made clear that He removed their excuse and dispelled their pretext, yet they did not submit and did not benefit from that respite.

His saying ﴿So We seized them suddenly﴾: the meaning is that when they rebelled under both conditions, God seized them suddenly wherever they were, so that this would be greater in regret. His saying ﴿while they were unaware﴾ means they did not perceive the punishment. The wisdom in relating this meaning is that those who hear this story and learn of it may take warning.

﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened for them blessings from the heaven and the earth, but they denied, so We seized them for what they used to earn﴾ ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by night while they are asleep?﴾ ﴿Or do the people of the towns feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them in the forenoon while they are at play?﴾ ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of God? None feel secure from the plan of God except the losing people﴾.

None feels secure from the plan of God except the people who are losers.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, explained in the first verse that those who disobeyed and rebelled were seized suddenly by God, He explained in this verse that, had they obeyed, God would have opened for them the doors of good things. So He said: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed﴾, meaning believed in God, His angels, His books, His messengers and the Last Day, ﴿and been mindful﴾ (of God) by avoiding what God has forbidden and prohibited, ﴿We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth.﴾ The blessings of the heaven are by rain, and the blessings of the earth are by plants and fruits, the abundance of livestock and cattle, and the attainment of security and safety. This is because the heaven takes the place of the father and the earth takes the place of the mother, and from them comes all benefit and good, by the creation and governance of God, may He be exalted. His saying: ﴿But they denied﴾ means the messengers, ﴿so We seized them﴾ with drought and famine, ﴿for what they used to earn﴾ of disbelief and disobedience.

Then He, may He be exalted, renewed the threat of the punishment of annihilation, saying: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾, and this is an interrogative in the sense of rebuke against them. The purpose is that He, may He be exalted, frightened them with the descent of that punishment upon them at the time in which they are in the utmost heedlessness, which is the state of sleep at night and the state of mid-morning (ḍuḥā) during the day, because that is the time in which a person is most inclined to busy himself with pleasures.

His saying: ﴿while they are at play﴾ may include being occupied with the affairs of this world, for these are play and amusement; and it may include their immersion in their disbelief, because that is like play in that it neither harms nor benefits.

Most of the reciters read ﴿أوَأمِنَ﴾ (a-wa-amina) with a fatḥa on the wāw, and here the wāw is the conjunction ('aṭf) which the interrogative hamza (hamzat al-istifhām) has entered, as it entered in His saying: ﴿أثُمَّ إذا ما وقَعَ﴾ [Yunus: 51] and His saying: ﴿أوَكُلَّما عاهَدُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah: 100]. This reading is more fitting with what comes before and after it, because before it is ﴿أفَأمِنَ أهْلُ القُرى﴾ and after it is ﴿أفَأمِنُوا مَكْرَ اللَّهِ﴾ and ﴿أوَلَمْ يَهْدِ لِلَّذِينَ يَرِثُونَ الأرْضَ﴾. Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿أوْ أمِنَ﴾ with the wāw sukūn (silent), and it is used in two ways:

The first: that it means one of two things, as in His saying: "Zayd or ʿAmr came," meaning: one of them came.

The second: that it is for iḍrāb (a turning away from what precedes it), as in your saying: "I am going out or I am staying," where you have turned away from going out and affirmed staying, as if you said: "No, rather I am staying." So the basis of this reading is that he made ﴿أوْ﴾ for iḍrāb, not on the basis that it nullifies the first, which is ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. The revelation of the Book, there is no doubt in it, from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿Or do they say﴾ [al-Sajdah: 1, 2, 3]. So the meaning of this verse is the equality of these kinds of punishment. If you wish, you may make ﴿أوْ﴾ here the one that means one of two things, and the meaning will be: "Do they feel secure from one of these punishments?"

His saying: ﴿ḍuḥā﴾. The ḍuḥā is the early part of the day, and its root meaning is manifestation, from the expression "ḍaḥā li-l-shams" when it became manifest to it (the sun).

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of God?﴾ The meaning of makr (plan/scheme) has already been explained linguistically, and the meaning of makr with respect to God, may He be exalted, was explained in Surat Āl ʿImrān at His saying: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 54]. His saying: ﴿Do they feel secure from the plan of God?﴾ indicates that what is meant is that His punishment comes upon them from where they do not perceive, and He said this as a warning. He named this punishment a "plan" figuratively (tawassuʿan), because when one of us wishes to scheme against his companion, he brings him into affliction from where he does not perceive it. So He named the punishment "plan" because it descends upon them from where they do not perceive. He made clear that none feels secure from the descent of God's punishment in this manner ﴿except the people who are losers﴾, namely those who, because of their heedlessness and ignorance, do not recognize their Lord and therefore do not fear Him. Whoever follows this path is the greatest of losers in this world and the Hereafter, because he has thrown himself into harm in this world and into the most severe punishment in the Hereafter.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 100–101:**

God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people that, if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins, and seal over their hearts so that they do not hear?﴾ ﴿These are the cities; We relate to you some of their news. Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before. Thus God seals the hearts of the disbelievers.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, had explained in the preceding verses the condition of the disbelievers whom God destroyed by total annihilation (al-isti'sal), both in summary and in detail, He followed this with an explanation that the purpose of mentioning these narratives is to produce a lesson (al-'ibrah) for all the legally responsible (al-mukallafin) regarding the interests of their religions and their acts of obedience. There are several issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** The reciters differed. Some read ﴿Has it not become clear﴾ (awa lam yahdi) with a yā' with a dot below, and some read it with a nūn. Al-Zajjaj said: If it is read with a yā' with a dot below, then his saying ﴿that if We willed﴾ (an law nasha'u) is in the nominative case as its subject (fa'il), meaning: Has it not become clear to those who succeed those earlier people and inherit their land and their dwellings, that this matter, namely that if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins just as We afflicted those before them, and We could destroy the inheritors just as We destroyed those who bequeathed the land? If it is read with a nūn, then it is in the accusative case, as if it were said: Have We not made clear to the inheritors this matter, meaning: Have We not explained to them that We afflicted Quraysh for their sins just as We afflicted those before them?

**The second issue:** The meaning is: Have We not made clear to those whom We raise up in the land after We have destroyed those who were there before them, so that We destroy them after them? This is the meaning of ﴿if We willed, We could afflict them for their sins﴾, i.e., the punishment for their sins. His saying ﴿and seal over their hearts﴾ means: if We do not destroy them with punishment, We seal over their hearts ﴿so that they do not hear﴾, i.e., they do not accept, they do not take admonition, and they do not desist. We said that the intended meaning is either destruction or the sealing of the heart, because destruction does not combine with the sealing of the heart: when He destroys a people, it is impossible for Him to seal their hearts.

**The third issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) used this verse, ﴿and seal over their hearts so that they do not hear﴾, to establish that God may prevent the servant from faith. The sealing (al-tab'), the stamping (al-khatm), the rust (al-rayn), the covering (al-kinan), the veil (al-ghishawah), the barring (al-sadd) and the prevention (al-man') are one and the same, as we have established in many verses.

Al-Jubba'i said: What is meant by this sealing is that God marks the hearts of the disbelievers with marks and signs by which the angels recognize that their owners will not believe; and that sign does not prevent them from faith.

Al-Ka'bi said: He attributed the sealing to Himself only because these people came to that disbelief at His command and trial. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But my calling only increased them in flight﴾ [Nuh: 6].

Know that the discussion about the reality of sealing and stamping has passed many times, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

**The fourth issue:** Is His saying ﴿and We seal﴾ disconnected from what precedes it, or is it conjoined to what precedes it? There are two opinions:

The first opinion: it is disconnected from what precedes it, because His saying ﴿We afflicted﴾ (asabna) is in the past tense, while His saying ﴿and We seal﴾ (wa natba'u) is in the future tense, and this conjunction is not preferable; rather it is disconnected from what precedes it, and the implied meaning is: and We, We seal over their hearts.

The second opinion: it is conjoined to what precedes it. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: It is conjoined to what is indicated by the meaning of ﴿Has it not become clear﴾, as if it were said: they are heedless of the guidance, and We seal over their hearts; or it is conjoined to His saying ﴿who inherit the land﴾. Then he said: It is not permissible for it to be conjoined to ﴿We afflicted them﴾, because they were disbelievers, and every disbeliever is sealed upon his heart, so His saying after that ﴿and We seal over their hearts﴾ would be in the manner of obtaining what is already obtained (tahsil al-hasil), and that is impossible. This is the statement of the author of al-Kashshaf in its strongest form, and it is weak; for being sealed upon arises only when a person persists and becomes firm in it. He first disbelieves, and then he becomes sealed in disbelief. So this does not contradict the validity of the conjunction.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿These are the cities; We relate to you some of their news﴾. His saying ﴿these﴾ (tilka) is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿the cities﴾ (al-qura) is a qualifier (sifah), and ﴿We relate to you﴾ (naqussu 'alayka) is the predicate (khabar). What is meant by ﴿these cities﴾ is the cities of the five peoples whom He described earlier, namely: the people of Noah, Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb. ﴿We relate to you some of their reports﴾, how they were destroyed. As for the reports of others than these peoples, We did not relate them to you. God specified the reports of these cities only because they were deceived by the long respite together with the abundance of blessings, so they imagined that they were upon the truth. So God mentioned them as a warning to the people of Muhammad (upon him be peace) to beware of acts like those.

Then God consoled him by His saying: ﴿Their messengers came to them with clear proofs﴾, meaning the prophets who were sent to them.

As for His saying ﴿but they were not going to believe in what they had denied before﴾, there are two opinions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: Those disbelievers would not have believed upon the sending of the messengers in what they had denied on the day when He took their covenant, when He brought them out from the loins of Adam; so they believed unwillingly, acknowledged with the tongue, and concealed the denial.

The second: Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿They were not going to believe﴾ after seeing the miracles in what they had denied before seeing those miracles.

The third: They would not have believed, even if We had brought them back to life after their destruction and returned them to the abode of obligation, in what they had denied before their destruction. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

The fourth: Before the coming of the Messenger they were persistent in disbelief, so these would not have believed after the coming of the messengers either.

The fifth: They would not have believed in the future time.

Then God, exalted is He, explained the cause of this non-acceptance, so He said: ﴿Thus God seals the hearts of the disbelievers﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: The kaf in ﴿thus﴾ (kadhalika) is in the accusative case, and the meaning is: like that which God sealed upon the hearts of the disbelievers of the past nations, He seals upon the hearts of the disbelievers who God has decreed will never believe. And God knows best the realities of matters.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi said: Those disbelievers would not have believed upon the sending of the messengers in what they had denied on the day when He took their covenant, when He brought them out from the loins of Adam; so they believed unwillingly, acknowledged with the tongue, and concealed the denial.

The second: Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿They were not going to believe﴾ after seeing the miracles in what they had denied before seeing those miracles.

The third: They would not have believed, even if We had brought them back to life after their destruction and returned them to the abode of obligation, in what they had denied before their destruction. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28].

The fourth: Before the coming of the Messenger they were persistent in disbelief, so these would not have believed after the coming of the messengers either.

The fifth: They would not have believed in the future time.

Then God, exalted is He, explained the cause of this non-acceptance, so He said: ﴿Thus God seals the hearts of the disbelievers﴾.

Al-Zajjaj said: The kaf in ﴿thus﴾ (kadhalika) is in the accusative case, and the meaning is: like that which God sealed upon the hearts of the disbelievers of the past nations, He seals upon the hearts of the disbelievers who God has decreed will never believe. And God knows best the realities of matters.

[Page 153]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We found not for most of them any covenant, and indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient.﴾ Concerning it there are several opinions:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: He means fulfilling the covenant which Allah took from them while they were in the loins of Adam, when He said:

صفحة ١٥٤
﴿Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes.'﴾ [al-A'raf: 172] When Allah took this covenant from them and they acknowledged it, and then they violated it, it was as though no covenant had been made with them. Therefore He said: ﴿And We found not for most of them any covenant.﴾

The second: Ibn Mas'ud said: The covenant here means faith (iman), and the evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Except for those who have taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾ [Maryam: 87], meaning: those who believed and said, "There is no god but Allah."

The third: that the covenant is an expression for establishing the proofs indicating the soundness of monotheism (tawhid) and prophethood. On this interpretation, the meaning is: We found not among most of them any fulfillment of the covenant.

* * *
Then He said: ﴿And indeed We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient﴾, i.e., indeed the matter and the report is that We found most of them to be defiantly disobedient, departing from obedience and turning away from the religion.

The Qur'anic text: ﴿Then after them We sent Moses with Our signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they wronged themselves by them. So see how was the end of the corrupters.﴾

Know that this is the sixth story among the stories that Allah the Exalted mentioned in this surah. In this story He gave more detail and explanation than in any of the other stories, because the miracles of Moses were stronger than the miracles of the other prophets, and the ignorance of his people was greater and more shameful than the ignorance of other peoples.

Know also that the pronoun in His words ﴿after them﴾ may refer to the prophets who have already been mentioned, and it may refer to the nations whose destruction was mentioned earlier.

As for His words "with Our signs" (bi-ayatina), there are several discussions (mabahith):

The first discussion: this verse indicates that a prophet must have a sign (ayah) and a miracle (mu'jizah) by which he is distinguished from others, for if he were not specially marked by this sign, accepting his word would not be more appropriate than accepting the word of anyone else.

The second discussion: this verse indicates that Allah the Exalted gave him many signs and many miracles.

The third discussion: Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "The first of his signs was the staff, then the hand. He struck the gate of Pharaoh with the staff, and Pharaoh was frightened by it, and his head turned white. Out of shame he dyed it black, so he was the first to dye (his hair)."

He said: "The last of the signs was the obliteration (al-tamsah)."

He said: "The staff has many benefits, some of which are mentioned in the Qur'an, such as His words: ﴿It is my staff; I lean on it, and I beat down leaves with it for my sheep, and in it I have other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18]."

Allah mentioned among those uses in the Qur'an His words: ﴿Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ [al-Baqarah: 60].

Ibn 'Abbas mentioned other things:

Among them: that he would strike the earth with it and it would bring forth plants.

Among them: that it would fight off thieves and the predators that targeted his sheep.

Among them: that it would glow at night like a candle.

Among them: that it would become like a long rope, by which water could be drawn from a deep well.

[Page 155]

Know that the benefits mentioned in the Qur'an are known. As for the matters not mentioned in the Qur'an, whatever is reported by a sound (sahih) report is accepted, and whatever is not, is not accepted. His statement that he would strike the earth with it and it would produce vegetation is weak, because the Qur'an indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, would turn to the staff for the water emerging from the rock, and he would not turn to it for seeking food.

As for His words ﴿but they wronged themselves by them﴾, that means they wronged by means of the signs that came to them. This is because wrong (zulm) is placing a thing in other than its proper place. Since those signs were overpowering and manifest, and then they disbelieved in them, placing denial in the place of acknowledgment and disbelief in the place of faith, that was a wrong on their part against those signs.

Then He said: "So see" (fa-nzur), meaning with the eye of your intellect, ﴿how was the end of the corrupters﴾, and how We dealt with them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 104–106:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Moses said, "O Pharaoh, indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds."﴾ ﴿It is incumbent upon me that I should not say about Allah except the truth. I have certainly come to you with clear evidence from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel.﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you should be of the truthful."﴾

Regarding the verse, there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that the kings of Egypt were called "Pharaohs," just as the kings of Persia were called "Khosrows" (Akasira). So it is as if he said, "O king of Egypt." His name was Qayus, and it was said: al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿Indeed I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾ contains an indication of that which proves the existence of God, exalted is He. For His saying, ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ indicates that the world is characterized by attributes for which it is in need of a Lord who nurtures it and a God who brings it into existence and creates it.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿It is incumbent upon me that I should not say about Allah except the truth.﴾ The meaning is that a messenger says only the truth. Thus the structure of the speech is as if he said: "I am a messenger of Allah, and a messenger of Allah says only the truth, therefore I say only the truth." Since the first premise was hidden and the second premise was evident and manifest, he mentioned that which proves the soundness of the first premise, which is His saying: ﴿I have certainly come to you with clear evidence from your Lord﴾, namely the manifest and overpowering miracle. And when he established the prophethood of himself, he derived from it the conveying of the command, which is His saying: ﴿so send with me the Children of Israel.﴾ When Pharaoh heard this speech he said: ﴿If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you should be of the truthful.﴾ Know that the proof of Moses, peace be upon him, was based on premises:

The first: that this world has a God who is powerful, knowing, and wise.

The second: that He sent him to them, by the evidence that He manifested the miracle in accordance with his claim. When this is the case, it is necessary that he be a true messenger.

The third: that when this is the case, everything that he conveys from Allah to them is true and sincere. Then, Pharaoh did not dispute with him over any of these premises except in demanding the miracle, and this gives the impression that he was agreeing to the soundness of the rest of the premises. We have mentioned in the Surah Ta-Ha that the scholars differed over whether Pharaoh was acquainted with his Lord or not. One who answers may say: the manifestation of a miracle first indicates the existence of a powerful, choosing God, and second indicates that God has made it stand in place of confirmation of that messenger. Perhaps Pharaoh was ignorant of the existence of the powerful, choosing God, and asked him to display that evidence, so that if he displayed it and brought it, that would be a proof of the existence of God first and of the soundness of his prophethood second. On this assumption, it does not follow from Pharaoh's limiting himself to demanding evidence that he acknowledged the existence of the acting, choosing God.

The third issue: Qari' Nafi' read ﴿ḥaqīqun ʿalayya﴾ with a doubled yāʾ, while the rest read with a sukun on the yāʾ and without doubling. As for Nafi's reading "fa-ḥaqīqun," it may be in the sense of the active participle (fāʿil). Al-Layth said: ḥaqqa al-shayʾ means "it became obligatory"; "yaḥiqqu ʿalayka an tafʿala kadha" and "ḥaqīqun ʿalayya an afʿalahu" in the sense of the active participle: "it is obligatory upon me to abandon speaking about Allah except with the truth." It may also be in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ūl), where the form faʿīl is placed in the position of maf'ūl. The Arabs say: "ḥaqqun ʿalayya an afʿala kadha," and "innī la-maḥqūqun ʿalayya an afʿala khayran," meaning: that is incumbent upon me, in the sense of "istaḥaqqa" (deserved).

Having understood this, we say: the argument of Nafi' for doubling the yāʾ is that ḥaqqa is transitive with ʿalā, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So the word of our Lord has come into effect against us﴾ [al-Saffat: 31] and He said: ﴿So the word has come into effect upon them﴾ [al-Isra': 16]. Thus "ḥaqīq" may be joined with the particle "ʿalā" in this respect. Also, His saying "ḥaqīq" is in the sense of "wājib" (obligatory), so just as "wajaba" is transitive with ʿalā, so too "ḥaqīq," if it is meant as "wajaba," is transitive with ʿalā. As for the reading of the common people, ﴿ḥaqīqun ʿalā﴾ with a sukun on the yāʾ, there are several aspects:

The first: the Arabs put bāʾ in the place of ʿalā; they say: "ramaytu ʿalā al-qaws" and "bi-al-qaws," and "jiʾtu ʿalā ḥālin ḥasanatin" and "bi-ḥālin ḥasanatin." Al-Akhfash said: this is like His saying: ﴿and do not sit on every path threatening﴾ [al-A'raf: 86]. Just as bāʾ occurred in His saying ﴿bi-kulli ṣirāṭin﴾ in the place of ʿalā, so likewise the word ʿalā occurred in the place of bāʾ in His saying: ﴿ḥaqīqun ʿalā an lā aqūla﴾. This aspect is confirmed by the reading of ʿAbd Allah: "ḥaqīqun bi-an lā aqūla." On this reading the construction is: "I am worthy to not say..." and on Nafi's reading it is in the nominative by inception, and its predicate is ﴿an lā aqūla﴾.

The second: the ḥaqq is that which is established and enduring, and ḥaqīq is an intensive form of it, and the meaning is: "I am firmly and continuously upon not saying except the truth."

The third: ḥaqīq here means "maḥqūq" (one who is verified), from your saying: "ḥaqaqtu al-rajul" when you verified him and knew him with certainty; and the particle "ʿalā" here is the one that is attached to essential, inherent attributes, as in His saying: ﴿the nature of Allah upon which He created mankind﴾ [al-Rum: 30]. And you say: "Fulan came to me in his form and habit," and "I knew him and verified him in such and such attributes." So the meaning of the verse is: "I have not known or verified except upon the saying of the truth." And Allah knows best.

As for His saying: ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾, that is, release them and let them go. Pharaoh had enslaved them in arduous labours, such as brick-making and carrying earth. At this speech Pharaoh said: ﴿If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you should be of the truthful.﴾ There are two discussions regarding this:

The first discussion: one may ask: how did he say to him, ﴿then bring it forth﴾, after his saying ﴿If you have come﴾?

صفحة ١٥٧
Its answer: if you have come from the One who sent you with a sign, then bring it to me and present it before me, so that your claim may be sound and your truthfulness established.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿He said, "If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you should be of the truthful"﴾ is a conditional clause occurring between two conditions. What is its ruling? Its answer: a parallel to it is the saying: "If you enter the house, then you are divorced, if you speak to Zayd." Here the element posterior in wording is anterior in meaning, and this meaning has been established previously.
