As for His saying: ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾, that is, release them and let them go. Pharaoh had enslaved them in arduous labours, such as brick-making and carrying earth. At this speech Pharaoh said: ﴿If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you should be of the truthful.﴾ There are two discussions regarding this:

The first discussion: one may ask: how did he say to him, ﴿then bring it forth﴾, after his saying ﴿If you have come﴾?

صفحة ١٥٧
Its answer: if you have come from the One who sent you with a sign, then bring it to me and present it before me, so that your claim may be sound and your truthfulness established.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿He said, "If you have come with a sign, then bring it forth, if you should be of the truthful"﴾ is a conditional clause occurring between two conditions. What is its ruling? Its answer: a parallel to it is the saying: "If you enter the house, then you are divorced, if you speak to Zayd." Here the element posterior in wording is anterior in meaning, and this meaning has been established previously.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 107–110 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿So he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the onlookers﴾ ﴿The eminent ones of the people of Pharaoh said, "Indeed, this is a knowledgeable sorcerer﴾ ﴿who wants to drive you out of your land. So what do you advise?"﴾.

Know that when Pharaoh demanded that Musa (peace be upon him) produce proof of the truth of his prophethood, God the Exalted showed that his miracle was the transformation of the staff into a serpent and the appearance of the white hand. The discussion of this verse falls under several aspects:

The first: a group of the naturalists (al-Tabi'iyyun) deny that the staff can be transformed into a serpent. They said: The proof of its impossibility is that permitting the staff to turn into a serpent necessitates the removal of certainty from the necessary knowledge (al-ulum al-darura), and that is false, and whatever leads to falsehood is false. We say that permitting it necessitates the removal of certainty from necessary knowledge, because if we allowed that a large serpent could be generated from a small staff, we would also allow that a strong adult human could be generated from a single straw or a single grain of barley. And if one allowed that, we would allow for this human we see now that he came into being just now in a single instant and not from two parents. We would also allow for Zayd whom we see now that he is not the Zayd we saw yesterday, but another person who came into being just now in a single instant. It is well known that whoever opens for himself the doors of these permissions, the majority of rational people will judge him to be mad, senile and insane. Furthermore, if we allowed this, we would allow that the mountains have turned into gold and the waters of the seas have turned into blood, and we would allow that the chaff in the dung heap of the house has turned into flour, and that the flour that was in the house has turned into dust. Permitting such things destroys necessary knowledge and leads a person into sophistry (al-safsata), and that is absolutely false, so whatever leads to it is also false.

If someone says: the permission of such things is specific to the age of the calling of the prophets, and this age is not like that; security has been established in this age from the permissibility of these conditions.

The answer to this is given from several aspects:

The first: if this permission exists in general, then specifying this permission to one time rather than another is something known only through an obscure proof. Thus whoever is ignorant of that obscure proof would be ignorant of the specificity of that permission to that particular time. Consequently, the majority of rational people who do not know that obscure proof would have to permit all the things we have mentioned and would not be certain of the impossibility of their occurrence. Since we see them certain of the impossibility of their occurrence, we know that what you have stated is corrupt.

The second: if we permitted such conditions in the age of the calling to prophethood, then the affirmation of the truth of prophethood would also be invalidated, for if it is permissible for the staff to turn into a serpent, it is permissible for the person we saw to be not the first person, but rather God annihilated the first person in a single instant and brought into existence another person who resembles him in all attributes. On this assumption we cannot know that this person whom we see now is the one we saw yesterday. Then it follows that doubt arises concerning those who saw Musa, Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them all), whether that person is the one they saw yesterday or not. It is well known that permitting this leads to discrediting prophethood and messengerhood.

The third: even if this age is not the age in which miracles are possible, it is the age in which karamat (marvels of the saints) are possible according to you, so their permissibility is binding on you. This is the sum of the discussion on this point.

Know that the affirmation of the possibility of the breaking of customary patterns from their courses is difficult and problematic. The rational thinkers have disagreed about it, and the people of knowledge have three positions on it:

The first position: the position of those who permit this without restriction, and this is the position of our companions (ashabuna, i.e. the Ash'aris). They permitted the generation of human beings and all kinds of animals and plants in a single instant, without any preceding matter, duration, root, or upbringing. They also permitted that an indivisible atom (al-jawhar al-fard) could be living, knowing, powerful, rational and dominant, without the presence of a structure, temperament, moisture or composition. They also permitted that a blind man in Andalusia could see in the darkness of night a spot at the farthest east, while a person with healthy sight does not see the rising sun in the brightness of day. This is the position of our companions.

The second position: the position of the natural philosophers (al-falasifa al-tabi'iyyin), which is that this is impossible without restriction. They claimed that these things can only come into existence and enter being in this particular manner and specific way. They said: by this way we have protected ourselves from being bound by the absurdities we have mentioned and the impossibilities we have explained. Know that although they claim that this does not bind them, in reality it does bind them with an unavoidable binding. Its explanation is that these events that occur in this world of ours either occur without a cause or with a cause. On either assumption, the position we have mentioned is binding. As for the view that they occur without any cause, this view is clearly false by sound reason; yet even with its permission, the stated consequence is binding, because if we permit the existence of things without a cause and without an originator, then how can there be security from permitting the generation of a human without two parents, and from permitting the transformation of a mountain into gold and of the sea into blood? For permitting the occurrence of some things without a cause is no more remote to reason than permitting the occurrence of all other things without a cause. Thus it is established on this assumption that the stated consequence is binding. As for the second assumption, namely affirming a cause and a governor for this world, that cause is either a necessitating agent by its essence or a free agent by choice.

As for the first assumption, the stated consequences are binding. Its explanation is that if the cause and its determining factor are necessitating by essence, it is necessary to be certain that the specification of each particular time with the particular event that occurred in it is due to the fact that the events of this world vary according to the variation of celestial configurations. For if this meaning were not taken into account, it would be impossible for an eternal, permanent cause to be the reason for the occurrence of a temporal, changing effect.

Once this is established, we say: how can there be security from there occurring in the heavens a strange configuration that necessitates the generation of a human in a single instant without two parents, and the transfer of the matter of a mountain from the mountainous form to the golden form or to an animal form? And then all the stated consequences return.

As for the second assumption, namely that the cause and determiner of the world is a free, chosing agent, there is no doubt that all the things mentioned are possible, because it is not impossible to say that this chosen agent creates by his will a human in a single instant without two parents, and the transfer of the matter of a mountain into gold and of the sea into blood. Thus it is established that the things they attribute to us as consequences apply under all assumptions and all sects, and that there is absolutely no way to refute them.

The third position: the position of the Mu'tazilites. They permit the breaking of customary patterns and their deviation from their courses in some cases but not others. Most of their shaykhs permit the generation of a human in a single instant without two parents, permit the transformation of water into fire and vice versa, and permit the generation of crops without a preceding seed. Then they said: it is not permissible for the indivisible atom to be described as knowing, powerful and living; rather the validity of these attributes is conditioned on the presence of a particular structure and a particular temperament. They claimed that when the sense organ is sound, the object of perception is present, and there is neither excessive closeness nor excessive distance, perception must occur; and when one of these conditions is missing, perception is impossible. In sum, the Mu'tazilites in some cases do not consider the courses of customary patterns, and claim that their change is possible and their breaking is permissible; while in other cases they claim that they are necessary and that their cessation or transformation is impossible. They have no fixed law among people and no known rule. Therefore their position is the most corrupt of the sayings.

Having learned these details, we say: the essences of bodies are identical in their entire quiddity (al-mahiyya), and whatever is valid for one thing is valid for its like. Therefore it must be valid for every body what is valid for another. If some attribute is valid for some bodies, it must be valid for all of them in the same manner. Since this is so, the body of the staff is receptive to the attributes by which it becomes a serpent, and since this is so, the transformation of the staff into a serpent is a matter possible in itself. It has been established that God the Exalted is capable of all possibles, so it is necessary to be certain that He is capable of turning the staff into a serpent, and that is what was sought.

This argument depends on establishing three premises: the establishment that bodies are identical in their entire essence; the establishment that the judgment of a thing is the judgment of its like; and the establishment that God the Exalted is capable of all possibles. When proof for the soundness of these three premises is established, the complete aim has been achieved. And God knows best.

His words: "fa-idha hiya" (and behold it), i.e. the staff, and it is feminine. And thuban (serpent) is the large male snake, according to all the lexicographers. As for its size, it is not mentioned in the Qur'an. Certain things have been related from the exegetes (al-mufassirun) about its description. From Ibn Abbas: it filled eighty cubits, then it rushed upon Pharaoh to swallow him, so Pharaoh leapt from his throne fleeing and defecated, and the people were routed, and twenty-five thousand of them died. It was also said: between its jaws was forty cubits; its lower jaw was placed on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace, and Pharaoh cried: "O Musa, take it, for I believe in you." When Musa took it, it returned to being a staff as it was. Regarding the description of that serpent as "clearly visible" (mubin), there are several aspects:

The first: to distinguish it from the deception the sorcerers brought, which is confusing to whoever does not know its cause; and by this the miracles of the prophets are distinguished from tricks and illusions.

The second: the meaning is that they witnessed it as a living serpent, so the matter was not confused for them regarding it.

The third: the meaning is that this serpent made clear the words of Musa (peace be upon him) from the words of a lying claimant.

* * *

As for his words: ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, nazaʿa (drew out) in the language means the removal of a thing from its place. So "nazaʿa yadahu" means he took his hand out of his pocket or from his armpit, according to the Exalted's words: ﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾ (al-Naml 12) and His words: ﴿And press your hand to your side﴾ (Ta-Ha 22). And His words: ﴿so behold, it was white for the onlookers﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it had a bright light that illuminated what was between the heaven and the earth.

Know that since whiteness appears as a defect, God the Exalted showed in another verse that it was without any harm (su').

If it is said: to what does His words "for the onlookers" (lil-nazirin) relate?

We say: it relates to His words "white" (bayda'), and the meaning is: behold, it was white for the spectators; and it would not be white for the spectators unless its whiteness were a wondrous whiteness outside the customary, such that people gather to look at it as spectators gather to see wonders. Several discussions remain here:

The first of them: in how many respects does the transformation of the staff into a serpent indicate the miracle?

The second: was this miracle greater, or the white hand? We have thoroughly examined these two questions in Surah Ta-Ha.

The third: a single miracle would have been sufficient, so combining the two would have been pointless.

Their reply: the multiplicity of proofs produces strength in certainty and removes doubt. Among the heretics (al-mulhidin) there is one who said: what is meant by the serpent (thu'ban) and by the white hand is one and the same thing, namely that the proof of Musa (peace be upon him) was strong, manifest and overpowering. That proof, insofar as it nullified the claims of the opponents and exposed their corruption, was like the great serpent that swallows up the proofs of the falsifiers; and insofar as it was manifest in itself, it was described as the white hand, as one says in common usage: "So-and-so has a white hand in such-and-such field of knowledge," meaning perfect capability and a manifest rank.

Know that interpreting these two miracles in this way amounts to rejecting what is transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) and denying Allah and His Messenger. And since we have shown that the turning of the staff into a serpent is possible in itself, what compels us to resort to this interpretation?

When Allah the Exalted mentioned that Musa (peace be upon him) displayed these two types of miracles, He related that the people of Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer.﴾ This was because sorcery was prevalent in that era, and there is no doubt that the ranks of the sorcerers were differing and varied, and there is no doubt that among them there would be one who reached the utmost limit and final degree in that knowledge. So the people claimed that Musa (peace be upon him), being at the extreme of the knowledge of sorcery, came with that quality; then they mentioned that he only brought that sorcery because he was seeking kingship and leadership.

If it is said: the saying ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾ is related by Allah in Surat ash-Shu'ara' as having been said by Pharaoh to his people, while here He relates that the people of Pharaoh said it; so how can the two be reconciled? Its answer is in two respects:

The first: there is no impediment to his having said it and their having said it too, so Allah related his saying there and their saying here.

The second: perhaps Pharaoh said it first, and the chiefs took it from him and said it to others, or they said it on his behalf to the rest of the people by way of conveying it, for when kings hold an opinion they mention it to the elite, and the elite mention it to the common people; so it is likewise here.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, al-Zajjaj mentioned three possibilities regarding it:

The first: the speech of the chiefs of Pharaoh's people was complete at His saying ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery﴾; then at this point Pharaoh said in reply to them: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ They supported the validity of this view with two arguments:

One of them: His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is addressed to a plural, not a singular, so it must be Pharaoh's speech to the people. For if we made it the people's speech to Pharaoh, they would have addressed him with the singular, not the plural.

It has been answered: it is permissible that they addressed him with the plural as an honouring of his station, since the great are referred to by the pronoun of plurality, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾ [Nuh: 1], ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

The second argument: when He mentioned His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, He said after it: ﴿They said: Delay him and his brother﴾, and there is no doubt that this is the people's speech, and He made it a reply to their saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾. So the one who said ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ must be other than those who said "delay him", and this indicates that the saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is the speech of someone other than the chiefs of Pharaoh's people.

It has been answered: it is not far-fetched that the people said ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾, then they said to Pharaoh and to the leading figures of his retinue ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, then followed it with their saying ﴿Delay him and his brother﴾; for servants and followers refer the matter of command and prohibition first to the master and the one they follow, and then mention what has occurred to their minds of the interest involved.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is part of the remainder of the people's speech. They argued for it with two arguments:

The first: it is coordinated with the people's speech without any separation, so it must be part of their speech.

The second: rank is taken into account in address, so His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ must be a address from the lower to the higher, and that requires that this be part of the remainder of the speech with Pharaoh.

It has been answered regarding this second argument that a leader who is obeyed may say to the assembled group of his kinsmen and subjects: "What do you advise?", his purpose being to console their hearts, bring joy to their breasts, and show from himself that he honours them and holds them in esteem. Then, those who said that this is part of the speech of Pharaoh's people mentioned two opinions:

One of them: the one addressed by this address is Pharaoh alone, for it is said to the obeyed leader: "What do you see in this affair?", meaning "What do you see, you alone?", the intent being that you alone stand in place of the whole group; the purpose of it is to draw attention to his perfection and the elevation of his rank and status.

The second: the one addressed by this address is Pharaoh together with the great men of his state and the eminent ones of his court, since they are the ones who independently decide matters of command and prohibition. And Allah knows best.

And if one allowed that, we would allow for this human we see now that he came into being just now in a single instant and not from two parents. We would also allow for Zayd whom we see now that he is not the Zayd we saw yesterday, but another person who came into being just now in a single instant. Permitting such things destroys necessary knowledge and leads a person into sophistry (al-safsata), and that is absolutely false, so whatever leads to it is also false.

If someone says: the permission of such things is specific to the age of the calling of the prophets, and this age is not like that; security has been established in this age from the permissibility of these conditions.

The answer to this is given from several aspects:

The first: if this permission exists in general, then specifying this permission to one time rather than another is something known only through an obscure proof. Thus whoever is ignorant of that obscure proof would be ignorant of the specificity of that permission to that particular time. On this assumption we cannot know that this person whom we see now is the one we saw yesterday. Then it follows that doubt arises concerning those who saw Musa, Isa and Muhammad (peace be upon them all), whether that person is the one they saw yesterday or not. It is well known that permitting this leads to discrediting prophethood and messengerhood.

The third: even if this age is not the age in which miracles are possible, it is the age in which karamat (marvels of the saints) are possible according to you, so their permissibility is binding on you. This is the sum of the discussion on this point.

From Ibn Abbas: it filled eighty cubits, then it rushed upon Pharaoh to swallow him, so Pharaoh leapt from his throne fleeing and defecated, and the people were routed, and twenty-five thousand of them died. It was also said: between its jaws was forty cubits; its lower jaw was placed on the ground and its upper jaw on the wall of the palace, and Pharaoh cried: "O Musa, take it, for I believe in you." When Musa took it, it returned to being a staff as it was. Regarding the description of that serpent as "clearly visible" (mubin), there are several aspects:

The first: to distinguish it from the deception the sorcerers brought, which is confusing to whoever does not know its cause; and by this the miracles of the prophets are distinguished from tricks and illusions.

The second: the meaning is that they witnessed it as a living serpent, so the matter was not confused for them regarding it.

The third: the meaning is that this serpent made clear the words of Musa (peace be upon him) from the words of a lying claimant.

* * *

As for his words: ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, nazaʿa (drew out) in the language means the removal of a thing from its place. So "nazaʿa yadahu" means he took his hand out of his pocket or from his armpit, according to the Exalted's words: ﴿And put your hand into your pocket﴾ (al-Naml 12) and His words: ﴿And press your hand to your side﴾ (Ta-Ha 22). And His words: ﴿so behold, it was white for the onlookers﴾. Ibn Abbas said: it had a bright light that illuminated what was between the heaven and the earth.

Know that since whiteness appears as a defect, God the Exalted showed in another verse that it was without any harm (su').

If it is said: to what does His words "for the onlookers" (lil-nazirin) relate?

We say: it relates to His words "white" (bayda'), and the meaning is: behold, it was white for the spectators; and it would not be white for the spectators unless its whiteness were a wondrous whiteness outside the customary, such that people gather to look at it as spectators gather to see wonders. Several discussions remain here:

The first of them: in how many respects does the transformation of the staff into a serpent indicate the miracle?

The second: was this miracle greater, or the white hand? We have thoroughly examined these two questions in Surah Ta-Ha.

The third: a single miracle would have been sufficient, so combining the two would have been pointless.

Their reply: the multiplicity of proofs produces strength in certainty and removes doubt. Among the heretics (al-mulhidin) there is one who said: what is meant by the serpent (thu'ban) and by the white hand is one and the same thing, namely that the proof of Musa (peace be upon him) was strong, manifest and overpowering. That proof, insofar as it nullified the claims of the opponents and exposed their corruption, was like the great serpent that swallows up the proofs of the falsifiers; and insofar as it was manifest in itself, it was described as the white hand, as one says in common usage: "So-and-so has a white hand in such-and-such field of knowledge," meaning perfect capability and a manifest rank.

Know that interpreting these two miracles in this way amounts to rejecting what is transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) and denying Allah and His Messenger. And since we have shown that the turning of the staff into a serpent is possible in itself, what compels us to resort to this interpretation?

When Allah the Exalted mentioned that Musa (peace be upon him) displayed these two types of miracles, He related that the people of Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer.﴾ This was because sorcery was prevalent in that era, and there is no doubt that the ranks of the sorcerers were differing and varied, and there is no doubt that among them there would be one who reached the utmost limit and final degree in that knowledge. So the people claimed that Musa (peace be upon him), being at the extreme of the knowledge of sorcery, came with that quality; then they mentioned that he only brought that sorcery because he was seeking kingship and leadership.

If it is said: the saying ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾ is related by Allah in Surat ash-Shu'ara' as having been said by Pharaoh to his people, while here He relates that the people of Pharaoh said it; so how can the two be reconciled? Its answer is in two respects:

The first: there is no impediment to his having said it and their having said it too, so Allah related his saying there and their saying here.

The second: perhaps Pharaoh said it first, and the chiefs took it from him and said it to others, or they said it on his behalf to the rest of the people by way of conveying it, for when kings hold an opinion they mention it to the elite, and the elite mention it to the common people; so it is likewise here.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, al-Zajjaj mentioned three possibilities regarding it:

The first: the speech of the chiefs of Pharaoh's people was complete at His saying ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery﴾; then at this point Pharaoh said in reply to them: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ They supported the validity of this view with two arguments:

One of them: His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is addressed to a plural, not a singular, so it must be Pharaoh's speech to the people. For if we made it the people's speech to Pharaoh, they would have addressed him with the singular, not the plural.

It has been answered: it is permissible that they addressed him with the plural as an honouring of his station, since the great are referred to by the pronoun of plurality, as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder﴾ [al-Hijr: 9], ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah﴾ [Nuh: 1], ﴿Indeed, We sent it down in the Night of Decree﴾ [al-Qadr: 1].

The second argument: when He mentioned His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, He said after it: ﴿They said: Delay him and his brother﴾, and there is no doubt that this is the people's speech, and He made it a reply to their saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾. So the one who said ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ must be other than those who said "delay him", and this indicates that the saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is the speech of someone other than the chiefs of Pharaoh's people.

It has been answered: it is not far-fetched that the people said ﴿Indeed, this is a knowing sorcerer﴾, then they said to Pharaoh and to the leading figures of his retinue ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, then followed it with their saying ﴿Delay him and his brother﴾; for servants and followers refer the matter of command and prohibition first to the master and the one they follow, and then mention what has occurred to their minds of the interest involved.

The second opinion: His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ is part of the remainder of the people's speech. They argued for it with two arguments:

The first: it is coordinated with the people's speech without any separation, so it must be part of their speech.

The second: rank is taken into account in address, so His saying ﴿So what do you advise?﴾ must be a address from the lower to the higher, and that requires that this be part of the remainder of the speech with Pharaoh.

It has been answered regarding this second argument that a leader who is obeyed may say to the assembled group of his kinsmen and subjects: "What do you advise?", his purpose being to console their hearts, bring joy to their breasts, and show from himself that he honours them and holds them in esteem. Then, those who said that this is part of the speech of Pharaoh's people mentioned two opinions:

One of them: the one addressed by this address is Pharaoh alone, for it is said to the obeyed leader: "What do you see in this affair?", meaning "What do you see, you alone?", the intent being that you alone stand in place of the whole group; the purpose of it is to draw attention to his perfection and the elevation of his rank and status.

The second: the one addressed by this address is Pharaoh together with the great men of his state and the eminent ones of his court, since they are the ones who independently decide matters of command and prohibition. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 111–114:

God, the Exalted, said: "They said: 'Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers, who will bring you every skilled sorcerer.' And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh; they said: 'Surely there will be a reward for us if we are the victors.' He said: 'Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.'"

Know that there are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "arjihi" without a hamza, with a kasra on the ha' and with the vowel extended (ishba'). 'Asim and Hamzah read "arjih" without a hamza and with the ha' sukun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "arji'hu" with a hamza and a damma on the ha'. Then Ibn Kathir extended the ha' according to his own principle, while the rest do not extend it. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "'Arjih' with a hamza and without a hamza are two dialects. It is said: 'arja'tu al-amr' and 'arjaytuhu' when you delayed it. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: '...and others await the command of Allah' [al-Tawbah: 106] and '...you may postpone whom you will' [al-Ahzab: 51]. Both verses were recited in the two dialects. As for the reading of 'Asim and Hamzah without a hamza and with the ha' sukun, al-Farra' said: 'It is the dialect of the Arabs, who pause on the pronominal ha' in connected speech when the letter before it is vowelled,' and he recited:

"fa-yuslihu al-yawma wa-yufsiduhu ghadan"

He said: 'They do the same with the feminine ta' (ha' al-ta'nith), so they say: "hadhihi Talhah qad aqbalat," and he recited:

"lamma ra'a an la da'ah wa la shibha'"

Then al-Wahidi said: 'This has no basis according to the Basran grammarians in analogy.' Al-Zajjaj said: 'This is a line of verse whose composer we do not know; had a well-known poet said it, he would have been told: "You erred."'

The second issue: Regarding His saying "arjih," there are two views:

The first: al-irja' means delay, so "arjih" means "delay him," i.e., delay his matter and do not hasten to judge concerning him, lest your haste become a proof against you. The intent is that they tried to oppose his miracle with their sorcery, so that this would be stronger in refuting the word of Musa, peace be upon him.

The second view, which is the view of al-Kalbi and Qatadah: "arjih" means "imprison him." The verifiers said: this view is weak for two reasons:

The first: that irja' in the language means delay, not imprisonment.

The second: that Pharaoh was not capable of imprisoning Musa after he had witnessed the state of the staff.

As for His saying, "And send into the cities gatherers," there are two issues:

The first issue: this verse indicates that there were many sorcerers in that time, for otherwise His saying "and send into the cities gatherers, who will bring you every skilled sorcerer" would not be valid. It also indicates that people's nature includes knowing opposition, and that when it is possible, there is no prophethood, and when it is impossible, prophethood is established. As for explaining what sorcery is, whether it has a reality or is merely deception, the detailed discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi related from Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji that he said: "Our companions differed about the word al-madinah (city) into three views:

The first view: that it is fa'ilah, because it is derived from their saying "madana bi-l-makan yamdunu mudunan," when he settled in it. The proponent of this view relies on the consensus of the reciters on hamzating al-madain, which is fa'ail, like sahaif and safinah (sahifah and safinah), and the yaʼ, when it is extra in the singular, is hamzated in the plural, like qaba'il and qabilah; and when it is from the root of the word, it is not hamzated in the plural, such as ma'ayish and ma'ishah.

The second view: that it is maf'ilah. On this view, the meaning of al-madinah is "the ruled one," from dana-hu yadinuhu. Our saying madinah is from dana, like ma'ishah from 'ash. Its plural is madayin on the pattern of mafa'il, like ma'ayish without a hamza, and it is a noun for the place and the land in which the ruler subjugated them, i.e., governed and overpowered them.

The third view: al-Mubarrad said: madinah originally was madyunah, from dana-hu when he overpowered and governed him. They found the movement of the damma on the ya' heavy, so they made it sukun and transferred its movement to the preceding letter. Two sukuns came together: the extra waw, which is the waw of the object, and the ya' which is part of the root. So the waw was deleted, because it is extra, and deleting the extra is preferable to deleting a root letter. Then they kasra'd the dal so that the ya' would be preserved, and it would not change into a waw because of the damma before it, so that the words with waw would not mix with the words with ya'. The same applies to mabi' (sold), makhit (sewn) and makil (measured)."

Then al-Wahidi said: "The correct view is that it is fa'ilah, because the reciters agree on hamzating al-madain."

The third issue: "And send into the cities gatherers" means: send into the cities of Upper Egypt men who will gather to you the sorcerers who are in them. Ibn 'Abbas said: The chiefs of the sorcerers were at the farthest cities of Upper Egypt. Al-Qadi related from Ibn 'Abbas that they were seventy sorcerers besides their chief, and the one who taught them was a Magian man from the people of Nineveh, the town of Yunus, peace be upon him, which is a village near Mosul. I say: this report is problematic, because the Magians are the followers of Zoroaster, and Zoroaster came after the coming of Musa, peace be upon him.

* * *

As for His saying, "Every skilled sorcerer will come to you," there are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-kulli sahhar," and the rest read "bi-kulli sahir." Whoever reads "sahhar" has as his argument that he was described as "alim" (skilled), and describing him thus indicates his perfection in it and his expertise in it; so it was fitting that he be named with the form that indicates intensity in sorcery. Whoever reads "sahir" has as his argument His saying: "And the sorcerers were thrown down" [al-A'raf: 120] and "that we may follow the sorcerers" [al-Shu'ara': 40]. "Sahara" is the plural of sahir, like kataba for katib and fajara for fajir. They also argued with His saying: "They bewitched the eyes of the people" [al-A'raf: 116], and the active participle of "sahharu" is sahir.

The second issue: The ba' in His saying "bi-kulli sahir" may mean "with," and it may be the ba' of transitivity. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: This verse indicates that sorcerers were numerous in that time, and this supports what the theologians say: that God makes the miracle of each prophet of the same kind as what dominated the people of that time. Since sorcery dominated the people of the time of Musa, peace be upon him, his miracle was similar to sorcery, though it differed from sorcery in reality. Since medicine dominated the people of the time of 'Isa, peace be upon him, his miracle was of the kind of medicine. And since eloquence dominated the people of the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), his miracle was necessarily of the kind of eloquence.

* * *

Then God, the Exalted, said: "And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh; they said: 'Surely there will be a reward for us if we are the victors.'" In it are issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "inna lana la-ajran" with a kasra on the alif, as a statement. The rest read it as a question. Then they differed: Abu 'Amr read it with a long hamza according to his principle, and the rest with two hamzas. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The interrogative is better in this place, because they wanted to know whether there would be a reward for them or not, and they were confident that the reward was theirs. The consensus of them in Surat al-Shu'ara' on the hamza for the interrogative strengthens this.

The argument of Nafi' and Ibn Kathir is that they intended the interrogative hamza, but they deleted it from the pronunciation, and the interrogative hamza may be deleted from the pronunciation while remaining in meaning, as in His saying: "And is this a favour with which you reproach me?" [al-Shu'ara': 22], where many people hold that its meaning is "awa-tilka" (is that...?) with the interrogative, and as in His saying: "This is my Lord" [al-An'am: 78], the implied meaning being "Is this my Lord?" It was also said: The intent is that the sorcerers established for themselves a great reward, because they said: "We must have a reward," and the indefiniteness is for magnification, like the saying of the Arabs: "Indeed he has camels (la-ibilan)" and "indeed he has sheep (la-ghanaman)," intending abundance.

The second issue: One might say: why was it not said: "And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh and said"?

Its answer: It is on the assumption of a questioner who asked: "What did they say when they came to him?" So he was answered with His saying: "They said: 'Surely there will be a reward for us,'" meaning a payment for victory.

If it is asked: His saying "And indeed you will be among those brought near" is conjoined (ma'tuf), so what is the thing it is conjoined to?

Its answer: It is conjoined to an omitted element, which the particle of affirmation has taken the place of. It is as if he said, affirming their statement, "Surely there will be a reward for us": "Yes, indeed there will be a reward for you, and indeed you will be among those brought near." He meant: I will not limit you to the reward, but I will add to it, and that addition is that I will make you among those brought near to me. The theologians said: This indicates that the reward is greatly valued only when it is joined with honour, and the proof of this is that when Pharaoh promised them a reward, he joined to it what indicates honour, namely the attainment of nearness.

The third issue: The verse indicates that all of creation knew that Pharaoh was a humble, abased, powerless slave; for otherwise he would not have needed to seek the help of the sorcerers in repelling Musa, peace be upon him. It also indicates that the sorcerers were not capable of transforming substances; for otherwise they would not have needed to ask Pharaoh for reward and wealth. For if they were capable of transforming substances, why did they not turn the dust into gold, why did they not transfer Pharaoh's kingdom to themselves, and why did they not make themselves the kings of the world and the leaders of the earth? The purpose of these verses is to alert a person to these subtleties, and that he should not be deceived by the words of the people of falsehood and lies. And Allah knows best.

The purpose of these verses is to alert a person to these subtleties, and that he should not be deceived by the words of the people of falsehood and lies. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 111–114:

God, the Exalted, said: "They said: 'Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers, who will bring you every skilled sorcerer.' And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh; they said: 'Surely there will be a reward for us if we are the victors.' He said: 'Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near.'"

Know that there are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "arjihi" without a hamza, with a kasra on the ha' and with the vowel extended (ishba'). 'Asim and Hamzah read "arjih" without a hamza and with the ha' sukun. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "arji'hu" with a hamza and a damma on the ha'. Then Ibn Kathir extended the ha' according to his own principle, while the rest do not extend it. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "'Arjih' with a hamza and without a hamza are two dialects. It is said: 'arja'tu al-amr' and 'arjaytuhu' when you delayed it. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: '...and others await the command of Allah' [al-Tawbah: 106] and '...you may postpone whom you will' [al-Ahzab: 51]. Both verses were recited in the two dialects. As for the reading of 'Asim and Hamzah without a hamza and with the ha' sukun, al-Farra' said: 'It is the dialect of the Arabs, who pause on the pronominal ha' in connected speech when the letter before it is vowelled,' and he recited:

"fa-yuslihu al-yawma wa-yufsiduhu ghadan"

He said: 'They do the same with the feminine ta' (ha' al-ta'nith), so they say: "hadhihi Talhah qad aqbalat," and he recited:

"lamma ra'a an la da'ah wa la shibha'"

Then al-Wahidi said: 'This has no basis according to the Basran grammarians in analogy.' Al-Zajjaj said: 'This is a line of verse whose composer we do not know; had a well-known poet said it, he would have been told: "You erred."'

The second issue: Regarding His saying "arjih," there are two views:

The first: al-irja' means delay, so "arjih" means "delay him," i.e., delay his matter and do not hasten to judge concerning him, lest your haste become a proof against you. The intent is that they tried to oppose his miracle with their sorcery, so that this would be stronger in refuting the word of Musa, peace be upon him.

The second view, which is the view of al-Kalbi and Qatadah: "arjih" means "imprison him." The verifiers said: this view is weak for two reasons:

The first: that irja' in the language means delay, not imprisonment.

The second: that Pharaoh was not capable of imprisoning Musa after he had witnessed the state of the staff.

As for His saying, "And send into the cities gatherers," there are two issues:

The first issue: this verse indicates that there were many sorcerers in that time, for otherwise His saying "and send into the cities gatherers, who will bring you every skilled sorcerer" would not be valid. It also indicates that people's nature includes knowing opposition, and that when it is possible, there is no prophethood, and when it is impossible, prophethood is established. As for explaining what sorcery is, whether it has a reality or is merely deception, the detailed discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi related from Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji that he said: "Our companions differed about the word al-madinah (city) into three views:

The first view: that it is fa'ilah, because it is derived from their saying "madana bi-l-makan yamdunu mudunan," when he settled in it. The proponent of this view relies on the consensus of the reciters on hamzating al-madain, which is fa'ail, like sahaif and safinah (sahifah and safinah), and the yaʼ, when it is extra in the singular, is hamzated in the plural, like qaba'il and qabilah; and when it is from the root of the word, it is not hamzated in the plural, such as ma'ayish and ma'ishah.

The second view: that it is maf'ilah. On this view, the meaning of al-madinah is "the ruled one," from dana-hu yadinuhu. Our saying madinah is from dana, like ma'ishah from 'ash. Its plural is madayin on the pattern of mafa'il, like ma'ayish without a hamza, and it is a noun for the place and the land in which the ruler subjugated them, i.e., governed and overpowered them.

The third view: al-Mubarrad said: madinah originally was madyunah, from dana-hu when he overpowered and governed him. They found the movement of the damma on the ya' heavy, so they made it sukun and transferred its movement to the preceding letter. Two sukuns came together: the extra waw, which is the waw of the object, and the ya' which is part of the root. So the waw was deleted, because it is extra, and deleting the extra is preferable to deleting a root letter. Then they kasra'd the dal so that the ya' would be preserved, and it would not change into a waw because of the damma before it, so that the words with waw would not mix with the words with ya'. The same applies to mabi' (sold), makhit (sewn) and makil (measured)."

Then al-Wahidi said: "The correct view is that it is fa'ilah, because the reciters agree on hamzating al-madain."

The third issue: "And send into the cities gatherers" means: send into the cities of Upper Egypt men who will gather to you the sorcerers who are in them. Ibn 'Abbas said: The chiefs of the sorcerers were at the farthest cities of Upper Egypt. Al-Qadi related from Ibn 'Abbas that they were seventy sorcerers besides their chief, and the one who taught them was a Magian man from the people of Nineveh, the town of Yunus, peace be upon him, which is a village near Mosul. I say: this report is problematic, because the Magians are the followers of Zoroaster, and Zoroaster came after the coming of Musa, peace be upon him.

* * *

As for His saying, "Every skilled sorcerer will come to you," there are issues:

The first issue: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "bi-kulli sahhar," and the rest read "bi-kulli sahir." Whoever reads "sahhar" has as his argument that he was described as "alim" (skilled), and describing him thus indicates his perfection in it and his expertise in it; so it was fitting that he be named with the form that indicates intensity in sorcery. Whoever reads "sahir" has as his argument His saying: "And the sorcerers were thrown down" [al-A'raf: 120] and "that we may follow the sorcerers" [al-Shu'ara': 40]. "Sahara" is the plural of sahir, like kataba for katib and fajara for fajir. They also argued with His saying: "They bewitched the eyes of the people" [al-A'raf: 116], and the active participle of "sahharu" is sahir.

The second issue: The ba' in His saying "bi-kulli sahir" may mean "with," and it may be the ba' of transitivity. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: This verse indicates that sorcerers were numerous in that time, and this supports what the theologians say: that God makes the miracle of each prophet of the same kind as what dominated the people of that time. Since sorcery dominated the people of the time of Musa, peace be upon him, his miracle was similar to sorcery, though it differed from sorcery in reality. Since medicine dominated the people of the time of 'Isa, peace be upon him, his miracle was of the kind of medicine. And since eloquence dominated the people of the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), his miracle was necessarily of the kind of eloquence.

* * *

Then God, the Exalted, said: "And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh; they said: 'Surely there will be a reward for us if we are the victors.'" In it are issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hafs, from 'Asim, read "inna lana la-ajran" with a kasra on the alif, as a statement. The rest read it as a question. Then they differed: Abu 'Amr read it with a long hamza according to his principle, and the rest with two hamzas. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The interrogative is better in this place, because they wanted to know whether there would be a reward for them or not, and they were confident that the reward was theirs. The consensus of them in Surat al-Shu'ara' on the hamza for the interrogative strengthens this.

The argument of Nafi' and Ibn Kathir is that they intended the interrogative hamza, but they deleted it from the pronunciation, and the interrogative hamza may be deleted from the pronunciation while remaining in meaning, as in His saying: "And is this a favour with which you reproach me?" [al-Shu'ara': 22], where many people hold that its meaning is "awa-tilka" (is that...?) with the interrogative, and as in His saying: "This is my Lord" [al-An'am: 78], the implied meaning being "Is this my Lord?" It was also said: The intent is that the sorcerers established for themselves a great reward, because they said: "We must have a reward," and the indefiniteness is for magnification, like the saying of the Arabs: "Indeed he has camels (la-ibilan)" and "indeed he has sheep (la-ghanaman)," intending abundance.

The second issue: One might say: why was it not said: "And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh and said"?

Its answer: It is on the assumption of a questioner who asked: "What did they say when they came to him?" So he was answered with His saying: "They said: 'Surely there will be a reward for us,'" meaning a payment for victory.

He meant: I will not limit you to the reward, but I will add to it, and that addition is that I will make you among those brought near to me. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 115–119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw or we will be the throwers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw." So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people, terrified them, and produced a great magic.﴾ ﴿And We revealed to Moses, "Throw your staff," and at once it swallowed up what they had falsely produced.﴾ ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and turned back humbled.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

Issue 1: Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said, regarding the "chapter of amma and imma": if you are commanding, forbidding or informing, it is pronounced with a fatha; if you are making a condition, expressing doubt or giving an option, it is pronounced with a kasra. In the fatha case you say: "As for Allah, worship Him; as for wine, do not drink it; as for Zayd, he has gone out."

As for the second type, you say when making a condition: "Imma tu'ti Zaydan fa-innahu yashkuruka" ("If you give Zayd, he will thank you"). Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So if you encounter them in war, then scatter [those behind them]﴾ [al-Anfal: 57]. And you say in expressing doubt: "I do not know who stood up: imma Zayd wa-imma 'Amr" ("either Zayd or 'Amr"). And you say in giving an option: "I have a house in Kufa, so either (imma) I will live in it, or (imma) I will sell it."

The difference between "imma" when it comes for doubt and "aw" (or) is that when you say: "Zayd or 'Amr came to me," it may be that you built your speech on certainty, then doubt overtook you and you said: "or 'Amr," so the doubt came to apply to both of them. The first of the two nouns with "aw" may be such that silence upon it is good, then doubt arises and you add the other noun to correct yourself. Do you not see that you say: "Your brother came," and you stop, then you doubt and say: "or your father?" But when you mention "imma," you are building your speech from the very beginning on doubt, and it is not permissible to say: "You struck imma 'Abd Allah," and stop.

As for the insertion of "an" in His saying ﴿imma an tulqiya﴾ and its omission in His saying ﴿imma yu'adhdhibuhum wa-imma yatubu 'alayhim﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106], al-Farra' said: "'An' has been inserted after 'imma' in this verse because it stands in the position of a command to choose, and it is in the accusative position, like the speaker's saying: 'Choose this or that.' It is as if they said: 'Choose that you throw or that we throw.' His saying ﴿imma yu'adhdhibuhum wa-imma yatubu 'alayhim﴾ contains no command to choose, do you not see that a command is not fitting here? For this reason 'an' is not in it. And Allah knows best."

Issue 2: His saying ﴿imma an tulqiya﴾ means his staff, and ﴿wa-imma an nakuna nahnu al-mulqin﴾ means: what is with us of ropes and staffs. So the object of the throwing is omitted. In the verse there is another subtle point: that the people observed good manners, in that they put Moses, peace be upon him, first in the mention. The people of Sufism said: when they observed this manners, Allah, may He be exalted, granted them faith by the blessing of observing this manners. Then they mentioned what indicates their desire that the initiation of the throwing be from their side, which is their saying ﴿wa-imma an nakuna nahnu al-mulqin﴾, because they mentioned the attached pronoun and emphasised it with the detached pronoun, and made the predicate definite rather than indefinite.

Know that when the people observed manners at first and showed what indicates their desire to begin with the throwing, Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Throw what you are going to throw.﴾ And there is a question: their throwing their ropes and staffs is an opposition to the miracle with magic, and that is disbelief, and commanding disbelief is disbelief. Since this is so, how is it permissible for Moses, peace be upon him, to say: "Throw"?

The answer to this is in several respects:

First: He, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded them only on condition that they know in their act that it would be true. If it was not so, there is no command there, like the saying of one of us to another: "Give me water from the jug." This speech is only a command on condition that water is in the jug. As for when there is no water in it, there is no command at all. Likewise here.

Second: The people had come only to throw those ropes and staffs, and Moses, peace be upon him, knew that they must do that, and the choice concerned only the precedence and the delay. At that point he permitted them to go first, out of contempt for their affair, indifference to them, and confidence in what Allah, may He be exalted, had promised him of support and strength, and that a miracle is never overcome by magic.

Third: He, peace and blessings be upon him, wished to nullify what they had brought of magic, and its nullification was possible only through their proceeding to display it. So he permitted them to bring that magic, so that he could proceed to nullify it. An example of this is that whoever wishes to hear the doubt of a heretic in order to answer it and expose its weakness and collapse, says to him: "Go on, say it, mention it, and exaggerate in stating it." His purpose from that is that when he answers it after this exaggeration,

Page 166

its weakness and collapse will become apparent to everyone. So it is here. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾. Those who hold that magic is pure deception have used this as evidence. The judge (al-Qadi) said: If magic were real, they would have bewitched their hearts, not their eyes; so it is established that what is meant is that they imagined wondrous states although the matter in reality was not in accordance with what they imagined. Al-Wahidi said: Rather, what is meant is: they bewitched the eyes of the people, that is, they turned them away from the soundness of their perception through those deceptions. It was said: they brought ropes and staffs, smeared those ropes with mercury, and put mercury inside those staffs; when the heat of the sun affected them, they moved and twisted around one another, and they were very numerous, so the people imagined that they moved and twisted by their own choice and power.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿and terrified them﴾, the meaning is that the common people feared the movements of those ropes and staffs. Al-Mubarrad said: ﴿istarhabuhum﴾ means "they frightened them," and the sin is extra. Al-Zajjaj said: they sought to produce the fear of the people until the people feared them, and that was by sending a group who called out at the moment of throwing those things: "O people, beware!" This is the "istirhab." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 115–119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw or we will be the throwers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw." So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people, terrified them, and produced a great magic.﴾ ﴿And We revealed to Moses, "Throw your staff," and at once it swallowed up what they had falsely produced.﴾ ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and turned back humbled.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

Issue 1: Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said, regarding the "chapter of amma and imma": if you are commanding, forbidding or informing, it is pronounced with a fatha; if you are making a condition, expressing doubt or giving an option, it is pronounced with a kasra. In the fatha case you say: "As for Allah, worship Him; as for wine, do not drink it; as for Zayd, he has gone out."

As for the second type, you say when making a condition: "Imma tu'ti Zaydan fa-innahu yashkuruka" ("If you give Zayd, he will thank you"). Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So if you encounter them in war, then scatter [those behind them]﴾ [al-Anfal: 57]. And you say in expressing doubt: "I do not know who stood up: imma Zayd wa-imma 'Amr" ("either Zayd or 'Amr"). And you say in giving an option: "I have a house in Kufa, so either (imma) I will live in it, or (imma) I will sell it."

The difference between "imma" when it comes for doubt and "aw" (or) is that when you say: "Zayd or 'Amr came to me," it may be that you built your speech on certainty, then doubt overtook you and you said: "or 'Amr," so the doubt came to apply to both of them. The first of the two nouns with "aw" may be such that silence upon it is good, then doubt arises and you add the other noun to correct yourself. Do you not see that you say: "Your brother came," and you stop, then you doubt and say: "or your father?" But when you mention "imma," you are building your speech from the very beginning on doubt, and it is not permissible to say: "You struck imma 'Abd Allah," and stop.

It is as if they said: 'Choose that you throw or that we throw.' His purpose from that is that when he answers it after this exaggeration,

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 115–119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw or we will be the throwers."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw." So when they threw, they bewitched the eyes of the people, terrified them, and produced a great magic.﴾ ﴿And We revealed to Moses, "Throw your staff," and at once it swallowed up what they had falsely produced.﴾ ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and turned back humbled.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

Issue 1: Al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i said, regarding the "chapter of amma and imma": if you are commanding, forbidding or informing, it is pronounced with a fatha; if you are making a condition, expressing doubt or giving an option, it is pronounced with a kasra. In the fatha case you say: "As for Allah, worship Him; as for wine, do not drink it; as for Zayd, he has gone out."

As for the second type, you say when making a condition: "Imma tu'ti Zaydan fa-innahu yashkuruka" ("If you give Zayd, he will thank you"). Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So if you encounter them in war, then scatter [those behind them]﴾ [al-Anfal: 57]. And you say in expressing doubt: "I do not know who stood up: imma Zayd wa-imma 'Amr" ("either Zayd or 'Amr"). And you say in giving an option: "I have a house in Kufa, so either (imma) I will live in it, or (imma) I will sell it."

The difference between "imma" when it comes for doubt and "aw" (or) is that when you say: "Zayd or 'Amr came to me," it may be that you built your speech on certainty, then doubt overtook you and you said: "or 'Amr," so the doubt came to apply to both of them. The first of the two nouns with "aw" may be such that silence upon it is good, then doubt arises and you add the other noun to correct yourself. Do you not see that you say: "Your brother came," and you stop, then you doubt and say: "or your father?" But when you mention "imma," you are building your speech from the very beginning on doubt, and it is not permissible to say: "You struck imma 'Abd Allah," and stop.

It is as if they said: 'Choose that you throw or that we throw.' His purpose from that is that when he answers it after this exaggeration,

We say: the meaning is that with the establishment of this truth, the substances they had falsified, namely those ropes and staffs, disappeared; at that point the victory became manifest; for this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they were overcome there﴾, for there is no victory more evident than that; ﴿and turned back humbled﴾, for there is no humiliation or abasement greater for the one in falsehood than the manifestation of the invalidity of his claim and his proof in a way in which no trick or doubt is possible at all. Al-Wahidi said: the word "ma" in His saying ﴿wa-batala ma kanu ya'malun﴾ may be in the sense of "alladhi" (that which), so the meaning is: the ropes and staffs with which they practised magic were nullified, that is, they ceased and went away through their disappearance; and it may be in the sense of the verbal noun, as if it were said: "their work was nullified." And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 7, verses 120–122**

[Page 168]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds,"﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

**The first issue:** The exegetes (mufassirun) said: those ropes and staffs were a load for three hundred camels. When Musa's serpent (peace be upon him) swallowed them and became a staff as it had been, some of the magicians said to others: "This is beyond magic; rather, it is a divine matter." Thus they took it as evidence that Musa (peace be upon him) was a truthful prophet sent from Allah, may He be exalted. The theologians (mutakallimun) said: this verse is one of the greatest proofs of the excellence of knowledge. That is because those people were knowledgeable about the reality of magic and aware of its limits. When they found that the miracle of Musa (peace be upon him) went beyond the bounds of magic, they knew that it was one of the divine miracles and not of the kind of human deceptions. Had they not been complete in the knowledge of magic, they would not have been able to make that inference, for they would have said: "Perhaps he is more advanced than us in the knowledge of magic, and so he was able to do what we were unable to do." Thus it is established that they were complete in the knowledge of magic. Because of their perfection in that knowledge, they moved from disbelief to belief. If this is the state of the knowledge of magic, then consider the state of a person's perfection in the knowledge of monotheism (tawhid).

**The second issue:** Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the magicians were cast down prostrate.﴾ They said: this verse indicates that someone other than them cast them down prostrate, and that was none other than Allah, the Lord of the worlds. This shows that the act of the servant is the creation of Allah, may He be exalted. Muqatil said: Allah, may He be exalted, cast them down prostrate.

The Mu'tazila (Mu'tazilah) said: the answer to this is in several respects:

*First:* when they witnessed the great signs and the overpowering miracles, they could not restrain themselves from falling prostrate, so it became as if someone had cast them down.

*Second:* al-Akhfash said: because of the speed with which they prostrated, it became as if someone else had cast them down, since they could not restrain themselves from falling prostrate.

*Third:* the verse does not state that someone cast them down to prostration, but we say that the one who cast them down was themselves.

The answer is: the creator of that motive (da'iyah) in their hearts is Allah, may He be exalted. Otherwise, in creating that firm motive, they would have needed another motive, and this would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. Furthermore, the basic capacity (qudrah) together with that firm motive becomes necessitating (mujibah) for the act. The creator of that necessitating cause is Allah, may He be exalted. Thus that act and effect are ascribed to Allah, may He be exalted. And Allah knows best.

**The third issue:** He, may He be exalted, first mentioned that they became prostrate, and then after that mentioned that they said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds.﴾ So what is the benefit of this, given that belief must precede prostration? The answer to this has several aspects:

*First:* when they attained knowledge, they prostrated to Allah, may He be exalted, immediately, and made that prostration a thanks to Allah for granting them knowledge and faith, and also a sign of their turning from disbelief to belief, and a display of humility and submission before Allah, may He be exalted. So it is as if they made that single prostration a sign of these three matters together.

*Second:* it is not far-fetched that when they went to prostrate, they said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds.﴾ On this interpretation, the question is resolved. The correct view is the first.

**The fourth issue:** The people of ta'lim (the Ta'limiyya) cited this verse, saying: the evidence that knowledge of Allah is not attained except through the statement of the Prophet is that those magicians, when they said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ their faith was not complete; then when they said: ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun,﴾ their faith was complete. This indicates our view.

The scholars answered this: when they said: ﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ Pharaoh said to them: "Do you mean me?" Then when they said: ﴿the Lord of Musa,﴾ he said: "Do you mean me, since I am the one who raised Musa?" Then when they said: ﴿and Harun,﴾ the doubt was removed, and everyone knew that they had rejected Pharaoh and believed in the God of the heavens.

It was said: the reason He singled out the two of them for mention, after their inclusion in the phrase "the worlds," is that the implied meaning is: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the one to whom Musa and Harun called to faith."

It was also said: He singled them out for mention as an honour and a mark of distinction, like His saying: ﴿And His angels and His messengers and Jibril and Mika'il﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 123–126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Pharaoh said, "You have believed in Him before I give you permission. Indeed, this is a scheme you have plotted in the city to drive its people out from it. But you will come to know.﴾ ﴿Surely I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all.﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾ ﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims."﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Ḥafṣ, read ﴿amintum﴾ with a single hamzah in the form of a statement, and likewise in Ṭā Hā and al-Shuʿarāʾ. ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abū Bakr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, read ﴿a-amintum﴾ with two hamzahs throughout the Qur'an, and the rest read with a single extended hamzah throughout it, in the form of a question. Al-Farrāʾ said: As for the reading of Ḥafṣ, ﴿amintum﴾, in the form of a statement without extension, its meaning is that He informs them of their belief in a manner of rebuke and disapproval of them. As for the reading with two hamzahs, its origin is ﴿a-amintum﴾, on the pattern of ʾafʿaltum.

The second issue: Know that when Pharaoh saw that the most knowledgeable of people in magic had acknowledged the prophethood of Mūsā, peace be upon him, in the presence of the great gathering, he feared that this would become a strong proof among his people for the validity of Mūsā's prophethood, so he immediately cast two kinds of doubt into the ears of the common people, so that this doubt would prevent the people from believing in the validity of Mūsā's prophethood, peace be upon him.

The first doubt: His saying, ﴿Indeed, this is a scheme you have plotted in the city.﴾ The meaning is: the belief of these people in Mūsā is not due to the strength of the evidence, but because they had colluded with Mūsā that if such and such happens, then we will believe in you and acknowledge your prophethood. Thus this belief came about through this means.

The second doubt: The aim of Mūsā and the magicians in what they colluded upon was to drive the people out of the city and to overthrow their rule. It is known to all rational people that leaving one's homeland and familiar blessings is among the most difficult of matters. So the accursed Pharaoh combined the two doubts, and no stronger than these two can be found in this domain. Muḥammad ibn Jarīr narrated, from al-Suddī, in a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd and other Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, that Mūsā and the chief of the magicians met, and Mūsā, peace be upon him, said: "Tell me, if I defeat you, will you believe in me and bear witness that what I have brought is the truth?" The magician said: "I will surely bring tomorrow a magic that no magic can overcome. By Allah, if you defeat me, I will surely believe in you." Pharaoh was watching them both and hearing their words. So this is the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, this is a scheme you have plotted.﴾ Know that this may have actually occurred, and it may also be that Pharaoh uttered this statement in the midst of the crowd so that it would divert the common people from believing in the prophethood of Mūsā, peace be upon him. Al-Qāḍī said: His saying, ﴿before I give you permission﴾, is evidence of the contradiction of Pharaoh in claiming divinity, for if he were a god he would not permit them to believe in Him while he calls them to the divinity of another. Then he said: This is from the abandonment by Allah, exalted is He, which manifests upon the falsifiers.

As for his saying, ﴿but you will come to know﴾, there is no doubt that it is the beginning of a threat. Then he did not confine himself to this general threat, but explained it, saying: ﴿Surely I will cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, then I will crucify you all.﴾ Cutting off the hand and foot on opposite sides is a well-known meaning: that he cut them from two different directions, either the right hand and the left foot, or the left hand and the right foot. As for crucifixion, it is well known. Thus he threatened them with these two great matters. They differed over whether this actually took place, and there is nothing in the verse that indicates either of the two matters. Some argued for its occurrence with several points:

The first: He, exalted is He, related about the chiefs of Pharaoh's people that they said to him: ﴿Will you leave Mūsā and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ Had he left those magicians and his people alive and not killed them, He would have mentioned them as well, and would have warned them against the corruption arising from them. It may be answered that they entered under his people, so there is no reason to single them out for mention.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, relating from them: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾, indicates that a severe, great affliction had befallen them, to the point that they asked Allah, exalted is He, to make them patient in it. It may be answered that they asked Allah, exalted is He, for patience in faith and for not paying heed to his threat.

The third: What is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that he did this, and cut their hands and feet on opposite sides. This is the more apparent, as an exaggeration on his part in warning the people against accepting the religion of Mūsā, peace be upon him. Others said: it did not occur from Pharaoh at all, but Allah, exalted is He, answered their supplication in their saying: ﴿and cause us to die as Muslims﴾, because they asked Him, exalted is He, that their death be from Him and not by this killing and cutting. This inference is close.

Then Allah, exalted is He, related from the people what is not permissible to occur from a believer in the face of this threat, the best of it being their saying to Pharaoh: ﴿And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us.﴾ They thereby made clear that what came from them does not necessitate a threat or the infliction of retribution upon them, but rather requires the opposite of that, namely that he emulate them in acknowledging the truth and avoiding falsehood when proof and evidence become manifest. It is said: "naqamtu anqimu" when you exaggerate in disliking a thing. This has already passed at His saying: ﴿Say, "O People of the Book, do you resent us?"﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 59]. Ibn ʿAbbās said: He means: We have committed no sin for which you punish us, except that we believed in the signs of our Lord. The intended meaning is the overwhelming miracles brought by Mūsā, peace be upon him, which none can produce except Allah, exalted is He.

Then they said: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience.﴾ The meaning of al-ifrāgh in language is pouring. It is said: "dirhamun mufraghun" when it is poured into its mould and is not struck. Its origin is from pouring out a vessel, which is pouring out all that is in it until the vessel is empty, and it comes from emptiness (farāgh). So it was used for patience by way of likening it to the state of emptying a vessel. Mujāhid said: The meaning is: pour upon us patience at the time of crucifixion and cutting. In the verse there are several benefits:

The first benefit: ﴿pour upon us patience﴾ is more complete than saying "send down upon us patience", because we have mentioned that pouring out a vessel is emptying what is in it entirely, so it is as though they asked Allah for all patience, not part of it.

The second benefit: His saying ﴿patience﴾ is mentioned in the indefinite form, and that indicates perfection and completeness, meaning complete, full patience, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96], meaning for a complete, full life.

The third benefit: that this patience is from their side and from their deeds, and then they asked it of Allah, exalted is He, and this indicates that the act of the servant does not come about except by Allah's creation and decree. Al-Qāḍī said: They only asked Him, exalted is He, for the graces that would call them to steadfastness and patience, and that is well known in supplications.

The answer: This is a departure from the apparent meaning, and moreover the evidence rejects it, because an act does not come about except upon the arising of a decisive motive, and the arising of that motive is only from Allah, mighty and majestic, so the whole is from Allah, exalted is He.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿and cause us to die as Muslims﴾, its meaning is: cause us to die upon the true religion that Mūsā, peace be upon him, brought. Concerning it there are two issues:

The first issue: Our companions argued that faith and submission do not come about except by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, and the manner of inference from it is clear. The Muʿtazilah interpret it as the provision of graces, and the discussion of that has already been known from what preceded.

The second issue: Al-Qāḍī argued from this verse that faith and submission are one and the same, saying: They first said: ﴿We believed in the signs of our Lord﴾, then they said secondly: ﴿and cause us to die as Muslims﴾. So it must be that this submission is that faith, and this indicates that each of them is the other. And Allah knows best.

They differed over whether this actually took place, and there is nothing in the verse that indicates either of the two matters. Some argued for its occurrence with several points:

The first: He, exalted is He, related about the chiefs of Pharaoh's people that they said to him: ﴿Will you leave Mūsā and his people to cause corruption in the land?﴾ Had he left those magicians and his people alive and not killed them, He would have mentioned them as well, and would have warned them against the corruption arising from them. It may be answered that they entered under his people, so there is no reason to single them out for mention.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, relating from them: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾, indicates that a severe, great affliction had befallen them, to the point that they asked Allah, exalted is He, to make them patient in it. It may be answered that they asked Allah, exalted is He, for patience in faith and for not paying heed to his threat.

The third: What is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that he did this, and cut their hands and feet on opposite sides. This is the more apparent, as an exaggeration on his part in warning the people against accepting the religion of Mūsā, peace be upon him.
