Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 127–128:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and to abandon you and your gods?" He said: "We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we are certainly dominant over them."﴾ ﴿Moses said to his people: "Seek help in God and be patient. Indeed the earth belongs to God; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever of His servants He wills, and the good outcome is for the God-fearing."﴾

Know that after this event occurred, Pharaoh did not confront Moses, nor seize him, nor imprison him; rather he let him go. So his people said: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land?﴾

And know that Pharaoh, whenever he saw Moses, feared him with the utmost fear. For this reason he did not confront him. However, his people did not know this, so they urged him to seize and imprison him. His saying ﴿to spread corruption in the land﴾ means: to corrupt for the people their religion which they followed; and if they corrupted their religions for them, they would use that as a means to seize the kingdom.

As for his saying ﴿and to abandon you﴾: the well-known reading is "wa-yadharaka" with a fatha (accusative). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned three possibilities in it:

First: that his saying "wa-yadharaka" is coordinated (ʿatf) with his saying ﴿to spread corruption﴾, because if they (Moses' people) were left and not prevented, this would lead to his abandoning and the abandoning of his gods; so it is as if they were left for that reason.

Second: that it is an answer to the interrogative with the waw (wa-), just as it is answered with the fa' (fa-), like the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"Was I not your neighbor, and would there not be between me and you affection and brotherhood?"

The implied meaning is: "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land, so that he abandons you and your gods?" Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Could it be from you that you leave Moses, and that Moses abandon you?"

Third: that it is in the accusative by the implied "an" (an): its estimate is, "Will you leave Moses and his people so that they spread corruption, and that he abandon you and your gods?" The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was also read "wa-yadharuka" with the nominative, coordinated with "atadharu" in the sense of "atadharuhu," and "wa-yadharuka," meaning "proceed against him," and this would be a resumed (mustaʾnaf) sentence or a circumstantial clause (hal), in the sense of: "Will you leave him while he abandons you and your gods?" Al-Hasan read "wa-yadharka" with the jazm (apocopate), and Anas read "wa-nadharaka" with the nun and the accusative, meaning: he diverts us from your worship, so we abandon it.

* * *

As for his saying ﴿and your gods﴾: Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ibn ʿUmar used to reject the common reading and would read "ilahataka" (your worship), saying: Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship. Ibn ʿAbbas said: as for the common reading "wa-alihataka," the intended meaning is the plural of ilah (god). On this reckoning, they have differed regarding it. It was said: Pharaoh had set up small idols for his people and commanded them to worship them, and said: "I am your Lord, the Most High, and the Lord of these idols"; this is his saying ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh used to worship idols. I say: What occurs to my mind is that if we say Pharaoh was not of complete reason, it would not be consistent with the wisdom of God the Exalted to send a messenger to him; and if he was rational, it would not be permissible for him to believe in himself that he was the creator of the heavens and the earth, and it would not be permissible for a great multitude of rational people to believe that about him, because its falsehood is known by the necessity of reason. Rather, the closer view is to say that he was a materialist (dahri) who denied the existence of the Maker, and he used to say: the regulator of this lower world is the stars; and as for the one who benefits the creation in this world and nurtures that group and sustains them, it is himself. So his saying ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ means: your nurturer, your benefactor, and your provider. And his saying ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38] means: I know of no one for you whose worship is obligatory upon you except me. If that was his doctrine, it is not far-fetched to say that he had taken idols in the forms of the stars, worshipped them, and drew near to them according to the religion of the star-worshippers. On this reckoning, there is no impediment to taking his exalted saying ﴿and your gods﴾ in its apparent sense. This is what I have on this matter, and God knows best.

Know that under all the aspects and possibilities, the people intended by mentioning this speech to incite Pharaoh to seize Moses, peace be upon him, and imprison him, and to inflict all kinds of punishment upon him. At this point Pharaoh did not mention the real state of affairs, which is that he was afraid of Moses, peace be upon him, but he said: ﴿We will kill their sons and spare their women, and we are certainly dominant over them.﴾ And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "sanaqtulu" with a fatha on the nun and with lightening (takhfif), while the rest read with a damma on the nun and with shadda (tashdid), for multiplication, meaning the sons of the Children of Israel and whoever believed in Moses, peace be upon him.

The second issue: Moses, peace be upon him, could cause corruption only through the clan and the faction. So we strive to reduce his clan and his faction, and that is by killing the sons of the Children of Israel and sparing their women. Then he explained that he was capable of that by his saying ﴿and we are certainly dominant over them.﴾ The intent of this is the abandonment of Moses and his people, not from incapacity or fear; and if he had intended to strike, he would have been able to. It is as if he gives his people the impression that he did not imprison or prevent him only because he paid him no heed and did not fear him. The exegetes differed: some said he used to do this as he had done at the beginning, at the birth of Moses; others said rather that he was prevented from it. The exegetes agreed that this threat occurred at a time other than the first time.

Then God, exalted is He, relates that Moses, peace be upon him, said to his people: ﴿Seek help in God and be patient.﴾ This indicates that what the chiefs said to Pharaoh, and what Pharaoh said to them, had reached Moses, peace be upon him, and he learned of it. At that point he said to his people: ﴿Seek help in God and be patient; indeed the earth belongs to God; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever of His servants He wills, and the good outcome is for the God-fearing.﴾ Here he commanded them two things and gave them two glad tidings.

As for the two things Moses, peace be upon him, commanded:

The first: seeking help in God, exalted is He.

The second: patience under God's trial.

He commanded them first to seek help in God because whoever knows that there is no governor in the world except God, exalted is He, his heart is expanded by the light of knowledge of God, exalted is He; and then the various kinds of trial become easy for him. Also, when a trial descends, he sees that it has occurred by the decree and measure of God, exalted is He, and his readiness by witnessing God's decree lightens for him the various kinds of trial.

As for the two glad tidings he gave:

The first: his saying ﴿indeed the earth belongs to God; He gives it as an inheritance to whomever of His servants He wills.﴾ This is Moses, peace be upon him, holding out hope to his people that God, exalted is He, would give them the land of Pharaoh as an inheritance after destroying him; and that is the meaning of inheritance, which is the transfer of a thing to a successor after a predecessor.

The second: his saying ﴿and the good outcome is for the God-fearing.﴾ It was said: the intent is the affair of the Hereafter only; it was said: the intent is the affair of this world only, namely victory, triumph, and support over enemies; and it was said: the intent is both matters together.

His saying ﴿for the God-fearing﴾ is an indication that whoever fears God, exalted is He, and is wary of Him, God helps him in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 127–128:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said: "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land and to abandon you and your gods?" Know that after this event occurred, Pharaoh did not confront Moses, nor seize him, nor imprison him; rather he let him go. So his people said: ﴿Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land?﴾

And know that Pharaoh, whenever he saw Moses, feared him with the utmost fear. For this reason he did not confront him. However, his people did not know this, so they urged him to seize and imprison him. His saying ﴿to spread corruption in the land﴾ means: to corrupt for the people their religion which they followed; and if they corrupted their religions for them, they would use that as a means to seize the kingdom.

As for his saying ﴿and to abandon you﴾: the well-known reading is "wa-yadharaka" with a fatha (accusative). The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) mentioned three possibilities in it:

First: that his saying "wa-yadharaka" is coordinated (ʿatf) with his saying ﴿to spread corruption﴾, because if they (Moses' people) were left and not prevented, this would lead to his abandoning and the abandoning of his gods; so it is as if they were left for that reason.

Second: that it is an answer to the interrogative with the waw (wa-), just as it is answered with the fa' (fa-), like the verse of al-Hutay'a:

"Was I not your neighbor, and would there not be between me and you affection and brotherhood?"

The implied meaning is: "Will you leave Moses and his people to spread corruption in the land, so that he abandons you and your gods?" Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "Could it be from you that you leave Moses, and that Moses abandon you?"

Third: that it is in the accusative by the implied "an" (an): its estimate is, "Will you leave Moses and his people so that they spread corruption, and that he abandon you and your gods?" The author of al-Kashshaf said: it was also read "wa-yadharuka" with the nominative, coordinated with "atadharu" in the sense of "atadharuhu," and "wa-yadharuka," meaning "proceed against him," and this would be a resumed (mustaʾnaf) sentence or a circumstantial clause (hal), in the sense of: "Will you leave him while he abandons you and your gods?" Al-Hasan read "wa-yadharka" with the jazm (apocopate), and Anas read "wa-nadharaka" with the nun and the accusative, meaning: he diverts us from your worship, so we abandon it.

As for his saying ﴿and your gods﴾: Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: Ibn ʿUmar used to reject the common reading and would read "ilahataka" (your worship), saying: Pharaoh was worshipped and did not worship. Ibn ʿAbbas said: as for the common reading "wa-alihataka," the intended meaning is the plural of ilah (god). On this reckoning, they have differed regarding it. It was said: Pharaoh had set up small idols for his people and commanded them to worship them, and said: "I am your Lord, the Most High, and the Lord of these idols"; this is his saying ﴿I am your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 24]. Al-Hasan said: Pharaoh used to worship idols. I say: What occurs to my mind is that if we say Pharaoh was not of complete reason, it would not be consistent with the wisdom of God the Exalted to send a messenger to him; and if he was rational, it would not be permissible for him to believe in himself that he was the creator of the heavens and the earth, and it would not be permissible for a great multitude of rational people to believe that about him, because its falsehood is known by the necessity of reason. **Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 7, verse 129:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said, "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us." He said, "It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and see how you will act."﴾

Know that when the people of Musa (peace be upon him) heard what Fir'awn had mentioned of threat and menace, they were frightened or alarmed, and they said: "We were harmed before you came to us and after you came to us." That is because the Children of Israel, before the coming of Musa (peace be upon him), were oppressed under the control of the accursed Fir'awn. He used to take the jizyah (poll tax) from them, make them work at hard labour, deprive them of comfort and luxury, kill their sons and spare their women. When God, may He be exalted, sent Musa (peace be upon him), their hope of the end of those harms and hardships grew strong. But when they heard that Fir'awn had renewed the threat a second time, their fear and grief increased greatly, and so they said this statement.

If it is said: Does not this saying indicate that they disliked the coming of Musa (peace be upon him), and that this would necessitate their disbelief?

The answer: When Musa (peace be upon him) came, he promised them the removal of those harms, so they assumed that they would be removed immediately. When they saw that they had not been removed, they returned to him to learn the manner of that promise. Musa (peace be upon him) then explained that the promise of their removal does not necessitate their removal at once, and he made clear to them that God, may He be exalted, would fulfil that promise for them at the time He had decreed for it. The upshot is that this was not an aversion to the coming of Musa (peace be upon him) with the message, but a seeking to know the manner of that promise. And God knows best.

Know also that when the people mentioned that, Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿It may be that your Lord...﴾. Sibawayh said: "ʿasā" (it may be; perhaps) expresses hope and apprehension. Al-Zajjaj said: Whatever God, may He be exalted, hopes for is necessarily realised.

One may say: This is weak, because the word "ʿasā" here is not the speech of God, may He be exalted, but rather a report of the speech of Musa (peace be upon him). Nevertheless, we say: such a statement, when it proceeds from a messenger whose prophethood has been established by manifest miracles (upon him blessings and peace), produces strength of soul and removes the brokenness and weakness that had entered it. Thus Musa (peace be upon him) strengthened their hearts with this statement and confirmed the promise for them, so that they would hold fast to patience and abandon blameworthy impatience. Then, by his saying ﴿and see how you will act﴾, he indicated what serves as an exhortation for them to hold fast to obedience to God, may He be exalted.

Know that the word "naẓar" (looking; seeing) may be used to mean the sort of looking that yields knowledge, which is impossible for God. It may be used to mean turning the pupil of the eye toward the thing seen in search of seeing it, which is also impossible for God. It may be used to mean waiting, which is also impossible for God. And it may be used to mean seeing, and the wording here must be taken in this sense. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, He sees that thing through its occurrence from you, because God, may He be exalted, does not requite them for what He knows of them, but only for what actually comes to pass from them.

If it is said: If you take this "naẓar" to mean seeing, a problem arises, because the fa' (then) in His saying ﴿fa-yanẓura﴾ indicates sequence, so God's seeing of those actions would have to come after the actions have occurred, and that would necessitate the coming into being of an attribute of God, may He be exalted.

We say: The connection of God's seeing to that thing is a relation that comes into being, and relations and attributions have no existence in concrete things. Therefore it does not follow that a real attribute came into being in the essence of God, may He be exalted. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 130–131:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We indeed seized the people of Pharaoh with years of drought and shortage of fruits, that perhaps they would take heed.﴾ ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours," and if evil afflicted them, they ascribed their misfortune to Moses and those with him. Unquestionably, their omen is with Allah, but most of them do not know.﴾

Page 175

Know that when Exalted Allah related about Moses, peace be upon him, that he said to his people, ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠ ... ⁠﻿⁠ ﴾, He therefore began here by mentioning what He sent down upon Pharaoh and his people of trials, one state after another, until the matter reached destruction, as a warning to the responsible persons to refrain from disbelief and from clinging to the denial of the messengers, out of fear of these trials descending upon them. So He said: ﴿And We indeed seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Sinin (years) is the plural of al-sanah (year). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: al-sanah has two meanings:

One of them: it is meant as the full year.

The other: it is meant as drought (jadb), which is the opposite of abundance (khisb).

Of what is meant as drought: this verse, and his saying ﷺ: "O Allah, make it upon them as years like the years of Joseph," and the saying of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "We do not fall into the year of sanah." Since al-sanah is intended to mean drought, they derived from it just as they derive from jadb. It is said: asnatu, just as it is said: ajdabu. The poet said:

And the men of Makkah are in drought, emaciated.

Abu Zayd said: Some Arabs say: "These are sinin (years)," and "I saw sinina," so they inflect the nun. Al-Farra' said similarly, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Called me from Najd, for its years ∗∗∗ have played with us, making us grey while making us beardless."

Al-Zajjaj said: al-sinin in the speech of the Arabs means the droughts; it is said: "the sanah touched them," meaning: the drought of the year and the severity of the year.

Having known this, we say: the exegetes said: ﴿We seized the people of Pharaoh with years﴾ means hunger and famine, year after year. So the years (were) for the people of the deserts, ﴿and shortage of fruits﴾ for the people of the towns.

* * *

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿that perhaps they would take heed﴾. Regarding this there are two issues:

The first issue: The apparent meaning of the verse is that Exalted Allah only sent these harms upon them so that they would turn from the way of rebellion and obstinacy to submission and servitude. This is because states of hardship soften the heart and make one desire what is with Allah. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted: ﴿When harm touches you at sea, those whom you call upon vanish except Him﴾ [al-Isra': 67], and His saying: ﴿And when harm touches him, he is one of lengthy supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51].

The second issue: al-Qadi said: this verse indicates that He, Exalted, did this intending that they would be mindful, not that they would persist in the disbelief they were upon.

Al-Wahidi answered this by saying: the words of trial (ibtila') and testing (ikhtibar) have come in the Qur'an, not with the meaning that Exalted Allah tests them, for that is impossible for Allah, Exalted, but with the meaning that He dealt with them in a manner resembling trial and testing. So it is here too. And Allah knows best.

Then Exalted Allah explained that when those trials descended upon them, they would proceed to what increases their disbelief and disobedience. So He said: ﴿But when good came to them, they said, "This is ours."﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: By "good" He means the pasture, abundance, fruits, livestock, expansion in provision, well-being and safety. And ﴿they said, "This is ours"﴾ means: we deserve it by the customary course of our abundant blessings and wide provisions; and they did not know that it was from Allah, so that they would thank Him for it and fulfil the right of the blessing in it. And His saying: ﴿And if evil afflicts them﴾

Page 176

means drought, famine, sickness, harm and calamity. ﴿They ascribed their misfortune to Moses and those with him﴾, meaning they regarded him as a bringer of ill omen, and said: this evil has only befallen us through the ill omen of Moses and his people. And tatayyur is tasha'um (ill omen) according to the saying of all the exegetes. His saying ﴿yattayyaru﴾ is originally yatatayyaru; the ta' was assimilated into the ta' ... the ta' was assimilated into the ta' ... [the Arabic here reads: the ta' was assimilated into the ta' (ṭā')], because they both come from one place, the tip of the tongue and the roots of the front teeth. And His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, their omen is with Allah﴾ – regarding al-ta'ir (the omen/bird) there are two views:

The first view: Ibn 'Abbas said: He means their ill omen is with Allah, Exalted, i.e., from Allah's side: the evil came only by the decree and judgment of Allah. Thus al-ta'ir here means ill omen. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted, in the story of Thamud: ﴿They said, "We augur ill from you and from those with you." He said, "Your omen is with Allah"﴾ [al-Naml: 47]. Al-Farra' said: The Jews considered the Prophet ﷺ an ill omen in Madinah, saying: "Our prices have risen and our rains have decreased since he came to us." Al-Azhari said: The ill omen was called ta'ir, tayr and tiyarah, because it was among the customs of the Arabs to take omens from birds and to be deterred by them, and to be pessimistic about their passing, the croaking of their crows, and their turning to the left when they were startled; so they named ill omen tayr, ta'ir and tiyarah, because of their pessimism regarding them.

Then Allah, Exalted, informed through the tongue of His Messenger that their tiyarah is false, so he said: "There is no tiyarah, and no hamah." The Prophet ﷺ used to seek good omen (tafa'ul) and did not take ill omen (tatayyur). The origin of fa'l is a good word, and the Arabs' view on fa'l and tiyarah was one; so the Prophet ﷺ affirmed fa'l and nullified tiyarah. Muhammad al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is necessary to mention a difference between the two categories, and the closer view is that human souls are purer and stronger than the souls of beasts and birds. So the word that passes over the tongue of a human can be used as evidence, unlike the flight of birds and the movements of animals, for their souls are weak, so it is not possible to use them as evidence for anything of the states.

The second view: concerning the interpretation of ta'ir, Abu 'Ubayd said: ﴿Unquestionably, their omen is with Allah﴾ means their portion (hazz). This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "Their omen is only what has been decreed for them and determined for them." The Arabs say: "I divided the wealth among the people and it flew (tayyartuhu) among them, so each of them got his share (sahm)," meaning that share came to him.

Know that according to both views, the meaning is: whatever good or evil befalls them is by the decree and determination of Allah, Exalted. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that all is from Allah, Exalted, because most of creation attribute events to visible causes and sever them from the decree and determination of Allah, Exalted. The truth is that all is from Allah, because every existing thing is either necessarily existent in itself or possibly existent in itself; the Necessary Existent is one, and whatever is other than Him is possibly existent in itself, and the possibly existent in itself does not exist except by the bringing into being of the Necessary Existent in itself. By this route all is from Allah, so attributing them to other than Allah is ignorance of the perfection of Allah, Exalted.

Al-Azhari said: The ill omen was called ta'ir, tayr and tiyarah, because it was among the customs of the Arabs to take omens from birds and to be deterred by them, and to be pessimistic about their passing, the croaking of their crows, and their turning to the left when they were startled; so they named ill omen tayr, ta'ir and tiyarah, because of their pessimism regarding them.

Then Allah, Exalted, informed through the tongue of His Messenger that their tiyarah is false, so he said: "There is no tiyarah, and no hamah." The Prophet ﷺ used to seek good omen (tafa'ul) and did not take ill omen (tatayyur). The origin of fa'l is a good word, and the Arabs' view on fa'l and tiyarah was one; so the Prophet ﷺ affirmed fa'l and nullified tiyarah. Muhammad al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is necessary to mention a difference between the two categories, and the closer view is that human souls are purer and stronger than the souls of beasts and birds. So the word that passes over the tongue of a human can be used as evidence, unlike the flight of birds and the movements of animals, for their souls are weak, so it is not possible to use them as evidence for anything of the states.

The second view: concerning the interpretation of ta'ir, Abu 'Ubayd said: ﴿Unquestionably, their omen is with Allah﴾ means their portion (hazz). This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "Their omen is only what has been decreed for them and determined for them." The Arabs say: "I divided the wealth among the people and it flew (tayyartuhu) among them, so each of them got his share (sahm)," meaning that share came to him.

Know that according to both views, the meaning is: whatever good or evil befalls them is by the decree and determination of Allah, Exalted. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ that all is from Allah, Exalted, because most of creation attribute events to visible causes and sever them from the decree and determination of Allah, Exalted. The truth is that all is from Allah, because every existing thing is either necessarily existent in itself or possibly existent in itself; the Necessary Existent is one, and whatever is other than Him is possibly existent in itself, and the possibly existent in itself does not exist except by the bringing into being of the Necessary Existent in itself. By this route all is from Allah, so attributing them to other than Allah is ignorance of the perfection of Allah, Exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 132–133:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to enchant us with, we will not be believers in you."﴾ ﴿So We sent upon them the flood and the locusts and the lice and the frogs and the blood, as distinct signs; but they were arrogant and were a criminal people.﴾

Page 177
Know that He, exalted is He, related about them in the first verse that, due to their ignorance, they attributed the events of this world not to the decree and destiny of God, exalted is He. Then in this verse He related about them another kind of ignorance and error: that they did not distinguish between miracles and magic, and they considered the whole of the signs, such as the transformation of the staff into a serpent, to be a form of magic. They said to Moses: "We will not accept anything from them at all." In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the word "mahma" (whatever), there are two opinions:

The first: its original form is "ma ma." The first "ma" is the "ma" of conditionality, and the second is the one added for emphasis of the conditional, just as it is added to the other conditional particles, as in their saying: "imma," "mimma," and "kayfama." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So if you overtake them in war﴾ [al-Anfal: 57], and it is like your saying: "in thaqafannahum" (if you overtake them). Then they replaced the alif of the first "ma" with "ha," out of dislike for repeating the word, so it became "mahma." This is the view of al-Khalil and the Basrans.

The second, which is the view of al-Kisa'i: the original is "mah," which carries the meaning of restraint, i.e., "restrain" (ikfuf), and it entered upon the conditional "ma," as if they said: "Restrain whatever sign you bring us, then it is such and such."

The second issue: Ibn 'Abbas said: When the people said to Moses: "Whatever sign you bring us from your Lord, it is for us from the category of magic, and we will not believe in it at all," Moses, peace be upon him, was a stern man, so at that point he invoked God against them, and God answered him, so He sent upon them the flood, continuous night and day, from Saturday to Saturday, until a man among them could not see sun or moon and could not manage to leave his house, and drowning came upon them. They cried out to Pharaoh and sought his help, so he sent to Moses, peace be upon him, and said: "Remove this punishment from us, for Egypt has become one sea. If you remove this punishment, we will believe in you." So God removed the rain from them and sent winds that dried the land, and there came forth from the plants what they had never seen the like of. They said: "This that we dreaded is better for us, but we did not realize it. By God, we will not believe in you, nor will we send the Children of Israel with you." So they broke the covenant. Then God sent upon them the locusts, which ate the plants, and the matter became grave for them until, when they flew, they covered the sun, and some of them fell upon others on the ground to the depth of a cubit, and they ate the plants. The people of Egypt cried out, so Moses, peace be upon him, prayed, and God, exalted is He, sent a wind that carried off the locusts and cast them into the sea. The people of Egypt saw that a remnant of their pasture and crops would suffice them. They said: "What remains is sufficient for us, and we will not believe in you." Then God sent upon them the lice after that, from Saturday to Saturday, and there was left in their land no green twig except that it devoured it. They cried out, and Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord, so God sent upon them a hot wind that burned them, and the wind carried them and cast them into the sea. Still they did not believe. Then God sent upon them the frogs after that, and there came out of the sea like the darkest night, and they fell into the garments and foods, so that a man among them would fall with a cubit's length of frogs upon his head. They cried out to Moses, peace be upon him, and swore by his God: "If you lift this punishment from us, we will surely believe in you." So God, exalted is He, was invoked and He caused the frogs to die, and sent upon them rain which carried them to the sea. Then they showed disbelief and corruption, so God sent upon them blood, and their rivers turned to blood, and they could not get sweet water, while the Children of Israel found sweet, pure water until hardship reached them. They cried out, and Pharaoh and the nobles of his people rode to the rivers of the Children of Israel, and whenever a man of them entered the river and scooped, it became blood in his hand. They remained seven days in humiliation, drinking nothing but blood. Pharaoh said: ﴿"If you remove from us the plague"﴾ to the end of the verse. This is the account accepted by most exegetes, though there are differences among them on many points.

As for the flood, al-Zajjaj said: "The tufan (flood) of anything is that which is abundant and encompassing, enveloping all the people, like a drowning that covers many cities; it is called tufan, and likewise a devastating killing is a tufan, and sudden death is a tufan." Al-Akhfash said: it is fu'lan from al-tawf (circling), because it circles around a thing until it covers it, and he said its singular in analogy is tufana. Al-Mubarrad said: al-tufan is a verbal noun like "al-rujhan" and "al-nuqsan," so there is no need to seek a singular for it.

Having understood this, we say: Most scholars hold that this flood is abundant rain, as we have related from Ibn 'Abbas. 'Ata' related from him that he said: the flood is death. Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, related with his chain a report from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The flood is death." This view is problematic, for if they had died, there would have been no benefit in sending the other kinds of punishment upon them. Rather, if this report were sound, the word "death" would have to be understood as the occurrence of the causes of death, such as heavy rain, great torrents, and the like. As for the locusts, they are well known, and the singular is "jaradah." A "majrud" plant is one whose leaves the locusts have eaten. Al-Lihyani said: "ard jardah" and "majrudah" is land that locusts have licked clean; when locusts strike the crop, it is said "jarada al-zar'" (they stripped the crop). The root of all this is "al-jard," which is taking a thing from another by way of scraping and grinding; from it comes the saying for a garment whose nap has gone: "jard," and "ard jaridah" is land without vegetation. As for the lice, they differed about it. It was said: it is the small locusts without wings, which are the young of locusts. And it is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: there was beside them a reddish dune, and Moses, peace be upon him, struck it with his staff, and it became lice, which fell upon their skins, their hair, the lashes of their eyes, and their eyebrows, and clung to their hides as if it were smallpox. They cried out, shouted, and fled to Moses, and he lifted it from them. They said: "Now we are certain that you are a knowing sorcerer; by the might of Pharaoh, we will never believe in you." Al-Hasan recited "wal-qaml" with a fatha on the qaf and a sukun on the mim, meaning the well-known lice. As for the blood, we have mentioned it. The author of al-Kashshaf related that it was said: God sent upon them nosebleeds. It is also narrated that Moses, peace be upon him, remained among them twenty years after he overcame the magicians, showing them these signs.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿distinct signs﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: ﴿mufassalat﴾ means clear and evident, such that it is not unclear to any sensible person that they are among the signs of God, which none other than Him can bring about.

The second: ﴿mufassalat﴾ means that there was a separation between some of them and others by a time in which their states were tested, and it was observed whether they would accept proof and evidence or persist in opposition and blind imitation. The exegetes said: the punishment would remain upon them from Saturday to Saturday, and between one punishment and the next there was a month. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿distinct signs﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying "ayat" (signs) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

His saying: ﴿so they were arrogant﴾ means arrogant toward the worship of God; ﴿and were a criminal people﴾ persisting in sin and transgression. It is also related that these mentioned kinds of punishment, at the time they occurred, were specific to the people of Pharaoh, and the Children of Israel were safe and at ease from them. There is no doubt that each of them is in itself a miracle, and its being specific to the Copt and not to the Israelite is another miracle.

If someone says: Since God, exalted is He, knew from the state of those peoples that they would not believe in those miracles, what is the benefit in their succession and the showing of many of them? Also, the people of Muhammad ﷺ asked for miracles and were not granted them, so what is the difference?

The answer: As for the view of our companions, God does what He wills and decrees what He desires. As for the view of the Mu'tazilah concerning the preservation of what is best, perhaps He knew from the people of Moses that some of them would believe upon the appearance of those additional miracles, and He knew from the people of Muhammad ﷺ that none of them would increase after the appearance of those manifest miracles except in disbelief and obstinacy. Thus the difference became evident. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 134–135:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the punishment (al-rijz) fell upon them, they said, "O Moses, call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you. If you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you."﴾ ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them at a term which they were to reach, behold, they broke their word.﴾

Know that we mentioned the meaning of al-rijz (punishment) at His saying: ﴿So We sent down upon those who wronged a punishment from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is a term for punishment. Then they differed concerning what is meant by this al-rijz. Some of them said: It is an expression for the five kinds mentioned of the punishment that was descending upon them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "al-rijz" means the plague (al-ta'un), which is the punishment that befell them, by which seventy thousand people of the Copts died in one day, and they were left unburied. Know that the first opinion is stronger, because the word "al-rijz" is a singular noun made definite by the article al-, so it refers to a known antecedent. Here the known antecedent is the five kinds that were mentioned earlier, whereas anything else is doubtful. Therefore, interpreting the word in terms of what is known is better than interpreting it in terms of what is doubtful.

Having understood this, we say: He, exalted is He, explained the abhorrent contradiction in which they were. For at times they denied Moses, peace be upon him, and at other times, in times of hardship, they resorted to him as a nation resorts to its prophet, and asked him to ask his Lord to lift that punishment from them. This implies that they conceded to him that he was a prophet whose supplication is answered. Then, after those hardships passed, they returned to denying him and attacking him, and they proceeded only to demand [a sign] of his magic. From this aspect, it becomes apparent that they contradicted themselves in these statements.

As for His saying, exalted is He, quoting them: ﴿call upon your Lord for us by what He has covenanted with you﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: "ma" in His saying ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ is verbal-masdariyyah (a masdarite particle), and the meaning is: by His covenant with you, which is prophethood. In this "ba'" (by) there are two possibilities:

The first possibility: it is connected to His saying ﴿call upon your Lord for us﴾, and the implied meaning is "call upon [Him] for us," seeking a means to Him through His covenant with you.

The second possibility: this "ba'" is an oath, and its answer is His saying ﴿we will surely believe you﴾, i.e., "We swear by God's covenant with you: ﴿if you remove the punishment from us, we will surely believe you.﴾"

As for His saying: ﴿and we will surely send the Children of Israel with you﴾: they had subjected the Children of Israel to severe toil, so they promised Moses, peace be upon him, in return for his supplication to remove the punishment from them, that they would believe in him, and would release the Children of Israel and send them with him to go with them wherever he wished.

As for His saying: ﴿But when We removed the punishment from them at a term which they were to reach﴾, the meaning is that We did not remove the punishment from them absolutely, nor did We remove the punishment from them in all instances; rather, We removed the punishment from them only until a specified term, and at that term We do not remove the punishment from them but destroy them by it.

As for His saying: ﴿behold, they broke their word﴾, it is the answer to "ma" (lammā), meaning: when We removed it from them, they immediately broke their word, hastened to it, and did not delay it; as soon as We removed it from them, they broke their word.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 136:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them and drowned them in the sea, because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾

Know that the meaning is that He, exalted is He, when He had removed the punishment from them before, many times and repeatedly, and they did not desist from their disbelief and ignorance, then, when they reached the appointed term, took vengeance upon them by destroying them through drowning. In language, intiqam (vengeance) is the removal of blessing through punishment. Al-yamm is the sea. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: al-yamm is the sea whose depth cannot be reached. It is said that it is the deep part of the sea and its main body of water. Its derivation is from tayammum (intending), because those who draw water from it intend it. By His saying, ﴿because they denied Our signs﴾, He, exalted is He, clarified that this vengeance was for that denial. As for His saying, ﴿and they were heedless of them﴾, the scholars differed over the pronoun in "of them" (ʿanha). It is said that it refers to the retribution indicated by His saying, ﴿We took vengeance﴾, and the meaning is: they were heedless of the retribution before its descent. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the signs, and this is the choice of al-Zajjaj. He said: because they did not take heed of the signs that descended upon them.

If it is said: heedlessness is not an act of man and does not occur by his choice, so how does the threat come upon heedlessness?

We say: what is meant by heedlessness here is turning away from the signs and not paying them any attention. They turned away from them until they became like those heedless of them.

If it is said: did they not add to their denial and heedlessness many other sins? So how can the vengeance be for these two and not for others?

We say: the verse does not state that He, exalted is He, took vengeance upon them for these two together, as a proof of the negation of anything else. The verse indicates that what is obligatory regarding the signs is to reflect upon them; therefore He blamed them for being heedless of them, and this indicates that blind imitation (taqlid) is a blameworthy path.

The Almighty said: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth, which We had blessed, and the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel because of their patience; and We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had been making and what they had been building.﴾

Know that Moses, peace be upon him, had told the Children of Israel: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land﴾ [al-A'raf: 129]. Here, when Allah, exalted is He, described the destruction of the people by drowning as a punishment, He described what He did for the believers of good things, namely that He made them inherit their land and their dwellings. So He said: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed﴾

[Page 181]

﴿to inherit the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾. The meaning of that oppression was that he (Pharaoh) would kill their sons, spare their women, impose the jizya (poll tax) on them, and use them in hard labour. The scholars differed over the meaning of ﴿the eastern and western parts of the earth﴾. Some understood it as the eastern and western parts of the land of al-Sham (Syria) and Egypt, because these were the lands under the control of Pharaoh, may Allah curse him. Also, His saying ﴿which We had blessed﴾ means blessed with fertility and abundance of provision, and that is fitting only for the land of al-Sham.

The second view: the intended meaning is the whole earth. This is because from among the Children of Israel came Dawud (David) and Sulayman (Solomon), who ruled the earth, and this indicates that "the earth" here is an ism al-jins (a generic noun, referring to the whole class of earth).

As for His saying ﴿and the fair word of your Lord was fulfilled for the Children of Israel﴾, it has been said: the intended meaning of ﴿the word of your Lord﴾ is His saying: ﴿And We wished to bestow favour upon those who were oppressed in the land﴾ [al-Qasas: 5] up to His saying ﴿what they were fearing﴾ [al-Qasas: 6]. Al-Husna is the feminine of al-Ahsan (the best), and it is an adjective of al-kalima (the word). The meaning of "was fulfilled for the Children of Israel" is: it passed over them and continued, from the saying of people: "tamma 'alayka al-amr" (the matter was completed for you) when it passed over you. It has also been said: the meaning of the fulfilment of the fair word is the carrying out of the promise that had preceded, namely the destruction of their enemy and their being made successors in the land. The carrying out was a completion of the speech, because a promise of something remains like a suspended thing; when the promised thing is realised, then the promise has been fulfilled for you and perfected.

His saying ﴿because of their patience﴾ means: that completion came about only through their patience. This suffices as an exhortation to patience and as an indication that whoever meets trial with impatience, Allah leaves him to it, and whoever meets it with patience and waiting for victory, Allah guarantees him relief.

ʿĀsim, in one transmission, read ﴿وَتَمَّتْ كَلِماتُ رَبِّكَ الحُسْنى﴾ (wa-tammat kalimatu rabbika al-husna, with the plural "kalimat"). A parallel to this is ﴿مِن آياتِ رَبِّهِ الكُبْرى﴾ [al-Najm: 18].

His saying ﴿We destroyed﴾ (wa-dammarna): al-Layth said: al-damar is total destruction. It is said: "dummira al-qawm yudammarun damaran," meaning they were destroyed.

His saying ﴿what Pharaoh and his people had been making﴾: Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means the craft (al-sani'), i.e., what they made.

His saying ﴿and what they had been building﴾: al-Zajjaj said: it is said "ʿarasha yaʿrishu" and "yaʿrushu" when one builds. It has been said: "wa-ma kanu yaʿrishun" refers to the trellised gardens, and from this is His saying: ﴿gardens trellised and untrellised﴾ [al-An'am: 141]. It has also been said: ﴿and what they had been building﴾ means what they raised of towering buildings in the sky, such as the tower of Haman and Pharaoh. The word "yaʿrishun" has been read with a kasra and with a damma (yaʿrishūn and yaʿrushūn), and al-Yazidi mentioned that the kasra is more eloquent. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "It has reached me that some people read ﴿yaghrisun﴾ (they plant), from the planting of trees, and I do not think that is anything but a scribal error by him." This is the last of what Allah, exalted is He, mentioned of the story of Pharaoh and his people and their denial of the signs of Allah, exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 138–139:**

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and they came upon a people devoted to their idols. They said, "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods." He said, "Indeed you are a people who act in ignorance."﴾ ﴿Indeed, these people—what they are engaged in will be destroyed, and what they have been doing is in vain.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, explained the kinds of His blessings upon the Children of Israel, by destroying their enemy and making them inherit their land and homes, He followed this with the greatest blessing, which is that He brought them across the sea in safety. In other surahs, Allah, the Exalted, explained how He led them through the sea in safety, namely by splitting the sea when Musa struck it with his staff and made it dry. Here He explains that when the Children of Israel saw a people devoted to worshipping their idols, they became ignorant, turned back, and said to Musa: ﴿make for us a god⦅ just as they have gods﴾. There is no doubt that these people, after witnessing the dazzling miracles that Allah, the Exalted, displayed through Musa against Pharaoh, and after seeing that He, the Exalted, destroyed Pharaoh and his armies and singled out the Children of Israel with kinds of safety and honor, still uttered this corrupt and false statement, which shows that they were in the utmost ignorance and the extreme of opposition.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾: it is said, "jawaza al-wadiya" when one crosses it and leaves it behind, and "jawaza bi-ghayrihi" means "he caused him to cross." It was also read as "jawwaznā," with the meaning "ajaznā." It is said, "ajaza al-makān" and "jawwazahu," meaning "jazahu" (he crossed it). ﴿Then they came upon a people devoted to their idols﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they persist in them and cling to them. It is said of everyone who clings to something and persists in it: "‘akafa ya‘kifu wa-ya‘kufu," and from this comes the term "mu‘takif" for one who stays in the mosque. Qatada said: those people were from the tribe of Lakhm, and they were settled in the countryside. Ibn Jurayj said: those idols were images of cows, and that was the first explanation of the story of the calf.

Then Allah, the Exalted, relates from them that they ﴿said, "O Musa, make for us a god just as they have gods."﴾ Know that it is impossible for a sensible person to say to Musa: "Make for us a god just as they have gods," meaning a creator and a governor, because what is produced by the making of Musa, and its determination, cannot be a creator of the world and its governor, and whoever doubts that is not of sound intellect. The more likely reading is that they asked Musa, peace be upon him, to designate for them idols and images through which they would draw near to Allah, the Exalted. This is the statement that Allah, the Exalted, related about the worshippers of idols when they said: ﴿We only worship them so that they bring us nearer to Allah in position﴾ [al-Zumar: 3].

Once you know this, someone may ask: why was this statement disbelief? We say: all the prophets, peace be upon them, agreed that worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted, is disbelief, whether one believes that other to be the god of the world or believes that worshipping it brings one closer to Allah, the Exalted, because worship is the utmost of glorification, and the utmost of glorification is fitting only for one from whom comes the utmost of bounty and honor.

If it is asked: did this statement come from all the Children of Israel, or from some of them?

We say: rather from some of them, because with Musa, peace be upon him, were the seventy chosen men, and among them were those who were too exalted for such a false question.

Then Allah, the Exalted, relates that Musa, peace be upon him, answered them, saying: ﴿Indeed you are a people who act in ignorance.﴾ The explanation of this ignorance is what was mentioned: that worship is the utmost of glorification, so it is fitting only for one from whom comes the utmost of bounty, and that is by creating the body, life, desire, power, and intellect, and by creating the things from which one benefits. The one capable of these things is none other than Allah, the Exalted, so worship must be fitting only for Him.

If they say: if their intention in worshipping those idols was to draw near through them to the glorification of Allah, the Exalted, what is the aspect of the ugliness of this worship?

We say: in that case they did not take them as gods at all, but rather they made them like a qiblah (direction of prayer), and that contradicts their saying: ﴿make for us a god just as they have gods.﴾ Know that the "mā" in His saying: ﴿just as they have gods﴾ may be a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle, meaning "as there has been established for them gods," and it may be a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). In their saying "lahum" there is a pronoun referring back to it, and "ālihatun" is an apposition (badal) from that pronoun, its meaning being: "like that which is for them gods."

Then Allah, the Exalted, relates that Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, these people—what they are engaged in will be destroyed.﴾ Al-Layth said: "al-tabār" is destruction. It is said: "tabira al-shay'u yatbaru tabāran," and "al-tatbīr" is annihilation, and from it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and We destroyed with complete destruction﴾ [al-Furqan: 39]. And the broken, crumbling gold is called "al-tibr." So His saying: ﴿what they are engaged in will be destroyed﴾ means: it will be annihilated and ruined. His saying: ﴿and what they have been doing is in vain.﴾ It has been said: "al-butlān" is the non-existence of a thing, either by the non-existence of its essence or by the non-existence of its benefit and purpose. What is meant by the vanity of their action is that no benefit and no averting of harm will return to them from that action. The full explanation of this matter is that the purpose of worship is that persistence in those actions becomes a cause for the firm establishment of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, in the heart, until that soul becomes happy through attaining that knowledge within it. So when a person occupies himself with worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted, his heart becomes attached to other than Allah, and that attachment becomes a cause for the heart's turning away from the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. When this verification becomes clear, it becomes clear that occupying oneself with worshipping other than Allah is destroyed, vain, and lost, and it is a striving toward achieving the opposite of this matter and its contradiction. This is because we have explained that the purpose of worship is the firm establishment of the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, in the heart, and occupying oneself with worshipping other than Allah removes the knowledge of Allah from the heart. Thus this is the opposite of the aim and the contradiction of what is sought. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 140:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has favoured you over the worlds?"﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, related about Musa (peace be upon him) that when they said to him, ﴿"Make for us a god just as they have gods"﴾, he (peace be upon him) mentioned several points in his reply:

The first of them: he passed judgment on them as ignorant, saying: ﴿"Indeed, you are a people who are ignorant."﴾

The second of them: he said: ﴿"Indeed, these people, what they are engaged in will be destroyed."﴾ That is, it is a cause of loss and ruin.

The third of them: he said: ﴿"And what they were doing is worthless."﴾ That is, this laborious activity will benefit them nothing in this world or in the religion.

The fourth of them: what he mentioned in this verse of astonishment at them, in a manner that necessitates denunciation and reproach, so he said: ﴿"Shall I seek for you a god other than Allah, while He has favoured you over the worlds?"﴾ The meaning is: a god is not something that is sought, requested, and taken. Rather, the god is Allah, who is capable of bestowing favours through creation, giving life, and all blessings. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿"while He has favoured you over the worlds"﴾. So this Existent is the god whom creation must worship, so how is it permissible to turn away from worshipping Him to worshipping other than Him?

Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: It is said: "I sought (baghaytu) for so-and-so something, and I sought for him," and He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿"They seek to cause you turmoil"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 47], meaning they seek for you. As for the case of the accusative of His saying (إلهًا) there are two possibilities:

The first: it is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). It is as if it were said: "I seek for you other than Allah as a worshipped one." In this case, the accusative of (غيرَ) is as the direct object.

The second: (إلهًا) is put in the accusative as the direct object, and (غيرَ) is in the accusative as a preposed circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), which if it were postponed would be a descriptive adjective, as you would say: "I seek for you a god other than Allah."

As for His saying: ﴿"while He has favoured you over the worlds"﴾, there are two opinions about it:

The first: the meaning is that He, may He be exalted, favoured them over the worlds of their time.

The second: that He, may He be exalted, singled them out with those overpowering signs, and the like of them was not given to anyone among the worlds, even though others were favoured with the rest of the qualities. An example of this: a man who learned one branch of knowledge, and another who learned many branches of knowledge besides that one. The person with the single branch of knowledge is preferred, by that one branch, over the person with many branches of knowledge; however, the person with many branches of knowledge is, in reality, preferred over the person with the single branch.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 141–142:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾

Know that this verse is explained in Surat al-Baqarah. The benefit of mentioning it in this place is that He, exalted is He, is the One who bestowed upon you this great blessing, so how is it fitting for you to occupy yourselves with worshipping other than Allah, exalted is He? And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr recited "wa'adna" (without an alif), while the rest recited "wa'adna" with an alif, on the pattern of mufa'alah (reciprocal form). The explanation of this recitation has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second issue: It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, promised the Children of Israel while he was in Egypt: if Allah destroys their enemy, he would bring them a Book from Allah containing the explanation of what they should do and what they should abstain from. When Pharaoh was destroyed, Musa asked his Lord for the Book. So this verse is about the manner in which the Torah was sent down. Know that He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And [recall] when We appointed for Musa forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51], and the detail of those forty is mentioned in this verse.

If it is said: What is the wisdom here in mentioning the thirty and then completing them with ten? Also, His saying: ﴿so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ is words devoid of benefit, since everyone knows that thirty together with ten makes forty.

We say: As for the answer to the first question, it is from several aspects:

The first aspect: He, exalted is He, commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to fast thirty days, and it was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty, he disliked the odor of his mouth, so he used the siwak (tooth-stick). The angels said: "We used to smell the fragrance of musk from your mouth, and you spoiled it with the siwak." Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Do you not know that the odor of the mouth of one who fasts is more fragrant to Me than the scent of musk?" So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to add ten days to them from Dhu al-Hijjah for this reason.

The second aspect regarding the benefit of this distinction: Allah commanded him to fast thirty days and to do in them what brings him near to Allah, exalted is He. Then the Torah was sent down to him in the remaining ten, and He also spoke with him in it. This is the benefit of dividing the forty into thirty and ten.

The third aspect: what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha indicates that Musa, peace be upon him, hastened to his Lord's appointment before his people. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?" He said: "They are close upon my trail."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83]. So it is permissible that Musa came to the mount at the completion of the thirty; then, when Allah informed him of the news of his people with the Samiri, he returned to his people before the completion of what Allah had promised him, then he went back to the appointment for another ten, and so the forty nights were completed.

The fourth aspect: Some of them said: there is no impediment that the first promise was attended by Musa alone, and the second promise was attended by the chosen ones with him so that they might hear the speech of Allah, exalted is He. Thus the promise differed according to the differing circumstances of those present. And Allah knows best.

As for the answer to the second question: He, exalted is He, only said: ﴿forty nights﴾ to remove the suspicion that those ten were part of the thirty; for it could be understood as "We completed it with ten of the thirty," as if it had been twenty and then He completed it with ten, making it thirty. So He removed this misconception.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The difference between *al-miqat* (appointed time) and *al-waqt* (time) is that *al-miqat* is that in which some action has been determined, whereas *al-waqt* is a time for something by a prior determination.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿forty nights﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: it was completed, reaching this number.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun﴾, the word "Harun" is an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan) to "his brother," and it was also read with a *damma* as a vocative. ﴿Take my place among my people﴾: be my successor among them. "And act righteously" means: be a reformer, or "act righteously" in what must be set right of the affairs of the Children of Israel, and whoever among them calls you to corruption, do not follow him nor obey him.

If it is said: Harun was Musa's partner in prophethood, so how did he make him a successor to himself? For the partner of a person is higher in status than his successor, and transferring a person from the higher rank to the lower would be a humiliation.

We say: Although the matter is as you have mentioned, Musa, peace be upon him, was nonetheless the origin of that prophethood.

If it is said: Since Harun was a prophet, and a prophet does only what is right, how then did he instruct him to act righteously?

We say: The purpose of this command is emphasis, like His saying: ﴿but that my heart may be assured﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 141–142:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a tremendous trial from your Lord.﴾

Know that this verse is explained in Surat al-Baqarah. The benefit of mentioning it in this place is that He, exalted is He, is the One who bestowed upon you this great blessing, so how is it fitting for you to occupy yourselves with worshipping other than Allah, exalted is He? And Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights. And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾

On this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu 'Amr recited "wa'adna" (without an alif), while the rest recited "wa'adna" with an alif, on the pattern of mufa'alah (reciprocal form). The explanation of this recitation has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The second issue: It is related that Musa, peace be upon him, promised the Children of Israel while he was in Egypt: if Allah destroys their enemy, he would bring them a Book from Allah containing the explanation of what they should do and what they should abstain from. When Pharaoh was destroyed, Musa asked his Lord for the Book. So this verse is about the manner in which the Torah was sent down. Know that He, exalted is He, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And [recall] when We appointed for Musa forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 51], and the detail of those forty is mentioned in this verse.

If it is said: What is the wisdom here in mentioning the thirty and then completing them with ten? Also, His saying: ﴿so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾ is words devoid of benefit, since everyone knows that thirty together with ten makes forty.

We say: As for the answer to the first question, it is from several aspects:

The first aspect: He, exalted is He, commanded Musa, peace be upon him, to fast thirty days, and it was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah. When he completed the thirty, he disliked the odor of his mouth, so he used the siwak (tooth-stick). The angels said: "We used to smell the fragrance of musk from your mouth, and you spoiled it with the siwak." Allah, exalted is He, revealed to him: "Do you not know that the odor of the mouth of one who fasts is more fragrant to Me than the scent of musk?" So Allah, exalted is He, commanded him to add ten days to them from Dhu al-Hijjah for this reason.

The second aspect regarding the benefit of this distinction: Allah commanded him to fast thirty days and to do in them what brings him near to Allah, exalted is He. Then the Torah was sent down to him in the remaining ten, and He also spoke with him in it. This is the benefit of dividing the forty into thirty and ten.

The third aspect: what Abu Muslim al-Isfahani mentioned in Surat Ta-Ha indicates that Musa, peace be upon him, hastened to his Lord's appointment before his people. The evidence for this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?" He said: "They are close upon my trail."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 83]. So it is permissible that Musa came to the mount at the completion of the thirty; then, when Allah informed him of the news of his people with the Samiri, he returned to his people before the completion of what Allah had promised him, then he went back to the appointment for another ten, and so the forty nights were completed.

The fourth aspect: Some of them said: there is no impediment that the first promise was attended by Musa alone, and the second promise was attended by the chosen ones with him so that they might hear the speech of Allah, exalted is He. Thus the promise differed according to the differing circumstances of those present. And Allah knows best.

As for the answer to the second question: He, exalted is He, only said: ﴿forty nights﴾ to remove the suspicion that those ten were part of the thirty; for it could be understood as "We completed it with ten of the thirty," as if it had been twenty and then He completed it with ten, making it thirty. So He removed this misconception.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights﴾, there are two discussions:

The first discussion: The difference between *al-miqat* (appointed time) and *al-waqt* (time) is that *al-miqat* is that in which some action has been determined, whereas *al-waqt* is a time for something by a prior determination.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿forty nights﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: it was completed, reaching this number.

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿And Musa said to his brother Harun﴾, the word "Harun" is an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan) to "his brother," and it was also read with a *damma* as a vocative. ﴿Take my place among my people﴾: be my successor among them. "And act righteously" means: be a reformer, or "act righteously" in what must be set right of the affairs of the Children of Israel, and whoever among them calls you to corruption, do not follow him nor obey him.

If it is said: Harun was Musa's partner in prophethood, so how did he make him a successor to himself? For the partner of a person is higher in status than his successor, and transferring a person from the higher rank to the lower would be a humiliation.

We say: Although the matter is as you have mentioned, Musa, peace be upon him, was nonetheless the origin of that prophethood.

If it is said: Since Harun was a prophet, and a prophet does only what is right, how then did he instruct him to act righteously?

We say: The purpose of this command is emphasis, like His saying: ﴿but that my heart may be assured﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 143 (part 1 of 3):**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me [Yourself], that I may look at You." He said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me." But when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Moses fell unconscious. And when he recovered, he said, "Glory be to You! I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers."﴾.

[Page 186]

Know that He, exalted is He, has explained the benefit for which Moses, peace be upon him, attended the appointed time, namely that his Lord spoke to him. The verse contains noble and lofty issues from the divine sciences.

**The first issue:** The verse indicates that He, exalted is He, spoke to Moses, peace be upon him. People differ concerning the speech of God (kalam Allah). Some say: His speech is an expression for the composed and arranged letters. Others say: His speech is a real attribute distinct from the letters and sounds.

As for those who hold the first view, the intelligent scholars agree that it must be originated, coming into existence after it was not. The Hanabila and the Hashwiyya claim that speech composed of letters and sounds is eternal. This view is too base for an intelligent person to give any attention to. That is because I once said: He, exalted is He, either speaks with these letters all together, or in succession and sequence. The first is false, because these heard and understood words are only understood if their letters follow one another. But if their letters existed all at once, that would not be meaningful at all. The second necessitates that it is originated, because when letters are in succession, the first passes away when the second comes. So the first is originated, since whatever is proven to be non-existent cannot be eternal. The second is also originated, since whatever whose existence is later than the existence of something else is originated. Thus it is established that, on the assumption that the speech of God, exalted is He, is an expression for mere letters and sounds, it is originated.

Having established this, we say to people: there are two positions here.

The first: the locus of those originated letters and sounds is the essence of God, exalted is He. This is the view of the Karramiyya.

The second: their locus is a body separate from the essence of God, exalted is He, like a tree or other things. This is the view of the Mu'tazila.

As for the second view, namely that the speech of God, exalted is He, is an attribute distinct from these letters and sounds, this is the view of most of the People of the Sunna and the Community (Ahl al-Sunna wa al-Jama'a). That attribute is eternal and without beginning. Those who hold this view have differed about what it was that Moses, peace be upon him, heard. The Ash'ariyya said: Moses, peace be upon him, heard that real, eternal attribute. They said: Just as seeing His essence is not impossible, even though His essence is neither a body nor an accident, likewise hearing His speech is not remote, even though His speech is not a letter or a sound. Abu Mansur al-Maturidi said: What Moses, peace be upon him, heard was discrete sounds and composed letters existing in the tree. As for the eternal attribute which is neither a letter nor a sound, that is absolutely not what Moses, peace be upon him, heard. This is the detailed account of the positions of people concerning hearing the speech of God, exalted is He.

**The second issue:** They differed over whether He, exalted is He, spoke to Moses alone or spoke to him together with other peoples. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates the first, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and his Lord spoke to him﴾ indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, was singled out for this honour, and specification by mention indicates the negation of the ruling for what is other than it. The judge (al-Qadi) said: Rather, the seventy chosen men at the appointed time also heard the speech of God, exalted is He. He said: This is because the purpose of bringing them was that they should inform the people of Moses, peace be upon him, of what took place there, and this purpose cannot be fulfilled except by hearing the speech. Also, God's speaking to Moses, peace be upon him, in this manner is a miracle, and the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, had already been established, so this meaning must be made manifest to others.

* * *

**The third issue:** Our companions (the Ash'ari scholars) said: This verse indicates that He, glorified is He, may be seen. Its demonstration is from four aspects:

The first: the verse indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, asked to see Him. There is no doubt that Moses, peace be upon him, knew what is obligatory, permissible and impossible for God, exalted is He. So if seeing were impossible for God, exalted is He, he would not have asked for it. Since he asked for it, we know that seeing is permissible for God, exalted is He.

The judge said: What the scholars who have achieved understanding have said about this consists of four views:

The first is what al-Hasan and others said: Moses, peace be upon him, did not know that seeing is not permissible for God, exalted is He. He said: With ignorance of this matter, a person may still know his Lord, His justice and His oneness. So it is not far-fetched that knowledge of the impossibility or permissibility of seeing depends on revelation.

The second: Moses, peace be upon him, asked for seeing on behalf of his people. They were ignorant of this and kept repeating the request to him, saying: ﴿We will not believe you until we see God plainly﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:55]. So Moses asked for seeing not for himself. When the prohibition came, it became clear that this was not a way to it. This is the method of Abu 'Ali and Abu Hashim.

The third: Moses, peace be upon him, asked his Lord, from Himself, for a knowledge that is overwhelming and necessary. The proponents of this interpretation differ. Some say: he asked his Lord for necessary knowledge. Others say: rather, he asked Him to manifest the overwhelming signs by which doubts and whisperings about knowing Him disappear, even though these are from His action, just as we say concerning the knowledge of the people of the Hereafter. This is what al-Ka'bi chose.

The fourth: The purpose of this request was that God, exalted is He, would mention from the revealed proofs what indicates the impossibility of seeing Him, so that the rational proof would be reinforced by the revealed proof. The reinforcement of proofs is something sought by intelligent people, and this is what Abu Bakr al-Asamm mentioned. This is the sum of the Mu'tazila's sayings on the interpretation of this verse.

Our companions said: As for the first aspect, it is weak, and the following points indicate this:

The first: the consensus of intelligent people that Moses, peace be upon him, was not of lower rank or standing in knowledge of God than the lowliest of the Mu'tazila. Since all of them know that seeing God, exalted is He, is impossible, and we suppose that Moses, peace be upon him, did not know this, his knowledge of God would be of a lower degree than the knowledge of each one of the lowliest Mu'tazila. This is false by the consensus of the Muslims.

The second: The Mu'tazila claim the necessary knowledge that everything that is seen must be opposite or in the state of being opposite. Then it is said: either Moses, peace be upon him, had this knowledge or he did not. If the first, then his permitting that the Exalted may be seen would necessitate permitting that the Exalted is located in a space and direction. Permitting this concept regarding God, exalted is He, necessitates unbelief according to the Mu'tazila, so it follows for them that Moses, peace be upon him, was an unbeliever. No intelligent person would say this.

If the second, then we say: since the knowledge that everything seen must be opposite or in the state of being opposite is a self-evident, necessary knowledge, and then we suppose that this knowledge was not present in Moses, peace be upon him, it follows that Moses, peace be upon him, did not possess all the necessary knowledges. Whoever is like this is insane, so it follows for them that they must judge that he, peace be upon him, was not of complete intellect but was insane, and that is unbelief by the consensus of the Community. Thus it is established that the claim that Moses, peace be upon him, did not know the impossibility of seeing, while we assume that He, exalted is He, is impossible to see, necessitates one of these two false divisions. So the claim is false. And God knows best.

As for the second interpretation, namely that he, peace be upon him, asked for seeing only for his people and not for himself, this is also corrupt, and the following points indicate this:

The first: If the matter were so, Moses would have said: "Show them, that they may look at You," and God, exalted is He, would have said: "They will not see Me." Since that is not what happened, this interpretation is void.

The second: If this request were a seeking of the impossible, He would have forbidden them from it, just as, when they said ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾, He forbade them from it by saying ﴿Indeed you are a people who are ignorant﴾.

The third: It was obligatory for Moses to establish conclusive proofs that God, exalted is He, cannot be seen, and to prevent his people from this request by those proofs. But for him not to mention any of those proofs at all, while their mention was an absolute obligation, would be an attribution of abandoning an obligation to Moses, peace be upon him, and that is not permissible.

The fourth: Those peoples who asked for seeing either believed in the prophethood of Moses, peace be upon him, or did not. If the first, the mere statement of Moses, peace be upon him, would have sufficed to prevent them from that false request, so there would be no need for this request which Moses, peace be upon him, mentioned. If the second, they would not have benefited from this answer, because they would say to him: "We do not accept that God prohibited seeing; rather, this is a saying you have fabricated against God, exalted is He."
