Thus it is established that on both assumptions there is no benefit for the people in the statement of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿Show me [Yourself], that I may look at You.﴾

As for the third interpretation, it is also far-fetched, and the following points indicate this:

The first: On this assumption the meaning of the verse would be: "Show me a sign, that I may look at Your sign," and then the object and the annexed noun would be omitted. But the context of the verse indicates the falsehood of this, namely His saying: ﴿"Look at Me"? He said: "You will not see Me"...﴾ and ﴿"...but look at the mountain..."﴾ and ﴿when His Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾. It is not permissible to apply all of this to the omission of the annexed noun.

The second: He, exalted is He, showed him, from the signs, things after which there is no further end, such as the staff, the white hand, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the overshadowing of the mountain. So how is it possible, after these circumstances, to request a clear and overwhelming sign?

The third: He, peace be upon him, was speaking with God without any intermediary. In this state, how would it be fitting for him to say: "Show me a overwhelming, clear sign which indicates that You exist"? It is well known that this statement is utterly corrupt.

The fourth: If what was sought were a sign indicating His existence, He would have given him that sign just as He gave him all the other signs, and there would have been no meaning to forbidding him from it. Thus it is established that this view is corrupt.

As for the fourth interpretation, which is to say that the purpose of it was to manifest a revealed sign that strengthens what reason has indicated, this too is far-fetched, because if that were the intent, it would have been obligatory for him to say: "I wish, O my God, that the impossibility of Your being seen be strengthened by proofs beyond what has become apparent to reason." Since he did not say that, but rather requested seeing, we know that all these interpretations are corrupt.

**The second proof from the aspects inferred from this verse, indicating that He, exalted is He, is permissible to be seen:** This is because if He, exalted is He, were impossible to see, He would have said: "I am not seen." Do you not see that if a man had a stone in his hand, and a person said to him, "Give me this that I may eat it," he would say to him, "This is not eaten," and would not say to him, "Do not eat"? But if there were an apple in his hand instead of the stone, he would say to him, "Do not eat it," meaning: this is something that is eaten, but you will not eat it. So when He, exalted is He, said ﴿You will not see Me﴾ and did not say "I am not seen," we know that this indicates that He, in His essence, is permissible to be seen.

[Page 189]

The third proof from the implications drawn from this verse: God, exalted is He, made His being seen conditional upon something possible, and what is conditioned upon something possible is itself possible. It follows that seeing (ru'yah) is possible in itself. We say that God, exalted is He, made His being seen conditional upon something possible because He made His being seen conditional upon the stillness of the mountain, as shown by His words, exalted is He: ﴿But if it remains in its place, then you will see Me﴾. The stillness of the mountain is something whose existence is possible in itself. Thus it is established that He made His being seen conditional upon something whose existence is possible in itself.

Once this is established, it must be that His being seen is possible in itself. For since that condition is something whose existence is possible, no impossibility follows from supposing it to occur. So, given the occurrence of that condition, either the reward, which is the occurrence of seeing, follows from it or it does not follow. If the occurrence of seeing follows from it, it is necessary to affirm with certainty that seeing is possible to occur. If the occurrence of seeing does not follow from it, this undermines the soundness of His statement that whenever that condition occurs, seeing occurs. And that is false.

If it is said: God made the occurrence of seeing conditional upon the stillness of the mountain while it is in motion, and the stillness of a mountain while it is in motion is impossible. Thus it is established that the occurrence of seeing is conditioned upon a condition whose occurrence is impossible, not upon a condition whose occurrence is possible, and therefore what you have claimed does not follow. The proof that the condition is the stillness of the mountain while in motion is this: the mountain, at the time when He made its stillness a condition for the occurrence of seeing, either was at rest or was in motion. If it was at rest, then seeing would have occurred by necessity of the conditional, and since it did not occur, we know that at that time the mountain was not stationary. And since it was not stationary, it was moving. Thus it is established that the mountain, at the time when He made its stillness a condition for the occurrence of seeing, was moving and not at rest. Thus it is established that the condition is the mountain's being stationary while it is in motion, and this is an impossible condition.

The answer is that considering the state of the mountain in terms of what it is in itself is different from considering its state in terms of its being either in motion or at rest. That it is impossible for it to be free of both motion and rest does not prevent considering its state in terms of its being either in motion or at rest. Do you not see that if you take a thing with the condition of its being existent, it is necessarily existent, and if you take it with the condition of its being nonexistent, it is necessarily nonexistent? But if you take it in terms of what it is, setting aside whether it is existent or nonexistent, it is possible to exist. Likewise here: what was made a condition in the wording is the stillness of the mountain, and this aspect is possible to exist. Thus it is established that the aspect made a condition is something possible to exist and possible to occur, and this aspect suffices to build the thesis upon. And God knows best.

The fourth proof from the implications drawn from this verse in establishing the permissibility of seeing: His words, exalted is He: ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾. This manifestation (tajalli) is seeing, and this is indicated by two aspects:

The first: knowledge of a thing makes that thing manifest, and seeing a thing also makes that thing manifest. However, seeing is more complete in making manifest than knowledge of it, and interpreting the word according to the more complete meaning is preferable.

The second: the purpose of mentioning this verse is to establish that a human being cannot bear the seeing of God, exalted is He, as evidenced by the fact that the mountain, despite its greatness, when it saw God, exalted is He, crumbled and its parts scattered. And if the meaning of manifestation were not what we have mentioned, this purpose would not be achieved. Thus it is established that His words, exalted is He, ﴿So when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble to dust﴾ mean that when the mountain saw God, exalted is He, its parts crumbled. And when this is the case, it is established that God, exalted is He, is permissible to be seen. At most, one might say: the mountain is inanimate, and an inanimate thing cannot see anything. But we say: it is not impossible to say that God, exalted is He, created in the essence of the mountain life, intellect, and understanding, and then created in it a seeing related to the essence of God, exalted is He. The evidence for this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿O mountains, echo His praises along with him, and the birds﴾ [Saba': 10]. Being addressed with this address is conditional upon the presence of life and intellect in it, and so likewise here. Thus by these four aspects, the indication of this verse that God, exalted is He, is permissible to be seen is established.

As for the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), they said: it has been established by rational and scriptural proofs that God, exalted is He, cannot be seen, so these apparent meanings must be redirected to interpretations.

As for their rational proofs, we have shown their weakness and their collapse in the books of rational theology, so there is no need to mention them here.

As for their scriptural proofs, the strongest thing they have in this matter is their reliance on His words, exalted is He: ﴿No vision can grasp Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103]. The subtle investigations and profound refinements concerning this verse have already been discussed in Surat al-An'am.

Know that the people (the Mu'tazilah) relied on this verse to deny seeing from several aspects:

The first: their reliance on His words: ﴿You will never see Me﴾. The argument is formulated as follows: this verse indicates that Moses, peace be upon him, will never see God at all, neither in this world nor in the Hereafter. And once this is established, it is established that no one sees Him at all. And once this is established, it is established that He, exalted is He, is impossible to be seen. These are three premises.

As for the first premise, its establishment is through several aspects:

The first: what has been reported from the lexicographers that the word "lan" (never) is for permanence. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this claim about the lexicographers is baseless, and no reliable book or sound transmission confirms it. Our companions (ashabuna) said: the evidence for its falsity is His words, exalted is He, concerning the Jews: ﴿But they will never wish for it, ever﴾ [al-Baqarah: 95], even though they wish for death on the Day of Resurrection.

The second: His words ﴿You will never see Me﴾ encompass all times, as shown by the soundness of making an exception for any time one wishes from this word, and the requirement of an exception is to exclude what would have been included in the wording without it. This too is weak, because the effect of an exception is to remove the soundness of the statement, not to remove its obligation, as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

The third: that the statement "I will never do such-and-such" conveys emphasis of negation, and its meaning is that doing it contradicts his state, as in His words: ﴿They could never create a fly, even if they gathered together for it﴾ [al-Hajj: 73]. This indicates that seeing is incompatible with divinity. The answer is that "lan" is for emphasizing the negation of what was asked about, and the question was about obtaining seeing at present. So His words ﴿You will never see Me﴾ are a negation of that desired thing. As for whether it conveys permanent negation, it does not. This is the summary of the discussion in establishing this issue.

As for the second premise: they said the speakers are two: one who says the believers see God and Moses also sees Him, and one who denies seeing for all. Affirming it for others other than Moses while denying it for Moses is a view that breaks the consensus (ijma'), and it is false.

As for the third premise: it is that everyone who denies the occurrence (of seeing) denies its soundness (possibility), so the claim that its soundness is established while its occurrence is denied is a view contrary to the consensus, and it is false.

Know that the building of this proof upon the soundness of the first premise means that once its weakness is established, this argument falls entirely.

The second argument of the people (the Mu'tazilah): God, exalted is He, related about Moses, peace be upon him, that he fell down unconscious (sa'iqan). If seeing were permissible, why did he fall unconscious when he asked for it?

The third argument: when he, peace be upon him, recovered, he said: "Glory be to You" (subhanaka). This expression is for declaring God free of imperfection (tanzih), so the intended meaning must be declaring God, exalted is He, free of what was mentioned before, and what was mentioned before is the seeing of God, exalted is He. Thus his saying "Glory be to You" was a declaring of Him free from being seen. Thus it is established by this that the denial of seeing is the declaring of God, exalted is He, free of imperfection, and the declaring of God free of imperfection is only from deficiencies and defects. Therefore seeing must be among the deficiencies and defects, and that is impossible for God. Thus it is established that seeing is impossible for God.

The fourth argument: God, exalted is He, related about Moses, when he recovered, that he said: ﴿I have repented to You﴾. If asking for seeing were not a sin, he would not have repented from it. And if it were not a sin that contradicts the soundness of faith, he would not have said: ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾.

Know that our companions said: seeing was permissible, but he, peace be upon him, asked for it without permission, and the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near. So the repentance was repentance from this matter, not from what they mentioned. This is the summary of the discussion on this verse, and God knows best the correct view.

* * *

The fourth issue in the discussion of this verse: it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Moses, peace be upon him, came with the seventy, and Moses ascended the mountain while the seventy remained at the foot of the mountain. God spoke to Moses, wrote for him a book on the tablets, and brought him near as one in private conversation (najiyy). When Moses heard the scratching of the pen, his longing greatly increased, so he said: ﴿My Lord, show me [Yourself], that I may look at You﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: the second object of "arini" (show me) is omitted, meaning "show me" Yourself, ﴿that I may look at You﴾. And there are questions regarding the wording of the verse:

The first question: "al-nazar" (looking): either it is an expression for seeing (ru'yah), or for its preliminary step, which is turning the healthy pupil toward the direction of the object seen, seeking to see it.

On the first interpretation the meaning would be: "show me, so that I may see You," and this is false.

On the second interpretation the meaning would be: "show me, so that I may turn the pupil toward You," and this is false for two reasons:

One: it requires affirming a direction for God, exalted is He.

The second: turning the pupil toward the direction of the object seen is a preliminary step for seeing, so making it like a result of seeing is false.

The answer: His words "show me" mean: enable me to be able to see You, so that I may look at You and see You.

The second question: why did He say ﴿You will never see Me﴾ and not "You will never look at Me," so that it would correspond to His words ﴿that I may look at You﴾?

The answer: since looking is a preliminary step to seeing, the intended thing is seeing, not the looking that has no seeing with it.

The third question: how is the shift in His words ﴿But look at the mountain﴾ connected to what precedes it?

The answer: its purpose is to magnify the matter of seeing, and that no one can bear to see God, exalted is He, except when God, exalted is He, strengthens him with His help and support. Do you not see that when the effect of manifestation and seeing appeared on the mountain, it crumbled and scattered? So this, from this aspect, indicates the magnification of the matter of seeing.

Regarding His saying, ﴿When His Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "tajalla" means it appeared and became clear. From it one says: "jalawtu al-carus" (I unveiled the bride) when you displayed her, and "jalawtu al-mir'ah wal-sayf" (I polished the mirror and the sword) when you removed the rust from them.

As for His saying, ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "dakkan" may be read with tanwin, and "dakkaa'" without tanwin. That is, He made it ground down level with the earth. One says: "dakaktu al-shay'" (I crushed the thing) when you pound it, "adukkuhu dakkan." And "al-dakkaa'" and "al-dakkawat" are the hills that stand raised up level with the earth. Accordingly, "al-dakk" is a verbal noun (masdar), and "al-dakkaa'" is a noun (ism).

Then al-Wahidi narrated with his chain from al-Akhfash, concerning His saying ﴿He made it crumble to dust﴾, that he said: "dakkahu dakkan" is an emphatic verbal noun, and it is permissible to take it as "dha dakk" (possessing crushing). He said: whoever reads "dakkaa'" with a long vowel intends "He made it a dakkaa'," i.e., a raised ground. This agrees with what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "He made it dust."

As for His saying, ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾, al-Layth said: "al-sac'q" is like the swooning (ghashy) that overtakes a person, and "al-sa'qah" is a fainting spell. One says: "sa'iqa al-rajulu" and "su'iqa," so whoever says "sa'iqa" then he is "sa'iq," and whoever says "su'iqa" then he is "mas'uq." It is also said: "sa'iqa" when he died, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So all those in the heavens and all those on earth will swoon﴾ [al-Zumar: 68], which they interpreted as death. And from it His saying: ﴿That Day of theirs in which they will be struck with swooning﴾ [al-Tur: 45], i.e., they will die. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "sa'iqa" originates from "al-sa'iqah" (the thunderbolt), which is also called "al-sa'iqah" from "sa'aqahu" when he struck him on the head.

Having understood this, we say: Ibn 'Abbas interpreted His saying, ﴿And Musa fell down unconscious﴾, as swooning, while Qatadah interpreted it as death. The first is stronger, because of His saying: ﴿Then when he regained consciousness﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: It is hardly said of the dead, "He regained consciousness from his death," but it is said of one who has fainted, "He regained consciousness from his fainting," because Allah, Exalted is He, said of those who died: ﴿Then We revived you after your death﴾ [al-Baqarah: 56].

As for His saying, ﴿He said: Glory be to You﴾, meaning: exalted are You above anyone asking You for anything without Your permission. ﴿I have turned to You in repentance﴾, and in this there are two views:
The first: ﴿I have turned to You in repentance﴾ from asking to see You in this world.
The second: ﴿I have turned to You in repentance﴾ from asking to see You without Your permission. ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾ in that You cannot be seen in this world; or it is said: ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾ in that asking of You is not permitted except with Your permission.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 144:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "O Musa, I have chosen you above the people by My messages and by My speech. So take what I have given you and be among the grateful."﴾

Know that when Musa (peace be upon him) asked to see Allah and Allah denied him that, Allah enumerated to him the various aspects of His great blessings that he had received, and commanded him to occupy himself with thanking Him for them. It is as if He said to him: "If I have withheld from you the vision, then I have given you such-and-such great blessings. So let your chest not be constricted because of the denial of the vision, and look at the rest of the kinds of blessings with which I have singled you out, and occupy yourself with thanking for them." The purpose is to console Musa (peace be upon him) regarding the denial of the vision. This is also one of the things that indicates that seeing Allah is permissible, for if it were impossible in itself, there would be no need to mention this much.

Know that al-Istifa' (choosing) is the extracting of the elite. So His words ﴿I have chosen you﴾ mean: I have taken you as an elite above the people. Ibn Abbas said: "He means: I have preferred you over the people." When He mentioned that He had chosen him, He mentioned the matter by which this choosing was achieved, saying: ﴿by My messages and by My speech﴾. Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read "bi-risalati" (in the singular), while the rest read "bi-risalati" (in the plural), because He revealed to him again and again. Whoever reads it in the singular, it is because risalah functions like a verbal noun, so it is permissible to use it in the singular in place of the plural. He said ﴿I have chosen you above the people﴾ and did not say "above the creation," because the angels may hear the speech of Allah without an intermediary, just as Musa (peace be upon him) heard it.

If it is said: How did He choose him above the people by his messages, when many people shared in the messengership?

We say: He, exalted is He, made clear that He singled him out from among people by the combination of the two matters: the messengership together with speech without an intermediary. This combination was not attained by anyone else. It is established that the distinction here arose because he heard that speech without an intermediary. The speech without an intermediary is a cause of greater nobility according to the apparent custom, for one who hears the speech of a great king directly from his mouth is of higher standing and more exalted rank than one who hears it through the mediation of chamberlains and deputies.

When He mentioned these two kinds of the great blessing, He said: ﴿So take what I have given you and be among the grateful﴾, meaning: take this blessing, and let your heart not be constricted because of your being denied the vision, and occupy yourself with thanking Allah for the success of obtaining this blessing. Occupying oneself with thanking for it is only by fulfilling its requirements, in knowledge and in action. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 145:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets [something] of everything, an admonition and a clear explanation of all things. So take hold of them with strength and order your people to take the best of them. I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that when the Exalted had explained that He had singled out Musa, peace be upon him, with the message, He mentioned in this verse the details of that message, saying: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) transmits from some of them that Musa fell down unconscious on the Day of 'Arafah, and God the Exalted gave him the Torah on the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr). They mentioned the number of the tablets, and their substance and length, that they were ten tablets. It was also said: seven. It was said: they were of emerald, brought by Jibril, peace be upon him. It was said: of green chrysolite and red ruby. Al-Hasan said: they were of wood that descended from the sky. Wahb said: they were of a solid rock which God softened for Musa, peace be upon him. As for the manner of writing, Ibn Jurayj said: Jibril wrote them with the pen with which he wrote the Reminder (al-Dhikr), and drew ink from the river of light.

And know that there is nothing in the wording of the verse that indicates the nature of those tablets or the manner of that writing. If that detail is established by a strong separate proof, it must be affirmed; otherwise, one must remain silent about it.

* * *
As for His saying: ﴿of everything﴾, there is no doubt that it is not meant in its general sense; rather, what is meant is everything that Musa and his people need in their religion, of what is lawful and unlawful, of what is good and what is bad.
* * *
As for His saying: ﴿an admonition and a clear explanation of all things﴾, it serves as an explanation of the general statement that He preceded with His saying: ﴿of everything﴾. This is because He divided it into two kinds: one is "admonition," and the other is "clear explanation" of what must be known of the rulings. Within admonition enters everything the Exalted mentioned of matters that produce desire for obedience and aversion from disobedience, and that is by mentioning promise and threat. When He first established that, He followed it with explaining the categories of rulings and detailing the lawful and the unlawful, saying: ﴿and a clear explanation of all things﴾. When He had explained that, He said to Musa: ﴿So take hold of them with strength﴾, i.e., with firm resolve and sincere intention. Then the Exalted commanded him to order his people to take the best of them. The apparent meaning of this is that there is a difference between the two obligations, so that this detailed distinction has a purpose. For this reason some exegetes said: the obligation upon Musa, peace be upon him, was more severe, because the Exalted did not grant him the concessions He granted to others. Others said: rather, He singled him out in that He charged him with delivering and conveying (the message), even though he shared with his people in what else was enjoined.

Regarding His saying: ﴿order your people to take the best of them﴾, there is a question: since the Exalted commanded that everything in the Torah be worshipped, it necessarily follows that all of it is enjoined, and the apparent meaning of ﴿take the best of them﴾ implies that among them there is what is not best, and that it is not permissible for them to take it; and that is contradictory. The scholars mentioned several answers to this:

The first: some of those obligations are good and some are better, such as retaliation (qisas), pardon, self-defence, and patience. That is, command them to compel themselves to take what is more inclusive of goodness and greater in reward, like His saying: ﴿And follow the best of what has been sent down to you﴾ [al-Zumar: 55] and His saying: ﴿Those who listen to the word and follow the best of it﴾ [al-Zumar: 18].

If they say: when the Exalted commanded taking the best, He prohibited taking the good, and that impugns its being good. We say: the command of God the Exalted to take the best is to be understood as recommendation (nadb), so that this contradiction disappears.

The second answer: Qutrub said: ﴿take the best of them﴾ means "with their goodness," and all of them are good, by His saying the Exalted: ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45], and by the saying of al-Farazdaq:

A house whose pillars are more mighty and taller.

The third answer: some said: "the good" includes the obligatory, the recommended, and the permissible, and the best of these three are the obligatory and the recommended.

Page 194
As for His saying: ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾, there are two views:

The first: the intended meaning is threat and warning against opposing the command of God the Exalted. On this reading there are two views:

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Mujahid said: the abode of the defiantly disobedient is Jahannam, i.e., let the mention of Jahannam be present in your minds so that you may beware of being among them.

The second: Qatadah said: I will cause you to enter Syria and show you the dwellings of the disbelievers who used to settle there, of the tyrants and the 'Amalaqah, so that you may take warning from them and from what they came to of punishment.

Al-Kalbi said: ﴿the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾ refers to the dwellings past which they used to pass when travelling, from the dwellings of 'Ad and Thamud and the generations whom God the Exalted destroyed.

The second view: the intended meaning is promise and glad tidings, that He, the Exalted, will make them heirs of the land of their enemies and their dwellings. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 146:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth without right; and even if they see every sign, they will not believe in it; and if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way; but if they see the way of error, they will take it as a way. That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them.﴾

In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned in the preceding verse His saying: ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-A'raf: 145], He mentioned in this verse how He will deal with them, saying: ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth﴾. Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited this verse as evidence that God may prevent a person from faith and turn him away from it, and this is clear. The Mu'tazila said: it is not possible to interpret the verse in the way you have stated, and this is indicated by several points:

The first point: al-Jubba'i said: it is not permissible that what is meant by it is that He, may He be exalted, turns them away from faith in His signs, because His saying ﴿I will turn away﴾ refers to the future, and God has already made clear that they disbelieved and denied before this turning away, since He described them as being arrogant on the earth without right, and that they, if they see the way of right guidance, do not take it as a way, and if they see the way of error, they take it as a way. Thus it is established that the verse indicates that disbelief had already occurred to them in the past time, and this indicates that what is meant by this turning away is not disbelief in God.

The second point: His saying ﴿I will turn away from My signs those who are arrogant on the earth﴾ is mentioned in the manner of punishment for arrogance and disbelief. So if what is meant by this turning away were their disbelief, its meaning would be that He created disbelief in them as a punishment for their embarking upon disbelief. It is known that punishing disbelief with the same kind of act for which one is punished is not permissible. Thus it is established that what is meant by this turning away is not disbelief.

صفحة ٤
The third point: if He turned them away from faith and prevented them from it, how could He say, along with that, ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 20], ﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the reminder?﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 49], ﴿And what prevented the people from believing?﴾ [al-Kahf: 55]. Thus it is established that interpreting the verse in this way is not possible, so it is necessary to interpret it in other ways.

As for the first interpretation: al-Ka'bi and Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: this statement is a completion of what God promised Musa, peace be upon him, regarding the destruction of his enemies. The meaning of "turning them away" is their destruction, so they will not be able to prevent Musa from conveying it, nor to prevent the believers from faith in it. This is similar to His saying: ﴿O Messenger, convey what has been sent down to you from your Lord; and if you do not, then you have not conveyed His message; and God will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]. So God willed to prevent the enemies of Musa, peace be upon him, from harming him, and from preventing him from carrying out what is incumbent upon him in conveying prophethood and messengership.

The second interpretation: what al-Jubba'i mentioned, saying: I will turn these arrogant ones away from attaining the honor and dignity that are in My signs, which are prepared for the prophets and the believers. He turns them away from that only by means of bringing humiliation and degradation upon them, and this proceeds in the manner of a punishment for their disbelief and their arrogance toward God.

The third interpretation: among the signs are some that cannot benefit one except after prior faith. So when they disbelieve, they have made themselves into a state in which they cannot benefit from those signs, and then God turns them away from them.

The fourth interpretation: when God knows from the condition of some of them that, if they witness those signs, they will not draw proof from them but will rather treat them lightly and not give them their due, then when God knows this of them, it is proper for God, may He be exalted, to turn them away from them.

The fifth interpretation: it is related from al-Hasan that he said: among the disbelievers are those who push their disbelief to the extent that, when they reach that limit, their hearts die. So what is meant by His saying ﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾ is these people. This is the whole of what has been said on this topic, and it has become clear that this verse does not contain strong evidence for the correctness of what he says regarding the question of the creation of actions. And God knows best.

The second issue: The meaning of "yatakabbarun" (they are arrogant): they consider themselves the best of creation, and that they have a right that is not held by others. This attribute, namely arrogance, belongs only to God, may He be exalted, because He is the One who possesses power and the excellence that no one else has; therefore He alone deserves to be the Arrogant. Some of them said: arrogance is displaying the greatness of the self over others. The attribute of arrogance is a blameworthy attribute in all of God's servants, and a praiseworthy attribute in God, majestic is His majesty, because He deserves to display it over whoever else exists, since that is a right in His case, whereas in the case of others it is false.

Know that He, may He be exalted, mentioned in this verse His saying ﴿without right﴾, because displaying arrogance over others may sometimes be with right, for the one who is in the right may be arrogant toward the one who is in falsehood. And in the well-known saying: "Arrogance toward the arrogant is a charity."

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and if they see the way of right guidance, they will not take it as a way﴾, there are discussions in it:

The first discussion: Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "al-rashad" with a fatha on the ra' and the shin, while the rest read it with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the shin. Abu 'Amr distinguished between them, saying: "al-rushd" with a damma on the ra' means righteousness (al-salah), as in His saying: ﴿But if you perceive in them maturity of judgment (rushdan)﴾ [al-Nisa': 6], i.e., righteousness. And "al-rashad" with both vowels as fatha means steadfastness in religion, as He said: ﴿that you have been taught of right guidance (rushdan)﴾ [al-Kahf: 66]. Al-Kisa'i said: they are two dialects with one meaning, like al-hazan and al-huzn, and al-saqam and al-suqum. It was also said: "al-rushd" with a damma is the noun, and with two fathas is the verbal noun.

The second discussion: "the way of right guidance" is an expression for the path of guidance and the true religion, and correctness in knowledge and action; and "the way of error" is what is opposed to that. Then He, may He be exalted, explained that this turning away occurred for two reasons:

One of them: their being deniers of God's signs.

The second: their being heedless of them, and what is meant is that they persisted in turning away from them until they became like one heedless of them. And God knows best.

The words of His Exalted Majesty: ﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter—their deeds have become void. Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾

Know that when Exalted God mentioned the reason for which He turned the arrogant away from His signs, by His saying: ﴿That is because they denied Our signs and were heedless of them﴾, He then explained the state of those deniers. It might have been supposed that they differ in the matter of punishment, because among them are some who perform some acts of righteousness. So God explained the state of all of them, whether one is arrogant or humble, whether one is of little goodness or of much goodness, and said: ﴿And those who denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, meaning by that their rejection of the promise and their audacity in acts of disobedience. Then God explained that their deeds are voided. The discussion of the true nature of ihbat (nullification of deeds) has already been presented in detail in Surat al-Baqarah, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

Then Exalted God said: ﴿Are they recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ In this there is an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: Are they recompensed except by what they used to do? Or: according to what they used to do.

Our companions (the Ash'arites) have used this verse as evidence against the position of Abu Hashim (al-Jubba'i) that the one who abandons an obligation deserves punishment merely by not performing the obligation, even if no act proceeds from him at the time of that obligation. They said: this verse indicates that there is no recompense except for action, and abandoning an obligation is not an action, so it must be that it is not requited; thus it is established that the recompense occurs only for the performance of its opposite. Abu Hashim answered: I do not name that punishment a recompense, so the argument falls.

Our companions answered this reply: recompense is so named because it "recompenses" (yajzi) and suffices as a deterrent from what is forbidden and as an incitement to what is commanded. If punishment is consequent upon the mere abandonment of an obligation, that punishment is sufficient as a deterrent from that abandonment, and so it is a recompense. Thus it is established that there is no way to refuse calling it a recompense. And God knows best.

[Page 6]

**His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the people of Moses took, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body that had a lowing. Did they not see that it does not speak to them or guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.﴾**

Know that the intended meaning of this verse is the story of al-Samiri's making of the calf. There are several issues concerning it.

**The first issue:** Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited *ḥilliyyihim* (ﷻ) with a kasrah on the ḥā' and the lām and a shaddah on the yā', for the sake of assimilation, as in *dulliyy*. The rest recited *ḥulliyyihim* with a ḍammah on the ḥā', a kasrah on the lām and a shaddah on the yā', as the plural of *ḥaly*, like *thady* and *thudiyy*. Some recited *min ḥulliyyihim* in the singular. *Al-ḥulliyy* is the name of what is adorned with gold and silver.

**The second issue:** It is said that the Children of Israel had a festival in which they adorned themselves, and they borrowed ornaments from the Copts (al-Qibṭ) for that day. When Allah drowned the Copts, those ornaments remained in the hands of the Children of Israel. Al-Samiri gathered those ornaments. He was a man obeyed among them, of high rank. They had asked Moses, peace be upon him, to make for them a god to worship, so al-Samiri fashioned a calf. Then people differed. Some said that he had taken a handful of dust from the hoofprint of Gabriel's horse, peace be upon him, and cast it into the inside of that calf, and it turned into flesh and blood, and a lowing came from it once. Al-Samiri said: "This is your god and the god of Moses!" Most of the commentators from the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that held that human reason and divine justice are foundational) said that he had made that calf hollow, and placed pipes in its interior in a specific shape, and placed that image in the path of the winds, so the wind entered the pipes and a particular sound came out resembling the lowing of a calf. Others said that he made that image hollow, and placed beneath it, in the place where he set up the calf, someone who blew into it from a place people did not notice, so they heard the sound from inside it like lowing. The proponent of this view said: "People today also do something similar with these statues in which they run water in the manner of fountains." By this method and others, he produced the sound from that image, and then he proclaimed to the people that this calf was their god and the god of Moses.

\* \* \*

Several questions remain concerning the wording of the verse.

**The first question:** Why does it say ﴿the people of Moses took﴾ when the one who took it was al-Samiri alone?

The answer has two aspects.

First: Allah attributed the act to them because one man among them carried it out, as one says: "The Banu Tamim said such and did such," while the speaker and the doer are one.

Second: They were desirous of taking it and content with it, so it is as though they all came together upon it.

**The second question:** Why does it say ﴿from their ornaments﴾ when the ornaments were not theirs, but had come into their hands by way of loan?

The answer: When Allah destroyed the people of Pharaoh, those possessions remained in their hands and became their property, like all their other possessions, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿How many gardens and springs they left behind, and crops and a noble station, and bounty in which they had delighted. Thus, and We made others inherit them.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 25–28]

**The third question:** Were those who worshipped the calf all of the people of Moses, or some of them?

The answer: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿the people of Moses took ... a calf﴾ implies generality. Al-Hasan said: "All of them worshipped the calf except Harun." He argued for this on two grounds.

First: the generality of this verse.

Second: the saying of Moses, peace be upon him, in this story: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my brother﴾ [al-A'raf: 151]. He singled out himself and his brother for the supplication, and this indicates that whoever differed from the two of them was not fit to be prayed for. Had they remained upon faith, the matter would not have been so.

Others said: Rather, there remained among the Children of Israel those who held firm in their faith, for that disbelief occurred only among specific people. The evidence for this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community that guides by the truth and by it acts justly﴾ [al-A'raf: 159].

**The fourth question:** Did that image turn into flesh and blood, as some of them said, or did it remain gold as it was before?

The answer: Those who held the first possibility argued for the soundness of their view on two grounds.

First: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a calf, a body that had a lowing.﴾ The word *jasad* is a name for the body made of flesh and blood. Some disputed this and said: rather, *jasad* is a name for every dense body, whether it is of flesh and blood or not.

Second argument: He, Exalted is He, ascribed to it a lowing, and that is only possible in a living animal. It was answered: since that sound resembled lowing, it is not far-fetched to apply the word "lowing" to it. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, recited (*ju'ār*), with a jīm and a hamzah, from *ja'ara*, meaning to cry out. This is what has been said on this matter.

Know that when He, Exalted is He, related their doctrine and their saying, He argued against the invalidity of that calf being a god with His saying: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them or guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.﴾ The argument's explanation is that this calf cannot speak to them, nor can it guide them to rightness and right guidance. Whoever is like this is either inanimate matter or a helpless animal, and in either case it is not fit for divinity.

Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to show that whoever is not speaking and does not guide to a way is not a god, because a god is the one who has command and prohibition, and that is only realized if he is speaking. Whoever is not speaking cannot issue commands or prohibitions, and the calf is incapable of commanding or prohibiting, so it was not a god.

The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that the condition for being a god is that he guide to truth and rightness, so whoever is misleading must not be a god.

If it is said: this implies that if it were valid for it to speak and guide, it would be permissible to take it as a god. Otherwise, if affirming that is like denying it in that it is not permissible to take it as a god, then there is no benefit in what you have mentioned.

The answer has two aspects.

First: It is not far-fetched that this is a condition for the attainment of divinity, so that the absence of it entails the absence of divinity, even though its presence does not entail the attainment of divinity.

Second: Whoever is able to speak to them and to guide them to good and evil is a god, and created beings are not able to guide; they are only able to describe guidance. As for establishing and setting up the proofs, none is capable of that except Allah, glorified and exalted is He.

Know that He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿and they were wrongdoers﴾, meaning they were wrongdoers to themselves, in that they turned away from the worship of Allah, Exalted is He, and occupied themselves with worshipping the calf. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 149:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when they were overcome with regret, and saw that they had gone astray, they said: "If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers."﴾

Know that they agreed that what is meant by His saying ﴿they were overcome with regret﴾ is that their remorse over the worship of the calf became intense, and they differed about the aspect for which this metaphor is apt.

The first aspect: al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that regret fell into their hands, that is, into their hearts, just as one says "a hardship befell his hand" (ḥaṣala fī yadayhi makrūh). Although it is impossible for a hardship that falls on the hand to occur literally, they applied to a hardship that falls on the heart and the soul the expression of it falling on the hand, so it is likewise here.

The second aspect: the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Kashshaf, by al-Zamakhshari) said: one says of a person who regrets, "he was overcome in his hand" (suqita fī yadihi), because it is the habit of one whose regret is intense to bite his hand in grief, so his regret comes to be "fallen into his hands," since his mouth has been placed into them.

The third aspect: falling (al-suqūṭ) is an expression for something descending from above to below, which is why they say "the rain fell" (saqaṭa al-maṭar), "something fell from your hand" (saqaṭa min yadika shay'), and "the woman miscarried" (asqatat al-mar'ah). Whoever undertakes an action undertakes it because he believes that action is good and correct, and that it will bring him honour and elevation. When it becomes clear to him that that action was false and corrupt, it is as if he has descended from the high to the low and fallen from above to below. For this reason one says of a man who errs: "that was a slip from him" (saqṭah), likening it to a fall to the ground. Thus it is established that applying the word "falling" to the state that arises at regret is permissible and commendable. It remains to ask: what is the benefit of mentioning the hand? We say: the hand is the instrument by which a person is able to take, control and preserve. The one who regrets is as if he is trying to remedy the state for which the regret arose and is occupied with correcting it, so it is as if he has fallen into the grip of his own self, in that after the arising of that regret he has occupied himself with remedying and correcting.

The fourth aspect: al-Wahidi related from some of them that this is derived from al-saqīṭ, which is what covers the ground in the mornings, resembling snow. One says of it: "the ground was saqīṭ-covered" (saqaṭat al-arḍ), just as one says of snow: "the ground was snowed upon" (thalajat al-arḍ) and "we were snowed upon" (thulijnā), meaning it was struck by snow. The meaning of "suqita fī yadihi" is that the saqīṭ fell into his hand. The saqīṭ melts at the slightest warmth and does not remain, so whoever has the saqīṭ fall into his hand gains nothing from it at all. This became an example for everyone who loses in his final outcome and gains nothing of value from his effort, and regret was the last of his affair.

The fifth aspect: some scholars said: the one who regrets is only said to have "fallen into his hand" because he becomes bewildered in his affair and is unable to carry out his deeds, and the primary instrument in deeds, for the most part, is the hand. The one who is incapable is in the position of one who has fallen, so when falling is linked with the hands it is understood that falling into the hand occurred because of complete incapacity. And it is said in common usage of one who does not find guidance in what he does: "his hand and his foot went astray" (ḍallat yaduhu wa rijluhu).

Page 9

The sixth aspect: it is the habit of the one who regrets to bow his head and rest it on his hand, leaning upon it, and at times he places it beneath his chin and part of his face, in a posture such that if his hand were removed he would fall upon his face. So the hand becomes that onto which one has fallen, since falling is settled upon it. His saying "suqita fī aydīhim" would then mean "suqita ʿalā aydīhim" (fallen upon their hands), like His saying: ﴿and I will crucify you upon the trunks of palm trees﴾ [Ṭaha: 71], meaning upon them. And God knows best.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿and saw that they had gone astray﴾, that is, they clearly perceived their error, as if they had seen it with their eyes. The judge (al-Qadi, ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: the delayed must be made prior, because regret and bewilderment occur only after knowledge; so it is as if He, exalted, said: "When they saw that they had gone astray, they were overcome with regret, because of the great grief that befell them." It may be said that there is no need for this transposition, because when a person becomes doubtful whether the deed he undertook is right or wrong, he may regret it, since undertaking what one does not know to be right or wrong is impermissible as corrupt or false. When this state appears, regret arises; then afterward knowledge is completed and it becomes clear that it was an error, corrupt and false. Thus it is established that on this reading there is no need to insist on transposition. Then He, exalted, explained that when this regret appeared, and they came to know that what they had done was false, they showed their turning to God, exalted, and they said: ﴿If our Lord does not have mercy on us and forgive us, we will surely be among the losers.﴾ This is the speech of one who acknowledges the great thing he undertook, regrets what proceeded from him, and begs his Lord for the pardon of his slip. Then they affirmed against themselves that they would be among the losers if God did not forgive them. This regret and seeking of forgiveness occurred only after the return of Musa (peace be upon him) to them. It was also read: "If You do not have mercy on us, our Lord, and forgive us" with the ta' (lam tarḥamnā rabbanā wa taghfir lanā), and "rabbanā" in the accusative as a vocative. This is the speech of the penitent, just as Adam and Eve, peace be upon them both, said: ﴿And if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us﴾ [al-A'raf: 23].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 150–151:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said, "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me. Did you hasten the command of your Lord?" And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by his head, dragging him toward himself. [Aaron] said, "Son of my mother! Indeed, the people overpowered me and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies rejoice over me, and do not place me among the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿[Moses] said, "My Lord, forgive me and my brother, and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that His saying, ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾, does not prevent him from having known about their affair beforehand regarding the worship of the calf, nor does it necessitate that, because it is possible that they became such upon his return and witnessing their conditions. Therefore, for this reason, they differed about it. Some people said: when he came upon them, he came to know of it. Abu Muslim said: rather, he already knew of it before, and this is closer to the truth, and several points indicate it:

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾ indicates that while he was returning he was angry and grieved, and he was returning to his people before reaching them. So this shows that before reaching them, peace be upon him, he already knew of this situation.

The second: He, exalted is He, mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha that He informed him of the occurrence of that event during the appointed time.

The second issue: Regarding al-asaf (grief/anger) there are two opinions:

The first: that al-asaf is intense anger. This is the view of Abu al-Darda', Ata', from Ibn Abbas, and the choice of al-Zajjaj, and they argued with His saying: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55], meaning, "when they angered Us."

The second, which is also the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Suddi: al-asif is the sorrowful. In the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, she said: "Abu Bakr is a man asif," meaning sorrowful. Al-Wahidi said: the two opinions are close, because anger arises from sorrow and sorrow from anger. For when something you dislike comes from one who is beneath you, you become angry, and when it comes from one who is above you, you become sorrowful. So one of these two states is called sorrow and the other anger. Based on this, Moses was angry at his people because of their worship of the calf, and grieved, because Allah had tested them, and He had said to him: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people after you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85].

As for His saying: ﴿Evil is what you have done in my absence after me﴾, its meaning is: "Evil is what you have done in standing in my place and being my successors after me." This address is directed either to the worshippers of the calf from al-Samiri and his followers, or to the leaders of the Children of Israel, namely Aaron, peace be upon him, and the believers with him. What indicates this is His saying: ﴿Take my place among my people﴾ [al-A'raf: 142]. According to the first interpretation, the meaning is: "Evil is what you have done in succeeding me by worshipping the calf instead of worshipping Allah." According to this second interpretation, the meaning is: "Evil is what you have done in succeeding me, since you were not prevented from worshipping other than Allah, the Exalted." Here there are questions:

First question: Where is the agent (fa'il) and the object of blame (al-makhsus bil-dhamm) that bi'sa requires?

Answer: The agent is a pronoun implied, explained by His saying: (mā khalaftumūnī), and the object of blame is omitted, its implied sense being: "Evil is the succession that you succeeded me in after me, your succession."

Second question: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿after me﴾ after His saying: ﴿you succeeded me﴾?

Answer: Its meaning is: "after what you saw from me of the oneness of Allah, the Exalted, the negation of partners from Him, and sincere worship to Him," or "after I used to lead the Children of Israel to monotheism and prevent them from worshipping the cow, when they said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾. And it is the right of successors to follow the course of those who appointed them."

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾, the meaning of 'ajalah (haste) is proceeding with a thing before its time, and for this reason it became blameworthy, whereas speed (sur'ah) is not blameworthy, because its meaning is doing a thing at the first of its times. Thus al-Wahidi said.

One might say: if haste were blameworthy, why did Moses, peace be upon him, say: ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84]? Ibn Abbas said the meaning of ﴿Did you hasten the command of your Lord?﴾ is: "the appointment of your Lord, so you did not wait for it?" Al-Hasan said: it is the promise of your Lord which He promised you of the forty [days]; and that is because they estimated that since He had not come on the thirtieth night, he had died. Ata' said: it means, "Did you hasten the wrath of your Lord?" Al-Kalbi said: "Did you hasten into worshipping the calf before the command of your Lord came to you?"

When He, exalted is He, mentioned that Moses returned angry, He then mentioned what that anger necessitated, and it was two matters:

The first: that he said: ﴿And he threw down the Tablets﴾, meaning those in which was the Torah. Since those Tablets were among his greatest miracles, and then he threw them down, this indicates the intensity of anger, because a person does not undertake such an act except when overwhelmed by a bewildering anger. It is narrated that the Torah was in seven sevenths; when he threw down the Tablets they broke, so he lifted six sevenths of them and one seventh remained. What was lifted contained the detailed explanation of everything, and what remained contained guidance and mercy. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: ("May Allah have mercy on my brother Moses. The report is not like seeing with one's own eyes. Allah, exalted is He, had informed him of the trial of his people, yet he knew that what He had informed him was true, and that he was holding firmly to what was in his hand.")

One might say: the Qur'an mentions only that he threw down the Tablets; as for his throwing them such that they broke, this is not in the Qur'an, and it is a great audacity against the Book of Allah, and such a thing does not befit the prophets, peace be upon them.

The second of the matters arising from that anger:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he threw down the Tablets and seized his brother by his head, dragging him toward himself.﴾ At this point there is a question for those who impugn the infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, which we mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha along with the correct answer. In sum, those who impugn the infallibility of the prophets say: he seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself, as a means of humiliation and belittling. Those who affirm the infallibility of the prophets say: he drew his brother's head toward himself so that he might speak to him privately and learn from him the manner of that event.

If it is said: why did he say: ﴿Son of my mother! Indeed, the people overpowered me﴾?

We say: the answer to this is that Aaron, peace be upon him, feared that the ignorant among the Children of Israel might imagine that Moses, peace be upon him, was angry with him just as he was angry with the worshippers of the calf. So he said to him: "Son of my mother, indeed the people overpowered me and did not obey me in abandoning the worship of the calf. I had forbidden them, but I did not have with me a group large enough to prevent them from this act by force. So do not do to me what will make my enemies rejoice, for they are your enemies too, since the people will take this action you are doing to me as humiliation, not honor."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Son of my mother﴾, know that Ibn Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, from Asim, read ﴿ibna ummi﴾ with a kasra on the mim, and in Ta-Ha likewise, on the assumption of "ummi" (my mother), so the ya' of possession was dropped, since the basis of the vocative is elision, and the kasra remained on the mim to indicate the possession, like His saying: (ya ibad). The rest read it with a fatha on the mim in both surahs, and regarding this there are two opinions:

One: that the two words were made a single name and it was built (mabni) because these two letters frequently occur together, so it became like a single word, similar to Hadramawt and Khamsata 'ashar.

Second: that it is on the elision of the alif that replaced the ya' of possession, and its origin is "ya ibna amma," as the poet said:

Ya ibnata 'amma, la talumi wahja'i
(O daughter of my paternal uncle, do not blame, and sleep on.)

His saying: ﴿Indeed, the people overpowered me﴾, meaning they did not heed my words, and they nearly killed me. So do not let the enemies rejoice over me, meaning the companions of the calf, and do not place me among the wrongdoing people who worshipped the calf, meaning do not make me a partner with them in Your punishment of them for their deed. At this point Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me﴾, meaning for what I undertook of this anger and harshness, ﴿and my brother﴾ for his leaving the severe rebuke of the calf worshippers, ﴿and admit us into Your mercy, for You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.﴾

Know that the complete discussion of these questions and answers concerning this story is mentioned in Surah Ta-Ha. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 152–153:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf [as a deity] will be overtaken by anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world. Thus do We recompense the fabricators.﴾ ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed—indeed, your Lord, after it, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is to explain the state of those who worshipped the calf.

Know also that the second object of the verb of taking (ittikhadh) is omitted, and the estimated meaning is: they took the calf as a god and an object of worship. This omitted element is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Moses"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88]. The exegetes have two approaches to this verse:

The first: The intended meaning of "those who took the calf" is those who directly engaged in worshipping the calf, and they are the ones concerning whom He said: ﴿will be overtaken by anger from their Lord﴾. According to this estimation, there is a question: those people were forgiven by Allah because they killed themselves as part of their repentance from that sin, and if Allah forgave them, how can it be said concerning them that ﴿anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world will overtake them﴾?

The answer to this: that anger occurred in this world, not in the Hereafter. The explanation of that anger is that Allah, exalted is He, commanded them to kill themselves. And the meaning of His saying ﴿and humiliation in the life of this world﴾ is that they had gone astray and so they were humbled.

If they say: the sin in His saying ﴿will overtake them﴾ denotes the future, so how can this be applied to a judgment of this world?

We say: this statement is a report of what Allah, exalted is He, informed Moses, peace be upon him, when He informed him of the trial of his people and their taking the calf. At that time He told him that anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world would overtake them. So this statement preceded their falling into killing and humiliation, and this interpretation is valid from this standpoint.

The second approach: The intended meaning of "those who took the calf" is their descendants who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. According to this estimation, there are two aspects to the verse:

The first aspect: The Arabs reproach the sons for the ugly deeds of their fathers, just as they do with the virtues. They say to the sons: "You did such and such," when only their forefathers did that. Likewise here, the Jews who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ are described as having taken the calf, even though their fathers did that. Then He judged concerning them that ﴿anger from their Lord will overtake them﴾ in the Hereafter, and ﴿humiliation in the life of this world﴾, as He said, exalted is He, describing them: ﴿and humiliation and destitution were imposed upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

The second aspect: The estimated meaning is ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾, i.e., those who directly engaged in it, ﴿will be overtaken by anger﴾, i.e., anger will overtake their children, and then the governing noun was omitted, indicated by the context.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, the meaning is that every fabricator in the religion of Allah, his recompense is the anger of Allah and humiliation in this world. Malik ibn Anas said: "There is no innovator except that he finds humiliation above his head," then he recited this verse, because the innovator is a fabricator in the religion of Allah.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed﴾, this indicates that whoever commits evil deeds must first repent from them, by abandoning them first and turning back from them, and then believe after that.

Second: he believes in Allah, exalted is He, and affirms that there is no god besides Him. ﴿Indeed, your Lord, after it, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This verse indicates that evil deeds in their entirety share the property that repentance from them necessitates forgiveness, because His saying ﴿those who committed evil deeds﴾ encompasses all of them. The estimated meaning is that whoever commits all evil deeds and then repents, Allah will forgive him. This is among the greatest things that convey good tidings and joy to the sinners. And Allah knows best.
