We say: this statement is a report of what Allah, exalted is He, informed Moses, peace be upon him, when He informed him of the trial of his people and their taking the calf. At that time He told him that anger from their Lord and humiliation in the life of this world would overtake them. So this statement preceded their falling into killing and humiliation, and this interpretation is valid from this standpoint.

The second approach: The intended meaning of "those who took the calf" is their descendants who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. According to this estimation, there are two aspects to the verse:

The first aspect: The Arabs reproach the sons for the ugly deeds of their fathers, just as they do with the virtues. They say to the sons: "You did such and such," when only their forefathers did that. Likewise here, the Jews who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ are described as having taken the calf, even though their fathers did that. Then He judged concerning them that ﴿anger from their Lord will overtake them﴾ in the Hereafter, and ﴿humiliation in the life of this world﴾, as He said, exalted is He, describing them: ﴿and humiliation and destitution were imposed upon them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61].

The second aspect: The estimated meaning is ﴿Indeed, those who took the calf﴾, i.e., those who directly engaged in it, ﴿will be overtaken by anger﴾, i.e., anger will overtake their children, and then the governing noun was omitted, indicated by the context.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus do We recompense the fabricators﴾, the meaning is that every fabricator in the religion of Allah, his recompense is the anger of Allah and humiliation in this world. Malik ibn Anas said: "There is no innovator except that he finds humiliation above his head," then he recited this verse, because the innovator is a fabricator in the religion of Allah.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But those who committed evil deeds and then repented after them and believed﴾, this indicates that whoever commits evil deeds must first repent from them, by abandoning them first and turning back from them, and then believe after that.

Second: he believes in Allah, exalted is He, and affirms that there is no god besides Him. ﴿Indeed, your Lord, after it, is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This verse indicates that evil deeds in their entirety share the property that repentance from them necessitates forgiveness, because His saying ﴿those who committed evil deeds﴾ encompasses all of them. The estimated meaning is that whoever commits all evil deeds and then repents, Allah will forgive him. This is among the greatest things that convey good tidings and joy to the sinners. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 154:**

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And when the anger subsided in Moses, he took up the tablets, and in their inscription was guidance and mercy for those who fear their Lord.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, described for us what came from him (Moses) while he was angry, He described in this verse what came from him when the anger had subsided.

In the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Regarding His statement, ﴿the anger subsided in Moses﴾ (sakata), there are several opinions.

The first opinion: this expression is used in the manner of metaphor (*istiʿarah*, a figure of speech in which one thing is described by the attributes of another). It is as if the anger was urging him on to what he did, telling him: "Say to your people such-and-such, throw down the tablets, and take your brother by the head towards you." When the anger departed, it was as if it had fallen silent.

The second opinion, which is the view of ʿIkrimah: the meaning is "Moses fell silent from the anger," and the expression is inverted, as they say: "I put the qalansuwa (cap) on my head," while the meaning is "I put my head into the cap."

The third opinion: the intended meaning of *sukūt* (silence/quiet) is calm and cessation. On this view, ﴿sakata ʿan Mūsā al-ghaḍab﴾ is permissible, but *ṣamata* (to keep silent, to shut the mouth) is not, because *sakata* means *sakana* (to become still), whereas *ṣamata* means to seal one's mouth from speech, and that is not appropriate with regard to anger.

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that when he (peace be upon him) came to know that his brother Harun had not been negligent, and his excuse became clear to him, at that point his anger calmed down. This was the time when he said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my brother﴾. As he supplicated for his brother, this signalled the cessation of his anger, because that was the first of the signs of his anger that had preceded regarding the two acts he had committed. So the opposite of those two acts was made like a sign of the calming of his anger.

**The third issue:** His statement ﴿he took up the tablets﴾ refers to the tablets mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and he threw down the tablets﴾. The apparent meaning of this indicates that none of them was broken or destroyed, and what has been said, that six-sevenths of the Torah were lifted up to heaven, is not the case.

As for His statement ﴿and in their inscription (nuskhatihā)﴾: *naskh* (copying; in the sense of transferring and conveying) refers to transmission and transformation. When you write a book from another book, letter by letter, you say: "I copied (nasakhtu) that book," as if you had transferred what was in the original into the second book.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: When Moses (peace be upon him) threw down the tablets, they broke, so he fasted for forty days. Then Allah, exalted is He, restored the tablets, and in them was the exact content of the first. According to this view, His statement ﴿in their inscription﴾ means "and in what was copied from them."

As for if we say that the tablets did not break, and Moses took them in their own form after he had thrown them down, and there is no doubt that they had been written from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), then they are also a copy (nasخ) on this assumption.

His statement ﴿guidance and mercy﴾ means ﴿guidance﴾ from misguidance, ﴿and mercy﴾ from punishment, ﴿for those who fear their Lord﴾, meaning those who are fearful of their Lord.

If it is asked: The construction would be "for those who fear their Lord (rabbahum)." What is the benefit of the *lām* in His statement ﴿li-rabbihim﴾?

We say that there are several answers to this:

The first: placing the verb after its object gives it a weakness, so the *lām* entered for emphasis. Its parallel is His statement: ﴿for dreams you interpret﴾ [Yusuf: 43].

The second: it is the *lām* of purpose (*lām al-ajl*), and the meaning is: "for those who fear for the sake of their Lord, not for show or for reputation."

The third: the preposition may be added to the object even when the verb is transitive, as in your saying: "I read in the sura" and "I read the sura," and "he cast his hand" and "he cast with his hand," and in the Qur'an: ﴿Does he not know that Allah sees?﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 14], and in another place: ﴿and they know that Allah...﴾ [al-Nur: 25]. On this view, His statement ﴿li-rabbihim﴾ has a *lām* that is a connecting and emphatic particle, like His statement: ﴿it followed closely upon you﴾ [al-Naml: 72]. We have already mentioned something similar regarding His statement: ﴿and do not believe except for one who follows your religion﴾ [Al ʿImran: 73].

[p. 14]

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 155 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Musa chose from his people seventy men for Our appointment. Then when the quake seized them, he said: "My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did? This is none but Your trial, by which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will. You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy on us, and You are the best of forgivers."﴾

In this verse there are several issues.

**The first issue: al-Ikhtiyar (choice, from the root "khayr", good; "iftiʿal" form).** It means taking the best or the choicest of something, as in: "ikhtara al-shay'" when one takes its best and its choicest part. The original form of ikhtara was ikhtayara. When the yāʾ moved and was preceded by a fatha, it was changed to an alif, as in qala and baʿa. For this reason the active and passive participles have the same form, so both are called mukhtar. The original forms were mukhtayir and mukhtayar, and the yāʾ in both was changed to an alif, so the two became identical in pronunciation.

To state the matter precisely: sound limbs, according to their original soundness, are suited both to doing and to not doing, and both to an act and to its opposite. As long as they remain in this balance, they cannot become the source of one side rather than the other, for otherwise a possibility would be preferred without a preponderant cause, which is impossible. So when a person judges that the act has a greater benefit and a preponderant good for him, he has judged that this side is better for him than its opposite. When this belief arises in the heart, the act becomes preferred over abstention. Without the judgment that one side is better than the other, the act could not come from him. Since the arising of an act from a living being depends on his judgment that doing it is better than leaving it, the living being's act is therefore called an act of choice (fiʿl ikhtiyari). And Allah knows best.

If it is objected: a person may kill himself, or throw himself from the top of a mountain, although he knows that this is not good but evil.

We reply: a person does not undertake to kill himself unless he believes that by this killing he will be freed from a greater harm, and a lesser harm in comparison with a greater harm is a good rather than an evil. On this assumption the objection falls away. And Allah knows best.

**The second issue: the grammar of "from his people" (min qawmihi).** The grammarians of the school said that the meaning is: "And Musa chose from among his people seventy." The word "min" (from) was deleted, the verb was connected directly to its object, and so it took the accusative. One says: "ikhtartu min al-rijal Zaydan" (I chose Zayd from among the men), and also "ikhtartu al-rijal Zaydan" (I chose Zayd of the men). They cited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"And among us is the one who chose men for generosity and largesse, when the violent winds blow."*

Abu Ali (al-Farisi) said: The basic principle in this category is that some verbs take a second object through one preposition, and then, by extension, the preposition is deleted so that the verb takes the second object directly. Of this kind is your saying: "ikhtartu min al-rijal Zaydan," then by extension one says "ikhtartu al-rijal Zaydan." Similarly, "astaghfiru Allah min dhanbi" (I seek Allah's forgiveness for my sin) and "astaghfiru Allah dhanbi," as the poet said:

*"I seek the forgiveness of Allah for a sin I cannot count."*

One also says: "amartu Zaydan bi-l-khayr" and "amartu Zaydan al-khayr," as the poet said:

*"I ordered you to the good, so do what you were ordered to do."*

And Allah knows best.

I have another view on this, namely that the intended meaning is: "And Musa chose his people for Our appointment," where "his people" refers to the notable ones among them, using the generic term for what is actually meant. The phrase "seventy men" is then an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan). On this view there is no need for the artificial explanations that they have mentioned.

**The third issue: the number and selection of those chosen.** They mentioned that Musa, peace be upon him, chose from his people twelve tribes, six from each tribe, which made seventy-two. He said: "Let two of you remain behind." They disputed about this, and he said: "Whoever among you remains behind will have a reward like that of whoever goes forth." So Kalib and Yusha' remained behind. It is also narrated that he did not find more than sixty elders, so Allah revealed to him that he should choose ten from the young men. He chose them, and they became elders overnight. He then commanded them to fast and purify themselves, and to purify their garments, and then he went forth with them to the appointed place.

* * *

**The fourth issue: was this choice for the appointment at which God spoke to Musa and Musa asked God to be seen, or for a different place?** Commentators have several opinions on this.

**The first opinion:** It was for the appointment of speech and of seeing (God). They said: He, peace be upon him, went forth with these seventy to Mount Sinai. When Musa approached the mountain, a column of cloud descended upon it until it enveloped the entire mountain, and Musa, peace be upon him, drew near and entered it. He said to the people: "Come near," and they drew near, until when they entered the cloud they fell down in prostration. They heard Him speaking to Musa, commanding and forbidding him: "Do this, and do not do that." Then the cloud dispersed, and they came to Him and asked to see Allah. They said: ﴿O Musa, we will not believe you until we see Allah plainly, and the thunderbolt seized you﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:55). This is the quake mentioned in this verse. So Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, if You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me. Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾ The meaning of this is their saying: ﴿Show us Allah plainly﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:153).

**The second opinion:** The intended appointment is an appointment different from the appointment of speech and of asking to see (God). According to this opinion they differed in several ways:

First: Although these seventy did not worship the calf, they did not separate themselves from the calf-worshippers when the latter were occupied with worshipping it.

Second: They did not strongly forbid the worship of the calf.

Third: When they went forth to the appointment in order to repent, they called upon their Lord and said: "Give us what You have not given anyone before us, and do not give it to anyone after us." So Allah the Exalted denounced this speech of theirs, and the quake seized them.

Those who held this view argued for the soundness of their position with several points:

The first: He, exalted is He, mentioned the story of the appointment of speech and of asking to see, then followed it with the story of the calf, and then followed it with this story. The apparent sense requires that this story be different from the earlier story. It is not denied that this could be a return to completing the discourse about the first story. But what is most fitting to eloquence is to complete the discourse about one story in one setting, and then to move from it, after its completion, to another. As for mentioning part of a story, then moving from it to another story, and then after completing that moving back to the remainder of the first story, this causes a kind of confusion and disorder, and it is preferable to preserve the speech of Allah, the Exalted, from such a thing.

The second: At the appointment of speech and of asking to see, no objection appeared there, except that they said ﴿Show us Allah plainly﴾. If the quake mentioned in this verse had occurred because of that saying, it would have been necessary to say: "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us say?" But since Musa did not say this, but said ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾, we know that this quake occurred because of their undertaking to worship the calf, not because of their undertaking to ask to see (God).

The third: Allah, the Exalted, mentioned in the appointment of speech and of seeing that Musa fell down unconscious, and that He made the mountain crumble to dust. As for the appointment mentioned in this verse, Allah, the Exalted, mentioned that the people were seized by the quake, and He did not mention that Musa, peace be upon him, was seized by the quake. How can it be said that he was seized by the quake, when he is the one who said: "If You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me"? The specific attribution of these rulings to each of these two appointments indicates a strong probability that one of them is other than the other.

Those who argued that this appointment is the appointment of speech and of asking to see argued that He, exalted is He, said in the first verse: ﴿And when Musa came to Our appointment﴾ (al-A'raf 7:143). This verse shows that the word "appointment" (mīqat) is specific to that appointment. So when He said in this verse: ﴿And Musa chose his people, seventy men, for Our appointment﴾, it is necessary that the intended appointment here be the very same appointment.

Their reply: This argument is weak, and there is no doubt that the points mentioned in support of the first opinion are stronger. And Allah knows best.

**The third opinion** concerning the explanation of this appointment is what is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, set out to the foot of a mountain. Harun fell asleep, and Allah took his soul. When Musa, peace be upon him, returned, they said: "It is he who killed Harun." So Musa chose seventy men from his people, and they went to Harun. Allah brought him back to life, and he said: "No one killed me." Then the quake seized them there. This is the whole of what has been said on this subject. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth issue: they differed about that quake.** It was said that it was a quake that caused death. Al-Suddi said: Musa said: "My Lord, how shall I return to the Children of Israel, when You have destroyed their best, and no one with me from them remains? What shall I say to the Children of Israel, and how will they trust me with anyone of them after this?" So Allah, the Exalted, brought them back to life. Thus the meaning of His saying ﴿If You had willed, You would have destroyed them before, and me﴾ is that Musa, peace be upon him, feared that the Children of Israel would accuse him concerning the seventy when he returned to them, and they would not believe that they had died. So he said to his Lord: "If You had willed, You would have destroyed us before our departure for the appointment," so that the Children of Israel would witness that, and not accuse me.

The second opinion: That quake was not death. Rather, when the people saw that awe-inspiring state, a trembling seized them and they shook, until their joints almost separated and their backs almost broke. Musa, peace be upon him, feared death, and at that point he wept and supplicated, and Allah removed that quake from them.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?﴾, the scholars said: It is not permissible for Musa, peace be upon him, to think that Allah, the Exalted, destroys a people for the sins of others, so the verse must be interpreted. There are two points concerning this:

The first: It is an interrogative with the meaning of denial, and the meaning is: You will not do that. As you say: "Will you humiliate the one who serves you?" meaning: You will not do that.

The second: al-Mubarrad said: It is an interrogative of entreaty, meaning: Do not destroy us.

As for His saying ﴿This is none but Your trial﴾, al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The pronoun in His saying "hiya" (it) refers to the trial, as you say: "This is none but Zayd," and "This is none but Hind." The meaning is: That trial into which the foolish fell was none but Your trial. You led some people astray by it so that they fell into error, and You preserved others from it so that they stood firm upon the truth. Then he emphasized the clarification that all of it is from Allah, the Exalted, saying: ﴿By which You lead astray whom You will and guide whom You will﴾. Al-Wahidi said: This verse is among the clear proofs against the Qadariyya, for whom no excuse remains in its presence.

The Mu'tazila said: The Jabriyya have no connection to this verse, because He, exalted is He, did not say: "You lead astray by it whom You will of Your servants from the religion." And because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿By which You lead astray﴾, meaning by the quake, and it is known that Allah does not lead anyone astray by a quake. Therefore this verse must be interpreted figuratively. As for His saying ﴿This is none but Your trial﴾, the meaning is: Your testing and the severity of Your imposing worship upon them, since when He showed the quake, He obligated them to endure it with patience.

As for His saying ﴿By which You lead astray whom You will﴾, there are several interpretations:

The first: By this testing You guide to Paradise and reward, on condition that the one charged believes and remains in faith, and You punish whom You will, on condition that he does not believe, or that if he believes he does not persevere in it.

The second: The intended meaning of "leading astray" is "destroying." The meaning is: You destroy whom You will by this quake, and You turn it away from whom You will.

The third: Since this testing was like a cause for the guidance of those who were guided and the straying of those who strayed, it was permissible for both to be ascribed to Him.

Know that these interpretations are broad, and the rational proofs indicate that the meaning must be what we have mentioned. Its establishment is from several aspects, and it is as follows:

The first point: the capacity that is suited to both faith and disbelief does not have its influence tilt toward one of the two sides over the other, except by virtue of a determining motive (*da'iyah mutarjjihah*, a decisive inclination). The creator of that motive is God, Exalted. When that motive comes into being, the act becomes necessary. Once these premises are established, it follows that guidance is from God, Exalted, and that misguidance is from God, Exalted.

The second point: none of the sensible people wills anything but faith, truth and sincerity. If the matter were by one's own choice and intention, then every person would have to be a believer and a follower of truth. Since the matter is not like that, it is established that everything is from God, Exalted.

The third point: if the attainment of guidance and knowledge were by the act of the servant, then, since the true belief is not distinguished in his perception from the false belief, it would be impossible for him to single out one of the two beliefs for acquisition and formation. But his knowledge that this belief is the truth and that the other is falsehood requires that he first know that belief as it actually is. It would then follow that the capacity to acquire the belief is conditional upon that true belief already being present, and this implies that a thing is conditional upon itself, which is impossible. Thus it is established that it is impossible for the attainment of guidance and knowledge to come about by the creating of the servant. As for the discussion of refuting those interpretations, it has been mentioned in this book more than once. And God knows best.

Then God, Exalted, relates of Musa (peace be upon him) that he said after that: ﴿You are our Protector, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of forgivers.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿You are our Protector﴾ conveys restriction (*ḥaṣr*, exclusivity). Its meaning is that there is no protector for us, no helper, and no guide except You. This is part of what was mentioned before, His saying: ﴿You send astray by it whom You will and guide whom You will.﴾ As for His saying ﴿so forgive us and have mercy upon us﴾, its intended meaning is that his taking the initiative with the words ﴿It is none but Your trial﴾ was a great audacity, so he asked God for its forgiveness and for overlooking it. As for His saying ﴿and You are the best of forgivers﴾, its meaning is that everyone other than You who pardons a sin does so either seeking a fine reputation, or seeking an abundant reward, or to remove a base stain from the heart. In sum, that forgiveness is for seeking benefit or for repelling harm. As for You, You forgive the sins of Your servants not seeking any recompense or purpose, but purely out of grace and generosity. Therefore it is necessary to affirm with certainty that You are ﴿the best of forgivers﴾. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 156:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And prescribe for us in this world a good, and in the Hereafter; indeed, we have turned back to You. He said, "My punishment – I afflict with it whom I will; but My mercy encompasses all things. So I will prescribe it for those who fear Me and give zakah and those who believe in Our verses."﴾

Know that this is part of the supplication of Musa (ﷺ) at the moment of witnessing the quaking (al-rajfah). His saying, ﴿And prescribe for us in this world a good﴾, means that he first affirmed that he has no guardian (wali) except Allah, the Exalted, which is His saying: ﴿You are our Guardian﴾. Then, what is expected from a guardian and helper is two matters:

The first: the repelling of harm.

The second: the attainment of benefit.

The repelling of harm takes precedence over the attainment of benefit. For this reason he began by asking for the repelling of harm, which is His saying: ﴿So forgive us and have mercy upon us﴾. Then he followed it with asking for the attainment of benefit, which is His saying: ﴿And prescribe for us in this world a good and in the Hereafter﴾. His saying: ﴿And prescribe﴾ means: make it obligatory for us. The word "kitabah" is mentioned with the meaning of making obligatory. His asking for good in this world and the Hereafter is like the supplication of the believers of this nation, concerning whom Allah, the Exalted, informed in His saying: ﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201].

And know that His being the Guardian of the servant is fitting for the servant to ask of Him the repelling of harms and the attainment of benefits, so that the effects of His generosity, bounty and divinity may be manifested. Also, the servant's occupation with repentance, humility and submission is fitting for asking these things. So he mentioned the first cause first, which is His being his Guardian, and based upon it the asking of these things. Then after it he mentioned the second cause, which is the servant's occupation with repentance and humility, saying: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You.﴾ The exegetes said: ﴿hudna﴾ means we repented and returned to You. Al-Layth said: al-hawd is repentance.

He mentioned this cause too because the cause that necessitates the goodness of asking for these things is nothing but the combination of these two matters: His being God, Lord and Guardian, and our being servants to Him who repent and are humble and submissive. The first is the covenant of the might of lordship, and the second is the covenant of the humility of servanthood. When both are obtained and combined, there is no cause stronger than them.

When Allah, the Exalted, related the supplication of Musa (peace be upon him), He mentioned after it what was His answer to Musa (peace be upon him), so He, the Exalted, said: ﴿He said, "My punishment – I afflict with it whom I will"﴾. Its meaning is that I punish whom I will, and no one has any objection against Me, because all belongs to Me, and whoever disposes of what is purely his own property, no one has the right to object to him. Al-Hasan recited "man asa'a" (whoever does evil), from the word isa'ah (evil-doing), and al-Shafi'i chose this recitation. His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ has many views. It was said that what is meant by His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ is that His mercy in this world has covered everything, while in the Hereafter it is specific to the believers, and to this points His saying: ﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear Me﴾. It was also said: existence is better than non-existence, and on this basis there is no existent except that His mercy has reached it, and the lowest level of it is its existence. It was said: good is sought in itself, and evil is sought incidentally, and what is sought in itself is dominant and prevailing, while what is sought incidentally is subordinate and overcome. The Mu'tazilah said: mercy is an expression for the will to good, and there is no living being except that Allah, the Exalted, has created it for mercy, pleasure and good, because if it is benefiting or able to benefit, then it is by Allah's mercy in many respects, and if pain occurs there, it has many compensations, and these are from Allah's blessing and mercy. For this reason He said: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things.﴾ Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: His saying: ﴿And My mercy encompasses all things﴾ is of the general term by which the specific is intended, like His saying: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾ [al-Naml: 23].

* * *

As for His saying: ﴿So I will prescribe it for those who fear Me and give zakah and those who believe in Our verses.﴾

Know that all of Allah's obligations are restricted to two kinds:

The first: the abstentions (turuk), which are the things it is obligatory for a person to leave, to guard against and to avoid. This kind is indicated by His saying: ﴿for those who fear Me﴾.

The second: the actions. Those obligations are either directed toward a person's wealth or toward his own self.

As for the first category: it is zakah, and to it points His saying: ﴿and give zakah﴾.

As for the second category: it includes what is obligatory upon a person in knowledge and action. As for knowledge, it is recognition (ma'rifah); as for action, it is affirmation by the tongue and action by the limbs, and prayer enters into them. To this whole is indicated His saying: ﴿and those who believe in Our verses﴾. Its parallel is His saying, exalted is He, at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿a guidance for the righteous, who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and from what We have provided them, they spend﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2–3].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 157:

Page 20

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins on them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and makes unlawful for them the vile things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them. So those who believe in him, honour him, help him, and follow the light which has been sent down with him—it is they who are the successful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that among the attributes of those for whom mercy is written in this world and the Hereafter are piety, giving zakat, and belief in the signs, He added to that that it is among their attributes to follow ﴿the Prophet, the unlettered, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. The scholars differed concerning this. Some said: the meaning is that they follow him by believing in his prophethood, since they found his description in the Torah; for it is not permissible that they follow him in his laws before he was sent to mankind. And as for His saying ﴿and the Gospel﴾, they said the meaning is that he will be found written in the Gospel, because it is impossible that they found him in it before God sent down the Gospel. Others said: rather, the meaning is those of the Children of Israel who lived during the time of the Messenger. So He, exalted is He, explained that these later ones will not have the mercy of the Hereafter written for them unless they follow the Messenger, the Prophet, the unlettered. The second view is closer, because following him before he was sent and appeared is not possible. So it is as though He, exalted is He, explained by this verse that this mercy is not attained by the Children of Israel except by those who were pious, gave zakat, and believed in the proofs in the time of Moses, and by those whose attribute in the days of the Messenger is that, together with that, they follow the unlettered Prophet in his laws.

Having known this, we say: He, exalted is He, described Muhammad (ﷺ) in this verse with nine attributes.

The first attribute: that he is a Messenger. This term, by custom, is specific to the one whom God has sent to creation to convey the obligations.

The second attribute: that he is a Prophet, which indicates that he is elevated in rank with God, exalted is He.

The third attribute: that he is unlettered. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of ﴿the unlettered﴾ is one who is in the state of the nation of the Arabs. He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: ("We are an unlettered nation; we do not write and we do not calculate"). Most of the Arabs did not write or read, and the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, was like that; for this reason He described him as unlettered. The people of verification said: his being unlettered in this sense was among his miracles, and its explanation is in several aspects:

The first: that he, upon him be prayers and peace, would recite to them the Book of God, exalted is He, composed in verse, time after time, without altering its words or changing its expressions. An Arab orator who extemporises a speech and then repeats it will inevitably add to it and subtract from it, by little or much. Then the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, although he did not write and did not read, recited the Book of God without addition, subtraction, or alteration. This was among the miracles, and to it refers His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We shall make you recite, and you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6].

The second: that if he had known how to write and read, he would have been suspected of perhaps having studied the books of the ancients, and thus acquired these sciences from that study. When he brought this great Qur'an, containing many sciences, without learning or study, that was a miracle. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿You did not recite any book before it, nor did you write it with your right hand; otherwise the falsifiers would have doubted﴾ [al-Ankabut: 48].

The third: that learning to write is an easy matter, for even the least intelligent and perceptive of people learn writing with little effort. So not learning it indicates a great deficiency in understanding. Then God, exalted is He, gave him the knowledge of the first and the last, and bestowed upon him sciences and realities that no human has attained; yet with that great strength of intellect and understanding, He made him such that he did not learn writing, which is easy to learn even for the least intelligent of creatures. So the combination of these two opposing states was like the combination of two opposites, and that is among the matters that break habit, and is like miracles.

Page 21

The fourth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. This indicates that his description and the soundness of his prophethood are written in the Torah and the Gospel; for if that were not written, mentioning this statement would be among the greatest things to repel the Jews and Christians from accepting his word, since persistence in lying and slander is among the greatest deterrents, and a sensible person does not strive for what would diminish his standing and repel people from accepting his word. So when he said that, it indicates that this description was mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel, and that is among the greatest proofs of the soundness of his prophethood.

The fifth attribute: His saying: ﴿who enjoins on them what is right﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible that His saying ﴿who enjoins on them what is right﴾ is a new sentence, and it is permissible that the meaning is "they find him written with them" that he ﴿enjoins on them what is right﴾. I say: the comprehensive principles of enjoining what is right are summed up in his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: ("Reverence for God's command and compassion for God's creation"). That is because what exists is either necessarily existent in its essence, or possibly existent in its essence. As for what is necessary in its essence, it is God, majestic is His majesty; and there is no good more noble than revering Him, manifesting servanthood to Him, showing humility and submission at the threshold of His might, acknowledging that He is described by attributes of perfection, free from deficiencies and defects, exalted above opposites and equals. As for what is possible in its essence: if it is not a living being, there is no way to bring benefit to it, since benefit is conditioned on life; yet still it is necessary to regard all of it with an eye of reverence, insofar as it is created by God, exalted is He, and insofar as every atom of created things, being a compelling proof and a dazzling demonstration of His unity and transcendence, must be regarded with an eye of honour. And insofar as God, exalted is He, has in every atom of created things wondrous secrets and hidden wisdoms, it is necessary to regard them with an eye of honour. As for if that created thing is of the animal kind, it is necessary to show compassion toward it to the utmost extent a human can, and this includes kindness to parents, maintaining ties of kinship, and spreading good. Thus it is established that his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: ("Reverence for God's command, and compassion for God's creation") is a comprehensive word encompassing all aspects of enjoining what is right.

The sixth attribute: His saying: ﴿and forbids them what is wrong﴾. What is meant by it is the opposites of the matters mentioned: worship of idols, speaking about God's attributes without knowledge, disbelief in what God sent down to the prophets, severing ties of kinship, and disobedience to parents.

The seventh attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and makes lawful for them the good things﴾. Some people said: what is meant by "the good things" is the things God has ruled to be lawful. This is far-fetched, for two reasons:

The first: on this reading the verse would become "and makes lawful for them the lawful things," which is pure repetition.

The second: on this reading the verse would lose its benefit, because we do not know which things God has made lawful, or how many they are. Rather, it is necessary that what is meant by "the good things" is the things that are pleasant by nature, because consuming them yields pleasure, and the default regarding benefits is permissibility. So this verse indicates that the default regarding everything the soul finds agreeable and the nature finds delightful is permissibility, unless there is a separate proof.

The eighth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and makes unlawful for them the vile things﴾. ʿAṭāʾ reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: he means carrion, blood, and what is mentioned in Surat al-Ma'idah up to His saying ﴿that is a transgression﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. I say: everything that the nature finds loathsome and the soul finds repugnant, its consumption causes harm, and the default regarding harms is prohibition; so its implication is that everything the nature finds loathsome, the default regarding it is prohibition, unless there is a separate proof. Upon this principle, al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, derived the prohibition of selling dogs, because he narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in the Sahihayn, that he said: ("The dog is vile, and its price is vile"). And if it is established that its price is vile, it must be unlawful, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and makes unlawful for them the vile things﴾. Also, wine is unlawful because it is an abomination (rijs), by the evidence of His saying: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90] up to His saying ﴿an abomination﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]; and the abomination is vile, by the consensus of the lexicographers upon it; and the vile is unlawful by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and makes unlawful for them the vile things﴾.

* * *

The ninth attribute: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾. In this there are two issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿĀmir alone read ʾāṣārahum in the plural, while the rest read ʾiṣrahum in the singular. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi said: iṣr is a verbal noun which applies to multiplicity while its form is singular, as is indicated by its being added to a plural, as in His saying: ﴿Had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sights﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. Whoever reads it in the plural intends various kinds of covenants that differ; and verbal nouns may be pluralised when their kinds differ, as in His saying: ﴿and you think about God, the thoughts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10].

The second issue: iṣr is the heavy burden that binds its bearer, that is, prevents him from movement because of its weight. What is meant by it is that the law of Moses, peace be upon him, was severe. As for His saying ﴿and the shackles that were upon them﴾, what is meant is the hardships that were in their acts of worship, such as cutting off the trace of urine, killing oneself in repentance, cutting off the sinning limbs, and tracing the veins out of the flesh. God made these shackles because prohibition prevents from action, just as a shackle prevents from action. It is also said: when the Children of Israel stood to pray they would wear coarse garments and bind their hands to their necks, out of humility before God, exalted is He. According to this view, "shackles" is not used metaphorically.

Know that this verse indicates that the default regarding harms is that they should not be legislated, because everything that is harmful is a burden and a shackle; and the apparent sense of this text requires non-legislation. This is akin to his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: ("There is no harm nor reciprocating harm in Islam"), and to his saying, upon him be prayers and peace: ("I was sent with the easy, tolerant, lenient monotheism"). This is a great principle in the Shari'ah.

Know that when He described Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, with these nine attributes, He said after them: ﴿So those who believe in him﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās said: meaning from among the Jews. ﴿and honour him﴾, meaning revere him. The author of al-Kashshaf said: the origin of ta'zir is prevention, and from it comes ta'zir, which is beating short of the prescribed punishment, because it prevents a return to what is ugly.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and help him﴾, that is, against his enemy; ﴿and follow the light which was sent down with him﴾, which is the Qur'an. It was also said: the guidance, the clarification, and the message. It was also said: the truth whose clarification is in the hearts like the clarity of light.

If it is said: how is it possible to take "light" here to mean the Qur'an? The Qur'an was not sent down with Muhammad; it was sent down with Gabriel.

We reply: its meaning is that it was sent down with his prophethood, because his prophethood appeared together with the appearance of the Qur'an.

Then, when He, exalted is He, mentioned these attributes, He said: ﴿It is they who are the successful﴾, that is, they are those who attain the sought goal in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 158 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all, [from] He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. There is no deity except Him; He gives life and causes death. So believe in Allah and His Messenger, the unlettered prophet who believes in Allah and His words, and follow him that you may be guided."﴾

Know that when He, the Exalted, said, ﴿So I will ordain it for those who fear Me﴾, and then explained that among the conditions for attaining mercy for those God-fearing people is that they follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, He affirmed in this verse his mission to all creation in its entirety. So He said: ﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all"﴾. In this statement there are two issues:

The first issue: This verse indicates that Muhammad, peace be upon him, was sent to all of creation. A group of Jews called the ʿIsawiyya (ʿIsawiyya), who are the followers of ʿIsa al-Isfahani, said: Muhammad is a truthful messenger sent to the Arabs, and not sent to the Children of Israel. Our proof against their statement is this verse, because His saying ﴿O mankind﴾ is an address that encompasses all people.

Then He said: ﴿indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all﴾, and this requires that he was sent to all people. Moreover, it is known by tawatur (mass transmission) from his religion that he claimed to be sent to all the worlds. Then it is either said that he was a true Messenger or that he was not so. If he was a true Messenger, lying about him is impossible, and it becomes necessary to affirm with certainty that he is truthful in everything he claims. Since it is established by tawatur and by the apparent meaning of this verse that he claimed to be sent to all creation, it is necessary that he was truthful in this claim, and that refutes the view of whoever says that he was sent only to the Arabs and not to the Children of Israel.

As for the statement of the one who says that he was not a true Messenger, this entails discrediting his being a Messenger to the Arabs and to others. Thus it is established that the claim that he is a messenger to some of creation and not others is an invalid and self-contradictory statement.

Given this is established, we say: As for His saying ﴿Say, "O mankind, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you all"﴾, among the scholars some said it is a general (ʿamm) term that has been subject to takhsis (specification), and others denied that. As for the first group, they said it has been subject to specification in two respects:

The first: He is a Messenger to people insofar as they are among the legally responsible (mukallafun). But if they are not among the legally responsible, he is not a Messenger to them. This is because he, peace be upon him, said: "The pen is lifted from three: from the child until he reaches puberty, from the sleeper until he awakens, and from the insane until he recovers."

The second: He is the Messenger of Allah to everyone to whom the news of his existence and the news of his miracles and laws has reached, so that it is possible for them to follow him at that point. But if we suppose a people in some corner of the world to whom the news of his existence and his miracles has not reached, they are not legally responsible for affirming his prophethood. Some people denied that the verse is subject to specification on these two grounds:

As for the first: its explanation is that His saying ﴿O mankind﴾ is an address, and this address encompasses only those who are legally responsible. Given this, the people included under His saying ﴿O mankind﴾ are none other than the legally responsible among mankind, and on this assumption it does not follow that His saying ﴿O mankind﴾ is a general term subject to specification.

As for the second: it is very unlikely to say that there exists in some corner of the earth a people to whom the news of the appearance of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the news of his miracles and laws has not reached. And when that is almost inconceivable, there is no need for us to commit to this specification.

The second issue: Although this verse indicates that Muhammad, peace be upon him, was sent to all creation, it contains no indication that other prophets, peace be upon them, were not sent to all creation. Rather, one must refer to the other evidences to determine whether any of the other prophets was sent to all creation or not. We say: A group of scholars held that no one other than him was sent to all creation, based on his saying, peace be upon him: "I have been given five things that no one before me was given: I have been sent to the red and the black; the earth has been made for me a place of prostration and a means of purification; I have been supported against my enemy by terror that strikes [them] from a distance of a month's journey; spoils have been made lawful for me though they were not lawful for anyone before me; and I was told, 'Ask, and it will be given you.' So I have kept it hidden as an intercession for my community."

It may be said: This report does not establish what is being sought, because it is not unlikely that what is meant is that the collection of these five was among the special privileges of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and was not granted to anyone else; and it does not follow from this collection being among his special privileges that each individual item of this collection is among his special privileges. Also, it has been said that Adam, peace be upon him, was sent to all his descendants, and on this assumption he was sent to all people. And that when Noah, peace be upon him, came out of the ark, he was sent to those who were with him, although all people at that time were none other than that people.

* * *

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, know that when He, the Exalted, commanded His Messenger to say to all people, "Indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you," He followed it with mention of what indicates the soundness of this claim.

Know that this claim is not complete, and its benefit does not become apparent, except by establishing four principles.

The first principle: Establishing that the world has a God who is living, knowing and powerful. What indicates this is what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿He to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. This is because the bodies of the heavens and the earth indicate their need for a Maker who is living, knowing and powerful, from many aspects mentioned in the Mighty Qur'an, and their explanation and establishment is mentioned in this commentary. We needed to establish this principle for the wisdom of legal obligation and the sending of messengers, because if the world had no influencer that affects its existence, or if it had an influencer but that influencer were a cause acting by necessity in its essence and not an agent acting by choice, then the affirmation of the sending of prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, would not be possible.

The second principle: Establishing that the God of the world is one, exalted above partner, equal and rival, and to this He points with His saying: ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾. We needed to establish this principle for the wisdom of legal obligation and the permissibility of sending messengers, because if the world had two gods, and one of the two gods sent a prophet to creation, then perhaps this person whom the messenger calls to worship this god was not created by him but was created by the second god. On this assumption, it would be obligatory for this person to worship and obey this god, so sending the messenger to him and imposing obedience upon him would be oppressive and false. But once it is established that God is one, then all creation is His servants, His obligation upon all is binding, and the submission of all to His commands and prohibitions is necessary. Thus it is established that if it is not established that God, the Exalted, is one, then sending messengers and sending down books containing obligations is not permissible.

The third principle: Establishing that He, the Exalted, is able to resurrect, to gather and to raise up, and to bring about the Resurrection. This is because, if this were not established, then engagement in obedience and abstention from disobedience would be futile and vain. To this principle He points with His saying: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾, for when He gave life at first, it is established that He is able to give life a second time, and so He is able to restore, gather and raise up. On this assumption, the first giving of life is a great favour, so it is not far from Him, the Exalted, to demand servitude from him, so that his performance of that obedience stands in place of thanks for the first giving of life. Also, since the first giving of life indicates His power to give life a second time, He is then able to deliver the recompense to him.

Know that once the soundness of these three principles is established, it is established that it is valid for Allah, the Exalted, to send messengers and to demand of creation the obligations, because on this assumption all creation are His servants and they have no master other than Him; moreover He is the bestower of the greatest blessings upon all; and moreover He is able to deliver recompense to them after their death. Each of these three reasons is a complete cause for the goodness of His imposing obligations upon creation. As for the first cause, it is good for a master to demand obedience and service from his servant. As for the second cause, it is good for a benefactor to demand gratitude and obedience from the one benefited. As for the third cause, it is good for one who is able to deliver complete recompense to the responsible person to impose upon him some kind of obedience. Thus it is evident that once the three principles are established by the proofs that Allah the Exalted mentioned in this verse, it is necessary to be certain that it is good for Allah to send messengers, and it is permissible for Him to single them out with various kinds of obligations. Thus it is established that the mentioned verses indicate that the world has a living, knowing, powerful God, that this God is one, and that it is good for Him to send messengers and to send down books.

* * *

Know that when He, the Exalted, established these principles by these proofs mentioned in this verse, He mentioned after it His saying: ﴿So believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. This ordering is most excellent, because when He first showed that the claim of the sending of prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, is a permissible and possible matter, He followed it with mention that Muhammad is a true messenger from Allah. For whoever seeks to establish a claim must first demonstrate its permissibility, then its actuality. Then He began with His saying: ﴿So believe in Allah﴾, because we have made clear that belief in Allah is the root, and belief in prophethood and messengership is a branch of it, and the root must be placed first. For this reason He began with ﴿So believe in Allah﴾, then followed it with ﴿and His Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, who believes in Allah and His words﴾.

Know that this is a reference to mentioning the miracles that indicate that he is a true prophet, and its explanation is that the miracles of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were of two kinds:

The first kind: the miracles that appeared in his blessed person. The greatest and most noble of these is that he was an unlettered man who had not learned from a teacher, had not studied a book, and had not happened to sit with any of the scholars, for Mecca was not a city of scholars, and the Messenger of Allah was never absent from Mecca for a long period such that it could be said that during that absence he learned many sciences. Then, despite that, Allah opened to him the door of knowledge and verification, and sent down upon him this Qur'an containing the sciences of the former and the latter people. So the appearance of these great sciences upon him, though he was an unlettered man who had not met a teacher nor studied a book, is among the greatest miracles, and to this He points with His saying: ﴿the unlettered Prophet﴾.

The second type of his miracles consists of the matters that appeared from the very essence of his being, such as the splitting of the moon and the gushing of water from between his fingers. These are called the Words of Allah, the Exalted. Do you not see that when the coming into being of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) was a strange matter, contrary to what is customary, Allah the Exalted named him a Word (kalima)? Likewise, since miracles are strange matters that break the normal course of things, there is no remoteness in calling them the Words of Allah the Exalted. This type is what is meant by His saying: ﴿He believes in Allah and His words﴾, that is, he believes in Allah and in all the miracles that Allah manifested through him. By this way, he established the proof that he was a truthful prophet from Allah.

Know that when the proofs that we have established confirmed the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), it was necessary that he mention, following this, the way by which his law can be known in detail, and this is nothing other than returning to his sayings and actions. To this is the allusion in the Exalted's saying: ﴿And follow him﴾.

Know that following (mutabaʿa) covers following in speech and following in action. As for following in speech, it is that the responsible person complies with everything he says regarding the two sides of command and prohibition, and encouragement and warning. As for following in action, it is an expression for performing the like of what the one followed did, whether it was on the side of doing or on the side of abstaining. Thus it is established that the wording ﴿and follow him﴾ covers both categories. It is also established that the apparent sense of a command is obligation, so the Exalted's saying ﴿and follow him﴾ is a proof that it is obligatory to submit to him in every command and prohibition, and it is obligatory to take him as a model in everything he did, except what a specific proof has excluded, namely the matters that have been established, by a separate proof, to be among the special privileges of the Messenger (ﷺ).

If it is said: The thing that the Messenger brought may be (done) on the basis that it was obligatory for him, and it may also be (done) on the basis that it was recommended. Given that he did it on the basis that it was recommended, if we did it on the basis that it was obligatory for us, that would be an abandonment and a breach of his pledge. The verse indicates the obligation of following him, so it is established that the Messenger's undertaking of that act does not indicate its obligation upon us.

We say: Following in action is an expression for performing the like of the act the one followed performed, as evidenced by the fact that whoever performs an act, and then another agrees with him in that act, it is said that he followed him in it; and if he did not perform it, it is said that he opposed him in it. So since performing the like of the followed one's act is following, and the verse indicates the obligation of following, it follows that the like of the Messenger's act (ﷺ) is obligatory upon the community.

There remains here that we do not know whether he (peace be upon him) did that with the intention of obligation or with the intention of recommendation. We say: the state of motives and resolutions is unknown, while the state of performing the apparent act and the sensible deed is known. Therefore it is necessary not to turn to the investigation of the state of resolutions and motives, since they are matters hidden from us, and to judge the obligation of following in the apparent action, since it is among the matters that can be observed. Thus this doubt is removed. Its formulation: this verse indicates that the basic principle regarding every act the Messenger performed is that it is obligatory upon us to perform its like, unless a specific proof excludes it.

Having known this, we say: when we want to judge the obligation of some deed among deeds,

we say: this deed's doing is better than its abandonment. When the matter is like that, then we know that the Messenger had performed it in general, because it is a necessary knowledge that the Messenger could not persist throughout his life in abandoning the better. So we know that he (peace be upon him) performed this better course. As for whether he performed the better of the two sides, that is doubtful, and the doubtful does not oppose the known. Thus it is established that he (peace be upon him) performed the better side. Whenever that is established, it is obligatory for us to do likewise, by His saying in this verse: ﴿and follow him﴾. This is a noble principle and a universal rule in knowing the rulings, pointing to the texts, by His saying: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but a revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm 53:3-4], so it is obligatory upon us to do likewise by His saying: ﴿and follow him﴾.

As for His saying: ﴿so that you may be guided﴾, there are two discussions:

The first: the word "laʿalla" is for hope, and that is not fitting for Allah, so it must be interpreted.

The second: its apparent meaning requires that He, the Exalted, intended guidance and faith from all the responsible persons, according to the Muʿtazila, and the discussion in establishing these two points has preceded in this book many times, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

**Commentary on the verse: "And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly."**

The Exalted said: ﴿And among the people of Moses is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾

Know that when the Exalted described the Messenger, and mentioned that it is obligatory upon creation to follow him, He mentioned that among the people of Moses (peace be upon him) there are those who followed the truth and were guided to it. He made clear that they are a group, because the word *ummah* (community) indicates multitude. The scholars differed over when this community came into being and in what era it existed.

It was said that they are the Jews who lived in the time of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) and embraced Islam, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and Ibn Suriya. The objection to this is that they were few in number, whereas the word *ummah* requires multitude. The answer to this can be that, since they were differing in religion, the term *ummah* could be applied to them, as in the Exalted's words: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a community﴾ [al-Nahl: 120].

It was also said that they are a people who walked upon the true religion that Moses brought, called people to it, and preserved it from distortion and alteration during the time when the Children of Israel had split apart and introduced innovations. It is possible that they remained upon this until the coming of Jesus, and then they entered his religion. It is also possible that they perished before that.

Al-Suddi and a group of exegetes said: When the Children of Israel disbelieved and killed the prophets, one tribe (*sibt*) remained among the twelve. They did not do what the others did, and they asked God to rescue them from among them. So God opened for them a passage (*nafaq*) in the earth, and they travelled through it until they emerged from beyond China.

Then these people differed. Some said that they remained adhering to the religion of Judaism until now. Others said that they are now upon the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), facing the Kaʿbah, having abandoned the Sabbath and adhered to Friday, not wronging one another, not envying one another, and no one from us reaches them nor any of them reaches us.

Some verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) said: This view is weak, because it must be said either: the news of Muhammad (ﷺ) reached them, or the news did not reach them.

If we say that his news reached them, and then they persisted in Judaism, then they are disbelievers, so how is it permissible to describe them as a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly?

And if we say that the news of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not reach them, this is far-fetched, because his news reached us, even though the motives for transmitting reports about them are not strong. How is it conceivable that the news of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him) would not reach them, when the world has been filled with his news and mention?

If they say: Has not the news of Gog and Magog reached us while our news has not reached them?

We say: This is disputed. From where is it known that our news has not reached them?

This is the sum of what has been said on this matter.

Having understood this, we say: His saying ﴿who guide by the truth﴾ means that they call people to guidance by the truth, ﴿and by it act justly﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: *ʿadl* is judgment by the truth. It is said: he judges by the truth and acts justly (*yaʿdilu*); he is a just arbiter (*hakam ʿadil*). From this is His saying: ﴿And you will never be able to act justly between wives﴾ [al-Nisa: 129], and His saying: ﴿And when you speak, be just﴾ [al-Anʿam: 152].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 160:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them into twelve tribes, as nations. And We revealed to Moses when his people asked him for water: Strike the rock with your staff. And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quail. Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse is to explain two aspects of the circumstances of the Children of Israel.

The first: He, exalted is He, made them into twelve tribes (asbat, sing. sibt, "tribe" or "lineage"). This was already mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, divided the Children of Israel into twelve groups, because they descended from twelve men, the sons of Ya'qub (Jacob). He distinguished them and did this so that they would not envy one another, lest chaos and disorder ensue among them. His saying ﴿And We divided them﴾ means: We made them into pieces (qita'), that is, groups (firaq), and distinguished some of them from others. It is also read "wa-qata'nahum" with the lighter pronunciation. Here there are two questions.

The first question: The specification (tamyiz) of numbers other than ten is singular, so what is the reason for its coming in the plural? Why was it not said "ithnay 'ashara sibtan" (twelve tribes)?

The answer: The meaning is "And We divided them into twelve clans (qabilah), and each clan is asbat," so he placed asbat in the position of qabilah.

The second question: He said ﴿twelve asbat﴾ although sibt is masculine, not feminine.

The answer: Al-Farra' said: He said it that way because He, exalted is He, mentioned after it ﴿umaman﴾, so the feminine gender went to the umam (nations). Then he said: If he had said "ithnay 'ashara" because sibt is masculine, it would have been permissible. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is ﴿And We divided them into twelve﴾ groups, "asbatan," so his saying ﴿asbatan﴾ is an adjective (na't) of an omitted noun, which is firqah (group). Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: His saying ﴿asbatan﴾ is not a specification, but rather a substitute (badal) for his saying ﴿twelve﴾.

As for his saying ﴿umaman﴾, the author of al-Kashshaf said: It is a substitute for ﴿twelve﴾, meaning: We divided them into nations, because each tribe was a great nation and a dense assembly in number, and each one was heading in a direction different from the other and hardly could they unite. It is also read "ithnatay 'ashirata" with the kasra on the shin.

The second aspect of the circumstances of the Children of Israel is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to Moses when his people asked him for water: Strike the rock with your staff.﴾ This story has also been mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. Al-Hasan said: It was only a rock which he encountered, and only a staff which he took.

Know that they sometimes needed water to drink during the wandering (al-tih), so God, exalted is He, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, to strike the rock with his staff. They would take it along with themselves and take from it the amount they needed. His saying ﴿fa-inbajasat﴾: al-Wahidi said: "fa-inbajasa al-ma'" and its inbijas means its bursting forth. It is said: "bajasa al-ma'u yabjusu," and "inbajasa" and "tabajjasa" when it gushes forth. This is the statement of the lexicographers. Then he said: Inbijas and infijar are the same, and on this basis there is no contradiction between the inbijas mentioned here and the infijar mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah. Others said: Inbijas is the water coming out in small quantity, and infijar is its coming out in abundance. The way to reconcile them is that the water began to come out slightly, then it became abundant. This distinction is related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned how He gave them drink, He mentioned secondly that He shaded them with clouds, and thirdly that He sent down upon them manna and quail. There is no doubt that the totality of these circumstances is a great blessing from God, exalted is He, because He facilitated for them food and drink in the best manner and warded off from them the harms of the sun.

Then He said: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you.﴾ The intended meaning is to restrict themselves to that food and to leave other than it.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾, and there is an ellipsis in it, because this statement is only fitting to mention if they had transgressed what God had commanded them. That may be by saying that they stored up (food) although God had forbidden them from it, or that they proceeded to eat at a time God had forbidden them from, or because they asked for something other than that although God had forbidden them from it. It is known that when the accountable person commits what is prohibited, he is a wrongdoer to himself. Therefore God, exalted is He, described them with it, and He drew attention with His saying: ﴿And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ This is because when the accountable person proceeds to disobedience, he harms no one but himself, inasmuch as he strives to make his own self deserving of great punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 161–162:

The Exalted said: ﴿And when it was said to them, "Dwell in this town and eat from it wherever you wish, and say, 'Hittah (a request for forgiveness),' and enter the gate prostrating; We will forgive you your sins, and We will increase the doers of good."﴾ ﴿So those who did wrong among them changed the word to other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon them a punishment from the sky for their wrongdoing.﴾

Know that this story is also mentioned, with explanation and elucidation, in Surat al-Baqarah.

It remains to be said: the wording of this verse differs from the wording of the verse in Surat al-Baqarah in several respects:

The first: In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and here He said: ﴿And when it was said to them, "Dwell in this town"﴾.

The second: In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿then eat﴾ with the fa' (fa, "then"), and here ﴿and eat﴾ with the waw (wa, "and").

The third: In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿raghadan (in abundance)﴾, and this word is not mentioned in this surah.

The fourth: In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿and enter the gate prostrating and say, "Hittah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and here He mentioned them in reverse order.

The fifth: In al-Baqarah He said ﴿We will forgive you your wrongs (khataya)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and here He said: ﴿We will forgive you your sins (khati'atikum)﴾.

The sixth: In Surat al-Baqarah He said ﴿and We will increase﴾ with the waw, and here He omitted the waw.

The seventh: In Surat al-Baqarah He said ﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], and here He said: ﴿So We sent upon them﴾.

The eighth: In Surat al-Baqarah He said ﴿for what they were defiantly disobeying (yafsuqun)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 59], and here He said: ﴿for what they were wronging (yazlimun)﴾.

Know that these wordings are close in meaning, and there is absolutely no contradiction between them, and it is possible to mention the benefits of these different wordings.

As for the first: In Surat al-Baqarah He said: ﴿Enter this town﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], and here He said: ﴿Dwell﴾. The difference is that entering the town must come first, then dwelling in it second.

As for the second: In al-Baqarah He said: ﴿Enter this town, then eat﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], with the fa'. Here He said: ﴿Dwell in this town and eat﴾ with the waw. The difference is that entering is a specific state which, once it occurs, passes away; for one is only "entering" at the very beginning of entering, and whatever follows that is dwelling, not entering.

Having established this, we say: entering is a state that is over and gone and has no continuity. Therefore it is fitting to mention the fa' of immediate sequence after it, which is why He said: ﴿Enter this town﴾. As for dwelling, it is a continuous, enduring state. So eating occurs together with it, not immediately after it, and the difference becomes clear.

As for the third: which is that He mentioned ﴿raghadan﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah and did not mention it here. The difference is that eating immediately after entering the town would be more pleasant, because the need for that food was more complete and perfect. And since that eating was more pleasant, He therefore mentioned in it the phrase ﴿raghadan﴾. As for eating while the town is being dwelt in, it is evident that it does not occur in a place of intense need unless the pleasure in it is complete, so He therefore left out the phrase ﴿raghadan﴾ there.

As for the fourth: which is His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿and enter the gate prostrating and say, "Hittah"﴾, while in Surat al-A'raf it is the reverse. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that it is fitting to place either of these two mentions before the other; but since the aim of both is to glorify God the Exalted and to show submission and humility, the situation does not differ according to the order of precedence and sequence.

As for the fifth: which is that He said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿khataya﴾ and here He said: ﴿khati'atikum﴾. This is an indication that these sins, whether they are few or many, are forgiven upon making this supplication and humble entreaty.

As for the sixth: which is that He, the Exalted, said in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿and We will increase﴾ with the waw, and here He omitted the waw. The benefit of omitting the waw is that it is a resumption (isti'naf), and the sense is as if someone said: "And what resulted after the forgiveness?" So it was said to him: ﴿We will increase the doers of good﴾.

As for the seventh: which is the difference between His saying ﴿fa-anzalna﴾ and His saying ﴿fa-arsalna﴾. This is because inzal (sending down) does not imply multiplicity, while irsal (sending) implies it. So it is as if He, the Exalted, began by sending down a small punishment, then made it abundant. This is similar to what we mentioned regarding the difference between His saying ﴿fa-inbajasat﴾ and His saying ﴿fa-infajarat﴾.

As for the eighth: which is the difference between His saying ﴿yazlimun﴾ and His saying ﴿yafsuqun﴾. This is because they are described as wrongdoers, since they wronged themselves, and as defiantly disobedient, since they departed from the obedience of God the Exalted. So the benefit of mentioning these two descriptions is to draw attention to the occurrence of both of these matters. This is what came to mind concerning the benefits of these different wordings, and the complete knowledge of them is with God the Exalted.
