﴿Ask them about the town that was by the sea, when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath, when their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them. Thus did We test them, because they were defiant.﴾

Know that this story is also mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. It contains several issues.

**The first issue:** His saying, ﴿Ask them﴾. The purpose is to know this story from them, because it had already become known to the Messenger from Allah, the Exalted. The purpose of mentioning this question is one of several things:

The first: the purpose of mentioning this question is to establish that they had committed this grave sin and flagrant disobedience, as a warning to them that their persistence in disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in his miracles is not something that has newly arisen in this time. Rather, this disbelief and persistence existed among their forebears from ancient times.

The second benefit: a person may say to another, "Is this matter such-and-such?" in order to show that he is well informed about that event and not unaware of its details. Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was an unlettered man who had learned no knowledge and had not studied any book, yet he related these stories as they occurred, without any discrepancy, addition or omission, this was regarded as a kind of miracle (mu'jiz, a supernatural proof of prophethood).

**The second issue:** Most scholars hold that that town was Aylah. It has also been said that it was Madyan, and it has been said that it was Tiberias. The Arabs call a city a *qaryah* (town). It is reported from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': "I have not seen men from cities more eloquent than al-Hasan and al-Hajjaj," meaning two men from the people of cities.

His saying, ﴿that was by the sea﴾, means near the sea, close to it and on its shore. *Al-hudur* (presence) is the opposite of absence, as in His saying: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196].

His saying, ﴿when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾, means they exceeded Allah's limit concerning it, namely by hunting on Saturday, which they had been forbidden to do. It was read as *ya'addūna* (they transgress), meaning *ya'tadūna* (they exceed bounds), with the *tā'* assimilated into the *dāl* and its vowel transferred to the *'ayn*. It was also read as *yu'iddūna* (they prepare), from *al-i'dād* (preparation), since they used to prepare hunting equipment on Saturday, although they were commanded not to occupy themselves on it with anything other than worship. *Al-sabt* (the Sabbath) is a verbal noun from *sabatat al-yahūd*, when the Jews honoured their Sabbath. So His saying, ﴿when they transgressed in the matter of the Sabbath﴾ means they transgressed in honouring this day. Likewise His saying, ﴿on their Sabbath day﴾ means the day of their honouring the matter of the Sabbath. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath﴾. It is further confirmed by the reading of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, *yawma asbātihim* (on the day of their Sabbaths). It was also read *lā yasbutūna* with a *ḍammah* on the *bā'*, and 'Alī (may Allah be pleased with him) read *lā yusbitūna* with a *ḍammah* on the *yā'*, from *asbatū* (they observed the Sabbath). It is reported from al-Hasan: *lā yusbatūna* in the passive form.

His saying, ﴿when their fish came to them﴾ is governed by His saying, ﴿they transgressed﴾. The meaning is: ask them when they transgressed at the time of the coming of the fish. His saying, ﴿on their Sabbath day openly﴾ means visible upon the water. *Shurra'an* is the plural of *shāri'* and *shāri'ah*. Everything that draws near something is *shāri'*; a house that is *shāri'ah* is one that is close to the road, and stars that are *shāri'ah* are ones that are close to setting. On this basis, the fish used to approach the town so that they could catch them.

Ibn 'Abbās and Mujāhid said: The Jews were commanded to observe the day that you (the Muslims) were commanded to observe, namely Friday, but they abandoned it and chose Saturday. So Allah tested them with it: hunting was forbidden to them on it, and they were commanded to honour it. When Saturday came, the fish would appear to them, and they would look at them in the sea. When Saturday ended, the fish would depart and would not return except on the following Saturday. That was a trial with which Allah tested them. This is the meaning of His saying, ﴿and on the day they did not observe the Sabbath, they did not come to them﴾.

His saying, ﴿Thus did We test them﴾ means: like that severe trial, We tested them because of their defiance. This indicates that whoever obeys Allah, the Exalted, Allah lightens his circumstances in this world and the Hereafter, and whoever disobeys, He tests him with various kinds of trials and afflictions.

Our companions (the Ash'arī scholars) have used this verse as evidence that it is not obligatory for Allah, the Exalted, to maintain *al-ṣalāḥ wa'l-aṣlaḥ* (what is most beneficial) for His servants, neither in religion nor in worldly affairs. This is because He, the Exalted, knew that the abundance of fish on Saturday might lead them to disobedience and disbelief. Had it been obligatory for Him to maintain what is most beneficial, He would have been obliged not to multiply these fish on that day, in order to protect them from that disbelief and disobedience. Since He did so, and did not heed their disbelief and disobedience, we know that maintaining what is beneficial and most beneficial is not obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 164–165:

His saying, ﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" they said, "As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment for what they used to defy.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿And when a community said﴾, is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying, ﴿when they transgressed﴾, and its grammatical ruling (hukm fi al-i'rab) is the same as its ruling.

His saying, ﴿a community among them﴾, means a group from the people of the town, from among their righteous ones, who exerted themselves (rakibu al-sa'b wa al-dhalul) in admonishing those fishermen, until they despaired of their accepting it, and so they said to other groups, "Why do you admonish a people...," meaning those who would not desist from their admonition.

His saying, ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy﴾, means: whom He will cause to perish (mukhtarimuhum) and cleanse the land of them, ﴿or punish with a severe punishment﴾ because of their persistence in evil. They only said this because they knew that admonition would not benefit them.

His saying, ﴿they said, "As an excuse before your Lord"﴾ contains two discussions:

The first discussion: Hafs, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read (ma'dhiratan) with a fatha (accusative), while the rest read it with a damma (nominative). As for the one who reads it in the accusative, al-Zajjaj said its meaning is: "We make an excuse, an excuse." As for the one who reads it in the nominative, the implied construction is: "This is an excuse," or "Our saying is an excuse," and it is the predicate (khabar) of this omitted subject.

The second discussion: al-Ma'dhira is a verbal noun (masdar) like al-'Udhr. Abu Zayd said: "I excused him (adhurahu) 'udhran and ma'dhiratan." The meaning of ʿadharahu linguistically is that he stood up to his excuse (qama bi-'udhrihi). It is also said: "his excuse." One says: "Who will excuse me?" meaning, who will stand up for my excuse? And "I excused so-and-so in what he did," meaning, I stood up for his excuse. Accordingly, the meaning of His saying, ﴿as an excuse before your Lord﴾ is that we stand up for our own excuse before Allah, Exalted, for when we prolong the enjoining of good and the forbidding of evil, we say: "We have done it," and thus we shall be excused. Al-Azhari said: al-Ma'dhira is a noun on the pattern maf'ila from ʿadhara yaʿdhuru, and it is used in place of the act of apologizing, as if they said: "Our admonition is an apology to our Lord." So the noun is placed in the position of the act of apologizing. It is said: "So-and-so apologized, an apology, an excuse, and a ma'dhira for his sin, so I excused him." His saying, ﴿and perhaps they will fear Him﴾ means: it is possible in our view that they will benefit from this admonition, so they will fear Allah and abandon this sin.

Having understood this, we say: there are two opinions regarding this verse.

The first opinion: among the people of the town, some hunted fish and went ahead with that sin, and some did not do so. This second category became two groups: some admonished the sinning group and restrained them from that act, and some remained silent about that admonition and objected to the admonishers, saying to them: "Why do you admonish them, knowing that Allah will destroy them or punish them?" That is: they had reached such persistence in this sin that they could hardly be prevented from it, so this admonition had no benefit and no effect, and therefore it was necessary to abandon it.

The second opinion: the people of the town were two groups: a group that committed the sin, and a group that refrained from it and admonished the first. When this group was occupied with admonishing the sinning, transgressing group that persisted in the ugly act, the sinning group said to the admonishing group: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish﴾ according to your claim? Al-Wahidi said: The first opinion is more sound, because if they were two groups, and His saying, ﴿as an excuse before your Lord﴾ was an address from the forbidding group to the transgressing group, they would have said: "and perhaps you will fear Him."

As for His saying, ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, it means: when they abandoned what the righteous had reminded them of, abandoning it as one who forgets what he has forgotten, ﴿We saved those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers who went ahead with the act of disobedience.﴾

Know that the wording of the verse indicates that the transgressing group perished, and the group forbidding evil was saved. As for those who said, ﴿Why do you admonish﴾, the commentators differed as to which of the two groups they belonged. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he withheld judgment on it. It is also related from him: both groups perished and the forbidding group was saved. Ibn ʿAbbas, when he recited this verse, would weep and say: "Those who remained silent about forbidding evil perished, and we see things we disapprove of, then we remain silent and say nothing." Al-Hasan said: the silent group is saved. Accordingly, two groups were saved and the third perished. They argued against this view that when they said, ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish﴾, this indicates that they were objecting to them in the strongest terms, and that they abandoned admonishing them only because it was dominant in their assessment that they would not pay attention to that admonition or benefit from it.

If it is said: abandoning admonition is disobedience, and forbidding it is also disobedience, so these abandoners of admonition and forbidders of it should enter under His saying, ﴿and We seized those who wronged﴾.

We say: this does not follow, because forbidding evil is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifaya). When some have performed it, it is lifted from the rest. Then He mentioned that He seized them with a wretched punishment (ʿadhabin bayis), and the apparent meaning is that this punishment is other than the transformation (maskh) mentioned later. His saying, ﴿with a wretched punishment﴾ means: a severe one. In this word there are readings:

One: "Ba'is" on the pattern fa'il (fa'īl). Abu ʿAli said: there are two aspects to it:

The first: that it is fa'il from ba'usa, yab'usu, ba's, when it becomes intense.

The second: what Abu Zayd said, that it is from al-bu's, which is poverty. It is said: the man becomes ba'is, ya'bas, bu's, ba's, and ba'is when he becomes poor, so he is ba'is, meaning poor. So His saying, ﴿with a wretched punishment﴾ means: a punishment possessing wretchedness.

The second reading is "Ba'isin" on the pattern of hadhir.

The third is "Ba'isin," with the hamza changed to a ya', like al-dhib for dhi'b.

The fourth is "Ba'yasin" on the pattern fay'al.

The fifth is "Bayyisin" on the pattern of rayyisin, with the hamza of ba'is changed to a ya' and the ya' assimilated into it.

The sixth is "Baysin," a lightened form of bayyisin, like hayn for hayyin.

These readings were transmitted by the author of al-Kashshaf. Then Allah, Exalted, made clear that, even with this punishment descending upon them, they remained defiant.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 164–165:

His saying, ﴿And when a community among them said, "Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish with a severe punishment?" they said, "As an excuse before your Lord, and perhaps they will fear Him."﴾ ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of, We saved those who forbade evil and seized those who wronged with a wretched punishment for what they used to defy.﴾

Know that His saying, ﴿And when a community said﴾, is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying, ﴿when they transgressed﴾, and its grammatical ruling (hukm fi al-i'rab) is the same as its ruling.

His saying, ﴿a community among them﴾, means a group from the people of the town, from among their righteous ones, who exerted themselves (rakibu al-sa'b wa al-dhalul) in admonishing those fishermen, until they despaired of their accepting it, and so they said to other groups, "Why do you admonish a people...," meaning those who would not desist from their admonition.

His saying, ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy﴾, means: whom He will cause to perish (mukhtarimuhum) and cleanse the land of them, ﴿or punish with a severe punishment﴾ because of their persistence in evil. They only said this because they knew that admonition would not benefit them.

His saying, ﴿they said, "As an excuse before your Lord"﴾ contains two discussions:

The first discussion: Hafs, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read (ma'dhiratan) with a fatha (accusative), while the rest read it with a damma (nominative). As for the one who reads it in the accusative, al-Zajjaj said its meaning is: "We make an excuse, an excuse." As for the one who reads it in the nominative, the implied construction is: "This is an excuse," or "Our saying is an excuse," and it is the predicate (khabar) of this omitted subject.

The second discussion: al-Ma'dhira is a verbal noun (masdar) like al-'Udhr. Abu Zayd said: "I excused him (adhurahu) 'udhran and ma'dhiratan." The meaning of ʿadharahu linguistically is that he stood up to his excuse (qama bi-'udhrihi). It is also said: "his excuse." One says: "Who will excuse me?" meaning, who will stand up for my excuse? And "I excused so-and-so in what he did," meaning, I stood up for his excuse. Accordingly, the meaning of His saying, ﴿as an excuse before your Lord﴾ is that we stand up for our own excuse before Allah, Exalted, for when we prolong the enjoining of good and the forbidding of evil, we say: "We have done it," and thus we shall be excused. Al-Azhari said: al-Ma'dhira is a noun on the pattern maf'ila from ʿadhara yaʿdhuru, and it is used in place of the act of apologizing, as if they said: "Our admonition is an apology to our Lord." So the noun is placed in the position of the act of apologizing. It is said: "So-and-so apologized, an apology, an excuse, and a ma'dhira for his sin, so I excused him." His saying, ﴿and perhaps they will fear Him﴾ means: it is possible in our view that they will benefit from this admonition, so they will fear Allah and abandon this sin.

Having understood this, we say: there are two opinions regarding this verse.

The first opinion: among the people of the town, some hunted fish and went ahead with that sin, and some did not do so. This second category became two groups: some admonished the sinning group and restrained them from that act, and some remained silent about that admonition and objected to the admonishers, saying to them: "Why do you admonish them, knowing that Allah will destroy them or punish them?" That is: they had reached such persistence in this sin that they could hardly be prevented from it, so this admonition had no benefit and no effect, and therefore it was necessary to abandon it.

The second opinion: the people of the town were two groups: a group that committed the sin, and a group that refrained from it and admonished the first. When this group was occupied with admonishing the sinning, transgressing group that persisted in the ugly act, the sinning group said to the admonishing group: ﴿Why do you admonish a people whom Allah is going to destroy or punish﴾ according to your claim? Al-Wahidi said: The first opinion is more sound, because if they were two groups, and His saying, ﴿as an excuse before your Lord﴾ was an address from the forbidding group to the transgressing group, they would have said: "and perhaps you will fear Him."

As for His saying, ﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾, it means: when they abandoned what the righteous had reminded them of, abandoning it as one who forgets what he has forgotten, ﴿We saved those who forbade evil and seized the wrongdoers who went ahead with the act of disobedience.﴾

Know that the wording of the verse indicates that the transgressing group perished, and the group forbidding evil was saved. As for those who said, ﴿Why do you admonish﴾, the commentators differed as to which of the two groups they belonged. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he withheld judgment on it. It is also related from him: both groups perished and the forbidding group was saved. Ibn ʿAbbas, when he recited this verse, would weep and say: "Those who remained silent about forbidding evil perished, and we see things we disapprove of, then we remain silent and say nothing." Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 166:

Then the One, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿So when they overstepped what they had been forbidden, We said to them: "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾

Among the matters discussed here:

The first question: ʿutuww (overstepping, rebellion) means refusal and disobedience. If they "overstepped" regarding what they had been forbidden, then they had obeyed, since they refused what they had been forbidden. It is known that this is not the intended meaning, so an implied element must be supplied. The sense is: "When they overstepped by abandoning what they had been forbidden," and then the word being added to (al-mudaf) is omitted. When they refused to abandon the forbidden act, that was committing the forbidden act.

The second question: Some people said that His words ﴿We said to them: "Be apes"﴾ are not speech, but rather what is meant is that He, exalted is He, did that. They said: In this is evidence that His words ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40] mean an act and not speech. Al-Zajjaj said: They were commanded to become like that by a word that was heard, and it is then so, which is more eloquent.

Know that interpreting this statement in this way is far-fetched, because one who is commanded to do an act must be able to do it, and those people were not able to turn themselves into apes.

The third question: Ibn ʿAbbas said: The people woke up as apes, humbled, and they remained so for three days, and the people saw them, and then they perished. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the young men of the people became apes, and the elders became swine. This statement goes against the apparent meaning. They differed over whether those who were transformed remained as apes, and whether these apes were of their offspring, or whether they perished and their line was cut off. There is no indication in the verse about this, and the discussion of transformation (maskh) and the matters it involves has already been treated exhaustively in surah al-Baqarah. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 167:

Know that when He (exalted is He) explained here some of the benefits of the actions of the Jews and the ugliness of their deeds, He mentioned in this verse that He had decreed for them humiliation and abasement until the Day of Resurrection. Sibawayh said: *adhdhana a'lam* (أذَّنَ أعْلَمَ, "he announced, he informed"). *Adhdhana* means he called out and shouted to inform. From this is His saying: ﴿Then a crier called out among them﴾ [al-A'raf: 44]. And the saying of the poet (*ta'adhdhana*) means the same as *adhdhana*, i.e., *a'lam* (he informed). The form *tafa''ala* (the Form V verbal pattern) here does not mean that he displayed something that is not in him. Rather, its meaning is *fa'ala* (the base form). So *ta'adhdhana* means *adhina* (he granted permission), as in His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾ [Yunus: 18], meaning *'ala* and *irtafa'a* (He is high and exalted), not that He displayed exaltedness from Himself, even though that quality was not in Him. As for His saying: ﴿He will surely send against them﴾, there are two points to discuss.

The first point: the lam in His saying (*la-yab'athanna*, "He will surely send") is the answer to the oath, because His saying *wa-idh ta'adhdhana* (and when your Lord declared) functions like an oath in that it is firm in asserting that report.

The second point: the pronoun in His saying *'alayhim* (against them) requires that it refer back to His saying: ﴿When they persisted in what they had been forbidden, We said to them, "Be apes, despised."﴾

[Page 35]

However, it is known that those who were transformed did not remain under the obligation of religious duties. Then the scholars differed. Some said: the intended meaning is their offspring and those of them who remained. Others said: rather, the intended meaning is all the Jews, for the people of the town were divided between righteous people and transgressors. The transgressors were transformed, and the humiliation was imposed on the rest. Most scholars said: this verse concerns the Jews whom the Messenger (ﷺ) encountered and invited to his law (*shari'a*, the revealed law). This view is closer to the truth, because the purpose of this verse is to frighten the Jews who lived in the time of the Messenger (ﷺ) and to deter them from remaining upon Judaism, for when they know that humiliation will remain upon them until the Day of Resurrection, they will be restrained.

The third point: there is no doubt that the intended meaning is the Jews who persisted in disbelief and Judaism. As for those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), they are excluded from this ruling.

As for His saying: ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾, this is an explicit statement that this punishment extends until the Day of Resurrection. That requires that this punishment occurs in this world. Regarding this, the scholars differed. Some said it is the imposition of the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects). It was said: it is contempt, humiliation and degradation, based on His saying: ﴿Abasement is stamped upon them wherever they are found﴾ [Al 'Imran: 112]. It was said: it is killing and fighting. It was said: it is expulsion and banishment from their homeland. The one who said this applied this verse to the people of Khaybar, Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir. This verse was revealed concerning the Jews to mean that they will have no dominion and no honor, that abasement will attach to them, and that humiliation will never leave them. When Allah (exalted is He) informed, during the time of Muhammad (ﷺ), about this event, and then we witnessed that the matter was indeed as He said, this was a truthful report of the unseen, and so it was a miracle. As for the transmitted report that the followers of al-Dajjal (the Antichrist) are the Jews, if it is authentic, its meaning is that they were Jews before his emergence, and then they submitted to his divinity, so they were mentioned by their former name. Otherwise, at the time they followed al-Dajjal, they would have come out of abasement and subjugation, and that contradicts this verse. Some scholars argued for the permanence of humiliation and degradation upon the Jews with His saying: ﴿Abasement is stamped upon them wherever they are found, except by a rope from Allah﴾. However, its indication is not strong, because the exception mentioned in this verse prevents a definite ruling that humiliation applies to them in all circumstances. As for the verse we are explaining, no restriction or exception occurs in it, so its indication of this meaning is very strong.

They differed about who it is that imposes this humiliation upon these Jews. Some said: the Messenger and his community. It was said: it may include the oppressive rulers among them, even if they were not commanded to carry this out when they humiliate them. The one who said this interpreted His saying *la-yab'athanna* (He will surely send) in the sense of His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers﴾ [Maryam: 83]. Since it is permissible for *irsal* (sending) to mean granting free rein and abstaining from preventing, the same applies to *ba'th* (sending). The one who said this also said: the intended meaning is Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar) and others up to this day. Then Allah (exalted is He) concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed your Lord is swift in punishment﴾, and the intended meaning is a warning of His punishment in the Hereafter together with humiliation in this world. ﴿And indeed He is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ to whoever repents from disbelief and Judaism and enters into faith in Allah and in Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 168:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We divided them in the earth into communities; among them are the righteous, and among them are others than that; and We tested them with good things and bad things, that perhaps they would return﴾

Page 36
Know that His saying "And We divided them" (waqatta'nahum) is one of the things that indicates that what was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿He will surely send against them﴾ refers to the whole of the Jews. The meaning of "qatta'nahum" is: We dispersed them with a severe dispersal. Therefore He said after it, ﴿in the earth, communities﴾. The apparent meaning of this is that there is no inhabited land except that there is a community of them in it, and this is the more common condition of the Jews, and the meaning of "qatta'nahum" is that there is hardly any town in which there is not a group of them.

Then He said: ﴿among them are the righteous﴾. It was said that the intended people are those who lived in the time of Musa (peace be upon him), because among them there was a community who guided by the truth. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: He means those who met the Prophet (ﷺ) and believed. His saying ﴿and among them are others than that﴾ means: among them are people other than that, and the intended are those who remained upon Judaism.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible that His saying ﴿and among them are others than that﴾ refers to those who are righteous, but whose righteousness was less than the righteousness of the first ones, because that is closer to the apparent meaning?

We say: His saying after that, ﴿that perhaps they would return﴾, indicates that what is meant by that is those who persisted in Judaism and departed from righteousness.

As for His saying ﴿and We tested them with good things and bad things﴾, meaning: We treated them as those who are tried and examined, with good things, which are blessings, abundance and well-being, and bad things, which are drought and hardships. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: each of the good things and the bad things calls to obedience; as for blessings, it is for the sake of encouragement (al-targhib), and as for afflictions, it is for the sake of warning (al-tarhib). His saying ﴿that perhaps they would return﴾ means: so that they might repent.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 169–170:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession who inherited the Book, taking the goods of this lower life and saying, "It will be forgiven us." And if goods like it came to them, they would take it. Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them, that they should not say about Allah except the truth, and they studied what is in it? And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Him. Will you not then reason?﴾ ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book and establish prayer — indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of the reformers.﴾

Know that His saying ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession﴾ apparently means that the first (group) is praised and the second is blameworthy. If that is so, then the meaning must be: there succeeded, after the righteous among them whose mention has preceded, a succession. Al-Zajjaj said: al-khalf (succession) is that which comes after you in place of what was taken from you; for this reason the generation that comes in the wake of a generation is called khalf, and it is also said khalaf. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: All people say "a khalf of truthfulness" and "a khalf of evil," and khalf for evil only.

The summary of the discussion: among the people of Arabic grammar, some say that khalf and khalaf are mentioned both for the good and for the bad. Others say that khalf is specific to blame; Labid said:

"And I remained in a khalf like the skin of a mangy camel."

Others say that khalf, used in blame, is derived from khulf, which is corruption. It is said of bad speech that it is khulf, and from it the well-known proverb: "He kept silent a thousand (times) and spoke one khalf (bad word)." The thing khalafa (became corrupt) yakhlafu, khulufan and khalafan, when it spoiled; likewise the mouth when its smell changes.

As for His saying ﴿taking the goods of this lower life﴾: Abu Ubayda said: all the goods of this world are ʿaraḍ with a fatha on the ra, it is said "the world is a present ʿaraḍ from which the pious and the wicked both eat." As for ʿarḍ with a sukun on the ra, it is what is other than gold and silver coins, and its plural is ʿurūḍ. So every ʿarḍ is an ʿaraḍ, but not every ʿaraḍ is an ʿarḍ. The meaning of His saying ﴿ʿaraḍ of this lower life﴾ is: the debris (ḥuṭām) of this lowly thing, meaning the world and what is enjoyed from it. In His saying ﴿this lower life﴾ there is belittling and disparagement. And "al-adnā" (lower) is either from dunuww meaning nearness, because it is immediate and near, or from the lowering and decline of the state and its scarcity.

The intended meaning is what they used to take of bribes in rulings, by distorting speech. Then Almighty God related about them that they regard that sin as trivial and say: "It will be forgiven us."

Then He said: ﴿And if goods like it came to them, they would take it.﴾ The intent is to inform of their persistence in sins. Al-Hasan said: this is an report of their greed for the world and that they are not satisfied with it. Then Almighty God explained the ugliness of their act, saying: ﴿Was not the covenant of the Book taken from them﴾ — that is, the Torah — ﴿that they should not say about Allah except the truth﴾. It was said the meaning is their being prevented from distorting the Book and changing the laws for the sake of taking bribes. And it was said: the meaning is that they said "this sin will be forgiven us" while persisting, and that is a false statement.

If it is said: this statement indicates that the ruling of the Torah is that the one who commits a major sin is not forgiven.

We say: they used to hold with certainty that this major sin was forgiven, whereas we do not hold with certainty to forgiveness, but we hope for forgiveness, and we say: even on the supposition that God punishes for it, that punishment is finite, not everlasting.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿and they studied what is in it﴾ — that is, they are mindful of what was taken from them, because they had recited it and studied it.

Then He said: ﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Him﴾ — from that vile, belittled bribery — ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾: it is said mastu bi-l-shay'i, and tamassaktu bihi, and istamsaktu bihi, and imtasaktu bihi (all meaning "I held fast to it"). Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read ﴿yumsikūna﴾ with a light (unshaddated) form, and the rest with the shadda. As for ʿAsim's proof, it is His saying ﴿fa-imsākun bi-maʿrūf﴾ [al-Baqara: 229], and His saying ﴿amsik ʿalayka zawjaka﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 37], and His saying ﴿fa-kulū mimmā amsakna ʿalaykum﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 4]. Al-Wahidi said: the shadda is stronger, because the shadda indicates multiplicity, and here multiplicity is intended; and because one says amsaktuhu, whereas one rarely says amsaktu bihi.

Having known this, we say: concerning His saying ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾ there are two opinions:

The first opinion: that it is in the nominative by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of the reformers﴾. The meaning: indeed We do not allow their reward to be lost, and this is like His saying ﴿Indeed those who believed and did righteous deeds — indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30]. This view is good, because when He mentioned the threat against the one who abandons holding fast to the Book, He followed it with the promise to the one who holds fast to it.

The second opinion: that it is in the genitive by way of conjunction (ʿaṭf) to His saying ﴿those who fear Him﴾, and His saying ﴿indeed We do not allow to be lost﴾ is an added clause mentioned to emphasize what precedes it.

If it is said: holding fast to the Book includes every act of worship, and among them is establishing the prayer; so why is it singled out for mention?

We say: to show the high rank of the prayer, and that it is the greatest of acts of worship after faith.
