It was said the meaning is their being prevented from distorting the Book and changing the laws for the sake of taking bribes. And it was said: the meaning is that they said "this sin will be forgiven us" while persisting, and that is a false statement.

If it is said: this statement indicates that the ruling of the Torah is that the one who commits a major sin is not forgiven.

We say: they used to hold with certainty that this major sin was forgiven, whereas we do not hold with certainty to forgiveness, but we hope for forgiveness, and we say: even on the supposition that God punishes for it, that punishment is finite, not everlasting.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿and they studied what is in it﴾ — that is, they are mindful of what was taken from them, because they had recited it and studied it.

Then He said: ﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear Him﴾ — from that vile, belittled bribery — ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾: it is said mastu bi-l-shay'i, and tamassaktu bihi, and istamsaktu bihi, and imtasaktu bihi (all meaning "I held fast to it"). Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read ﴿yumsikūna﴾ with a light (unshaddated) form, and the rest with the shadda. As for ʿAsim's proof, it is His saying ﴿fa-imsākun bi-maʿrūf﴾ [al-Baqara: 229], and His saying ﴿amsik ʿalayka zawjaka﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 37], and His saying ﴿fa-kulū mimmā amsakna ʿalaykum﴾ [al-Mā'ida: 4]. Al-Wahidi said: the shadda is stronger, because the shadda indicates multiplicity, and here multiplicity is intended; and because one says amsaktuhu, whereas one rarely says amsaktu bihi.

Having known this, we say: concerning His saying ﴿And those who hold fast to the Book﴾ there are two opinions:

The first opinion: that it is in the nominative by way of the inchoative (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of the reformers﴾. The meaning: indeed We do not allow their reward to be lost, and this is like His saying ﴿Indeed those who believed and did righteous deeds — indeed We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good work﴾ [al-Kahf: 30]. This view is good, because when He mentioned the threat against the one who abandons holding fast to the Book, He followed it with the promise to the one who holds fast to it.

The second opinion: that it is in the genitive by way of conjunction (ʿaṭf) to His saying ﴿those who fear Him﴾, and His saying ﴿indeed We do not allow to be lost﴾ is an added clause mentioned to emphasize what precedes it.

If it is said: holding fast to the Book includes every act of worship, and among them is establishing the prayer; so why is it singled out for mention?

We say: to show the high rank of the prayer, and that it is the greatest of acts of worship after faith.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 171:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We raised the mountain above them as though it were a canopy, and they thought it was about to fall upon them: "Take what We have given you with determination, and remember what is in it, so that you may become righteous."﴾

Abu 'Ubayda said: The origin of *al-natq* (ٱلنَّتْق) is uprooting a thing from its place and hurling it. It is said: "He *nataqa* what was in the saddlebag," meaning he threw it out and poured it out. A woman is called *natiq* and *mintaq* when she has many children, because she casts her children out (*ramy*) in abundance. So the meaning of ﴿We raised the mountain﴾ is: We uprooted it from its base and placed it above them. As for His saying ﴿as though it were a canopy﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: "as though it were a roof (*saqifa*)." The *zulla* is everything that shades you, whether the ceiling of a house, a cloud, or the wing of a wall; its plural is *zulal* and *zilal*. This story is mentioned in Surah al-Baqara.

﴿And they thought it was about to fall upon them﴾: The exegetes said: they knew and were certain. The people of meanings (*ahl al-ma'ani*) said: it became firmly established in their souls that it would fall upon them if they opposed it. This is the most apparent meaning of *zann* (ظن, here: thought/supposition). The discussion of it has already passed at His saying ﴿those who think that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 46].

It is narrated that they refused to accept the rulings of the Torah because of their severity and heaviness, so God raised the Mount (*al-Tur*) over their heads to the size of their army, which was a farsakh by a farsakh. It was said to them: "If you accept it with what is in it, well and good; otherwise it will surely fall upon you." When they looked at the mountain, each one of them fell prostrate on his left eyebrow while looking with his right eye, out of fear of its falling. For this reason you do not see a Jew prostrate except on his left eyebrow while looking with his right eye, and they say: "This is the prostration by which the punishment was lifted from us."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Take what We have given you with determination﴾: that is, "And We said: take what We have given you," or saying: "Take what We have given you of the Book with determination and resolve to bear its hardships and obligations." ﴿And remember what is in it﴾ of the commands and prohibitions, that is, remember what is in it of reward and punishment. It is also permissible that what is meant is: "Take what We have given you of this great sign with strength, if you are able to bear it," like His saying: ﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman: 33]. And [remember] what is in it of the evidence of His overwhelming power, so that you may become righteous, [turning away from] what you are upon.

[Page 39]

The Almighty's statement: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "Only our fathers associated partners [with Allah] before, and we were descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, and perhaps they will return.﴾

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when the Almighty had explained the story of Moses, peace be upon him, together with its ramifications, in the most complete manner, He mentioned in this verse what serves as establishing the proof against all the responsible persons (mukallafun). Regarding the interpretation (tafsir) of this verse there are two opinions.

The first: This is the view of the exegetes (mufassirun) and the people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar). It is what Muslim ibn Yasar al-Juhani narrated: that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about this verse, and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being asked about it, and he said: 'Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, created Adam, then wiped his back, and brought forth from it descendants. He said: "I created these for Paradise, and they will work by the deeds of the people of Paradise." Then He wiped his back and brought forth from it descendants, and said: "I created these for the Fire, and they will work by the deeds of the people of the Fire."' A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what is the point of works?' He said, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Indeed, when Allah creates a servant for Paradise, He makes him work by the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of Paradise, and so he enters Paradise. And when He creates a servant for the Fire, He makes him work by the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of the Fire, and so Allah enters him into the Fire.'"

And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created Adam, He wiped his back, and there fell from his back every soul of his descendants until the Day of Resurrection." Muqatil said: Indeed Allah wiped the right side of Adam's back, and there came forth from it descendants, white, like the likeness of ants, moving. Then He wiped the left side of his back, and there came forth from it descendants, black, like the likeness of ants. He said: "O Adam, these are your descendants."

Then He said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes.﴾ He said to the white ones: "These are in Paradise by My mercy, and they are the companions of the right hand." And He said to the black ones: "These are in the Fire, and I do not care, and they are the companions of the left hand." Then He returned them all into the loins of Adam. So the people of acceptance (ahl al-qabul) remain confined until all the people of the covenant come forth from the loins of men and the wombs of women.

And the Almighty said concerning one who broke the first covenant: ﴿And We did not find most of them to be keepers of a covenant﴾ [al-A'raf: 102]. This view has been held by many of the early exegetes, such as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: that he (Adam) saw among his descendants a people who had light. He said: "O Lord, who are they?" He said: "The prophets." And he saw one who was the most luminous of them, and he said: "Who is he?" He said: "Dawud." He said: "What is his lifespan?" He said: "Seventy years." Adam said: "That is little; I have given him forty years from my lifespan." Adam's lifespan was a thousand years. When Adam's lifespan reached nine hundred and sixty years, the Angel of Death came to him to seize his soul. He said: "There remain forty years of my term." He said: "Did you not give them to your son Dawud?" He said: "I had not intended to give anyone any part of my term." At that point it was written for every soul its term.

As for the Mu'tazilah: they are unanimous that it is not permissible to interpret this verse in this manner, and they argued for the falsity of this view with several arguments.

The first argument they gave: They said: The statement ﴿from their loins﴾ undoubtedly makes ﴿from their loins﴾ a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Children of Adam﴾, so the meaning is: "And when your Lord took from the loins of the Children of Adam." On this reading, Allah did not mention that He took anything from Adam's back.

The second argument: If what was meant is that He, the Exalted, brought forth from Adam's back some descendants, He would not have said ﴿from their loins﴾ but rather "from his loin," because Adam has only one back. Likewise His statement ﴿their descendants﴾: had it been Adam, it would have said "his descendants."

[Page 40]

The third argument: He, the Exalted, related of those descendants that they said: ﴿Only our fathers associated partners [with Allah] before﴾, and this speech is fitting for the children of Adam, since he, peace be upon him, was never a polytheist.

The fourth argument: Taking a covenant (mithaq) is possible only from a rational being. So if Allah had taken the covenant from those ants (dharr), they would have to be rational. And if they were rational and were given that covenant while in possession of their reason, it would have been necessary that they remember at this time that they were given the covenant before entering this world. For a person who has experienced a great and awe-inspiring event, it is not permissible, while being rational, to forget it completely, so that he recalls nothing of it at all, neither a little nor a lot. By this same argument transmigration (tanasukh) is refuted. For we say: If our souls had previously been in other bodies before these bodies, it would have been necessary that we now remember that we were in another body before this body. Since we do not remember that, the doctrine of transmigration is false. So if our reliance in refuting transmigration is nothing but this argument, and this very argument applies in this question, it is necessary to adopt what it requires. For if it is permissible to say that at the time of the covenant we were given the pledge and the covenant while we do not remember anything of it at this time, then why is it not also permissible to say that we were in another body before this body while we do not remember anything of those states in this body? In sum, there is no difference between this view and the doctrine of the transmigrationists. If it is not far-fetched to commit to this view, then it is not far-fetched either to commit to the doctrine of transmigration.

The fifth argument: All the creatures whom Allah created from the children of Adam are a great number and a vast multitude. So the aggregate resulting from those descendants reaches an enormous size and quantity, while the loins of Adam, despite their smallness, are far too narrow to contain that aggregate.

The sixth argument: Bodily structure (bunyah) is a condition for the occurrence of life, reason and understanding. For if it were not so, it would not be far-fetched that every particle of the dust (habaʾ) could be rational, understanding, and authoring many works in the subtle sciences. Opening this door leads to committing to absurdities. And since it is established that bodily structure is a condition for life, each one of those particles cannot be knowing, understanding and rational, unless it acquires a capacity from bodily structure, flesh and blood. If that is so, then the totality of those persons who came into existence from the first creation of Adam until the end of the Resurrection cannot be contained by the expanse of this world. So how can it be said that they all came into being at once in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him?

The seventh argument: They said: This covenant either was taken from them at that time, so that it would be a proof against them at that time, or so that it would be a proof against them upon their entry into the abode of this world. The first is false, because there is a consensus that by virtue of that measure of covenant they do not become deserving of reward and punishment, praise and blame. Nor can it be that the purpose of it was that it would become a proof against them upon their entry into the abode of this world, since they did not mention that covenant in this world, so how could it become a proof against them in adhering to faith?

The eighth argument: Al-Ka'bi said: The condition of those descendants cannot be higher in understanding and knowledge than the condition of children. And since legal responsibility (taklif) is not directed at a child, how can it be directed at those beings?

Al-Zajjaj answered him, saying: Since it is not far-fetched that Allah should give reason to the ant, as He said: ﴿A female ant said: "O ants…"﴾ [al-Naml: 18], and that He should give understanding to the mountains so that they glorify, as He said: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with Dawud﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79], and as Allah gave reason to the camel so that it prostrated to the Messenger, and to the palm tree so that it heard and submitted when it was called, so too here.

[Page 41]

The ninth argument: Those ants at that time either were of complete reason and capacity, or they were not. If the first, then they were necessarily under legal responsibility, and they would remain under legal responsibility only if they knew Allah through reasoning. And if they were so, their circumstances at that time would not be distinguished from their circumstances in this worldly life. So if legal responsibility in this world depended on the prior occurrence of that covenant, then legal responsibility at the time of that covenant would depend on the prior occurrence of another covenant, and it would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. As for the second: that is, if it is said that at the time of that covenant they were neither of complete reason nor of complete capacity, then in that case addressing them and imposing legal responsibility upon them is impossible.

The tenth argument: The statement of the Almighty: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from. He was created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 5–6]. If those ants were rational, understanding and complete, they would have existed before this gushing fluid, and there would be no meaning for "man" except that thing. In that case, man would not have been created from a gushing fluid, and that is a rejection of the text of the Qur'an.

If they say: Why is it not permissible to say that He created him with complete reason and understanding at the time of the covenant, then He removed his reason, understanding and capacity, and then He created him again in the mother's womb and brought him out into this life?

We say: This is false, because if the matter were so, He would not have created him from a drop of semen as an original creation; rather it would have had to be a creation by way of restoration (i'adah). And the Muslims have unanimously agreed that his creation from a drop of semen is the originating creation (al-khalq al-mubtada'). This indicates that what you have mentioned is false.

The eleventh argument: That those ants either are the very same people or are other than them, and the second is false by consensus. What remains is the first. We say: Either it is said that they remained understanding, rational and capable while they were a drop, a clot and a lump of flesh, or they did not remain so. The first is false by the self-evident judgment of reason. The second requires saying that man came to have life four times: the first at the time of the covenant, the second in this world, the third in the grave, and the fourth on the Resurrection. And that he suffered death three times: death after the life obtained in the first covenant, death in this world, and death in the grave. This number contradicts the number mentioned in the Almighty's statement: ﴿Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice﴾ [Ghafir: 11].

The twelfth argument: The statement of the Almighty: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12]. If this view of the ants were correct, then those ants would be the human being, since he is the one addressed, the one rewarded and the one punished. But that is false, because those ants were not created from a drop, a clot, or a lump of flesh, while the text of the Book is evidence that man was created from a drop and a clot. That is the Almighty's statement: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾, and His statement: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is! From what thing did He create him? From a drop He created him﴾ [Abasa: 17–19]. These are the sum of the arguments mentioned to show that this view is weak.

[Page 42]

The second view on the interpretation of this verse is that of the people of reflection and rational inquiry: God brought forth the offspring, who are the children, from the loins of their fathers. This bringing forth means that they were a drop of semen, and God brought them forth in the wombs of their mothers, made them a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then made them human beings, well-formed and complete creatures. Then He made them bear witness against themselves through the signs of His oneness that He had placed in them, the wonders of His creation, and the marvels of His workmanship. Through this bearing witness, it was as though they had said "Yes," even though no statement was made with the tongue. There are parallels to this in the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat: 11]

[Page 42, continued]

Among them is the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82] And the saying of the Arabs:

*The wall said to the peg, "Why do you split me?"*
*He said, "Ask him who is hammering me."*
*For the one behind me... has not left me alone behind me.*

And the poet's words:

*The basin is full and says, "Enough for me!"*

This type of metaphor and figurative speech is well known in discourse, so it is necessary to interpret the speech in this way. This, then, is the discussion in establishing these two views. This second view is entirely free of criticism. And even supposing this view is valid, it would not contradict the validity of the first view. The question is only whether the first view is valid or not.

If someone asks: "What, then, is your preferred position on this?"

We say: here there are two points of discussion:

The first: Is it valid to hold that the covenant was taken from the *dharr* (atoms, or tiny offspring)?

The second: Supposing it is valid to hold this, is it possible to make it an interpretation of the wording of this verse?

As for the first point: those who deny it have relied on the rational proofs that we mentioned and established, and it is possible to answer each of them with a convincing argument.

As for the first of the rational arguments mentioned, namely that if the covenant had indeed been taken, we would be obligated to remember it now:

We say: The one who creates the knowledge of the occurrence of past states is God, Exalted is He, because this knowledge is rational and necessary (*ḍarūrī*, i.e., self-evident). Necessary knowledge is created by God, Exalted is He. Given that this is so, it is valid for Him, Exalted is He, to create it.

If they say: "If you permit this, then permit the claim that before this body we were in other bodies by way of transmigration (*tanāsukh*, the passing of souls from body to body), even though we do not now remember the states of those bodies!"

We say: The difference between the two matters is clear. For if we were in other bodies and remained in them for years and eons, it would be customarily impossible to forget them. But the taking of this covenant occurred in the briefest time and the shortest period, so forgetting it is not improbable. This clear difference is decisive in establishing the validity of this distinction. For a person who remains at a single action for many years cannot forget it, whereas if he practices a single action for only a moment, he may forget it. Thus the difference has become evident.

As for the second argument, namely that it is said: the totality of those atoms is impossible to be present all together in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him.

We say: According to us, the bodily structure is not a condition for the occurrence of life, and the indivisible atom (*al-jawhar al-fard*, the partless substance) is capable of life and reason. So when we make each of those atoms an indivisible substance, why do you say that the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, cannot contain all of them? However, this answer is only complete if we say that the human being is an indivisible substance and a partless part of the body, according to the view of some of the early thinkers. But if we say that the human being is the rational soul (*al-nafs al-nāṭiqah*), and that it is a substance that is neither spatially located nor an accident inhering in a located thing, then the question is removed.

[Page 43]

As for the third argument, namely his saying: "The benefit of taking the covenant is that it would be a proof at that time or in the present life."

Our answer is to say: God does what He wills and decrees what He desires. Moreover, do not the Mu'tazilah, when they wish to establish the doctrine of the weighing of deeds and the speaking of the limbs, say: "It is not improbable that for some of the responsible persons, the hearing of these things would be a grace (*luṭf*, divine favor that facilitates obedience)"? Likewise here, it is not improbable that for some of the angels, in distinguishing the blessed from the wretched at the time of taking the covenant, there would be a grace. It has also been said that God will remind them of that covenant on the Day of Resurrection. The remaining arguments are weak, and the discussion of them is easy and simple.

As for the second point: supposing the validity of the view that the covenant was taken from the *dharr*, is it possible to make it an interpretation of this verse? We say: the three arguments mentioned earlier prevent this, because His saying: ﴿When your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring﴾ — we have shown what is meant by it, namely that He took from the loins of the children of Adam. Furthermore, if this offspring had been taken from the loins of Adam, He would have said: "from his loins, his offspring," and not "from their loins, their offspring."

The defenders of this view answered this objection: it has been authentically transmitted from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he interpreted this verse in this way, and it is not possible to criticize the interpretation of the Messenger of God.

We say: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that God brought forth the *dharr* from the loins of the children of Adam. This is to be understood to mean that God knows that a certain person will beget a certain son, and that son will beget another, and so on. According to the order in which He knows they will enter existence, He brings them forth and distinguishes some of them from others. As for the claim that God brings forth all that offspring from the loins of Adam, there is nothing in the wording of the verse that proves this, nor is there anything in the verse that proves its falsehood. However, a report (*khabar*) has indicated it. Thus the bringing forth of the offspring from the loins of the children of Adam is established by the Qur'an, and the bringing forth of the offspring from the loins of Adam is established by the report. Given this, there is no contradiction or conflict between the two matters, so it is necessary to adopt both together, in order to preserve the verse and the report from criticism as far as possible. This is the end of the discussion in establishing this point.

* * *

The second issue: Nafi' (Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān), Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū ʿUmar recited *dhurriyyātihim* (ذُرِّيّاتِهِمْ) with the *alif*, in the plural, while the rest recited *dhurriyyatahum* (ذُرِّيَّتَهم), in the singular.

Al-Wāḥidī (Abū al-Ḥasan al-Wāḥidī, the exegete) said: *al-dhurriyyah* (the offspring) may be used for both the singular and the plural. Whoever recites it in the singular has dispensed with pluralizing it, and since it may be used for the plural, it is like *al-bashar* (mankind), which is used for the singular, as in His words: ﴿This is not a human (*bashar*)﴾ [Yusuf: 31], and for the plural, as in His words: ﴿Shall mere humans (*abashar*) guide us?﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6], and His words: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 10]. Just as *bashar* is not pluralized either by the regular plural or by the broken plural, likewise *dhurriyyah* is not pluralized. Whoever pluralizes it says: even if *dhurriyyah* is singular, there is no difficulty in its being pluralized, and if it is already a plural, its pluralization is also acceptable, for you have seen that broken plurals have been pluralized, as in *al-ṭuruqāt* (the roads) and *al-jadarāt* (the walls). This is the view preferred by Yunus (ibn Ḥabīb, the grammarian).

As for His words: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes."﴾ — we say: According to the view of those who affirm the first covenant, all these things are to be taken according to their apparent meanings. But according to the view of those who deny it, they are to be taken as an analogy (*tamthīl*), and the meaning is that God established for them proofs of His lordship, and their intellects bore witness to it. Thus this became like what would occur if He had made us testify against ourselves and acknowledge His oneness.

As for His words: *shahidnā* (ﺷَهِدْنا, "we testify"), there are two views on it:

The first view: it is part of the speech of the angels. This is because when they said "Yes," God said to the angels, "Bear witness," and they said, "We bear witness." According to this view, it is good to pause at His words: ﴿They said, "Yes."﴾ because the speech of the offspring ends here. As for His words: ﴿Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ its meaning is: the angels said, "We bear witness against them with their acknowledgment, lest they say what we did not acknowledge," so the particle *lā* ("not") has been dropped, as in His words: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl: 15], meaning "lest it shake with you." This is the view of the Kufans. According to the Basrans, its implied meaning is: "We bore witness out of aversion to their saying..."

The second view: His words *shahidnā* are part of the remaining speech of the offspring. According to this interpretation, His words: ﴿Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ are connected to His words: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves﴾, and the meaning is: "He made them testify concerning themselves to such and such, lest they say on the Day of Resurrection: 'Indeed, we were unaware of this,'" or "out of aversion to their saying that." According to this interpretation, it is not permissible to pause at His words *shahidnā*, because His words *an yaqūlū* ("that they say") are connected to what precedes it, namely His words *wa-ashhadahum* ("and He made them testify"), so it is not permissible to separate it from that.

The readers differed concerning the words *an yaqūlū* (أنْ يَقُولُوا, "that they say") and *an taqūlū* (أنْ تَقُولُوا, "that you say"). Abū ʿAmr recited them all with the *yāʾ* (third-person), because the preceding speech was in the third person: His words ﴿from the children of Adam, from their loins﴾ and ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves﴾, so that "they" would not say. The rest recited with the *tāʾ* (second-person), because a second-person address has occurred in the speech, namely His words: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ "They said, 'Yes, we testify.'" Both readings are good, because the absent persons are, in meaning, the addressed persons.

As for His words: ﴿Or you should say, "Indeed, our fathers associated partners with God before, and we were only their offspring after them."﴾ The exegetes said: the meaning is that the purpose of this making them testify is that the unbelievers should not say, "We only associated partners because our fathers did so, and we imitated them in that association." This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ The conclusion is that when God took the covenant from them, they were prevented from holding on to this excuse.

As for those who understood the verse to mean merely the establishment of proofs, they said: the meaning of the verse is that We established these proofs and made them manifest to the intellects, out of aversion to their saying on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this," for no warner had alerted us to it, or out of aversion to their saying that they associated partners only by way of imitating their forefathers, because the establishing of proofs for monotheism remains with them, so they have no excuse for turning away from it and turning instead to imitation and following the fathers.

Then He said: ﴿And thus We detail the verses﴾. The meaning is: just as We have explained and clarified in this verse, We have clarified the rest of the verses, so that they might reflect upon them, return to the truth, and turn away from falsehood. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. It has also been said: that is, [We detail the verses concerning] what covenant He took from them regarding monotheism.

There is also a third view regarding the verse: that human souls exist before the bodies, and the acknowledgment of the existence of God is a necessary consequence of their essences and realities. This knowledge does not need acquisition or seeking to attain it. This matter, however, is only fully disclosed through obscure rational investigations, which cannot be mentioned in this book. And God knows best.

[Page 39]

The Almighty's statement: ﴿And when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves: "Am I not your Lord?" They said: "Yes, we testify." [This] lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection: "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ ﴿Or lest you should say: "Only our fathers associated partners [with Allah] before, and we were descendants after them. Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?"﴾ ﴿Thus do We detail the signs, and perhaps they will return.﴾

Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when the Almighty had explained the story of Moses, peace be upon him, together with its ramifications, in the most complete manner, He mentioned in this verse what serves as establishing the proof against all the responsible persons (mukallafun). Regarding the interpretation (tafsir) of this verse there are two opinions.

The first: This is the view of the exegetes (mufassirun) and the people of transmitted reports (ahl al-athar). It is what Muslim ibn Yasar al-Juhani narrated: that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, was asked about this verse, and he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) being asked about it, and he said: 'Indeed Allah, glorified and exalted is He, created Adam, then wiped his back, and brought forth from it descendants. He said: "I created these for Paradise, and they will work by the deeds of the people of Paradise." Then He wiped his back and brought forth from it descendants, and said: "I created these for the Fire, and they will work by the deeds of the people of the Fire."' A man said: 'O Messenger of Allah, then what is the point of works?' He said, peace and blessings be upon him: 'Indeed, when Allah creates a servant for Paradise, He makes him work by the deeds of the people of Paradise until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of Paradise, and so he enters Paradise. And when He creates a servant for the Fire, He makes him work by the deeds of the people of the Fire until he dies upon one of the deeds of the people of the Fire, and so Allah enters him into the Fire.'"

And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created Adam, He wiped his back, and there fell from his back every soul of his descendants until the Day of Resurrection." Muqatil said: Indeed Allah wiped the right side of Adam's back, and there came forth from it descendants, white, like the likeness of ants, moving. Then He wiped the left side of his back, and there came forth from it descendants, black, like the likeness of ants. He said: "O Adam, these are your descendants."

Then He said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ They said: ﴿Yes.﴾ He said to the white ones: "These are in Paradise by My mercy, and they are the companions of the right hand." And He said to the black ones: "These are in the Fire, and I do not care, and they are the companions of the left hand." Then He returned them all into the loins of Adam. So the people of acceptance (ahl al-qabul) remain confined until all the people of the covenant come forth from the loins of men and the wombs of women.

And the Almighty said concerning one who broke the first covenant: ﴿And We did not find most of them to be keepers of a covenant﴾ [al-A'raf: 102]. This view has been held by many of the early exegetes, such as Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, Ikrimah and al-Kalbi. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: that he (Adam) saw among his descendants a people who had light. He said: "O Lord, who are they?" He said: "The prophets." And he saw one who was the most luminous of them, and he said: "Who is he?" He said: "Dawud." He said: "What is his lifespan?" He said: "Seventy years." Adam said: "That is little; I have given him forty years from my lifespan." Adam's lifespan was a thousand years. When Adam's lifespan reached nine hundred and sixty years, the Angel of Death came to him to seize his soul. He said: "There remain forty years of my term." He said: "Did you not give them to your son Dawud?" He said: "I had not intended to give anyone any part of my term." At that point it was written for every soul its term.

As for the Mu'tazilah: they are unanimous that it is not permissible to interpret this verse in this manner, and they argued for the falsity of this view with several arguments.

The first argument they gave: They said: The statement ﴿from their loins﴾ undoubtedly makes ﴿from their loins﴾ a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Children of Adam﴾, so the meaning is: "And when your Lord took from the loins of the Children of Adam." On this reading, Allah did not mention that He took anything from Adam's back.

The second argument: If what was meant is that He, the Exalted, brought forth from Adam's back some descendants, He would not have said ﴿from their loins﴾ but rather "from his loin," because Adam has only one back. Likewise His statement ﴿their descendants﴾: had it been Adam, it would have said "his descendants."

[Page 40]

The third argument: He, the Exalted, related of those descendants that they said: ﴿Only our fathers associated partners [with Allah] before﴾, and this speech is fitting for the children of Adam, since he, peace be upon him, was never a polytheist.

The fourth argument: Taking a covenant (mithaq) is possible only from a rational being. So if Allah had taken the covenant from those ants (dharr), they would have to be rational. And if they were rational and were given that covenant while in possession of their reason, it would have been necessary that they remember at this time that they were given the covenant before entering this world. For a person who has experienced a great and awe-inspiring event, it is not permissible, while being rational, to forget it completely, so that he recalls nothing of it at all, neither a little nor a lot. By this same argument transmigration (tanasukh) is refuted. For we say: If our souls had previously been in other bodies before these bodies, it would have been necessary that we now remember that we were in another body before this body. Since we do not remember that, the doctrine of transmigration is false. So if our reliance in refuting transmigration is nothing but this argument, and this very argument applies in this question, it is necessary to adopt what it requires. For if it is permissible to say that at the time of the covenant we were given the pledge and the covenant while we do not remember anything of it at this time, then why is it not also permissible to say that we were in another body before this body while we do not remember anything of those states in this body? In sum, there is no difference between this view and the doctrine of the transmigrationists. If it is not far-fetched to commit to this view, then it is not far-fetched either to commit to the doctrine of transmigration.

The fifth argument: All the creatures whom Allah created from the children of Adam are a great number and a vast multitude. So the aggregate resulting from those descendants reaches an enormous size and quantity, while the loins of Adam, despite their smallness, are far too narrow to contain that aggregate.

The sixth argument: Bodily structure (bunyah) is a condition for the occurrence of life, reason and understanding. For if it were not so, it would not be far-fetched that every particle of the dust (habaʾ) could be rational, understanding, and authoring many works in the subtle sciences. Opening this door leads to committing to absurdities. And since it is established that bodily structure is a condition for life, each one of those particles cannot be knowing, understanding and rational, unless it acquires a capacity from bodily structure, flesh and blood. If that is so, then the totality of those persons who came into existence from the first creation of Adam until the end of the Resurrection cannot be contained by the expanse of this world. So how can it be said that they all came into being at once in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him?

The seventh argument: They said: This covenant either was taken from them at that time, so that it would be a proof against them at that time, or so that it would be a proof against them upon their entry into the abode of this world. The first is false, because there is a consensus that by virtue of that measure of covenant they do not become deserving of reward and punishment, praise and blame. Nor can it be that the purpose of it was that it would become a proof against them upon their entry into the abode of this world, since they did not mention that covenant in this world, so how could it become a proof against them in adhering to faith?

The eighth argument: Al-Ka'bi said: The condition of those descendants cannot be higher in understanding and knowledge than the condition of children. And since legal responsibility (taklif) is not directed at a child, how can it be directed at those beings?

Al-Zajjaj answered him, saying: Since it is not far-fetched that Allah should give reason to the ant, as He said: ﴿A female ant said: "O ants…"﴾ [al-Naml: 18], and that He should give understanding to the mountains so that they glorify, as He said: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [Allah] with Dawud﴾ [al-Anbiya: 79], and as Allah gave reason to the camel so that it prostrated to the Messenger, and to the palm tree so that it heard and submitted when it was called, so too here.

[Page 41]

The ninth argument: Those ants at that time either were of complete reason and capacity, or they were not. If the first, then they were necessarily under legal responsibility, and they would remain under legal responsibility only if they knew Allah through reasoning. And if they were so, their circumstances at that time would not be distinguished from their circumstances in this worldly life. So if legal responsibility in this world depended on the prior occurrence of that covenant, then legal responsibility at the time of that covenant would depend on the prior occurrence of another covenant, and it would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. As for the second: that is, if it is said that at the time of that covenant they were neither of complete reason nor of complete capacity, then in that case addressing them and imposing legal responsibility upon them is impossible.

The tenth argument: The statement of the Almighty: ﴿So let man look at what he was created from. He was created from a gushing fluid﴾ [al-Tariq: 5–6]. If those ants were rational, understanding and complete, they would have existed before this gushing fluid, and there would be no meaning for "man" except that thing. In that case, man would not have been created from a gushing fluid, and that is a rejection of the text of the Qur'an.

If they say: Why is it not permissible to say that He created him with complete reason and understanding at the time of the covenant, then He removed his reason, understanding and capacity, and then He created him again in the mother's womb and brought him out into this life?

We say: This is false, because if the matter were so, He would not have created him from a drop of semen as an original creation; rather it would have had to be a creation by way of restoration (i'adah). And the Muslims have unanimously agreed that his creation from a drop of semen is the originating creation (al-khalq al-mubtada'). This indicates that what you have mentioned is false.

The eleventh argument: That those ants either are the very same people or are other than them, and the second is false by consensus. What remains is the first. We say: Either it is said that they remained understanding, rational and capable while they were a drop, a clot and a lump of flesh, or they did not remain so. The first is false by the self-evident judgment of reason. The second requires saying that man came to have life four times: the first at the time of the covenant, the second in this world, the third in the grave, and the fourth on the Resurrection. And that he suffered death three times: death after the life obtained in the first covenant, death in this world, and death in the grave. This number contradicts the number mentioned in the Almighty's statement: ﴿Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice﴾ [Ghafir: 11].

The twelfth argument: The statement of the Almighty: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12]. If this view of the ants were correct, then those ants would be the human being, since he is the one addressed, the one rewarded and the one punished. But that is false, because those ants were not created from a drop, a clot, or a lump of flesh, while the text of the Book is evidence that man was created from a drop and a clot. That is the Almighty's statement: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾, and His statement: ﴿Woe to man, how ungrateful he is! From what thing did He create him? From a drop He created him﴾ [Abasa: 17–19]. These are the sum of the arguments mentioned to show that this view is weak.

[Page 42]

The second view on the interpretation of this verse is that of the people of reflection and rational inquiry: God brought forth the offspring, who are the children, from the loins of their fathers. This bringing forth means that they were a drop of semen, and God brought them forth in the wombs of their mothers, made them a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then made them human beings, well-formed and complete creatures. Then He made them bear witness against themselves through the signs of His oneness that He had placed in them, the wonders of His creation, and the marvels of His workmanship. Through this bearing witness, it was as though they had said "Yes," even though no statement was made with the tongue. There are parallels to this in the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth, "Come willingly or unwillingly." They said, "We come willingly."﴾ [Fussilat: 11]

[Page 42, continued]

Among them is the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82] And the saying of the Arabs:

*The wall said to the peg, "Why do you split me?"*
*He said, "Ask him who is hammering me."*
*For the one behind me... has not left me alone behind me.*

And the poet's words:

*The basin is full and says, "Enough for me!"*

This type of metaphor and figurative speech is well known in discourse, so it is necessary to interpret the speech in this way. This, then, is the discussion in establishing these two views. This second view is entirely free of criticism. And even supposing this view is valid, it would not contradict the validity of the first view. The question is only whether the first view is valid or not.

If someone asks: "What, then, is your preferred position on this?"

We say: here there are two points of discussion:

The first: Is it valid to hold that the covenant was taken from the *dharr* (atoms, or tiny offspring)?

The second: Supposing it is valid to hold this, is it possible to make it an interpretation of the wording of this verse?

As for the first point: those who deny it have relied on the rational proofs that we mentioned and established, and it is possible to answer each of them with a convincing argument.

As for the first of the rational arguments mentioned, namely that if the covenant had indeed been taken, we would be obligated to remember it now:

We say: The one who creates the knowledge of the occurrence of past states is God, Exalted is He, because this knowledge is rational and necessary (*ḍarūrī*, i.e., self-evident). Necessary knowledge is created by God, Exalted is He. Given that this is so, it is valid for Him, Exalted is He, to create it.

If they say: "If you permit this, then permit the claim that before this body we were in other bodies by way of transmigration (*tanāsukh*, the passing of souls from body to body), even though we do not now remember the states of those bodies!"

We say: The difference between the two matters is clear. For if we were in other bodies and remained in them for years and eons, it would be customarily impossible to forget them. But the taking of this covenant occurred in the briefest time and the shortest period, so forgetting it is not improbable. This clear difference is decisive in establishing the validity of this distinction. For a person who remains at a single action for many years cannot forget it, whereas if he practices a single action for only a moment, he may forget it. Thus the difference has become evident.

As for the second argument, namely that it is said: the totality of those atoms is impossible to be present all together in the loins of Adam, peace be upon him.

We say: According to us, the bodily structure is not a condition for the occurrence of life, and the indivisible atom (*al-jawhar al-fard*, the partless substance) is capable of life and reason. So when we make each of those atoms an indivisible substance, why do you say that the loins of Adam, peace be upon him, cannot contain all of them? However, this answer is only complete if we say that the human being is an indivisible substance and a partless part of the body, according to the view of some of the early thinkers. But if we say that the human being is the rational soul (*al-nafs al-nāṭiqah*), and that it is a substance that is neither spatially located nor an accident inhering in a located thing, then the question is removed.

[Page 43]

As for the third argument, namely his saying: "The benefit of taking the covenant is that it would be a proof at that time or in the present life."

Our answer is to say: God does what He wills and decrees what He desires. Moreover, do not the Mu'tazilah, when they wish to establish the doctrine of the weighing of deeds and the speaking of the limbs, say: "It is not improbable that for some of the responsible persons, the hearing of these things would be a grace (*luṭf*, divine favor that facilitates obedience)"? Likewise here, it is not improbable that for some of the angels, in distinguishing the blessed from the wretched at the time of taking the covenant, there would be a grace. It has also been said that God will remind them of that covenant on the Day of Resurrection. The remaining arguments are weak, and the discussion of them is easy and simple.

As for the second point: supposing the validity of the view that the covenant was taken from the *dharr*, is it possible to make it an interpretation of this verse? We say: the three arguments mentioned earlier prevent this, because His saying: ﴿When your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring﴾ — we have shown what is meant by it, namely that He took from the loins of the children of Adam. Furthermore, if this offspring had been taken from the loins of Adam, He would have said: "from his loins, his offspring," and not "from their loins, their offspring."

The defenders of this view answered this objection: it has been authentically transmitted from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he interpreted this verse in this way, and it is not possible to criticize the interpretation of the Messenger of God.

We say: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that God brought forth the *dharr* from the loins of the children of Adam. This is to be understood to mean that God knows that a certain person will beget a certain son, and that son will beget another, and so on. According to the order in which He knows they will enter existence, He brings them forth and distinguishes some of them from others. As for the claim that God brings forth all that offspring from the loins of Adam, there is nothing in the wording of the verse that proves this, nor is there anything in the verse that proves its falsehood. However, a report (*khabar*) has indicated it. Thus the bringing forth of the offspring from the loins of the children of Adam is established by the Qur'an, and the bringing forth of the offspring from the loins of Adam is established by the report. Given this, there is no contradiction or conflict between the two matters, so it is necessary to adopt both together, in order to preserve the verse and the report from criticism as far as possible. This is the end of the discussion in establishing this point.

* * *

The second issue: Nafi' (Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān), Ibn ʿĀmir, and Abū ʿUmar recited *dhurriyyātihim* (ذُرِّيّاتِهِمْ) with the *alif*, in the plural, while the rest recited *dhurriyyatahum* (ذُرِّيَّتَهم), in the singular.

Al-Wāḥidī (Abū al-Ḥasan al-Wāḥidī, the exegete) said: *al-dhurriyyah* (the offspring) may be used for both the singular and the plural. Whoever recites it in the singular has dispensed with pluralizing it, and since it may be used for the plural, it is like *al-bashar* (mankind), which is used for the singular, as in His words: ﴿This is not a human (*bashar*)﴾ [Yusuf: 31], and for the plural, as in His words: ﴿Shall mere humans (*abashar*) guide us?﴾ [al-Taghabun: 6], and His words: ﴿You are only human beings like us﴾ [Ibrahim: 10]. Just as *bashar* is not pluralized either by the regular plural or by the broken plural, likewise *dhurriyyah* is not pluralized. Whoever pluralizes it says: even if *dhurriyyah* is singular, there is no difficulty in its being pluralized, and if it is already a plural, its pluralization is also acceptable, for you have seen that broken plurals have been pluralized, as in *al-ṭuruqāt* (the roads) and *al-jadarāt* (the walls). This is the view preferred by Yunus (ibn Ḥabīb, the grammarian).

As for His words: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves, "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes."﴾ — we say: According to the view of those who affirm the first covenant, all these things are to be taken according to their apparent meanings. But according to the view of those who deny it, they are to be taken as an analogy (*tamthīl*), and the meaning is that God established for them proofs of His lordship, and their intellects bore witness to it. Thus this became like what would occur if He had made us testify against ourselves and acknowledge His oneness.

As for His words: *shahidnā* (ﺷَهِدْنا, "we testify"), there are two views on it:

The first view: it is part of the speech of the angels. This is because when they said "Yes," God said to the angels, "Bear witness," and they said, "We bear witness." According to this view, it is good to pause at His words: ﴿They said, "Yes."﴾ because the speech of the offspring ends here. As for His words: ﴿Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ its meaning is: the angels said, "We bear witness against them with their acknowledgment, lest they say what we did not acknowledge," so the particle *lā* ("not") has been dropped, as in His words: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it should shake with you﴾ [al-Nahl: 15], meaning "lest it shake with you." This is the view of the Kufans. According to the Basrans, its implied meaning is: "We bore witness out of aversion to their saying..."

The second view: His words *shahidnā* are part of the remaining speech of the offspring. According to this interpretation, His words: ﴿Lest you should say on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this."﴾ are connected to His words: ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves﴾, and the meaning is: "He made them testify concerning themselves to such and such, lest they say on the Day of Resurrection: 'Indeed, we were unaware of this,'" or "out of aversion to their saying that." According to this interpretation, it is not permissible to pause at His words *shahidnā*, because His words *an yaqūlū* ("that they say") are connected to what precedes it, namely His words *wa-ashhadahum* ("and He made them testify"), so it is not permissible to separate it from that.

The readers differed concerning the words *an yaqūlū* (أنْ يَقُولُوا, "that they say") and *an taqūlū* (أنْ تَقُولُوا, "that you say"). Abū ʿAmr recited them all with the *yāʾ* (third-person), because the preceding speech was in the third person: His words ﴿from the children of Adam, from their loins﴾ and ﴿And He made them testify concerning themselves﴾, so that "they" would not say. The rest recited with the *tāʾ* (second-person), because a second-person address has occurred in the speech, namely His words: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ "They said, 'Yes, we testify.'" Both readings are good, because the absent persons are, in meaning, the addressed persons.

As for His words: ﴿Or you should say, "Indeed, our fathers associated partners with God before, and we were only their offspring after them."﴾ The exegetes said: the meaning is that the purpose of this making them testify is that the unbelievers should not say, "We only associated partners because our fathers did so, and we imitated them in that association." This is what is meant by His words: ﴿Will You destroy us for what the falsifiers did?﴾ The conclusion is that when God took the covenant from them, they were prevented from holding on to this excuse.

As for those who understood the verse to mean merely the establishment of proofs, they said: the meaning of the verse is that We established these proofs and made them manifest to the intellects, out of aversion to their saying on the Day of Resurrection, "Indeed, we were unaware of this," for no warner had alerted us to it, or out of aversion to their saying that they associated partners only by way of imitating their forefathers, because the establishing of proofs for monotheism remains with them, so they have no excuse for turning away from it and turning instead to imitation and following the fathers.

Then He said: ﴿And thus We detail the verses﴾. The meaning is: just as We have explained and clarified in this verse, We have clarified the rest of the verses, so that they might reflect upon them, return to the truth, and turn away from falsehood. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿so that they may return﴾. It has also been said: that is, [We detail the verses concerning] what covenant He took from them regarding monotheism.

There is also a third view regarding the verse: that human souls exist before the bodies, and the acknowledgment of the existence of God is a necessary consequence of their essences and realities. This knowledge does not need acquisition or seeking to attain it. This matter, however, is only fully disclosed through obscure rational investigations, which cannot be mentioned in this book. And God knows best.
