Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 177:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Evil is the example of the people who denied Our signs and were wronging themselves.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said, after likening them to the dog, ﴿That is the example of the people who denied Our signs﴾, and by this He deterred from disbelief and denial, He emphasized it in the mode of deterrence by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Evil is the example﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-Layth said: sa'a (ساء) yasu'u is a verb that is both intransitive and transitive. It is said: sa'a al-shay' yasu'u, meaning "the thing is ugly" (sa'in, ساء, "ugly"), when it is repugnant; and sa'ahu yasu'uhu, meaning "it displeased him" (masa'ah, مساءة). The grammarians said: its estimated form is: "evil is the example, the example of the people," with mathalan (مَثَلًا, "example") in the accusative as a tamyiz (specification), because when you say sa'a, it is permissible to mention something other than mathalan; so when you mention a type, you have distinguished it from the rest of the types. As for your saying al-qawm (القَوْمُ, "the people"), its nominative case is on two grounds:

The first: that it is a mubtada' (subject), and your saying sa'a mathalan (ساءَ مَثَلًا) is its predicate (khabar).

The second: that when you said sa'a mathalan, you were asked: "Who is it?" and you said "al-qawm," so its nominative case is because it is the predicate of an omitted mubtada'. Al-Jahdari recited: sa'a mathalu al-qawm (ساءَ مَثَلُ القَوْمِ), "evil is the example of the people."

The second issue: the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿evil is the example﴾ requires that this example be described as evil, and that is not permissible, because this example was mentioned by God, exalted is He, so how could it be described as evil? Also, it serves to deter from disbelief and to call to faith, so how could it be described as evil? Therefore, what is described as evil must be what the example conveys of their denial of the signs of God, exalted is He, and their turning away from them, to the point that in this likening they became like the panting dog.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and were wronging themselves﴾, it is either coordinated with His saying "denied" (كَذَّبُوا), so that it enters within the scope of the relative clause, in the sense of "those who combined denial of the signs of God with wronging themselves"; or it is a sentence disconnected from the relative clause, in the sense of "and they wronged none but themselves by denial." As for the fronting of the object (تَقْدِيمُ المَفْعُولِ), it is for restriction (لِلِاخْتِصاصِ), as if it were said: "and they restricted the wronging to themselves, and the effect of that wronging did not pass beyond them to others."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 178:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the one who is guided; and whomever He sends astray, it is those who are the losers.﴾

In the verse there are two issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, had described the misguided with the aforementioned description and made known their condition through the aforementioned parable, He clarified in this verse that guidance is from Allah, and that misguidance is from Allah, exalted is He. At this point the Mu'tazilah were confounded, and they mentioned many interpretations (ta'wil) of it:

The first, which al-Jubba'i mentioned and al-Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) approved, is that what is meant is: whomever Allah guides to Paradise and reward in the Hereafter, he is the one who is guided in this world, the one who follows the path of right conduct in what he has been charged with. Thus Allah, exalted is He, clarified that He guides to reward in the Hereafter only those who have this description, and whomever He misguides from the path of Paradise, ﴿it is those who are the losers﴾.

The second: Some have said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the estimated meaning is: whomever Allah guides, so he accepts and holds fast to His guidance, he is the one who is guided; and whomever He misguides, by his not accepting, he is the loser.

The third: that what is meant by "whomever Allah guides" is that whoever Allah has described as being guided, he is the one who is guided, because that is like praise, and Allah's praise is only attained with regard to one who is described by that praiseworthy attribute. And "whomever He misguides", i.e., whoever Allah has described as being astray, ﴿it is those who are the losers﴾.

The fourth: that what is meant by "whomever Allah guides" is guidance through subtle favours (alṭaf) and an increase in guidance, so he is the one who is guided; and "whomever He misguides" means he is deprived of that because of the bad choice that proceeded from him, so by this cause he is excluded from being affected by those subtle favours, and he is among the losers.

Know that we have shown that decisive rational proofs have established that guidance and misguidance occur only from Allah, in several ways:

The first: that the act depends on the occurrence of the motive, and the occurrence of the motive is only from Allah, so the act is only from Allah.

The second: that the opposite of Allah's knowledge is impossible to occur; so whoever Allah knows will have faith, he cannot be capable of disbelief, and vice versa.

The third: that every person intends to acquire faith and knowledge, so when disbelief occurs after it, we know that it is not from him but from another.

Then we say:

As for the first interpretation: it is weak, because it takes His saying "whomever Allah guides" to refer to guidance in the Hereafter to Paradise, and His saying "he is the one who is guided" to refer to being guided to the truth in this world, and this entails incoherence in the composition, rather it is necessary that guidance and being guided refer to one thing, so that the speech is well composed.

As for the second: it is an undertaking to supply an additional supposition, which is contrary to the wording, and if the door to such suppositions were opened, negation would turn into affirmation and affirmation into negation, and the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, would cease to be a proof, for each person could supply in the verse whatever he wishes, and then everything would cease to convey meaning.

As for the third: it is weak, because the saying of one who says: "So-and-so guided so-and-so" does not at all indicate in the language that he described him as being guided. Analogizing this to His saying "So-and-so misled so-and-so and declared him an unbeliever" is an analogy within language, and it is in the extreme of corruption. The fourth is also false, because every subtle favour that lies within Allah's capacity, He has already bestowed, according to the Mu'tazilah, upon all the disbelievers, so interpreting the verse in this manner is far-fetched. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: His saying ﴿fa-huwa al-muhtadi﴾ (he is the one who is guided) may retain the yā' (ي) in it according to the original form, and it may be dropped seeking lightness, as has been said regarding a verse in the Kitab (of Sibawayh):

fa-ṭirtu bi-munṣulī fī yaʿmalātin dawāmiyal-ayd yakhbiṭnaʾs-sarīḥa
And from its verses also:
ka-khawāfī rīshi ḥamāmatin najdiyyatin ∗∗∗ masḥat bi-māʾi al-bayni ʿaṭfa al-athmadi

Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili said: he means "ka-khawāfī" with the yā' dropped.

As for His saying ﴿wa-man yuḍlil﴾ (and whomever He sends astray): he means "and whomever Allah sends astray and forsakes," ﴿it is those who are the losers﴾, i.e., they lost both this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 179 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind. They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾

This verse is the second proof in this place for the soundness of our school's position on the question of the creation of actions (khalq al-af'al) and the will of created beings. Its explanation is in several aspects.

The first: He, exalted is He, stated explicitly that He created many of the jinn and mankind for Hell, and there is no addition to the clarity of God's statement.

The second: When He, exalted is He, informed about them that they are among the people of the Fire, then if they were not among the people of the Fire, God's knowledge would turn into ignorance and His true report into falsehood. All of that is impossible, and what leads to an impossibility is itself impossible. So their not entering the Fire is impossible. Whoever knows that a thing is impossible is unable to will it. Thus it is established that He, exalted is He, is unable to will that He not cause them to enter the Fire; rather, He must will that He cause them to enter the Fire. This is what the wording of the verse indicates.

The third: The one who is able to disbelieve, if he is not able to believe, then the One who created in him the ability to disbelieve has willed that He cause him to enter the Fire. If he is able to disbelieve and to believe together, then the preponderance of one of the two sides over the other is impossible without a preponderant cause (murajjih). If that preponderant cause arises from himself, it necessitates an infinite regress (tasalsul). If it arises from Him, exalted is He, then since He is the Creator of the motive (da'iyah) that necessitates disbelief, He has certainly created him for the Fire.

The fourth: If He, exalted is He, had created him for Paradise and helped him to acquire what necessitates entering Paradise, and then we assume that the servant strove to acquire disbelief, which necessitates entering the Fire, then the servant's will has been fulfilled and God's will has not been fulfilled. It would then follow that the servant is more capable and more powerful than God, exalted is He, and no rational person says that.

The fifth: The rational person does not will disbelief and ignorance, which necessitate deserving the Fire. Rather, he wills faith and knowledge, which necessitate deserving reward and entering Paradise. So when disbelief and ignorance occur contrary to the servant's intention and the opposite of his effort and striving, it must be that their occurrence is not from the servant, but must be from God, exalted is He.

If they say: the servant only strove to acquire that corrupt, false belief, because the matter became confused for him and he thought it was the true, sound belief.

We say: In that case, he fell into this ignorance only because of that earlier ignorance. If his advancing toward that earlier ignorance was due to another ignorance, then an infinite regress follows, and that is impossible. And if it ends at an ignorance that arose from the beginning, not because of a previous ignorance, then the argument has been directed and the proof and demonstration have been confirmed. Thus it is established that these rational proofs speak in agreement with what the explicit statement of His saying, glorified and exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind.﴾

The Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds human beings create their own actions) said: It is not possible that the meaning of this verse is what you have mentioned, because many verses indicate that He willed from all of them obedience, worship, goodness and righteousness. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ [al-Fath: 8-9]. He said: ﴿And We did not send any messenger except to be obeyed by permission of Allah﴾ [al-Nisa: 64]. He said: ﴿And We have certainly diversified it among them that they may remember﴾ [al-Furqan: 50]. He said: ﴿It is He who sends down upon His servant verses of clear evidence to bring you out from darknesses into the light﴾ [al-Hadid: 9]. He said: ﴿And We sent down with them the Scripture and the balance so that people may maintain justice﴾ [al-Hadid: 25]. He said: ﴿He calls you that He may forgive you of your sins﴾ [Ibrahim: 10]. He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56]. Similar verses are many. We know by necessity that it is not permissible for contradiction to occur in the Qur'an. So we know that it is not possible to take His saying, ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind,﴾ according to its apparent meaning.

The second aspect: He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see﴾, and He mentioned that only as a reproach against them. If they had been created for the Fire, they would not have been able to believe at all, and according to this assumption, it would be ugly to reproach them for abandoning faith.

The third aspect: If He had created them for the Fire, He would have had no blessing upon any of the disbelievers at all, because the benefits of this world, compared to the eternal punishment, are like a drop in the sea. It would be like someone who hands a person a sweet poisoned thing: he is not considered a benefactor to him. So too here. Since the Qur'an is full of the abundance of God's blessings upon all creation, we know that the matter is not as you have mentioned.

The fourth aspect: Praise and blame, reward and punishment, encouragement and warning, nullify this doctrine which they support.

The fifth aspect: If He, exalted is He, had created them for the Fire, He would necessarily have created them from the beginning in the Fire, because there would be no benefit in leading them gradually toward the Fire by creating disbelief in them.

The sixth aspect: His saying ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell﴾ has an apparent meaning that is abandoned, because Hell is the name of that specific place, and it is not permissible that the specific place be what is meant by it. Thus it is established that what God, exalted is He, intended by creating them must be understood as omitted. So it is as if He said: "And We have certainly created them in order that they disbelieve and thus enter Hell." So the verse, according to their view, has its apparent meaning abandoned. Therefore it must be built upon His saying: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me﴾, because its apparent meaning is valid without omission.

The seventh aspect: If the meaning is that when He created them in order that they disbelieve and thus arrive at Hell, the matter in their interpretation returns to saying that this lam is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), yet they interpret it as the lam of consequence although there is no entitlement to the Fire. We have said it of a consequence that is realized together with the entitlement to the Fire, so our statement is more appropriate. Thus it is established by these aspects that it is not possible to take this verse according to its apparent meaning, and so it is necessary to turn to interpretation (ta'wil). Its explanation: Since the consequence for many of the jinn and mankind is entering the Fire of Hell, it is permissible to mention this lam in the sense of consequence. There are many parallels to this in the Qur'an and in poetry. As for the Qur'an, there is His saying: ﴿And thus We diversify the verses, and that they may say: "You have studied"﴾ [al-An'am: 105]. It is known that He did not diversify them so that they would say that, but when they said that, the use of this expression became appropriate. Also, He said: ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs adornment and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead astray from Your way﴾ [Yunus: 88]. Also, He said: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. They did not pick him up for this purpose, but since the outcome of their affair was that, this expression became appropriate. As for poetry, there are verses. He said:

For death the mothers bear their young, just as for the ruin of time dwellings are built.

And he said:

Our wealth we gather for the heirs, and our houses we build for the ruin of time.

And he said:

For him is an angel calling every day: "Give birth for death, and build for ruin."

And he said:

And O mother of Simak, do not grieve, for for death is what the mother bears.

This is the end of the people's response regarding the answer.

Know that turning to interpretation is only proper when it has been established by proof that reason forbids taking this expression according to its apparent meaning. But since it has been established by proof that there is no truth except what the apparent meaning of the expression indicates, turning to interpretation in such a context is pointless. As for the verses by which they held to establish the Mu'tazilah doctrine, they are countered by the surging seas full of verses indicating the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah). Among them is what precedes this verse, which is His saying: ﴿Whomever Allah guides, he is the guided; and whomever He leaves astray, it is those who are the losers﴾, which is the explicit statement of our doctrine. And what follows this verse, which is His saying: ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them step by step from where they do not know. And I will give them time; indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-A'raf: 182-183]. Since what precedes this verse and what follows it are nothing but what strengthens our position and reinforces our doctrine, the Mu'tazilah's argument for the obligation to interpret this verse is extremely weak.

* * *

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear﴾, there are two issues in it.

The first issue: Our companions have argued with this verse for the soundness of their position regarding the creation of actions. They said: There is no doubt that those disbelievers had hearts with which they understood their worldly interests, and there is no doubt that they had eyes with which they saw visible things and ears with which they heard words. So it is necessary that the meaning of this verse be restricted to what pertains to religion: that they did not understand with their hearts what pertains to the interests of religion, and that they did not see or hear what pertains to the interests of religion.

Once this is established, we say: It is established that He charged them with attaining religion while their hearts, sights and hearing were not suitable for that. This operates in the manner of preventing something and turning away from it while commanding it, and that is what is sought. The Mu'tazilah said: If they were like that, it would be ugly of God to charge them, because charging one who has no capacity to act is ugly and unbecoming of the All-Wise. Therefore it is necessary to interpret the verse as meaning that by their great turning away from the proofs and their not paying attention to them, they became like one who has no understanding heart, no seeing eye, and no hearing ear.

The answer: When a person's aversion to something becomes firmly rooted, that firmly rooted aversion becomes an obstacle preventing him from understanding the speech that proves the soundness of the thing, and an obstacle preventing him from seeing its merits and virtues. This is a necessary inner state that every rational person finds within himself. For this reason they said in the well-known proverb: "Your love for a thing makes you blind and deaf."

Once this is established, we say: Groups of disbelievers reached, in their enmity toward the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and in their hatred of him, and in the intensity of their aversion to accepting his religion and acknowledging his prophethood, this degree and even more. And it is known by necessity that the arising of hatred and love in the heart is not by a person's choice; rather, it arises in the heart, whether a person wishes it or dislikes it.

When this is established, we say: it has become clear that the arising of this aversion and enmity in the heart is not by the servant's choice, and it has been established that whenever this aversion and enmity arise in the heart, a person cannot, with that deep-rooted aversion and intense enmity, attain understanding and knowledge. Once this is established, the doctrine of compulsion (*jabr*, the view that human acts are predetermined and not chosen) follows necessarily, with no escape from it.

It is related from the Commander of the Faithful, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, that he gave a sermon explaining this meaning, and it is of the utmost excellence. Shaykh Ahmad al-Bayhaqi related in his book *Manaqib al-Shafiʿi* (*The Virtues of al-Shafiʿi*), may Allah be pleased with him, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he addressed the people and said: "The most wondrous thing in man is his heart. In it are sources of wisdom and their opposites. If hope beckons to it, greed infatuates it; if greed stirs it, covetousness destroys it; if despair destroys it, regret kills it; if anger befalls it, rage intensifies; if it is made happy by contentment, it becomes wretched through discontent; if fear reaches it, sorrow preoccupies it; if calamity strikes it, impatience kills it; if it finds wealth, richness makes it insolent; if poverty grips it, affliction occupies it; if hunger exhausts it, weakness keeps it sitting. So every shortfall in it is harmful, and every excess in it is corrupting."

I say: this passage is of the utmost majesty and nobility, and it is like one who has looked into the secret of the question of qadar (divine decree) and predestination, because the actions of the limbs are tied to the states of the hearts, and every state of the heart is grounded in another state that came before it. When a person comprehends this, he knows that there is no escape from acknowledging compulsion.

The Shaykh al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, in his book *al-Ihya'* (*The Revival of the Religious Sciences*), mentioned a section establishing the doctrine of compulsion.

Then he said: If it is said: "I find within myself that if I wish to act, I act, and if I wish to refrain, I refrain; so my act is accomplished by me, not by another." Then he said: Suppose you have found this within yourself. We would say: Do you find within yourself that if you wish to will something, you will it, and if you wish not to will it, you do not will it? I do not think you would say that, for otherwise the matter would regress infinitely. Rather, whether you will or do not will, you will that thing, and when you will it, whether you will it or not, you do it. So neither your willing it is by you, nor is the occurrence of your act after the occurrence of your willing by you. Thus man is compelled in the form of one who chooses.

**The second issue:** Scholars have used the words of the Exalted, ﴿They have hearts with which they do not understand﴾, as evidence that the locus of knowledge is the heart, because He, the Exalted, negated understanding and comprehension from their hearts in a context of blame. This is valid only if the locus of understanding and comprehension is the heart, and Allah knows best.

As for His words, ﴿They are like cattle; rather, they are more astray﴾, its explanation is that man and the rest of the animals share the powers of nature: the nutritive, the growth-producing, and the reproductive. They also share in the benefits of the five external and internal senses, and in the states of imagination, reflection, and recollection. The distinction between man and the other animals lies in the rational and discerning faculty, which guides him to knowledge of truth for its own sake and to good for the sake of acting upon it. When the unbelievers turned away from considering the states of intellect and reflection, from knowing the truth, and from acting upon good, they became like cattle.

Then He said: ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾, because animals have no capacity to attain these virtues, whereas man was given the capacity to attain them. Whoever turns away from acquiring great virtues while having the capacity to attain them is in a worse state than one who does not acquire them due to incapacity. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾. And the wisest of poets said:

The spirit, with the Lord of the Throne, is its origin,
and the dust of the earth is the root of the body and frame.
The Sovereign, the Compassionate, joined the two together
so that they might be fit to receive command and trials.
So the spirit is in a state of estrangement, and the body is in a homeland;
then recognize the rights of the stranger far from his homeland.

Other interpretations have been given of His words, ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾. It has been said: because cattle obey Allah, the Exalted, whereas the unbeliever does not obey. Muqatil said: they are more misguided in the way than cattle, because cattle know their Lord and remember Him, whereas they do not know their Lord nor remember Him. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Rather, they are more astray﴾, because cattle perceive their benefits and harms, so they strive to obtain their benefits and guard against their harms. These unbelievers and obstinate people, most of them know that they are obstinate, yet they persist in it and cast themselves into the Fire and into punishment. It has also been said that they flee always toward their owners and those who look after their welfare, whereas the unbeliever flees from his Lord and his God who has bestowed upon him blessings without limit. It has been said: because they go astray when there is no guide with them, but when a guide is with them they rarely go astray. These unbelievers have had prophets come to them and books sent down to them, yet they increase in misguidance.

Then Allah concluded the verse by saying: ﴿Those are the heedless﴾. ʿAta' said: heedless of what Allah has prepared for His friends of reward and for His enemies of punishment.

صفحة ٥٤

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 180 (part 1 of 2):**

God's words: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, described those created for Hell by His words, ﴿Those are the heedless﴾, He then commanded the remembrance of God, exalted is He, saying: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them.﴾ This is as if to alert that what brings about entry into Hell is heedlessness of the remembrance of God, and what delivers one from the punishment of Hell is the remembrance of God, exalted is He. Those of spiritual taste and direct witnessing (ahl al-dhawq wa al-mushahada) find in their souls that the matter is so. When the heart becomes heedless of the remembrance of God and turns toward this world and its desires, it falls into the state of greed and the bitter cold of deprivation (zamharir al-hirman), and it never ceases to move from one desire to another, from one pursuit to another, and from one darkness to another. But when the gate of the remembrance of God and the knowledge of God is opened upon the heart, it is freed from the fires of calamities and from the regrets of losses, and it perceives the knowledge of the Lord of the earth and the heavens.

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: God's words ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ are mentioned in four surahs:

The first of them is this surah.

The second is at the end of Surat Bani Isra'il, in His words: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful; whichever you call, to Him belong the most beautiful names. And do not be too loud in your prayer or too quiet therein, but seek between that a way.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:110]

The third is at the beginning of Ta-Ha, namely His words: ﴿Allah — there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:8]

The fourth is at the end of al-Hashr, namely His words: ﴿He is Allah, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ [al-Hashr 59:24]

Having known this, we say: the "names" (al-asma') are words that indicate meanings. They are beautiful only through the beauty of their meanings and their concepts. There is no sense of "beauty" with respect to God, exalted is He, except the mention of attributes of perfection and qualities of majesty, and these are confined to two types: the absence of His need for anything other than Him, and the affirmation that everything other than Him is in need of Him.

[Page 55]

Know that we have a book on the explanation of God's names, rich in subtleties and noble in realities, which we named *Lawami' al-Bayyinat fi Tafsir al-Asma' wa al-Sifat*. Whoever wishes to investigate it thoroughly should refer to it. Here we mention some flashes and points from it. We say: the names of God can be divided in many respects.

The first respect: we say that a name is either a name for the Essence (dhat), or for a part of the parts of the Essence, or for an attribute external to the Essence and subsisting in it. As for the name of the Essence, it is what is called the Greatest Name (al-ism al-a'zam), and in uncovering what is hidden in it of investigations there are secrets. As for the name of a part of the Essence, it is impossible with respect to God, exalted is He, because this is only applied to an essence composed of parts, and everything that is like this is contingent (mumkin). The Necessary Being (wajib al-wujud) cannot have a part.

As for the name of an attribute, we say: an attribute is either real (haqiqiyya), or relational (idafiyya), or negative (salbiyya), or what is composed of these three. These are four, because it is either a real attribute together with a relation, or together with a negation; or a negative attribute together with a relation; or a combination of a real attribute, a relation, and a negation. As for a real attribute free of relation, it is like our saying "existent" according to one who says that existence is an attribute, or our saying "one" according to one who says that unity is a second attribute, and like our saying "living," for life is a real attribute free of connections and relations. As for a purely relational attribute, it is like our saying "mentioned" and "known." As for a negative attribute, it is like our saying "the Holy, the Perfect in peace" (al-Quddus al-Salam). As for a real attribute together with a relation, it is like our saying "Knowing" and "Powerful," for knowledge is a real attribute and it has a connection to the known, and power is a real attribute and it has a connection to the powerful object. As for a real attribute together with a negation, it is like our saying "Eternal, without beginning" (qadim azali), for it is an expression of a being that has no beginning. As for a relational attribute together with a negation, it is like our saying "First," for He is the one who preceded others and was not preceded by others. As for a real attribute together with a relation and a negation, it is like our saying "Wise," for He is the one who knows the realities of things and does not do what it is not fitting to do. The attribute of knowledge is a real attribute, and that this attribute is connected to the known things is a relation and a connection, and that He is not an agent of what is not fitting is a negation.

Having known this, we say: negations are infinite and relations are also infinite. His being the Creator of created things is a relational attribute; His giving life and causing death are specific relations; and His being the Provider is another specific relation. Through these two types of considerations there arise names for God, exalted is He, that have no limit, because His objects of power are infinite. Since there is no way to know the true reality of His Essence, and the way to know Him is only through knowing His acts, whoever has greater insight into the secrets of His wisdom in His creation has greater knowledge of God's names. And since this is a sea with no shore and no end, likewise there is no end to knowing the Most Beautiful Names of God.

The second type of division of God's names is what the mutakallimun (the scholastic theologians) have said: that the attributes of God, exalted is He, are of three kinds: what is necessary (wajib), what is possible (jA'iz), and what is impossible (mustahil) for God, exalted is He. For God, according to each of these three categories, there are specific names.

The third type of division of God's names: the attributes of God, exalted is He, are either essential (dhatiyya), or meaningful (ma'nawiyya), or attributes of acts (sifat al-af'al).

[Page 56]

The fourth type of division of God's names, exalted is He: either it is permissible to apply them to other than God, exalted is He, or it is not permissible.

As for the first category, it is like our saying: the Generous, the Merciful, the Mighty, the Subtle, the Great, the Creator. These words may be applied to servants, although their meaning with respect to God, exalted is He, differs from their meaning with respect to servants.

As for the second category, it is like our saying: Allah, the Most Merciful (al-Rahman).

As for the first category: when these are restricted by specific qualifiers, they reach a state in which they cannot be applied except to God, exalted is He, like our saying: "O Most Merciful of the merciful," "O Most Generous of the generous," and "O Creator of the heavens and the earths."

The fifth type of division of God's names: it is said that among the names of God are those that may be mentioned alone, like our saying: "O Allah," "O Most Merciful," "O Living," "O Wise." And among them are those that are not like this, like our saying "the Causer of Death" (mumit) and "the Harmer" (darr). It is not permissible to mention them alone; rather it must be said: "O Giver of Life, O Causer of Death, O Harmer, O Benefiter."

The sixth type of division of God's names, exalted is He: it is said that the first thing known of the attributes of God, exalted is He, is that He is the one who originates things, giving preponderance to their existence over their non-existence. This is because we only know His existence, glorified is He, through the inference from the existence of contingent beings to Him. When the proof indicates that this sensible world is contingent in its existence and non-existence by its essence, the intellect judges that it needs a preponderant cause that gives preference to its existence over its non-existence, and that preponderant cause is none other than God, glorified is He. Thus it is established that the first thing known of Him, exalted is He, is that He is the one who gives preponderance and is the effective cause. Then we say: that preponderant cause either gives preponderance by way of necessity, or by way of possibility. The first is false, for otherwise the world would have eternally persisted by its eternal cause, and that is false. So what remains is that it has been given preponderance by way of possibility. And His being the one who gives preponderance by way of possibility is nothing other than His being Powerful, exalted is He. Thus it is established that what is known of Him, after knowing that He is the preponderant cause, is that He is Powerful. Then, after this, we infer from the perfection and soundness of His acts that He is Knowing. Then, when we know that He, exalted is He, is Powerful and Knowing, and we know that the Powerful Knower cannot but be Living, we know from His being Powerful and Knowing that He is Living. From this it becomes clear that knowledge of His attributes, exalted is He, and of His names, is not on one level; rather, knowledge of them consists of ordered kinds of knowledge, some of which are derived from others.

The second issue: God's words ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names﴾ imply restriction (hasr), and their meaning is that the most beautiful names belong only to God, exalted is He. Rational proof may indicate the soundness of this meaning. This is because a being either exists necessarily by its own essence, or exists contingently by its own essence. The one that exists necessarily by its essence is none other than the One, namely God, glorified is He. As for everything other than that One, it is contingent by its essence, and everything contingent by its essence is in need, in its quiddity (mahiyya), in its existence, and in all its real, relational, and negative attributes, of the bestowal of the Necessary Being by its essence. Were it not for this, it would remain in pure non-existence and sheer negation. So God, glorified is He, is perfect in His essence, and the perfection of everything else is obtained by His generosity and beneficence. Thus every perfection, majesty, and nobility belongs to Him, glorified is He, by His essence, through His essence, and in His essence, while for others it is by way of loan. And what belongs to other than Him from its own essence is poverty, need, deficiency, and non-existence. Thus this clear proof establishes that the most beautiful names belong only to God, and the most beautiful attributes belong only to God, and that everything other than Him is drowned in the sea of annihilation and deficiency.

* * *

The third issue: this verse indicates that the names of God belong only to God, and the most beautiful attributes belong only to God, and so it is necessary that they be described by beauty and perfection. This indicates that every name which does not convey an attribute of perfection and majesty in the named one may not be applied to God, glorified is He. On this basis, it is reported from Jahm ibn Safwan that he said: "I do not apply to the Essence of God, exalted is He, the term 'thing' (shay')." He said: "Because the term 'thing' applies to the lowest and most base of things and those furthest from the ranks of nobility, and if that is so, it must be decided that it does not confer on the named one any honor, rank, or majesty."

Given that this is established, we say: it has been established by the requirement of this verse that the names of God must indicate nobility and perfection, and it has been established that the term "thing" is not so; therefore it is forbidden to name God by being a "thing." He said: "God forbid that this be a dispute about whether He is in Himself a reality, an essence, and existent. The dispute is only over the mere wording: whether it is correct to name Him by this word or not. As for our saying that He is the Originator of things, it is a name that indicates praise, majesty, and nobility, so applying this name to God is true." Then he reinforced this argument with other kinds of proofs:

The first: God's words ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 42:11]. Its meaning is: "there is not a like of His like anything." Undoubtedly, the very thing is a like of the like of its own self. Since it has been established by reason that everything is a like of the like of its own self, and the Qur'anic proof indicates that the like of the like of God is not a thing, this is an explicit statement that He, exalted is He, is not named by the name of "thing." And no one may say that the (al-kaf) in His words ﴿like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura 42:11] is a superfluous particle with no benefit, for to interpret the words of God as idle, pointless, and without benefit is far-fetched.

The second argument: God's words ﴿Creator of all things﴾ [al-An'am 6:102]. If God, exalted is He, were included under the name of "thing," it would follow that He is the creator of Himself, and that is impossible. It cannot be said that this is a general statement to which specification has been applied, for we say that this is a statement that must be examined. We say: it has been established by the well-known custom that they treat the majority as if it were the whole, and treat the rare exception as if it were nonexistent.

Having established this, we say: when the majority and the predominant part is present, and the exceptional, rare part is outside it, they attach that majority to the whole, attach that rare exception to the non-existent, apply the word "all" to it, and regard that rare exception as an instance of the specification of a general term.

Once you understand this, we say: if the term "thing" (shay') is truly applicable to God Most High, then the greatest of all things would be God Most High, and restricting it to such a designation would amount to falsehood. Therefore it must be believed that God Most High is not named by the name "thing", so that this prohibited consequence does not befall us.

The third argument: this name is not found in the Book of God nor in the Sunnah of His Messenger, and we have not seen any of the early generations (al-salaf) say in their supplication "O Thing." Therefore it is obligatory to refrain from it. The proof that it is not found in the Book of God is that the verse in which this name is supposedly included is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?" Say: "God is witness between me and you."﴾ [al-An'am: 19]. We have already explained in Surat al-An'am that this verse does not indicate the intended meaning, so the discussion about it falls away.

If someone says: our statements "existent," "mentioned," "essence," and "known" are terms that do not indicate nobility and majesty, so you must say that it is not permissible to apply them to God Most High. We say: the correct position in this matter is detailed distinction. We say: what do you mean by your saying that God Most High is a thing, an essence, and a reality? If you mean that God Most High in Himself is an essence, a reality, established, existent, and a thing, then He is so without any doubt or ambiguity. But if you mean whether it is permissible to call upon Him with these terms or not, we say: it is not permissible; for we have seen the early generations saying: "O Allah, O Merciful, O Compassionate," and so on through the rest of the noble names, and we have neither seen nor heard that anyone says: "O Essence, O Reality, O Concept, O Known." Therefore, refraining from such terms in the context of calling upon and supplicating to God Most High is obligatory. And God knows best.

The fourth issue: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ indicates that God Most High possesses beautiful names, and that a person is obligated to call upon God by them. This indicates that the names of God are tawqifi (revealed/fixed by scripture) and not conventional (istilahi). What confirms this is that it is permissible to say "O Generous (jawwad)," but it is not permissible to say "O Liberal (sakhiy)," nor "O Intelligent (aqil), O Physician (tabib), O Jurist (faqih)." This indicates that the names of God Most High are tawqifi and not conventional.

The fifth issue: the verse indicates that the name is other than the named, because it indicates that the names of God are many, since the word "names" (asma') is plural, and plural denotes three or more. Thus it is established that God's names are many, and there is no doubt that God is one, so it is necessarily certain that the name is other than the named. Also, His saying: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ requires the attribution of the names to God, and the attribution of a thing to itself is impossible. Also, if it were said: "And to God belong the essences," it would be false; but when He said: ﴿And to God belong the names,﴾ it was true, and this indicates that the name is other than the named.

* * *

The sixth issue: His saying: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ indicates that a person does not call upon his Lord except by those Most Beautiful Names, and this calling cannot be realized unless he knows the meanings of those names, and knows by proof that He has a God and a Lord, a Creator, described by those noble and sanctified attributes. When he knows this by proof, then it is fitting for him to call upon his Lord by those names and attributes. Moreover, that supplication has many conditions, mentioned in detail in the book (al-Minhaj) of Abu 'Abdullah al-Halimi. The best of what is in it is that he should be mindful of two matters: the first: the might of Lordship (izzat al-Rububiyyah); and the second: the humility of servanthood (dhillat al-Ubudiyyah). Then the supplication is fitting and the mention of that remembrance is greatly effective. But if he is not like this, it is of little benefit. I will give an example of this meaning: whoever wishes to say "Allahu Akbar" at the opening of his prayer (tahrimah) must in his intention bring to mind as much as he can of the traces of God Most High in the creation of his own self, his body, and his powers, intellectual, sensory, or motive. Then he should proceed from himself to bring to mind the traces of God's wisdom in the creation of all people, all animals, all kinds of plants and minerals, and the celestial phenomena of thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts found in every part of the world. Then he should bring to mind the traces of God Most High's power in the creation of the earths, mountains, seas, and deserts. Then he should bring to mind the traces of God Most High's power in the creation of the layers of the lower and upper elements. Then he should bring to mind the traces of God Most High's power in the creation of the layers of the heavens in their vastness and greatness, and in the creation of the bodies of the luminaries, the fixed stars and the planets. Then he should bring to mind the traces of God Most High's power in the creation of the Kursi and the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary. Then he should bring to mind the traces of His power in the creation of the Great Throne encompassing all these existents. Then he should bring to mind the traces of His power in the creation of the angels, the bearers of the Throne and the Kursi, and the hosts of the spiritual world. He continues to bring to mind from these ranks and levels the utmost that his understanding, intellect, remembrance, thought, and imagination can reach. Then, upon bringing to mind all these spiritual and corporeal beings, with their varying degrees and differing stations and ranks, he says: "Allahu Akbar," and by his saying "Allah" he points to the Existent who created these things and brought them out from non-existence into existence, and arranged them with the attributes and qualities they possess; and by his saying "Akbar" he means that He, in His greatness, majesty, might, exaltedness, and self-sufficiency, is not likened to these things, but rather He is greater than to be said to be greater than these things. So when you know this one example, measure the remembrance attained together with knowledge and awareness, and then there will open upon your intellect a breath of the secrets deposited beneath His saying: ﴿And to God belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾.

* * *

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names﴾, there are issues in it:

The first issue: Hamzah recited "yalhudun," and 'Asim and al-Kisa'i agreed with him in (Surat) al-Nahl. Al-Farra' said: "yalhudun" and "yulhidun" are two dialects: it is said "lahadtu lahdan" and "alhadtu." The lexicographers said: the meaning of ilhad (deviation) in the language is inclining away from the intended course. Ibn al-Sikkit said: the mulhid is one who turns away from the truth, introducing into it what is not part of it; it is said: "alhada fi al-din" and "lahada." Abu 'Amr, one of the lexicographers, said: ilhad is turning away from uprightness and deviating from it, and from it comes the lahd (the niche dug in the side of a grave). Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: the more preferred is the recitation of the common readers, because of His saying: ﴿and whoever intends therein deviation (ilhad)﴾, and ilhad is more common in their speech, as in their saying "mulhid," and you hardly hear the Arabs say "lahid."

The second issue: The verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said: deviation concerning the names of God occurs in three ways:

The first: applying the blessed and pure names of God to other than God, such as the disbelievers who used to name idols as "gods (alihah)," and from this that they named idols al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and al-Manat; the derivation of al-Lat is from al-Ilah, of al-'Uzza from al-'Aziz, and of Manat from al-Mannan. Musaylimah the liar titled himself "al-Rahman."

The second: that they name God with what it is not permissible to name Him, such as naming one who called Him the father of the Messiah, and the saying of the majority of Christians: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and like the Karramiyyah, who apply the term "body (jism)" to God, may He be glorified, and name Him by it; and like the Mu'tazilah who sometimes say in the course of their speech: "If God did such and such, He would be foolish, deserving of blame," and these expressions indicate bad manners. Our companions said: not everything whose meaning is sound may be applied verbally to God, for it has been established by proof that He, glorified is He, is the Creator of all bodies, yet it is not permissible to say: "O Creator of worms, apes, and ticks"; rather, it is obligatory to exalt God above such remembrances, and to say: "O Creator of the earth and the heavens, O Remover of stumbles, O Rahim of tears," and other beautiful and noble remembrances.

The third: that the servant mentions his Lord with a term whose meaning he does not know and whose referent he does not conceive, for perhaps its referent is something not befitting the majesty of God. These three divisions are deviation in the names.

If someone says: Does the occurrence of the first in applying its term to God Most High necessitate that all words derived from it be applied to Him without restriction?

We say: In my view, the truth is that this is not necessary with regard to God Most High, nor with regard to the angels and prophets. Its explanation: the word "taught ('allama)" occurs regarding God Most High in verses, among them His saying: ﴿and He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]; ﴿and taught you what you did not know﴾ [al-Nisa': 113]; ﴿and We taught him knowledge from Us﴾ [al-Kahf: 65]; ﴿The Most Merciful, taught the Qur'an﴾ [al-Rahman: 1-2]. Yet it is not permissible to say of God Most High "O Teacher (mu'allim)." Also occurs His saying: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], yet in my view it is not permissible to say "O Lover (muhibb)." As for the prophets: regarding Adam, peace be upon him, it occurs: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], yet it is not permissible to say that Adam was disobedient and erring. And regarding Musa, peace be upon him, it occurs: ﴿O father, hire him﴾ [al-Qasas: 26], yet it is not permissible to say that he, peace be upon him, was a hired laborer. The principle is that these potentially misleading terms must be confined to what is transmitted; as for extending the use to words derived from them, in my view this is prohibited and not permissible.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾, which is a threat and warning to whoever deviates concerning God's names. The Mu'tazilah said: the verse has indicated the affirmation of action for the servant, and that the recompense is based upon his action and deed.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 181:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We have created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾, informing that many of the two weighty things (al-thaqalan) are created for the Fire, He followed it with His saying: ﴿And among those whom We created is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾, to show also that many of them are created for Paradise. Know that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the story of Musa His saying: ﴿And among the people of Musa is a community who guide by the truth and by it act justly﴾ [al-A'raf: 159]. When Allah, exalted is He, repeated this statement here, most of the exegetes (mufassirun) took it that what is meant by it is the people of Muhammad (ﷺ). Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it refers to this community. It is also narrated that he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: ("This applies to them, and Allah has given the people of Musa the like of it"). And from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, that he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse and said: ("Among my community there will be a people upon the truth until Isa ibn Maryam descends"). Ibn Abbas said: it means the community of Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates that no era is ever devoid of those who stand for the truth, act upon it and guide to it, and that they never agree upon falsehood in any of the eras, because it is not possible that what is meant is either: the time of the existence of Muhammad (ﷺ), which is the time in which this verse was revealed; or that there has occurred some era in which a people with the described attribute arose; or what we have mentioned, that no era is free of a people described by this attribute. The first is invalid, because it was evident to all people that Muhammad and his companions were upon the truth, so interpreting the verse in this sense removes it from benefit. The second is also invalid, because everyone knows by necessity that there has occurred some era among past eras in which a group of those upon the truth existed. Thus only the third division remains. And it is more indicative that no era has been devoid of a people of those upon the truth, and that their consensus is a proof (hujjah). On this reckoning, this indicates that the consensus of all nations is a proof.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 182–183:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them step by step (from where) they do not know.﴾ ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted mentioned the state of the community that guides and is just, He returned to mention those who deny the signs of Allah the Exalted and the threat that awaits them. So He said: ﴿And those who deny Our signs﴾. This includes all deniers. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): the intended meaning is the people of Makkah. But this is far-fetched, because the general wording covers everyone, except what evidence has excluded.

As for His saying: ﴿We will lead them step by step﴾, *al-istidraj* (gradual leading, from the root *darajah*, "degree") is the form *istifʿal*, meaning either ascending or descending, degree by degree. From it comes *daraja al-ṣabiyy* ("the child walked") when he brought his steps close together; and *adraja al-kitab* ("he folded the book"), meaning he rolled it up piece by piece; and *daraja al-qawm* ("the people died"), meaning some of them died one after another. It is also possible that this word is derived from *al-darj*, which is the wrapping and folding of a thing part by part.

Having known this, the meaning is: We will bring them closer to that which destroys them, and multiply their punishment from where they do not know what is intended for them. This is because whenever they commit a crime or engage in a sin, Allah opens for them a door of blessing and good in this world. So they grow in insolence, immersed in corruption and persistent in error. Through the succession of those blessings they advance in sins. Then Allah seizes them all at once while they are at their most heedless. For this reason ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), when the treasures of Kisra were brought to him, said: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from being led on step by step, for I heard You say: ﴿We will lead them step by step (from where) they do not know.﴾"

Then He said: ﴿And I give them respite; indeed, My plan is firm.﴾ *Al-imla'* in the language means granting delay and lengthening the term; its opposite is *al-iʿjal* (hastening). *Al-maliyy* is a long period of time, and from it is His saying: ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46], meaning for a long while. It is said: *malwah*, *mulwah* and *milawah* of time, meaning a long period. So the meaning of ﴿And I give them respite﴾ is: I grant them time and lengthen the duration of their lives so that they may persist in sins, and I do not hasten to punish them for their disobedience, so that they may abandon it through repentance and turning back. As for His saying: ﴿indeed, My plan is firm﴾, Ibn ʿAbbas said: He means that My scheme is strong. *Al-matin* of anything is the strong one; it is said *matuna matanatan*.

Know that our companions (the Ashʿarites) argued in the matter of qadar and qada' by these three expressions: *al-istidraj*, *al-imla'* and *al-kayd al-matin*. All of them indicate that Allah the Exalted intends for the servant that which drives him to disbelief and distance from Allah the Exalted. This is the opposite of what the Muʿtazilah say.

Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i replied that the meaning of *al-istidraj* is that Allah led them into punishments until they fall into them from where they do not know, leading them to that so that they fall into it suddenly. This punishment may be in this world, like killing and annihilation, and it may be the punishment of the Hereafter. He said: Some of the Mujbirah (determinists) have said that the meaning is: "We will lead them to disbelief from where they do not know." He said: This is corrupt, because Allah the Exalted has informed of their disbelief having already occurred. So what He leads them to is a future act, because the *sin* in His saying ﴿sa-nastadriju-hum﴾ (the *sa-* prefix) indicates the future. And it is not necessary that the meaning be that He leads them to another disbelief, since He may cause them to die before He brings them into another disbelief. So the meaning is what we have said. Moreover, Allah the Exalted does not punish the disbeliever by creating in him another disbelief, since disbelief is his own act, and He punishes him only for his own deed.

As for His saying ﴿And I give them respite﴾, its meaning is: I keep them alive in this world while they persist in disbelief, and I do not hasten to punish them, because they cannot escape Me and cannot overpower Me. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿indeed, My plan is firm﴾, because His plan is His punishment, and He called it a plan because it descends upon the servants from where they do not perceive.

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: His saying ﴿And those who deny Our signs, We will lead them step by step﴾ means what we mentioned: whenever they increase in persistence in sin and disbelief, Allah increases them in blessing and good in this world. Their success in worldly pleasures then becomes a cause of their persistence in turning away from the remembrance of Allah and their distance from returning to obedience to Allah. This is a state we witness in some people, and if this is a sensed and observed matter, how can it be denied?

The second: Suppose that what is meant is leading them to punishment. Even so, this also refutes the claim that He intends for His servant nothing but good and righteousness. For when Allah knew that this leading and this respite may increase him in arrogance, disbelief, corruption and deserving severe punishment, then if He intended good for him, He would have caused him to die before he became deserving of those increases in punishment. Rather, in His wisdom and His care for interests, it would have been required that He not create him at all, to preserve him from this punishment; or that He create him but cause him to die before he reaches the stage of obligation; or that He create him only in Paradise, to preserve him from the calamities of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. But since He created him in this world and cast him into the peril of obligation, prolonged his life and empowered him to commit sins, while knowing that this yields nothing but more disbelief, wickedness and deserving of punishment, we know that He did not create him except for punishment and for the Fire, as He explained in the preceding verse, which is His saying:

[Page 62]

﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind.﴾

I am greatly amazed at these Muʿtazilah, for they see the Qur'an as a sea without shore, filled with these verses and with rational proofs that are decisive and in agreement with them. Yet they are content, in interpreting these verses, with these weak aspects and feeble expressions. However, my knowledge that what Allah wills comes to be removes this amazement. And Allah knows best.
