Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 184:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not reflected? There is no madness in their companion; he is only a clear warner.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had exaggerated in threatening those who turn away from His signs and are heedless of contemplating His proofs and clear evidences, He returned to answering their doubts. So He said: ﴿Have they not reflected upon their companion? There is no madness in him.﴾ Tafakkur (reflection, the seeking of meaning by the heart) is the seeking of meaning with the heart. This is because the thinking of the heart is what is called looking (nazar), intellectual apprehension of a thing, contemplation of it and pondering over it. Just as seeing with the eye is a specific state of disclosure and clarity, and has a preliminary step, which is turning the pupil toward the object seen in order to obtain that sight with the eye, so too seeing with insight, which is called knowledge and certainty, is a specific state of disclosure and clarity, and has a preliminary step, which is turning the pupil of the intellect toward the various aspects in order to seek that disclosure and manifestation. This is what is called the looking (nazar) of the intellect and its thinking. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have they not reflected?﴾ is a command to thought, contemplation, pondering and deliberation in order to seek knowledge of things as they truly are, with complete recognition. In the wording there is an omitted element, and the implied meaning is: "Have they not reflected so that they would know there is no madness in their companion?" Madness (jinnah) is a state of insanity, like the sitting (jilsah) and the kneeling (rukbah). The entry of "min" (from) in His saying ﴿min jinnatin﴾ requires that there be no kind of madness in him at all.

Know that some of the ignorant among the people of Makkah used to attribute madness to him, for two reasons:

The first: his action, peace be upon him, was contrary to their action, because he, peace be upon him, turned away from this world and turned toward the Hereafter, occupied with calling to God. So his conduct was contrary to their way, and they believed that he was mad. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood at night on al-Safa calling out to each clan of Quraysh, saying, 'O children of so-and-so, O children of so-and-so,' warning them of God's punishment and retribution. One of them said, 'Your companion here is surely mad, he persisted in shouting all this night.'" So God, exalted is He, revealed this verse and urged them to reflect on the matter of the Messenger, peace be upon him, so that they would know that he called only to warn, not to what the ignorant attributed to him.

The second: when the revelation descended upon him, peace be upon him, a remarkable state would overcome him; his face would change and his color would turn pale, and a state resembling a swoon would come over him. The ignorant would say that it was madness. So God, exalted is He, made clear in this verse that there is no kind of madness in him. This is because he, peace be upon him, was calling them to God and establishing decisive proofs and dazzling clear evidences, in eloquent words that reached such a degree of eloquence that the earlier and later generations were unable to match them. He had good character, pleasant companionship, an approved way and a pure conduct, and he was constant in good deeds, by which he became an exemplar for the rational beings of the worlds. It is known by necessity that such a person cannot be described as mad. And when this is established, it becomes clear that his striving in calling to the religion was only because he is a clear warner, sent by the Lord of the worlds to frighten the disbelievers and to encourage the believers. Since the consideration of the matter of prophethood is a consequence of establishing the proofs of monotheism, it is therefore mentioned right after it what indicates monotheism.

Then He said: ﴿Have they not considered the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and what things God has created, and that perhaps their term has drawn near? So in what discourse after this will they believe?﴾ Know that the proofs of the dominion of the heavens and the earth for the existence of the Wise, Eternal Creator are many, and we have explained them in this book repeatedly and in various ways, so there is no benefit in repeating them.

Then He said: ﴿and what things God has created﴾. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that the proofs for *tawhid* (the oneness of God) are not confined to the heavens and the earth. Rather, every single atom (*dharra*) of the world of bodies and spirits is a manifest demonstration and an overwhelming proof of *tawhid*. Let us establish this meaning with an example. We say: when light falls through a window of a house, the atoms and motes become visible. Let us suppose the discussion concerns one of those atoms. We say: it indicates the Wise Creator from infinitely many aspects. This is because it is specifically confined to a particular place among the countless places in the void that has no limit, and for every place among those infinite places that we suppose this atom to occupy, its specific confinement to that particular place was among the possibilities and permissibles. A possibility must have a specifier and a determiner. If that specifier is a body, the question returns concerning it; and if it is not a body, then it is God, glorified is He. Also, that atom cannot be free of motion and rest, and everything of this kind is originated (*muhdath*). Every originated thing's origination must necessarily be specific to a determined time, while it was permissible for it to occur before or after that. Its specification to that determined time in which it originated must therefore be by the specification of an eternal specifier. If that specifier is a body, the question returns concerning it; and if it is not a body, then it is God, glorified and exalted is He. Also, that atom is equal to the rest of bodies in occupying space and in having volume, and it differs from them in color, shape, nature, taste and all other attributes. Its specification with all those attributes by which it differs from the rest of bodies must be among the permissibles, and the permissible must have a preponderator. If that preponderator is a body, the first inquiry returns concerning it; and if it is not a body, then it is God, glorified is He. Thus it is established that this atom indicates the existence of the Creator from infinitely many aspects and infinitely many considerations. The same holds for all parts of the corporeal and spiritual world, its simples and composites, its lowly things and its exalted things. At this point the truth of the poet's words becomes clear to you:

*And in everything there is a sign
indicating that He is One.*

When you have understood this, the benefit of His saying ﴿and what things God has created﴾ becomes apparent to you. When God, exalted is He, had drawn attention to these wondrous secrets and subtle details, He followed it with what necessitates strong encouragement to undertake this reflection and contemplation, and so He said: ﴿and that perhaps their term has drawn near﴾. The word *an* (that) in His saying ﴿and that perhaps﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy (*an*), its estimate being *annahu ʿasa* (that it is perhaps), and the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*). The meaning is: perhaps their terms have drawn near, so they die in disbelief and arrive at the Fire. When this possibility exists, it is obligatory for the rational person to hasten to this reflection and to be prompt in this insight, striving to free the soul from this intense fear and this great peril. When God, exalted is He, had mentioned these manifest clarifications and rational proofs, He said: ﴿So in what discourse after this will they believe?﴾ This is because if they do not believe in this Qur'an, with what it contains of these [Page 64] manifest reminders and overwhelming clear signs, then how would He be satisfied from them with belief in anything else? Know that this verse indicates many matters.

The first matter: *taqlid* (blind imitation) is not permissible, and inquiry and reasoning are indispensable. The evidence that this is so is His saying: ﴿Have they not considered?﴾

The second matter: the affair of prophethood is a branch of *tawhid*. The evidence for this is that when He said: ﴿He is only a clear warner﴾, He followed it with mention of what indicates *tawhid*. Had the matter not been so, there would be no need for this statement.

The third matter: al-Jubba'i and al-Qadi held onto His saying ﴿So in what discourse after this will they believe?﴾ to show that the Qur'an is not eternal. They said: because *hadith* (discourse/report) is the opposite of *qadim* (eternal), and also the word *hadith* by custom indicates that it came into being recently. For this reason it is said: "This thing is *hadith* (new), and is not *ʿatīq* (old)," so they make *hadith* the opposite of *ʿatīq*, which is what has long existed. It is also said of speech: it is *hadith*, because it comes into being moment after moment upon the ears.

Our answer to this is: it is to be understood as referring to the wording, the words, and there is no dispute about their being originated.

The fourth matter: contemplation of the dominion of the heavens and the earth is not possible except after knowing their divisions.

The detailed explanation of their divisions is this: everything other than God, exalted is He, is either a spatially extended thing (*mutahayyiz*), or an accident inhering in a spatially extended thing, or neither spatially extended nor inhering in one. As for the spatially extended, it is either simple or composite. The simples are either supernal or lower. The supernal are the spheres and the stars, and what we have mentioned includes the Throne and the Footstool; it also includes the Garden and the Fire, the Frequented House, and the Raised Ceiling. Study the details of these categories thoroughly. The lower simples are the layers of the four elements, and included in them are the seas, mountains and deserts. The composites are four: the supernal phenomena, minerals, plants and animals. Study thoroughly the details of the species of these four genera. As for the accidents inhering in spatially extended things, their genera come close to forty, and under each genus there are many species. Then, when the rational person reflects on the wonders of their rulings, their necessary consequences, their effects and their causes, it is as if he has plunged into a sea without shore.

As for the third division, namely that the existent is neither spatially extended nor inhering in a spatially extended thing, it has two kinds: either it is connected to bodies by governing and moving them, and this is called the spirits (*arwah*), or it is not so, and these are the holy substances (*al-jawahir al-qudsiyya*) freed from the attachments of bodies.

As for the first kind, the highest and most noble of them are the eight holy spirits that carry the Throne, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And above them on that day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ [al-Haqqa: 17]. Following them are the holy spirits indicated by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And you see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. Following them are the inhabitants of the Footstool, to whom He alludes in His saying: ﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Footstool encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 255]. Following them are the holy spirits in the layers of the seven heavens, and to them He alludes in His saying: ﴿By those who line up in ranks, and those who drive with a driving, and those who recite the reminder﴾ [al-Saffat: 1–3]. Among their attributes is that they do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they glorify Him night and day without slackening; they do not precede Him in speech, and they act by His command.

Know that what we have mentioned and detailed of God's dominion and sovereignty is like a drop in the sea. Perhaps God, glorified is He, has a thousand thousand worlds beyond this world, and for each of them He has a throne greater than this Throne, a footstool higher than this Footstool, and heavens wider than these heavens. How can the intellect of man encompass the full dominion and sovereignty of God, after hearing His saying: ﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 31]? So when a person brings these divisions to mind and wishes to plunge into understanding the secrets of His wisdom and divinity, the saying of the angels is understood: ﴿Glory be to You, we have no knowledge except what You have taught us﴾ [al-Baqara: 32].

How well Abu al-ʿAla al-Maʿarri said:

*O people, how many spheres belong to God,
through which the stars run, and the sun and the moon!*

*Here upon God are our past and our future,
so in other regions than Him we have no stake.*

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 186:

His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him, and He leaves them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾

Know that in this verse He, exalted is He, returns once more to describing the condition of the misguided deniers, saying: ﴿Whomever Allah leaves astray, there is none to guide him.﴾ Know that our companions' (ashab) use of this verse as evidence that guidance and misguidance are from Allah is like what preceded in the previous verse, and the interpretations of the Mu'tazilah and our answer to them are like what was previously mentioned, so there is no benefit in repeating them. His saying: ﴿and He leaves them in their transgression﴾ is a resumptive (isti'naf) nominative clause, cut off from what comes before it. Abu 'Amr read "wa-yadharuhum" with the yā' (third person) and a raised rā' (ḍammah), because the name of Allah, glorified is He, precedes it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the yā' and the jazm (apocopate). The explanation of this, as Sibawayh says, is that it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the position (mawḍi') of the fā' and what follows it in His saying: ﴿there is none to guide him﴾, because the position of the fā' and what follows it is jazm, as the answer to the conditional clause. So "wa-yadharuhum" is taken as conjoined to the position that is jazm.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 187:**

The Most High says: ﴿They ask you about the Hour, "When will it arrive?" Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord. None but He will reveal it at its time. It has weighed heavily upon the heavens and the earth. It will not come upon you except suddenly." They ask you as though you were well-informed about it. Say: "Its knowledge is only with God, but most people do not know."﴾

Know that there are two ways of understanding the arrangement (nazm) of the verse:

The first: When the Most High spoke about tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, qada' (divine decree) and qadar (divine measuring), He followed this with speech about the return (ma'ad), because we have explained that the universal themes of the Qur'an are none other than these four.

The second: When the Most High said in the preceding verse, ﴿and perhaps their term has drawn near﴾, as a motivation toward perseverance in repentance and reform, He said after it, ﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾, so that it would be firmly established in hearts that the time of the Hour is hidden from creation. This would move the responsible people (mukallafun) to hasten to repentance and to the performance of obligations. There are several issues in the verse:

**First issue:** They differed about who this questioner was. Ibn Abbas said: A group of Jews said, "O Muhammad, tell us when the Hour will establish itself," and this verse was revealed. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: The Quraysh said, "O Muhammad, between us and you there is kinship, so tell us when the Hour will be."

[Page 66]

**Second issue:** The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The Hour" (al-sa'ah) is among the names that have become dominant, like "the star" for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). The Resurrection was named "the Hour" either because it comes suddenly, or because the reckoning of creation will be concluded in it in a single hour, so it was named "the Hour" for this reason, or because despite its length it is like a single hour for creation.

**Third issue:** The word ﴿ayyan﴾ (أيّانَ) means asking about the time that will come; it is a question about time. The sum of the matter is that ayyan has the meaning of matā ("when"). Regarding its derivation there are two opinions:

The well-known view is that it is derived from ayn (أين, "where"). Ibn Jinni rejected this and said: ayyan is a question about time, while ayna is a question about place, so how could one be derived from the other?

The second view, which Ibn Jinni chose, is that its derivation is from ayy (أيّ) with the pattern fa'lan from it, because its meaning is "which time," and the word ayy is a form from awaytu ilayhi ("I took refuge in him"), because a part takes refuge in the place of the whole, leaning upon it. Thus Ibn Jinni said: al-Sulami read ﴿iyyan﴾ with a kasra on the hamza.

**Fourth issue:** ﴿Mursaha﴾ (مُرْساها): "al-Mursa" here is a verbal noun meaning irsa' ("establishing, settling"), as in the Most High's words: ﴿In the name of God is its sailing and its anchoring﴾ [Hud: 41], that is, its running and its anchoring. Irsa' means establishment, and one says rasa yarsu when something becomes fixed. The Most High said: ﴿and the mountains He has set firm﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 32]. So rusuww is not a term for mere stability in general; rather, it is a term for the stability of a thing when it is heavy, and from it come the anchoring of a mountain and the anchoring of a ship. Since the heaviest thing upon creation is the Hour, as shown by the Most High's words ﴿it has weighed heavily upon the heavens and the earth﴾, God therefore named its occurrence and its fixed establishment as irsa'.

* * *

Then the Most High said: ﴿Say: "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾, meaning: no one knows the time at which the Resurrection will take place except God, glory be to Him. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, God has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34], and His saying: ﴿and that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it﴾ [al-Hajj: 7], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. When Jibril asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said, "When is the Hour?", he (peace be upon him) said: "The one asked about it does not know more than the one asking." The scholars who investigated the matter said: The reason the Hour is concealed from the servants is that if they do not know when it will be, they will be cautious of it, and this makes them more inclined to obedience and more restrained from disobedience. Then the Most High emphasized this meaning, saying: ﴿None but He will reveal it at its time﴾. Tajliyah (التجلية) is making a thing manifest, and tajalli is its becoming apparent. The meaning is: He does not manifest it at its specified time ﴿except He﴾, that is, none can manifest its specified time by informing and announcing except Him.

Then the Most High said: ﴿It has weighed heavily upon the heavens and the earth﴾. The intended meaning is describing the Hour as heavy. A parallel to this is the Most High's saying: ﴿and they leave behind them a heavy day﴾ [al-Insan: 27]. Also, the Most High described the quaking of the Hour as great, saying: ﴿Indeed, the quake of the Hour is a great thing﴾ [al-Hajj: 1], and He described its punishment as severe, saying: ﴿And they are not drunk, but the punishment of God is severe﴾ [al-Hajj: 2].

Having known this, we say: The exegetes have several interpretations of the Most High's words ﴿it has weighed heavily upon the heavens and the earth﴾:

Al-Hasan said: Its coming weighed heavily upon the heavens and the earth, because when it comes the heavens will be split open, the sun and moon will be wound up, the stars will be scattered, and it will weigh heavily upon the earth, because on that day the earth will be changed into another earth, and the mountains and seas will be annihilated.

Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: This day is extremely heavy upon the people of the heavens and the earth, because in it is their annihilation and destruction, and that is heavy upon hearts.

Some said: This day is of great weight upon hearts, because creation knows that after it they will go to resurrection, reckoning and questioning, and fear of God on a day such as this is intense.

Al-Suddi said:

[Page 67]

﴿Thaqulat﴾ means: it was hidden in the heavens and the earth, and none of the near angels or the messenger prophets knew when its occurrence and taking place would be.

Some said: ﴿It has weighed heavily upon the heavens and the earth﴾ means: obtaining knowledge of its specified time has become burdensome for the people of the heavens and the earth. Just as it is said of a load that cannot be carried that it has become heavy on its bearer, so too it is said of knowledge that God has reserved for Himself that it is heavy upon them.

Then He said: ﴿It will not come upon you except suddenly﴾. This too is an emphasis of what came before and an affirmation that it is of such a nature that it will not come except suddenly, unexpectedly, at a time when creation is heedless. It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Hour will surprise people. A man will be repairing his place, a man will be watering his livestock, a man will be displaying his goods in his market, and a man will be lowering and raising his scale." Al-Hasan also narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, the Hour will surely come, and a man will be raising a morsel to his mouth, and the Hour will come between him and that."

* * *

Then the Most High said: ﴿They ask you as though you were well-informed about it﴾. In this there are two issues:

**First issue:** Regarding ﴿hafiyy﴾ (حَفِيٌّ) there are several meanings:

The first: al-Hafiyy means one who is kind and gentle. Ibn al-A'rabi said: One says "hafa bi" (حفى بي) with great kindness, and "tahaffa bi" (تحفّى بي) with tahaffi; al-hafa is good speech and good meeting. From it is the Most High's saying: ﴿Indeed, He has always been kind to me﴾ [Maryam: 47], meaning kind and gentle, who answers my supplication when I call upon Him. According to this interpretation, the meaning is: they ask you as though you were kind to them and gentle in companionship with them. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada and al-Suddi. This view is supported by what is narrated in its explanation: "The Quraysh said to Muhammad (peace be upon him): Between us and you there is kinship, so tell us when the Hour will be. Then the Most High said: ﴿They ask you as though you were well-informed about it﴾," meaning: as though you were a friend to them and kind, in the sense that you would not be kind to them as long as they remain in disbelief.

The second view: ﴿hafiyy ʿanha﴾ means: one who asks much about it and is intensely eager to know it. According to this view, ﴿hafiyy﴾ is on the pattern fa'il from ihfa', which is insistence and importunity in asking. Whoever asks much about a thing and searches for it, knows it. Abu Ubayda said: It is from their saying "tahaffa fi al-mas'alah," meaning he went to the utmost in it. So the Most High's words ﴿as though you were well-informed about it﴾ mean: as though you had asked much about it and exerted yourself greatly in seeking its knowledge. The author of al-Kashshaf said: This construction conveys emphasis, and from it comes ihfa' al-sharib (trimming the moustache very closely) and ihfa' al-baql (uprooting the herbs completely). One says "ahfa fi al-mas'alah" when he presses hard in asking, and "hafiya bi fulan" or "tahaffa bihi" when he is extremely good to him. According to this interpretation, the first two views are close to each other.

**Second issue:** Regarding His saying ﴿ʿanha﴾ (عنها, "about it") there are two possibilities:

The first: There is inversion in the construction, and the meaning is: they ask you about it as though you were well-informed about it. Then the word "bi-ha" (بها) was omitted because the speech is long, and because it is understood, so that no ambiguity arises from its omission.

The second: The meaning is: they ask you as though you were kind to them, because the word hafiyy may be construed sometimes with the preposition bi (ب) and at other times with ʿan (عن). This second possibility is reinforced by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "ka'anaka hafiyyun bi-ha."

**Third issue:** His saying ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when will it arrive?﴾ is a question about the time of the Hour's establishment. His second statement, ﴿They ask you as though you were well-informed about it﴾, is a question about the reality of the Hour's weight, its severity and its awe-inspiring character. Therefore there is no repetition.

He answered the first with His saying: ﴿Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾.

[Page 68]

He answered the second with His saying: ﴿Its knowledge is only with God﴾. The difference between the two cases is that the first question was about the time of the Hour's establishment, while the second question was about the measure of its severity and awe-inspiring character. The greatest of God's names in awe and majesty is His saying, when the question is about the measure of the severity of the Resurrection, the name that denotes the utmost awe, which is our saying: "Allah." Then the Most High concluded this verse with His saying: ﴿but most people do not know﴾. In this there are several meanings:

One of them: but most people do not know the reason for which I have concealed knowledge of its specified time from creation.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on Surah 7, verse 188:

Concerning his words, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I possess no power to benefit or harm myself, except as God wills. And if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good, and no harm would have touched me. I am only a warner and a bringer of glad tidings to a people who believe.﴾

There are several matters concerning this verse.

**The first matter:** On the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are several views.

The first: His words, ﴿I possess no power to benefit or harm myself﴾, mean: I do not claim knowledge of the unseen. ﴿I am only a warner and a bringer of glad tidings.﴾ A parallel to this is His words, may He be exalted, in Surah Yunus: ﴿They say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?" Say: I possess no power to harm or benefit myself, except as God wills. For every nation there is a term.﴾ [Yunus 10:48–49]. It is related that the people of Mecca said: "O Muhammad, will your Lord not inform you of the cheapness and dearth of prices, so that we may buy and profit, and of the land that becomes barren, so that we may migrate to fertile land?" God then revealed this verse.

The third: Some have said: When the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, returned from the expedition against Bani al-Mustaliq, a wind arose on the road and the riding animals fled from it. The Prophet ﷺ was informed of the death of Rifa'ah in Medina, and this caused vexation to the hypocrites. He said: "Look for where my she-camel is." Then Abdullah ibn Ubayy said, among his people: "Do you not marvel at this man, who informs of the death of a man in Medina, yet does not know where his camel is?" The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Some hypocrites have said such and such, and my she-camel is in this ravine, its halter caught on a tree." They found it as he had said. Then God revealed: ﴿Say: I possess no power to benefit or harm myself, except as God wills.﴾

**The second matter:** Know that when the people demanded that he inform them of the unseen, and demanded that he give them abundant wealth and great dominion, He stated that his power is limited and his knowledge is little. He made clear that every servant is like this, and that complete power and all-encompassing knowledge belong to God alone. How, then, could a servant acquire this power and this knowledge?

Our companions argued, in the question of the creation of acts, from His words: ﴿I possess no power to benefit or harm myself, except as God wills.﴾ Faith is a benefit and disbelief is a harm, so it is necessary that neither comes about except by the will of God. This indicates that faith and disbelief come about only by the will of God, glorified is He. The argument for this, which we have mentioned many times, is that if the power to disbelieve were not capable of faith, then the creator of that power would be willing disbelief. And if it were capable of faith, then the creator of that power would be willing faith. And if it were capable of faith, it would be impossible for disbelief to proceed from it instead of faith, except when a decisive motive arises. Then the creator of that decisive motive would be willing disbelief.

Page 69

Thus it is established that in every case the servant does not possess power to benefit or harm himself, except as God wills.

The judge (al-Qadi) answered this argument in several ways:

The first: Although the apparent meaning of His words, ﴿I possess no power to benefit or harm myself, except as God wills﴾, is general in its wording, we have mentioned that the occasion of its revelation was that the unbelievers said: "O Muhammad, will your Lord not inform you of the time of cheap prices before they rise, so that we may buy the cheap goods and profit from them when prices are high?" Thus the general wording is understood in light of its occasion of revelation. By "benefit" is meant the acquisition of wealth and other things, and by "harm" is meant the time of drought, sickness, and other such things.

The second: What is meant is: I possess no power to benefit or harm myself in matters connected with knowledge of the unseen. The proof that this is the intended meaning is His words: ﴿And if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good.﴾

The third: What is meant is: I possess no power over harm and benefit for myself beyond the measure that God wills to empower me with and enable me to do. The purpose of this statement is to show that he has no power over anything except when God empowers him to it.

Know that all of these answers are, in their entirety, departures from the apparent meaning of the wording. How could one turn to them, when we have established the decisive rational proof that the truth is only what the apparent wording of this verse indicates? And God knows best.

**The third matter:** The Messenger ﷺ argued for his lack of knowledge of the unseen with His words: ﴿And if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good.﴾ They differed about what is meant by this "good." It was said that it means acquiring the benefits of this world and its goods, and warding off its calamities and harms, and this includes what relates to fertility and drought, profits and gains.

It was also said that it means what relates to the matter of religion. That is: if I knew the unseen, I would know that calling people to the true religion would have an effect in this case but not in that case, so how could I occupy myself with calling this group rather than that one?

It was also said that it means what relates to answering questions. The meaning is: if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good.

The answer concerning these matters about which they asked him is like the question about the time of the Hour and similar things.

As for His words: ﴿And no harm would have touched me﴾, there are two views:

The first view: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The statement is complete at His words, ﴿And if I knew the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good.﴾ Then He said: ﴿And no harm would have touched me﴾, meaning: I am not insane. This is because they had attributed madness to him, as we mentioned in His words: ﴿There is no madness in their companion﴾. In my view this view is very far-fetched and would disrupt the coherence of the verse.

The second view: That it is the completion of the first statement. The meaning is: If I knew the unseen, I would have acquired abundant good through obtaining benefits, and I would have guarded against evil until I became such that no harm would touch me. Since the matter was not so, it became clear that knowledge of the unseen is not attained by me. And since he had shown earlier that he has no power except over what God empowers him to, and knows only what God gives him knowledge of, He said: ﴿I am only a warner and a bringer of glad tidings to a people who believe.﴾ "Warner" is an intensive form signifying a warning of punishment for committing sins and abandoning obligations, and "bringer of glad tidings" is an intensive form signifying glad tidings of reward for performing obligations and abandoning sins.

As for His words: ﴿to a people who believe﴾, there are two views:

One of them: He is a warner and a bringer of glad tidings to both believers and unbelievers, but He mentioned one of the two groups and omitted mention of the second, because mention of one implies the other, as in His words: ﴿Garments that protect you from the heat﴾ [al-Nahl 16:81], meaning and from the cold.

The second: Although he, peace and blessings be upon him, is a warner and a bringer of glad tidings to all, the ones who benefit from that warning and glad tidings are the believers. For this reason God singled them out for mention. We have elaborated on this meaning in our commentary on His words, may He be exalted: ﴿A guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:2].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 189–190 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul and made from it its mate, that he might find tranquility in her. And when he covered her, she bore a light burden and carried it about. But when she became heavy, they both called upon Allah, their Lord, "If You give us a righteous [child], we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them a righteous [child], they attributed to Him partners in what He had given them. But Allah is exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾

Know that in this verse He, the Exalted, returns to establishing the matter of tawhid (the oneness of God) and refuting shirk (associating partners with God). In it there are several issues:

The first issue: It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿It is He who created you from a single soul﴾ that it refers to the soul of Adam, ﴿and made from it its mate﴾, meaning Hawwa' (Eve), whom Allah created from a rib of Adam, peace be upon him, without any harm. ﴿When he covered her﴾, Adam, ﴿she bore a light burden and carried it about. But when she became heavy﴾, meaning the child became heavy in her womb, Iblis came to her in the form of a man and said: "What is this, O Hawwa'! I fear that it may be a dog or a beast. And how do you know from where it will come out? From your posterior, so that it kills you, or your belly will be split?" Hawwa' was frightened and mentioned that to Adam, peace be upon him, and they remained in distress about it. Then he came to her and said: "If you ask Allah to make it righteous, sound like you, and to make its birth easy from your belly, name it ʿAbd al-Harith." The name of Iblis among the angels was al-Harith. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿But when He gave them a righteous [child], they attributed to Him partners in what He had given them. But Allah is exalted above what they associate with Him.﴾ That is, when Allah gave them a sound, righteous child, they made for Him a partner, meaning Adam and Hawwa' made for Him a partner, and by it is meant al-Harith. This is the complete story.

Know that this interpretation is corrupt, and the following points indicate it:

First: He said: ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate with Him﴾, and this indicates that those who committed this shirk were a group.

Second: He said after it: ﴿Do they associate with Him that which creates nothing and is itself created?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 191]. This indicates that the purpose of this verse is the refutation of those who made idols partners with Allah the Exalted, and there is no mention in this verse of what happened to the accursed Iblis.

Third: If the intended one were Iblis, He would have said: "Do they associate that which creates nothing?" using "ma" and not "man," because the rational being is mentioned with the form "man," not "ma."

Fourth: Adam, peace be upon him, was the most knowledgeable of people about Iblis, and he knew all the names, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 31]. So he must have known that the name of Iblis is al-Harith. So call upon them, and let them respond to you, if you are truthful.﴾

Know that this verse is among the strongest proofs that the meaning of His words ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they associate﴾ is not what was mentioned concerning the story of Iblis. For if that were the meaning, this verse would be entirely unrelated to it, and that would be the utmost corruption in the arrangement (nazm) and sequence of the text. Rather, the meaning is what we have mentioned in the other answers: the purpose of the preceding verse is a refutation of the idol-worshippers. There are several issues (masa'il) concerning the verse:

[p. 74]

The first issue: the purpose of this verse is to establish the proof that idols are not fit for divinity. Thus His words ﴿Do they associate with Him those who create nothing, while they are themselves created?﴾ mean: "Do they worship what is not able to create anything, while they themselves are created?" That is, while they are created beings, meaning the idols.

If it is asked: How did He use the singular ﴿creates﴾ and then the plural, saying ﴿while they are themselves created﴾? And also, how did He use the masculine plural suffix (waw and nun) for things other than humans?

As for the first question, the answer is that the word ﴿ma﴾ (what) can refer to one, two, or many. It is a form of the singular by the apparent sense of its wording, but it can also be understood as plural. Allah therefore took both aspects into account: He used the singular ﴿creates﴾ in observance of the apparent ruling of the wording, and the plural ﴿they are created﴾ in observance of the meaning.

As for the second question, namely how the plural with waw and nun can be used for non-rational beings: we say that when its worshippers believed that they perceive and discern, this expression came in accordance with what they believe and imagine. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And each in an orbit is swimming﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40], His saying: ﴿And the sun and the moon—I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4], and His saying: ﴿O ants, enter your dwellings﴾ [al-Naml: 18].

The second issue: His saying ﴿Do they associate with Him those who create nothing, while they are themselves created?﴾ Our companions (the Ash'aris) have used this verse as evidence that the servant is neither an originator nor a creator of his actions. They said: Because He criticized the divinity of bodies on the basis that they create nothing, and this criticism would only be valid if, supposing they were creators of something, the criticism of their divinity would not apply. This implies that whoever is a creator is a god. So if the servant were the creator of his own actions, he would be a god. Since that is false, we know that the servant is not the creator of his own actions.

* * *

As for His saying ﴿They cannot help them, nor can they help themselves﴾: He means that the idols do not help those who obey them, nor do they defend themselves against those who disobey them. ﴿Nasr﴾ means assistance against an enemy. The meaning is that the one worshipped must be capable of bringing benefit and repelling harm, and these idols are not like that. So how is it proper for a rational person to worship them?

Then He said: ﴿nor can they help themselves﴾, that is, they cannot repel any harm from themselves. For whoever wishes to break them will find that they cannot prevent it.

Then He said: ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will not follow you.﴾ Know that since He established in the previous verse that these idols have no power over any matter, He demonstrated in this verse that they have no knowledge of anything. The meaning is that this deity worshipped by the polytheists is known from its condition to be such that, just as it neither benefits nor harms, it likewise cannot be expected to follow when called to good. Nor does it distinguish the condition of one who addresses it from one who remains silent. Then He strengthened this statement with His saying: ﴿It is the same for you whether you call them or remain silent.﴾ This is similar to His saying: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]. We have already mentioned the issues in that verse, except that the difference here is that in that verse a verb is conjoined to a verb, whereas here a noun is conjoined to a verb. This is because His saying ﴿Did you call them?﴾ is a verbal sentence, while His saying ﴿Or are you silent?﴾ is a nominal sentence.

Know that it is established that conjoining a nominal sentence to a verbal sentence is not permitted except for a benefit and a wisdom. That benefit is that the form of the verb indicates renewal and occurrence, state after state, whereas the form of the noun indicates permanence, stability, and continuity.

[p. 75]

Having understood this, we say: These polytheists, whenever they fell into a serious matter or a predicament, would humble themselves before those idols; and when that event did not occur, they remained quiet and silent. So it was said to them: There is no difference between your initiating the call to them and your continuing in your silence and stillness. This is the benefit of this expression. Then Allah reinforced the explanation that they are not fit for divinity, saying: ﴿Indeed, those whom you call upon besides Allah are servants like you.﴾ There is a question here: how is it proper to describe them as servants, when they are inanimate objects? The answer to this has several aspects:

First: when the polytheists claimed that they harm and benefit, it necessarily followed that they must believe them to be rational and understanding. Therefore these expressions came in accordance with their beliefs. For this reason He said: ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you,﴾ and He did not say "let them (feminine) respond," and He said ﴿Indeed, those who [alladhina]﴾ and did not say "those who (feminine) [allati]."

The second answer: this trivial expression was used in the context of mockery of them. That is, at best they could be living and rational beings. If that were established, then they would be servants like you, and they have no superiority over you. So why did you make yourselves servants and make them gods and lords? Then He refuted that they are servants like you, saying: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk?﴾ Then He confirmed this explanation by His saying: ﴿So call upon them, and let them respond to you.﴾ The meaning of this calling is seeking benefits and removing harms from them. The lam in His saying ﴿so let them respond﴾ is the lam of command, in the sense of incapacitating them (ta'jiz). The meaning is that when it became clear to every rational person that they are not able to respond, it became clear that they are not fit to be worshipped. A parallel to this is the statement of Abraham (peace be upon him) to his father: ﴿Why do you worship what neither hears nor sees and cannot avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. And His saying: ﴿If you are truthful﴾ means: in your claim that they are gods and deserving of worship. Since these three certain proofs have established that they are not fit for worship, it is obligatory for the rational person not to turn toward them, and not to occupy himself except with the worship of the God who is All-Powerful, All-Knowing, Ever-Living, All-Wise, the Bringer of harm and benefit.

There is no doubt that when each of these limbs possesses what befits it of the moving and perceiving faculties, it is superior to what it would be if it were devoid of these faculties. So a foot capable of walking and a hand capable of grasping are superior to a hand and foot devoid of the power of movement and life, and a seeing eye and a hearing ear are superior to an eye and ear devoid of the power of sight and hearing, and of the power of life. When this is established, it becomes clear that man is far superior to these idols; indeed, there is absolutely no comparison between the excellence of man and the excellence of these idols. And if this is so, how is it fitting for the most excellent, most perfect and most noble to occupy himself with worshipping the most base and lowest, from which he perceives absolutely no benefit, neither in bringing about a benefit nor in averting a harm? This is the manner of presenting this proof which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse.

Page 76

Some of the ignorant among the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) have clung to this verse as an argument for affirming these limbs for Allah, exalted is He. They said: He, exalted is He, made the absence of these limbs in these idols a proof of their lack of divinity. So if these limbs were not present in Allah, exalted is He, their absence would be a proof of the lack of divinity, and that is false. Therefore it is necessary to affirm these limbs for Allah, exalted is He. The answer to this is given from two aspects:

The first aspect: the purpose of this verse is to show that man is superior and more perfect in state than the idol, because man has a walking foot, a grasping hand, a seeing eye and a hearing ear, whereas the idol's foot does not walk, its hand does not grasp, its eye does not see and its ear does not hear. And if this is so, man is superior and more perfect in state than the idol, and for the most excellent and most perfect to occupy himself with worshipping the most base and lowest is ignorance. This is the intended meaning of mentioning this statement, not what the delusion of these ignorant people has led them to.

The second aspect of the answer: the purpose of mentioning this statement is to establish the argument that He mentioned before this verse, namely His saying: ﴿And they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves﴾. That is, how can it be good to worship one who cannot bring about benefit or harm? Then Allah, exalted is He, confirmed this by stating that these idols do not possess walking feet, grasping hands, seeing eyes or hearing ears. When the matter is so, they are not capable of benefiting or harming, and it is impossible for them to be gods. As for the God of the world, exalted and sanctified is He, although He is exalted above these limbs and organs, He is described as having perfect power to benefit and harm, and He is described as having perfect hearing and sight. Thus the difference between the two categories becomes clear.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then call your partners, then plot against me﴾, al-Hasan said: they used to threaten the Messenger, peace be upon him, with their gods, so Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then call your partners, then plot against me﴾, so that it may become apparent to you that they have no power to bring harm upon me in any way whatsoever. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr wrote the yā' in (kīdūnī) (plot against me), while the rest omitted it. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿So do not give me respite﴾. Al-Wahidi said: the explanation of this is that the fawasil (verse endings) resemble qawafi (rhyme endings), and they omitted these yā's when they were in the rhyme positions, as in the line of poetry:

*He touches the saddle-pads in his dwelling with his hands, like a weary Jew.*

Those who wrote them did so because the original form is with the yā'. The meaning of His saying: ﴿So do not give me respite﴾ is: do not delay me, and hasten in your plotting against me, you and your partners.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿إنَّ ولِيِّيَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي نَزَّلَ الكِتابَ وهو يَتَوَلّى الصّالِحِينَ﴾ ﴿والَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِهِ لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ نَصْرَكم ولا أنْفُسَهم يَنْصُرُونَ﴾ ﴿وإنْ تَدْعُوهم إلى الهُدى لا يَسْمَعُوا وتَراهم يَنْظُرُونَ إلَيْكَ وهم لا يُبْصِرُونَ﴾.

[Page 77]

اعْلَمْ أنَّهُ لَمّا بَيَّنَ في الآياتِ المُتَقَدِّمَةِ أنَّ هَذِهِ الأصْنامَ لا قُدْرَةَ لَها عَلى النَّفْعِ والضُّرِّ بَيَّنَ بِهَذِهِ الآيَةِ أنَّ الواجِبَ عَلى كُلِّ عاقِلٍ عِبادَةُ اللَّهِ تَعالى، لِأنَّهُ هو الَّذِي يَتَوَلّى تَحْصِيلَ مَنافِعِ الدِّينِ ومَنافِعِ الدُّنْيا، أمّا تَحْصِيلُ مَنافِعِ الدِّينِ، فَبِسَبَبِ إنْزالِ الكِتابِ، وأمّا تَحْصِيلُ مَنافِعِ الدُّنْيا، فَهو المُرادُ بِقَوْلِهِ: ﴿وهُوَ يَتَوَلّى الصّالِحِينَ﴾ وفِيهِ مَسائِلُ:

Know that when he had explained in the preceding verses that these idols have no power to benefit or harm, he explained in this verse that it is obligatory for every rational person to worship God, Exalted is He, because He is the One who takes charge of obtaining the benefits of religion and the benefits of this world. As for obtaining the benefits of religion, it is through the sending down of the Book; and as for obtaining the benefits of this world, it is what is meant by His words: ﴿and He takes charge of the righteous﴾. And there are several issues concerning this:

المَسْألَةُ الأُولى: قالَ الواحِدِيُّ رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ: قَرَأ القُرّاءُ ولِيِّي بِثَلاثِ ياءاتٍ، الأُولى ياءُ فَعِيلٍ وهي ساكِنَةٌ، والثّانِيَةُ لامُ الفِعْلِ وهي مَكْسُورَةٌ، قَدْ أُدْغِمَتِ الأُولى فِيها فَصارَ ياءً مُشَدَّدَةً، والثّالِثَةُ ياءُ الإضافَةِ، ورُوِيَ عَنْ أبِي عَمْرٍو: ولِيَّ اللَّهُ بِياءٍ مُشَدَّدَةٍ، ووَجْهُ ذَلِكَ أنَّهُ حَذَفَ الياءَ الَّتِي هي لامُ فَعِيلٍ، كَما حَذَفَ اللّامَ مِن قَوْلِهِمْ فاماليت بِهِ فالهَ، ثُمَّ أُدْغِمَتْ ياءُ فَعِيلٍ في ياءِ الإضافَةِ، فَقِيلَ ولِيَّ اللَّهُ وهَذِهِ الفَتْحَةُ فَتْحَةُ ياءِ الإضافَةِ، وأمّا الباقُونَ فَأجازُوا اجْتِماعَ ثَلاثِ ياءاتٍ، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ.

First issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: The reciters read *waliyyiya* with three yā's. The first is the yā' of the pattern *fa'īl*, which is sukūn (unvowelled); the second is the lām of the verb, which is kasrah (vowelled with kasra); the first was assimilated into it, so it became a shaddah-marked yā'; and the third is the yā' of possession (*yā' al-iḍāfah*). It is narrated from Abū 'Amr that he read *waliyya Allāh* with a single shaddah-marked yā'. The explanation for this is that he dropped the yā' which is the lām of *fa'īl*, just as the lām is dropped in their saying *fa-mālaytu bihi fa-lahu* (?). Then the yā' of *fa'īl* was assimilated into the yā' of possession, so it was said *waliyya Allāh*, and this fatḥah is the fatḥah of the yā' of possession. As for the rest, they permitted the combination of three yā's. And God knows best.

المَسْألَةُ الثّانِيَةُ: ﴿إنَّ ولِيِّيَ اللَّهُ﴾ أيِ الَّذِي يَتَوَلّى حِفْظِي ونُصْرَتِي هو اللَّهُ الَّذِي أنْزَلَ الكِتابَ المُشْتَمِلَ عَلى هَذِهِ العُلُومِ العَظِيمَةِ النّافِعَةِ في الدِّينِ ويَتَوَلّى الصّالِحِينَ بِنَصْرِهِمْ، فَلا تَضُرُّهم عَداوَةُ مَن عاداهم، وفي ذَلِكَ يَأْمَنُ المُشْرِكِينَ مِن أنْ يَضُرَّهُ كَيْدُهم، وسَمِعْتُ أنَّ عُمَرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ العَزِيزِ ما كانَ يَدَّخِرُ لِأوْلادِهِ شَيْئًا، فَقِيلَ لَهُ فِيهِ فَقالَ: ولَدِي إمّا أنْ يَكُونَ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ أوْ مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ، فَإنْ كانَ مِنَ الصّالِحِينَ فَوَلِيُّهُ اللَّهُ، ومَن كانَ لَهُ ولِيًّا فَلا حاجَةَ لَهُ إلى مالِي، وإنْ كانَ مِنَ المُجْرِمِينَ فَقَدْ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿فَلَنْ أكُونَ ظَهِيرًا لِلْمُجْرِمِينَ﴾ [القَصَصِ: ١٧] ومَن رَدَّهُ اللَّهُ لَمْ أشْتَغِلْ بِإصْلاحِ مُهِمّاتِهِ.

Second issue: ﴿Indeed, my protector is God﴾, i.e., the One who takes charge of my protection and support is God, who sent down the Book containing these great and beneficial sciences of religion, and who takes charge of the righteous by supporting them, so the enmity of those who oppose them does not harm them. In this, the one who is pious is safe from the plots of the polytheists harming him. I have heard that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz did not save anything for his children. He was asked about this, and he said: "My son is either among the righteous or among the wrongdoers. If he is among the righteous, then God is his protector, and whoever has God as his protector has no need of my wealth. And if he is among the wrongdoers, then God, Exalted is He, has said: ﴿So I will never be a helper to the criminals﴾ [al-Qasas 28:17], and whomever God abandons, I will not concern myself with setting right his affairs."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verses 197–198:

As for His saying: ﴿Those whom you invoke besides Him cannot help you, nor can they help themselves﴾, there are two opinions on it.

The first opinion: the intended meaning is to describe the idols with these attributes.

If it is said: these things have already been mentioned in the preceding verses, so what is the benefit of repeating them? We say: al-Wahidi said: this meaning is repeated because the first mention is made by way of rebuke, and this mention is made by way of distinguishing between the one who is worthy of worship and the one who is not. It is as if it were said: the God who is worshipped must be such that He takes care of the righteous, and these idols are not like that, so they are not fit for divinity.

The second opinion: these described states are attributes of those polytheists who invoke other than Allah. That is, the disbelievers used to threaten the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his companions, so Allah the Exalted said: they have no power over anything. Rather, they have reached such a degree of ignorance and foolishness that even if you called them and displayed the greatest kinds of proof and evidence, they would absolutely not hear it with their minds.

If it is said: the polytheists were not mentioned before; only the idols were mentioned, so how can what was said be correct?

We say: their mention has preceded in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say: Call upon your associates, then plot against me﴾.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you see them looking at you, yet they do not see﴾, if we take these attributes as referring to the idols, we say: the meaning of their "looking" is that they face the people with their faces, from the saying "two mountains facing each other (mutanazirani)," i.e., opposite each other. And if we take them as referring to the polytheists, the meaning is: although they look at people, yet due to their intense aversion to the truth, they have not benefited from that looking and seeing, so they became as if they were blind. This verse indicates that looking (naẓar) is other than seeing (ru'yah), because He, the Exalted, affirmed looking and negated seeing, and that indicates difference. This argument was answered, and it was said: its meaning is "you suppose they are looking at you while in reality they are not looking," i.e., you think they are looking at you while they do not perceive you. And the use of "seeing" in the sense of "supposing" occurs; the Exalted said: ﴿And you see people as drunk, and they are not drunk﴾ [al-Hajj: 2].
