Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 199:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Take what is given freely, enjoin what is customary, and turn away from the ignorant.﴾

Know that when the Most High explained in the first verse that Allah is the One who takes charge of the believers, and that the idols and those who worship them cannot cause harm or injury, He explained in this verse the upright path and the straight way in dealing with people, saying: ﴿Take what is given freely and enjoin what is customary.﴾ The lexicographers said: *al-'afw* (what is given freely) is the surplus, and whatever comes without strain.

Having understood this, we say: the rights that are exacted from people and taken from them either admit of leniency and forbearance, or they do not.

As for the first category, it is what is meant by His words ﴿Take what is given freely﴾. It includes abandoning strictness in everything related to financial rights. It also includes treating people with good character and avoiding harshness and roughness, as the Most High said: ﴿Had you been harsh and hard-hearted, they would have scattered from around you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159]. Among this category is calling creation to the true religion with gentleness and kindness, as the Most High said: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Nahl: 125].

As for the second category, which does not admit of leniency and forbearance, the ruling concerning it is to enjoin *al-ma'ruf* (what is known as good). *Al-'urf*, *al-'arifah* and *al-ma'ruf* all mean every matter known to be necessary to perform, and whose existence is better than its absence. This is because if this category were confined to taking what is given freely, without enjoining what is known as good and without disclosing the reality of the situation, that would be an attempt to alter the religion and nullify the truth, and that is not permitted. Furthermore, when one enjoins what is known as good, encourages it, forbids what is disapproved and warns against it, some of the ignorant may be provoked into foolishness and harm. For this reason the Most High said at the end of the verse: ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾. In another verse He said: ﴿When they pass by vain talk, they pass by with dignity﴾ [al-Furqan: 72], and He said: ﴿And those who turn away from vain talk﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 3], and He said describing the people of Paradise: ﴿They hear therein no vain talk nor sinful speech﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 25]. When your intellect comprehends this division, you will know that this verse contains the noble qualities of character in what concerns a person's dealings with others.

'Ikrimah said: When this verse was revealed, [the Prophet] (ﷺ) said: "O Jibril, what is this?" He said: "O Muhammad, your Lord says: it is that you join ties with one who has severed them with you, give to one who has withheld from you, and pardon one who has wronged you."

The scholars said: Jibril's explanation corresponds to the wording of the verse, for if you join ties with one who severed them with you, you have pardoned him; and if you give to one who withheld from you, you have enjoined what is known as good; and if you pardon one who wronged you, you have turned away from the ignorant.

Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: There is no verse in the Qur'an that gathers the noble qualities of character better than this verse.

The exegetes have another interpretation of this verse. They said: ﴿Take what is given freely﴾ means: what is given to you from their wealth without effort; take what they bring to you willingly, and do not ask about what lies beyond that. They said: This was before the obligation of alms (*sadaqah*), and when the verse of the obligation of zakat (obligatory alms) was revealed, this verse became abrogated (*mansukh*) except for His words ﴿and enjoin what is customary﴾, meaning by manifesting the true religion and establishing its proofs; ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾, meaning the polytheists. They said: This is abrogated by the verse of the sword. According to this view, the whole verse is abrogated except His words ﴿and enjoin what is customary﴾.

Know that restricting His words ﴿Take what is given freely﴾ to what he mentioned is a restriction of the absolute without evidence. Moreover, if we take this statement to refer to paying zakat, the imposition of zakat in specified amounts is not incompatible with it, because the collector of zakat is commanded not to take the best of people's wealth and not to press the one who pays too harshly. Therefore the imposition of zakat is not a cause for this verse to become abrogated.

As for His words ﴿and turn away from the ignorant﴾, what is intended by it is the command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to be patient with their bad character, and not to respond to their base words or their vile deeds with the like. It contains no indication that he was prohibited from fighting, because it is not impossible that he (ﷺ) be commanded to turn away from the ignorant together with being commanded to fight the polytheists. For it is not contradictory to say that the Lawgiver does not match their foolishness with the like, but nevertheless fought them. And if combining the two commands is possible, then there is no need to posit abrogation. However, the literalist exegetes are fond of multiplying the abrogating and the abrogated without necessity or need.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 200:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should stir you, then seek refuge in Allah. Indeed, He is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Abu Zayd said: "When the saying of the Exalted was revealed, ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾, the Prophet ﷺ said: 'How, O Lord, when there is anger?' Then there was revealed: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should stir you…﴾"

The second issue: Know that nazgh (evil suggestion, stirring) of Satan is an expression for his whisperings and prodding in the heart with what he beautifies to the person of sins. From Abu Zayd: "nazaghtu bayna al-qawm" means I corrupted what was between them. It has also been said: al-nazgh is agitation (al-iz'aj), and it is most often at the time of anger; its root is agitation by movement toward evil. The sense of the discourse is that when He commanded him to ʿurf (customary good conduct), a foolish person might at that point become agitated and display foolishness; so at that point the Exalted commanded him to refrain from confronting him, saying: ﴿And turn away from the ignorant﴾. Since it is known that when the foolish person proceeds to foolishness, anger and rage are stirred and a person does not remain in a state of safety, and in that state Satan finds room to drive that person toward what is not fitting, therefore the Exalted, for this purpose, set forth what serves as a remedy, saying: ﴿So seek refuge in Allah﴾. The discussion of the explanation of seeking refuge (al-istiʿadhah) has already preceded at the beginning of the Book, in full detail.

The third issue: Those who object to the infallibility (ʿismah) of the prophets have argued with this verse, saying: If it were not permissible for the Messenger to commit disobedience or sin, He would not have said to him: ﴿And if an evil suggestion from Satan should stir you, then seek refuge in Allah﴾.

The answer to this is in several respects:

First: The essence of this statement is that He, the Exalted, said to him: If there occurs in your heart a stirring from Satan, just as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you should associate [others with Allah], your deeds would surely become worthless﴾ [az-Zumar: 65], and that does not indicate that he associated. And He said: ﴿Had there been within them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22], and that does not indicate that there were gods within them.

Second: Suppose we grant that Satan whispers to the Messenger, peace be upon him; yet this does not impair his infallibility. What impairs his infallibility is only if the Messenger accepted his whisper, and the verse does not indicate that. From al-Sha'bi, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There is not a person except that with him is a devil." They said: "And you, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "And I, but Allah helped me against him, so he submitted. He came to me and I seized his throat, and had it not been for the supplication of Sulayman, he would have become prostrate in the mosque." This is like an indication that Satan whispers to the Messenger ﷺ. And the Exalted said: ﴿And We did not send before you any messenger or prophet except that when he spoke, Satan threw [something] into his wish﴾ [al-Hajj: 52].

Third: Suppose we grant that Satan whispers and that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is affected by the effect of his whisper; yet we restrict this state to leaving what is better and more preferable. He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, there is a veiling over my heart, and I seek forgiveness from Allah seventy times in a day and a night."

The fourth issue: Seeking refuge in Allah in this state means that a person remembers the great blessings of Allah upon him and the severity of His punishment, and each of these two matters calls him to turn away from what the nature demands and to turn toward what the Law commands.

The fifth issue: Although this address was specifically directed by Allah to the Messenger, it is a general discipline for all the responsible (mukallafin), because seeking refuge in Allah in the manner we have described is a preventive grace (lutf) against the effect of Satan's whisperings. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed﴾ ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾ [an-Nahl: 98]. And since it is established by the text that this seeking of refuge has an effect in repelling Satan's stirring, it is obligatory to be constant in it in most circumstances.

The sixth issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, He is Hearing, Knowing﴾ indicates that seeking refuge by the tongue alone benefits only when knowledge of the meaning of seeking refuge is present in the heart. It is as if the Exalted said: Mention the wording of seeking refuge with your tongue, for I am Hearing; and call to mind the meanings of seeking refuge with your intellect and heart, for I am Knowing of what is in your inner self. In reality, verbal utterance without heartfelt knowledge is of no benefit or effect.

[Page 81]

Al-Razi, *Mafatih al-Ghayb*, commentary on Surah 7, verse 201:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who have taqwa (God-consciousness), when a passing thought from Satan touches them, remember, and then they see clearly.﴾ ﴿But their brothers (the devils) drag them further into error, and they do not hold back.﴾ There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Know that in the previous verse God explained that Satan may incite the Messenger (ﷺ), and He explained that the remedy for this condition is seeking refuge in God. Then in this verse He explained that the state of the God-conscious surpasses the state of the Messenger in this matter, because the Messenger only experiences from Satan the *nazgh* (an incitement), which is like the beginning of whispering, whereas for the God-conscious He allowed something beyond it, namely that a *ṭā'if* (passing thought) from Satan touches them. This touching is necessarily more intense than the incitement.

The second issue: Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read *ṭayf* (طَيْفٌ) without an alif, while the rest read *ṭā'if* (طائِفٌ) with an alif. Al-Wahidi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: They differed concerning *al-ṭayf*. It has been said that it is a *maṣdar* (verbal noun). Abu Zayd said: one says *ṭāfa yaṭūfu ṭawfan wa ṭawafan* when he comes and goes, and *aṭāfa yuṭīfu iṭāfatan* when he begins to circle around the people and come to them from their sides, and *ṭāfa al-khayāl yaṭīfu ṭayfan* when the phantom visits in a dream. Ibn al-Anbari said: It is permissible that *ṭayf* originally was *ṭayyif*, but they found the doubling burdensome, so they deleted one of the two yā's and kept a single quiescent yā'. According to the first view it is a *maṣdar*, and according to what Ibn al-Anbari said it is of the pattern of *hayn* and *hayyin*, *mayt* and *mayyit*. What supports the correctness of Ibn al-Anbari's view is the reading of Sa'id ibn Jubayr: (إذا مَسَّهم طَيِّفٌ) with the doubling. This is the original form of *ṭayf*. Then *al-junūn* (madness), *al-ghaḍab* (anger) and *al-waswasah* (whispering) were called *ṭayf*, because it is a passing impulse from Satan that resembles the passing image of a phantom. Al-Azhari said: *al-ṭayf* in the speech of the Arabs means madness. Then anger was called *ṭayf*, because the angry person resembles the madman. As for *al-ṭā'if*, it may have the meaning of *al-ṭayf*, like *al-'āfiyah* and *al-'āqibah* and similar words whose *maṣdar* came in the pattern *fā'il* and *fā'ilah*. Al-Farra' said concerning this verse: *al-ṭā'if* and *al-ṭayf* are the same, and it is what is like the phantom that visits a person. Some of them said: *al-ṭayf* is like a passing thought, and *al-ṭā'if* is like a fleeting idea.

The third issue: Know that anger is only stirred up in a person when he regards an action of the one who is angered against him as ugly, then believes in himself that he is capable, and believes that the one who is angered against him is incapable of repelling it. When these three beliefs are present, and he is in the darkness of the world of bodies, he is deceived by the outward appearances of affairs. But when a light from the unseen world is revealed to him, these three beliefs disappear in many ways.

As for the first belief, which is judging that action to be ugly on the part of the one who is angered against, when it is revealed to him that he only undertook that deed because God created in him a firm, decisive motive, and whenever God creates that motive in him, it is impossible for him not to proceed with that deed, then when this meaning becomes clear, the anger departs. Also, it may occur to a person that God knew this state of his, and when it is so, there is no way for him to abandon it. At that point his anger flees. To this the peace and blessings of God be upon him alluded when he said: "Whoever knows the secret of God in predestination, calamities become easy for him."

As for the second and third beliefs, namely his belief in himself that he is capable, and that the one who is angered against him is incapable, these two beliefs are also corrupt in several respects:

The first: he believes that however much the other has wronged him in the deed, God was capable of it, and he (the offender) was a captive in the grip of God's power, and then He overlooked it.

The second: just as the one who is angered against is incapable in the hand of the angry person, so too the angry person is incapable in relation to the power of God.

The third: that the angry person remembers what God commanded him, namely to refrain from carrying out his anger, and to return to not harming and not alienating.

The fourth: that he remembers that if he carries out his anger and takes revenge, he becomes a partner of the harmful beasts and the deadly serpents, and if he abandons revenge and chooses pardon, he becomes a partner of the great prophets and the friends of God.

The fifth: that he remembers that perhaps that weak one may turn strong and capable over him, and then he would avenge himself upon him in the worst way; but if he pardons, that is a kindness from him toward him. In sum, what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿when a passing thought from Satan touches them, they remember﴾ is the three beliefs we have mentioned, and what is meant by His saying: ﴿they remember﴾ is the aspects we have mentioned that show the weakness of those beliefs. His saying: ﴿then they see clearly﴾ means that when these remembrances come into their minds, immediately the touch of Satan's phantom departs, and insight, disclosure and illumination arise, and deliverance from Satan's whispering is attained.

The fourth issue: His saying: ﴿then they see clearly﴾. The meaning of *idhā* (إذا) here is that of suddenness (*lil-mufājaʾah*), like your saying: "I went out, and suddenly Zayd (was there)." And *idhā* in His saying: ﴿when it touches them﴾ requires an answer (*jazāʾ*), like your saying: "I will come to you when the dates turn red."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 202:

Page 82

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and their brothers extend them in error﴾, there are several issues.

The first issue: the scholars differed over what the pronoun in His saying ﴿and their brothers﴾ refers back to, on two views.

The first view, which is the most apparent, is that the meaning is: "and the brothers of the devils extend the devils in error." This is because the devils of mankind are brothers to the devils of the jinn, so the devils of mankind lead people astray, and that constitutes an extension (imdad) from them to the devils of the jinn in misguidance and leading astray.

The second view is that the brothers of the devils are the people who are not God-fearing (muttaqun), for the devils become a supply (madad) for them in it. Both views are based on the premise that every disbeliever has a brother among the devils.

The second issue: the meaning of extension (imdad) is strengthening that whispering, persisting in it, and occupying the soul away from considering its ugliness and its faults.

The third issue: Nafi' read (yamuddunahum) with a dammah on the yaa' and a kasrah on the meem, from al-imdad, while the rest read (yamuddunahum) with a fathah on the yaa' and a dammah on the meem. Both are dialects: madda yamuddu and amadda yumiddu. It has also been said that madda means "to pull," while amadda means "to supply."

Al-Wahidi said: most of what occurs in the Revelation that is praiseworthy and desirable is in the form amdadtu (af'altu), as in His saying: ﴿We extend them with it, of wealth and children﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55], and His saying: ﴿And We extended them with fruit﴾ [al-Tur: 22], and His saying: ﴿Will you extend me with wealth?﴾ [al-Naml: 36]. What is contrary to that is in the form madadtu, as He said: ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 15]. So the preferred reading here is the reading of the majority, which is the fathah on the yaa'. Whoever puts a dammah on the yaa' uses the verb for its opposite, as in His saying: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 21], and His saying: ﴿then they do not refrain﴾. Al-Layth said: al-iqsar is restraining oneself from a thing. Abu Zayd said: "So-and-so refrained (aqsara) from evil, and so he refrains (yuqsiru) iqsaran when he holds back from it and ceases." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Then they do not refrain from error and leading others astray; as for the one who is astray (ghawi), he is in error, and as for the one who leads astray (mughwi), he is in leading others astray."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And when you do not bring them a sign, they say, "Why have you not fabricated it?" Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord. This is insights from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe."﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted had explained in the previous verse that the devils of the jinn and of mankind do not fall short in misleading and leading astray, He explained in this verse a kind of misguidance and leading astray: they used to demand specific signs and particular miracles out of obstinacy (ta'annut), as in His saying: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us"﴾ (Al-Isra: 90). Then He mentioned that he (ﷺ) did not bring them what they asked for. At that, they said: ﴿Why have you not fabricated it?﴾

Al-Farra' said: The Arabs say "ijtabaytu al-kalam" (I fabricated the speech), "ikhtalaqtuhu" (I invented it), and "irtajaltuhu" (I composed it extemporaneously), when you invent it from your own self. The meaning is: "Why have you not fabricated it, invented it, and brought it from yourself?" because they used to say: ﴿This is nothing but a fabricated lie﴾ (Saba': 43). Or it is said: "Why did you not propose it to your god and object of worship, if you are truthful that Allah

[Page 83]

accepts your supplication and answers your request?" At this, Allah commanded His Messenger to state the sufficient answer, which is His saying: ﴿Say, "I only follow what is revealed to me from my Lord."﴾ Its meaning: It is not for me to propose anything to my Lord concerning any matter; rather I await revelation. Whatever He honors me with, I say. Otherwise, the duty is silence and abandoning proposals. Then He explained that the absence of bringing those miracles that they proposed does not undermine the purpose, because the appearance of the Qur'an in accordance with his claim is a far-reaching and dazzling miracle. When this one miracle appears, it is sufficient to establish prophethood, so asking for more is a matter of obstinacy. He then mentioned three terms in describing the Qur'an:

The first: His saying: ﴿This is insights from your Lord.﴾ The root of "basira" (insight) is seeing. Since the Qur'an is a cause of insights of the intellects concerning the proofs of monotheism, prophethood, and the Hereafter, it was given the name "basira," by naming the cause with the name of the effect (tasmiyat al-sabab bi-ism al-musabbab).

The second: His saying: ﴿and guidance﴾. The difference between this rank and what precedes it is that people, regarding the knowledge of monotheism, prophethood, and the Hereafter, are of two types:

One of them: Those who have reached in these knowledges a point where they became as those who witness them, and they are the people of certainty of sight (ʿayn al-yaqin).

The second: Those who did not reach that limit, but they arrived at the levels of those who reason by proof, and they are the people of certainty of knowledge (ʿilm al-yaqin). So the Qur'an, with regard to the first group, who are the foremost (al-sabiqun), is insights; with regard to the second group, who are the moderate (al-muqtasidun), is guidance; and with regard to the common believers, is mercy. Since the three groups are all among the believers, He rightly said: ﴿for a people who believe.﴾

[p. 84]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾**

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, magnified the status of the Qur'an by saying, ﴿This is insight from your Lord﴾, He followed it with saying, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ In this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *al-Insat* (silence) means keeping quiet, and *al-Istima'* (listening). It is said: *nassata*, *anssata*, and *intassata*, all with one meaning.

**The second issue:** There is no doubt that His saying, ﴿So listen to it and be silent﴾, is a command, and the apparent meaning of a command is obligation. Therefore its implication is that listening and silence are obligatory. People have differing opinions on this.

**The first opinion:** This is the view of al-Hasan and of the literalists (*Ahl al-Zahir*): we apply this verse in its general sense. Wherever a person recites the Qur'an, it becomes obligatory on everyone to listen to it and remain silent. Accordingly, on this view, silence is required for passers-by and for teachers of children.

**The second opinion:** It was revealed concerning the prohibition of speaking during prayer. Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "They used to speak during prayer, so this verse was revealed and they were commanded to be silent." Qatada said: "A man would come while they were praying and ask them, 'How many rak'ahs have you prayed, and how many remain?' They would speak during the prayer about their needs, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

**The third opinion:** The verse was revealed concerning abandoning loud recitation behind the imam. Ibn Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited in the obligatory prayer, and his companions recited behind him raising their voices, so they confused him," and so this verse was revealed. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions.

**The fourth opinion:** It was revealed concerning silence during the khutbah (sermon). This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, and 'Ata'. This opinion is also reported from al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Many people have considered this opinion far-fetched and said: "The wording is general, so how can it be restricted to this one form?" I say that this opinion is extremely distant, because the word *idha* (when) indicates a condition and does not indicate repetition. The evidence for this is that if a man says to his wife, "When you enter the house, you are divorced," and she enters the house once, she is divorced with one divorce; but if she enters the house a second time, she is not divorced, by consensus, because the word *idha* does not indicate repetition.

Having established this, we say: His saying, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, indicates only the obligation of silence once. When we have made listening obligatory during the recitation of the Qur'an in the khutbah, we have fulfilled the requirement of the wording, and no indication remains in the wording beyond this form. Even if we grant that the wording indicates generality, we still say it is in accordance with the verse. This is because, according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, the imam remains silent, and then the follower recites al-Fatihah during the imam's silence. As Abu Salama said: "The imam has two pauses, so seize the opportunity to recite during whichever of them you wish." This objection was raised by al-Wahidi in *al-Basit*.

One may say: The imam's silence is either obligatory or not obligatory. The first is invalid by consensus, and the second implies that it is permissible for him not to remain silent. If he does not remain silent, then the follower's recitation must coincide with the imam's recitation, and that leads to abandoning listening and abandoning silence during the imam's recitation, which contradicts the text. Furthermore, this silence has no defined limit or fixed measure, and the pause that followers need differs according to their speed and slowness. Sometimes the follower cannot complete al-Fatihah within the length of the imam's silence, and then the mentioned harm follows. Also, the imam remains silent only so that the follower can complete the recitation, and then the imam becomes like a follower and the follower like an imam, because the imam during this silence becomes like one who follows the follower, and that is not permissible. Thus it is established that this objection raised by al-Wahidi is not valid.

Al-Wahidi raised a second objection to the use of this verse as evidence. He said: "Silence means abandoning loud recitation, and the Arabs call one who abandons loud recitation 'silent' (*munsit*), even if he recites to himself when he does not make anyone hear."

One may say: Allah, exalted is He, first commanded him to listen, and occupation with recitation prevents him from listening, because hearing (*sama'*) is one thing and listening (*istima'*) is another. Listening is an expression for being in such a state that one comprehends that spoken discourse in its complete form. Allah, exalted is He, said to Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:13), and what is meant is what we have mentioned. When this is established and it becomes clear that occupation with recitation is among the things that prevent listening, we know that the command to listen implies a prohibition of reciting.

**The third objection, which is the one relied upon:** The jurists have agreed that it is permissible to specify the general meaning of the Qur'an by a single-narration report (*khabar al-wahid*). Suppose the generality of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ requires the follower's silence during the imam's recitation. Nevertheless, the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, "There is no prayer for one who does not recite the Opening of the Book (al-Fatihah)," and his saying, "There is no prayer except with the Opening of the Book," are more specific than that generality. It is established that specifying the general meaning of the Qur'an by a single-narration report is necessary, so it is necessary to turn to specifying the general meaning of this verse by this report. This objection is sound.

**The fourth objection:** We say: The school of Malik, which is also the earlier view of al-Shafi'i, holds that it is not permissible for the follower to recite al-Fatihah in the audibly recited prayers, acting upon the implication of this text, and that it is obligatory for him to recite in the silently recited prayers, because this verse has no indication regarding that case. This too is a sound objection.

**A fifth opinion regarding the verse** is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ is addressed to the disbelievers at the beginning of the call to Islam, and not to the Muslims. This is a sound and fitting view, and its explanation is as follows. Allah, exalted is He, related before this verse that groups of disbelievers were asking for specific signs and specific miracles. When the Prophet, peace be upon him, did not bring them, they said, "Why have you not chosen them?" So Allah commanded His Messenger to reply to their words, saying: "It is not for me to propose to my Lord; it is only for me to await the revelation." Then Allah, exalted is He, explained that the Prophet ﷺ left off bringing those miracles they had proposed as proof of the validity of prophethood, because the Qur'an is a complete miracle, sufficient in establishing prophethood. Allah, exalted is He, expressed this meaning by His saying: ﴿This is insight from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾.

If we say that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾ means the follower's recitation behind the imam, then no connection would exist between this verse and what precedes it in any way, the arrangement would be broken, and the order would be corrupted. That is not befitting the speech of Allah, exalted is He. Therefore it must mean something other than this. The explanation is that when He claimed that the Qur'an is insight, guidance, and mercy inasmuch as it is a miracle indicating the truthfulness of Muhammad, peace be upon him, this quality does not become manifest except under a specific condition: that when the Prophet, peace be upon him, recites the Qur'an to those disbelievers, they listen to it and remain silent until they comprehend its eloquence and encompass the many sciences it contains. Then the Qur'an's miraculous nature, as an indication of the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ, becomes clear to them, so they seek with this Qur'an to find the other miracles, and the truth of His description of the Qur'an as (insight, guidance, and mercy) becomes evident to them. Thus it is established that when we interpret the verse in this way, the arrangement holds together and the order becomes good and meaningful. But if we interpret the verse as prohibiting the follower from reciting behind the imam, the arrangement collapses and the order is disrupted. Therefore it is established that interpreting it as we have mentioned is preferable.

Having established this, it becomes clear that His saying, ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it﴾, is addressed to the disbelievers during the Messenger's recitation of the Qur'an to them, in the context of arguing that it is a miracle proving the truthfulness of his prophethood. At this point, the opponents' use of this verse as evidence falls away in every respect.

Several considerations strengthen the view that the verse should be interpreted as we have mentioned:

**The first consideration:** Allah, exalted is He, related about the disbelievers that they said: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you will overcome﴾ (Fussilat 41:26). When He related this about them, it was fitting that He command them to listen and be silent, so that they could come to understand the many aspects of the Qur'an that reach the level of inimitability.

**The second consideration:** Allah, exalted is He, said before this verse: ﴿This is insight from your Lord, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe﴾. Thus He decreed with certainty and definiteness that this Qur'an is a mercy for the believers.

Then He said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent, that you may receive mercy.﴾ If those addressed by His saying, ﴿So listen to it and be silent﴾, were the believers, He would not have said, ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾, because He had already definitively decreed before this verse that the Qur'an is a mercy for the believers. How could He then say immediately afterward, without any separation, "perhaps listening to the Qur'an will be a mercy for the believers"? But if we say that those addressed by His saying, ﴿So listen to it and be silent﴾, are the disbelievers, then His saying, ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾ is correct, because the meaning is: "So listen to it and be silent, that perhaps you will come to know the signs of its inimitability, and then believe in the Messenger and become recipients of mercy." It is thus established that if we interpret the verse as we have said, the phrase ﴿that you may receive mercy﴾ is fitting, whereas if we said the address is to the believers, the particle *la'alla* ("perhaps") would not be appropriate here. Therefore it is established that interpreting the verse according to the explanation we have given is preferable. In that case, the opponent's use of it as evidence falls away in every respect, because we have demonstrated by proof that this address does not include the believers, but rather addressed the disbelievers at the beginning of the period of conveying the revelation and the call.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 7, verse 205 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and in awe, without loudness of speech, in the mornings and the evenings, and do not be among the heedless﴾. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent﴾, [it should be understood that] a reciter recites the Qur'an with a loud voice so that they are able to hear the Qur'an, and it is known that this reciter is none other than the Messenger, peace be upon him. This verse therefore takes the place of a command from God to Muhammad (ﷺ) to recite the Qur'an to the people with a loud, elevated voice, and He commanded him to do so only so that the purpose of conveying the revelation and the message would be achieved.

Then, He, exalted is He, followed that command by commanding him in this verse to remember his Lord within himself. The benefit of this is that a person's benefit from remembrance (dhikr) is only complete when the remembrance occurs in this manner, because with this condition it is closer to sincerity (ikhlas) and humble supplication (tadarru').

The second issue: He, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to remember Him, restricted by conditions:

The first condition: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾. What is meant by remembering God within oneself is that one is aware of the meanings of the invocations that one says with one's tongue, while keeping in mind the attributes of perfection, might, exaltedness, majesty and greatness. This is because remembrance by the tongue, if it is empty of remembrance by the heart, is without benefit. Do you not see that the jurists have agreed that if a man says "I sell" and "I buy" while not knowing the meanings of these words and understanding nothing from them, the sale and purchase is not concluded? Likewise here. From what we have mentioned, rulings follow:

The first ruling:
I heard that some of the great men among the people of the hearts, when he wished to order one of the seekers (murids) to seclusion and remembrance, would order him to seclusion and purification for forty days. Then, upon completing this period and attaining complete purification, he would recite to him the ninety-nine Names, and say to that seeker: Observe the state of your heart upon hearing these Names. For every Name whose hearing your heart finds its effect strengthened and its longing greatened, know that God only opens the doors of unveilings (mukashafat) upon you by means of persistence in remembering that very Name. This is a good and subtle method in this field.

The second ruling:
The scholars of kalam (mutakallimun) said: This verse indicates the affirmation of the speech of the self (kalam al-nafs), because when He, exalted is He, commanded His Messenger to remember his Lord within himself, it became necessary to acknowledge the occurrence of inner (nafsani) remembrance, and there is no meaning to the speech of the self except that.

[Page 87]

If they say: Why could it not be that what is meant by inner remembrance is knowledge and recognition?

We say: This is false, because a human being has no power to acquire knowledge of a thing from the start, for he either seeks it while it is present or while it is absent. The first is false, because it entails acquiring what is already acquired, which is impossible. The second is false, because what is not conceived is something the mind is unaware of, and one who is unaware of a thing cannot be seeking it. Thus it is established that a human being has no power to acquire conceptions, and therefore it is impossible for a command to be directed to it. The verse indicates the command to inner remembrance, so inner remembrance must be a meaning distinct from recognition, knowledge and conception, and that is what was to be proven.

The third ruling:
He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾, and He did not say "remember your God" or any other of the names. In this context He named Him by the name of His being Lord, and attributed Himself to him, and all of this indicates the utmost mercy, nearness, favour and benevolence. The intended purpose is that the servant become joyful upon hearing this name, because the word "Lord" implies nurturing and bounty, and upon hearing this name the servant recalls the kinds of God's blessings upon him, while in reality his intellect cannot reach even the least of their kinds, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you were to count the blessing of God, you could not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34; al-Nahl: 18]. So when this station is unveiled in the heart, hope grows strong. Then when he hears after that His saying: ﴿humbly and in awe﴾, fear becomes great. At that point, in the heart arise the causes of hope and the causes of fear, and at that point faith is perfected, as he, peace be upon him, said: "If the fear of the believer and his hope were weighed, they would balance." However, here there is a subtlety: hearing the word "Lord" necessitates hope, and hearing the words "humility" and "awe" necessitates fear. So since the beginning was with what necessitates hope, we know that the side of hope is stronger.

The second condition among the conditions regarded in remembrance: the occurrence of humility (tadarru'), to which the words of the Exalted refer: ﴿humbly﴾. This condition is regarded, and it is indicated by the Qur'an and by reason. As for the Qur'an, it is His saying in Surat al-An'am: ﴿Say: Who delivers you from the darknesses of land and sea, when you call upon Him humbly and secretly?﴾ [al-An'am: 63]. As for reason: the perfection of a human being's state is achieved only through the unveiling of two matters:

One of them: the might of Lordship. This aim is accomplished only by His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾.

The second: by witnessing the humiliation of servanthood, and this is perfected only by His saying: ﴿humbly﴾. So the transition from remembrance to humility resembles descending from the ascent (mi'raj), and the transition from humility to remembrance resembles ascending, and by both the ascent of the holy spirits is completed. Here there is an inquiry: knowledge of God necessarily entails humility and fear, and heartfelt remembrance cannot be separated from humility and fear, so what is the benefit of requiring this humility and fear? It is answered that knowledge does not necessarily entail humility and fear absolutely, for it may be firmly established in a person's intellect that God does not punish anyone, since such punishment is harm to another with no benefit to the Truth. If that is so, He does not punish; and when one believes this, humility and fear are not perfected. For this reason God explicitly stated that they are necessary.

It is also answered that fear is of two kinds:

The first: fear of punishment, which is the station of beginners.

The second: fear of majesty, which is the station of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun). This fear cannot cease, and whoever knows God's majesty better has this fear more perfect in his heart. And it has been answered regarding this answer that the people of unveilings have two stations: the unveiling of beauty (jamal) and the unveiling of majesty (jalal). When they are unveiled to beauty, they live; when they are unveiled to majesty, they are overwhelmed; and in the station of remembrance it is necessary to observe both sides.

[Page 88]

The third condition: His saying: ﴿and in awe﴾. In another reading: (and in secrecy, khufyah). Al-Zajjaj said: its original form is "khawfah," and the waw was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it. I say: this fear occurs in several aspects:

First: fear of shortcoming in deeds.

Second: fear of the final outcome (khatimah). The verifiers' fear is of the beginning (sabiqah), because what was decreed in the opening (fatihah) is what becomes manifest in the ending, and for this reason he, peace be upon him, used to say: "The pen has dried with what will be until the Day of Resurrection."

Third: fear that, how can I match God's blessings, which have no limit or end, with my deficient acts of obedience and my insufficient remembrances? Shaykh Abu Bakr al-Wasiti used to say: "Thanks is polytheism." They asked me about this statement and I said: perhaps the meaning, and God knows best, is that whoever tries to match the aspects of God's kindness with his thanks has committed polytheism, because on this reckoning it becomes as if the servant says: "From You is the blessing and from me is the thanks," and there is no doubt that this is polytheism. But when one offers thanks together with fear of shortcoming and with acknowledgement of humiliation and submission, then the scent of servanthood is perceived in it.

As for the second reading, His saying: (and in secrecy, khufyah): secrecy, for beginners, is intended to preserve acts of worship from the taints of showing off (riya') and reputation-seeking; and for those who have reached the end and are brought near, its source is jealousy (ghayrah). That is because when love is perfected it necessitates jealousy, and when this immersion is complete and annihilation (fana') is attained, remembrance occurs at the time of concealment, based on His, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever knows God, his tongue becomes silent."

The fourth condition: His saying: ﴿and without loudness of speech﴾. What is meant by it is that this remembrance should occur in a manner intermediate between loudness and whispering, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud nor silently, but seek a way between that﴾ [al-Isra': 110], and He said of Zakariyya, peace be upon him: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. Ibn 'Abbas said: the interpretation of His saying ﴿without loudness of speech﴾ is that one should remember one's Lord in a way that makes oneself hear, because what is intended is the occurrence of oral remembrance, and oral remembrance, when it is such that it makes oneself hear, then the imagination is affected by that remembrance, and the affecting of the imagination causes strength in the spiritual, heartfelt remembrance, and each of these three pillars continually grows stronger, and the lights of these remembrances reflect from one to another, and these reflections become a cause of greater strength, clarity, unveiling and ascent from the lowland of the darknesses of the world of bodies to the lights of the Governor of light and darkness.

* * *

The fifth condition: His saying: ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾. Here there are issues:

The first issue: regarding the word "al-ghuduww" there are two views:

The first view: it is a verbal noun, as one says ghadawtu aghdu ghadwan and ghuduwwan, and from it His saying: ﴿its going forth in the morning is a month's journey﴾ [Saba': 12], meaning its going forth for travel. Then the time of going forth (ghuduww) was called ghuduww, just as one says: "the morning has drawn near," meaning its time, and "the evening has drawn near," meaning its time.

The second view: that al-ghuduww is the plural of ghudwah. Al-Layth said: al-ghuduww is a plural like al-ghadawat, and the singular of al-ghadawat is ghudwah. As for ﴿al-asal﴾, al-Farra' said: its singular is asal, and the singular of al-asal is al-asil. He said: it is said "we came to them in the evenings" (mu'assilin), meaning at the times of the evenings (al-asal). It is also said that al-asil is derived from al-asl (origin), and the day with its night begins with the onset from the beginning of the night, and the end of each day's daylight is connected to the beginning of the night of the following day, so the end of the day was called asil, because it is adjacent to what is the origin (asl) of the following day.

The second issue: the mornings and the evenings were singled out for this remembrance, and the wisdom in it is that at the morning-time a person passes from sleep, which is like death, to wakefulness, which is like life, and the world passes from darkness, which is a privative nature, to light, which is an existential nature.

[Page 89]

As for the evenings, the matter is the opposite, because in them a person passes from life to death, and the world passes from pure light to pure darkness. At these two times these two kinds of wondrous, powerful, overwhelming change occur, and none is able to bring about such change except the God described by manifest wisdom and boundless power. Because of this marvelous wisdom, God, exalted is He, singled out these two times for the command to remember. Some people have said: He mentioned these two times and the intended meaning is persistence in remembrance and constancy in it to the extent possible. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding His saying: ﴿Those who remember God standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ [al-A'raf: 191]: "Were a fourth state to occur to the son of Adam besides these states, God would have commanded remembrance in it." What is meant by this is that He, exalted is He, commanded remembrance continually.

Sixth restriction: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾. The meaning is that His saying ﴿in the mornings and the evenings﴾ indicates that remembrance must be present at all times, and His saying ﴿And do not be among the heedless﴾ indicates that the remembrance of the heart must be constant, and that a person must not be heedless for a single moment of recalling the majesty and greatness of Allah to the extent of human capacity and human power. The verification of this matter is that there is a wondrous relationship between the spirit and the body, because every effect that occurs in the essence of the spirit descends from it to the body, and every state that occurs in the body ascends from it as results to the spirit. Do you not see that when a person imagines a sour thing, his teeth become set on edge, and when he imagines a disagreeable state and becomes angry, his body grows hot? These are effects that descend from the spirit to the body. Also, when a person persists in an action of the actions and repeats it many times and many times, a strong, firmly rooted disposition (malakah) arises in the essence of the soul. These are effects that ascend from the body to the soul.

Having understood this, we say: When verbal remembrance is present in such a way that a person makes himself hear it, an effect from that verbal remembrance arises in the imagination. Then from that imaginal effect there ascends an increase of lights and manifestations to the essence of the spirit. Then from those spiritual illuminations there are reflected additional effects to the tongue, and from it to the imagination, and then once more to the intellect. These lights continue to be reflected from these mirrors, some onto others, some strengthening others and some completing others. Since there is no end to the increase of the lights of the levels, there is necessarily no end to the journey of the knowers through these lofty, holy stations, and that is a sea without shore and a goal without end.

Know that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself﴾, although its apparent form is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), is in fact general in regard to all those who are accountable, and for each person there is a particular rank and a specific station according to the readiness of the essence of his rational soul, as He said in describing the angels: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164].

[Page 90]

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate.﴾ In this there are several issues:

The first issue: When Allah encouraged His Messenger to remember Him and to persist in it, He followed this with what strengthens his motives in that, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship.﴾ The meaning is that the angels, despite the utmost of their nobility, the extreme of their purity, their protection from sin, and their freedom from the drivers of desire and anger and the occurrences of resentment and envy, are constant in servitude, prostration, humility and submissiveness. A human being, although afflicted with the darknesses of the material world and inclined toward human pleasures and human impulses, is more deserving of persistence in obedience. For this reason, ʿIsa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿And He has enjoined on me prayer and zakat as long as I live﴾ [Maryam: 31], and He said to Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

The second issue: The Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists, those who liken Allah to creation) held to His saying: ﴿those who are with your Lord﴾, and said that the word ʿinda (with/at) indicates place and direction.

Its answer: We have mentioned the many rational and traditional proofs in this surah, at the explanation of His saying: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], that it is impossible for Allah, Exalted is He, to be located in a place or direction.

When this is established, we say: it is necessary to resort to interpretation (ta'wil) in this verse, and its explanation is in several aspects:

The first aspect: He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And He is with you﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], and there is no doubt that this companionship is by grace and mercy, not by direction. So likewise here. Also, it has come in the divine reports that He, Exalted is He, said: "I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake." There is no disagreement that this "withness" is not for the sake of place and direction, so likewise here.

The second aspect: The intended meaning is nearness by honor. It is said: the vizier has a great nearness to the amir, and the intended meaning is not nearness by direction, for the doorkeeper and the carpet-layer may be nearer to the king in direction, space and place than the vizier. Thus we know that the nearness that is considered is nearness by honor, not nearness by direction.

The third aspect: This is an honoring of the angels by attributing them to Allah, in that He caused them to dwell in the place that He honored and exalted, and made it the abode of lights, the ascent of spirits, acts of obedience and noble gifts.

The fourth aspect: The reason Allah said, regarding the angels: ﴿those who are with your Lord﴾, is that they are the messengers of Allah to creation, just as it is said: the caliph has a great army with him, even if they are dispersed throughout the land. So likewise here. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: Abu Bakr al-Asamm, may Allah have mercy on him, held to this verse as proof that the angels are superior to humans, because when Allah commanded His Messenger to worship and remember Him, He said: ﴿Indeed, those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship.﴾ The meaning is: you are then more deserving and more entitled to worship. This statement is only sound if the angels are superior to him.

The fourth issue: He mentioned first, among their acts of obedience, that they glorify (Allah), and you know that tasbih (glorification) is an expression for declaring Allah exempt from every imperfection, and this belongs to knowledge and cognitions. Then, when He mentioned glorification, He followed it with mention of prostration, and this belongs to the actions of the limbs. This order indicates that the basis of obedience and servitude is the actions of the heart, and the actions of the limbs branch from it. Also, His saying: ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾ conveys restriction, and its meaning is: they do not prostrate to anyone other than Allah.

If it is said: How is this reconciled with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely﴾ [al-Hijr: 30], and the intended meaning is that they prostrated to Adam?

The answer: Shaykh al-Ghazali said: Those who prostrated to Adam were the angels of the earth; as for the great angels of the heavens, no.

It has also been said: His saying ﴿and to Him they prostrate﴾ indicates that they did not prostrate to anyone other than Allah, so this indicates generality. And His saying "they prostrated to Adam" is specific, and the specific takes precedence over the general.

Know that the verses indicating that the angels are wholly immersed in servitude are many, such as His saying, Exalted is He, reporting about them: ﴿And indeed, we are those who stand in ranks﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are those who glorify﴾ [al-Saffat: 165–166], and His saying: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying with the praise of their Lord﴾ [al-Zumar: 75]. And Allah knows best.

And may Allah bless our master Muhammad, the unlettered Prophet, and his family and companions, and grant them abundant peace.
